title: Is there a Django for Node.js? A NestJS guide for Django developers
description:
Django's pitch has always been the batteries. You start a project and you already have an ORM, migrations, users, sessions, permissions, forms, email, file storage, translations, caching and an admin. Add Django REST Framework and Celery, and a team can build a B2B product without assembling anything.

So when a Django team has to build something in TypeScript (a backend next to a frontend that's already TypeScript, a team that wants one language, a company that standardized on Node), the first question is usually "is there a Django for Node.js?". For a long time the honest answer was "not really": Express and a pile of libraries you pick yourself.

Nest is the closest thing to a yes. It gives a backend one structure (modules, dependency injection, controllers, validation, guards), and its first-party packages now cover most of Django's batteries: sign-in and sessions, permissions, email, file storage, translations, background jobs, scheduling, caching, rate limiting and configuration. It doesn't cover all of them, and I'll say plainly which ones are missing, starting with the admin.

This post is the tour I'd give a Django team on day one: the tools, the structure, each Django battery and its Nest counterpart with code on both sides, how it ships, and the differences that will actually bite.

The short version

Django Nest
startproject, startapp, runserver nest new, nest g resource, npm run start:dev
Apps and INSTALLED_APPS modules and their imports
Models, makemigrations, migrate Drizzle or TypeORM, and their migration tools
Views, DRF viewsets, urls.py controllers with route decorators
Forms, DRF serializers a validation pipe, with Zod or class-validator
Middleware middleware, guards and interceptors
django.contrib.auth, sessions @nestjs/authentication
Permissions, DRF permission classes @nestjs/authorization policies
settings.py @nestjs/config
send_mail() @nestjs/mail
default_storage, django-storages @nestjs/storage
gettext, .po files @nestjs/i18n
Celery, Celery beat @nestjs/bullmq, @nestjs/schedule
Signals, transaction.on_commit() @nestjs/event-emitter, @nestjs/outbox
The cache framework, DRF throttling @nestjs/cache-manager, @nestjs/throttler
Management commands, manage.py shell standalone scripts, the REPL
TestCase, APIClient @nestjs/testing with Supertest
drf-spectacular @nestjs/swagger
Channels gateways
The admin nothing first-party

Every row has its own section below. The docs have the same mapping as a reference page, with a link to the full chapter for each row: Coming from Django.

Your tools, translated

Before any code, here's what replaces the things around it:

Django world Nest world
Python Node.js (a current LTS release) and TypeScript
pip, requirements.txt or pyproject.toml npm, package.json
PyPI the npm registry
A virtualenv node_modules, per project, with nothing to activate
django-admin startproject npx @nestjs/cli new
manage.py runserver npm run start:dev, which restarts on every save
manage.py startapp nest generate resource
manage.py test, pytest npm test, with Vitest
mypy the TypeScript compiler, on every build
Black, Ruff Prettier and oxlint, set up by nest new
Gunicorn or uWSGI Node.js itself: node dist/main.js

npm run start:debug starts the app with the Node inspector attached, and VS Code or WebStorm connects to it the way PyCharm attaches to a Django process.

Project layout

nest new orders-api gives you a small src/ folder. As the app grows, the convention is one folder per feature, like a Django app, each with its module, and tests next to the code they test:

src/
  main.ts                    # what runserver and wsgi.py do
  app.module.ts              # the root module: your INSTALLED_APPS
  database/
    schema.ts                # tables, if you use Drizzle
  orders/
    orders.module.ts
    orders.controller.ts     # views.py and urls.py
    orders.controller.spec.ts
    orders.service.ts        # services.py, or your fat model's methods
    orders.repository.ts     # the queries
    create-order.schema.ts   # serializers.py
  payments/
    payments.module.ts
    ...
test/
drizzle/                     # generated migrations

Apps become modules

A Django project lists its apps in INSTALLED_APPS, and Django finds their models, URLs, templates and admin classes by convention. A Nest application is a tree of modules, and each one lists what it contains:

// orders/orders.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { OrdersController } from './orders.controller.js';
import { OrdersRepository } from './orders.repository.js';
import { OrdersService } from './orders.service.js';

@Module({
  controllers: [OrdersController],
  providers: [OrdersService, OrdersRepository],
  exports: [OrdersService],
})
export class OrdersModule {}

The root module imports the feature modules, which is what INSTALLED_APPS does:

// app.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { OrdersModule } from './orders/orders.module.js';
import { PaymentsModule } from './payments/payments.module.js';

@Module({
  imports: [OrdersModule, PaymentsModule],
})
export class AppModule {}

Nothing is discovered. A controller that isn't listed serves no routes. That feels like ceremony for about a week, and then it's the thing you like: what the app does at startup is written down in its modules.

Modules are also a boundary that Django apps don't have. Any Django app can import any other app's models. In Nest, a provider is visible only inside its own module, unless the module exports it and another module imports the module. On a big codebase, that's what stops "payments" from quietly reaching into "orders".

Services and dependency injection

Django has no dependency injection: a view imports the models and functions it needs. Nest code lives in providers, classes marked @Injectable(), and Nest creates them and passes them to the constructors that ask for them:

// orders/orders.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Mailer } from '@nestjs/mail';
import { OrdersRepository } from './orders.repository.js';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(
    private readonly ordersRepository: OrdersRepository,
    private readonly mailer: Mailer,
  ) {}
}

private readonly in the constructor declares and assigns the field in one step. The business logic a Django project keeps in fat models or a services.py goes in providers like this one, and a test replaces the repository or the mailer by passing another one in, with no mock.patch on import paths.

Models and migrations

Here's the first real difference: Nest has no ORM of its own. Its first-party integrations are Drizzle, where the schema is TypeScript and queries read like SQL, and TypeORM, where models are decorated classes and feel closer to Django's. Prisma and MikroORM work too. I'll use Drizzle here, because its migrations work the way makemigrations does.

A Django model:

# orders/models.py
class Order(models.Model):
    class Status(models.TextChoices):
        PENDING = "pending"
        PAID = "paid"
        SHIPPED = "shipped"

    customer = models.ForeignKey(Customer, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    status = models.CharField(
        max_length=16, choices=Status.choices, default=Status.PENDING
    )
    total_cents = models.IntegerField()
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

The same table with Drizzle, where the row type is inferred from the table:

// database/schema.ts (customers is declared in this file too)
import { integer, pgEnum, pgTable, timestamp, uuid } from 'drizzle-orm/pg-core';

export const orderStatus = pgEnum('order_status', [
  'pending',
  'paid',
  'shipped',
]);

export const orders = pgTable('orders', {
  id: uuid().primaryKey().defaultRandom(),
  customerId: uuid('customer_id')
    .notNull()
    .references(() => customers.id, { onDelete: 'cascade' }),
  status: orderStatus().notNull().default('pending'),
  totalCents: integer('total_cents').notNull(),
  createdAt: timestamp('created_at').notNull().defaultNow(),
});

export type Order = typeof orders.$inferSelect;

makemigrations becomes npx drizzle-kit generate, which writes SQL migration files from the changes to the schema, and migrate becomes npx drizzle-kit migrate. With TypeORM, migration:generate and migration:run do the same job.

Queries go through the injected database. Order.objects.filter(customer_id=..., status="pending").order_by("-created_at") becomes:

// orders/orders.repository.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectDrizzle } from '@nestjs/drizzle';
import { and, desc, eq } from 'drizzle-orm';
import type { NodePgDatabase } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres';
import { orders } from '../database/schema.js';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersRepository {
  constructor(@InjectDrizzle() private readonly db: NodePgDatabase) {}

  findPending(customerId: string) {
    return this.db
      .select()
      .from(orders)
      .where(
        and(eq(orders.customerId, customerId), eq(orders.status, 'pending')),
      )
      .orderBy(desc(orders.createdAt));
  }
}

A query runs when it's awaited. There's no lazy QuerySet that a template evaluates later, so nothing hits the database by accident, and an N+1 shows up in your own code, where you can see it. Load related rows with a join or Drizzle's relational queries, as select_related() and prefetch_related() do.

transaction.atomic() becomes a callback, whose queries commit when it resolves and roll back when it throws:

async place(customerId: string, items: NewOrderItem[]) {
  return this.db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    const [order] = await tx
      .insert(orders)
      .values({ customerId, totalCents: sumOf(items) })
      .returning();
    await tx
      .insert(orderItems)
      .values(items.map((item) => ({ ...item, orderId: order.id })));
    return order;
  });
}

Queries in the transaction go through tx, not through the injected database. That's the one mistake everybody makes once.

Views and URLs become controllers

A DRF viewset and its router:

# orders/views.py
class OrderViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    serializer_class = OrderSerializer
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]

    def get_queryset(self):
        return Order.objects.filter(customer=self.request.user.customer)

# urls.py
router = DefaultRouter()
router.register("orders", OrderViewSet, basename="order")
urlpatterns = [path("api/", include(router.urls))]

In Nest, a controller declares its routes with decorators, so there's no urls.py:

// orders/orders.controller.ts
import {
  Body,
  Controller,
  Delete,
  Get,
  HttpCode,
  Param,
  ParseUUIDPipe,
  Post,
} from '@nestjs/common';
import { CurrentUser } from '@nestjs/authentication';
import type { User } from '../users/user.js';
import {
  createOrderSchema,
  type CreateOrderDto,
} from './create-order.schema.js';
import { OrdersService } from './orders.service.js';

@Controller('orders')
export class OrdersController {
  constructor(private readonly ordersService: OrdersService) {}

  @Get()
  findAll(@CurrentUser() user: User) {
    return this.ordersService.findForCustomer(user.id);
  }

  @Get(':id')
  findOne(@CurrentUser() user: User, @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string) {
    return this.ordersService.findOne(user, id);
  }

  @Post()
  create(
    @CurrentUser() user: User,
    @Body({ schema: createOrderSchema }) dto: CreateOrderDto,
  ) {
    return this.ordersService.place(user, dto);
  }

  @Delete(':id')
  @HttpCode(204)
  cancel(@CurrentUser() user: User, @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string) {
    return this.ordersService.cancel(user, id);
  }
}

What to notice, coming from DRF:

  • @Controller('orders') is the URL prefix, and each method decorator adds a path. app.setGlobalPrefix('api') adds the api/ from urls.py.
  • Route parameters arrive as strings. ParseUUIDPipe or ParseIntPipe converts and checks one, like a path converter.
  • A POST answers 201 by default and everything else 200. @HttpCode() changes it.
  • A handler returns the body, and Nest serializes it as JSON. get_object_or_404() becomes throw new NotFoundException() in the service.
  • There's no IsAuthenticated above, and it isn't missing: with @nestjs/authentication, every route requires a signed-in user unless it's marked @Public().

There are no generic viewsets. The five methods above are the whole of a ModelViewSet, written out, and nest g resource writes that boilerplate for you. I'd argue it's a fair trade: a new developer reads one file and knows every route.

Serializers become schemas

A DRF serializer validates input and shapes output. In Nest those are two separate jobs.

Input is validated before the handler runs, by a pipe. Here's a DRF serializer:

# orders/serializers.py
class OrderItemSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    product_id = serializers.UUIDField()
    quantity = serializers.IntegerField(min_value=1, max_value=20)

class CreateOrderSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    items = OrderItemSerializer(many=True, allow_empty=False)
    note = serializers.CharField(max_length=500, required=False)

The same rules as a Zod schema, which also gives the DTO its type:

// orders/create-order.schema.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

export const createOrderSchema = z.object({
  items: z
    .array(
      z.object({
        productId: z.uuid(),
        quantity: z.int().min(1).max(20),
      }),
    )
    .min(1),
  note: z.string().max(500).optional(),
});

export type CreateOrderDto = z.infer<typeof createOrderSchema>;

The controller above passes it with @Body({ schema: createOrderSchema }), and one line in main.ts turns validation on for the whole app:

app.useGlobalPipes(new StandardSchemaValidationPipe());

An invalid body gets a 400 that lists every failed rule, like is_valid(raise_exception=True). Valibot and ArkType work the same way, and if you'd rather have a declarative class, class-validator DTOs with ValidationPipe are the closest thing to a Serializer subclass.

Here's the gotcha I'd warn every Django developer about: TypeScript types don't exist at runtime. @Body() dto: CreateOrderDto with no schema and no pipe accepts whatever JSON the client sent, and the type annotation checks nothing. Python developers expect the opposite, because a serializer always runs.

Output needs no serializer. A handler returns a plain object, and its JSON is the response. To leave a field out, such as a password hash, don't select it, or return an object without it.

Users, sign-in and permissions

django.contrib.auth gives you a User model, password hashing, sessions and permission tables. @nestjs/authentication gives you the sign-in parts, and leaves the users to you:

  • Users are your table. The package never reads it. It asks your code for a user by id, and a user is whatever type your app defines. No AbstractUser, no AUTH_USER_MODEL.
  • Passwords are hashed by PasswordHasher, with scrypt at OWASP's parameters, the job of make_password() and check_password(). An unknown email takes as long to check as a wrong password, and needsRehash() tells you when to upgrade an old hash on sign-in, as Django does.
  • Sessions are server-side, in an HttpOnly, Secure cookie, like the database session backend, and SignInService.signIn() is login(). The one thing Django does that the package doesn't: it creates no tables. Sessions go in your database through a store you write against its interfaces, with the package's own tests to check it.
  • Every route is closed by default. @Public() opens one, which turns login_required inside out. @CurrentUser() is request.user.
  • What you'd install django-allauth for is in the box: email verification, password reset links, TOTP two-factor authentication, magic links, sign-in with Google and other OpenID Connect providers, access and refresh tokens, and API keys that users create and revoke.

Permissions are code, not rows. Django stores add_order, change_order and friends per model, assigns them to groups, and checks them with has_perm(). @nestjs/authorization replaces those, and DRF's permission classes, with policies. Here's a DRF object permission:

# orders/permissions.py
class IsOrderOwnerOrStaff(permissions.BasePermission):
    def has_object_permission(self, request, view, obj):
        user = request.user
        return user.is_staff or obj.customer_id == user.customer.id

The same check as a policy, with a staff-only refund next to it:

// orders/order.policy.ts
import { Policy } from '@nestjs/authorization';
import type { User } from '../users/user.js';
import type { Order } from './order.js';

@Policy()
export class OrderPolicy {
  view(user: User | null, order: Order) {
    if (!user) {
      return false;
    }
    return user.roles.includes('staff') || order.customerId === user.id;
  }

  refund(user: User | null) {
    return !!user?.roles.includes('staff');
  }
}

A check that needs only the user goes on the route, as @Can(OrderPolicy, 'refund'). A check that needs the record, the has_object_permission() case, goes in the service once the record is loaded:

async findOne(user: User, id: string) {
  const order = await this.ordersRepository.findById(id);
  if (!order) {
    throw new NotFoundException();
  }
  await this.authorizationService.authorize(OrderPolicy, 'view', user, order);
  return order;
}

authorize() throws when the policy says no, which answers 403, or 401 to a guest. And like authentication, the authorization guard denies by default: a route with no check declared is closed. Roles and groups are fields on your user, stored however you like. For organizations, members and roles in a B2B app, the docs have a multi-tenant SaaS tutorial.

Settings become configuration

settings.py is Python that runs at startup and usually reads os.environ. @nestjs/config reads .env files and environment variables, and validates them before the app starts, so a missing DATABASE_URL is a startup error, not a 500 on the first request:

// app.module.ts
import { ConfigModule } from '@nestjs/config';
import { z } from 'zod';

@Module({
  imports: [
    ConfigModule.forRoot({
      isGlobal: true,
      validationSchema: z.object({
        DATABASE_URL: z.url(),
        SMTP_URL: z.url(),
        DEBUG: z.stringbool().default(false),
      }),
    }),
  ],
})
export class AppModule {}

There's no global settings object to import. A provider that needs a value injects ConfigService and calls get(), or getOrThrow() for a required one.

Email

send_mail() becomes Mailer from @nestjs/mail. Here's the usual Django version, rendering a template and sending it:

# orders/emails.py
def send_order_confirmation(order):
    html = render_to_string("emails/order_confirmation.html", {"order": order})
    send_mail(
        f"Your order #{order.number}",
        strip_tags(html),
        None,
        [order.customer.email],
        html_message=html,
    )

In Nest, a mail is a class that returns the subject, the template's name and the values the template reads:

// notifications/order-confirmation.mail.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Mailable } from '@nestjs/mail';
import type { Order } from '../orders/order.js';

@Injectable()
export class OrderConfirmationMail implements Mailable<{ order: Order }> {
  render({ order }: { order: Order }) {
    return {
      subject: `Your order #${order.number}`,
      template: 'order-confirmation',
      context: { order },
    };
  }
}

A service sends it, and the type of data comes from the mail class:

await this.mailer.send(OrderConfirmationMail, {
  to: { name: customer.name, address: customer.email },
  data: { order },
});

Templates escape every value, as Django's do. In development, FileMailTransport writes each mail to a file instead of sending it, like the file email backend; in production, SMTP or Resend sends it; and in tests, InMemoryMailTransport keeps what was sent, like mail.outbox.

Files and translations

django-storages becomes @nestjs/storage: named disks (a local folder, S3, or R2 and other S3-compatible stores) behind one API. default_storage.save() is put(), .url() is url(), and a private file gets a signed link:

// invoices/invoices.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectDisk, StorageDisk } from '@nestjs/storage';

@Injectable()
export class InvoicesService {
  constructor(@InjectDisk('private') private readonly files: StorageDisk) {}

  async store(orderId: string, pdf: Buffer) {
    const key = `invoices/${orderId}.pdf`;
    await this.files.put(key, pdf, { contentType: 'application/pdf' });
    return this.files.signedUrl(key, { expiresIn: '15m' });
  }
}

Uploads stream straight onto a disk with uploadToDisk(), rather than through memory or a temp file.

gettext and .po files become @nestjs/i18n, with a JSON catalog per language. Keys are typed, so _("Order not found") turns into a key that fails to compile if you misspell it:

throw new NotFoundException(this.i18n.t('orders.notFound', { args: { id } }));

Plurals follow each language's rules, like ngettext(), and the locale comes from Accept-Language, a query parameter, a cookie or the user's saved language, the job LocaleMiddleware does. Validation messages and exceptions get translated too.

Celery, beat and signals

A Celery task becomes a job on a BullMQ queue, which runs on Redis, the way Celery usually does. Here's a task and the call that queues it:

# orders/tasks.py
@shared_task
def generate_invoice(order_id):
    ...

generate_invoice.delay(order.id)

In Nest, a processor class takes the queue's jobs:

// invoices/invoice.processor.ts
import { Processor, WorkerHost } from '@nestjs/bullmq';
import type { Job } from 'bullmq';

@Processor('invoices')
export class InvoiceProcessor extends WorkerHost {
  async process(job: Job<{ orderId: string }>) {
    // ...
  }
}

A service adds a job to the queue it injects, as delay() does:

// constructor(@InjectQueue('invoices') private readonly invoices: Queue) {}
await this.invoices.add('generate', { orderId: order.id });

The processor is a provider like any other, so it injects your services. No separate Celery app with its own settings: workers run in the app's process, or in another process that starts the same modules.

Celery beat becomes @Cron() from @nestjs/schedule, on any provider's method. A scheduled method runs on every instance of the app, so on more than one instance, add @OnOneInstance() from @nestjs/locks.

Signals become events, emit() and @OnEvent() from @nestjs/event-emitter. There's no post_save, because there's no model layer to send it: emit the event from the service that saved the row, which I'd argue is where you wanted it anyway.

And transaction.on_commit(), for "send the email only once the order is saved", has a stronger version: @nestjs/outbox writes the message in the same transaction as the order and delivers it after the commit, retrying until it's sent, even if the process dies in between.

Caching, rate limiting, CSRF and templates

  • Caching: @nestjs/cache-manager gives you get(), set() and del() like django.core.cache, and CacheInterceptor caches whole responses like cache_page.
  • Rate limiting: @nestjs/throttler limits requests per client and window, like DRF's throttle classes, with @Throttle() and @SkipThrottle() per route.
  • CSRF: app.enableCsrfProtection() refuses state-changing requests from other origins, using the Sec-Fetch-Site and Origin headers browsers send, so there's no token to put in forms.
  • Templates: most Nest apps are APIs with a separate frontend. If you render HTML on the server, set a view engine such as Handlebars and return a template's context from a handler marked @Render('products/detail').

Management commands and the shell

A management command becomes a script that starts the app's modules without the HTTP server:

// scripts/close-stale-carts.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { AppModule } from '../app.module.js';
import { CartsService } from '../carts/carts.service.js';

const app = await NestFactory.createApplicationContext(AppModule);
await app.get(CartsService).closeStale();
await app.close();

For commands with arguments, options and help text, nest-commander gives you what BaseCommand does. And manage.py shell has a counterpart in Nest's REPL, where every provider is at hand: await get(OrdersService).findOne(...).

The admin

Nest has no admin. It's the one Django battery with no first-party counterpart, and for a team that runs its back office in the Django admin, it's the biggest thing you give up. I'd rather you hear that from me now than find out in week three.

What teams do instead:

  • A third-party admin panel. AdminJS has a Nest integration and generates CRUD screens from your models.
  • A database GUI for the people who only browse and fix rows.
  • Internal pages in your own frontend, on the same API and the same policies as the rest of the app. That's more work up front, and it means one permission model instead of two.

Testing

TestCase and APIClient become a testing module and Supertest. This test creates only the controller, with a fake service in place of the real one:

// orders/orders.controller.spec.ts
import { Test } from '@nestjs/testing';
import type { INestApplication } from '@nestjs/common';
import request from 'supertest';
import { vi } from 'vitest';
import { OrdersController } from './orders.controller.js';
import { OrdersService } from './orders.service.js';

describe('OrdersController', () => {
  let app: INestApplication;
  const ordersService = { findForCustomer: vi.fn() };

  beforeAll(async () => {
    const moduleRef = await Test.createTestingModule({
      controllers: [OrdersController],
      providers: [{ provide: OrdersService, useValue: ordersService }],
    }).compile();
    app = moduleRef.createNestApplication();
    await app.init();
  });

  afterAll(() => app.close());

  it('lists orders', async () => {
    ordersService.findForCustomer.mockResolvedValue([]);
    await request(app.getHttpServer()).get('/orders').expect(200, []);
  });
});

For a test of the whole app, import AppModule and swap providers with overrideProvider(). One thing Django spoils you with: its test runner creates a test database, runs migrations and wraps each test in a transaction. Nest doesn't. Point DATABASE_URL at a test database, run the migrations before the suite, and clean the tables between tests (Testcontainers makes the first part painless).

OpenAPI and health checks

drf-spectacular becomes @nestjs/swagger, which builds the OpenAPI document from your controllers and schemas and serves Swagger UI, the closest thing to DRF's browsable API. Health endpoints for your load balancer come from @nestjs/terminus, with checks for the database, other services, disk and memory.

Shipping it

A Django app ships as Python code behind Gunicorn or uWSGI, often with a separate Celery worker. A Nest app ships as compiled JavaScript plus its node_modules, almost always in a container. A production Dockerfile, built in one stage and run in another:

FROM node:24-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev

FROM node:24-slim
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/package.json ./
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
CMD ["node", "--enable-source-maps", "dist/main.js"]

Three things to check that Gunicorn handled for you:

  • Graceful shutdown. Call app.enableShutdownHooks() in main.ts, so onApplicationShutdown() runs on SIGTERM and connections close cleanly.
  • The process gets the signal. Use the exec form, CMD ["node", ...], not npm start, which doesn't reliably forward signals.
  • More cores means more processes. Gunicorn starts several workers; one Node process uses one core for your code. Run several containers, or several processes per container, behind the load balancer.

And run migrations as a release step (drizzle-kit migrate), not on startup, so two instances starting at once don't race, the same advice you'd follow with manage.py migrate.

Moving over without a rewrite

You don't have to port a Django codebase to start using Nest:

  • Start with a new service, not a port. The next thing you need gets written in Nest, behind the same proxy or ingress, against the same Postgres if that's simpler. Nest doesn't care that Django created the tables: point Drizzle at them, and drizzle-kit pull writes a schema from the existing database.
  • Share the contract, not the code. If your DRF API publishes an OpenAPI document, generate a TypeScript client from it for the Nest service, and the other way round with @nestjs/swagger.
  • Move endpoints only when you'd rewrite them anyway, one path at a time behind the proxy.

What's actually different

The syntax takes a week. These take longer.

One process serves many requests at once. A Gunicorn worker handles one request at a time. Node runs your code on one thread with an event loop: while a request waits for Postgres, the others run. That's why one Node process handles thousands of concurrent connections, the promise Django's async views make, but everywhere and by default. The flip side: CPU-heavy work in a handler, such as resizing an image or a long loop over a big list, stalls every other request in that process. Move it to a queue or a worker thread. If your service is mostly number crunching or data science, Python is the better home, and I'd say so to anyone.

await everything. Database drivers and HTTP clients are asynchronous. A forgotten await doesn't block, it lets the code carry on before the query has finished, and the bug shows up somewhere else. The no-floating-promises lint rule catches most of them, and nest new turns it on, so keep npm run lint in CI.

No thread-local request. There's no global request to reach for from a helper. Pass the user into the service, or read per-request state from AsyncLocalStorage, which follows a request through every await.

Everything is wired explicitly. Django finds your models, admin classes, management commands and templates by convention. Nest configures nothing because a package is installed, and runs nothing because a file exists.

Batteries are separate packages. Django is one package, released as a whole. Nest's core and each first-party package are installed separately, so a project carries only what it uses. Upgrade them together.

Types are a compile-time check. I said it above and I'll say it again, because it's the one that bites Python developers: a type annotation describes what you expect and checks nothing at runtime. A request body, a raw query's rows, a queue message: only a schema checks them.

Numbers are doubles. There's no Decimal. Keep money in integer cents, or use a decimal library and your database's numeric type, which most drivers return as a string anyway.

ES modules. A new project imports local files with a .js extension, even from .ts files, because that's the name of the compiled file. It looks wrong for about a day.

When I'd stay on Django

To be fair to Django: if the admin is how your company runs, if your team is all Python and happy, or if the backend lives next to data science and machine learning code in Python, stay. Django's maturity, its admin and its ecosystem of reusable apps are real advantages, and a rewrite to get TypeScript is rarely worth it on its own.

Nest is a good fit when the new thing is a new service, when the people building it also write the TypeScript frontend, or when you want one language from the browser to the database, with batteries close to the ones you're used to.

Getting started 

npx @nestjs/cli new orders-api
cd orders-api
npm run start:dev

Then nest g resource orders, and you have a module, controller, service, DTOs and tests to hold up against the Django app in your head. The Coming from Django page in the docs keeps this mapping as a reference, with a link from each row to its full chapter.

If something here doesn't match how you'd do it in Django, tell me. It's written for you, and it's easy to fix.

Coming from Java or .NET instead? Here's the same tour for Spring Boot and for ASP.NET Core.

title: Understanding Failure Patterns in LLM-Based Mathematical Optimization Modeling
description:
arXiv:2611.33351v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Industrial optimization involves complex constraints, making optimization modeling difficult to automate. Large language models (LLMs) have been explored for generating optimization models from natural language, but their reliability in end-to-end settings remains limited, often producing non-executable, infeasible, or feasible but incorrect solutions. In this work, we study failure modes in LLM-based optimization modeling by decomposing the process into three components: mathematical reasoning, solver usage, and domain knowledge, and constructing datasets that target each aspect. Using these datasets, we analyze how different components relate to errors and find that they are associated with different types of failure, although these relationships are not always strong or consistent. Furthermore, while combining these components improves execution reliability, feasible but incorrect solutions remain the dominant failure mode, suggesting a remaining gap between executability and correctness. These findings highlight limitations of current dataset designs and suggest the importance of data that better capture constraint completeness and formulation accuracy to enhance reliability.

title: HumblePRM: Improving VLM Abstention in Ambiguous Situations through Process Reward Modeling
description:
arXiv:2611.33452v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliable deployment of Vision Language Models (VLMs) requires that a model's expressed confidence remain grounded in what it can actually see, and that it recognize when the visual evidence is too ambiguous to commit to a confident response. Standard post-training uses outcome reward models (ORMs) that supervise only the final decision, rewarding a confident answer regardless of whether the image supports one, while existing methods either tend to detect uncertainty post-hoc or assume an objective verdict always exists. We instead split multimodal reasoning into two stages: perception, where the model must factually describe the scene, and calibration, where it must judge whether that evidence is sufficient to commit to a conclusion. We introduce HumblePRM, a lightweight process reward model (PRM) that scores each stage independently, rewarding agreement between evidence and expressed confidence rather than outcome correctness alone. Training with HumblePRM increases abstention due to uncertainty on ambiguous inputs considerably while leaving accuracy on clear images roughly unchanged. We also find that the improvement transfers to Gemma 4 E4B, a larger, popular edge model. Our findings show that process reward supervision is a promising route to VLMs with better calibrated abstention, ensuring more reliability rather than unpredictable behavior.

title: Fine-Tuning Without Gradients? Closed-Form, LLM-Written Classifiers on a Frozen Encoder
description:
arXiv:2611.33972v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Can a classifier computed in closed form on a frozen encoder match gradient fine-tuning? We present closed-form weight-space programming (WSP): a large language model (LLM), used as a design assistant, writes programs that read a frozen masked language model through cloze-style prompt templates at several layers, fit closed-form heads (shrinkage discriminant analysis, kernel ridge regression and the encoder's label-word prior) on labelled data, and select among a pool of candidate heads by cross-fitting. No gradient is computed and no encoder weight changes. We instantiate the framework on RoBERTa-large. On 11 development datasets with 512 to 8,192 training labels, WSP is ahead of full fine-tuning (FT) and LoRA at every label budget (by 0.3 to 0.6 points on average; the registered non-inferiority tests pass) and within 0.5 points of prompt-based fine-tuning (PFT); these datasets also shaped the recipe. With fewer labels its lead over FT and LoRA grows: 1.2 to 3.5 points with 64 and 128 labels, and 3.8 to 5.3 points in the few-shot setting of 16 labels per class, where WSP is again within half a point of PFT on the development datasets. On six held-out datasets, WSP stays ahead of LoRA and within half a point of FT on average, although with six datasets no registered test passes, and PFT is ahead, by 1.30 points with 8,192 labels. WSP never collapses and is deterministic, but it needs one encoder pass per template (17 here). We report all eight recipe versions, every decision that saw test results, and 27 ideas that did not help.

title: MonoQPM: Splitting Features into Concepts for Inherent Interpretability and Predictive Performance
description:
arXiv:2611.33252v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Alongside superposition, polysemanticity is one of the primary obstacles to achieving interpretable deep neural networks. While these phenomena are typically intrinsically linked, the Quadratic Programming Enhanced Model (QPM) naturally decouples them. By representing classes with a sparse binary assignment of very few features, QPM prevents superposition by design on its final features but still exhibits polysemanticity. However, measuring polysemanticity is an open problem. This work proposes a utility-focused approach to measuring polysemanticity by quantifying the decrease in interference-induced activation errors, which yields the practical utility of tighter prediction sets using Conformal Prediction (CP). We explicitly disentangle the polysemantic features of QPM into monosemantic concepts to create the Monosemantic QPM (MonoQPM). Because its features are disentangled, MonoQPM acts as a significantly more efficient Conformal Predictor. Additionally, we introduce CUBCars, a dataset providing ground truth information about shared concepts. Using this and other datasets, we demonstrate that polysemanticity emerges in QPM across all tested architectures, but is effectively alleviated by MonoQPM. For instance, MonoQPM guarantees 88% coverage using Adaptive Prediction Sets on ImageNet with just 66% of the frozen QPM's set size.

title: Benchmarking Segmentation Models for Scalable Mangrove Mapping with Sentinel-1/2 Imagery
description:
arXiv:2611.33369v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mangroves are dynamic coastal ecosystems that contribute to carbon storage, coastal protection and biodiversity conservation, but are vulnerable to climate change. Very-high-resolution imagery such as Pl\'eiades enables detailed mangrove mapping but it is costly and have a low revisit rate. Large-scale monitoring requires free and regularly available data such as Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 but their spatial resolution poses challenges for detailed mangrove mapping. In this work, we benchmark deep learning approaches for mangrove mapping from Sentinel-1 radar and Sentinel-2 optical imagery using reference maps derived from very-high-resolution Pl\'eiades imagery. We compare four segmentation configurations based on CROMA and BigEarthNet-pretrained ResNet50 representations with different segmentation decoders. We construct a mangrove mapping dataset covering French Guiana, Suriname, and Amap\'a. CROMA + UPerNet achieves the best performance, with an F1-score of 0.9218 and an IoU of 0.8549. These results highlight the potential of pretrained multimodal Earth observation representations and open Sentinel data to support mangrove resilience through scalable monitoring.

title: A 3D Simulator for Passive SPAD Imaging
description:
arXiv:2611.33498v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Passive single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) cameras provide short-exposure observations for low-light perception, but collecting task annotations for these sensors remains difficult, and annotated datasets are scarce. We present a 3D simulation pipeline that generates realistic photon detections together with camera-motion and semantic labels, enabling perception models to be trained on synthetic SPAD observations and applied directly to real-world data. The pipeline couples controllable scene geometry and motion with a sensor-informed observation model that accounts for photon shot noise, dark counts, and spatial crosstalk. We evaluate the pipeline through calibrated photon-count comparisons and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer across three downstream perception tasks. We show that classifiers trained only on synthetic SPAD data achieve high accuracy on real low-light recordings at illumination levels less than 2 lux, without real-data fine-tuning. Similarly, we apply models trained entirely on simulated camera sweeps to real-world camera-rotation estimation and achieve mean absolute rotation errors of less than 1 degree on real 20-degree and 30-degree sweeps at 0.5 and 5.0 lux, when deployed zero-shot. We additionally train semantic segmentation models on synthetic data with automatically generated dense labels and perform direct inference on real-world low-light recordings; the results further demonstrate the usefulness of synthetic dense supervision for real low-light perception. Our simulator thus provides a practical source of annotated training data for real SPAD perception.

title: Parallel Coding Agents Keep Colliding? Give Each One a Lane
description:
You start two coding agents on the same repo. One adds a discount to the pricing API, the other shows the new price in the cart. Both report success. Then you merge, and one of them has rewritten a file the other one owned.

Running agents in parallel is easy to start. Keeping them out of each other's way is the actual work. This article is a practical setup for that: give each agent a lane, write the lanes down, define how agents hand work to each other, merge in a fixed order, and keep one reviewer. If you're still deciding whether you need more than one agent at all, read Single Agent, Subagents or an Agent Team? first. This one assumes you've decided, and the agents are already colliding.

What a lane is

A lane is three things that belong to one agent and nobody else:

  • A checkout. Its own working directory, so edits on disk can't overwrite each other.
  • A branch. Its own line of history, so you can review and merge it separately.
  • A set of files. The paths it is allowed to change.

The first two are solved by tooling. The third is a decision you have to make and write down, and it's the one that's usually missing.

Step 1: Give each agent its own checkout with git worktrees

The git worktree docs put it in one line: "A git repository can support multiple working trees, allowing you to check out more than one branch at a time." Each worktree is a separate directory on its own branch, sharing the same repository history.

The main coding agents now build on this:

  • Claude Code: claude --worktree feature-auth creates a worktree under .claude/worktrees/feature-auth/ on a new branch worktree-feature-auth, per the worktrees docs. Custom subagents can always run in their own worktree with isolation: worktree in their frontmatter.
  • Codex (ChatGPT desktop app): the worktrees page says worktrees "let Codex run multiple independent chats in the same project without interfering with each other." By default Codex works in a detached HEAD state, and you can create a branch from the chat header.
  • Cursor: in the Agents Window, Cursor creates a separate checkout when you start an agent in a worktree, and runs setup commands from .cursor/worktrees.json, per the worktrees docs.

Two practical notes from those docs. A worktree is a fresh checkout, so dependencies and gitignored files such as .env aren't there until you set them up (Claude Code has .worktreeinclude, Cursor has setup-worktree). And, as the Codex page puts it, "Git only allows a branch to be checked out in one place at a time." That rule protects you: two agents can't silently share one branch.

If you'd rather do it by hand, plain git works with any agent:

git worktree add -b lane/api .worktrees/api
git worktree add -b lane/ui .worktrees/ui

Step 2: Write the lanes in a shared task file

Worktrees isolate files on disk. They don't stop two agents from changing the same file in their own copies. You find that out at merge time, which is the most expensive moment to find out.

So the file ownership goes in a file every agent reads before it starts. I keep it at the repo root as TASKS.md:

# TASKS.md (one lane per agent)

## lane: api
branch: lane/api
owns: src/api/
status: in progress
task: add a discount parameter to get_price

## lane: ui
branch: lane/ui
owns: src/ui/
status: in progress
task: show the discounted price in the cart

Each agent's prompt then says: work only in your branch, change only the paths under owns, and if you need a change outside them, write a hand-off note instead (Step 3). Claude Code's agent-teams docs give the same advice for teams, which don't get worktrees: "Two teammates editing the same file leads to overwrites. Break the work so each teammate owns a different set of files."

Instructions alone aren't proof, so I check them. This script reads TASKS.md, asks git which files each lane branch changed since main, and flags files outside a lane and files touched by more than one lane. It only reads.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Check that each agent's branch only touched the files its lane owns.
Reads TASKS.md and git history only. Usage: python3 lane_check.py [BASE]"""
import re, subprocess, sys
from collections import defaultdict

base = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "main"
lanes = re.findall(r"^## lane: (\S+)\nbranch: (\S+)\nowns: (.+)$",
                   open("TASKS.md").read(), re.M)

def changed(branch):
    out = subprocess.run(["git", "diff", "--name-only", f"{base}...{branch}"],
                         capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout
    return out.split()

touched_by = defaultdict(list)
problems = 0
for name, branch, owns in lanes:
    prefixes = [p.strip() for p in owns.split(",")]
    files = changed(branch)
    print(f"lane {name} ({branch}): {len(files)} file(s) changed")
    for f in files:
        touched_by[f].append(name)
        if not any(f.startswith(p) for p in prefixes):
            problems += 1
            print(f"  OUTSIDE LANE  {f}")

for f, names in sorted(touched_by.items()):
    if len(names) > 1:
        problems += 1
        print(f"SHARED FILE  {f}  <- {', '.join(names)}")

print("OK: every lane stayed in its files" if not problems
      else f"{problems} problem(s): fix before merging")
sys.exit(1 if problems else 0)

I tested it on a small invented repo with the two lanes above. To be clear: no agent ran here. I made the "agent" edits by hand with commits, to reproduce the collision from the intro: the UI lane also changed src/api/client.py, which belongs to the API lane, and the API lane changed it too. This is the real output, run on 26 Nov 2026 with git 2.47.3 and Python 3.13.5:

$ git worktree add .worktrees/api2 lane/api
Preparing worktree (checking out 'lane/api')
fatal: 'lane/api' is already used by worktree at '/tmp/shop/.worktrees/api'
[exit 128]
$ python3 /tmp/lane_check.py
lane api (lane/api): 2 file(s) changed
lane ui (lane/ui): 2 file(s) changed
  OUTSIDE LANE  src/api/client.py
SHARED FILE  src/api/client.py  <- api, ui
2 problem(s): fix before merging
[exit 1]
$ git merge-tree --write-tree --name-only lane/api lane/ui
876743633a0717c0cd987ad594fbd1b26bbc968d
src/api/client.py

Auto-merging src/api/client.py
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/api/client.py
[exit 1]

The first command shows git refusing to put one branch in two worktrees. The lane check names the file and both lanes before any merge. git merge-tree --write-tree performs a trial merge of the two branches; per its docs it "does not make any new commits and does not read from or write to either the working tree or index". It confirms the conflict.

Step 3: Hand off instead of reaching across

The UI agent had a real reason to touch client.py: it needed something from the API side. The fix isn't to forbid that need. It's to route it to the lane that owns the file. I use a short hand-off note, appended to TASKS.md under the owner's lane. For the demo, an example would look like this:

### hand-off: ui -> api
need: client.py should expose the discounted price endpoint
why: cart.html shows the discounted price (lane/ui)
blocking: yes, ui shows a placeholder until this lands
done when: get_price(item_id, discount) is reachable from client.py

Five lines: who asks whom, what, why, whether it blocks, and how to tell it's done. The owning agent picks it up, and the asking agent reverts its out-of-lane edit. In the demo, after the UI lane reverted client.py:

$ python3 /tmp/lane_check.py
lane api (lane/api): 2 file(s) changed
lane ui (lane/ui): 1 file(s) changed
OK: every lane stayed in its files
[exit 0]

Step 4: Merge in a fixed order

My rule (my own, not from the docs): merge the lane that others depend on first. Here the UI needs the API, so lane/api goes first, then lane/ui, and the tests run after each merge, not once at the end. If the second merge breaks something, you know which lane did it. Write the order into TASKS.md before the agents start, so nobody argues about it at the end.

Both merges went through cleanly in the demo, and afterwards git worktree remove cleaned up both lanes.

Step 5: One reviewer for all lanes

Parallel agents can produce work faster than one person can read it. My rule here is also my own: one reviewer, human or a dedicated review agent, reads every lane's diff before it merges, and nothing merges on the writing agent's own say-so. A reviewer who sees all lanes is the one who notices that two "independent" tasks made opposite assumptions.

When to stop adding agents

Claude Code's agent-teams docs are direct about this: token costs scale linearly, coordination overhead grows, and "beyond a certain point, additional teammates don't speed up work proportionally." They suggest starting with 3 to 5 teammates for most workflows and add: "Three focused teammates often outperform five scattered ones." Their overview of parallel approaches adds that running several sessions or subagents at once multiplies token usage.

My own signals that the next agent won't help:

  • You can't give it a set of files no other lane touches.
  • Hand-off notes start outnumbering finished tasks.
  • The reviewer is the queue: lanes wait for review more than they wait for work.

At that point, fewer lanes with bigger tasks usually beats more lanes with smaller ones.

Checklist

  1. One agent, one worktree, one branch.
  2. Write each lane's files in TASKS.md before any agent starts.
  3. Set up each worktree: dependencies and .env aren't copied by default.
  4. Out-of-lane change needed? Hand-off note to the owner, not a direct edit.
  5. Run a lane check before merging: files outside lanes, files shared by lanes.
  6. Merge the depended-on lane first; run tests after each merge.
  7. One reviewer reads every diff.
  8. Can't give a new agent its own files? Don't add it.

Where to go next

Lanes, hand-offs and shared state are one part of a bigger design question. Multi-Agent Orchestration: The Complete Guide covers it framework-agnostic in 40 pages: when not to go multi-agent, five coordination patterns (sequential pipeline, fan-out/fan-in, supervisor-workers, dynamic handoff, maker-checker/debate), task boundaries and roles, handoffs and shared state, and five failure modes, including state collisions and diffused accountability.

How do you split work between parallel agents today: by files, by branches, or by trusting them to stay out of each other's way?

This article was written with the assistance of AI and reviewed by the author.

title: How fast should an aesthetic clinic reply to a new enquiry?
description:
As fast as you can do reliably, and the target I built Conduit around is seconds, day or night. I cannot give you a study that says exactly how quickly a person loses interest, because I do not have one and will not make one up. What I can show you is how to measure your own reply times and decide what is worth fixing.

A new enquiry usually arrives when someone has just decided to ask. If the first reply arrives after they have asked the next clinic as well, you are competing for a decision that was almost made. Here is how to look at it.

Why does reply speed matter for a clinic?

Because the person who writes to you is comparing clinics while the question is fresh. The Conduit model of the problem is simple: an enquiry arrives at night, goes cold by morning, and some of those people book somewhere else. That is the first of the two gaps I built the product to close, the other being past patients who are never reminded that a review is due.

How many people go elsewhere is the unknown. Our home page check assumes 40% of after-hours enquiries go to another clinic, and the page labels that as an assumption you should change. Your own data beats it.

How do you measure your current reply time?

  1. 1Collect a month of enquiries from your inbox, forms, chat and phone log.
  2. 2For each, note the time it arrived and the time of the first real reply.
  3. 3Mark whether it arrived inside or outside opening hours.
  4. 4Work out the typical gap for each group, and the longest gaps.
  5. 5Check how many of the slowest ones ever booked.

A spreadsheet is enough. The last step is the most useful, because it replaces a general belief with a count from your own clinic. If the slow ones booked anyway, the problem is smaller than you think.

What is a good reply, not only a fast one?

A reply that moves the person forward. 'We have received your message' is an acknowledgement, not a reply. A good first reply answers the question asked, says what happens next and offers a way to book.

  • It answers the actual question or says who will
  • It asks the health questions your practitioner needs, before anything is booked
  • It offers a time to book, not 'let us know'
  • It stays inside the wording rules: no offers, no medicine names, no promises

The last point is where speed and compliance meet. A fast reply written quickly is the most likely place for a slip, which is why Conduit checks reply templates before they are used and your clinic approves each one.

What are the options for evenings and weekends?

The same four as in the after-hours cost article: reply next morning, extend hours or roster someone, send an automatic acknowledgement, or use a system that replies in seconds and carries the enquiry to a booked consultation. Each fixes a different part of the problem.

The staffed option is the most human and the most expensive in wages, which you know better than I do. The automatic acknowledgement costs little but does not book anything. A system that replies and books, like the Grow plan, sits in between. Combine them if it suits your clinic.

What should a reply never do?

  • Give medical advice. Clinical questions go to your team.
  • Skip consent and the health questions to be quick.
  • Ask for photos over a social platform's direct messages.
  • Push the person with a deadline.

In Conduit the health questions and consent come first, and photos arrive by private link. Speed is only worth having when the reply is safe to send.

Does a fast reply replace your coordinator?

No. It answers the first message and carries the enquiry to a booked consultation. Your coordinator and your practitioner take it from there. If an enquiry is booked at midnight and nobody confirms it until Friday, the patient will notice.

So plan the handover as carefully as the first reply. Decide who looks at new bookings each morning and what they check. A fast front end with a slow back end moves the delay, not removes it.

What about phone calls?

Treat them the same way. A missed call at 7 pm is an enquiry with a timestamp, and a voicemail nobody plays until Monday is a slow reply. Add the phone log to your month of records so the numbers reflect how people actually reach you.

The Pro plan, priced on a call after we see your clinic, adds an AI agent on your clinic number, set up with you. It does not give medical advice, and I would not describe it as a replacement for the people who talk to your patients. Whether it fits depends on how many calls you miss, which only your phone records can tell you.

How do you decide what to do?

Measure for a month, then compare the cost of each option with the value of the enquiries you lose, using the formula in the after-hours article. If the number is small, reply next morning and move on. If it is large, test one option for a month.

Grow is priced on a call after we see your clinic, plus a one-off setup of about A$400, with no minimum term. You can see how it replies on your own clinic by booking a 20-minute demo, where we run a test enquiry through the system so you can see each step.

title: Differentially Private Policy Optimization in Linear MDPs with Adversarial Rewards
description:
arXiv:2611.33469v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) in personalized services often relies on sensitive interaction data. Motivated by the need to protect these data, we study differentially private (DP) policy optimization in episodic linear Markov decision processes (MDPs) with unknown transitions and adaptive adversarial linear rewards under full-information feedback. This setting poses two key challenges: past trajectories are repeatedly reused for policy evaluation, and reward choices may depend on previously released private statistics. The proposed algorithm combines batched proximal policy optimization (PPO) updates with optimistic policy evaluation, using private regression statistics and reward estimates to protect both trajectories and reward functions under joint differential privacy (JDP). With all other parameters fixed, our high-probability regret bound retains the same leading $\widetilde{O}\left(K^{3/4}\right)$ dependence on the number of episodes $K$ as the corresponding non-private bound for batched optimistic PPO. The additional privacy terms scale as $\widetilde{O} \left(K^{5/8}\right)$ and $\widetilde{O} \left(K^{1/2}\right)$. Thus, privacy incurs only lower-order additive costs in $K$, even under adaptive adversarial rewards.

title: Anatomy-Aware Pseudo-Labels and Homotopy-Annealed Hausdorff Supervision for Semi-Supervised Pancreas Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2611.33425v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Confidence-gated co-training assumes that pseudo-label errors are uncertain and concentrated at organ boundaries. We argue that for pancreas CT, where the target organ is a single connected structure and detached fragments are anatomically implausible, the dominant failures arise at three levels: where the organ is, what its boundary should look like, and how a correct boundary is penalized. Anatomical Rectification relabels implausible fragments of a teacher prediction as confident background, without adding any loss or parameter; an audit confirms that its rejections are overwhelmingly detached hallucinations and that thin, tail-like slices are not eroded. Boundary Grafting transplants labelled surface regions with their annotation into unlabeled volumes, replacing unreliable boundary pseudo-labels with ground truth. The residual error is coherent surface displacement, weakly penalized by permutation-invariant Dice and cross-entropy losses. Homotopy-Annealed Hausdorff (HAH) supervision anneals a distance-weighted penalty from an annotation-anchored objective that is convex in the prediction to a Hausdorff surrogate, admitting the prediction-dependent distance term only after the predicted surface becomes reliable. On NIH pancreas CT, under the standard semi-supervised split, the full method reaches 84.60% Dice and 4.97 voxels 95HD, improving all four metrics over compared methods; on MSD Task07, 78.90% Dice and 4.19 voxels 95HD. We further contribute PanTS-SSL, a semi-supervised evaluation protocol derived from the public 9,901-case PanTS corpus, with a curated 1,015-volume main pool, labelled tiers of 50, 100 and 250 volumes, an 80-case tumor track, shift probes for acquisition and anatomy change, and a fixed 901-volume test set. On it, the method exceeds the co-training baseline at 100 labels, scales to 85.29% Dice at 250 labels, and reaches 85.50% Dice at 100 labels with HAH.

title: On Grokking and the Dynamics of Generalization
description:
arXiv:2611.33825v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We extend the signal-channel theory of grokking introduced by Litman and Guo by relating training dissipation and evaluation transfer to population risk. For preconditioned gradient flows with time-dependent kernels, we distinguish two sources of limited evaluation visibility, namely small cumulative dissipation and weak transfer. We obtain quantitative bounds for task visibility and establish their stability under signal filtering and changes of evaluation distribution. We describe how task directions enter the effective signal channel through spectral activation or transport. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the transferred signal to decrease squared population risk and derive classification error bounds under margin assumptions. These results yield sufficient conditions for the same training trajectory to generalize under one evaluation distribution while failing under another. We show that differences in spectral learning rates can produce arbitrarily long delays between low training loss and low population risk. By relating classification accuracy to the distribution of margin crossing times, we construct a family of gradient flows in which the generalization delay tends to infinity, while both the duration of the transition from zero to full accuracy and the corresponding variation of population risk tend to zero. These phenomena occur without feature evolution during training. Finally, we prove that the occurrence and timing of generalization cannot generally be inferred from training dynamics alone, but depend on the geometry of evaluation transfer and its relation to the target.

title: From ITP to Debian testing: how my Rust CLI got into Debian
description:
In October 2026, a small terminal tool I wrote, Crumb, became a Debian package. It
was accepted from the NEW queue into unstable on 28 October, reached testing on
31 October, and a newer release (1.4.1) followed it into testing on 10 November.

I'm not a Debian Developer. I'm a contributor, which means every upload went through a
sponsor who reviewed and signed it. Getting there taught me more about how a Linux
distribution actually works than anything I'd read before, so this is the path as it
really happened, including the parts that went wrong.

What Crumb is

Crumb is a terminal tool written in Rust ("your terminal, with an agent that actually
gets the work done"), released under the MIT licence. Packaging it meant fitting a
modern Rust project into Debian's rules: every dependency available inside Debian,
every file with clear licensing, and every build reproducible in a clean environment.

Step 1: say you're doing it (the ITP)

Debian starts with a public note of intent. I filed an Intent to Package (ITP),
bug #1151280, on Debian's bug tracker. It tells everyone a package is coming and
prevents two people from doing the same work. The bug tracker is entirely email-driven,
which was my first culture shock.

Step 2: build it the way Debian builds it

Debian doesn't trust "works on my machine". I built Crumb with sbuild, inside a
clean chroot that has nothing installed except what the package declares. Then I ran
lintian (a static checker for packaging mistakes) and autopkgtest (tests run
against the installed package).

This is where real problems surfaced:

  • Crumb's own test suite failed inside the Debian build, because Debian removes Cargo.lock during the build and one test depended on it. I fixed it with a patch, and the fix went upstream too (crumb#233).
  • Salsa CI (Debian's GitLab CI) found that the tests needed a CA certificate store, so the package gained a ca-certificates dependency.
  • My first autopkgtest was only a superficial smoke test. After review from my sponsor, I replaced it with real tests.

The lesson: Debian's tooling isn't bureaucracy. It's a set of independent checks that
catch assumptions your own CI never questions.

Step 3: dependencies

A Rust package can only use crates already in Debian. Crumb needed rust-reedline
0.52.1, and I now
co-maintain that package in Debian alongside kpcyrd.

Step 4: find a sponsor (the RFS)

Contributors can't upload directly. I uploaded the package to mentors.debian.net and
filed a Request for Sponsorship (RFS). Simon Quigley, a Debian Developer on the
Rust team, reviewed it, asked for changes, and sponsored the upload.

Having a sponsor is the best part of the process. Every review taught me a convention I
didn't know existed.

Step 5: the NEW queue

Brand-new packages land in NEW, where Debian's ftpmasters check, by hand, that
every file is properly licensed and redistributable. Crumb was accepted into unstable on
28 October 2026.

Step 6: britney and the road to testing

From unstable, packages migrate to testing automatically, once britney (Debian's
migration tool) is satisfied: enough days without release-critical bugs, builds on the
release architectures, and no regressions in packages that depend on it. Its "excuses"
page explains exactly what is blocking a package. Crumb reached testing on 31
October, and version 1.4.1-1 followed on 10 November.

The lesson I wish I'd known on day one

While working on other Rust packages with the Debian Rust team, I learnt that when
upstream ships files without their source (pre-built or generated assets), you don't
just skip installing them. You repack the source so those files aren't in Debian's
source package at all (in Rust team packaging, via excludes in debcargo.toml).
Debian ships source you can actually rebuild, not just binaries you can trust.

What came next

Getting one package in opened the door to more: I now work with the Debian Rust
team on release-critical bugs. One fix (blosc2) went the whole way from my bug report to an
upload and an upstream merge, another (rustls) shipped in another developer's upload
with my patch, and for a third (lopdf) upstream merged my fix while Debian shipped its own.

If you want your software in Debian

  1. Read the Debian New Maintainers' Guide, and package something small first.
  2. File the ITP early; it signals intent and attracts help.
  3. Build with sbuild from day one. Fix what lintian and autopkgtest tell you.
  4. Find your language team (for Rust, the Debian Rust team) and ask questions.
  5. Expect reviews; they're how you learn.

Links:

  • Crumb in Debian: https://tracker.debian.org/pkg/crumb
  • The ITP: https://bugs.debian.org/1151280
  • Crumb: https://github.com/elixpo/crumb.elixpo

title: Refusal Is Not Scored: A Coverage Limit in Content-Based Bias Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2611.33690v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bias audits of conversational models often discard refusals (responses such as "I can't assist with that request") before scoring, a filtering step which is rarely examined as a measurement decision even though it determines which responses an audit is capable of evaluating. This work examines what the step removes, applying seven bias-evaluation instruments spanning both deployed paradigms, three dictionary-based and four LLM-as-judge, to two intersectional datasets of 360 generated responses each. In both datasets, the filter removed a demographically skewed subset produced entirely by one of the three responder models, which refused North Korean prompts at 2.15 times the rate of American prompts on declarative content and 1.76 times on operational content. We then remove the filter and pass every refusal to all seven instruments. Bias-Lexicon scores refusals as clean, and including them shrinks the nationality disparity it reports. HurtLex appears to register the disparity, but we trace this entirely to a single lexicon entry matching the token "can" in "I can't". The LLM judges either flag most responses or rate refusals as unbiased. For the two judges that discriminate, including refusals lowers the nationality disparity they report, and no instrument identifies the refusal disparity. The failure is therefore a coverage limit upstream of scoring rather than a calibration gap that a better lexicon or judge prompt would be expected to close, which makes the behavioral channel an instrument is sensitive to a question of construct validity rather than one of method selection.
