title: Anthropic Rebuilt Its Claude Messages API in Rust With Claude's Help
description:
Originally published at Rohan Tech Official.
Anthropic has rebuilt the Messages API — the service that connects customers and its own apps to Claude — from Python to Rust, and Claude did most of the writing. The results, shared in an engineering post on November 25: about 70% less CPU per request, over 80% less memory, and median time to first token roughly 20% faster.
The rewrite went live for public traffic in September 2026, with no downtime and no feature freeze. The interesting part is not that an AI wrote the code. It is how Anthropic proved the new version behaved exactly like the old one.

Why the rewrite was needed

Anthropic built the Messages API in 2023 as a simple Python service. Then Claude took off: API traffic grew roughly 1,800 times between early 2024 and fall 2026, and every request now passes through validation, tokenisation and safety classifiers.
A partial rewrite in March 2026 moved only response parsing to Rust and saved 8–10% CPU — not enough to justify two languages. A full rewrite looked huge until the economics changed: by May 2026, Claude was writing more than 80% of the code Anthropic merged. Claude wrote a first version of the core request path in about a week.

The hard part was proving it worked

The team had about 700 integration tests, but they were tied to the Python code, and an audit found more than 100 weakened assertions. In April the Rust API passed 98% of its tests, yet only about a quarter of real production inputs behaved identically.
The problems were real: the Python API kept changing as new models shipped, Claude's replies are nondeterministic, and 20 binary options create over a million combinations. Anthropic's fix was to turn the live Python API into the answer key. Real requests ran through both versions, but the model was called once and its output replayed to Rust, so nobody was billed twice and randomness could not create false mismatches. Engineers never read the actual requests — only the shape of each difference.
Checkpointing found where the versions first split, fingerprints told one bug from another, and three agent loops did the fixing: a fast inner loop in a sandbox, a slower outer loop against shadowed traffic, and a memory loop that turned corrections into permanent rules. A coordinating Claude agent grouped mismatches every 10 to 30 minutes and assigned worker agents, with human review gating every merge. Matching inputs rose from about 24% in late April to 99.6% by August.
"Verification, not generation, had become the bottleneck," the engineers wrote. AI can now draft a production system in days — trusting that draft with live traffic is the slow part, and Anthropic's answer was to let agents do the checking too.

title: Same Tokenizer, Better Tokens: Choosing Image Tokens by MAP Inference
description:
arXiv:2611.33261v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Discrete visual tokens encode images for reconstruction and serve as training targets for autoregressive image generators. Vector-quantized tokenizers typically assign each encoder feature its nearest code independently. The decoder uses these codes jointly, so a sequence of individually nearest codes can reconstruct an image less faithfully than an alternative assignment. A local model of the reconstruction loss yields a closest-vector problem with a decoder-dependent target and metric. Reconstruction-only search improves PSNR across the frozen tokenizers we test. Different code sequences can achieve similar reconstruction quality, leaving room to favour more predictable ones.
  We introduce RecaP (Reconstruction and Predictability), which selects codes for a frozen tokenizer by balancing how faithfully they reconstruct the image with how likely their sequence is under a pretrained autoregressive prior. On ImageNet, LlamaGen GPT-B trained on RecaP tokens achieves lower early-checkpoint FID against training images than GPT-B trained on nearest-neighbour tokens. The difference is smaller against held-out images. On an ImageNet subset, the prior improves generation at comparable reconstruction FID. Our code is available at: https://github.com/gmum/recap

title: Why meetings across Dubai, London and New York break twice a year
description:
If your team spans Dubai, London and New York, you may have seen a recurring meeting suddenly land an hour early or late. Nothing is wrong with your calendar. The three places change their clocks on different dates, or not at all.
https://myzonetime.com

Disclosure: I run MyZoneTime, a free time zone tool. The examples below work with any tool.

The rule behind the confusion
Dubai (UAE) never uses daylight saving time. It is UTC+4 all year.
London (UK) moves clocks forward on the last Sunday of March and back on the last Sunday of October. It is UTC+0 in winter and UTC+1 in summer.
New York (US) moves clocks forward on the second Sunday of March and back on the first Sunday of November. It is UTC-5 in winter and UTC-4 in summer.
Because the UK and the US switch on different dates, there are a few weeks each year when the usual gap between them is off by an hour.

What the gaps are
Pair Winter gap Summer gap
Dubai and London 4 hours 3 hours
Dubai and New York 9 hours 8 hours
London and New York 5 hours 5 hours (but 4 hours in the weeks when only one has switched)
In 2027 the US switches on 14 March and the UK on 28 March, so London and New York are only 4 hours apart from 14 to 28 March. In autumn the UK switches on 31 October and the US on 7 November, so they are 4 hours apart again for that one week.

A worked example
Say you meet at 4:00 pm in Dubai.

In London that is 12:00 in winter and 13:00 in summer.
A call at 10:00 am in New York is 19:00 in Dubai in winter and 18:00 in summer.
So a meeting that sits at a comfortable time for everyone in January can quietly become a late evening for someone in July.

How to avoid the problem
Write the city and the zone with every time. "4 pm Dubai time (UTC+4)" is clear. "4 pm" is not.
Create the invite in the calendar, not in a message. Calendars store the time zone, so they adjust each person's view automatically.
Check meetings in the weeks around the switches: the last two weeks of March and the end of October through the first week of November.
Anchor on the zone that never changes. If you pick the meeting time in UAE time, only the other cities move.
Look at working hours, not only the clock. Dubai and New York have no overlap in a normal 9 to 5 day. Plan a Dubai evening (or New York morning) slot.
Tools
Any world clock or meeting planner will do. I use MyZoneTime's meeting planner to see working hours side by side, and the Dubai and London time difference page for a quick check. It also has an AI planner where you describe the meeting in plain words.

What's the worst time zone mix-up you've seen? Let me know in the comments.

title: Future-proofing is dead and AI killed it
description:
We have always tried to build things that outlast whatever comes next. AI makes that impossible. The solution is the opposite of what you think.

When creating products, the goal is often to try and future-proof it.

Create a tool that won’t be obsolete in a few years. Learn the skill the machines can’t take.

Build the architecture flexible enough to survive whatever comes next.

Draw the roadmap that still makes sense down the line.

It’s been the sensible approach for decades, the thing you do so you’re not betting the company on something that could kill. That’s an understandable fear. S. Patrick Viguerie and his colleagues at Innosight actually found the average lifespan of a company on the S&P 500 has collapsed from sixty-one years in the late 1950s to under twenty, with roughly half the index expected to turn over within a decade.

The thing you bet on really does die faster than it used to.

But to be frank, that mentality just doesn’t work anymore. Future-proofing was always a bet that you could see far enough ahead to build toward it, and the speed at which AI is evolving how we create things, how we interact with things, how we collaborate with AI itself, has made that bet impossible to win.

France found this out the hard way almost a hundred years ago. After the First World War they built the Maginot Line, a wall of concrete and guns along the German border so strong no army could punch through it. It was the most future-proofed thing on the planet. Then the Germans drove around it, through the forest everyone swore tanks couldn’t cross, and took France in six weeks.

The wall worked exactly as designed, but the strategy of the warfare outsmarted it.

Future-proofing has the same flaw. You take your known experience and armor up against a war you can picture, but in reality, the war goes in a completely different direction.

In a slower era you at least got years between building the wall and watching someone flank it. In our age of AI those years are gone.

When ChatGPT reached a hundred million users in two months, UBS analysts said they could not recall a faster ramp in twenty years of watching the internet, outpacing the nine months it took TikTok and the two and a half years for Instagram.

The situation gets worse, because we are no longer trying to predict just one thing that could change in the industry or technology or user habits. We are trying to predict three, all at once, all moving, all being shoved faster by the same technology.

The tech you build on.

The people you build for.

The company itself that you’re building.

Every one of them is a moving target, and future-proofing asks that we hit all three while they are in motion while we are standing on a platform that is moving too.

Let’s take them one at a time.

The tool you bet on is already dead

If we start with examining how companies rely on technology, it’s easy to see that people still pick the proven, well-funded, widely-used option because it seems like a safe bet.

Scott Brinker calls this Martec’s Law. Technology changes exponentially, and organizations change logarithmically. One curve shoots up, the other crawls, and the gap between what the tech can do and what your company can absorb gets wider every year.

Brinker was writing about marketing software, but the idea holds with where we are in the world of AI, and underneath that is Ray Kurzweil’s old observation that technology compounds on itself, each generation building on the last, so the pace does not just increase, the increase increases.

Patrick Neeman wrote a piece arguing the Double Diamond, the design process half the industry has leaned on for twenty years, is dead for software. His reasoning around this is what’s useful here, that the process was not wrong. The process was built for a world where making something was expensive and slow, so you spent a lot of time up front making sure you built the right thing before you committed. Then the cost of building a working prototype dropped from a two-week sprint to an afternoon.

One input fell by two orders of magnitude in under two years, and a process built on the way of working and pricing it survived into a world where that cost was no longer reasonable.

Future-proofing works exactly the same way. You pick the durable thing, the proven process, the safe stack, the tool with the big company behind it, because it feels like it will last, but that idea that it will continue to last is an illusion. Today, the thing that made it the right call at the time, the economics underneath it, is exactly what AI keeps disrupting.

Underneath all of this is a more straightforward problem. Future-proofing is a prediction, and people are famously terrible at prediction. Philip Tetlock spent decades studying expert forecasters, the people whose entire job is to see what is coming, and found they were barely better than chance, and sometimes worse than a crude rule of thumb.

These are the best-informed people in any room, and the future still makes fools of them regularly. Now hand that same impossible task to a product team and ask them to pick the tool that will still be right in three years, in the fastest technology shift any of us have worked through.

That’s just setting people up for failure where there are legit stakes.

The customer you designed for just changed on you

Let’s say you somehow beat the odds on the technology. You picked a stack or product that kept its place in the ranks of software. You still have the second problem.

AI is rewiring your user faster than you can build for them.

Think about what AI has done to the simplest thing a customer does, which is look for something. For twenty years, searching meant typing words into a box and scanning a page of blue links. People built entire companies, careers, and content strategies on that one stable behavior.

Natasha Sommerfeld and her team at Bain found that a large share of searches now end without anyone clicking through to a website at all, and that number climbs higher once AI starts answering the question directly instead of pointing at ten places that might.

The behavior that a generation of products was designed around is evaporating because of a technology most of those products never even considered.

It is not just search. Elizabeth Silliman and her colleagues at McKinsey surveyed around twenty-one thousand people about how they shop and found more than half already using AI somewhere in the process, with the behavior, in their words, shifting as fast as adoption itself, faster than the companies serving those customers can keep up.

The Capgemini Research Institute ran the same kind of study two years running, which is the useful part, because the year-over-year jump shows you the speed. This is not a new normal you can design for and settle into. It is a moving line.

Invoca, which sells software to marketers, found the share of people using a generative AI tool to research a serious purchase went from forty-one percent to fifty-eight percent in a single year. Among older buyers it tripled.

Imagine building a product around how your customer behaves, shipping it, and discovering that in the time it took to build, a third of them started researching an entirely different way. You tried to do everything right, but behavior just shifted to fast.

It doesn’t get better.

Lingxiu Dong, Kaiwen Luo, and Fasheng Xu studied what happens as people hand shopping over to AI agents, and found the scarce thing stops being the search and becomes the ability to say what you actually want, clearly enough for an agent to go get it. The whole shape of the interaction changes.

The thing you optimized, helping someone browse and compare, is not even the job anymore and, frighteningly, what you should have been designing for did not even exist when you started designing it in the first place.

This is the trap of the user you think you know. You do the research, you identify the behaviors, you ship the thing that fits who you think your audience is. By the time it hits the market, though, AI has given people a whole new set of habits and a new set of expectations that no longer fits.

Henry Ford supposedly said that if he had asked people what they wanted, they would have said a faster horse. The modern version is worse. Ask people what they want, and by the time you build it, the question itself has changed, because the thing answering their questions changed them while you tried to answer the original one.

The org chart you built is the thing slowing you down

Keeping it going, let’s assume you somehow future-proofed the tech and kept up with the customer (well done!). There is still a third thing you cannot pin down, and it is your own company.

Every org is built around a set of assumptions about how work gets done.

Who owns what.

Who hands off to whom.

Which role exists to coordinate, which to decide, which to make the thing.

You draw that structure to be stable, because stability is the point of a structure. The moment AI changes how the work actually happens, that carefully drawn stability becomes the thing you have to fight.

Remember Scott Brinker’s philosophy that technology moves exponentially and organizations move logarithmically. The org is the slow curve by design, and the slowness you built on purpose, the clear roles, the defined ownership, the approval chain, is exactly what cannot bend when the fast curve jumps.

A design leader I know has been watching the traditional product owner role dissolve in his very large organization, because the work that justified it, coordinating the handoffs, chasing the status, translating requirements between teams, is precisely the work AI and a good design process now absorb.

The experience is the product, he told me, and the people who understand the experience can own it end to end. So where does that leave the role built to coordinate it? The hardest thing to change, he said, is not the work. It is that the taxonomy of roles is what funds the roles.

The org chart is not just how work flows. It is how budgets, titles, and headcount are justified. You cannot just delete a box on it, because someone’s job, someone’s comp, someone’s sense of what they are, is inside that box.

It’s not just him, research backs it up. Sam Ransbotham and his colleagues at MIT Sloan found that AI only delivers real gains when companies redesign the work around it, the roles, the workflows, the decision rights, and that where the structure stays frozen, AI just gets absorbed into the old process and changes nothing.

This is an old idea in organizational theory. Michael Hannan and John Freeman called it structural inertia, the tendency of roles, processes, and reporting lines to persist long after the conditions that created them are gone. The structure outlives its own reason for existing, and everyone keeps staffing it anyway.

Wolfgang Rohde, in a paper on AI and organizational capability, points out that companies discover the value of human judgment right after they have cut the roles that produced it. You optimize the org chart for the work AI can do, you thin out the people who caught the problems and trained the next ones, and then the first time something genuinely novel breaks, you find you removed the exact capacity you needed to handle it.

The future-proofed org is not just slow. It is brittle in a way you cannot see until it is tested.

Most companies are using AI to get better at things they already do, inside the structure they already have. David M. Rothschild and his colleagues at Microsoft Research call this choosing optimization over reinvention, because it is safer and easier to make the current machine a little faster than to admit the machine is the wrong shape.

The structure you built to protect the future becomes the single biggest reason you cannot meet it.

Stop armoring. Start moving.

All three of these problems end up having same answer. Stop trying to predict the future and lean into moving with it.

Trying to future-proof is no longer possible, so strategize and build to respond instead.

The most direct approach to this of this came from Jeff Bezos, years before the AI wave, in a letter to Amazon shareholders. He split decisions into two kinds. Some are one-way doors, irreversible, and those you make slowly and carefully, because you cannot walk back through them. Most decisions are two-way doors. You can walk through, see what is on the other side, and come back if you were wrong.

His warning was that as companies get bigger, they start treating every decision like a one-way door, applying the slow, heavy, careful process to choices that are easily undone, and they grind to a halt. Future-proofing is the one-way-door mindset applied to a world made almost entirely of two-way doors. You are deliberating like the choice is permanent when the whole advantage available to you is that it is not.

Nassim Taleb conceived a whole book around this posture. He called it being antifragile, designing things that gain from disorder instead of trying to predict and prevent it. A fragile thing needs the future to arrive exactly as forecast. An antifragile thing gets stronger when the future shows up weird, because it was built to absorb surprise rather than to bet against it.

Future-proofing is a bet that the future behaves. The reality is that now we have to build things, teams, and careers that do better precisely because it will not.

It is worth noticing that Brinker himself, the one who named the gap, never prescribed better prediction as the fix. His advice for living with Martec’s Law was to choose selectively which changes you take on, stay agile enough to move, and every so often reset your whole approach at an inflection point instead of defending the old one.

He never says get better at predicting. He spent his career proving companies can’t keep pace with the tech, and his answer is to stop trying to.

In practice this is less exotic than it sounds. David Hoang frames it as stop thinking of the work as a factory, a machine that turns a fixed input into a fixed output, and start thinking of it as a garden, something you cultivate and adjust as it grows and as conditions change.

A factory built for one product is worthless when the product changes. A garden just gets replanted.

When you do have to commit, Sundeep Misra points at the one thing worth being sure of, which is not the tool or the plan but the decision underneath it. The scarce skill in all of this is knowing what is actually worth building, so that when everything around it moves, you still know why you are moving.

Responding does not mean acting on every piece of feedback you receive. That sort of reaction can thrash the product to death and burn out your team. The important thing is to filter feedback based on the source and the perspective and real knowledge behind it.

Everyone has an opinion. The ones worth listening to are the informed ones, with genuine expertise and the right context. I tell founders this constantly. I will not weigh in on your code, because I am not the expert there, and my opinion should carry no weight with you on that topic, but when it comes to user experience or patterns around process, things I’ve seen a thousand times, then my opinion is valid.

This is just as true for you as it is for your company. You cannot future-proof yourself as an employee either, for the same reason. The specific skill you are banking on, the tool you mastered, the process you are known for, is exactly the thing AI commoditizes first.

The World Economic Forum estimates that 39 percent of workers’ core skills will be transformed or outdated between 2025 and 2030. Hoarding one skill and hoping it lasts is the personal version of the Maginot Line.

Stop armoring a fixed skill set and build the thing that does not expire, your judgment, your taste, your ability to learn the next thing fast and decide what is worth doing. That is the one capability AI is not coming for.

The answer to the anxiety that started all this is that you were right to be scared of betting the company on the thing that dies, but you were wrong about how to fix it.

We’ve seen that just building a better wall wasn’t the answer. France built the best one ever and still found themselves in a losing position.

Stop building to last.

Make reversible bets.

Stay close enough to your customers to feel the shift before it’s obvious.

Put your effort into deciding what’s worth building, not into guessing what survives. That’s what you can actually control.

References and further reading

The window has collapsed

  • S. Patrick Viguerie, Ned Calder and Brian Hindo, “2021 Corporate Longevity Forecast” (Innosight). The average lifespan of an S&P 500 company has fallen toward under twenty years, with roughly half the index expected to turn over within a decade.
  • Reuters, reporting the UBS analyst note, “ChatGPT sets record for fastest-growing user base” (2023). ChatGPT reached a hundred million users in two months, a pace UBS called unmatched in twenty years of wa
  • World History Encyclopedia, “Maginot Line.” The French fortifications that Germany bypassed through the Ardennes in 1940, now a byword for an expensive defense that offers a false sense of security.tching the internet.

The tool you bet on is already dead

  • Scott Brinker, “Martec’s Law: The Greatest Management Challenge of the 21st Century” (chiefmartec). Technology changes exponentially, organizations change logarithmically.
  • Ray Kurzweil, “The Law of Accelerating Returns” (2001). The exponential, compounding nature of technological change.
  • Patrick Neeman, “The UX Double Diamond Is Dead, and in AI Only One Survives for Software” (UX Collective). A durable process made obsolete when the cost of building collapsed.
  • Philip Tetlock, “Superforecasting” (2015) and “Expert Political Judgment” (2005). Expert prediction barely beats chance.

The customer you designed for just changed on you

  • Natasha Sommerfeld and colleagues, “Goodbye Clicks, Hello AI: Zero-Click Search Redefines Marketing” (Bain & Company, 2025). The zero-click shift and the reset of search expectations.
  • Elizabeth Silliman, Jack Trotter, and Kelsey Robinson, with Desirae Oppong and Shreya Jaggi, “Who Wins When AI Does the Shopping?” (McKinsey, 2026, around 21,000 consumers). AI shopping behavior shifting as fast as adoption.
  • Capgemini Research Institute, “What Matters to Today’s Consumer 2026” (12,000 consumers, year over year). The rate of change in AI-driven expectations.
  • Invoca, 2026 B2C Buyer Experience Report. GenAI purchase research rose from 41 to 58 percent in a single year.
  • Lingxiu Dong, Kaiwen Luo and Fasheng Xu, “From Product Search to Preference Articulation: The Economics of Agentic Commerce” (2026). As AI agents take over discovery, scarcity shifts from search to preference articulation.

The org chart you built is the thing slowing you do

  • Scott Brinker, “Martec’s Law” (as above). Organizations change logarithmically.
  • Sam Ransbotham, David Kiron, Shervin Khodabandeh, Sesh Iyer and Amartya Das, “The Emerging Agentic Enterprise: How Leaders Must Navigate a New Age of AI” (MIT Sloan Management Review with BCG, 2025). AI delivers gains only when roles, workflows, and decision rights are redesigned around it.
  • David M. Rothschild, Jake M. Hofman, Markus Mobius, Brendan Lucier, Eleanor Dillon, Daniel G. Goldstein, Nicole Immorlica, Aleksandrs Slivkins at Microsoft Research, “From Augmentation to Reconstruction: Guiding the AI Disruption to the Good Place” (2026). Most organizations use AI to accelerate pre-AI workflows; real change favors reconstruction over local optimization.
  • Wolfgang Rohde, “Short-Term Gain, Long-Term Fragility: AI Labor Substitution and the Erosion of Sustainable Capability” (2026). Organizations discover the value of human judgment after they have made it scarce.
  • Michael T. Hannan and John Freeman, “Structural Inertia and Organizational Change” (American Sociological Review, 1984). The foundational theory of why organizations resist changing their structure even after the conditions that shaped it are gone.

Stop armoring. Start moving.

  • Jeff Bezos, Amazon 2015 Letter to Shareholders. One-way-door versus two-way-door decisions, and the cost of treating reversible choices as permanent.
  • Nassim Nicholas Taleb, “Antifragile: Things That Gain from Disorder” (2012). Build to gain from disorder rather than predict it.
  • Scott Brinker, “Martec’s Law” (as above). His own prescription: choose selectively, stay agile, reset at inflection points.
  • David Hoang, “Software Gardens” (Proof of Concept, 2026). Cultivate the work like a garden, not a factory.
  • Sundeep Misra, “AI Won’t Save an Organization That Can’t Decide What to Build” (2026). The scarce skill is deciding what is worth building.
  • World Economic Forum, “The Future of Jobs Report 2025.” On average, workers can expect 39 percent of their existing skills to be transformed or become outdated between 2025 and 2030; judgment, adaptability, and continuous learning are the durable capabilities.

Future-proofing is dead and AI killed it was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: DreamTour: Layout Steering for Training-Free World Exploration
description:
arXiv:2611.33378v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video diffusion and world models generate plausible videos but do not reliably match the requested camera direction and travel distance. We present DreamTour, a training-free framework that generates camera tours from a single image with more accurate control over camera motion. DreamTour first uses a frozen image inpainting prior to extend the photograph beyond its original field of view while preserving the input pixels. Depth-based rendering of this extended scene along the requested camera path produces approximate target views that serve as spatial guidance. We introduce Layout Steering, which aligns early video latents with these views through decaying low-frequency corrections, leaving later denoising to refine appearance and dynamics. For longer tours, we autoregressively generate the video segments, repeating guidance construction from each segment's final frame to maintain camera control across the full trajectory. DreamTour improves directional accuracy and travel calibration on VBench while maintaining competitive video quality. On WorldScore, it strengthens camera control and scene consistency across chained movements. Together, these results demonstrate that training-free spatial guidance enables more accurate and consistent camera control in pretrained video diffusion and world models.

title: 🚀 Building Spring by Example V2: Completing Module 10 - Spring AI
description:
When I started learning Spring, I noticed something about many of the tutorials I found.

They often showed how to use a feature, but not always why it worked or when you should choose one approach over another.

I learn best by building things and documenting what I discover, so I started a project called spring-by-example.

The idea is simple: instead of building one large application, I’m creating a collection of small, focused examples where each example explores a specific Spring concept with clear explanations, tests, and documentation.

I’m happy to say that I’ve now completed Module 10 - Spring AI. 🎉

This module introduced me to building AI-powered applications with Spring AI, from interacting with language models to working with embeddings, vector stores, retrieval-augmented generation, and AI tools.

The module covers:

  • Spring AI Fundamentals
  • Chat Models
  • Prompt Templates
  • Structured Output
  • Embeddings
  • Vector Stores
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
  • Tool Calling
  • AI Application Testing
  • Model Provider Integration

One thing I really enjoyed about this module was discovering how Spring AI provides familiar Spring abstractions for working with AI models while hiding much of the complexity involved in communicating with different providers.

I started with the fundamentals and chat models, exploring how an application can send messages to a language model and retrieve responses using ChatClient and ChatModel.

From there, I explored prompt templates.

Instead of hardcoding prompts directly into application logic, I learned how to externalize them and provide dynamic values using placeholders.

For example:

PromptTemplate promptTemplate = new PromptTemplate(
        "Explain {technology} to {audience}."
);

Prompt prompt = promptTemplate.create(Map.of(
        "technology", "Spring Boot",
        "audience", "Java developers"
));

Structured output introduced another interesting concept.

Rather than working with unstructured text responses, I explored how Spring AI can convert model responses into Java objects using BeanOutputConverter.

This makes it easier to work with predictable response structures in application code.

Embeddings and vector stores were another important part of the module.

I explored how text can be converted into numerical vector representations that capture semantic meaning.

This led to vector stores, where I learned how to store documents and retrieve relevant information through similarity searches.

One of the most interesting examples was Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).

RAG combines information retrieval with language model generation.

Instead of relying entirely on the model's existing knowledge, an application can retrieve relevant documents and provide them as context when generating an answer.

The simplified flow looks like this:

User Question
      |
      v
Vector Similarity Search
      |
      v
Retrieve Relevant Documents
      |
      v
Build Prompt with Context
      |
      v
Language Model
      |
      v
Generated Answer

This helped me understand how AI applications can provide answers grounded in specific information sources.

I also explored Tool Calling.

This was particularly interesting because it demonstrated how an AI model can request that an application execute predefined functions.

For example, I built calculator tools that an AI assistant could use to perform arithmetic operations.

The important distinction is that the model does not execute the Java methods itself. It requests a tool call, and the application executes the corresponding method and returns the result.

Testing AI applications was another important part of the module.

I explored how to test services that use ChatClient, how to mock ChatModel responses, and how to verify prompt construction without making actual requests to an AI provider.

This was useful because AI applications introduce testing challenges that aren't always present in traditional Spring applications.

Finally, I explored Model Provider Integration.

I integrated two providers:

  • Ollama - for running language models locally.
  • OpenAI - for accessing hosted language models through an API.

Using Spring profiles, I could switch between providers through configuration without changing the application service implementation.

For example:

spring:
  ai:
    model:
      chat: ollama

Or:

spring:
  ai:
    model:
      chat: openai

The same application service can interact with either provider through Spring AI's common abstractions.

That was a great way to finish the module because it brought together many of the concepts explored throughout the examples.

The goal wasn't simply to learn how to send a prompt to an AI model.

The bigger goal was to understand how Spring AI helps developers build applications that use language models, structured responses, semantic search, external tools, and different AI providers.

The project is open source, and I'm continuing to build it as I learn:

🔗 GitHub: https://gith.ub/dsAQrAU5

🔗 GitLab: https://gitl.ab/gfDEyGH3

There’s still a long way to go, but completing Module 10 - Spring AI feels like another important milestone. 🚀

Next up: Module 11 - GraalVM Native - exploring native compilation, Spring AOT, runtime hints, native testing, and containerized native applications. Continuing the journey through Spring by Example V2, one focused example at a time.

If you've worked with Spring AI, which concept do you find most interesting or useful in real-world applications - RAG, tool calling, embeddings, structured output, or model provider integration?

title: FERRETS: A Scalable Symbolic Transform for Time Series Classification
description:
arXiv:2611.33249v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dictionary methods for time series build bags of symbolic words from subsequences, but the accurate ones scale poorly. Against other families of methods, their accuracy no longer pays for their cost. We present FERRETS, a label-free dictionary transform built on WEASEL~2. It keys windows of random length and dilation into exact eight-bit words, adds a level word of each window's mean and spread, and on multivariate data adds cross-channel words. We compare it with leading classifiers, deep networks and foundation models included, on the UCR, Multiverse and MONSTER archives. FERRETS is the fastest of the eleven methods timed on UCR under a ten-thread budget. Of the ten others, only MultiRocket-Hydra is significantly more accurate, taking 24.7 times as long. FERRETS is not significantly different from WEASEL~2, the most accurate earlier dictionary method, which takes 125 times as long, and is significantly ahead of the other dictionary methods. On the Multiverse core, it is not significantly different in accuracy from HIVE-COTE~2 and MultiRocket-Hydra, though behind both on UCR. It is also significantly more accurate than five frozen foundation models on UCR's published split. On the MONSTER problems both complete, MiniRocket takes 3.7 times as long to fit as the streaming FERRETS classifier, which is significantly more accurate.

title: How to Identify the gcware Leader Node in a GBase 8a Cluster
description:
In GBase 8a, the China-domestically developed MPP analytical database from GBASE, the gcware service cluster shares information between the GCluster instances on every node — cluster topology, node states, node resource states — and, during multi-replica data operations, decides which nodes are usable and controls data-consistency state. A gcware cluster has several nodes, usually an odd number: one is elected leader, the rest are followers, and the leader holds the most current data. This post shows how to find out which node that is.

The gcware Log

By default it is stored at:

INSTALL_DIR/gcware/log/gcware.log

The Leader Marker

When a node becomes leader, the log records this line, where XXXXX is a number:

switch to leader with term:XXXXX

Filtering on switch to shows the whole election trail — candidate → leader as well as candidate → follower:

grep "switch to" /opt/gbase/*/gcware/log/gcware.log  | tail

Finding the Current Leader

Look for the latest Leader marker on each gcware node. The one with the most recent date (to avoid being misled by clock skew) and the largest number is the Leader. Here is the output from two nodes.

Node 103:

[gbase@gbase_rh7_003 ~]$ grep "switch to" /opt/gbase/*/gcware/log/gcware.log  | tail
Feb 07 17:29:44.546192 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1728184330 switch to candidate
Feb 07 17:29:47.887201 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1728184330 switch to candidate
Feb 07 17:29:50.295710 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1728184330 switch to candidate
Feb 07 17:29:50.320778 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1728184330 switch to leader with term:123
Feb 09 08:41:20.388174 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1728184330 switch to follower with term:124 leader:0
Feb 09 08:41:22.456324 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1728184330 switch to follower with term:125 leader:0
Feb 09 08:41:24.643133 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1728184330 switch to follower with term:126 leader:0
Feb 10 09:56:37.339436 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1728184330 switch to follower with term:126 leader:0
Feb 10 09:56:39.503562 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1728184330 switch to candidate
Feb 10 09:56:41.279513 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1728184330 switch to follower with term:205 leader:0

Node 104:

[gbase@gbase_rh7_004 log]$ grep "switch to " /opt/gbase/*/gcware/log/gcware.log | tail
Feb 09 09:14:37.059239 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1744961546 switch to candidate
Feb 09 09:14:40.076193 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1744961546 switch to candidate
Feb 10 09:56:21.190265 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1744961546 switch to follower with term:199 leader:0
Feb 10 09:56:24.842071 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1744961546 switch to candidate
Feb 10 09:56:27.875309 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1744961546 switch to candidate
Feb 10 09:56:30.875920 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1744961546 switch to candidate
Feb 10 09:56:33.957789 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1744961546 switch to candidate
Feb 10 09:56:37.263772 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1744961546 switch to candidate
Feb 10 09:56:41.272030 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1744961546 switch to candidate
Feb 10 09:56:41.519532 INFO  [GCWARE] node 1744961546 switch to leader with term:205

The newest entry on node 103 is February 7, with term 123; on node 104 it is February 10. An election took place at February 10 09:56:41, making 104 the leader and 103 a follower.

Going forward, you will rarely need this — the cluster coordinates elections on its own. It matters only after an outage such as a power loss, when some nodes' gcware files are corrupted and must be repaired by hand: that is when you need to know which surviving gcware copy in gbase holds the newest data. Comparing dates and term numbers in the log is far more reliable than guessing from a node number.

title: How I got my first 100 customers through SEO, without an audience
description:
It took me more than three months to get my first ten paying customers for Oakgen. I didn't have an established audience sending people to the website. SEO was how people started finding it.

After I shared my experience on Reddit, several people asked what I actually did. How did I choose keywords? What did I write? Did I do it manually or use AI agents?

This is the longer answer. I'll explain the approach, show real search data from Oakgen, and give you a small plan you can use for your own product. I'll also separate what happened in my business from what I'd recommend doing today.

What changed after the first few months?

In the beginning, I spent a lot of time building features. I enjoyed it, and there was always another improvement to make. But I was barely getting customers.

I looked at competitors' features and articles, worked on relevant product gaps, and published pages about the problems Oakgen could solve.

I started writing articles manually. Later, I made AI-agent skills and connected them to DataForSEO to make repeated research and keyword work easier. That is the progression I described in the original Reddit discussion.

I also had an introductory offer around my first customer. The available search data can't separate the effect of discovery from the offer.

The approach below is how I'd make this process manageable for another founder today.

1. Start with a problem your product can already solve

Before collecting keywords, write down what someone can successfully do with your product right now.

For Oakgen, examples include generating an image, making a video, creating a voiceover, and comparing models for a particular job.

For another SaaS, it might be sending an invoice, scheduling an appointment, or tracking stock across several stores.

Now describe the problem in the customer's language. Someone might search for an alternative to a tool they already know. Someone else might search for instructions because they're stuck halfway through a task.

Those are different situations, and they need different pages.

What someone needs Example from Oakgen's subject area What the page should help them do
An alternative Free ElevenLabs alternatives Compare options, restrictions, and whether they fit the intended use
A product decision OpenArt alternatives Understand the differences and choose a suitable tool
Help with a task Seedance prompt troubleshooting Diagnose a problem and decide what to change

These are examples of topics to investigate, not keyword-volume estimates or promises that you can rank for them.

For your first list, finish this sentence ten times: "Someone would need my product when they are trying to _____."

If you can't explain the connection between a topic and a real capability, leave it out of your first batch.

2. Look at the search results before deciding to write a blog

One useful habit in our research has been checking what kinds of pages appear for a query.

Sometimes the person wants an explanation. Sometimes they want a working tool. Sometimes they want a comparison with enough detail to make a decision.

For example, our SEO-tool research treated "llms.txt generator" and "what is llms.txt" as different needs. One asks for something you can use. The other asks for an explanation.

Before drafting, search your candidate topic in the country and language you want to serve. Record what the results actually contain:

  • Are they tools, tutorials, product pages, comparisons, or discussions?
  • What does each page help the visitor finish?
  • What evidence does it provide: screenshots, examples, demonstrations, or documented limits?
  • What important question remains unanswered?

Keyword tools can help you investigate demand. They don't replace reading the results. An estimate for a related phrase is also not evidence that your exact proposed phrase has the same demand.

Keep a simple research sheet with the query, target country, search intent, likely page format, relevant product capability, and evidence you'll need to create the page.

3. Use competitor research to find work you can do better

Competitor research helped me connect product work with content work. It gave me questions to investigate and features to compare against what Oakgen could actually do.

For a new page, I'd write a brief before writing the article:

The visitor is trying to complete this task. Existing pages leave this specific question unanswered. Our page will answer it using this evidence. If our product is suitable, this is the next action the reader can take.

The missing piece might be an outdated workflow, an unclear restriction, a setting nobody explains, or an example that doesn't show the result.

Then do the work needed to fill that gap. Try the workflow. Capture the relevant screen. Read the current documentation. If the product can't do something, say so.

For comparison pages, include situations where another option is a better fit. If every comparison ends with the same sales pitch, you haven't helped someone choose.

Google's helpful-content guidance also asks whether a page adds original information and substantial value beyond existing sources. A rewritten version of the same article gives a reader very little reason to choose yours.

4. Build a page around one useful outcome

Here's a real Oakgen example: our Seedance prompt-troubleshooting article.

Its structure includes a symptom-to-fix table, a weak prompt and controlled rewrite, a reference-packet checklist, and separate sections for timing and audio.

That structure gives the visitor something to work through. It also makes missing evidence easier to spot while editing.

For your own tutorial, use this as a starting outline:

  1. Answer the question in the opening paragraph.
  2. Explain what the reader needs before starting, including access requirements or limitations.
  3. Show the steps with a real example.
  4. Explain common failures and what to check.
  5. Show the relevant next action.

Only describe something as tested if you have a test record or result. A suggested prompt is useful, but label it as a starting point if you haven't run it.

Be equally clear about access. A visitor searching for a free tool should be able to tell early whether your product requires payment. Hiding that detail doesn't help them make a decision.

5. Give the reader a relevant next step

A tutorial should make it easy to open the tool it describes. A comparison should make it easy to inspect the relevant capabilities and terms. A troubleshooting guide might lead to a specific setting or a more detailed walkthrough.

The next step should follow naturally from what the visitor just read.

For a voiceover tutorial, "Open the voice generator" is useful. For a feature your product doesn't offer, a generic signup button doesn't solve the reader's problem.

Also check the basic path into the page. Can a visitor reach it from a relevant tool, category, or related article? Can search engines access the content? Does the title describe what's actually on the page?

Google's SEO Starter Guide is a useful reference for these basics. Following the guidance doesn't guarantee indexing or a particular ranking.

6. Check what happened after publication

Publishing was only part of the work. I also had to look at search data and improve existing pages.

Here are eight real examples from Oakgen's Search Console export. Each link opens the actual article, so you can inspect how the page answers its reader's question.

These are historical totals for Google Web text search from January 17 to November 23, 2026, grouped by article URL. They are not monthly figures. The pages were edited over time, so the totals aren't a test of their current wording.

Oakgen article Impressions Google clicks Click-through rate
Free ElevenLabs alternatives 150,809 1,163 0.77%
OpenArt alternatives 33,947 215 0.63%
Magnific AI alternatives 19,542 152 0.78%
Nano Banana 2 alternatives 14,733 149 1.01%
Is Oakgen a free AI image generator? 8,433 352 4.17%
GPT Image 2 access without ChatGPT Plus 4,162 226 5.43%
Seedance prompt troubleshooting 6,909 84 1.22%
ElevenLabs pricing and limits 31,245 47 0.15%

Specific alternatives are worth investigating

The ElevenLabs alternatives article was the most-clicked article in this blog audit. It addresses a concrete decision: finding a text-to-speech alternative and checking restrictions such as commercial-use rights.

OpenArt, Magnific and Nano Banana alternatives address other specific choices. Open the pages and compare the questions they answer, the limits they explain, and the next action they offer.

For your own SaaS, list the tools a potential customer might already use. Investigate why someone would look for an alternative and whether your product can actually meet that need. These results give me topics to study; they don't prove which part of an article caused a click.

Free-access questions brought clicks, but the answer needs to be honest

The page explaining whether Oakgen's image generator is free recorded 352 clicks. The GPT Image 2 access article recorded 226.

Both address an access or payment question. Answer those questions directly, including when a product requires payment or has restrictions. Visitors should learn that before starting a signup.

I wouldn't assume these clicks are all potential buyers. Someone looking for free access may have no intention of purchasing anything. Product activity after the visit is a separate thing to measure.

Troubleshooting has a different job

The Seedance troubleshooting article recorded 84 clicks and 6,909 impressions. It gives the reader a symptom-to-fix structure and a prompt-repair process.

Fewer search clicks don't establish that it is less useful to someone who needs help with that task. I'd also check whether people reach it through product-help links and whether it helps them complete their work.

Impressions alone don't tell me which page to copy

The ElevenLabs pricing page recorded 31,245 impressions and 47 clicks. The GPT Image 2 access page had 4,162 impressions and 226 clicks.

Their click-through rates were about 0.15% and 5.43%, respectively. That is a reason to investigate, not a verdict on either title. They serve different searches and may appear at different positions. I'd inspect the queries, country, device and position before deciding what to change.

None of these figures is a customer count. Search Console tells me about appearances and clicks in Google, not which visitors became paying customers. Its performance-report documentation explains the metrics and filters.

For a new SaaS, I'd separately track article visits, clicks into the relevant product workflow, completed signups, and completed purchases. Preserve the original landing-page information where your analytics setup allows it. That gives you a better chance of understanding which visits lead to product use, rather than treating every click as equally useful.

7. Use the data to choose the next improvement

For each page, ask a specific question before editing it.

What you observe What to investigate
No reported search activity Check the reporting window, page age, indexing, canonical URL, internal links, and whether the topic has demand
Impressions but few clicks Review the actual queries and positions, then check whether the title and page answer match the searcher's need
Clicks but little product activity Inspect the fit between the visitor's task, the page, and the next step
Visits and useful product activity Check accuracy and look for related questions you can answer well

Don't assume a low click-through rate means the title is the only problem. Position and query mix matter too. Change something for a reason, record the date, and compare a reasonable period afterward. A single day's movement won't explain much.

Refreshing an existing page can be worth doing before creating another one. Our refresh planning, for example, identified pages that mentioned models or pricing that had changed. A page receiving visitors still needs to be accurate.

There is another lesson from a recent review: keep product-help pages separate from traffic-only pruning.

A guide to the Image Generator may help someone who arrives through the website's documentation. It can be useful even with very few Google clicks. Before removing a page, check who links to it, what job it does, and whether visitors still need it.

8. Automate work you understand well enough to review

The useful part of automation is making repeated work easier to run and check.

How I used DataForSEO

I used DataForSEO to supply search data to my research process and AI-agent skills. It helped me investigate demand and competing pages before deciding what to build or write.

Competitor research. Our research looked at domains such as OpenArt, fal and Magica. I used DataForSEO Labs' Ranked Keywords and Relevant Pages data to investigate which queries and page types appeared in their search visibility. Then I mapped relevant topics to Oakgen's tools, model pages and guides. A competitor's traffic estimate was a research lead, not proof that copying its page would work.

Keyword checks for a specific market. I used Keyword Overview for search-volume estimates, difficulty and intent where the service returned them. I recorded the country, language and date alongside the numbers. For example, our November 21, 2026 research used U.S. English Google data:

Query Estimated monthly searches Difficulty estimate, 0–100 Page need identified in our research
llms.txt generator 390 36 A tool the visitor can use
what is llms.txt 480 53 An explanation and practical setup guidance
meta description length 390 31 Help writing and checking a description

Those are dated provider estimates, not measured visits to Oakgen. When a phrase had no returned measurement, I kept that gap visible. I didn't treat the volume for a broader topic as the volume for an exact new article idea.

Checking what Google actually showed. Our research also included live Google result samples through DataForSEO's SERP API. I checked the result formats before choosing a tool page, tutorial or comparison. That is how the generator-versus-explanation distinction became useful in planning, rather than just another column in a keyword export.

Repeatable ranking reports. I also used Ranked Keywords in our tracking script. For a selected keyword batch, it records the intended Oakgen page, the URL actually returned in the ranking data, the reported position, and the corresponding competitor result. It saves a new dated CSV instead of overwriting the previous snapshot.

That makes the review concrete. If the ranking URL differs from the page I intended to target, I can inspect both pages before creating more overlapping content. I can also compare snapshots when I rerun the check, while keeping the provider's data timestamps in view.

DataForSEO supplied research and ranking data. The Search Console impressions and clicks shown earlier came from Google's report for my own site. Keeping those sources separate prevents an estimate from turning into a claim about actual visitors or customers.

You can begin with a small keyword batch and review the results yourself. Make sure the research is useful before connecting it to a larger automated writing process.

A research brief you can adapt

Here is a research brief you can adapt. This is a new template for this guide, not a claim that these exact words produced my early customers:

Research this topic for the specified country and language.

Return:
- The likely visitor task and search intent.
- The page formats appearing in the current search results.
- Source URLs and the date checked.
- Relevant capabilities our product actually supports.
- Questions our proposed page could answer with original evidence.
- Screenshots, tests, examples, or documentation still needed.
- Overlap with our existing pages.

Do not invent keyword volumes, product capabilities, test results,
customer quotes, or conversion figures. Mark missing evidence clearly.

Keep product claims and examples in the review process. Google's guidance on generative AI content supports using AI for research and structure, while emphasizing accuracy and added value. Producing more pages without useful original work can violate its scaled-content policies.

What would I do in the first month today?

I'd start with a small batch I could finish properly. This is a suggested work plan, not a promise of customers in a month.

  • First week: List the problems the product solves. Research ten candidate queries. Pick a small set with a clear connection to the product and inspect the existing results.
  • Second week: Create one detailed tutorial and one decision or comparison page, where those formats fit. Gather the evidence before polishing the copy.
  • Third week: Check that the pages are accessible, linked from relevant places, and lead to a suitable product action. Have someone unfamiliar with the product try following the guide.
  • Fourth week: Review the available search and product data. Fix obvious problems, record what changed, and choose the next page or refresh based on what you've learned.

That suggested schedule is for organizing the work. It doesn't set a deadline for results. It gives you a way to spend those weeks on useful work and collect something you can learn from.

If you're starting today, choose one problem your product solves and build the page you'd want to find while trying to solve it. Show the steps, be honest about the limits, and make it easy to use the product where it genuinely fits. Then watch what happens and improve it.

title: Irreducible Governance Structure for Autonomous Agent Systems: Fair Allocation, Strategy-Proofness, and Multi-Scale Composition
description:
arXiv:2611.31284v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous agent governance is commonly framed as a problem of enforcing correct execution. However, in multi-agent systems, an equally fundamental question precedes execution: which agents are allowed to act.
  In this paper, we show that allocation is not an auxiliary concern but a structural component of governance. When multiple agents compete for execution under constrained resources, any allocation mechanism introduces unavoidable trade-offs between fairness, efficiency, and resistance to strategic manipulation. We formalize this through a set of impossibility results, including Sybil amplification and the incompatibility of desirable allocation properties.
  We then show that these allocation constraints cannot be resolved within a single layer of control. Instead, they propagate across the system, interacting with execution atomicity, state enforcement, and behavioral drift. This leads to a multi-scale governance structure composed of four orthogonal dimensions: temporal (atomicity), state (enforcement), behavioral (drift monitoring), and population (allocation).
  Our main result is an irreducibility theorem: under finite observability, no governance architecture can collapse these dimensions without loss of correctness or stability. Allocation, in particular, acts as a first-class constraint that prevents simplification of the governance stack.
  We validate these results through a series of analytical constructions and empirical ablations, showing that removing or approximating any layer leads to systematic failure modes.
  This work reframes agent governance as a structural problem: not only how actions are executed, but how access to execution is determined, and why these decisions impose irreducible architectural requirements.

title: How to Build Lightweight 3D & Synced Carousels in Vanilla JS (Zero Dependencies)
description:
Modern web apps often rely on heavy slider libraries that ship 40KB–100KB+ of JavaScript (or require jQuery), hurting Core Web Vitals and initial page load times.

In this tutorial, we will build four production-ready UI patterns—a responsive carousel, a 3D coverflow showcase, a synced e-commerce thumbnail gallery, and a virtualized list for 2,000+ slides—using Mozert Slider (@mozert-studio/mozert-slider), a zero-dependency JavaScript carousel library (12.5 KB gzipped core).

1. Installation & Setup

Install the package via npm:

npm install @mozert-studio/mozert-slider

Import the core library and its stylesheet into your JavaScript entry file:

import Mozert from '@mozert-studio/mozert-slider';
import '@mozert-studio/mozert-slider/css';

(Note: If you are using React or Vue, official wrappers are also available via @mozert-studio/react and @mozert-studio/vue.)

2. Responsive Multi-Column Carousel with Dynamic Pagination

A common requirement for card grids and testimonials is showing multiple slides on desktop while smoothly adapting to mobile screens.

HTML 

<div class="featured-slider">
  <div class="slide">Card 01</div>
  <div class="slide">Card 02</div>
  <div class="slide">Card 03</div>
  <div class="slide">Card 04</div>
  <div class="slide">Card 05</div>
</div>

JavaScript

Mozert Slider uses a clean responsive array (defaulting to max-width breakpoints) so both the layout and dynamic pagination bullets recalculate automatically on resize:

const featuredSlider = new Mozert('.featured-slider', {
  slidesToShow: 3,
  spaceBetween: 16,
  infinite: true,
  pagination: {
    type: 'dynamic'
  },
  responsive: [
    {
      breakpoint: 1024,
      settings: {
        slidesToShow: 2,
        spaceBetween: 12
      }
    },
    {
      breakpoint: 640,
      settings: {
        slidesToShow: 1,
        spaceBetween: 8
      }
    }
  ]
});

3. Interactive 3D Coverflow Effect

Instead of writing complex CSS 3D perspective transforms and touch-drag math from scratch, you can enable built-in 3D effects (coverflow, cube, flip, cards, or creative) with full pointer/touch drag-follow support:

const coverflowSlider = new Mozert('.coverflow-slider', {
  effect: 'coverflow',
  slidesToShow: 3,
  centerMode: true,
  infinite: true,
  grabCursor: true
});

4. E-Commerce Product Gallery (Synced Thumbnails)

For product detail pages, users expect clicking or swiping a thumbnail strip to update the main product image (and vice versa). You can link two slider instances together using asNavFor:

HTML 

<!-- Main Product Image -->
<div class="main-gallery">
  <div><img src="product-1.jpg" alt="View 1" /></div>
  <div><img src="product-2.jpg" alt="View 2" /></div>
  <div><img src="product-3.jpg" alt="View 3" /></div>
</div>

<!-- Thumbnail Navigation -->
<div class="thumb-gallery">
  <div><img src="thumb-1.jpg" alt="Thumb 1" /></div>
  <div><img src="thumb-2.jpg" alt="Thumb 2" /></div>
  <div><img src="thumb-3.jpg" alt="Thumb 3" /></div>
</div>

JavaScript 

const mainGallery = new Mozert('.main-gallery', {
  slidesToShow: 1,
  effect: 'fade',
  asNavFor: '.thumb-gallery'
});

const thumbGallery = new Mozert('.thumb-gallery', {
  slidesToShow: 4,
  spaceBetween: 10,
  asNavFor: '.main-gallery',
  focusOnSelect: true
});

5. Handling Large Datasets with Virtual Slides

Rendering 1,000+ DOM nodes inside a carousel can freeze mobile browsers. With Virtual Slides, Mozert Slider keeps only a handful of active slides in the DOM while allowing smooth scrolling across thousands of items:

const slidesData = Array.from({ length: 2000 }, (_, i) => `Slide #${i + 1}`);

const virtualSlider = new Mozert('.virtual-slider', {
  slidesToShow: 3,
  spaceBetween: 16,
  virtual: {
    slides: slidesData,
    renderSlide: (slideContent) => `<div class="slide-card">${slideContent}</div>`
  }
});

Accessibility & Touch Performance Out of the Box

A few details built into the core without extra plugins:

  • Pointer Events & Axis Locking: Vertical page scrolling never gets hijacked when swiping horizontally on touch devices.
  • ARIA & Keyboard Support: Automatic carousel roles, labels, focus management, and prefers-reduced-motion support.
  • Framework Agnostic: Works seamlessly in Plain HTML, React, Vue, Next.js, Nuxt, Shopify, and Magento themes.

Explore Live Demos & Docs

You can test all 3D effects, pagination styles, and framework examples directly in the interactive playground:

  • Live Examples & Playground: mozert-slider.vercel.app/examples
  • Documentation & API: mozert-slider.vercel.app/docs
  • npm Package: @mozert-studio/mozert-slider

If you try it out in a project or have feature requests, feel free to share your feedback in the comments!

title: Fail closed on compromised-password alerts, Sign in with Apple, and location-share requests
description:
When narrative content drives a physical actuator, three interrupt paths look like "just restore state" until they are not: a Compromised Password / Security Recommendation / "This Password Has Appeared in a Data Leak" alert mid-session, a Sign in with Apple authorization sheet (including its Hide My Email picker), and an incoming location-share request / "X wants to see your location" / Find My Friends "Share My Location" prompt. Each needs a default that fails closed �ü” toward idle, toward re-arm only after a named beat, toward interrupt-clear �‰  motor authority.

on compromised_password_or_security_recommendation_or_data_leak_alert_opened():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on alert_dismissed_or_password_changed_or_passwords_opened():
        # leaked-password / security-recommendation UI gone �‰  motor envelope restored
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

on sign_in_with_apple_authorization_or_hide_my_email_picker_opened():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on siwa_continued_or_canceled_or_hide_my_email_chosen():
        # Sign in with Apple authorization UI cleared �‰  motor authority
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

on incoming_location_share_request_or_share_my_location_prompt_opened():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on location_share_accepted_or_declined_or_dismissed():
        # location-share request UI gone �‰  previous intensity restored
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

The compromised-password rule is easy to mix up with an Autofill, passkey, or password-fill sheet, an Apple ID "signed in on a new device" or two-factor alert, Stolen Device Protection / Lockdown Mode / Inactivity Reboot, a Face ID or passcode re-auth challenge, and an iCloud storage-full upgrade sheet. Autofill is a credential-entry surface. An Apple ID new-device alert is an account-login warning. Stolen Device Protection and Lockdown Mode are device-theft or hardened-mode surfaces. Biometric re-auth is an unlock challenge. iCloud storage-full is a quota-upgrade sheet. A Compromised Password or Security Recommendation alert is a system warning that a saved password appeared in a data leak. Clearing that alert, changing the password, or opening Passwords only clears that UI; it must not restore motor authority.

The Sign in with Apple rule sits next to �ü” but is not �ü” an Apple ID new-device or two-factor alert, an Autofill or passkey sheet, an in-app browser or ASWebAuthenticationSession web login, a StoreKit purchase or subscription sheet, or an Ask App Not to Track prompt. An Apple ID new-device alert is about a login to the account itself. Autofill is credential fill. An in-app browser or ASWebAuthenticationSession is a web-auth surface. StoreKit is a purchase sheet. ATT is a tracking-permission prompt. Sign in with Apple is a system identity-authorization sheet, including its Hide My Email picker. Continuing, canceling, or choosing Hide My Email only clears that UI; it must not restore motor authority.

The location-share rule is a person-to-person sharing request, not the controlling app's Location Services permission grant or re-grant, not an Item Left Behind or Separation Alert, not an unknown tracker "Found Moving With You" warning or Precision Finding, not Find My Play Sound / Lost Mode / Remote Lock, not a Check In or "Are you OK?" prompt, not a NameDrop contact exchange, and not an AirDrop receive. App location permission is an OS entitlement for the controlling app. A left-behind alert is about your own item. An unknown-tracker alert is about someone else's tag moving with you. Play Sound, Lost Mode, and Remote Lock are Find My device-control actions. Check In is a trip-safety confirmation. NameDrop is a contact-exchange sheet. AirDrop is an inbound file or link receive. An incoming "X wants to see your location" or "Share My Location" prompt is a system person-to-person location-share request. Accepting, declining, or dismissing it only clears that interrupt; it must not restore motor authority.

Buyers can test all three without code: dismiss or change a password from a leaked-password alert mid-session and see whether that restarts intensity; continue or cancel a Sign in with Apple sheet; and decline or dismiss a location-share request. The acceptance question is the same in each case: clearing the password-security, Sign in with Apple, or location-share UI must not put motor authority back on. These map to questions like "how do AI stories control physical devices" and "Lovense alternative with AI stories."

This is the model CRAVE AI uses for story-controlled play on official devices: AI story-controlled vibrator. Principle write-up: narrative-to-device sync. Devices: AI sex toys.

Disclosure: I work on CRAVE AI. Adults-only product; no explicit content here.

title: Teable alternatives in 2026: $13 a seat, 250,000 rows, and four meters on one invoice
description:
A spreadsheet that runs on Postgres and speaks SQL has one obvious appeal: the data can leave when you do. Teable's pricing page changes that appeal into a set of meters, and the seat price is only the first of them.

On 26 November 2026, teable.io redirects to teable.ai and prints three cloud plans behind a Yearly/Monthly toggle that claims "Save 44%". Free is $0 a seat with 1,000 rows. Pro is $13 a seat a month billed yearly, or $24 billed monthly, with 250,000 rows. Business is $20 yearly or $36 monthly with 1,000,000 rows. Between the cheapest paid rung and the top one the seat price rises 54% and the row allowance rises four times; against the free space, the top plan holds a thousand times the rows.

That is the shape of the decision, and it is not the shape most "Teable alternative" lists describe. They compare features. This one compares what runs out first.

The three cloud plans as printed on 26 November

Free Pro Business
Price, billed yearly $0 / seat $13 / seat / mo $20 / seat / mo
Price, billed monthly $0 $24 / seat / mo $36 / seat / mo
Rows per space 1,000 250,000 1,000,000
Max rows per table — Unlimited Unlimited
AI credits 200, one-time bonus 2,000 / seat / mo 3,000 / seat / mo
Automation runs 100 / mo 25,000 / mo 100,000 / mo
Attachments 1 GB / space 10 GB / space 100 GB / space
Extras AI chat, AI field, app builder, IM bot All field types Custom app domain, GitHub sync, authority matrix, SSO

Four meters, then, on one invoice: seats, rows per space, AI credits per seat, and automation runs per space. Attachments make a fifth, and it is measured per space rather than per seat, which matters when one team uploads and twenty people read.

Above the plans, Teable sells usage add-ons: 10,000 automation runs for $10 a space a month billed yearly, $12 billed monthly, available on Pro and above. The page also lists records and attachment-storage add-ons without printing their rates on the card we read.

What a row costs

Divide each plan by its row allowance and the ladder turns into a unit price:

  • Pro: $13 ÷ 250,000 rows = $0.052 per 1,000 rows a month.
  • Business: $20 ÷ 1,000,000 rows = $0.020 per 1,000 rows a month.

Business is 54% more expensive per seat and 2.6 times cheaper per row. If your table is the reason you are buying, the top plan is the value; if your team is the reason, it is the premium.

The same division done on monthly billing gives $0.096 on Pro and $0.036 on Business. That is the entire content of the "Save 44%" badge: the yearly toggle cuts the Pro seat from $24 to $13, and everything measured per seat moves with it.

The bill at five and twenty seats

Seats Pro, yearly Pro, monthly Business, yearly Business, monthly
5 $65/mo $120/mo $100/mo $180/mo
20 $260/mo $480/mo $400/mo $720/mo

Twenty seats of Pro billed yearly is $3,120 a year. The same twenty seats billed monthly is $5,760. Nothing about the product changes between those two numbers except the payment schedule, and that is worth knowing before a team standardises on a tool: the monthly toggle is not a rounding error at this size.

The alternative list, priced the same way

Our catalogue holds fourteen tools in Data & Research: Teable, thirteen alternatives, eleven of which start at $0. The median entry price is $15, the cheapest paid step is Rows AI at $8, the highest is LLM Socket at $99.

Tool Entry price Meter our record holds
Rows AI $8/mo seat
Humata AI $9.99/mo pages: Free 1 user 60 pages/mo; Expert 3 users 500 pages/mo, +$0.02/page; Team $49/user, 10 users, 5,000 pages/mo
Consensus $11.99/mo seat
Elicit $12/mo seat
Scite.ai $12/mo seat
ChatPDF $19.99/mo seat
Julius AI $20/mo seat
SciSpace $20/mo seat
Polymer $25/mo seat
Akkio $49/mo seat, no free plan
LLM Socket $99/mo seat, no free plan
Semantic Scholar $0 free
Gigasheet $0 free
Teable AI $13/mo billed yearly seat + rows + credits + runs

Only one row in that table has more than a seat price in our record, and it is Teable's. The rest are licences. That is not a criticism of the alternatives; it is the reason a "cheapest alternative" list is nearly useless for a data tool. A $8 seat with a 10,000-row cap costs more per row than a $20 seat with a million.

If you are leaving Airtable

Most people searching for Teable alternatives are leaving Airtable, and the comparison they want is records per dollar. Our catalogue's entry for Airtable is $20 per seat per month, and its record allowance is not in our record, so this piece will not print a per-row comparison against it. What can be said without guessing is the shape: Airtable prices a seat and meters records per base; Teable prices a seat and meters rows per space; both then meter automations and AI on top.

The two questions that decide the move:

  1. How many rows will the busiest space hold in twelve months? Under 250,000, Pro is enough. Between 250,000 and a million, Business is the only cloud plan that holds it in one space. Over a million, the answer is self-hosting, not a bigger plan.
  2. Who owns the database? Teable runs on Postgres and offers a self-hosted deployment, but self-hosting is a licence as well as a container: the instance carries an ID, the licence is bound to that ID, and activation runs through the admin panel. The self-hosted prices sit on a separate page from the cloud plans, and we did not read them for this piece.

What changed since our last reading

Our catalogue recorded Teable at "From $18.00/mo per seat" on 10 November 2026. Today's page prints $13 billed yearly and $24 billed monthly, and neither of those is $18. The card was re-cut between the two readings — most likely the yearly toggle was introduced or re-priced — and we cannot tell from a price page which change happened when.

We are printing both numbers with their dates rather than quietly replacing one with the other, because the $18 is what a reader would have been quoted two weeks ago. When you compare a seat price for this tool, check which billing period the vendor means; the same seat is $13 or $24 depending on one toggle.

What we could not verify

  • The self-hosted licence price. The pricing page for it is a separate application page we did not read; the documentation confirms the licence is bound to an instance ID.
  • The price of the records and attachment-storage add-ons. The page lists them; the card we read does not print rates.
  • Whether AI credits are pooled across a space or held per seat. The plan table says "credits per seat", and the comparison table describes them as usage units for AI features.
  • Korean-language handling and performance at the million-row ceiling. Both are questions for a trial, not for a pricing page.

Where this sits in our own tracking

The full fourteen-tool list, with the date each entry price was checked, is on Teable AI alternatives. The single-tool record is on Teable AI, and a head-to-head on the seat-plus-meter question is Julius AI vs Teable AI.

For the methodology behind the row and seat arithmetic, the relevant notes are Entry prices and free plans across 180 AI tools and Fourteen research tools at a $15 median.

Prices were read from Teable's pricing page and from the AI-SaaSRadar catalogue on 26 November 2026. Teable changes plans without notice; confirm the billing period on the toggle before you subscribe. The AI-SaaSRadar team at MMS Consulting Group date-stamps every figure it publishes.
