title: What staging validation teaches us about production debugging
description:
The moment after an alert

Imagine a customer reports a request that failed once and cannot be reproduced locally. A production observability change deserves its own staging test because it touches request handling and data retention. Without a useful record, the team is left comparing assumptions.

Reconstruct before changing code

A representative test should cover middleware placement, route capture, redaction, persistence, access, and restart behavior. Begin with the route and time window, correlate nearby application messages, and compare status and duration. Keep a clear distinction between facts in the record and hypotheses about the cause.

Turn evidence into a fix

Write a short acceptance checklist for the routes that matter and run it after configuration or version changes. Build the smallest safe reproduction from sanitized inputs, add a regression check, and verify the behavior after the change.

Improve the next response

Avoid enabling broad payload inspection in production until the expected data and access controls are understood. Close the incident by noting what evidence was missing and whether the telemetry policy should change. The useful outcome is a repeatable debugging path, not a bigger pile of logs.

Learn more: TracerNest

title: GaokaoMathGen: Chinese Gaokao Mathematics Finale Problem Generation Controlled by Latent Reasoning Structures
description:
arXiv:2611.31823v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generating Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problems requires controlling not only the included skills, but also the underlying mathematical kernel and solution path. Existing LLM-based methods mainly rely on surface-level specifications, while the realized difficulty of generated problems cannot be determined directly from prompted targets. Therefore, we propose GaokaoMathGen, a framework for Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problem generation controlled by latent reasoning structures. It extracts standardized latent reasoning structures from seed problems and performs constrained synthesis using skills, methods, a core identity, and a pivot step as structural controls. We further estimate realized difficulty through logical-quality filtering, fixed-solver decoding effort, structural features, and solver-output search signals. Experiments show that semantic normalization improves cross-annotator comparability and that 78.0% of 609 scored candidates pass the logical-quality filter. In a teacher audit of the 60 highest-effort candidates, all were judged to reach finale or penultimate problem difficulty, and only one exhibited a severe logical issue. These results support latent reasoning structures as effective control signals for generating high-difficulty mathematical problems.

title: Feature-Based Explainability of Transformer Scoring Models: A Fidelity-First Framework for Automated Writing Assessment
description:
arXiv:2611.33175v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Transformer-based automated writing scoring models can achieve strong agreement with human scores while providing limited transparency into the response characteristics associated with their predictions. This study evaluated a feature-based post-hoc explanation approach in which explanatory fidelity was established before feature importance was interpreted. English Language Arts responses from three writing prompts in Grades 6 and 8 were analyzed, with about 12,700 responses per prompt and separate DeBERTa-v3-base research models for Expression and Conventions. Each response was represented by 61 interpretable linguistic and writing-quality features. Four approaches - theory-driven composites, hierarchical feature groupings, exploratory factor analysis, and Random Forest surrogates - were compared in their ability to reproduce DeBERTa predictions. Random Forest surrogates produced the largest observed R2 values across all six prompt-by-trait conditions, with held-out R2 values from .81 to .95. SHAP analyses showed substantial overlap in high-importance features across traits, with 75% to 90% of the top 20 features shared. Trait differentiation occurred mainly through relative feature weighting: Expression showed greater importance for lexical and conceptual indicators, whereas Conventions showed greater importance for sentence-level and syntactic-control indicators. Under researcher-defined mappings, rubric correspondence was 90%-95% for Expression and 12%-18% for Conventions. These percentages are descriptive and conditional on the mappings and available linguistic features. The findings support a fidelity-first framework for examining apparent scoring priorities while distinguishing post-hoc evidence about model behavior from direct explanation of transformer internals.

title: Quizzes and vocabulary lists made from one text
description:

A teacher who pastes a reading passage into a model and asks for ten quiz questions gets them back in seconds. The trouble begins at marking time. One answer appears nowhere in the passage, another is a loose paraphrase that nobody can point to, and a third is a fact the learner could only know from outside the text. Word lists go wrong in a parallel way: a "dictionary form" that no dictionary holds, a translation taken from the wrong sense, an example sentence the passage never contained. Both problems have one cure. Everything the model returns must point at a place in the passage, and a short program, not a tired person, should be able to confirm that the place exists. title: Game Evidence: 6 Presigned Browser Rules for Direct Upload to Private User Document Storage
description:
A browser upload becomes a security boundary the moment game evidence contains an account name, a moderation report, or a tournament document. Short answer: let the browser send bytes straight to private object storage with a short-lived, narrowly scoped presigned URL, but let the application choose the object key, record the expected metadata, and authorize every later download.

Do not treat a successful upload as a completed workflow. The storage write and the application state change are separate operations, and retries can duplicate one without repeating the other.

I've been paged by missed scheduled work and duplicate queue delivery. That experience leaves one useful reflex here: make completion idempotent, then make the reconciler boring. A client can close its tab after storage accepts the last byte but before it tells the application. It can also repeat the completion request after a timeout. Both outcomes are normal distributed-system states, not exceptional stories.

Can browser uploads preserve privacy for PDF and DOCX user documents?

Split the path into a control plane and a data plane. The application authenticates the player or tournament operator, decides whether the upload is allowed, selects an opaque object key, records an expected media type and maximum size, and returns a time-limited upload capability. The browser uses that capability to transfer the file directly. The application never proxies the body.

That division keeps large files away from application workers without giving the browser general storage credentials. It also preserves the important ownership decision: a user may request a destination, but cannot choose another tenant's prefix or turn a filename such as ../../appeals/admin.pdf into an authorization decision. The original filename is display metadata. It is not an object key.

Six controls belong in the issue-and-complete flow:

  1. Authenticate before issuing an upload capability.
  2. Generate the object key on the server and bind it to the authenticated owner.
  3. Constrain the accepted size and media type in both application policy and the signed request where the storage interface permits it.
  4. Use a short expiry and one logical upload session per intended object.
  5. Keep the bucket private; possession of an object name must not grant a read.
  6. Complete idempotently, then verify stored metadata before marking the document available.

File extensions are weak evidence. A .pdf name and a browser-supplied content type can help reject obvious mistakes, but neither proves that the bytes are safe. If documents feed a moderation console, add an asynchronous inspection state such as pending_scan; only a successful policy check should move the record to available. Until then, download authorization returns no link.

Cost follows the retry boundary

The awkward window starts after object storage acknowledges the write and ends when the application commits its document record. A direct upload makes that window visible. Hiding it behind an application proxy doesn't remove it; it only moves the same state transition into a longer-running request.

Use a small state machine: issued, uploaded, pending_scan, available, rejected, and expired. Store the upload ID, owner ID, server-generated key, declared byte count, media type, creation time, and a completion idempotency key. A completion request for an already completed upload should return the existing document result. A request whose object metadata differs from the recorded declaration should fail closed, for example with 409 Conflict; a conditional state write can use 412 Precondition Failed when another worker won the transition.

The long-tail case matters. Suppose a 2 GB replay archive finishes, the browser loses its connection before receiving the application's completion response, and a queue consumer receives the same completion message twice. The first consumer verifies metadata and advances the state. The second reads that terminal state and returns success without creating another document or scheduling another scan. If no completion message arrives, a scheduled reconciler lists old issued sessions, checks the exact server-generated key, and either advances a matching object or expires the session. The reconciler must use bounded batches and the same idempotent transition as the request path, because a repair job that invents a second write path will eventually produce a second class of incident.

Quiet is good.

The preventative Go path below keeps product-specific signing behind an interface. The handler owns policy; an adapter owns the storage service's signing format. The example numbers are local policy choices, not universal limits.

package upload

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/rand"
    "encoding/hex"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "path/filepath"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const maxDocumentBytes int64 = 25 << 20

var allowedTypes = map[string]bool{
    "application/pdf": true,
    "application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document": true,
}

type Signer interface {
    SignUpload(ctx context.Context, key, mediaType string, maxBytes int64, expiresAt time.Time) (string, error)
}

type Sessions interface {
    Create(ctx context.Context, session Session) error
}

type Session struct {
    ID          string
    OwnerID     string
    ObjectKey   string
    MediaType   string
    MaxBytes    int64
    OriginalName string
    State       string
    ExpiresAt   time.Time
}

type Request struct {
    OwnerID     string
    Filename    string
    MediaType   string
    Size        int64
}

type Response struct {
    UploadID string
    URL      string
    Expires  time.Time
}

func Issue(ctx context.Context, signer Signer, sessions Sessions, now time.Time, req Request) (Response, error) {
    if req.OwnerID == "" || !allowedTypes[req.MediaType] {
        return Response{}, errors.New("upload is not permitted")
    }
    if req.Size <= 0 || req.Size > maxDocumentBytes {
        return Response{}, fmt.Errorf("size must be between 1 and %d bytes", maxDocumentBytes)
    }

    id, err := randomID()
    if err != nil {
        return Response{}, err
    }
    ext := strings.ToLower(filepath.Ext(req.Filename))
    if ext != ".pdf" && ext != ".docx" {
        return Response{}, errors.New("unsupported filename extension")
    }

    expires := now.Add(15 * time.Minute)
    key := "evidence/" + req.OwnerID + "/" + id
    session := Session{
        ID: id, OwnerID: req.OwnerID, ObjectKey: key,
        MediaType: req.MediaType, MaxBytes: req.Size,
        OriginalName: filepath.Base(req.Filename), State: "issued", ExpiresAt: expires,
    }
    if err := sessions.Create(ctx, session); err != nil {
        return Response{}, err
    }
    url, err := signer.SignUpload(ctx, key, req.MediaType, req.Size, expires)
    if err != nil {
        return Response{}, err
    }
    return Response{UploadID: id, URL: url, Expires: expires}, nil
}

func randomID() (string, error) {
    b := make([]byte, 16)
    if _, err := rand.Read(b); err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    return hex.EncodeToString(b), nil
}

In production, create the session and capability in an order your cleanup process understands. If signing fails after the session is stored, the session can expire without exposing an object. If the database write fails first, issue no capability. Don't log the returned URL: while it remains valid, it is a credential.

Evaluate single-request and multipart recovery with failure budgets

A single presigned upload is the simplest option when the file fits comfortably inside one request and a retry from byte zero is acceptable. Multipart transfer is for a different operational envelope: large files, unstable client connections, or retry costs high enough that resending completed parts hurts users. It adds state. The application must track a multipart upload identifier, constrain part ownership, list or record completed parts, complete exactly once, and abort abandoned sessions.

Path Operational advantage Main catch Prefer it when
Application proxy One place for synchronous inspection and policy App workers carry every byte and long requests consume capacity Bytes must be inspected before they may enter storage
Direct single request Few states and a small client A failed request restarts from byte zero Documents are bounded and connections are dependable
Direct multipart Completed parts can survive a retry More session, cleanup, and completion state Large files or unreliable networks make full retries unacceptable

Multipart completion deserves the same idempotency rule as document completion. Record the expected upload identifier and object key before issuing part capabilities. Accept part numbers only inside the session's declared range. On completion, verify the returned part set rather than trusting an arbitrary list from the browser. Abort abandoned multipart sessions on a schedule, but never infer ownership from a client-supplied key.

I'm not sure where the right multipart threshold sits for every game or network; your mileage may vary. Resolve it with the actual file-size distribution, mobile failure rate, retry bytes, and support burden. A threshold copied from another system is just folklore.

Implement access control beyond the initial write

Private storage is necessary, but it is not the complete policy. A download endpoint should authenticate the requester, load the document record by an opaque application ID, check tenant and role policy, confirm that the state is available, and only then issue a short-lived read capability for the recorded object key. Never accept a raw object key from a query string and sign it on demand.

Keep audit events around the decisions: upload capability issued, upload completed, inspection result recorded, download authorized, and document deleted. Avoid recording capability URLs or document contents. Useful operational dimensions include state-transition latency, expired-session count, multipart abort count, completion conflicts, inspection backlog age, and denied download count. Alert on symptoms that require action, especially a growing oldest-item age; a raw count often rises simply because traffic rose.

Cross-origin policy is another authorization layer, not the primary one. Permit only the application origins and methods needed by the browser flow, and test the browser's preflight behavior before deployment. A permissive origin rule does not make a leaked capability broader than its signature, but it removes a useful constraint and makes mistakes harder to spot.

There is also a compliance boundary. A storage architecture diagram does not establish regulatory authorization. If a procurement program requires FedRAMP, verify the relevant service, deployment, data flow, and authorization status through the program's official materials; do not infer compliance from API compatibility.

Rollout criteria for keeping an application proxy

Direct-to-storage upload is not suitable when policy requires synchronous inspection before any byte may land in object storage, when clients cannot perform the required signed request, or when every upload must be transformed as part of a single application transaction. In those cases, stick with a bounded proxy or a dedicated ingestion service and pay the capacity cost deliberately.

The catch with presigned access is that the URL is a temporary bearer capability. Keep its scope narrow and expiry short, avoid logs and analytics fields that capture it, and reauthorize downloads rather than handing out permanent links. For highly sensitive evidence, a one-time application-mediated download can be the clearer control even though it adds load.

For the common gaming evidence path, the decision rule is plain: use direct single-request upload for bounded PDF and DOCX documents; graduate large replay or media payloads to multipart only after measurements justify the extra states; retain application proxies where pre-storage inspection is mandatory. In every path, the database record is the authorization source, the storage key is server-generated, and duplicate completion is harmless.

Sources

  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • https://www.fedramp.gov/

title: Five AI Assistants Compared — Only With Dated, Public Figures
description:
I keep being asked how ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok and DeepSeek compare. I look for a simple table as much as anyone. The honest version is less tidy: the companies do not publish the same numbers, on the same definitions, at the same time.

So this is not a ranking. It is a dated collection of facts I could verify in public sources, plus a clear note about what I could not verify. Where I have no reliable official figure, I leave the cell empty instead of filling it with a guess.

Why the numbers are hard to compare

"Users" can mean weekly or monthly, a single app or a whole family of products, a person who opened the app once or a paying account. OpenAI has talked about weekly users. Google has talked about monthly users of the Gemini app, not of every Gemini feature inside Search or Android. Anthropic, xAI and DeepSeek have not, as far as I can find, published a comparable official consumer user count I would put next to those figures.

Treat the table as a set of labelled measurements, not as a podium.

The table, with dates

Assistant Public start (documented) Official-scale user figure I could cite Other public fact What I am not claiming
ChatGPT (OpenAI) 30 November 2022, as a free research preview built on the GPT-3.5 series On 29 September 2026, OpenAI's DevDay recap referred to "our collective 1.2B weekly users." The Verge reported the same day that OpenAI said ChatGPT had 1.2 billion weekly users. I am quoting both, because the word "collective" in the recap is not defined on that page. ChatGPT was the first of these five to reach a mass consumer audience. I am not treating "collective" and "ChatGPT only" as proven to be the same number.
Claude (Anthropic) 14 March 2023, after a closed alpha with partners No comparable official consumer user count that I can cite Anthropic was founded in 2021 by former OpenAI employees, including Dario Amodei (CEO) and Daniela Amodei (president). I will not invent a monthly or weekly user number for Claude.
Gemini (Google) Early access to Bard in March 2023; the Gemini brand was unified in February 2024 On 11 August 2026, Google wrote that the Gemini app had surpassed 1 billion monthly users. That figure is about the app, not about every place Gemini appears in Search or other Google products. Google described it as the fastest-growing product in its history, and the 14th Google product to pass a billion users. A monthly app user is not comparable, one-for-one, with a weekly user somewhere else.
Grok (xAI) Announced 3 November 2023; early access followed for X subscribers No comparable official user count that I can cite Reuters reported on 6 January 2026 that xAI had raised $20 billion in a Series E round. That is a funding fact, not a user count. A funding round is not a measure of how many people use the assistant.
DeepSeek The company was founded in 2023. The New York Times and TechCrunch covered the free chatbot app that appeared on 10 January 2025 and then spread quickly. No official current user count or official valuation I am willing to present as comparable DeepSeek drew a lot of attention in January 2025 for releasing capable models at a low price point. That moment is well documented. Later user figures in secondary blogs are inconsistent, so I am leaving them out. I will not recycle an unsourced download or valuation number.

Two other measurements people mix in

User counts are only one lens, and they favour products that sit in a consumer app.

Consumer popularity. In June 2026, TechCrunch wrote that Claude was gaining among paying consumers, and that ChatGPT was still far and away the most popular AI with consumers, with Sensor Tower data showing Claude still a long way behind. That is a consumer-market statement, dated June 2026.

Enterprise API spend. Menlo Ventures' "2026: The State of Enterprise AI" report, published 3 November 2026, estimated that Anthropic had 55 percent of enterprise LLM API spend, OpenAI 31 percent, and Google 9 percent, based on a survey of nearly 400 U.S. enterprise decision-makers, fielded in September 2026. Anthropic and OpenAI together were 86 percent, up from 67 percent a year earlier. Two caveats belong next to that sentence: the figure is spend, not seat count, and Menlo lists Anthropic as a portfolio company.

If someone tells you "Claude overtook ChatGPT," ask "on which measure, and in which month?" Both of the measurements above can be true at the same time.

What I do with a table like this

I use it to stop arguments that cannot be settled with the public record.

  • If you need the product most people have already heard of, ChatGPT is still the one with the large, officially discussed consumer reach.
  • If you care about a Google account you already have, Gemini's official app figure is large, and it is a monthly figure for the app, not a claim about every Google surface.
  • If you care about enterprise API budgets, Menlo's 2026 survey is one data point, with the conflicts of interest stated.
  • If you care about Grok or DeepSeek, I would look at the product and the licence in front of you, not at a fake user column.

I would not pick a daily coding assistant from this table alone. I wrote a separate piece about how ChatGPT and Claude feel on development tasks. That is a different question, and it should stay a different question.

A habit worth keeping

When a chart on social media shows five logos and one winner, look for three things: the date, the exact wording of the metric, and a link to a primary source. If any of those is missing, treat the chart as decoration.

The five assistants in this article are real products with real differences. The public numbers we have about them are just not the same kind of number. It is better to say that than to invent a ranking.

I'm Saulius, an independent full-stack, automation and electronics developer in Kaunas, Lithuania. You can also find me on Dev.to and LinkedIn.

title: PRIOR: Pre-Call Reasoning in SFT and Its Influence on Tool-Use Retention under RL
description:
arXiv:2611.33648v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool use learned during supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is not always retained during reinforcement learning (RL). We study how properties of SFT data may affect this retention by constructing Low, Medium, and High SFT datasets with approximately matched token budgets but different tool-call depths. Under the same RL recipe, the three initializations reach similar RL training accuracy yet exhibit markedly different tool-use dynamics: tool initiation increases in Low, declines in Medium, and collapses in High. We observe that these datasets also differ substantially in the amount of reasoning preceding each tool call. In particular, High trajectories contain considerably less pre-call reasoning, motivating the hypothesis that pre-call reasoning may affect how well tool use is calibrated and, consequently, whether the corresponding behaviors are retained during RL. An idealized theoretical analysis provides a selective-retention view of this process: advantages in overall and tool-conditioned accuracy can be preserved under outcome-only optimization, while tool initiation increases only when tool-using trajectories are more successful than the tool-free alternative. Guided by this analysis, we rank the original High trajectories by average pre-call reasoning length and retain the highest-ranked examples while approximately matching cumulative SFT token exposure. This simple filtering strategy improves post-RL accuracy and tool-conditioned final-answer success without consistently increasing tool initiation across multiple benchmarks. These results suggest that pre-call reasoning is a useful dimension of SFT supervision for understanding and improving tool-use retention under downstream RL.

title: Measuring and Predicting Image-Token Repair Boundaries in Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.33388v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Degraded images make vision-language models answer wrongly. Using synthetic paired blur, noise, and low light, we trace which clean image states can still repair those answers from the vision encoder through the language model. In four encoder models, 12 to 23 ranked tokens recover half of the full-patch effect, whereas random orders require four to fifteen times as many; encoder-free Gemma needs 22.2 versus 53.1. Full-block repair expires at a model-specific language-model crossing. The matched reverse-direction intervention is algebraically identical to text-token restoration, so its gap from image restoration measures a redundancy band rather than an independent predictor. A clean-image gray-ablation crossing independently predicts held-out repair with 1.53-layer error, against 3.65 for shared depth. Gemma MMBench has the only large attention-to-repair point gap; Gemma GQA does not. Restormer provides a non-oracle consistency check on two models.

title: SMM panel API'lerine bağlanmadan önce: /api/v2 standardı, CORS ve anahtarı sunucuya hiç göndermemek
description:
SMM panelleri, yani takipçi, beğeni ve izlenmeyi binlik fiyatla satan toptan mağazalar, neredeyse hep aynı API'yi kullanır. Takip ettiğimiz panellerin 144'ü herkese açık bir sipariş API'si yayımlıyor ve bunların çoğu aynı panel yazılımlarının ortak sözleşmesini konuşuyor.

Bu yazıda o sözleşmeyi, tarayıcıdan denemenin neden çoğu zaman başarısız olduğunu ve bir test aracını kullanıcının API anahtarına hiç dokunmadan nasıl kurduğumuzu anlatıyorum.

Ortak sözleşme

Yaygın panel yazılımları API'yi /api/v2 yolunda açar. Ama bu evrensel değil: yolu her zaman panelin kendi API sayfasından okuyun, tahmin etmeyin.

İstek her zaman aynı biçimde: POST, gövde application/x-www-form-urlencoded, içinde key ve action.

curl -s -X POST 'https://panel-adresi.example/api/v2' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
  --data 'key=API_ANAHTARINIZ&action=services'

Dört eylem işin büyük kısmını görür:

action Ne yapar Para harcar mı
services Kataloğu listeler: servis numarası, ad, kategori, binlik fiyat, alt ve üst miktar Hayır
balance Hesap bakiyesini okur Hayır
status Bir siparişin durumuna bakar Hayır
add Sipariş verir Evet

Entegrasyondan önce ilk üçüyle başlayın. add gerçek bakiyeden düşer.

Tarayıcıdan denemek neden çoğu zaman olmaz

Bir paneli tarayıcıdan, fetch ile denemek istediğinizde isteğin büyük ihtimalle CORS duvarına çarptığını görürsünüz. Panellerin çoğu başka bir kökenden gelen isteğe izin veren Access-Control-Allow-Origin başlığını göndermiyor. Bu bir hata değil: API'ler sunucudan sunucuya kullanılmak üzere kurulmuş.

Kolay çözüm, isteği kendi sunucunuzdan geçiren bir proxy yazmak. Ama o zaman kullanıcının API anahtarı, yani parasına erişen kimlik bilgisi, sizin sunucunuzdan geçer ve sizin loglarınıza düşebilir.

Anahtarı hiç görmeyen bir test aracı

Panel API test aracımızı tam tersini seçerek kurduk:

  • İstek doğrudan kullanıcının tarayıcısından panele gider. Arkada bir proxy rotası yok, hiçbir şey depolamaya yazılmıyor, hiçbir şey loglanmıyor. Tarayıcının ağ panelini açtığınızda tek bir istek görürsünüz: panelin alan adına.
  • Panel CORS'u reddederse araç bunu sessizce bir sunucu üzerinden çözmeye çalışmaz; size aynı isteğin curl karşılığını verir.
  • curl komutunda anahtar bilerek yer tutucu olarak yazılır. Gerçek anahtarı terminalde yerine koyarsınız, böylece ekran görüntüsüne düşmez.

Bedeli açık: panellerin çoğunda "tarayıcıdan gönder" düğmesi CORS hatasıyla döner ve işi curl ile bitirirsiniz. Karşılığında bir kimlik bilgisinin bizim tarafımızda hiç bulunmadığını, kodu okumadan da ağ panelinden doğrulayabilirsiniz.

Hangi paneli bağlamalı?

Bir entegrasyon için en önemli ölçü özellik listesi değil, uç noktanın ayakta olması: çalışmayan bir API'nin hiçbir özelliği yoktur. Bu yüzden araç sayfasında, son 30 günün erişilebilirlik ölçümlerine göre sıralı bir liste var; her satırda 30 günlük uptime, medyan yanıt süresi ve güven puanı yazıyor.

Bağlantılar

  • Panel API test aracı: panelcompare.com/tr/tools/panel-api-tester
  • API sunan paneller: panelcompare.com/tr/best/smm-panel-with-api
  • Günlük fiyat endeksi: panelcompare.com/tr/price-index
  • Bizim kendi API'miz (anahtarsız, CORS açık): panelcompare.com/api-docs

Açıklama: PanelCompare'i ben yürütüyorum. Sitede etiketli bir sponsor alanı ve ortaklık linkleri var; ikisi de fiyat ve erişilebilirlik ölçümlerini değiştirmiyor.

description:
Agent Platform Workbench

AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Feature

You can now tune SQL queries using AI. Available starting with version 1.6.2 of the google_ml_integration extension, the ai.tune_sql function uses an LLM along with query execution plans, schemas, and runtime stats to recommend query optimizations. The function identifies performance bottlenecks and provides recommendations for query rewrites, indexes, statistics collection, Grand Unified Configuration (GUC) flags, and table analyze and vacuum operations. This feature is in Preview.

For more information, see Tune SQL queries using AI and Database advisor flags.

Apigee X

Announcement

On November 2, 2026, we released an updated version of Apigee.

Note: Rollouts of this release began today and may take four or more business days to be completed across all Google Cloud zones. Your instances may not have the features and fixes available until the rollout is complete.

Feature

EKM health monitoring

You can now monitor EKM health and configure alerts for EKM-related issues using Cloud Logging. For more information, see EKM health monitoring.

App Engine flexible environment Python

Feature

Support for the Python 3.15 runtime is in Preview.

App Engine standard environment Python

Feature

Support for the Python 3.15 runtime is in Preview.

BigQuery

Feature

Lakehouse caching for cross-cloud data access is generally available (GA). Cross-cloud caching is disabled by default. You can opt in to caching on a Lakehouse federated catalog or a BigQuery cross-cloud connection to cache remote files in your Google Cloud region. This helps reduce cross-cloud egress costs and accelerate subsequent queries.

For more information, see About cross-cloud data access and Query remote data.

Feature

Lakehouse supports the following remote catalog providers for cross-cloud data access. This feature is generally available (GA).

  • Databricks Unity Catalog on Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud
  • AWS Glue Data Catalog on AWS
  • Snowflake Horizon Catalog on AWS, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud
  • Workday Data Lake on AWS or Google Cloud

This feature lets you configure federated catalog endpoints to synchronize catalog metadata and query Apache Iceberg tables in remote catalogs directly from Google Cloud using BigQuery, Managed Service for Apache Spark, and Apache Spark without migrating data or building complex ETL pipelines. You can route background metadata refresh and queries over the public internet or privately over Cross-Cloud Interconnect, and protect cross-cloud data access with VPC Service Controls service perimeters. For Databricks Unity Catalog, you can also use user identity federation to propagate end-user identities on queries for permission enforcement and audit logging.

For more information, see About cross-cloud data access, Query remote data, and Use VPC Service Controls with federated catalog endpoints.

Feature

You can now monitor the performance, adoption, latency, and costs of your data agents and their conversations by using Google Cloud Observability in BigQuery. This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

You can use the AI.PARSE_DOCUMENT function to extract layout elements such as titles, headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, and images by using the Document AI layout parser to convert unstructured documents into structured JSON data.

This function is generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now use BigQuery change history and continuous queries for Apache Iceberg managed tables in Lakehouse.

You can use the APPENDS table-valued function (TVF) to track rows appended to Apache Iceberg managed tables over a specified time range, and use BigQuery continuous queries to read incoming data from and write output rows to Apache Iceberg managed tables.

This feature is generally available (GA).

For more information, see Work with change history and Introduction to continuous queries.

Feature

The SECURE_CONTEXT function is now available in Preview. SECURE_CONTEXT returns the value of a request-scoped secure context parameter provided at query runtime, allowing logical views to dynamically filter and evaluate data based on context variables such as user attributes, department IDs, or tenant identifiers.

Feature

The Data Engineering Agent now supports BigQuery AI, ML, and object functions and statements in generated Dataform SQLX pipelines and agent instruction files.

This feature is generally available (GA).

Bigtable

Libraries

Node.js

7.5.1 (2026-10-28)

Bug Fixes
  • bigtable: Use ReadonlyMap for EncodedKeyMap implements clause (#9709) (f803bff)

Cloud Asset Inventory

Feature

The following resource type is publicly available through the ExportAssets, ListAssets, BatchGetAssetsHistory, QueryAssets, Feed, SearchAllResources, and SearchAllIamPolicies APIs.

  • Cloud Scheduler
    • cloudscheduler.googleapis.com/Job

Cloud Load Balancing

Feature

Distributed tracing with Cloud Trace is available in Preview for Global external Application Load Balancers, Regional external Application Load Balancers, Regional internal Application Load Balancers, and Cross-region internal Application Load Balancers. Attach a telemetry policy to a load balancer's forwarding rule to generate trace spans that conform to W3C Trace Context and OpenTelemetry, and get end-to-end visibility into requests from clients through the load balancer to your backends. For more information, see Distributed tracing overview.

Feature

For mutual TLS (mTLS) on Application Load Balancers, frontend mTLS validation relaxations are generally available.

The ALLOW_VALIDATION_RELAXATIONS client validation mode on the Client Authentication (ServerTlsPolicy) resource allows you to configure specific X.509 certificate validation exceptions to standard client certificate validation rules. This simplifies migrations of legacy workloads while maintaining an active security posture.

This mode supports the following client certificate validation relaxation parameters:

  • ALLOW_MISSING_EKU: Bypasses Extended Key Usage validation if the EKU extension is absent in the client certificate.

  • ALLOW_SHA1_HASHING: Permits client certificates signed with the legacy SHA-1 algorithm.

  • ALLOW_EXPIRED_LEAF_CERTIFICATE: Evaluates expired leaf certificates by validating them as of 1 second prior to their actual expiration time.

This feature is available for all Application Load Balancer types.

For more information, see Client validation modes.

Cloud NGFW

Feature

Advanced malware sandbox (WildFire) integrates dynamic machine learning (ML) and cloud-based behavioral sandboxing to perform deep inspection of network-routed file transfers and block zero-day malware before it reaches your workloads. Advanced malware sandbox is available in the Cloud Next Generation Firewall Enterprise tier. For more information, see Advanced malware sandbox overview and Configure Advanced malware sandbox in your network.

This feature is available in General Availability.

title: LGCount: Layout-Guided Diffusion for Zero-Shot Object Counting
description:
arXiv:2611.33344v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Class-agnostic counting requires the user to specify what to count, usually with a class name or a few annotated boxes. We propose a richer text-based specification: a structured layout that names the target, the region that holds it, the distractors to ignore. A prompt upsampler writes this layout from the image and the requested category alone, and an image-editing diffusion model, adapted into a single-step counter, turns it into a density map. Because counting datasets pair each image with a single valid density map, a counter trained on it learns to ignore the layout. We therefore train on synthetic counterfactuals in which one image admits several valid density maps, so that the layout cannot be ignored. On FSC-147 we improve on the previous zero-shot state of the art and we set the best reported result on LOOKALIKES while being told the least about each image. A single photograph can be counted by category, by region, or by granularity without retraining.
