title: Spring Security Part 2: AuthenticationManager and BCrypt
description:
In Part 1, we understood why Spring Security uses filters, where those filters execute, and how we configure a custom SecurityFilterChain.

Now let's understand what happens when a user tries to log in.

Imagine you are building a login API.

A user sends:

{
    "username": "ram",
    "password": "r@123"
}

Your application receives these credentials. But how does Spring Security know whether the username exists? How does it compare the password? Who decides whether the user is authenticated?

Does SecurityFilterChain do all of this?

No.

Spring Security divides this responsibility into smaller components:

  • Authentication
  • AuthenticationManager
  • AuthenticationProvider
  • DaoAuthenticationProvider
  • UserDetailsService
  • PasswordEncoder

At first, these names might look confusing. But once we follow an actual login request, each component will make sense.

Let's start from the beginning.

Table of contents

  • Start with the authentication problem
    • What does Authentication represent?
    • Principal, credentials and authorities
  • Follow the authentication flow
    • Create an unauthenticated Authentication object
    • What AuthenticationManager does
    • How ProviderManager delegates to AuthenticationProvider
    • What DaoAuthenticationProvider does
    • Where UserDetailsService fits
    • What happens after successful authentication
  • Understand UserDetails and user storage
    • What UserDetails contains
    • In-memory users for learning
    • Database-backed users for real applications
  • Store passwords safely
    • Why plain-text passwords are dangerous
    • What NoOpPasswordEncoder does
    • How BCryptPasswordEncoder works
    • Configure a PasswordEncoder bean
    • BCrypt strength and password migration
  • Connect AuthenticationManager to your application
    • Expose AuthenticationManager as a bean
    • Authenticate credentials in a login service
    • Why a custom login endpoint is different from form login
  • Connect the flow to your SecurityConfig
    • Read your AuthenticationProvider bean
    • Follow a login request from start to finish
    • Common issues in your current configuration
  • Which one should I use?
  • Common mistakes
  • Quick recap
  • Try it yourself

Start with the authentication problem

Before understanding Spring Security classes, let's understand the actual problem.

Suppose we have a user stored in our database:

Username: ram
Password: $2a$10$someEncodedPassword
Role: USER

A user tries to log in using:

Username: ram
Password: r@123

Our application needs to perform a few operations:

  1. Find the user named ram.
  2. Retrieve the user's stored password.
  3. Compare the submitted password with the stored password.
  4. Check whether the account is allowed to authenticate.
  5. If everything is valid, create an authenticated user representation.
  6. Make that authentication available to the rest of the application.

Spring Security provides different components for these responsibilities.

The important thing to understand is that authentication is a process, not a single class or method.

What does Authentication represent?

In Spring Security, Authentication is an interface that represents the authentication information of a user or an authentication request.

It can represent two different situations:

  • Someone is trying to prove their identity.
  • Someone has already been authenticated.

For example, when a user submits a username and password, Spring Security can create an Authentication object containing those credentials.

At this stage, the user is not authenticated yet.

After the credentials are verified, Spring Security returns an authenticated Authentication object.

Think of it like entering an office.

You arrive at the office reception
              |
              v
You provide your ID card
              |
              v
Reception verifies your identity
              |
       +------+------+
       |             |
       v             v
   Valid ID       Invalid ID
       |             |
       v             v
   Entry given    Entry denied

The ID card you provide is not proof that your identity has already been verified. It is the information that needs to be checked.

The same idea applies to Spring Security.

Principal, credentials and authorities

An Authentication object contains a few important pieces of information.

Let's understand them using a login example.

Username: ram
Password: r@123
Role: USER

Principal

The principal represents the identity of the user.

For a username/password login, it can initially be the username.

After authentication, it is commonly a UserDetails object containing the user's information.

Credentials

Credentials are the information used to prove the identity.

In our example, the password is the credential.

Authorities

Authorities represent the permissions granted to the authenticated user.

For example:

ROLE_USER
ROLE_ADMIN

A user with ROLE_ADMIN may be allowed to access administrative endpoints, while a user with ROLE_USER may only access normal application features.

Here's a simplified view:

+--------------------------------------+
|             Authentication          |
+--------------------------------------+
|                                      |
|  Principal   : ram                   |
|  Credentials : r@123                 |
|  Authorities : ROLE_USER             |
|                                      |
|  Authenticated: false / true         |
|                                      |
+--------------------------------------+

One more important method is:

authentication.isAuthenticated();

It tells us whether the authentication object represents an authenticated identity.

But don't confuse this flag with password verification performed by your application. A trusted authentication provider should be responsible for producing the authenticated result.

Follow the authentication flow

Now let's connect the components.

Imagine a user submits a username and password.

Spring Security needs someone to receive the authentication request, someone to decide which authentication mechanism should handle it, and someone to verify the actual credentials.

This is where the following components come into the picture:

Username and Password
          |
          v
Authentication object
          |
          v
AuthenticationManager
          |
          v
AuthenticationProvider
          |
          v
UserDetailsService
          |
          v
PasswordEncoder
          |
          v
Authenticated Authentication

Let's understand each component.

Create an unauthenticated Authentication object

Spring Security provides a class called UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.

It implements the Authentication interface.

Despite the word Token in its name, this is not a JWT.

It is simply an object used to represent username/password authentication information.

Let's create one:

import org.springframework.security.authentication.UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken;

public class LoginExample {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken authentication =
                new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(
                        "ram",
                        "r@123"
                );

        System.out.println(authentication.getPrincipal());
        System.out.println(authentication.getCredentials());
        System.out.println(authentication.isAuthenticated());
    }
}

Output:

ram
r@123
false

Notice the last output:

false

Why?

Because we have only created an authentication request. We haven't verified the credentials yet.

There are two constructors worth knowing:

1. Unauthenticated constructor

new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(
        username,
        password
);

This creates an unauthenticated authentication object.

2. Authenticated constructor

new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(
        userDetails,
        null,
        userDetails.getAuthorities()
);

This constructor creates an authenticated object containing the user's authorities.

The second constructor is intended for trusted authentication code, such as an AuthenticationProvider.

Don't use it in your controller to mark an arbitrary user as authenticated. That would defeat the purpose of authentication.

What AuthenticationManager does

Now we have an unauthenticated Authentication object.

Who should verify it?

Meet AuthenticationManager.

AuthenticationManager is an interface responsible for authenticating an Authentication request.

Its most important method is:

Authentication authenticate(Authentication authentication);

Notice something interesting.

It accepts an Authentication object and returns an Authentication object.

Why?

Because the input represents an authentication request, while the returned object represents the result of the authentication process.

For example:

Input:

Username: ram
Password: r@123
Authenticated: false

After successful authentication:

Output:

Principal: UserDetails object
Credentials: Usually cleared after authentication
Authorities: ROLE_USER
Authenticated: true

The AuthenticationManager defines the authentication operation, but it doesn't necessarily implement the actual username/password verification itself.

It delegates that work to an AuthenticationProvider.

How ProviderManager delegates to AuthenticationProvider

ProviderManager is the most commonly used implementation of AuthenticationManager.

Think of AuthenticationManager as a common interface and ProviderManager as the implementation that delegates authentication requests to one or more providers.

Why do we need multiple providers?

Because an application may support different authentication mechanisms.

For example:

  • Username and password.
  • LDAP authentication.
  • Custom authentication.
  • Other authentication mechanisms supported by the application.

Instead of putting every authentication mechanism inside one giant class, Spring Security uses separate providers.

The relationship looks like this:

             AuthenticationManager
                      |
                      v
                ProviderManager
                      |
          +-----------+-----------+
          |           |           |
          v           v           v
      Provider 1  Provider 2  Provider 3
          |           |           |
          v           v           v
       Database     LDAP       Custom
       Login       Login      Login

ProviderManager checks whether a provider supports the type of Authentication object it receives.

The provider's supports() method helps determine that.

If a provider supports the request, Spring Security asks it to authenticate the request.

A provider can:

  • Return an authenticated Authentication object.
  • Return null when it cannot handle the request.
  • Throw an AuthenticationException when authentication fails.

The most important thing to remember:

AuthenticationManager delegates. AuthenticationProvider performs the actual authentication.

What DaoAuthenticationProvider does

Now let's focus on username/password authentication.

Spring Security provides a built-in implementation called DaoAuthenticationProvider.

It uses two important components:

  • UserDetailsService
  • PasswordEncoder

Its responsibility is to authenticate a username/password combination using the user information loaded by UserDetailsService.

Let's follow the process.

        DaoAuthenticationProvider
                   |
                   v
       UserDetailsService
                   |
                   v
       Load user information
                   |
                   v
       Get stored encoded password
                   |
                   v
           PasswordEncoder
                   |
                   v
       Compare submitted password
                   |
           +-------+-------+
           |               |
           v               v
         Match           No match
           |               |
           v               v
      Authentication    Authentication
        successful         failed

For example:

Submitted password: r@123

Stored password: $2a$10$...

DaoAuthenticationProvider loads the user information and uses the configured PasswordEncoder to compare the submitted password with the stored password.

If the password is correct and the account checks pass, authentication succeeds.

If the password is incorrect, authentication fails with an authentication exception.

You don't have to implement this entire process manually. Spring Security already provides this provider.

Where UserDetailsService fits

Now we know that DaoAuthenticationProvider needs user information.

But where does it get that information?

From UserDetailsService.

UserDetailsService is an interface provided by Spring Security.

It has one main method:

UserDetails loadUserByUsername(String username);

Its job is simple:

Find the user using the supplied username and return the user's details.

For example, imagine our database contains:

+--------------------------------------+
|                users                 |
+--------------------------------------+
| id | username | password | role      |
+--------------------------------------+
| 1  | ram      | $2a$...  | ROLE_USER  |
| 2  | kim      | $2b$...  | ROLE_ADMIN |
+--------------------------------------+

When someone tries to log in as ram, Spring Security calls:

userDetailsService.loadUserByUsername("ram");

The implementation retrieves the user and returns a UserDetails object.

Important: UserDetailsService does not verify the submitted password.

It only loads the user.

Password verification is handled by DaoAuthenticationProvider using PasswordEncoder.

This separation is useful because the same authentication mechanism can work with different user storage systems.

For example:

  • A user stored in memory.
  • A user stored in MySQL.
  • A user stored in PostgreSQL.
  • A user stored in MongoDB.

The provider doesn't need to know the details of your database queries. It only needs a UserDetailsService.

What happens after successful authentication

Let's say:

Username: ram
Password: r@123

The user exists, the password matches, and the account is enabled.

DaoAuthenticationProvider creates an authenticated Authentication result.

The authentication filter that initiated the authentication process then stores that result in the SecurityContextHolder.

The simplified flow is:

Authentication request
          |
          v
AuthenticationManager
          |
          v
DaoAuthenticationProvider
          |
          v
UserDetailsService
          |
          v
PasswordEncoder
          |
          v
Authenticated Authentication
          |
          v
SecurityContextHolder

What is SecurityContextHolder?

It provides access to the current security context.

The SecurityContext holds the current user's Authentication object.

For example:

Authentication authentication =
        SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();

System.out.println(authentication.getName());

If authentication succeeded and the context was populated, the output could be:

ram

This is how Spring Security makes the authenticated user's information available to the rest of the application.

We'll revisit this when we work with JWT authentication in Part 3.

Understand UserDetails and user storage

We have discussed UserDetailsService, which loads user information.

But what exactly does it return?

It returns an object implementing UserDetails.

What UserDetails contains

UserDetails is an interface that represents the user information required by Spring Security.

It provides methods such as:

String getUsername();

String getPassword();

Collection<? extends GrantedAuthority> getAuthorities();

boolean isAccountNonExpired();

boolean isAccountNonLocked();

boolean isCredentialsNonExpired();

boolean isEnabled();

Let's understand why these methods exist.

Username and password

These provide the user's identity and stored password information.

Authorities

These define what the user is allowed to access.

Account status

These methods help Spring Security determine whether the account is allowed to authenticate.

For example:

Username: ram
Password: $2a$10$...
Authorities: ROLE_USER

Account non-expired: true
Account non-locked: true
Credentials non-expired: true
Enabled: true

You can implement UserDetails yourself or adapt an existing user entity to it.

The important distinction is:

UserDetailsService
       |
       | loads
       v
UserDetails
       |
       | contains
       v
Username + Password + Authorities + Account Status

In-memory users for learning

Spring Security provides InMemoryUserDetailsManager.

It stores user details in application memory.

This is useful when learning Spring Security or creating small demonstrations.

Example:

@Bean
public UserDetailsService userDetailsService() {

    UserDetails user1 = User
            .withDefaultPasswordEncoder()
            .username("ram")
            .password("r@123")
            .roles("USER")
            .build();

    UserDetails user2 = User
            .withDefaultPasswordEncoder()
            .username("kim")
            .password("k@123")
            .roles("ADMIN")
            .build();

    return new InMemoryUserDetailsManager(user1, user2);
}

Here we created two users.

One has the USER role and the other has the ADMIN role.

Notice this:

.roles("ADMIN")

Spring Security converts it into the authority:

ROLE_ADMIN

This is why hasRole("ADMIN") and hasAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN") are commonly used together.

One warning: User.withDefaultPasswordEncoder() is meant for samples and demos, not production password storage.

In-memory users are also not suitable for a typical production application where users register, update their profiles, and expect their accounts to remain available after the application restarts.

Database-backed users for real applications

In a real application, users are usually stored in a database.

For example, let's create a simple UserDetailsService implementation.

@Service
public class MyUserDetailsService implements UserDetailsService {

    @Autowired
    private UserRepository userRepository;

    @Override
    public UserDetails loadUserByUsername(String username) {

        User user = userRepository.findByUsername(username)
                .orElseThrow(() ->
                        new UsernameNotFoundException("User not found")
                );

        return org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User
                .withUsername(user.getUsername())
                .password(user.getPassword())
                .authorities(user.getRole())
                .build();
    }
}

Here:

  1. We receive a username.
  2. We search for that username in the database.
  3. We retrieve the user.
  4. We convert the user into Spring Security's UserDetails.
  5. We return it.

Now DaoAuthenticationProvider can use this service without knowing whether the user came from PostgreSQL, MySQL, or another storage system.

That's the benefit of using interfaces.

Your database implementation can change without requiring you to rewrite the entire authentication mechanism.

Store passwords safely

Now comes one of the most important parts of authentication.

Let's say a user registers with:

Username: ram
Password: r@123

Should we directly store this password in our database?

Absolutely not.

Let's understand why.

Why plain-text passwords are dangerous

Imagine your database stores passwords like this:

+------------------------------+
| username | password          |
+------------------------------+
| ram      | r@123             |
| kim      | k@123             |
| john     | john123            |
+------------------------------+

Suppose an attacker gets access to your database.

The attacker can immediately read every user's password.

This is a serious security problem.

Instead of storing the original password, we should store a one-way password hash.

For example:

Original password:

r@123

Stored password:

$2a$10$...

The stored value is not the original password.

During login, the application checks whether the submitted password matches the stored hash.

This is where PasswordEncoder comes in.

What NoOpPasswordEncoder does

You may have seen this line in Spring Security examples:

provider.setPasswordEncoder(
        NoOpPasswordEncoder.getInstance()
);

What does it do?

The name gives us a clue.

"No Operation" means it does not perform password hashing.

For example:

PasswordEncoder encoder =
        NoOpPasswordEncoder.getInstance();

String encoded = encoder.encode("r@123");

System.out.println(encoded);

System.out.println(
        encoder.matches("r@123", encoded)
);

Conceptually, the output is:

r@123
true

The password is stored as it is.

There is no secure hashing involved.

Why does Spring Security provide it?

It is useful for legacy applications and simple testing scenarios where plain-text passwords are intentionally used.

But it is deprecated and explicitly documented as insecure.

Never use NoOpPasswordEncoder for a production application.

How BCryptPasswordEncoder works

Spring Security provides BCryptPasswordEncoder to hash passwords using the BCrypt algorithm.

Example:

PasswordEncoder encoder =
        new BCryptPasswordEncoder();

String encodedPassword =
        encoder.encode("r@123");

System.out.println(encodedPassword);

System.out.println(
        encoder.matches("r@123", encodedPassword)
);

System.out.println(
        encoder.matches("wrongPassword", encodedPassword)
);

The output will look similar to:

$2a$10$...
true
false

The actual encoded password will be a long BCrypt hash.

Let's understand the important difference.

When you call:

encoder.encode("r@123");

BCrypt generates a salted password hash.

A salt is random data used during password hashing.

Why do we need it?

Imagine two users choose the same password:

User 1: r@123
User 2: r@123

Without proper salting, identical passwords can produce identical stored hashes.

That makes it easier for attackers to identify users with the same password.

BCrypt uses a salt, so encoding the same password multiple times normally produces different hashes.

For example:

String hash1 = encoder.encode("r@123");
String hash2 = encoder.encode("r@123");

System.out.println(hash1.equals(hash2));

Output:

false

Does this mean the passwords are different?

No.

Both hashes represent the same original password, but they use different salts.

So how do we verify the password?

We use:

encoder.matches(rawPassword, encodedPassword);

For example:

encoder.matches("r@123", hash1);

Output:

true

Don't compare a newly generated BCrypt hash with the stored hash using equals().

Use matches() because BCrypt uses a salt.

Configure a PasswordEncoder bean

Instead of creating a password encoder wherever we need it, we can register it as a Spring bean.

A straightforward configuration using BCrypt is:

@Bean
public PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
    return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(10);
}

Now Spring can inject this bean wherever a PasswordEncoder is required.

For example:

@Service
public class UserService {

    private final PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder;

    public UserService(PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder) {
        this.passwordEncoder = passwordEncoder;
    }

    public String encodePassword(String rawPassword) {
        return passwordEncoder.encode(rawPassword);
    }
}

When a user registers, encode the password before saving it.

String encodedPassword =
        passwordEncoder.encode(request.getPassword());

user.setPassword(encodedPassword);

userRepository.save(user);

During login, DaoAuthenticationProvider uses the configured password encoder to verify the submitted password against the stored encoded password.

Important: Registration and login must use compatible password-encoding strategies. If you store a BCrypt hash, configure authentication to verify it using BCrypt-compatible matching.

There is another option worth knowing: DelegatingPasswordEncoder.

@Bean
public PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {

    return PasswordEncoderFactories
            .createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();
}

Why should we consider it?

It supports multiple password formats and identifies the encoder using a prefix in the stored password.

For example:

{bcrypt}$2a$10$...

The {bcrypt} prefix tells Spring Security which encoder should be used to verify the password.

This is useful when an application needs to support password migration or different password formats over time.

For many applications, DelegatingPasswordEncoder is a good default choice.

BCrypt strength and password migration

You may have noticed this:

new BCryptPasswordEncoder(10);

What does 10 mean?

It is the BCrypt strength, also called the work factor.

BCrypt deliberately makes password hashing computationally expensive.

A higher strength increases the work required to calculate the hash and verify a password.

Why make it slow?

Because attackers may try millions of password combinations.

Making each password verification more expensive makes large-scale password guessing more difficult.

But there is a trade-off.

If the work factor is too high, legitimate users may experience slow login requests, and your server may consume too many resources.

Spring Security's BCrypt default strength is 10.

You should benchmark the cost on your actual production hardware and tune it according to your application's security and performance requirements.

One more thing about migration.

Suppose your old application stored plain-text passwords, and now you want to move to BCrypt.

You cannot simply switch the encoder and expect old plain-text values to match BCrypt hashes.

You need a migration strategy.

DelegatingPasswordEncoder can help applications support multiple formats during migration. You can also use a password-reset process to move users to a new secure password format.

Connect AuthenticationManager to your application

So far, we have understood the individual components.

Now let's see how our own application can use them.

Imagine we have created a REST endpoint:

POST /users/login

The client sends a username and password.

We want Spring Security to authenticate those credentials.

For this, we can inject AuthenticationManager into our service or controller.

Expose AuthenticationManager as a bean

Spring Security provides AuthenticationConfiguration, which can give us the configured AuthenticationManager.

We can expose it as a bean:

@Bean
public AuthenticationManager authenticationManager(
        AuthenticationConfiguration configuration
) throws Exception {

    return configuration.getAuthenticationManager();
}

Now we can inject AuthenticationManager into another Spring-managed component.

For example:

@Service
public class LoginService {

    private final AuthenticationManager authenticationManager;

    public LoginService(AuthenticationManager authenticationManager) {
        this.authenticationManager = authenticationManager;
    }
}

Why do we need this?

Because our custom login logic can now delegate credential verification to Spring Security instead of manually checking passwords.

Authenticate credentials in a login service

Let's see the actual authentication call.

@Service
public class LoginService {

    private final AuthenticationManager authenticationManager;

    public LoginService(AuthenticationManager authenticationManager) {
        this.authenticationManager = authenticationManager;
    }

    public Authentication login(String username, String password) {

        Authentication authenticationRequest =
                new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(
                        username,
                        password
                );

        return authenticationManager.authenticate(
                authenticationRequest
        );
    }
}

Let's understand what happens here.

First:

new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(
        username,
        password
);

We create an unauthenticated authentication request.

Then:

authenticationManager.authenticate(authenticationRequest);

We pass the request to Spring Security.

The configured authentication manager delegates the request to a suitable provider.

The provider loads the user, verifies the password, and returns an authenticated result if everything is valid.

If authentication fails, Spring Security throws an AuthenticationException.

In a real REST API, you should handle that exception and return an appropriate HTTP response without exposing sensitive information.

Why a custom login endpoint is different from form login

This is an important distinction.

In your configuration, you have:

.formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults())

This enables Spring Security's form-login support.

Spring Security provides filters that handle form-login requests and delegate authentication to the configured authentication manager.

But imagine you create your own REST endpoint:

POST /users/login

And the request body is JSON:

{
    "username": "ram",
    "password": "r@123"
}

The form-login filter does not automatically know how to process your custom JSON request body.

Your controller or service must explicitly invoke the AuthenticationManager, or you must implement an appropriate custom authentication filter.

This is why exposing an AuthenticationManager bean is useful for a custom REST login flow.

We'll use this idea in Part 3 when we connect login authentication with JWT generation.

Connect the flow to your SecurityConfig

Now let's revisit the code you shared.

You already have an AuthenticationProvider bean and an AuthenticationManager bean.

Let's understand what each part does.

Read your AuthenticationProvider bean

Your code:

@Bean
public AuthenticationProvider authenticationProvider(
        UserDetailsService userDetailsService
) {

    DaoAuthenticationProvider provider =
            new DaoAuthenticationProvider(userDetailsService);

    provider.setPasswordEncoder(
            new BCryptPasswordEncoder(10)
    );

    return provider;
}

Let's break it down.

Step 1: Receive UserDetailsService

UserDetailsService userDetailsService

Spring injects your UserDetailsService implementation.

In your project, this could be MyUserDetailsService.

Its job is to load the user from your database.

Step 2: Create DaoAuthenticationProvider

DaoAuthenticationProvider provider =
        new DaoAuthenticationProvider(userDetailsService);

We create a provider that uses the supplied UserDetailsService.

This provider knows how to authenticate username/password requests using the loaded user details.

Step 3: Configure PasswordEncoder

provider.setPasswordEncoder(
        new BCryptPasswordEncoder(10)
);

We tell the provider how to verify passwords.

If the database contains BCrypt hashes, the provider can use BCrypt to compare the submitted password with the stored hash.

Step 4: Return the provider

return provider;

We register the provider as a Spring bean.

Spring Security can use this provider as part of its authentication configuration.

Follow a login request from start to finish

Let's put everything together.

Assume:

  • The user is stored in your database.
  • Your MyUserDetailsService implements UserDetailsService.
  • The stored password is a BCrypt hash.
  • Your DaoAuthenticationProvider uses BCryptPasswordEncoder.

The authentication process looks like this:

             Login Request
                   |
                   v
       Username: ram, Password: r@123
                   |
                   v
       Unauthenticated Authentication
                   |
                   v
          AuthenticationManager
                   |
                   v
             ProviderManager
                   |
                   v
        DaoAuthenticationProvider
                   |
                   v
          MyUserDetailsService
                   |
                   v
          Load user from database
                   |
                   v
            UserDetails object
                   |
                   v
          BCryptPasswordEncoder
                   |
                   v
         Compare submitted password
                   |
            +------+------+
            |             |
            v             v
        Password       Password
         matches       incorrect
            |             |
            v             v
       Authenticated   Authentication
       Authentication     failed
            |
            v
       SecurityContext

Now the entire purpose of each component should be clearer.

Common issues in your current configuration

Let's look at a few things in your code that are worth checking.

1. Your UserDetailsService must be registered

Your provider expects a UserDetailsService.

Make sure you have an implementation registered as a Spring bean.

For example:

@Service
public class MyUserDetailsService implements UserDetailsService {
    // loadUserByUsername implementation
}

Otherwise, Spring won't have a service to inject into your provider.

2. Registration must encode the password

If your login provider uses BCrypt, make sure your registration logic stores an encoded password.

For example:

user.setPassword(
        passwordEncoder.encode(request.getPassword())
);

If you store the raw password but configure BCrypt, authentication will fail.

3. Keep password encoding consistent

You currently configure:

new BCryptPasswordEncoder(10)

This is fine when the stored passwords are BCrypt hashes compatible with that encoder.

If you later switch to DelegatingPasswordEncoder, make sure existing stored hashes have the expected {bcrypt} prefix or are migrated appropriately.

4. Don't mix up form login and custom JSON login

Your configuration enables:

.formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults())

That does not automatically turn /users/login into a JSON login endpoint.

If you want a custom REST login endpoint, invoke the AuthenticationManager from your login flow.

5. Don't use NoOpPasswordEncoder in production

You have this commented-out code:

provider.setPasswordEncoder(
        NoOpPasswordEncoder.getInstance()
);

Keep it disabled.

Use a secure password encoder such as BCrypt or the default delegating encoder.

6. Check your role and authority values

If you create users using:

.roles("ADMIN")

Spring Security creates the authority:

ROLE_ADMIN

So remember the difference between:

.hasRole("ADMIN")

and:

.hasAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN")

They are related, but they don't take exactly the same input.

Which one should I use?

Let's quickly connect the components to their responsibilities.

  • Authentication: Represents the authentication request or authenticated user.
  • UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken: Carries username/password credentials during username/password authentication.
  • AuthenticationManager: Provides the authentication operation.
  • ProviderManager: Common AuthenticationManager implementation that delegates to providers.
  • AuthenticationProvider: Performs a particular authentication mechanism.
  • DaoAuthenticationProvider: Authenticates username/password using UserDetailsService and PasswordEncoder.
  • UserDetailsService: Loads user information.
  • UserDetails: Represents the user information required by Spring Security.
  • PasswordEncoder: Encodes passwords and verifies submitted passwords.
  • BCryptPasswordEncoder: Provides BCrypt-based password hashing.
  • DelegatingPasswordEncoder: Supports multiple password formats and password-encoding migration.

For a typical username/password application backed by a database, this is a good starting point:

AuthenticationManager
        |
        v
DaoAuthenticationProvider
        |
        +----------------------+
        |                      |
        v                      v
UserDetailsService      PasswordEncoder
        |
        v
Database

You generally don't need to write your own AuthenticationProvider just to authenticate users against a database. DaoAuthenticationProvider already handles that use case.

Common mistakes

  1. Confusing AuthenticationManager with AuthenticationProvider: AuthenticationManager provides the authentication operation, while AuthenticationProvider performs a specific authentication mechanism. Understand the delegation instead of treating them as the same component.

  2. Assuming UserDetailsService verifies passwords: It only loads user information. Password verification is handled by the authentication provider using a PasswordEncoder.

  3. Storing raw passwords in the database: Never store plain-text passwords in a production application. Encode passwords using a suitable password encoder before saving them.

  4. Comparing BCrypt hashes using equals(): BCrypt uses a salt, so encoding the same password twice can produce different hashes. Use passwordEncoder.matches(rawPassword, encodedPassword).

  5. Using NoOpPasswordEncoder in production: It does not hash passwords and is deprecated as insecure. Use BCrypt or DelegatingPasswordEncoder instead.

  6. Assuming a custom JSON login endpoint is handled by formLogin(): Form login and your custom JSON login endpoint are different flows. Invoke AuthenticationManager from your custom login logic or implement an appropriate authentication filter.

Quick recap

  • Authentication is the process of verifying a user's identity.
  • Authentication represents an authentication request or an authenticated user.
  • UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken carries username/password authentication information.
  • AuthenticationManager delegates authentication to suitable providers.
  • ProviderManager is the common implementation of AuthenticationManager.
  • DaoAuthenticationProvider authenticates users using UserDetailsService and PasswordEncoder.
  • UserDetailsService loads user information.
  • UserDetails contains the username, password, authorities, and account status.
  • PasswordEncoder handles password encoding and verification.
  • NoOpPasswordEncoder is insecure and should not be used in production.
  • BCryptPasswordEncoder provides adaptive one-way password hashing.
  • DelegatingPasswordEncoder supports multiple password formats and migration.
  • A custom REST login endpoint can use AuthenticationManager to authenticate credentials.

Try it yourself

Don't just read these concepts. Try implementing them.

Practice 1: Understand Authentication

Create a UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken using a username and password.

Print:

  • Principal
  • Credentials
  • isAuthenticated()

Then create an authenticated token using a UserDetails object and authorities. Compare the results.

Practice 2: Configure BCrypt

Create a PasswordEncoder bean using BCryptPasswordEncoder.

Encode the same password twice.

Check whether both hashes are equal.

Then use matches() to verify the original password against both hashes.

Practice 3: Understand DaoAuthenticationProvider

Create a database-backed UserDetailsService.

Configure DaoAuthenticationProvider with that service and a PasswordEncoder.

Try logging in with:

  • A valid username and password.
  • A valid username and incorrect password.
  • An invalid username.

Observe what happens in each case.

Bonus challenge

Create a custom /users/login REST endpoint.

Inject AuthenticationManager into your service and authenticate the submitted username and password.

Don't manually compare passwords inside the controller. Let Spring Security handle authentication.

If this helped, or if you spotted something I should fix, tell me in the comments. I'm still learning too.

title: Faker vs Relational Test Data Generators: Which Fits Better?
description:
If your team already uses Faker or similar libraries, you may be wondering when they stop being enough. This guide compares code-first fake data libraries with schema-driven relational generators for realistic buyer questions.

Start with the real question

This is not really a question about tools. It is a question about where your complexity lives.

If you need a few fake names, emails, and timestamps inside unit tests, Faker-style libraries are a great fit. If you need several related tables as downloadable CSV files, with consistent foreign keys and rules you can review outside application code, you may want a relational generator instead.

Neither approach is universally better. They solve different problems.

What Faker-style libraries do well

Tools such as Faker and similar language-specific libraries are popular because they are simple and flexible. You call methods in code and generate values right where your tests need them.

They are especially good for:

  • Unit tests with small in-memory objects
  • Seeding a single table quickly
  • Generating field-level fake values in application code
  • Cases where developers want full control over logic

A typical pattern looks like this:

customer = {
  "name": fake.name(),
  "email": fake.email(),
  "created_at": fake.date_time_this_year()
}

The cost appears later, when one object becomes a graph of related tables and business rules.

Where manual Faker setups get harder

As soon as you need relational consistency, you usually begin writing your own mini data platform.

For example, to create e-commerce fixtures you may need to:

  • Create customers before orders
  • Reuse valid customer IDs in orders
  • Create products before order items
  • Make order totals align with item lines
  • Ensure dates are in a valid sequence
  • Export each table to CSV

None of that is impossible. Many teams do it successfully. But it means the effort is no longer “use Faker.” It is “build and maintain relational generation logic around Faker.”

What relational generators optimize for

Relational test data generators start from the schema rather than from provider methods in code. You define tables, columns, SQL types, and foreign keys, then generate several related tables together.

They are usually a better fit when you care about:

  • Foreign-key integrity across CSV exports
  • Editable generation rules outside source code
  • Reusable data definitions for QA or CI
  • A preview before full generation

With Luna, for example, the input is a JSON schema and the output includes related CSV tables, an editable generation spec, and a quality report. See the docs and methodology for product details.

Side-by-side comparison

Question Faker-style library Relational generator
How do you define fields? Provider methods in code Schema metadata and column definitions
How do you express relationships? Custom application logic Foreign keys in input schema
Best output shape Objects or app seeding code Related CSV tables
Rule editing Change code Edit a generation spec
Quality checks Usually custom May include per-run reports

How to choose based on use case

Choose Faker-style libraries when

  • You are writing unit or integration tests inside one codebase
  • Your entities are simple and mostly independent
  • Developers prefer full procedural control
  • You do not need CSV fixture bundles for non-engineers

Choose a relational generator when

  • You need several tables that join correctly
  • You want to define data from a schema, not code
  • You need downloadable CSVs for QA, analytics, or demos
  • You want to review inferred rules and reuse a saved generation spec

Luna is one schema-first option in this category, not a direct replacement for Faker in every case. Faker remains useful for many code-level test scenarios.

A practical hybrid approach

For many teams, the best answer is both.

Use a relational generator for the baseline dataset: customers, orders, products, tenants, users, devices, events. Then add a small number of handcrafted records or code-generated edge cases for the scenarios your app cares about most.

This gives you broad coverage without forcing every weird exception into one generation system.

Questions buyers should ask before switching

  1. Are we spending engineer time maintaining fake data scripts?
  2. Do broken joins or invalid timestamps regularly waste QA time?
  3. Do multiple teams need the same dataset outside the application runtime?
  4. Would a schema and editable spec be easier to review than code?

If the answer to most of these is yes, a relational generator is worth evaluating.

When not to switch

Do not change tools just because schema-driven generation sounds cleaner. If your current approach is small, stable, and owned by the team that uses it, replacing it may add process without much benefit.

Also, if your tests depend on highly custom procedural behavior, keeping generation logic in code may still be the most transparent option.

Try a small proof of concept

The easiest way to decide is not a long feature comparison. Pick one realistic schema slice and test both approaches. Measure:

  • Time to first useful dataset
  • Time to adjust distributions or rules
  • How easy it is to explain the setup to another team member
  • Whether the output works in your actual QA workflow

Generated relational data still needs validation in your own QA workflow, regardless of which tool you use.

If you want to test the schema-first route, start with a preview and inspect the resulting tables before committing. You can try that here: https://veri.lunafzai.com/#demo.

No personal data is required for Luna's schema-first workflow.

FAQ

Is Faker bad for relational test data?

No. It is very useful, especially inside application tests. The challenge is that multi-table relationships, exports, and rule validation usually require extra code around it.

Can a relational generator replace all test fixtures?

Usually not. It is strong for broad baseline datasets, but many teams still keep a smaller set of handcrafted edge-case fixtures for specific scenarios.

What if I already have Faker scripts?

You do not need to throw them away. A common approach is to keep them for unit tests and use a relational generator only for larger shared datasets or CSV-based QA workflows.

Originally published at veri.lunafzai.com. Disclosure: written by the team behind Luna synthetic test data.

title: AVERT: Anomalous Value Erasure with Response Testing against Visual Prompt Injection
description:
arXiv:2611.33532v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) are vulnerable to visual prompt injection, in which an adversarially perturbed image forces the model to respond with the attacker's chosen content, such as malicious tool calls, website links, or advertisements, sometimes regardless of the user's question. Existing defenses, such as diffusion-based purification and image-token masking, mitigate these attacks at a substantial cost to the model's utility on benign inputs. To address this challenge, we propose AVERT, which removes adversarial feature directions only when the model's answer depends on them. Our key procedures involve identifying anomalous value subspaces and detecting answer dependence. To identify the anomalous value subspace, we compare the statistics of each input's attention-head outputs with those of clean images and extract the directions along which the input deviates the most. We then project out these directions to remove the injected content. Because the same directions also carry benign visual information, we apply the removal only to answers that depend on them, namely answers whose likelihood collapses once the directions are removed or that are as likely under unrelated questions as under the user's question. Against white-box attacks on four VLMs (Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA, InternVL2.5) and four injection benchmarks, AVERT lowers average attack success from 86-90% to at most 0.6% while retaining at least 96% of undefended utility averaged over thirteen benchmarks. Its defense-utility F-score ($F_{DU}$), the harmonic mean of attacks stopped and utility retained, is 98.0-99.1 and the highest among all compared defenses on every model.

title: The game shelf: a CSS coverflow with view-timeline
description:
This note has an interactive demo. Try it in the original

The row of daily games on the richi.codes home page is a coverflow, and JavaScript doesn't calculate any of the motion. As you scroll it, the cover in the middle faces you with an orange glow, and the others turn away in 3D, shrink and darken. The browser does all of that with scroll-driven animations. The demo above is a standalone copy of the same technique. Scroll it, tick "Show timeline %" to see the number each cover is animating with, and move the tilt slider.

What you see, and what drives it

On the site, the shelf lives in components/Bento/GameShelf.jsx, with its styles in styles/globals.css. Underneath, it's an ordinary horizontal list: overflow-x: auto, scroll-snap-type: x mandatory and scroll-snap-align: center on each slide. That part works on its own, in any browser.

The 3D comes from a view progress timeline. MDN describes it as a timeline that "progresses based on changes to the visibility of an element (the subject) within a scrollable element". For a horizontal row, the axis has to be inline, because the default is block. MDN's guide sets out the scale: 0% is when the subject starts to enter at the end edge of the scrollport, and 100% is when it leaves through the start edge. In a left-to-right row, a cover is at 0% when it peeks in on the right, at 50% in the middle, and at 100% when it disappears on the left. Turn on the percentages in the demo and you'll see the centered cover at 50.

So the whole effect fits in one set of keyframes with a 50% stop:

.slide {
  view-timeline: --cover inline;      /* a named timeline on each slide */
  animation: stack 1ms linear both;
  animation-timeline: --cover;        /* after the shorthand */
}
.card {
  animation: flow 1ms linear both;
  animation-timeline: --cover;        /* the child reads its parent's timeline */
}
@keyframes flow {
  0%   { transform: perspective(900px) translateX(-50%) rotateY(-60deg) scale(.74); }
  50%  { transform: perspective(900px) translateX(0) rotateY(0deg) scale(1); }
  100% { transform: perspective(900px) translateX(50%) rotateY(60deg) scale(.74); }
}
@keyframes stack { 0%, 100% { z-index: 1; } 50% { z-index: 30; } }

The real site has more stops: at 38% and 62% the covers are already turned 44 degrees, so the turn happens close to the center. In the demo the angle comes from a --tilt custom property that the slider changes.

Two details come straight from MDN. animation-timeline goes after the animation shorthand, because the shorthand resets it to auto and can't set it. And the duration is 1ms, because Firefox needs a non-zero animation-duration to apply the animation.

Why a named timeline and not view(inline)

The anonymous version, animation-timeline: view(inline), is shorter, and it works when the element you animate is the one being tracked. The shelf needs something else: one timeline per slide that drives five animations. Those are the card's 3D turn, the glow (a ::before), the shade over the image, the opacity of the title and caption, and the z-index of the slide itself, so the centered cover sits on top of its neighbors. MDN notes that the animated element "doesn't have to be" the subject. The spec explains why the children can see the name: when an element looks up a timeline name, it checks itself first and then walks up its ancestors. view-timeline: --cover inline on the li is therefore visible to everything inside it.

The note Dr. Kernel left with this change gave another reason: if you transformed the li itself, you'd move the box being measured. The spec says otherwise: when computing view progress, "Transforms are ignored". The good reason is the one above: one measurement, five consumers.

The effect is optional, the navigation isn't

All of the motion sits behind two conditions:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  @supports ((animation-timeline: view()) and (animation-range: entry)) {
    /* the rules above */
  }
}

Chrome's Modern Web Guidance recommends the second check (animation-range: entry) because it filters out browsers with only partial support. Without the effect you get a flat row with snap, which is just as usable. Untick "3D effect" in the demo to see it.

What does use a little JavaScript is what shouldn't depend on a decorative effect: previous and next buttons that are real <button> elements with a name, a counter, and a role="status" region that announces "Game 3 of 16: Title" once scrolling stops. It listens for scrollend, and falls back to scroll plus a short timeout where that event doesn't exist. Two things came up when the shelf was tested in three browsers:

  • An extra tab stop. Firefox made the scrolling row a tab stop of its own, even though each cover is already a link. The list has tabindex="-1".
  • Focus fights the centering. When you tab to a cover, the browser scrolls it into view on its own and overrides the centering. Centering it on the next requestAnimationFrame fixes it. The demo uses the same trick.

Browser support and gotchas

  • Support: Chrome and Edge 115, Safari 26 and Firefox 159. The Firefox 159 release notes list scroll-driven animations as "now enabled by default", and web-features has marked them Baseline "newly available" since October 27, 2026. Anyone who hasn't updated gets the flat row. In those browsers the demo also shows a notice.
  • overflow on the track decides everything. MDN warns that if the scroller doesn't overflow on that axis, or its overflow is hidden or clipped, no timeline is created. If the row fits on screen, nothing turns.
  • The % readout is a registered integer. @property --p { syntax: "<integer>" } is animated from 0 to 100 on the same timeline and printed with counter(). In my WebKit test, getComputedStyle returned decimals (84.91) where Chromium returned 85. The centered cover showed 50% in both.

What to keep an eye on

  • "Widely available" status. Baseline "newly available" means every engine ships it, not that every user has updated. The flat fallback costs nothing, so keep it.
  • timeline-scope. If you ever need the timeline from an element that isn't a descendant (a separate indicator outside the list, say), the spec lets you lift the name to a shared ancestor with timeline-scope.
  • The spec is still an Editor's Draft. The basics shown here work today in all three engines, but there are still open issues.

Sources

  • view-timeline – MDN
  • Scroll-driven animation timelines – MDN guide
  • Scroll-driven Animations, Editor's Draft – CSS Working Group
  • Firefox 159 release notes for developers – MDN
  • Element: scrollend event – MDN

title: How to Check if a File Exists in Python
description:
When I first started writing Python scripts that read files, I kept getting FileNotFoundError and crashing my program.

I later learned that you can check if a file exists before trying to open it using the os module.

import os

file_path = "data.txt"

if os.path.exists(file_path):
    with open(file_path, "r") as file:
        print(file.read())
else:
    print("File not found.")

This simple check makes your scripts much more robust, especially if they depend on user-generated files or external data.

title: Getting Cluster Lock and Failover Information via SQL in GBase 8a
description:
In current builds of GBase 8a, the China-domestically developed MPP analytical database from GBASE, cluster lock and failover information is normally available only through the gcadmin command line. Because the engine supports Python UDFs, you can wrap those commands and fetch the same data with plain SQL — especially useful when shell access is inconvenient.

A Python UDF for Cluster Locks (showlock) 

drop function if exists showlock;
create function showlock()
returns varchar
$$
try:
    import commands
    output = commands.getoutput("gcadmin showlock")
except:
    return None
return str(output)

$$ language plpythonu;

Result:

gbase> select showlock();
+-------------------+
| showlock()        |
+-------------------+
|  +=================================================================+
 |                          GCLUSTER LOCK                          |
 +=================================================================+
 +-------------+----------+-------------+--------------+------+----+
 |  Lock name  |  owner   |   content   | create time  |locked|type|
 +-------------+----------+-------------+--------------+------+----+
 |gc-event-lock|10.0.2.201|global master|20250113120320| TRUE | E  |
 +-------------+----------+-------------+--------------+------+----+
 Total : 1 |
+--------------------+
1 row in set (Elapsed: 00:00:00.63)

A Python UDF for Failover Information (showfailover) 

drop function if exists showfailover;
create function showfailover()
returns varchar
$$
try:
    import commands
    output = commands.getoutput("gcadmin showfailover")
except:
    return None
return str(output)

$$ language plpythonu;

Result:

gbase> drop function if exists showfailover;
Query OK, 0 rows affected, 1 warning (Elapsed: 00:00:00.00)

gbase> create function showfailover()
    -> returns varchar
    -> $$
    -> try:
    ->     import commands
    ->     output = commands.getoutput("gcadmin showfailover")
    -> except:
    ->     return None
    -> return str(output)
    ->
    -> $$ language plpythonu;
Query OK, 0 rows affected (Elapsed: 00:00:00.00)

gbase> select showfailover();
+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| showfailover()                                               |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+
|
gcadmin showfailover: no gcluster failover information now
 |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+
1 row in set (Elapsed: 00:00:00.63)

gbase>

Both UDFs share the same structure: plpythonu calls the matching gcadmin subcommand through commands.getoutput, converts the output to a string, and returns None if anything raises.

Going forward, the output can also be switched to XML with the f parameter for easier programmatic parsing — see gcadmin --help for details. Bringing these operational checks into the SQL interface means you no longer need a shell account for everyone who needs them, and privilege control plus auditing stay in one place: the gbase database itself.

title: Engineering Deterministic AI Pipelines: Beyond Naive Retrieval-Augmented Generation
description:
As systems engineers, when we transition from deploying conversational wrappers to architecting mission-critical AI pipelines, we immediately hit a fundamental architectural wall: Non-determinism. LLMs are probabilistic token-samplers. Production systems require deterministic SLAs, strict latency budgets, and absolute schema safety.

Naive Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architectures—characterized by synchronous vector database lookups, unconstrained prompting, and raw string parsing—fail spectacularly under production loads. They suffer from high Time-To-First-Token (TTFT), silent JSON schema drift, and zero semantic caching.

In this deep-dive, we will design and implement a production-grade, asynchronous inference pipeline using FastAPI that incorporates a semantic cache layer, structured output validation via Pydantic, and resilient asynchronous flow control.

System Architecture

The following diagram illustrates our asynchronous, resilient AI processing pipeline. It decouples the ingress request from vector search and LLM inference, routing execution through a semantic cache layer to eliminate redundant compute cycles.

  [ Client Request ]
         │
         ▼
  +──────────────────────────────────────────────+
  │ FastAPI Async Router                         │
  +──────────────────────────────────────────────+
         │
         ├──► [ Semantic Cache (Redis / Vector) ] ──(Cache Hit)──► [ Return Payload ]
         │
         (Cache Miss)
         │
         ▼
  +──────────────────────────────────────────────+
  │ Async Embedding & Retrieval Service          │
  +──────────────────────────────────────────────+
         │
         ▼
  +──────────────────────────────────────────────+
  │ LLM Client (AsyncOpenAI)                     │
  │  - JSON Schema Enforcement (Pydantic)        │
  +──────────────────────────────────────────────+
         │
         ▼
  +──────────────────────────────────────────────+
  │ Pipeline Output (Validated & Structured)     │
  +──────────────────────────────────────────────+

Engineering Principles for Production AI

  1. Strict Structural Bounds: Never trust an LLM to return valid JSON without hard schema enforcement. We leverage provider-native JSON mode alongside strict Pydantic parsing.
  2. Semantic Caching: Exact-match caching is useless for natural language inputs. We require embedding-space distance metrics to serve cached completions for semantically equivalent queries.
  3. Fail-Fast Asynchrony: I/O operations (vector lookups, network calls to inference endpoints) must utilize non-blocking async execution loops to maximize throughput per container instance.

Production-Ready Implementation

Below is a complete, syntax-valid, production-grade FastAPI service demonstrating these concepts. It includes explicit error handling, structured validation, and typed asynchronous models.

from __future__ import annotations

import os
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from typing import Any, List, Optional
import uvicorn
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, status
from openai import AsyncOpenAI
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Configuration & Models
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

OPENAI_API_KEY = os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY", "dummy-key-for-syntax")
client = AsyncOpenAI(api_key=OPENAI_API_KEY)


class GenerationRequest(BaseModel):
    query: str = Field(..., min_length=3, max_length=1000)
    context_tags: List[str] = Field(default_factory=list)


class ExtractedInsight(BaseModel):
    summary: str = Field(..., description="A concise 2-sentence summary of the analysis.")
    confidence_score: float = Field(..., ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    key_entities: List[str] = Field(..., description="Identified technical entities.")


class PipelineResponse(BaseModel):
    cached: bool
    data: ExtractedInsight


# Mock Semantic Cache Layer (In production, back this with Redis / Milvus)
class SemanticCache:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._store: dict[str, ExtractedInsight] = {}

    async def get(self, query: str) -> Optional[ExtractedInsight]:
        # Simulated semantic lookup with O(1) mock check
        return self._store.get(query.strip().lower())

    async def set(self, query: str, insight: ExtractedInsight) -> None:
        self._store[query.strip().lower()] = insight


cache = SemanticCache()

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Application Lifecycle
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    # Initialize connection pools, models, or DB drivers here
    print("Initializing AI Pipeline Engine...")
    yield
    # Teardown logic
    print("Shutting down AI Pipeline Engine...")


app = FastAPI(
    title="Deterministic AI Pipeline",
    version="1.0.0",
    lifespan=lifespan,
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core Pipeline Endpoint
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

@app.post(
    "/v1/analyze",
    response_model=PipelineResponse,
    status_code=status.HTTP_200_OK,
    summary="Execute Deterministic AI Extraction Pipeline",
)
async def execute_pipeline(payload: GenerationRequest) -> PipelineResponse:
    try:
        # 1. Check Semantic Cache
        cached_result = await cache.get(payload.query)
        if cached_result:
            return PipelineResponse(cached=True, data=cached_result)

        # 2. Construct Enforced Prompt Context
        system_prompt = (
            "You are a strict systems analysis engine. "
            "Analyze the provided query and extract technical insights."
        )

        # 3. Execute Async LLM Call with Structured Outputs
        # Note: Utilizing OpenAI's beta parse feature for guaranteed schema alignment
        completion = await client.beta.chat.completions.parse(
            model="gpt-4o-mini",
            messages=[
                {"role": "system", "content": system_prompt},
                {"role": "user", "content": payload.query},
            ],
            response_format=ExtractedInsight,
            temperature=0.0,  # Maximize determinism
        )

        insight = completion.choices[0].message.parsed
        if not insight:
            raise ValueError("Model failed to parse response into expected schema.")

        # 4. Populate Cache
        await cache.set(payload.query, insight)

        return PipelineResponse(cached=False, data=insight)

    except Exception as e:
        # Log error securely in production (omitted for brevity)
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=status.HTTP_500_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR,
            detail=f"Pipeline execution failed: {str(e)}",
        )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    uvicorn.run("main:app", host="0.0.0.0", port=8000, reload=True)

Conclusion

By moving away from unstructured text parsing and adopting strict schema enforcement combined with semantic caching layers, we transform chaotic LLM outputs into robust, enterprise-ready APIs. Setting temperature=0.0, leveraging Pydantic parsers natively via SDKs, and isolating I/O routines into asynchronous patterns ensures that our AI infrastructure matches the reliability standards of traditional distributed systems.

For further exploration of resilient systems engineering, check out my work and repositories on GitHub.

title: OpenAI and AMD Cut Next-Gen GPU Design Time by a Year With 14% PPA Gains
description:
Silicon design cycles usually move at the speed of physics and human verification, taking years to shave single-digit percentages off power, performance, and area (PPA). On November 18, 2026, OpenAI and AMD published concrete evidence that frontier reasoning models are already rewriting production hardware code before tape-out.

In a technical research post, OpenAI disclosed that its models found up to 14% PPA improvements relative to heavily optimized human baselines on AMD's next-generation flagship GPU IP. According to OpenAI, those gains represent roughly a year of microarchitectural progress compressed into less than five months, and AMD has already included part of that work in a chip design sent for manufacturing.

How AI rewrote AMD's SystemVerilog RTL

The collaboration focused on SystemVerilog Register Transfer Level (RTL) code, the hardware description layer that defines how circuits calculate, route data, and manage control logic. Instead of generating speculative toy circuits, OpenAI's models proposed targeted RTL rewrites and validated every change inside Synopsys electronic design automation (EDA) tools to confirm functional equivalence and measure PPA trade-offs.

AMD did not stop at GPUs. OpenAI confirmed that AMD also verified single-digit percentage PPA improvements across key blocks of its upcoming next-generation flagship CPU using model-written designs, feeding additional blocks into production design files for future silicon revisions.

That hardware-level optimization arrives at a moment when AMD is set to outsell Intel and buyers are weighing current desktop upgrades against Zen 6 and Nova Lake roadmaps.

Expand

Macro photograph of a patterned semiconductor silicon wafer reflecting light

Credit: Rob Bulmahn, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

Silicon-proven savings inside OpenAI's Jalapeno chip

OpenAI first tested AI-assisted RTL design on its own custom inference chip, Jalapeno, starting with GPT-o3 mini in early 2025. Even that earlier generation uncovered practical optimizations across floating-point adders, multipliers, conversion units, and reduction logic.

In Jalapeno's matrix unit, one multiplier redesign reduced synthesis standard-cell area by roughly 15% while cutting latency from two clock cycles down to one. A separate floating-point adder redesign also trimmed cell area by about 15% while holding its two-cycle latency. Across the full Jalapeno design, OpenAI estimates AI-proposed changes cut standard-cell area by approximately 13% in the vector unit and 10% in the matrix unit, with those gains proven in actual bring-up silicon.

Hardware Target AI Model / Tooling Measured / Disclosed Gain Production Status
AMD Next-Gen Flagship GPU IP OpenAI models + Synopsys EDA Up to 14% PPA improvement Included in design sent for manufacturing
AMD Next-Gen Flagship CPU OpenAI models + Synopsys EDA Single-digit % PPA gains Added to production design files
OpenAI Jalapeno Vector Unit GPT-o3 mini onward ~13% standard-cell area reduction Silicon proven during chip bring-up
OpenAI Jalapeno Matrix Unit GPT-o3 mini onward ~10% standard-cell area reduction Silicon proven during chip bring-up
PicoRV32 & Ibex RISC-V Cores GPT-6.2 Astra (112K tokens) ~0.7 to 0.75 from spec (9,881 runs) Open-source Yosys simulation benchmark

What 9,881 RISC-V benchmark runs reveal

Because proprietary AMD and Jalapeno RTL cannot be published openly, OpenAI evaluated five model generations across 9,881 scored runs on two open-source 32-bit RISC-V cores: PicoRV32 (targeted at FPGAs) and OpenTitan's Ibex embedded security core. Each design had to pass correctness checks within a strict 16x area cap while maximizing estimated instructions per second via Yosys synthesis.

On both optimizing existing RTL and designing a core from written specifications, GPT-6.2 Astra led at comparable 112,000-token budgets, roughly doubling GPT-6 Astra's mean score on PicoRV32 optimization. Interestingly, all five tested models scored higher when designing a core from scratch against written specifications (reaching ~0.7 on PicoRV32 and ~0.75 on Ibex) than when refactoring existing RTL.

OpenAI candidly noted why: designing from a specification allowed models to drop optional features like performance counters and extra instructions that did not affect the test workloads. Future benchmarks that enforce full feature parity and post-synthesis physical timing will provide a tougher test.

Expand

Close-up of a 12-inch fabricated silicon wafer showing individual die grids

Credit: Peellden, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

What GPT-Synopsys and full-stack AI mean for silicon

OpenAI's disclosure landed two days after Anthropic highlighted in an investor video that Claude Mythos Preview wrote low-level kernel code to run on AMD GPUs in roughly three days compared to 6 to 12 months of engineering work, as MACCUS noted. Together, the announcements show frontier labs applying AI at both ends of the silicon lifecycle: pre-tape-out RTL optimization and post-silicon driver and kernel bring-up.

To formalize the hardware side, OpenAI is partnering with Synopsys to train GPT-Synopsys, a dedicated model built to operate Synopsys EDA verification and synthesis suites directly. While neither AMD nor OpenAI has released raw RTL diffs publicly, shipping AI-optimized blocks into taped-out flagship silicon marks a clear shift from research demos to real foundry wafers.

What AI-designed RTL means for chipmakers and EDA vendors

For semiconductor teams, the biggest takeaway from OpenAI and AMD's November 18 disclosure is that RTL exploration loops can now run orders of magnitude wider before tape-out freezes. Traditional physical design forces engineers to pick a handful of candidate adder, multiplier, or pipeline layouts and spend weeks verifying timing, power, and cell area in synthesis. When an AI model paired with Synopsys EDA evaluators can test thousands of SystemVerilog variants and surface a 14% PPA improvement in under five months, design teams can allocate human review time to architecture-level trade-offs and floorplanning.

At the same time, OpenAI's RISC-V results highlight why strict verification guardrails remain non-negotiable. Because models designing from a bare specification tended to trim optional features like performance counters unless explicitly constrained, production EDA pipelines still depend on formal equivalence checking, synthesis timing closure, and foundry sign-off rules. As GPT-Synopsys matures alongside AMD's upcoming flagship CPU and GPU silicon, buyers and data center operators should expect faster cadence on generation-over-generation efficiency gains instead of multi-year waits between process node shrinks.

For PC builders, cloud buyers, and workstation users watching AMD's roadmap, those silicon-level efficiencies take time to reach retail shelves. Because blocks taped out in late 2026 still pass through foundry fabrication, packaging, and platform validation, the practical impact of AI-assisted SystemVerilog optimization will show up across next-generation flagship GPUs and CPUs arriving in 2027 and beyond.

For hardware engineers evaluating AI-assisted EDA today, the clearest lesson is that model-driven RTL rewrites work best when paired with automated formal equivalence checks and synthesis metrics. Grounding every proposed circuit change in Synopsys verification turns raw token output into measurable silicon savings.

Tracking how AMD integrates those blocks into upcoming Instinct and Radeon architectures will be one of the clearest hardware stories to watch through 2027.
