title: CROSS-Calib: Selective Channel Calibration for Ultrasound Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2611.31684v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ultrasound imaging provides views of internal tissue in real time for medical diagnosis. However, ultrasound signals may be affected by interference, and correcting errors and removing transient interference while preserving valid echoes remains challenging. We propose CROSS-Calib, a channel recovery method that uses predictions from other channels as references for amplitude and phase calibration, while a gate using context selectively combines calibrated measurements with predicted echoes to retain usable samples and repair unreliable ones. On the in vivo test set, CROSS-Calib outperforms all baseline models under gain errors and transient interference, while phantom tests show that the model restores cyst contrast with echo widths of wire targets close to the clean reference. CROSS-Calib can perform channel calibration and selective repair before beamforming to improve echo usability and image quality.

title: Cloudflare-E-Mail-Fehler: E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED, E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED und 429 behoben
description:
Cloudflare-E-Mail-Fehler tauchten am 24. November 2026 in deutlich mehr Logs auf, als Cloudflare E-Mail-Versand im Workers-Free-Plan verfügbar machte. Der Haken steckt in einer Zeile des Changelogs: Im Free-Plan kannst du nur an verifizierte Zieladressen in deinem eigenen Account senden.

Probiere Apidog heute aus

Kurzantwort: E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED bedeutet, dass du im Workers-Free-Plan bist und der Empfänger keine verifizierte Zieladresse ist: verifiziere sie oder upgrade auf Workers Paid – und versuche es niemals erneut. E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED (Workers-Binding), HTTP 429 (REST-API) und 451 4.7.1 (SMTP) bedeuten, dass du das tägliche Sendelimit deines Accounts erreicht hast: stelle die Nachricht in die Warteschlange und versuche es später erneut oder beantrage ein höheres Limit.

Was die Cloudflare-E-Mail-Fehler bedeuten

Der Cloudflare Email Service meldet ein Problem auf drei Wegen: Das Workers-Binding wirft einen String-code, die REST-API liefert einen HTTP-Status plus einen numerischen Code, und SMTP antwortet mit einem Reply-Code. Alle drei teilen sich denselben Satz von Account-Limits.

Problem Workers-Binding REST-API SMTP Erneut versuchen?
Empfänger in deinem Plan nicht erlaubt E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED 403, Code 10208 550 5.7.1 bei RCPT TO Nein
Tägliches Sendelimit erreicht E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED 429 451 4.7.1 Später
Sende- oder Parallelitätslimit E_RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED 429, Code 10004 451 4.7.1 Ja, mit Backoff
Empfänger auf der Suppression-Liste E_RECIPIENT_SUPPRESSED 400 Nachricht abgelehnt Nein
Account wegen Reputation pausiert E_ACCOUNT_SUSPENDED 403, Code 10207 Nicht aufgeführt Nein

Quellen: Cloudflares Limits-Seite, die Workers-API-Fehlercodes und die SMTP-Response-Codes, gelesen am 26. November 2026.

Der entscheidende Punkt: Die REST-Fehlertabelle enthält einen 429-Eintrag, 10004 (email.sending.error.throttled), und SMTP verwendet 451 4.7.1 sowohl für das Ratenlimit als auch für das Tageslimit. Nur das Binding verrät dir, welches Limit du erreicht hast.

E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED im Workers-Free-Plan beheben

E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED ist eine Planregel, kein vorübergehender Fehler. Im Workers-Free-Plan akzeptiert der E-Mail-Versand nur verifizierte Zieladressen in deinem Account. Jede andere Adresse schlägt bei jedem Versuch auf dieselbe Weise fehl – versuche es also niemals erneut.

Es gibt drei Auswege:

  1. Verifiziere die Adresse. Gehe im Dashboard zu Compute > Email Service > Email Routing > Destination Addresses, füge die Adresse hinzu und klicke auf den Link in Cloudflares Bestätigungs-E-Mail. Ein Account kann 200 Zieladressen enthalten.
  2. Upgrade auf Workers Paid. Paid sendet an beliebige Empfänger, mit 3.000 E-Mails pro Monat inklusive und 0,35 USD pro 1.000 danach, laut Email-Service-Preisseite.
  3. Behalte Free für interne Mails. Alerts und Reports an dein eigenes Team passen in Free, und Sendungen an verifizierte Adressen umgehen das Kontingent und die Tageslimits in jedem Plan.

Über SMTP zeigt sich dieselbe Regel früher in der Session. Cloudflare lehnt das unverifizierte RCPT TO mit 550 5.7.1 ab. Wenn dein Client dann trotzdem DATA sendet, schlägt die gesamte Nachricht mit 554 5.7.1 fehl und kein Empfänger erhält sie – auch verifizierte nicht. Teile gemischte Empfängerlisten vor dem Senden auf.

Verwechsle das nicht mit E_RECIPIENT_NOT_ALLOWED, das aus allowed_destination_addresses deines eigenen Bindings stammt.

E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, HTTP 429 und 451 4.7.1 beheben

Neue Accounts starten mit einem konservativen Tageskontingent, das mit deinem Sendeverhalten, deiner Zustellbarkeit und deinem Account-Status wächst. Cloudflare veröffentlicht den Startwert nicht und passt ihn pro Account an.

Behandle ein Tageslimit als „heute nicht“. Schnelle Wiederholungen helfen nicht. Stattdessen:

  • Lege die Nachricht in einer Warteschlange oder Tabelle mit einem not_before-Zeitstempel einige Stunden in der Zukunft ab.
  • Wenn wieder Kapazität verfügbar ist, priorisiere Transaktionsmails (Passwort-Resets, Rechnungen) vor Massenmails.
  • Wenn du mehr Spielraum brauchst, nutze das Formular „Need a higher limit?“ unten auf der Limits-Seite.

Ein Ratenlimit ist etwas anderes: Es ist kurzlebig, daher ist exponentielles Backoff mit Jitter das richtige Werkzeug. Unser Leitfaden zu Retries mit exponentiellem Backoff erklärt die Mathematik, und HTTP 429 Too Many Requests erklärt den Statuscode selbst.

Die Fehler in einem Worker behandeln

Das Binding liefert dir das klarste Signal, also verzweige nach error.code. Dieser Worker wiederholt nur das Ratenlimit, verzögert das Tageslimit und schlägt bei allem Dauerhaften sofort fehl:

const PERMANENT = new Set([
  "E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED", "E_RECIPIENT_NOT_ALLOWED",
  "E_RECIPIENT_SUPPRESSED", "E_VALIDATION_ERROR", "E_ACCOUNT_SUSPENDED",
]);

async function sendEmail(env: Env, msg: EmailMessageBuilder) {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt++) {
    try {
      return { status: "sent", id: (await env.EMAIL.send(msg)).messageId };
    } catch (err: any) {
      if (err instanceof TypeError) return { status: "bad_input", reason: err.message };
      if (err.code === "E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED") return { status: "defer" };
      if (PERMANENT.has(err.code)) return { status: "failed", reason: err.code };
      if (err.code !== "E_RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" && err.code !== "E_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR") throw err;
      const wait = 2 ** attempt * 500 + Math.random() * 250;
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, wait));
    }
  }
  return { status: "defer" };
}

Das Binding ist eine Zeile in wrangler.jsonc: "send_email": [{ "name": "EMAIL" }]. Ein TypeError ohne code bedeutet, dass dein send()-Argument nicht zum Interface passt (kein Empfänger oder eine EmailAddress ohne name): ein Bug, den du beheben musst, kein Sendevorgang zum Wiederholen.

Einen 429 von der REST-API behandeln

Der REST-Endpoint ist POST https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/{account_id}/email/sending/send mit einem Bearer-API-Token. Fehler kommen im Standard-Cloudflare-Envelope zurück, lies also errors[0].code:

const BASE = process.env.CF_API_BASE ?? "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4";

async function sendViaRest(accountId, token, payload, attempt = 0) {
  const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/accounts/${accountId}/email/sending/send`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`, "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(payload),
  });
  const body = await res.json();
  if (body.success) return { status: "sent", id: body.result.message_id };

  const code = body.errors?.[0]?.code;
  if (res.status === 403 && code === 10208) return { status: "failed", reason: "recipient_plan_restricted" };
  if (res.status === 429 || res.status >= 500) {
    if (attempt >= 3) return { status: "defer" };
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 2 ** attempt * 1000 + Math.random() * 500));
    return sendViaRest(accountId, token, payload, attempt + 1);
  }
  return { status: "failed", reason: `${res.status}:${code}` };
}

Da ein REST-429 beide Limits bedeuten kann, begrenze die Wiederholungen und übergib die Nachricht nach der letzten an deine Warteschlange. Das konfigurierbare CF_API_BASE ist später wichtig, wenn du diesen Client auf einen Mock zeigst.

Prüfe auch den Success-Body. Bei aktiviertem Drop suppressed recipients kann ein 200 dennoch Adressen in suppressed_recipients oder permanent_bounces auflisten, und diese Empfänger haben nichts bekommen.

451 4.7.1 und 550 5.7.1 über SMTP behandeln

Cloudflares SMTP-Submission läuft auf smtp.mx.cloudflare.net, Port 465, nur implizites TLS. Der Benutzername ist der Literal-String api_token und das Passwort ist ein API-Token mit Email Sending: Edit. Port 587 mit STARTTLS wird nicht unterstützt.

Mit Nodemailer landet der Reply-Code auf err.responseCode:

import nodemailer from "nodemailer";

const transport = nodemailer.createTransport({
  host: "smtp.mx.cloudflare.net", port: 465, secure: true,
  auth: { user: "api_token", pass: process.env.CF_EMAIL_TOKEN },
});

try {
  await transport.sendMail({ from: "alerts@yourdomain.com", to, subject, text });
} catch (err) {
  if (err.responseCode === 451 || err.responseCode === 421) scheduleRetry(); // temporary
  else if (err.responseCode === 550 || err.responseCode === 554) markFailed(err.response);
  else throw err;
}

Eine 4xx-Antwort ist vorübergehend; eine 5xx ist dauerhaft. 535 5.7.8 bedeutet ein falscher Benutzername oder Token, und 550 5.7.1 Sender denied bedeutet, dass die MAIL FROM-Domain nicht unter dem Account des Tokens onboarded ist.

Wann wiederholen und wann aufhören

Die Entscheidung läuft auf eine Frage hinaus: Wird dieselbe Anfrage später erfolgreich sein, ohne dass du etwas änderst?

Suppression-Fehler verdienen Aufmerksamkeit. Cloudflare unterdrückt eine Adresse nach Hard Bounces (7 Tage, oder ohne Ablauf, wenn das Postfach nicht existiert), Soft Bounces (standardmäßig 24 Stunden) und validierten Spam-Beschwerden (kein Ablauf). Laut den Suppression-List-Docs zählen unterdrückte Sendungen nicht zu deinem Kontingent und erscheinen als Rejected in den Logs. Wiederhole keine solche Sendung und lösche eine Beschwerde-Suppression nicht, bevor die Person erneut einwilligt.

Du suchst noch einen Anbieter? Sieh dir unseren Überblick zu kostenlosen E-Mail-APIs an.

Die Fehlerpfade mit der Apidog CLI aus deinem Coding-Agent testen

Fehlerzweige werden am wenigsten getestet, weil ein echter 429 schwer auszulösen ist und ein echtes Tageslimit einen Tag kostet. Lass deinen Coding-Agent die Fehlerfälle stattdessen mit der Apidog CLI bauen: Mock-Expectations liefern Cloudflares exakte Fehler-Bodies, und dein Client läuft dagegen.

Installiere die CLI und den Agent-Skill einmalig:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

Dann gib deinem Agent einen Prompt:

In Apidog project <id>, add Cloudflare's POST /accounts/{account_id}/email/sending/send
endpoint with 200, 403 and 429 responses. Create mock expectations: when the body "to"
is stranger@example.com, return 403 with errors[0].code 10208; when header X-Scenario is
throttle, return 429 with errors[0].code 10004. Then list the endpoint and its mocks.

Der Agent findet den Endpoint, liest das Payload-Schema, validiert sein JSON und schreibt die Mocks:

apidog endpoint list --project <id> --method POST
apidog cli-schema get mock-create
apidog cli-schema validate mock-create --file mock-403.json
apidog mock create --project <id> --file mock-403.json
apidog mock list --project <id>

Richte CF_API_BASE auf die Mock-URL des Projekts, die im Endpoint in Apidog angezeigt wird, und führe die Tests deines REST-Clients aus. Der 403-Fall sollte recipient_plan_restricted ohne Wiederholungen zurückgeben, und der Throttle-Fall sollte dreimal wiederholen und dann verzögern. Wenn der echte Endpoint angebunden ist, kann der Agent Testfälle erstellen und sie mit apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <id> -e <envId> -r cli,junit ausführen. Der Leitfaden Apidog CLI in Claude Code führt durch diesen Loop.

Wenn diese Agent-Runs erst einmal Teil deiner Woche sind, kannst du sie mit Sharkly als Tasks auf einem Board an dein Team verteilen: Jeder Coding-Agent, auch Claude Code und Codex, läuft auf deinem eigenen Rechner mit deinem eigenen Plan, und du prüfst, was er abliefert, bevor es gemergt wird. Der Einstieg ist kostenlos.

Fazit

Diese Fehler verlangen gegensätzliche Reaktionen. E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED ist dauerhaft, bis du die Adresse verifizierst oder auf Workers Paid wechselst – also schlage schnell fehl. E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, 429 und 451 4.7.1 drehen sich um Volumen – also verzögere und versuche es später erneut. Teste beide Pfade, bevor du deine erste echte Sendung verschickst.

FAQ

Funktioniert der Cloudflare Email Sending im Workers-Free-Plan? Ja, seit dem 24. November 2026, aber nur an verifizierte Zieladressen in deinem Account. Das Senden an alle anderen erfordert Workers Paid.

Wie viele E-Mails kann ich pro Tag senden? Cloudflare veröffentlicht keine feste Zahl. Neue Accounts starten mit einem konservativen Tageslimit, das mit der Reputation steigt, und du kannst über das Formular auf der Limits-Seite eine Erhöhung beantragen.

Zählen Sendungen an verifizierte Adressen zu meinem Kontingent? Nein. Sendungen an verifizierte Zieladressen sind in jedem Plan kostenlos und zählen nicht zum monatlichen Kontingent oder zu den täglichen Sendelimits.

Sollte ich einen 429 von der Cloudflare Email REST API erneut versuchen? Ja, einige Male mit exponentiellem Backoff und Jitter. Wenn er bestehen bleibt, gehe davon aus, dass du das Tageslimit erreicht hast, und verschiebe die Nachricht in eine aufgeschobene Warteschlange.

Warum ist meine SMTP-Sendung mit 554 5.7.1 fehlgeschlagen? Ein Empfänger wurde bei RCPT TO mit 550 5.7.1 abgelehnt, meist eine unverifizierte Adresse im Workers-Free-Plan, und dein Client hat trotzdem DATA gesendet. Cloudflare lehnt dann die gesamte Nachricht ab.

title: An unreadable log file now stops caddy-analyze with exit 1
description:
On 26 November 2026, GitHub Trending's daily list is led by agent tooling: cursor/plugins gained 416 stars that day, mvanhorn/last30days-skill gained 945, google-labs-code/stitch-skills gained 355, and mjmirza/app-store-compliance gained 858. Trendshift's weekly list for the same date shows three coding-agent CLIs gaining the most stars that week: pingdotgg/t3code +7.9k, stablyai/orca +5.1k, and google-gemini/gemini-api-cli +2.5k (weekly gains, not totals; totals on 26 November were 79.5k, 138.1k and 3.2k). Hacker News' front page carries an agent essay at 929 points. The causal link to this article is short: when scripts and agents are the main callers of a CLI, the exit status is the only machine readable proof that the work ran, so a tool that prints an error and exits 0 is a silent failure in the control plane.

lenny-ts/caddy-analyzer#150 is one concrete case. caddy-analyzer is a zero-dependency Go CLI with 45 stars for analysing Caddy v2 access logs. It was failing exactly that contract.

The reproduction

Issue #136, opened 17 November 2026, gives a two-line reproduction:

caddy-analyze /tmp/this-file-does-not-exist.log
echo $?

The reported output was an error line followed by no log entries found, and the printed status was 0. The issue's acceptance criteria ask for four things: a non-zero status for a missing or unreadable file, an error that identifies the file, defined and tested behaviour for partial failures across several inputs, and tests for missing and unreadable files.

The cause sits in pkg/reader/reader.go. FileReader.Read started a reader goroutine and printed errors from inside it, but returned no error to its caller. runOnceMode in cmd/root.go had nothing to propagate, so the command ended as a successful empty analysis.

The change

The pull request was opened by Indra Prasetya and merged on 21 November 2026. Four commits are in the branch. The first two, d96bc9c and 1676a03, are authored by Indra Prasetya. The last two, including the head commit a807e0a, are authored by maintainer lenny-ts. The repository belongs to the maintainer. The final merge includes his follow-up work on read errors in followed logs, so this is a joint branch rather than a claim that every commit is mine.

The diff is 6 files, +188 and -15 lines:

File Added Removed
pkg/reader/reader.go 58 11
pkg/reader/follow_cancel_test.go 53 0
cmd/root.go 37 2
cmd/top.go 26 2
pkg/reader/reader_test.go 12 0
cmd/fanin_test.go 2 0

At the merge head, FileReader.Read checks every path with os.Stat before it starts the goroutine. Missing paths are recorded through a sync.Once guard, which keeps the first error, and the available paths still stream. If no path is available, Read returns the error immediately. The interface also gains an Err() method so a streaming error can be read after the lines channel drains. runOnceMode returns that error, which is what turns it into exit 1.

The missing-path branch now reaches the process exit code.

Using os.Stat rather than open and close is deliberate. An input can be a FIFO, and opening it twice would block the second attempt. The partial failure rule is now explicit: readable inputs are still analysed, the first open error is preserved, and the command exits non-zero.

The verification

The pull request reports three checks: go test ./pkg/reader/... passed in 0.42s, go test ./cmd/... passed in 0.02s, and go build ./... produced no output. Those are the figures recorded in the PR, not measurements I repeated on this host.

The before and after pair is the part that matters for automation. Before the change, a missing input printed a message and echo $? returned 0. After the change, the same command reports error reading /tmp/this-file-does-not-exist.log: open /tmp/this-file-does-not-exist.log: no such file or directory, and echo $? returns 1. A caller can now branch on the status and still read the filename from stderr.

Two details came from the maintainer's commits, not the original patch. Follow mode with several files reads them concurrently, because a blocked first file used to starve the rest. The Err() method was added so errors raised after streaming starts are not lost. Both are visible in the six-file diff at a807e0a.

What the trend means here

The agent tooling wave makes the command line a machine-facing interface. A human sees no log entries found and moves on; a cron job or an agent sees only the status code. This fix changes one line of that contract, from 0 to 1, and it took 6 files and 4 commits because the error had to travel from a goroutine through the reader interface to the command entry point. That is the honest size of a small reliability fix in a tool with several input sources.

Issue #136 remains closed. The four acceptance criteria are covered by the new tests and the recorded behaviour, including the partial failure case that the issue asked to define.

Sources: caddy-analyzer#150, its merge head a807e0a and issue #136, retrieved 26 November 2026. Trend sources: Trendshift weekly, GitHub Trending daily, Hacker News and dev.to trending, retrieved 26 November 2026.

title: Scalpel and Brush: Pruning and Targeted Weight Editing of a Small Language Model by a Single LLM Agent
description:
arXiv:2611.33426v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: It has recently been shown that an LLM can itself edit the weights of a language model, yet it remains unclear which part of such a result is due to the agent and which part is reproduced by a random edit of the same shape, by an instruction in the prompt, or by a standard procedure without an LLM. We unify repair and pruning as sparse weight edits to optimize a metric we specify, using BLEU as an example: three tasks -- targeted weight repair ("brush"), structured MLP neuron pruning ("scalpel", zeroing pruned weights), and layer removal with repair - are assigned to a DeepSeek Harness agent powered by DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, with up to 50 dev evaluations. We study Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct in three independent runs per task, with final evaluation on two hidden splits. On ordinary differential equations, changing at most 0.0084% of weights raised test BLEU by 24-32% on second-order equations and by a factor of 1.8-2.5 on equations with polynomial right-hand sides. An independent substitution check showed that higher BLEU reflects notation alignment rather than improved correctness. Masks that remove 12.5-15% of MLP neurons shrink the model by 9.4-11.2% with mean BLEU loss of at most 0.01 on both hidden splits, whereas standard pruning with equal shares per layer failed the constraint at all tested shares. On seven-class GoEmotions classification, edits raise macro-F1 from 0.100 to 0.396-0.451 on test and from 0.175 to 0.455-0.476 on holdout. A ridge-based classifier written into agent-selected weight rows yields macro-F1 of 0.424 and 0.464. Pruning search with the same evaluation limit removes 15.9% of neurons versus 14-21.4% for agent runs passing the hidden check. Standard procedures without an LLM reproduce much of the performance once given the location and form of intervention found by the agent; a comparison of agentic and non-agentic search remains open.

title: Antares-Smaug: Adversarial Names, Tokens and Attack Rewrites: Sanitisers Miss Unseen Generalisations
description:
arXiv:2611.31347v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Laya is an open decision model: given a text, a question and K named options with descriptions, it returns one probability per option in a single pass, and software may act on the answer unseen. We attack six Laya models with 81 programmatic edits of 566 synthetic items (injected sentences, label leaks, edited descriptions, decoy options, invisible and look-alike characters, floods) and report the share of correctly answered items hijacked or lost, with bootstrap intervals. Attack wordings that no defence was built from win the attacker's option on 59% of items for released Laya and 36% for fine-tune v1 (trained on 109 written injections). An injection works through the option name: a sentence naming an option steers the released model even when negated (32%), while an imperative naming no option does not (5%). Option descriptions barely matter (2%). Character edits alone cost v1 up to 72% of right answers. A sanitiser frozen before any held-out result cuts the attacks it was built from by 72% but held-out sentence attacks by 27%, and an attacker who picks the best of 34 held-out strings per item restores success to 84% (mean string 18%). The same oracle takes the model fine-tuned on the four build families of injected sentences from 5% (mean string) to 58%. Fine-tuning on build families only (against an unchanged-rows control) cuts held-out sentence attacks (three held-out families) from 33% to 3% but character edits only from 25% to 20%. A label-free check that deletes the option names and measures the shift flags held-out sentence attacks (AUROC 0.95) but not character edits (0.46), and thresholds set on dev schemas for 5% false alarms gave 8% to 18% on an unseen schema and other languages. All data are synthetic with LLM labels, on one backbone. Several planned runs (other checkpoints, a second seed, some fine-tunes) were not run.

Project Connections let applications evaluate flags defined in another Vercel project within the same team, without managing SDK keys.

Previously, sharing flags between projects required copying a server SDK key into an environment variable and managing it manually. Connected projects authenticate using their deployment’s identity. For local development, vercel env pull retrieves your project’s OIDC token.

Manage access from the Connections page under your project's Flags section, or with vercel flags connections in the CLI. Connections grant read-only access across all environments. The consumer deployment determines the flag environment (production deployments evaluate production flags).

In the consumer application, create an adapter with the source project’s ID.

Access can be revoked without redeploying.

Project Connections are available on all plans and require @flags-sdk/vercel 1.6.0 or later, or @vercel/flags-core 1.11.0 or later when using the core library directly. Managing connections from the CLI requires Vercel CLI 63.0.0 or later.

title: No Fixed Configuration Is Best: Context- and Cost-Aware Tuning of LLM Pipelines, with an Application to Schema Matching and Mapping
description:
arXiv:2611.31864v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The numeric settings of a multi-stage LLM pipeline (a compound AI system) are the usual target of tuning. We tuned all of them for an LLM pipeline for schema matching and mapping, with accuracy and cost as joint objectives, and we show what this buys, what it cannot buy, and where the remaining accuracy is. First, tuning buys cost and a little accuracy. On 35 tasks, with whole groups of tasks held out from tuning, one tuned configuration gains 2.9 points of top-1 accuracy (HR@1) over the default at 18% more cost, and another keeps the accuracy of the default at 32% lower cost. Second, the accuracy depends on a choice that numeric tuning cannot reach. Restricting the search for each source column to one assigned target table changes HR@1 by +30 points on a MIMIC-III to OMOP task and by -52 points on a task built from database views, more than numeric tuning gains on nine of ten test tasks. Neither setting is right for all tasks: on the larger set of 41 tasks used for the remaining results, mean HR@1 is 75.7% with the restriction (the default) and 83.1% without it. Third, choosing the setting per task is not enough either: even an oracle that picks the better setting for each task reaches only 87.8% on the 41 tasks, because the better setting differs between the columns of one task. The pipeline therefore runs both settings, and an LLM judge chooses among their candidate answers on the 26% of columns on which they disagree. This reaches 91.5% HR@1 on the 41 tasks, at 5.9 times the cost of the default, about one cent per column.

title: EgoCARBS: Egocentric Video Meets Active Acoustics for Kitchen Action Understanding
description:
arXiv:2611.33565v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Egocentric video records what a person looks at, but often misses what their body does: the hands leave the frame, and arm motion goes unseen. An exocentric camera recovers this context, but it must be installed wherever the activity happens. Active acoustic sensing can recover it from the wearables themselves: a device's speaker emits inaudible chirps, and its microphone senses the motion of the hands, arms, and nearby objects from their echoes. Yet no public dataset pairs it with egocentric video. We present EgoCARBS, with two deliverables. The first is a multimodal dataset and benchmark: 15 participants cook unscripted meals in their own kitchens wearing camera glasses and an off-the-shelf smartwatch that both sense with active acoustics, synchronized with egocentric and exocentric video and the watch's audio and IMU, with 4,019 verb-noun action annotations in 11.4 hours. The second is a study of what the wearables add to egocentric video. On verb recognition, they add at least as much as an exocentric camera for participants seen in training, and even more for new participants, for whom the exocentric camera does not help. Active acoustics alone provides most of this gain, and helps most where the camera does not see the hands. Trimmed action recognition, detection, and anticipation remain open. We will release the data, our data collection and annotation tools, and pre-trained models.

title: Your Watchdog Stops Stuck Threads With Thread.stop and Java 21 Throws Instead
description:
The report server
has a watchdog.

Every minute
it looks for report threads
that have run too long,
and kills them.

if (elapsed > limit) {
worker.stop();
}

Some reports
hang on a bad query.

Some loop forever
on bad data.

The watchdog
has kept the server alive
since 2014.

Then the upgrade.

Java 17
to Java 21.

Tests green.

The first stuck report
did not die.

The watchdog
threw instead:

java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException

The exception
was logged
inside the watchdog's own loop,
once a minute,
and the stuck thread
kept its connection
and its memory.

By the afternoon
there were thirty of them.

Here is what changed.

Thread.stop
was deprecated
in Java 1.2,
in 1998.

It was never safe.

It throws ThreadDeath
wherever the thread happens to be,
and releases every lock
it holds,
mid-update.

Java 18 marked it
for removal.

Java 20
turned it into a method
that only throws.

It still compiles,
with a warning
nobody reads.

It still links.

It just
does nothing useful,
loudly.

The tests passed
because nothing in them
ever got stuck.

Here is what to do.

Find every call first.

The JDK ships a tool for it:

jdeprscan --for-removal --release 21 app.jar

Then replace force
with interruption.

future.cancel(true)

interrupts the thread.

Blocking calls
throw InterruptedException.

Long loops
must check
Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()
and leave.

Give the query
its own timeout
on the statement,
so the database ends it
instead of you.

For code you cannot change,
a library that loops
and never checks,
run it in a separate process
with a deadline,
and destroy the process.

Processes can be killed.

The operating system
takes back
the memory,
the connections
and the locks.

Threads, in Java,
no longer can be.

A method that only throws
looks like a feature
right up until
the day you need it.

Search for the ones
your emergencies depend on
before you upgrade.

– Serguey Asael Shinder
