title: OrdiHand-GS: Ordinal-Guided Tracking and Hand-Refined Gaussian Avatars for Digital Signers
description:
arXiv:2611.33465v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Digital signers, also known as signing avatars, convey sign language through animated virtual humans, where visual fidelity and linguistic intelligibility hinge primarily on the hands. When one hand crosses over the other, two failure modes dominate. First, monocular expressive-human tracking suffers from ordinal depth ambiguity: either hand can satisfy the same 2D landmarks, and the baseline tracker orders wrists at chance level on 365 annotated overlapping frames from How2Sign. Second, hand appearance remains blurred in neural rendering even after geometry is corrected. We propose OrdiHand-GS to address these errors separately. Relative depth from a video depth estimator and apparent hand size vote, with confidence weighting and abstention, for a front-back relation, which enters expressive-human tracking as a hinge on median hand-surface depth. A source-conditioned residual head then refines the local positions of hand-associated UV Gaussians with the avatar backbone and renderer frozen. We instantiate the framework with GUAVA. Against matched unconstrained refinement, wrist-order accuracy rises from 32.9% to 77.3% at a cost of 0.39 pixels of reprojection error, while a random-sign placebo gives no balanced-accuracy gain. A 2x2 factorial evaluation attributes most of the interaction-rendering improvement to tracking-stage refinement, with a smaller additional benefit from the residual.

title: What I learned building twelve 3D temples for a website nobody asked for
description:
I wanted to see whether a cultural site could feel like somewhere instead of documentation.

So I built Twelve Halls: twelve temples, each with its own deity, each answering one kind of question — love, money, work, health, travel, family. You land in front of a door. You push it. The incense lights, the room opens, and you can ask a question drawn from a Chinese astrological chart.

This is not a launch post. It is a list of things that turned out to matter.

1. A door is worth more than a menu

The first version was a grid of twelve cards, like every other site. The bounce told the story. So I rebuilt the entry as a 3D door you push open. Same content, same links. People started entering halls.

The lesson isn't "use 3D". It's that one small physical gesture does more for attention than a well-designed list.

2. Texture budget is the whole game

Each hall is a single scene with pre-baked lighting. Target: a few hundred kilobytes per hall, so a phone on 4G loads it without a spinner. That meant WebP, aggressive compression, and a separate smaller texture set for phones — and giving up reflections nobody would see at 6cm.

// rough budget per hall
// scene: 1 pre-baked equirect-equivalent background
// + deity plate + particle layer
// mobile: 1024px texture set, desktop: 2048px

3. The reading has to quote its source

The chart side is Zi Wei Dou Shu: twelve palaces, fourteen major stars, four transformations. It runs entirely in the browser — birth data never leaves the device. That is both a privacy decision and an honesty one.

But the part I care about is citation. Every reading quotes the classical passage it leans on, with volume and section, from public-domain editions. Not because it makes the reading true, but because it lets the reader argue with it.

4. A wishing tree beats a spinner

The site has a tree where visitors hang wishes. It began as decoration. It ended up being the thing people write to me about — reading strangers' wishes turns out to be more compelling than any feature I designed.

5. Bilingual is not translation

English and Chinese are not two files of the same text. The Chinese page assumes familiar vocabulary; the English page has to explain what a palace is before using the word. Same site, different teaching.

No metrics to sell. If you want to walk through it: h00ai.com — free, no account.

The classical library, if you care more about the source texts than the 3D: h00ai.com/en/classics

Happy to answer anything about the rendering approach, the calendar math, or the source texts.

title: Implementing CAPTCHA and Email Verification for 3 Go Signup Gates
description:
CAPTCHA spends user patience to reduce automated signup volume; email verification spends another interaction to establish mailbox control. For an edtech application offering email and password accounts, that trade is usually justified when bulk registration threatens enrollment capacity. TL;DR: use CAPTCHA before admitting expensive signup work, require email verification before activation, and cap accounts per address. Neither check makes a student trustworthy or establishes school membership, and a person controlling many mailboxes can pass both.

Consider a bounded production rehearsal: I would model a course launch receiving 100 signup attempts per second, then ask what happens if a successful challenge immediately produces an active session. Those are planning assumptions, not an observed incident. The dangerous transition is easy to miss: a volume check has become permission to access course resources, even though the application has not established mailbox control or decided what that account may read. Adding an email check repairs one boundary; it does not turn the signup flow into an authorization system.

Keep the boundary.

The lesson is an invariant: each gate must authorize only the next piece of work for which it supplies evidence. A challenge admits a signup attempt. Mailbox verification admits activation under the application's policy. An authenticated session still needs authorization before it can read a student's work. This distinction is worth more than an impressive bot score when someone has to defend the enrollment SLO during a launch.

Does CAPTCHA or email verification stop fake signups better?

CAPTCHA is the volume control. Email verification is the mailbox-control check. They fail against different attacks, so declaring one the universal winner hides the operational question: which unwanted work should the application refuse, and at which point can it refuse it?

A challenge can reject automated attempts before those attempts consume downstream capacity. It does not establish identity. Email verification rejects applicants who cannot prove access to the address they supplied, but an operator who controls a disposable mailbox can complete that verification. Calling the resulting account a verified person would overstate the evidence.

A human with many mailboxes can pass both.

That leaves two distinct limits to design. A per-address account cap prevents repeated creation against the same address; it does not stop a mailbox farm. A broader admission policy must bound attempted work too, because even failed registration can consume challenge validation, email delivery, storage, and support capacity. Neither a CAPTCHA widget nor an email code substitutes for that budget.

For the rehearsal above, suppose 20 percent of 100 attempts per second reach the email stage. That produces a planning load of 20 email operations per second before retries, resends, and bursts; it is an assumption to test, not a provider throughput claim. Provisioning only for successful account creations would miss the work that rejected applicants already caused. Measure attempts at each boundary, and include resend behavior in the capacity model before choosing dependency limits.

Define an SLO for legitimate signup completion and track challenge abandonment separately from email completion. Track sign-in and session establishment separately as well. A low completion rate could mean successful abuse rejection, inaccessible challenges, or delayed mail; collapsing those outcomes into one availability number makes the dashboard easier to read and the on-call decision harder to make.

Buy versus build follows the evidence boundary

The useful comparison is between responsibilities, rather than a row of products all pretending to solve the same problem. A challenge provider and an authentication platform can both belong in the design. Buying either still leaves the platform team responsible for deciding when an account becomes active and what an authenticated student can access.

Option Responsibility to evaluate Suitable when Limitation and work retained
Cloudflare Turnstile Managed challenge with server-side validation The team wants to buy challenge operation Does not establish mailbox control; admission and activation policy remain application responsibilities
Google reCAPTCHA Managed bot assessment The team wants a managed abuse signal A challenge or assessment result is not a student's identity; the application must decide how the signal affects enrollment
Supabase Auth Email and password authentication with email confirmation The application wants authentication in that platform Confirmation proves mailbox access, while per-address policy and course authorization still need explicit decisions
Auth0 Managed application authentication The team wants to buy identity-service operation Signup admission and course-access policy remain application responsibilities; buying authentication does not identify a student
Keycloak Self-hosted identity management with email verification Operational control is worth running the identity service Deployment, upgrades, capacity planning, and signup abuse policy add on-call work
Application-owned admission policy Combines trusted evidence with account limits The platform needs explicit control over activation Requires durable state, concurrency control, security review, and an owner for the policy

Infrai combines a self-describing REST API with one key, one wallet, one bill across 295 routes and 20 modules. Public discovery exposes request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so wiring the verification handoff begins with reading its contract rather than learning another SDK; examples in 10 languages include Go. The single key reduces credential wiring when enrollment needs authentication and other backend operations, while public schemas let the platform team inspect the contract before configuring credentials.

That convenience has a boundary. A shared backend provider concentrates dependency and credential decisions, whereas separate services let the platform choose challenge and identity components independently. Neither arrangement establishes a measured availability advantage here. Choose on the operations the team is willing to own, the evidence its policy requires, and the consequences of dependency concentration.

The runnable path below exercises the application policy first, then shows the verification transport. It makes no assumptions about provider request fields or response shapes.

Implement the 3 gates before connecting the signup flow

First, make challenge acceptance a prerequisite for progressing through signup. Second, require mailbox-control evidence bound to the same attempt and email address before activation. Third, enforce the per-address account cap atomically with account creation. Running both verification checks adds one verification call compared with using only one; the cap is application state rather than another identity claim.

Save this program as main.go and run it with go run main.go. It executes all three steps locally using explicitly simulated evidence, including a rejected challenge, an unverified mailbox, a successful admission, an idempotent retry, and a second attempt against the same address. The program is an executable policy rehearsal, not a password store or a provider client.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Evidence struct {
    AttemptID string
    Email string
    CaptchaOK bool
    EmailOK bool
    Expires time.Time
}

type Account struct {
    ID int
    Email string
}

type Admission struct {
    mu sync.Mutex
    byAttempt map[string]Account
    byEmail map[string]Account
}

func (a *Admission) admit(attempt, email string, e Evidence, now time.Time) (Account, error) {
    a.mu.Lock()
    defer a.mu.Unlock()
    if existing, ok := a.byAttempt[attempt]; ok {
        if existing.Email != email {
            return Account{}, fmt.Errorf("attempt reused with another address")
        }
        return existing, nil
    }
    if attempt == "" || email == "" || e.AttemptID != attempt || e.Email != email {
        return Account{}, fmt.Errorf("evidence binding rejected")
    }
    if !now.Before(e.Expires) {
        return Account{}, fmt.Errorf("evidence expired")
    }
    if !e.CaptchaOK {
        return Account{}, fmt.Errorf("challenge gate rejected")
    }
    if !e.EmailOK {
        return Account{}, fmt.Errorf("mailbox gate rejected")
    }
    if _, exists := a.byEmail[email]; exists {
        return Account{}, fmt.Errorf("per-address account cap reached")
    }
    account := Account{ID: len(a.byEmail) + 1, Email: email}
    a.byAttempt[attempt] = account
    a.byEmail[email] = account
    return account, nil
}

func main() {
    now := time.Now()
    admission := Admission{
        byAttempt: make(map[string]Account),
        byEmail: make(map[string]Account),
    }
    email := "student@example.org"
    cases := []struct {
        attempt string
        captcha bool
        mailbox bool
    }{
        {"launch-a", false, false},
        {"launch-b", true, false},
        {"launch-c", true, true},
        {"launch-c", true, true},
        {"launch-d", true, true},
    }
    for _, c := range cases {
        evidence := Evidence{
            AttemptID: c.attempt,
            Email: email,
            CaptchaOK: c.captcha,
            EmailOK: c.mailbox,
            Expires: now.Add(5 * time.Minute),
        }
        account, err := admission.admit(c.attempt, email, evidence, now)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Println(c.attempt, err)
            continue
        }
        fmt.Println(c.attempt, "admitted account", account.ID)
    }
}

Read the result as a decision check: the first two attempts must be refused, the next two must return the same account ID, and the last must hit the address cap. The five-minute evidence lifetime is a local policy choice for this exercise, not a vendor token lifetime. The booleans are fixtures. In an integration, only trusted server-side verification may supply those values; accepting them from a browser would let an attacker manufacture approval.

Notice the retry path. A repeated operation returns its existing account instead of applying the creation again, while reuse against another address is rejected. It returns a creation result, not a session or permission to read an account. The caller must retain the same operation identity across retries, and authentication must remain a separate decision.

The mutex makes checking the cap and recording creation atomic inside this one process. It does not coordinate replicas. Before putting the policy behind multiple application instances, move those invariants into durable transactions and uniqueness constraints, and define an email comparison policy instead of assuming raw string equality is enough. A restart erases these maps. Shipping that storage model would lose both the cap and retry protection precisely when a deployment or incident makes retries likely.

The code checks evidence before admission; the surrounding workflow must also place CAPTCHA before expensive downstream work. A final activation check alone cannot protect the email budget if every rejected applicant has already triggered delivery. Account creation, password handling, email delivery, and session issuance are integration responsibilities outside this local program.

For the provider handoff, save the following separate Go program as verify.go and run it with go run verify.go. Set INFRAI_API_ORIGIN to the documented HTTPS API origin, without a trailing slash, and INFRAI_API_KEY to a server credential. Set CAPTCHA_VERIFY_BODY and EMAIL_VERIFY_BODY to complete JSON request bodies from public discovery's respective schemas, and set CAPTCHA_OPERATION and EMAIL_OPERATION to distinct stable operation IDs retained across retries. Supply only requests bound to the same trusted signup attempt. No request fields are guessed here.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func required(name string) string {
    value := os.Getenv(name)
    if value == "" { panic("missing " + name) }
    return value
}

func verify(client *http.Client, route, body, operation string) ([]byte, error) {
    if !json.Valid([]byte(body)) { return nil, fmt.Errorf("invalid JSON request") }
    origin := required("INFRAI_API_ORIGIN")
    if !strings.HasPrefix(origin, "https://") {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("HTTPS origin required")
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        request, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, origin+route, bytes.NewBufferString(body))
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer " + required("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        request.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        request.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", operation)
        response, err := client.Do(request)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        payload, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(response.Body, 2<<20))
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := response.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 30 { return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry deferred beyond local budget") }
                if requested := time.Duration(seconds)*time.Second; requested > delay {
                    delay = requested
                }
            } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if requested := time.Until(deadline); requested > delay { delay = requested }
            }
            if delay > 30*time.Second { return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry deferred beyond local budget") }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("verification status %d: %s", response.StatusCode, payload)
        }
        return payload, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10*time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(_ *http.Request, _ []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    checks := []struct { route, body, operation string }{
        {"/v1/captcha/verify", "CAPTCHA_VERIFY_BODY", "CAPTCHA_OPERATION"},
        {"/v1/auth/email/verify", "EMAIL_VERIFY_BODY", "EMAIL_OPERATION"},
    }
    for _, check := range checks {
        payload, err := verify(client, check.route, required(check.body), required(check.operation))
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        fmt.Printf("%s result requires schema validation: %s\n", check.body, payload)
    }
}

This is a transport inspection program: it performs the two verification calls and prints their responses, but creates no account and grants no access. Don't run it with production student data on a shared terminal. HTTP success alone must never populate the policy's approval booleans; a production adapter must evaluate the documented verification result, bind it to the attempt and address, and reject missing or negative evidence. The program intentionally cannot activate an account without that adapter. In the live workflow, perform the challenge first and continue only after its result is accepted; email verification happens after the applicant has completed the email step.

The four-attempt retry limit and 30-second maximum wait are local budgets. A longer Retry-After defers the operation rather than retrying early. Stable operation IDs express retry intent, but token reuse and idempotency guarantees must still be checked against each capability's contract; a shared header convention is not proof that every verification operation is replayable.

When should legitimate enrollment take a different path?

The recommendation applies to public signup where automated volume is a credible capacity risk. It should not become a demand that every authenticated student solve a challenge on every ordinary sign-in. An invitation-based enrollment flow has different admission evidence, and a platform with meaningful accessibility requirements needs a usable recovery path when a legitimate applicant cannot complete the challenge.

Preserve the security boundary when reducing friction: removing a challenge from a trusted enrollment path need not remove mailbox verification or course authorization. Conversely, requiring both checks does not justify granting an unrestricted session, promising the elimination of disposable accounts, or claiming protection against a human operating many addresses. Set activation and session policy explicitly, then measure how much legitimate enrollment it costs.

The acceptance criterion is concrete: unwanted signup work stays within the platform's capacity budget, legitimate students can complete enrollment within its SLO, and each account receives only the access its evidence supports.

Sources

References for the authentication boundaries and alternatives discussed above:

  • OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • Cloudflare Turnstile server-side validation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/get-started/server-side-validation/
  • Google reCAPTCHA server-side verification: https://developers.google.com/recaptcha/docs/verify
  • Supabase password-based authentication: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/passwords
  • Auth0 authentication documentation: https://auth0.com/docs/authenticate
  • Keycloak server administration guide: https://www.keycloak.org/docs/latest/server_admin/index.html

title: Spring Beans Explained: Component, Service, Repository and Scope
description:
When I started learning Spring Boot, I kept seeing annotations like @Component, @Service, and @Repository everywhere.

Initially, I thought they were just different ways of telling Spring to create objects. But then I started wondering:

  • Why do we need three different annotations?
  • What exactly is a Spring Bean?
  • Why does Spring create only one object by default?
  • What is the difference between DAO and Repository?
  • How should I organize my Spring Boot application?

These questions might look simple, but understanding them makes a huge difference when you start building real backend applications.

In this post, we'll understand these concepts step by step using a small library application.

Versions used in this post:

  • Java 17
  • Spring Boot 4.2.0
  • Spring Framework 7.1.0

The examples use Java 17-compatible syntax, so the concepts also apply to earlier Spring Boot projects that support Java 17.

Table of contents

  • First understand Spring beans
    • A Java object is not automatically a Spring bean
    • How Spring finds classes with component scanning
  • @Component
  • @Service
  • @Repository
  • DAO and Repository
  • @Scope("prototype")
    • Singleton is the default
    • What prototype actually means
    • The singleton and prototype trap
  • Ideal Layer Structure for a Spring Boot Application
    • The responsibility of each layer
    • A request travels through the layers
    • A practical package structure
  • What else belongs in this foundation
    • Constructor injection
    • Keep services stateless
  • Which one should I use?
  • Common mistakes
  • Quick recap
  • Try it yourself

First understand Spring beans

Before jumping into annotations, let's understand something important.

What exactly is a Spring Bean?

A Spring Bean is simply a Java object that is created, configured, and managed by the Spring IoC container.

Let's understand what that means.

A Java object is not automatically a Spring bean

Consider a normal Java class:

public class BookService {

    public void getBooks() {
        System.out.println("Fetching books...");
    }
}

We can create its object using the new keyword:

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        BookService service = new BookService();

        service.getBooks();
    }
}

Output:

Fetching books...

This is a perfectly valid Java program.

But there is one important thing missing.

Spring doesn't know anything about the service object we created using new.

We created that object ourselves, so we are responsible for managing it.

Now imagine an application with hundreds of classes. Some classes depend on other classes, and those classes depend on even more classes.

Managing all these objects manually becomes difficult.

This is where Spring comes in.

What problem does Spring solve?

Spring takes responsibility for creating objects and connecting their dependencies.

This is called Inversion of Control (IoC).

Normally, our code controls object creation. With IoC, we hand that responsibility over to the Spring container.

The container responsible for this is called the IoC container or Spring container.

Two commonly used container interfaces are:

  • BeanFactory: The basic container functionality.
  • ApplicationContext: A more feature-rich container used by most Spring applications.

How Spring finds classes with component scanning

Now the next question is:

How does Spring know which objects it needs to create?

We need to tell Spring which classes should become beans.

One way is through annotations such as @Component, @Service, and @Repository.

Another way is through Java configuration using @Bean.

For now, let's focus on annotations.

When we create a Spring Boot application, we generally have this annotation on our main class:

@SpringBootApplication
public class LibraryApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        SpringApplication.run(LibraryApplication.class, args);
    }
}

One important thing to know is that @SpringBootApplication includes @ComponentScan.

Component scanning means Spring searches specified packages for classes that are eligible to become beans.

By default, Spring Boot scans the package containing the main application class and its subpackages.

For example:

com.example.library
|
+-- LibraryApplication.java
|
+-- service
|   +-- BookService.java
|
+-- repository
|   +-- BookRepository.java
|
+-- support
    +-- BookFormatter.java

Spring can discover the annotated classes inside these packages.

Behind the scenes

The process looks something like this:

        SpringApplication.run()
                  |
                  v
         Spring ApplicationContext
                  |
                  v
          Component Scanning
                  |
                  v
       Find annotated component classes
                  |
                  v
          Register Bean Definitions
                  |
                  v
          Create Spring Beans
                  |
                  v
        Inject their dependencies

Notice something important.

Spring first discovers eligible classes and registers their bean definitions.

A bean definition is essentially a recipe containing information about how a bean should be created.

The actual object is created and managed by the container according to that definition.

Now let's understand the annotations that make this possible.

@Component

@Component is the most generic stereotype annotation provided by Spring.

In simple words:

Use @Component when you want Spring to manage a class, but that class doesn't fit into a more specific application layer.

For example, consider a class responsible for formatting book titles.

import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class BookFormatter {

    public String format(String title) {

        return "Book: " + title;
    }
}

That's it!

Spring can now detect this class during component scanning and register it as a bean.

We can inject it into another class using constructor injection.

@Service
public class BookService {

    private final BookFormatter formatter;

    public BookService(BookFormatter formatter) {

        this.formatter = formatter;
    }

    public String getFormattedTitle(String title) {

        return formatter.format(title);
    }
}

Example output:

Book: Effective Java

The output comes from calling:

System.out.println(
    bookService.getFormattedTitle("Effective Java")
);

Why do we need @Component?

Imagine that you have several supporting classes:

  • BookFormatter
  • EmailFormatter
  • DateUtility
  • NotificationHelper

These classes are not necessarily services or repositories.

They are simply supporting components used by different parts of your application.

This is where @Component fits perfectly.

Behind the scenes

Spring recognizes @Component during component scanning and registers the class as a bean definition.

Later, when another bean requests BookFormatter through dependency injection, Spring supplies the managed instance.

One important point:

@Component is also the base stereotype for several other Spring annotations, including @Service and @Repository.

We'll understand why that matters next.

@Service

Now imagine Asha is building a library application.

Users should be able to search for books, borrow books, and return books.

Where should we write the logic for borrowing a book?

Should we write it inside the controller?

Should we put it directly inside the database access class?

Neither is a good choice.

We need a separate place for business logic.

This is where @Service comes in.

@Service identifies a class that belongs to the service layer of an application.

The service layer handles business operations and coordinates different parts of the application.

Example:

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class BookService {

    public void borrowBook(Long bookId) {

        System.out.println(
            "Book borrowed successfully. ID: " + bookId
        );
    }
}

Output:

Book borrowed successfully. ID: 101

We can also inject other beans into our service.

For example:

@Service
public class BookService {

    private final BookRepository bookRepository;

    public BookService(BookRepository bookRepository) {

        this.bookRepository = bookRepository;
    }

    public void borrowBook(Long bookId) {

        bookRepository.findBookById(bookId);

        System.out.println("Book borrowed successfully.");
    }
}

Here, BookService coordinates the operation and delegates database access to BookRepository.

Why not use @Component instead?

Technically, you could.

Both annotations make a class eligible for component scanning.

But their meaning is different.

@Component says:

"This is a Spring-managed component."

@Service says:

"This is a Spring-managed component that belongs to the business logic layer."

Using the appropriate annotation makes your application easier to understand and maintain.

Behind the scenes

@Service is itself annotated with @Component.

Conceptually, its relationship looks like this:

            @Component
                 |
          +------+------+
          |             |
      @Service     @Repository

This is why Spring can discover a class annotated with @Service during component scanning.

Spring also recognizes its service-layer role, which can be useful for framework features and application tooling.

@Repository

We have learned that the service layer handles business logic.

But where should we write code that communicates with the database?

For example:

  • Fetch a book by ID.
  • Save a new book.
  • Update book information.
  • Delete a book.

These responsibilities belong to the persistence or data access layer.

This is where @Repository comes in.

@Repository identifies a class that performs data access operations.

Example:

import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository;

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;

@Repository
public class InMemoryBookRepository {

    private final Map<Long, String> books = Map.of(
        1L, "Effective Java",
        2L, "Clean Code"
    );

    public Optional<String> findBookById(Long id) {

        return Optional.ofNullable(books.get(id));
    }
}

Output:

Optional[Effective Java]

The example uses an in-memory Map instead of an actual database so that we can focus on the responsibility of the repository.

Later, we'll replace this implementation with JDBC and Spring Data JPA.

But wait, there is something special about @Repository.

Spring provides an additional feature called exception translation.

Different persistence technologies can produce different types of database-related exceptions.

Spring can translate supported persistence exceptions into its common DataAccessException hierarchy.

This provides a consistent way of handling data access failures.

For example, instead of your service layer needing to understand every database provider's exception type, it can work with Spring's data access exception abstraction.

However, this doesn't mean every exception thrown inside a repository is automatically translated.

The exception translation infrastructure works with supported persistence exceptions.

Behind the scenes

@Repository is also a specialization of @Component.

Therefore, Spring discovers it during component scanning.

It can additionally serve as a marker for Spring's persistence exception translation infrastructure.

DAO and Repository

While learning Spring Boot, you will frequently encounter two terms:

  1. DAO
  2. Repository

Are they the same?

Not exactly, although people sometimes use these terms interchangeably.

Let's understand the difference.

What is DAO?

DAO stands for Data Access Object.

It is a design pattern used to separate database-related operations from the rest of the application.

For example:

public interface BookDao {

    Optional<String> findBookById(Long id);

    void saveBook(String title);

    void deleteBook(Long id);
}

The DAO provides methods for interacting with the data source.

Its implementation might use JDBC, SQL, or another persistence technology.

The main goal is to prevent database access logic from spreading across the application.

What is Repository?

A Repository is a pattern that provides a collection-like abstraction for accessing domain objects.

Think about a library.

You don't necessarily care how the application retrieves a book from the database.

You simply want to perform operations such as:

  • Find a book.
  • Save a book.
  • Delete a book.
  • Find all books.

A repository provides this kind of abstraction.

For example:

public interface BookRepository {

    Optional<Book> findById(Long id);

    Book save(Book book);

    void deleteById(Long id);

    List<Book> findAll();
}

Here, the caller works with books rather than worrying about SQL statements or database connections.

What is the actual difference?

The distinction is mostly about the abstraction and design perspective.

DAO generally focuses on isolating data access operations and persistence technology.

Repository generally focuses on providing domain-oriented access to objects.

In real Spring applications, the two terms often overlap.

For example, Spring developers commonly call a class BookRepository even when it performs traditional DAO-style database operations.

Also remember that @Repository is an annotation, while DAO and Repository are architectural patterns or abstractions.

They are not competing annotations.

A useful distinction for later:

Spring Data JPA provides a Repository abstraction and automatically creates implementations for supported repository interfaces.

We will explore that in Part 3.

@Scope("prototype")

Now let's understand something interesting about Spring beans.

When Spring creates a bean, does it always create a new object whenever we request it?

No!

By default, Spring uses singleton scope.

But sometimes we need a new object every time we request a bean.

This is where bean scopes become important.

A bean scope determines how Spring manages the instances created from a bean definition.

Singleton is the default

Singleton is the default scope in Spring.

It means Spring maintains one shared bean instance per bean definition inside a particular Spring container.

Consider this class:

import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class BookFormatter {

    public String format(String title) {

        return "Book: " + title;
    }
}

Now suppose we request this bean twice:

BookFormatter first =
    context.getBean(BookFormatter.class);

BookFormatter second =
    context.getBean(BookFormatter.class);

System.out.println(first == second);

Output:

true

Why?

Because both references point to the same Spring-managed object.

Behind the scenes

             Spring Container
                    |
                    v
             BookFormatter Bean
                    |
             +------+------+
             |             |
             v             v
           first         second
             \             /
              \           /
               Same Object

Notice that singleton in Spring does not mean a globally unique object across the entire JVM.

It means one instance per bean definition per Spring container.

What prototype actually means

Now imagine that we are generating reports.

Each report operation needs a separate ReportDraft object containing its own temporary state.

Using the same object repeatedly could cause unwanted state to be shared.

We can use prototype scope.

@Scope("prototype") tells Spring to create a new bean instance every time that bean is requested from the container.

Example:

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Scope;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
@Scope("prototype")
public class ReportDraft {

    public ReportDraft() {

        System.out.println("New ReportDraft created");
    }
}

Now request this bean twice:

ReportDraft first =
    context.getBean(ReportDraft.class);

ReportDraft second =
    context.getBean(ReportDraft.class);

System.out.println(first == second);

Output:

New ReportDraft created
New ReportDraft created
false

Why is the output false?

Because Spring created two separate objects.

The first and second references point to different instances.

Behind the scenes

             Spring Container
                    |
                    v
             ReportDraft Bean
                    |
             +------+------+
             |             |
             v             v
        New Object 1   New Object 2
             |             |
           first         second

The same bean definition acts as a recipe for creating multiple objects.

A small but important point:

You can also write the scope using the Spring constant:

@Scope(ConfigurableBeanFactory.SCOPE_PROTOTYPE)

This avoids manually typing the scope name.

Does prototype mean one object per HTTP request?

No.

Prototype means one new instance per bean request or dependency resolution.

Spring also provides web-specific scopes such as request and session, which have different lifecycles.

The singleton and prototype trap

There is one behaviour that surprises many beginners.

Suppose we have a singleton service that depends on a prototype bean.

@Component
@Scope("prototype")
public class ReportDraft {
}

Now inject it directly into a service:

@Service
public class ReportService {

    private final ReportDraft reportDraft;

    public ReportService(ReportDraft reportDraft) {

        this.reportDraft = reportDraft;
    }
}

The service is singleton by default.

The ReportDraft dependency is resolved when Spring creates the service.

That means the service receives one prototype instance during its own creation.

Even when you call different methods on the service, the same injected reportDraft reference is used.

This is not what some developers expect.

How do we get a new prototype instance whenever we need one?

Use ObjectProvider.

import org.springframework.beans.factory.ObjectProvider;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class ReportService {

    private final ObjectProvider<ReportDraft> reportDraftProvider;

    public ReportService(
        ObjectProvider<ReportDraft> reportDraftProvider
    ) {

        this.reportDraftProvider = reportDraftProvider;
    }

    public ReportDraft createDraft() {

        return reportDraftProvider.getObject();
    }
}

Now we can request a fresh instance whenever needed:

ReportDraft first = reportService.createDraft();

ReportDraft second = reportService.createDraft();

System.out.println(first == second);

Output:

false

Every call to getObject() asks the Spring container for another prototype instance.

Behind the scenes

          Singleton ReportService
                    |
                    v
          ObjectProvider<ReportDraft>
                    |
             +------+------+
             |             |
             v             v
      getObject()    getObject()
             |             |
             v             v
        ReportDraft   ReportDraft
          Object 1      Object 2

One more important lifecycle detail:

Spring initializes prototype beans, but it does not manage their complete destruction lifecycle.

For example, Spring does not automatically invoke configured destruction callbacks for prototype instances.

The application using those objects is responsible for cleaning up resources they hold.

This is another reason why prototype scope should be used thoughtfully.

Ideal Layer Structure for a Spring Boot Application

So far, we have learned about components, services, repositories, and bean scopes.

Now let's put everything together.

Suppose Asha is building a library management system.

The application needs to support:

  • Registering books.
  • Fetching books.
  • Borrowing books.
  • Returning books.
  • Deleting books.

We could write everything inside one class.

But imagine maintaining that class after adding 50 more features.

It would quickly become difficult to understand and modify.

Instead, we divide our application into layers.

This is commonly called Layered Architecture.

The idea is simple:

Each layer should have a specific responsibility.

The responsibility of each layer

A typical Spring Boot backend application contains these layers:

1. Controller Layer

The controller handles incoming HTTP requests.

Its responsibilities include:

  • Receiving requests.
  • Reading request parameters and request bodies.
  • Validating request input.
  • Calling the appropriate service.
  • Returning an HTTP response.

Common annotations:

  • @Controller
  • @RestController
  • @RequestMapping
  • @GetMapping
  • @PostMapping

2. Service Layer

The service layer contains business logic.

Its responsibilities include:

  • Executing business rules.
  • Coordinating multiple repositories.
  • Validating business conditions.
  • Managing application operations.
  • Defining transaction boundaries where appropriate.

Common annotation:

  • @Service

3. Repository Layer

The repository layer handles persistence.

Its responsibilities include:

  • Saving records.
  • Fetching records.
  • Updating records.
  • Deleting records.
  • Executing database queries.

Common annotation:

  • @Repository

4. Entity Layer

Entities represent objects that are mapped to database tables when using JPA.

For example, a Book entity might contain:

public class Book {

    private Long id;

    private String title;

    private String author;

}

In a JPA application, we will add the appropriate persistence annotations.

5. DTO Layer

DTO stands for Data Transfer Object.

DTOs are used to transfer data between different application boundaries.

For example, we might return a BookResponse containing only the book ID and title instead of exposing every field of the database entity.

6. Configuration Layer

This package contains application configuration.

For example:

  • Database configuration.
  • Security configuration.
  • Bean configuration.
  • External service configuration.

A request travels through the layers

Let's understand the complete flow.

Suppose Ravi sends this request:

GET /api/books/101

How does the request travel through our application?

             CLIENT
                |
                | HTTP Request
                v
        +------------------+
        |    CONTROLLER    |
        |                  |
        | Receives Request |
        +------------------+
                |
                | Calls Service
                v
        +------------------+
        |     SERVICE      |
        |                  |
        | Business Logic   |
        +------------------+
                |
                | Calls Repository
                v
        +------------------+
        |    REPOSITORY    |
        |                  |
        | Database Access  |
        +------------------+
                |
                | SQL / Persistence
                v
        +------------------+
        |     DATABASE     |
        +------------------+
                |
                | Query Result
                v
        +------------------+
        |    REPOSITORY    |
        +------------------+
                |
                v
        +------------------+
        |     SERVICE      |
        +------------------+
                |
                v
        +------------------+
        |    CONTROLLER    |
        +------------------+
                |
                | HTTP Response
                v
              CLIENT

The important thing to notice is the direction of responsibility.

The controller does not directly communicate with the database.

The service does not need to know how SQL queries are executed.

The repository does not need to know how HTTP requests work.

Each layer focuses on its own responsibility.

This separation makes the application easier to test, maintain, and extend.

A practical package structure

Here is a recommended package structure for a Spring Boot application:

com.example.library
|
+-- LibraryApplication.java
|
+-- controller
|   +-- BookController.java
|   +-- UserController.java
|
+-- service
|   +-- BookService.java
|   +-- UserService.java
|
+-- repository
|   +-- BookRepository.java
|   +-- UserRepository.java
|
+-- entity
|   +-- Book.java
|   +-- User.java
|
+-- dto
|   +-- BookRequest.java
|   +-- BookResponse.java
|
+-- config
|   +-- SecurityConfig.java
|
+-- exception
    +-- GlobalExceptionHandler.java
    +-- BookNotFoundException.java

Why should we follow this structure?

Imagine tomorrow you want to change your database from MySQL to PostgreSQL.

Ideally, most of your changes should remain inside the persistence-related parts of the application.

Your business logic should not need to know whether you're using MySQL, PostgreSQL, or another supported database.

Similarly, changing the HTTP response format should not require rewriting your database access logic.

This is the main benefit of separating responsibilities.

One important clarification:

This structure is a recommended convention, not something Spring automatically enforces.

Also, don't create additional layers just for the sake of having more packages. Every layer should have a clear responsibility.

What else belongs in this foundation

There are a few related concepts worth understanding before moving to database operations.

Constructor injection

We already used constructor injection in our examples.

But why is it preferred?

Consider this approach:

@Service
public class BookService {

    @Autowired
    private BookRepository bookRepository;
}

This is called field injection.

It works, but it has some disadvantages:

  • Dependencies are not obvious from the constructor.
  • Testing the class without Spring becomes more difficult.
  • The dependency cannot easily be declared as final.

Instead, prefer constructor injection:

@Service
public class BookService {

    private final BookRepository bookRepository;

    public BookService(BookRepository bookRepository) {

        this.bookRepository = bookRepository;
    }
}

Notice that we don't need @Autowired here.

When a Spring bean has only one constructor, Spring can use that constructor for dependency injection automatically.

This makes dependencies explicit and allows us to use final fields.

Keep services stateless

Remember that singleton is the default bean scope.

That means the same service instance can handle multiple requests.

Now consider this example:

@Service
public class BookService {

    private String currentUser;

    public void processRequest(String username) {

        currentUser = username;

        // Perform some operation
    }
}

There is a problem here.

Imagine two users accessing the application simultaneously.

User A sets:

currentUser = Asha

Before Asha's operation finishes, another request sets:

currentUser = Ravi

Now the first request might accidentally read Ravi's information.

This is a concurrency problem caused by shared mutable state.

A better approach is to keep request-specific information in method parameters and local variables:

@Service
public class BookService {

    public void processRequest(String username) {

        System.out.println(
            "Processing request for " + username
        );
    }
}

Output for two calls:

Processing request for Asha
Processing request for Ravi

The rule of thumb:

Prefer stateless singleton services.

Use local variables for temporary operations instead of storing request-specific data in instance fields.

Which one should I use?

Now that we've covered the annotations, let's understand when to use each one.

Use @Component when:

  • You have a general-purpose helper class.
  • The class does not specifically belong to the service or persistence layer.
  • You want Spring to manage a supporting component.

Example: BookFormatter, EmailHelper.

Use @Service when:

  • You are implementing business logic.
  • You are coordinating multiple repositories.
  • You are implementing application use cases.

Example: BookService, PaymentService.

Use @Repository when:

  • You are implementing data access logic.
  • Your class interacts with a database.
  • You are isolating persistence operations.

Example: BookRepository implementation, UserRepository implementation.

Use @Scope("prototype") when:

  • You need a fresh bean instance for each container lookup.
  • You have a stateful object whose temporary state should not be shared.
  • The object's lifecycle makes prototype scope appropriate.

Example: ReportDraft.

What should be my default choice?

For most Spring Boot backend applications:

  • Use singleton scope by default.
  • Use @Service for business logic.
  • Use @Repository for custom persistence classes.
  • Use @Component for general-purpose supporting classes.
  • Use prototype scope only when you actually need it.

You don't need to manually change every bean's scope.

Common mistakes

Let's look at six mistakes beginners frequently make.

1. Using new instead of dependency injection

Creating dependencies manually using new bypasses Spring's bean management.

For Spring-managed dependencies, prefer constructor injection.

2. Using @Component everywhere

Technically, it works for many classes, but it hides their intended responsibilities.

Use @Service for business logic and @Repository for persistence classes.

3. Making every bean prototype

Prototype scope is not automatically better than singleton scope.

Most service and repository classes are stateless, so singleton is generally the right default.

4. Expecting an injected prototype bean to refresh automatically

Injecting a prototype bean directly into a singleton resolves that dependency only when the singleton is created.

Use ObjectProvider when you need a fresh prototype instance repeatedly.

5. Putting database operations inside controllers

Controllers should handle HTTP requests, not SQL queries or database connections.

Delegate business operations to services and persistence operations to repositories.

6. Storing request-specific data in singleton beans

Multiple requests can access the same singleton bean.

Avoid storing mutable, request-specific information in its instance variables.

Use method parameters and local variables instead.

Quick recap

Let's quickly revise everything.

  • A Spring Bean is an object managed by the Spring IoC container.
  • Spring uses component scanning to discover annotated classes.
  • @Component identifies a general-purpose Spring-managed component.
  • @Service identifies a service-layer component.
  • @Repository identifies a data-access component and supports persistence exception translation.
  • DAO is a pattern for isolating data access operations.
  • Repository provides a domain-oriented abstraction for accessing objects.
  • Singleton is the default bean scope in Spring.
  • @Scope("prototype") creates a new instance for each bean request.
  • Injecting a prototype bean directly into a singleton does not give you a new instance on every method call.
  • ObjectProvider can be used to request fresh prototype instances when needed.
  • A typical Spring Boot application separates Controller, Service, Repository, Entity, DTO, and Configuration responsibilities.
  • Constructor injection is generally preferable to field injection.
  • Keep singleton services stateless whenever possible.

Try it yourself

Practice idea:

Create a small Library Management application with these classes:

  • BookFormatter using @Component.
  • BookService using @Service.
  • BookRepository using @Repository.
  • ReportDraft using @Scope("prototype").

Inject these classes into one another using constructor injection.

Run the application and verify that:

  1. Spring discovers all your annotated classes.
  2. Your service can call the repository.
  3. Your formatter can be injected into your service.
  4. Two singleton lookups return the same object.
  5. Two prototype lookups return different objects.

Bonus experiment:

Inject a prototype bean directly into a singleton service. Compare its behaviour with an implementation using ObjectProvider.

Try to understand why the two approaches produce different results.

If this helped, or if you spotted something I should fix, tell me in the comments. I'm still learning too.

title: Daemons can now send traces to Vercel Tracing
description:
Vercel Daemons can now send OpenTelemetry traces to Vercel Tracing, allowing you and your agents to inspect background worker operations alongside the rest of your project's traces.

Vercel provides each daemon with a Unix socket for receiving OTLP/HTTP traces and sets the socket's path in VERCEL_OTEL_SOCKET_PATH.

Upgrading @vercel/otel to version 2.3.0 or later enables automatic trace export for Node.js daemons using the default configuration. The SDK detects this socket and sends the spans your worker records to Vercel.

These spans are available through the Vercel CLI, which can search by service name within a project and return JSON for your agents.

Learn more in the daemon tracing documentation.

Read more

title: Code availability is not enough: schemas for documenting and extending data analysis
description:
arXiv:2611.33167v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A data analysis involves a sequence of decisions, from data cleaning to model specification, each of which can affect the reported result. Reproducing that result is not the same as understanding the sequence of decisions that produced it and the reasons for each: the code mixes those decisions with implementation details, while the manuscript states the major decisions and their rationale but scatters them across its sections and often leaves out the minor ones. A reader may then ask how the result would change under a different decision: the question itself is easy to pose, but implementing it is often non-trivial in practice. In this work, we propose a schema that represents a data analysis as a collection of decisions in natural language, from which large language models (LLMs) can generate and validate analysis scripts directly. This workflow can also expand a single analysis into a full multiverse of alternatives, specified in an alternative file, ready for comparison. We demonstrate the proposed workflow in two applications. In the first, we construct a schema for a published regression analysis of heaped smoking data and show that it reproduces the reported estimates, and that a reviewer-suggested alternative can be specified through the alternative file and turned into code automatically. In the second, where no schema is provided, we show how the workflow serves instead as a reproducibility check, applied to the many-analysts football study. As an intermediate representation between the manuscript and code scripts, our schema gives a self-contained account of an analysis and makes it extensible from a reader's perspective.

title: Your Tests Take Twenty Minutes and You Have Stopped Running Them
description:
When you joined, the test suite finished in about two minutes. Now it takes twenty. You still run it before you push, most of the time. But during the day you have started making several changes at once, running nothing, and hoping. When something fails, you spend an hour working out which of your six changes caused it.

Your tests are feedback, and like any feedback, it loses most of its value when it arrives late.

There is useful research on how waiting changes the way people work. Jakob Nielsen, building on a 1968 paper by Robert Miller, describes three rough limits. A tenth of a second feels instant. One second is about as long as you can wait without your train of thought breaking. At ten seconds, people start to drift off to other tasks. Twenty minutes is far beyond all three. Nobody sits and watches a suite that long, so they stop asking it questions.

That is the real cost. Not the twenty minutes, but the questions you no longer ask. Did this small change break anything? You would have checked in two minutes. You will not check in twenty.

So treat the slowness as a problem worth your time, not as weather.

Measure first. Most test tools can report which tests take longest. Often a handful of slow ones dominate the total, perhaps a few that start a real database or wait on a fixed timer.

Run less, more often. Most tools let you run only the tests for the file you are working on, or only those affected by your change. Keep the full suite for before you push and in the pipeline.

Look at the slowest tests one at a time. Can a sleep become a wait for a condition? Can a test that starts the whole application check the same thing at a lower level? Can tests run in parallel?

And raise it with your team, with numbers. The suite has gone from two minutes to twenty in a year, and here are the ten tests that cause half of it. That is a much easier conversation than the tests are slow.

A fast answer you check every few minutes is worth more than a perfect one you have stopped asking for.

– Asael Shinder

title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake
description:
arXiv:2611.31301v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/
