title: We put our CI runners behind an egress proxy and the Java tests ignored it and waited two minutes for every call
description:
In September our network team moved the CI runners into a new subnet whose only way out to the internet is a Squid proxy. They set HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY in the runners' environment, ran a few curl commands through it, and told us nothing should notice.

Almost nothing did. curl, npm and pip all read those variables. Maven took its dependencies from our Nexus, which sits inside the network and needs no proxy. The build stage of our label service went green. The contract test stage, which calls each carrier's sandbox from Java, ran for forty one minutes and failed with nineteen connection timeouts.

The JVM does not read HTTPS_PROXY. Java's HTTP clients take their proxy from system properties, https.proxyHost and https.proxyPort, and without them they connect directly. The firewall drops direct traffic leaving that subnet instead of refusing it, so every attempt waited for the kernel to give up. Linux retries a SYN six times by default, doubling the wait from one second, which comes to about a hundred and twenty seven seconds per connection, and our tests set no connect timeout of their own.

Our first fix did nothing. We put the properties in MAVEN_OPTS and the tests still went direct. MAVEN_OPTS configures the JVM that runs Maven. Surefire runs the tests in a forked JVM, which takes its arguments from argLine and inherits nothing from Maven's.

What works is JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS. Every JVM reads it from its environment at startup, forked or not, and says so on stderr with the line Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS. The runner image now builds it from the same values as HTTPS_PROXY. The exclusions needed translating as well. NO_PROXY is a comma separated list in which .internal.example.com covers a whole domain. Java's http.nonProxyHosts, which it also uses for HTTPS, is separated by pipes and wants *.internal.example.com.

The contract tests now set a five second connect timeout, so a network that drops packets fails the stage in seconds, not in forty minutes. The first step of every Java job prints the proxy properties the JVM actually sees, so the next change to the network shows up in a log line before it shows up as a timeout.

An environment variable is a convention, and only the programs that agreed to it follow it. Ask each runtime where it gets its proxy from, not the shell.

– Sergey Shinder

title: 29 tells of AI slop, written as lint rules
description:
Ask an AI coding agent for a landing page and you can usually tell it was generated within a second. Purple-to-blue gradient, a pill badge above a centred headline that says "Supercharge your workflow", three feature cards with emoji icons, everything fading up on scroll.

I've been collecting those tells while building unslop, a design playbook coding agents read before they build. The playbook makes the agent better, but not perfect, so unslop also ships a linter: unslop lint scans HTML, JSX, TSX, Vue, Svelte, Astro and CSS and says how to fix each tell it finds.

Here are all 29 checks, grouped the way the linter groups them. Each one is a regex with good and bad examples that run in CI, so a check that starts flagging good code fails the build.

npx @deliverwebsite/unslop lint src

Copy

1. banned-phrase (error): A phrase that signals generated copy.

Fix: Say what the product does and for whom, with a concrete detail (a number, a feature name, a result).

<h1>Supercharge your workflow</h1>

2. vague-social-proof (warning): Vague social proof reads as filler.

Fix: Use a specific, checkable claim: "2,400 clinics send reminders with Pulsebook", or a named quote.

<p>Trusted by thousands of teams</p>

3. placeholder-copy (error): Placeholder content.

Fix: Write real-looking content: a named product, believable numbers, real feature names.

<p>Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet</p>

4. vague-button (warning): Button or link text that doesn't say what happens.

Fix: Name the outcome: "Start 14-day trial", "See pricing", "Book a 20-minute call".

<button>Get started</button>

5. emoji-heading (warning): Heading starts with an emoji, a common stand-in for a real icon or idea.

Fix: Drop the emoji, or use one icon from the project's icon set with a consistent size and stroke.

<h3>🚀 Fast deploys</h3>

6. made-up-stat (warning): A round, unsourced stat that reads as made up.

Fix: Use a real figure with its source, or remove it. In drafts, mark sample numbers so nobody ships them as fact.

<p>Ship 10x faster</p>

7. tell-word (warning): A word that has become a tell of generated copy, used more than once.

Fix: Replace it with the concrete fact it stands for: what is quiet, how was it made, for whom.

<p>Quiet software.</p><p>Thoughtfully built.</p>

8. dot-separators (warning): Little dots between words used as decoration.

Fix: Use space, a line break or a list. Keep a separator only where items are a genuine inline list, such as a footer.

<p>Fast · Private · Yours · Forever</p>

9. numbered-sections (warning): Numbered section labels (01, 02, 03) as decoration.

Fix: Number things only when order matters, such as the steps of a setup. Otherwise let the headings carry the section.

<span>01</span><span>02</span><span>03</span>

Markup and accessibility

10. tailwind-motion-without-reduced (warning): Tailwind animation with no reduced-motion variant in this file.

Fix: Use motion-safe:animate-… or add motion-reduce:animate-none.

<div class="animate-bounce"></div>

11. img-without-alt (error): Image without alt text.

Fix: Add alt text that says what the image shows, or alt="" if it is purely decorative.

<img src="/hero.png">

12. clickable-div (warning): Click handler on a div or span, which keyboards and screen readers can't use.

Fix: Use a for actions and an for navigation.

<div onClick={open}>

13. dead-link (warning): Link that goes nowhere (href="#").

Fix: Link to a real destination, or use a

if it performs an action.
<a href="#">Pricing</a>

14. arrow-everywhere (warning): Arrows on many buttons and links in this file.

Fix: An arrow means "this goes somewhere". Keep it on the one primary link, if any, and let button text do the work.

<a>Pricing →</a><a>Docs →</a><button>Start <ArrowRight /></button>

15. italic-headline-word (warning): One word set in italic inside a headline for flair.

Fix: Set the headline in one style. Use emphasis only where the sentence would be read with stress.

<h1>Software that <em>listens</em></h1>

16. sparkle-icon (warning): Sparkle icon, the stock symbol for "AI".

Fix: Show what the feature does instead: an icon for the action itself, or no icon.

<Sparkles size={16} />




Colour, type and motion

17. purple-blue-gradient (error): Purple/indigo gradient, the most recognised default of generated interfaces.

Fix: Use a neutral base and one accent chosen from the product. If you need depth, use a subtle tint of that accent.

<div class="bg-gradient-to-r from-purple-600 to-blue-500">

18. default-indigo-accent (warning): The framework's default indigo/violet accent is used throughout.

Fix: Pick an accent from the product or brand, define it as a token (e.g. --accent), and use it only for what matters.

<a class="bg-indigo-600"></a><b class="text-indigo-600"></b><i class="ring-indigo-500"></i>

19. gradient-text (warning): Gradient text used more than once in this file.

Fix: Use weight and size for emphasis. Keep gradient text to one moment, if any.

<h1 class="bg-clip-text"></h1><h2 class="bg-clip-text"></h2>

20. neon-glow (warning): Coloured glow shadow, a signature of generated dark-mode pages.

Fix: Use a soft neutral shadow for elevation, or none. Show focus with an outline, not a glow.

<div class="shadow-purple-500/50">

21. glassmorphism (warning): Frosted-glass blur on several surfaces in this file.

Fix: Keep blur for one overlay that needs it (a sticky header over content). Use solid surfaces elsewhere.

<nav class="backdrop-blur-md"></nav><div class="backdrop-blur-lg"></div>

22. decorative-motion (warning): Decorative looping motion with no job.

Fix: Remove it, or replace it with motion that explains something: a value updating, a list receiving an item.

<div class="animate-blob"></div>

23. animate-layout (warning): Transition on layout properties or all.

Fix: Animate only transform, opacity and filter, and name the properties you transition.

<button class="transition-all">

24. css-motion-without-reduced (error): Animation with no prefers-reduced-motion handling in this file.

Fix: Add @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) with a complete still state.

@keyframes in { from { opacity: 0 } }

25. default-font (warning): A font generated interfaces reach for by default (Inter for UI, Instrument Serif for display).

Fix: Choose a typeface for a reason that fits the product, and set a type scale for it. Keep it only if you chose it on purpose.

font-family: Inter, sans-serif;

26. focus-removed (error): Focus outline removed with no visible replacement nearby.

Fix: Keep a visible focus state: :focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: 2px; }.

button:focus { outline: none; }

27. pulsing-dot (warning): Pulsing green dot.

Fix: Show a live indicator only for something that is actually live, and update it from real state.

<span class="h-2 w-2 rounded-full bg-green-500 animate-ping"></span>

28. coloured-left-border (warning): Coloured left border used as decoration on several blocks.

Fix: Separate blocks with space or a neutral rule. Keep a coloured edge for one meaningful state, such as an error callout.

<div class="border-l-4 border-blue-500"></div><div class="border-l-4 border-purple-500"></div>

29. hero-glow-blob (warning): Large blurred shape, usually a coloured glow behind the hero.

Fix: Remove it. If the hero needs depth, use the product screenshot and one surface colour.

<div class="absolute rounded-full bg-violet-500 blur-3xl"></div>

How to use it

Put the playbook where your agent reads it, then lint what it builds:

npx @deliverwebsite/unslop init   # writes AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / Cursor / Copilot rules
npx @deliverwebsite/unslop lint   # exits 1 on errors, --strict fails on warnings too

To skip a line on purpose, add an unslop-ignore comment on it, or unslop-ignore-next-line above it.

It's free and open source (MIT for the code, CC BY 4.0 for the playbook): https://github.com/deliverwebsite/unslop. Made by DeliverWebsite.

Which tell is missing? I'm adding new checks every day this week.

Made by DeliverWebsite UI. Free React components: ui.deliverwebsite.com

title: Your AI agent marked the form accessible. It had only checked contrast.
description:
Say you ask your AI agent to build a "request a visitor badge" form at example.com. The pull request comes back with a green line in the notes: "Accessibility: pass." The only check that ran was a contrast test on the button colours.

A single automated check was treated as a result about the whole form.

This is a fictional illustration of how Design Decision Method reports accessibility work, not a case study or a measured result. The product details below are invented for the example. It is also not a repeat of the broader handoff and evidence labels in step 6. This post is about a narrower mistake: turning one accessibility check into a claim the interface cannot support.

What you may report

The docs (Release 2.2.4) already ask the agent, when it delivers the work, to label each result as proposed, heuristic review, automated check, manual test, or user research, and to say what it did not test.

The procedure on the main branch is more specific about accessibility. Its checks are prompts, not the complete standard. It asks the agent to combine automated checks with manual keyboard testing and relevant assistive-technology pairs, to record what was not tested, and to distinguish those evidence levels. If a reference file cannot be opened, the procedure on the main branch says to say so and mark the affected checks as unverified, rather than claiming them.

An honest note for the visitor-badge form might look like this:

Automated check: Contrast on the text and button colours used. No failures found. This cannot support a claim about overall accessibility.
Manual test: The three fields and the submit control can be reached from the keyboard, in a logical order, with a visible focus. Tested once on a desktop keyboard. Not tested on a phone.
Heuristic review: Error text for a bad host email sits next to the field (the placeholder is name@example.com). Markup only. Not tested with a screen reader.
Proposed: People complete a badge request without help. Not tested. No user research.
Not tested: screen reader, zoom and reflow, mobile keyboard, a native app — and web checks would not validate a native one.

Nothing in that note invents a measurement. Nothing in it claims that a standard was met.

What you may not claim

The procedure on the main branch is direct about the limit. An automated check can support specific rule failures. It cannot support overall accessibility or usability. "Accessibility: pass" is the second kind of statement.

When the project supplies no other standard, the procedure on the main branch uses WCAG 2.2 level AA as the default web design and verification target, and says a stronger project or legal requirement wins. That is a target to design toward. It is not a result you can report from a contrast check, and the procedure on the main branch tells the agent not to claim certification, or that a standard was met, without evidence for that claim. Flag a conflict with a stronger requirement instead of quietly lowering accessibility.

The same limit applies across platforms. For native apps, the procedure on the main branch points to the platform's accessibility guidance and tools. Do not claim that web checks validate native accessibility. If example.com later needs an iOS version of the badge request, the contrast run on the website does not speak for that app.

Why this matters

Agents are good at running a checker and writing a confident summary. The dangerous part is the upgrade: from "these colours passed a contrast check" to "the form is accessible." Readers of the pull request cannot see the gap unless the note says what was actually tested.

The docs (Release 2.2.4) already require that gap to be visible: say what you did not test. The procedure on the main branch fills in the accessibility detail — keyboard, assistive technology, native tools, and unverified checks — so the summary cannot outrun the evidence.

The method does not claim this saves time. That has not been measured. It also does not guarantee an accessible interface. What it gives you is a report that stays inside what the checks can support.

Try it

Design Decision Method is a lightweight design decision workflow for developers building interfaces with AI agents. It follows the open Agent Skills format and is MIT licensed. Install paths for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and Codex are in the README.

  • Read the DDM docs
  • Accessibility baseline and verification
  • Acceptance and evidence labels
  • Repository README and install notes

title: Cloudflare E-posta Hataları: E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED, E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED ve 429 Hatası Çözümü
description:
Cloudflare Email hataları: E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED, günlük limitler ve yeniden deneme stratejisi

Cloudflare Email hataları, Cloudflare'ın Email Sending özelliğini Workers Free planında kullanıma sunduğu 24 Kasım 2026 tarihinden itibaren çok daha fazla logda görünmeye başladı. İşin püf noktası, changelog'daki tek bir satırda saklı: Free planında yalnızca kendi hesabınızdaki doğrulanmış hedef adreslere gönderim yapabilirsiniz.

Apidog'u bugün deneyin

Kısa cevap: E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED, Workers Free planında olduğunuz ve alıcının doğrulanmış bir hedef adresi olmadığı anlamına gelir: adresi doğrulayın ya da Workers Paid planına yükseltin ve asla yeniden denemeyin. E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED (Workers binding), HTTP 429 (REST API) ve 451 4.7.1 (SMTP) ise hesabınızın günlük gönderim limitine takıldığınız anlamına gelir: mesajı kuyruğa alın ve daha sonra yeniden deneyin veya daha yüksek bir limit talep edin.

Cloudflare Email hataları ne anlama geliyor

Cloudflare Email Service, tek bir sorunu üç farklı şekilde bildirir: Workers binding bir string code fırlatır, REST API bir HTTP durum kodu ile sayısal bir kod döndürür, SMTP ise bir yanıt kodu ile cevap verir. Üçü de aynı hesap limitlerini paylaşır.

Sorun Workers binding REST API SMTP Yeniden denemeli mi?
Alıcı planınızda izinli değil E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED 403, kod 10208 RCPT TO aşamasında 550 5.7.1 Hayır
Günlük gönderim limitine ulaşıldı E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED 429 451 4.7.1 Daha sonra
Gönderim hızı veya eşzamanlılık limiti E_RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED 429, kod 10004 451 4.7.1 Evet, backoff ile
Alıcı bastırma listesinde E_RECIPIENT_SUPPRESSED 400 Mesaj reddedildi Hayır
Hesap itibar nedeniyle askıya alındı E_ACCOUNT_SUSPENDED 403, kod 10207 Listelenmemiş Hayır

Kaynaklar: Cloudflare'ın Limits sayfası, Workers API error codes ve SMTP response codes, 26 Kasım 2026 tarihinde okundu.

Önemli nokta şu: REST hata tablosunda tek bir 429 girdisi var, 10004 (email.sending.error.throttled), ve SMTP hem hız limiti hem de günlük limit için 451 4.7.1 kullanıyor. Hangi limite takıldığınızı yalnızca binding size söyler.

Workers Free planında E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED hatasını düzeltmek

E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED geçici bir arıza değil, bir plan kuralıdır. Workers Free planında Email Sending yalnızca hesabınızdaki doğrulanmış hedef adreslerini kabul eder. Diğer tüm adresler her denemede aynı şekilde başarısız olur, bu yüzden asla yeniden denemeyin.

Üç çıkış yolunuz var:

  1. Adresi doğrulayın. Dashboard'da Compute > Email Service > Email Routing > Destination Addresses yolunu izleyin, adresi ekleyin ve Cloudflare'ın doğrulama e-postasındaki bağlantıya tıklayın. Bir hesap 200 hedef adresi barındırabilir.
  2. Workers Paid planına yükseltin. Paid planı herhangi bir alıcıya gönderim yapmanıza izin verir; aylık 3.000 e-posta dahildir ve sonrasında Email Service fiyatlandırma sayfasına göre 1.000 e-posta başına 0,35 dolar ücret alınır.
  3. Dahili e-posta için Free planında kalın. Kendi ekibinize giden uyarılar ve raporlar Free planına uygundur ve doğrulanmış adreslere yapılan gönderimler her planda kotayı ve günlük limitleri atlar.

SMTP üzerinden aynı kural oturumun daha erken bir aşamasında ortaya çıkar. Cloudflare, doğrulanmamış RCPT TO adresini 550 5.7.1 ile reddeder. İstemciniz buna rağmen DATA komutunu gönderirse, doğrulanmış alıcılar da dahil olmak üzere hiçbir alıcının mesajı almamasıyla birlikte tüm mesaj 554 5.7.1 ile başarısız olur. Karışık alıcı listelerini göndermeden önce ayırın.

Bunu, kendi binding'inizin allowed_destination_addresses ayarından kaynaklanan E_RECIPIENT_NOT_ALLOWED hatasıyla karıştırmayın.

E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, HTTP 429 ve 451 4.7.1 hatalarını düzeltmek

Yeni hesaplar, gönderim davranışınıza, teslim edilebilirliğinize ve hesap durumunuza göre artan temkinli bir günlük kota ile başlar. Cloudflare başlangıç sayısını yayınlamaz ve bu sayıyı hesap bazında ayarlar.

Günlük limiti "bugün olmaz" olarak değerlendirin. Hızlı yeniden denemeler bu limiti temizlemez. Bunun yerine:

  • Mesajı, birkaç saat sonrasına ayarlanmış bir not_before zaman damgasıyla bir kuyruğa veya tabloya park edin.
  • Kapasite geri geldiğinde işlemsel e-postaları (şifre sıfırlamaları, makbuzlar) toplu e-postaların önünde tutun.
  • Daha fazla alana ihtiyacınız varsa, Limits sayfasının altındaki "Need a higher limit?" formunu kullanın.

Hız limiti farklıdır: kısa ömürlüdür, bu yüzden jitter'lı üstel backoff doğru araçtır. Üstel backoff ile yeniden deneme rehberimiz matematiği ele alıyor ve HTTP 429 Too Many Requests durum kodunun kendisini açıklıyor.

Hataları bir Worker içinde ele almak

Binding size en net sinyali verir, bu yüzden error.code üzerine dallanın. Bu Worker yalnızca hız limitini yeniden dener, günlük limiti erteler ve kalıcı olan diğer her şeyde hızla başarısız olur:

const PERMANENT = new Set([
  "E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED", "E_RECIPIENT_NOT_ALLOWED",
  "E_RECIPIENT_SUPPRESSED", "E_VALIDATION_ERROR", "E_ACCOUNT_SUSPENDED",
]);

async function sendEmail(env: Env, msg: EmailMessageBuilder) {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt++) {
    try {
      return { status: "sent", id: (await env.EMAIL.send(msg)).messageId };
    } catch (err: any) {
      if (err instanceof TypeError) return { status: "bad_input", reason: err.message };
      if (err.code === "E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED") return { status: "defer" };
      if (PERMANENT.has(err.code)) return { status: "failed", reason: err.code };
      if (err.code !== "E_RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" && err.code !== "E_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR") throw err;
      const wait = 2 ** attempt * 500 + Math.random() * 250;
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, wait));
    }
  }
  return { status: "defer" };
}

Binding, wrangler.jsonc içinde tek bir satırdır: "send_email": [{ "name": "EMAIL" }]. code içermeyen bir TypeError, send() argümanınızın arayüzle uyuşmadığı anlamına gelir (alıcı yok veya name eksik bir EmailAddress): yeniden denenecek bir gönderim değil, düzeltilecek bir hatadır.

REST API'den gelen 429 hatasını ele almak

REST uç noktası POST https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/{account_id}/email/sending/send ve Bearer API token'ı ile çalışır. Hatalar standart Cloudflare zarfında geri döner, bu yüzden errors[0].code değerini okuyun:

const BASE = process.env.CF_API_BASE ?? "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4";

async function sendViaRest(accountId, token, payload, attempt = 0) {
  const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/accounts/${accountId}/email/sending/send`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`, "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(payload),
  });
  const body = await res.json();
  if (body.success) return { status: "sent", id: body.result.message_id };

  const code = body.errors?.[0]?.code;
  if (res.status === 403 && code === 10208) return { status: "failed", reason: "recipient_plan_restricted" };
  if (res.status === 429 || res.status >= 500) {
    if (attempt >= 3) return { status: "defer" };
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 2 ** attempt * 1000 + Math.random() * 500));
    return sendViaRest(accountId, token, payload, attempt + 1);
  }
  return { status: "failed", reason: `${res.status}:${code}` };
}

Bir REST 429 her iki limitten de kaynaklanabildiği için, yeniden denemeleri sınırlayın ve son denemeden sonra mesajı kuyruğunuza teslim edin. Yapılandırılabilir CF_API_BASE daha sonra, bu istemciyi bir mock'a yönlendirdiğinizde önem kazanır.

Ayrıca başarı yanıt gövdesini de kontrol edin. Drop suppressed recipients seçeneği açıkken, bir 200 yanıtı yine de suppressed_recipients veya permanent_bounces içinde adresler listeleyebilir ve bu alıcılar hiçbir şey almamıştır.

SMTP üzerinden 451 4.7.1 ve 550 5.7.1 hatalarını ele almak

Cloudflare'ın SMTP gönderimi smtp.mx.cloudflare.net üzerinde, 465 portunda, yalnızca örtük TLS ile çalışır. Kullanıcı adı birebir api_token string'idir ve parola, Email Sending: Edit iznine sahip bir API token'ıdır. STARTTLS ile 587 portu desteklenmez.

Nodemailer ile yanıt kodu err.responseCode üzerine düşer:

import nodemailer from "nodemailer";

const transport = nodemailer.createTransport({
  host: "smtp.mx.cloudflare.net", port: 465, secure: true,
  auth: { user: "api_token", pass: process.env.CF_EMAIL_TOKEN },
});

try {
  await transport.sendMail({ from: "alerts@yourdomain.com", to, subject, text });
} catch (err) {
  if (err.responseCode === 451 || err.responseCode === 421) scheduleRetry(); // temporary
  else if (err.responseCode === 550 || err.responseCode === 554) markFailed(err.response);
  else throw err;
}

4xx yanıtı geçicidir; 5xx ise kalıcıdır. 535 5.7.8 hatalı bir kullanıcı adı veya token'ı, 550 5.7.1 Sender denied ise MAIL FROM alan adının token'ın hesabı altında tanımlanmadığını gösterir.

Ne zaman yeniden denemeli, ne zaman durmalı

Karar tek bir soruya indirgeniyor: aynı istek, siz hiçbir şeyi değiştirmeden daha sonra başarılı olur mu?

Bastırma hataları dikkat gerektirir. Cloudflare bir adresi sert bounce'lar sonrasında (7 gün veya posta kutusu yoksa süresiz), yumuşak bounce'lar sonrasında (varsayılan olarak 24 saat) ve doğrulanmış spam şikayetleri sonrasında (süresiz) bastırır. Bastırma listesi belgelerine göre, bastırılmış gönderimler kotanıza sayılmaz ve loglarda Rejected olarak görünür. Bunları yeniden denemeyin ve kişi tekrar onay verene kadar bir şikayet bastırmasını silmeyin.

Hâlâ sağlayıcı mı seçiyorsunuz? Ücretsiz e-posta API'leri derlememize göz atın.

Hata yollarını kodlama ajanınızdan Apidog CLI ile test etmek

Hata dalları en az test edilen kısımlardır çünkü gerçek bir 429 tetiklemek zordur ve gerçek bir günlük limit bir güne mal olur. Kodlama ajanınızın başarısızlık senaryolarını Apidog CLI ile oluşturmasına izin verin: mock beklentileri Cloudflare'ın birebir hata gövdelerini döndürür ve istemciniz bunların üzerinde çalışır.

CLI'yı ve ajan becerisini bir kez kurun:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com/?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation   # pick your agent when prompted

Ardından ajanınıza tek bir istem verin:

In Apidog project <id>, add Cloudflare's POST /accounts/{account_id}/email/sending/send
endpoint with 200, 403 and 429 responses. Create mock expectations: when the body "to"
is stranger@example.com, return 403 with errors[0].code 10208; when header X-Scenario is
throttle, return 429 with errors[0].code 10004. Then list the endpoint and its mocks.

Ajan uç noktayı bulur, payload şemasını okur, JSON'unu doğrular ve mock'ları yazar:

apidog endpoint list --project <id> --method POST
apidog cli-schema get mock-create
apidog cli-schema validate mock-create --file mock-403.json
apidog mock create --project <id> --file mock-403.json
apidog mock list --project <id>

CF_API_BASE değişkenini projenin mock URL'sine (Apidog'da uç noktada gösterilir) yönlendirin ve REST istemcinizin testlerini çalıştırın. 403 senaryosu sıfır yeniden denemeyle recipient_plan_restricted döndürmelidir, throttle senaryosu ise üç kez yeniden denemeli ve ardından ertelemelidir. Gerçek uç nokta bağlandığında, ajan test senaryoları oluşturabilir ve bunları apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <id> -e <envId> -r cli,junit ile çalıştırabilir. Claude Code'da Apidog CLI rehberi bu döngüyü adım adım anlatıyor.

Bu ajan çalıştırmaları haftalık rutininizin bir parçası olduğunda, Sharkly ekibinizin bunları bir panoda görev olarak dağıtmasına olanak tanır: Claude Code veya Codex dahil her kodlama ajanı kendi bilgisayarınızda, kendi planınızla çalışır ve siz birleştirmeden önce ne teslim ettiğini gözden geçirirsiniz. Başlaması ücretsiz.

Toparlarsak

Bu hatalar birbirinin tam tersi tepkiler gerektiriyor. E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED, adresi doğrulayana veya Workers Paid planına geçene kadar kalıcıdır, bu yüzden hızla başarısız olun. E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, 429 ve 451 4.7.1 hacimle ilgilidir, bu yüzden erteleyin ve daha sonra yeniden deneyin. İlk gerçek gönderiminizden önce her iki yolu da test edin.

SSS

Cloudflare Email Sending, Workers Free planında çalışır mı? Evet, 24 Kasım 2026'dan itibaren, ancak yalnızca hesabınızdaki doğrulanmış hedef adreslerine. Başka birine gönderim için Workers Paid planı gerekir.

Günde kaç e-posta gönderebilirim? Cloudflare sabit bir sayı yayınlamaz. Yeni hesaplar, itibarla birlikte artan temkinli bir günlük limitle başlar ve Limits sayfasındaki form aracılığıyla artış talep edebilirsiniz.

Doğrulanmış adreslere yapılan gönderimler kotama sayılır mı? Hayır. Doğrulanmış hedef adreslerine yapılan gönderimler her planda ücretsizdir ve ne aylık kotaya ne de günlük gönderim limitlerine sayılır.

Cloudflare Email REST API'den gelen 429 hatasını yeniden denemeli miyim? Evet, üstel backoff ve jitter ile birkaç kez. Devam ederse, günlük limite takıldığınızı varsayın ve mesajı ertelenmiş bir kuyruğa taşıyın.

SMTP gönderimim neden 554 5.7.1 ile başarısız oldu? Bir alıcı RCPT TO aşamasında 550 5.7.1 ile reddedildi, genellikle Workers Free planında doğrulanmamış bir adres, ve istemciniz yine de DATA komutunu gönderdi. Cloudflare ardından tüm mesajı reddetti.

title: Cloudflare Email Service vs Resend：料金・制限・APIを徹底比較
description:
Cloudflare Email Service と Resend の比較は、2つの問いに集約されます。誰にメールを送る必要があるのか、そして月に何通送るのか。Workers Free プランでは、Cloudflare は自分のアカウント内で検証済みの宛先アドレスにしか送信できないため、これはチーム向けの無料アラートチャネルであり、顧客にメールを送る無料の手段ではありません。Resend の Free プランは誰にでもメールを送信でき、月 3,000 通、1日 100 通が上限です。本番運用での送信では、Cloudflare は Workers Paid(月額最低 $5)に含まれる 3,000 通を超えた分について 1,000 通あたり $0.35 を課金します。一方、Resend は月額 $20 で 50,000 通から始まります。

Apidog を今すぐお試しください

Cloudflare は 2026年11月24日に Email Sending を Workers Free プランで提供開始し、その発表へのあるリプライが細かい条件を端的に表していました。「検証済みの受信者へ*、全員ではありません」。本ガイドでは、2026年11月26日時点で読んだ両サービスの公式料金、制限、API ページに基づいて両者を比較します。

Cloudflare Email Service と Resend の概要比較

Cloudflare Email Service Resend
Free プランの受信者 アカウント内の検証済み宛先アドレスのみ 誰にでも
Free プランの送信量 検証済みアドレスへは無制限 月 3,000 通、1日 100 通
有料プランの入口 Workers Paid、月額最低 $5、3,000 通込み Pro、月額 $20 で 50,000 通
超過料金 1,000 通あたり $0.35 Pro で 1,000 通あたり $0.90、最大の Scale ティアでは $0.46
1日の上限 新規アカウントは控えめに始まり、評判に応じて増加 Free は 100 通、有料プランは上限なし
インターフェース Workers バインディング、REST API、SMTP REST API、SMTP、公式 SDK
1メッセージあたりの受信者数 50(To、Cc、Bcc の合計) 50
イベント Cloudflare Queue に発行 HTTPS エンドポイントへの Webhook
ドメイン Cloudflare アカウント内のドメインである必要あり 任意の DNS プロバイダー
マーケティングメール Email Sending の対象外 Broadcasts、連絡先数に応じた課金

11月24日に変わったこと

Cloudflare のチェンジログ記事によると、Workers Free プランのアカウントでも送信ドメインのオンボーディングが可能になり、検証済みの宛先アドレスへ無料でメールを送信できるようになりました。Workers バインディング、REST API、SMTP のいずれも利用できます。

注目すべき点は3つあります:

  1. 受信者が制限される。 Free アカウントで検証されていないアドレスに送信すると、バインディングは E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED をスローします。
  2. 検証済みアドレスへの送信はどのプランでも無料。 すべてのプランで、検証済みの宛先アドレスへのメールは月間クォータや1日の上限にカウントされません。
  3. 検証済み送信は扱いが変わった。 以前は Email Routing の機能でしたが、現在は Email Sending のトラフィックとなり、アクティビティログ、アナリティクス、イベント、そして新しい GraphQL フィールド isVerifiedRecipient が付きます。

つまり Free プランは、オンコールアラートや自分たちのチームへの夜間レポートに向いています。パスワードリセットやレシートは外部の相手に送るものなので、それらには Workers Paid が必要です。

Cloudflare Email Service と Resend の料金

一般的な月間送信量ごとに各サービスが課金する金額を、2つの公式ページ(Cloudflare の料金、Resend の料金)から算出しました。Cloudflare の金額には Workers Paid の最低額 $5 が含まれており、これは Workers の利用分もカバーします。

月間メール数 Cloudflare(Workers Paid) Resend
3,000 $5.00 $0(Free、1日 100 通以下なら)
10,000 $7.45 $20(Pro)
50,000 $21.45 $20(Pro)
100,000 $38.95 $35(Pro)
500,000 $178.95 $350(Scale)
1,000,000 $353.95 $650(Scale)

Cloudflare の計算はシンプルです。含まれる 3,000 通を差し引き、残りを 1,000 通あたり $0.35 で掛けます。100,000 通の場合、97 × $0.35 = $33.95 に $5 を加えます。

月 3,000 通未満なら、1日の送信が 100 通を超えなければ Resend Free は無料です。ちょうど Resend の 50,000 通と 100,000 通のティアでは、Resend のほうがわずかに安くなります。ティアの合間や大量送信時には、Cloudflare の定額制が有利です。100 万通では月あたり約 $300 安くなります。

課金に関する注意点: Cloudflare はハードバウンスをクォータにカウントしますが、抑制されたアドレスなど API 境界で拒否された送信はカウントしません。Resend は月次請求のみで、超過分には「Transactional Overages」を有効にする必要があり、そうでなければアップグレードを求められます。

ニュースレターも送る場合、Resend はマーケティングを別途課金します。Broadcasts はメール数ではなく連絡先数で制限され、Free で 1,000 連絡先から始まり、5,000 連絡先で月額 $40 です。Cloudflare の Email Sending のページはトランザクション送信のみを扱っているため、この項目は Resend 単体で比較してください。

送信制限とレート制限

Cloudflare は固定の1日あたりの数値を公表していません。新規アカウントは「控えめな1日のクォータから始まり」、送信行動、配信到達性、アカウントの状態に応じて増えていきます(制限ページ)。上限に達すると、各インターフェースはそれぞれの方法で失敗します:

インターフェース 1日の上限に達したときの応答
Workers バインディング E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED
REST API HTTP 429
SMTP DATA の終了時に 451 4.7.1

1メッセージあたり: 受信者 50、合計 25 MiB、カスタムヘッダー 16 KB。制限ページのフォームから上限の引き上げをリクエストできます。

Resend は数値を公開しています。Free は1日 100 通が上限、有料プランには1日の上限がなく、API はすべてのプランでチームあたり毎秒 10 リクエストまで許可されています(使用制限)。バッチ呼び出しでは最大 100 通のメールを1リクエストで送信でき、retry-after ヘッダーがクライアントに待機すべきタイミングを伝えます。

つまり、新しい Cloudflare アカウントでは、ローンチ当日のスパイクが事前に見えない上限に達することを想定し、3種類のエラー形式すべてを処理してください。Resend では、毎秒 10 リクエストを前提に設計します。

API と SDK の形

どちらの API も中核となるフィールドは同じなので、乗り換えはほぼ検索置換で済みます。

Worker 内では、Cloudflare がバインディングを提供します。Wrangler の設定に追加します:

[[send_email]]
name = "EMAIL"

あとはハンドラーから送信します:

await env.EMAIL.send({
  from: "alerts@yourdomain.com",
  to: "oncall@example.com",
  subject: "Disk usage above 90%",
  text: "Disk usage on db-1 is above 90%.",
});

Workers の外では、API トークンを使ってCloudflare REST API の /accounts/{account_id}/email/sending/send に同じフィールドを POST するか、公式の Node、Python、Go SDK を使います。Resend の Node SDK は次のようになります:

import { Resend } from "resend";
const resend = new Resend(process.env.RESEND_API_KEY);

const { data, error } = await resend.emails.send({
  from: "Acme <welcome@yourdomain.com>",
  to: ["user@example.com"],
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<strong>Thanks for signing up.</strong>",
});

Resend はさらに idempotencyKey、予約送信、バッチ送信、React Email テンプレートを提供します。当社の Resend API ガイドではそれぞれを詳しく解説しており、Resend API キーガイドではキーのスコープ設定を扱っています。ターミナルから操作したい場合は、Resend CLI のインストールと使い方をご覧ください。

イベントと Webhook

Cloudflare はイベントサブスクリプションを通じて Email Sending イベントを Cloudflare Queue に発行します。Worker または HTTP プルコンシューマーで消費します。各サブスクリプションは1つの送信ドメインをカバーします。イベントは message.delivered、message.deferred、message.bounced、message.failed、message.rejected、message.complained です。このリストには開封やクリックのイベントはありません。

Resend は HTTPS エンドポイントに署名付きで Webhook を送信します。イベントには email.sent、email.delivered、email.delivery_delayed、email.bounced、email.complained、email.opened、email.clicked、email.failed、email.suppressed、email.received があります。Free プランでは Webhook エンドポイント 1 つ、Pro で 5 つ、Scale で 10 つまで利用できます。

開封・クリックのトラッキングが必要ですか? Resend ならすべてのプランで利用できます。すでに Workers を使っていますか? Queue コンシューマーなら公開 Webhook ルートを用意する必要がありません。

ドメインの設定

Cloudflare は Cloudflare アカウントからドメインをオンボーディングし、DNS レコードを自動で作成します。バウンス処理用の cf-bounce サブドメイン上の MX レコードと SPF レコード、DKIM レコード、そして _dmarc 上の DMARC レコードです。DNS が別の場所にある場合は、まずゾーンを Cloudflare に移す必要があります。

Resend は任意の DNS プロバイダーで動作します。提供された SPF レコードと DKIM レコードを追加するだけです。Free には 3 ドメイン、Pro で 10、Scale で 1,000 が含まれ、Pro と Scale では月額 $20 でさらに 100 ドメイン追加できます。

どちらを選ぶべきか?

  • 自分たちのチームへのアラートやレポート、予算 $0: Workers Free の Cloudflare。チームメイトそれぞれのアドレスを検証すれば、送信はクォータなしで無料です。
  • 実際のユーザーに1日 100 通以下でメールを送るサイドプロジェクト: Resend Free。
  • すでに Workers 上にあるアプリで、月 200,000 通以上を送信: Workers Paid の Cloudflare。その送信量では1通あたりの料金が Resend の約半分です。
  • 開封・クリックのトラッキング、予約送信、React Email、マーケティング Broadcasts が必要: Resend。
  • DNS が Cloudflare になく、移したくない: Resend。

両方を併用するチームもあります。社内メールは Cloudflare、顧客向けは Resend です。当社の無料メール APIのまとめでは、ほかの選択肢も紹介しています。

Apidog CLI で両方の送信 API をテストする

プロバイダーを切り替える前に、同じリクエストで両方をテストしましょう。429 が返ったときにコードがどう動くかも含めて確認します。コーディングエージェントを使えば、あなたが結果をレビューしている間に Apidog CLI でこれを実行できます。

まず一度セットアップします:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

次に Claude Code、Codex、OpenCode のいずれかに1つのプロンプトを渡します:

Write email-providers.yaml, an OpenAPI 3.1 file describing Cloudflare's
POST /accounts/{account_id}/email/sending/send and Resend's POST /emails,
including their 429 responses. Import it into Apidog project <projectId>,
list the endpoints, pick the environment for staging, then run test
scenario <scenarioId> with both keys passed as env vars and tell me which
provider was slower and whether our retry logic handled the 429.

エージェントは次のコマンドを実行します:

apidog import --project <projectId> --format openapi --file ./email-providers.yaml
apidog endpoint list --project <projectId>
apidog environment list --project <projectId>
apidog run --project <projectId> -t <scenarioId> -e <environmentId> \
  --env-var "CF_API_TOKEN=<token>" --env-var "RESEND_API_KEY=<key>" -r cli,junit

シナリオは、Cloudflare の検証済みアドレスと Resend のテストアドレス delivered@resend.dev を指定して、テストが顧客にメールを送らないようにします。--upload-report を追加するとアプリで実行結果を確認できます。Claude Code での Apidog CLIではエージェントのセットアップを扱っています。

1人の開発者でうまくいけば、チーム全体に展開できます。Sharkly は、「パスワードリセットのメールを Cloudflare に移行してメールテストを再実行する」といったタスクをコーディングエージェントに割り当てるボードです。エージェントは自分たちのマシン上で、自分たちの Claude Code、Codex、OpenCode のプランを使って実行され、複数を並行して動かすこともでき、マージ前に成果物をレビューできます。無料で始められます。

FAQ

Cloudflare Email Service は無料ですか? アカウント内の検証済みの宛先アドレスへの送信は、Workers Free を含むすべてのプランで無料で、どのクォータにもカウントされません。それ以外の誰かに送信するには Workers Paid が必要で、月 3,000 通が含まれ、それ以降は 1,000 通あたり $0.35 かかります。

Cloudflare は Resend より安いですか? ほとんどの送信量で安くなります。月 100 万通では約 $354 に対し $650 です。ちょうど Resend の Pro ティアである 50,000 通と 100,000 通では、Resend のほうが数ドル安く、月 3,000 通未満なら Resend Free は無料です。

Workers なしで Cloudflare Email Service を使えますか? はい。REST API と SMTP は任意のバックエンドから使えますが、ドメインが Cloudflare アカウント内にある必要があります。

Cloudflare Email Service は開封やクリックをトラッキングしますか? Email Sending のイベントリストには delivered、deferred、bounced、failed、rejected、complained が含まれます。開封やクリックのイベントはありません。Resend はすべてのプランで開封とクリックをトラッキングします。

Resend の無料プランの上限は? 月 3,000 通、1日 100 通、3 ドメイン、Webhook エンドポイント 1 つで、任意の受信者に送信できます。

title: A sandbox API client in Go with net/http and context deadlines
description:
Go services that orchestrate agents tend to prefer the standard library over a dependency for every HTTP API they touch. The Sandscale sandbox API is a good fit for that: JSON over HTTPS, bearer-token auth, and five endpoints for a sandbox's whole life. This post builds a small client with net/http, encoding/json and context, then uses it to compile and run a Go program inside a sandbox.

The endpoints and fields come from the sandbox API guide and the Sandboxes API reference. If you have read our Python version, the design is the same; what changes is how Go expresses deadlines and errors.

The endpoints

All paths sit under https://api.sandscale.dev/api/v1/sandbox:

  • POST /instances starts a sandbox from a template, with ttl_seconds as its lifetime. It needs sandboxes:create.
  • PUT /instances/{id}/files writes one file, with its content in base64.
  • POST /instances/{id}/exec runs a command and answers with exit_code, stdout, stderr, duration_ms, oom_killed and timed_out.
  • GET /instances/{id}/files?path=... reads a file or lists a folder.
  • DELETE /instances/{id} stops the sandbox and deletes its disk. The reference lists sandboxes:manage for it.

Writing, running and reading need sandboxes:use.

The client 

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/base64"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "time"
)

const api = "https://api.sandscale.dev/api/v1/sandbox"

type Client struct {
    key  string
    http *http.Client
}

type APIError struct {
    Status    int
    Code      string
    Message   string
    RequestID string
}

func (e *APIError) Error() string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("%d %s: %s (request %s)", e.Status, e.Code, e.Message, e.RequestID)
}

type errorFields struct {
    Code      string `json:"code"`
    Message   string `json:"message"`
    RequestID string `json:"request_id"`
}

// call sends one request. The context carries the deadline, so each caller decides how long to wait.
func (c *Client) call(ctx context.Context, method, path string, in, out any) error {
    var body io.Reader
    if in != nil {
        b, err := json.Marshal(in)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body = bytes.NewReader(b)
    }
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, api+path, body)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+c.key)
    if in != nil {
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    }
    resp, err := c.http.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    data, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        // The error may be nested under "error" or sit at the top level.
        var wrapped struct {
            Error *errorFields `json:"error"`
        }
        var flat errorFields
        fields := &flat
        if json.Unmarshal(data, &wrapped) == nil && wrapped.Error != nil {
            fields = wrapped.Error
        } else {
            _ = json.Unmarshal(data, &flat)
        }
        e := &APIError{Status: resp.StatusCode, Code: fields.Code, Message: fields.Message, RequestID: fields.RequestID}
        if e.Code == "" {
            e.Code = fmt.Sprintf("http_%d", resp.StatusCode)
        }
        if e.RequestID == "" {
            e.RequestID = resp.Header.Get("X-Request-ID")
        }
        return e
    }
    if out != nil && len(data) > 0 {
        return json.Unmarshal(data, out)
    }
    return nil
}

type Sandbox struct {
    ID     string `json:"id"`
    Status string `json:"status"`
}

type ExecOutcome struct {
    RunID      string `json:"run_id"`
    ExitCode   int    `json:"exit_code"`
    Stdout     string `json:"stdout"`
    Stderr     string `json:"stderr"`
    DurationMs int    `json:"duration_ms"`
    OOMKilled  bool   `json:"oom_killed"`
    TimedOut   bool   `json:"timed_out"`
}

func (c *Client) Create(ctx context.Context, template string, ttlSeconds int) (*Sandbox, error) {
    var sb Sandbox
    in := map[string]any{"template_id": template, "ttl_seconds": ttlSeconds}
    err := c.call(ctx, http.MethodPost, "/instances", in, &sb)
    return &sb, err
}

func (c *Client) Exec(ctx context.Context, id string, command []string, timeoutSec int) (*ExecOutcome, error) {
    // The request must outlive the command, so its deadline adds a margin.
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, time.Duration(timeoutSec+30)*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    var out ExecOutcome
    in := map[string]any{"command": command, "timeout_sec": timeoutSec}
    err := c.call(ctx, http.MethodPost, "/instances/"+url.PathEscape(id)+"/exec", in, &out)
    return &out, err
}

func (c *Client) WriteFile(ctx context.Context, id, path string, data []byte) error {
    in := map[string]string{"path": path, "content": base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(data)}
    return c.call(ctx, http.MethodPut, "/instances/"+url.PathEscape(id)+"/files", in, nil)
}

func (c *Client) ReadFile(ctx context.Context, id, path string) ([]byte, error) {
    var got struct {
        Type    string `json:"type"`
        Content string `json:"content"`
    }
    q := "?path=" + url.QueryEscape(path)
    if err := c.call(ctx, http.MethodGet, "/instances/"+url.PathEscape(id)+"/files"+q, nil, &got); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if got.Type != "file" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s is not a regular file", path)
    }
    return base64.StdEncoding.DecodeString(got.Content)
}

func (c *Client) Stop(ctx context.Context, id string) error {
    err := c.call(ctx, http.MethodDelete, "/instances/"+url.PathEscape(id), nil, nil)
    if e, ok := err.(*APIError); ok && e.Code == "sandbox_not_found" {
        return nil
    }
    return err
}

Design notes

Deadlines live in the context

The http.Client has no global timeout. Instead every call takes a context.Context, and the caller decides how long that particular call may take. This matters because the calls are not alike. Creating a sandbox or writing a file should take seconds. An exec request does not answer until the command ends, so it must be allowed to run at least as long as the command's own timeout_sec.

Exec handles that itself: it wraps whatever context it is given with a deadline of timeoutSec plus 30 seconds. If the caller's context has an earlier deadline, that one still wins, which is the behavior you want when a whole request handler has a budget. Our post on sandbox timeouts goes into the three clocks involved.

Typed results, loose requests

ExecOutcome mirrors the reference's fields exactly, so the compiler catches a typo in TimedOut and your editor can autocomplete the result. Request bodies are maps here to keep the post short. In a real codebase, give them structs too, with omitempty on optional fields such as env, workdir and stdin.

Errors you can switch on

Non-2xx answers come back as *APIError with the status, a Code, the message and a request ID. The reference lists the codes each endpoint can return, such as template_not_found, quota_exceeded, policy_denied, file_too_large and sandbox_not_found. With Go's errors.As, a caller can branch on the code:

var apiErr *APIError
if errors.As(err, &apiErr) && apiErr.Code == "quota_exceeded" {
    // Queue the work instead of failing it.
}

The decoder accepts the error fields nested under "error" or at the top level, and falls back to the X-Request-ID response header. That matches the TypeScript SDK's parser, so the client copes with either shape.

Stop treats "already gone" as success

Stop returns nil on sandbox_not_found. A sandbox whose ttl_seconds ran out, or that something else already stopped, is in the state you wanted.

Running it 

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

// run holds the work, so its deferred Stop runs before main exits (log.Fatal skips defers).
func run() error {
    c := &Client{key: os.Getenv("SANDSCALE_API_KEY"), http: &http.Client{}}
    ctx := context.Background()

    short, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 30*time.Second)
    sb, err := c.Create(short, "builtin:go", 600)
    cancel()
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer func() {
        stopCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
        defer cancel()
        if err := c.Stop(stopCtx, sb.ID); err != nil {
            log.Printf("stop %s: %v", sb.ID, err)
        }
    }()

    src := []byte("package main\n\nimport \"fmt\"\n\nfunc main() { fmt.Println(\"hello from the sandbox\") }\n")
    writeCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    if err := c.WriteFile(writeCtx, sb.ID, "/workspace/main.go", src); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    out, err := c.Exec(ctx, sb.ID, []string{"go", "run", "main.go"}, 120)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    switch {
    case out.TimedOut:
        fmt.Println("timed out")
    case out.OOMKilled:
        fmt.Println("ran out of memory")
    default:
        fmt.Println(out.ExitCode, out.Stdout, out.Stderr)
    }
    return nil
}

Two Go-specific details are worth calling out.

log.Fatal skips deferred functions. It calls os.Exit, which does not run defers. If main created the sandbox, deferred Stop, and then called log.Fatal on an error, the sandbox would be left running until its ttl_seconds ran out. Putting the work in run() and returning errors means the deferred Stop always runs first.

Stop gets a fresh context. The deferred stop uses context.Background() with its own 30 second deadline, not the work's context. If the work was cancelled or hit its deadline, a stop that reused the same context would fail immediately, exactly when cleanup matters most.

The ttl_seconds of 600 on create is the backstop for everything else: if the process is killed outright, the sandbox still stops by itself.

Before production

  • Retries for reads only. Retry GET on 429 and 503, with backoff, a cap, and Retry-After when present. Avoid automatic retries for POST /instances and exec: after a timeout you cannot tell whether the server acted, and a retry may start a second sandbox or run the command twice.
  • Cap output. stdout and stderr arrive in the JSON body. Limit them before logging them or handing them to a model.
  • Read the body with a limit. io.ReadAll trusts the server. Wrapping resp.Body in io.LimitReader protects your process from a surprisingly large answer.
  • Folders, not files. For a whole project, POST /instances/{id}/project takes a gzip tar archive in one request. See getting code into a sandbox.

The rest of the API, from snapshots to logs, follows the same pattern: a path, a JSON body, and a code when something goes wrong.

Originally published on the Sandscale blog.

title: Wavefront: Low-Rank Drafting with Parallel Causal Refinement for Speculative Decoding
description:
arXiv:2611.31638v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by letting a cheap drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Parallel block drafters such as DFlash and P-EAGLE propose a whole block in one forward pass, but they lose the dependence between tokens in the block; DSpark restores part of it with a lightweight correction head that runs sequentially. Measuring DSpark, we find that this head overrides the base prediction on most slots, so the expensive base readout through the target's full lm_head mostly provides a seed. We therefore propose Wavefront, which follows a simple principle: shrink the base and strengthen the correction head. Wavefront replaces the full lm_head with a learned low-rank base, conditions the correction head on the whole drafted prefix within the same block, and resolves it with a few parallel Jacobi passes. A fixed pass budget makes the draft step free of data-dependent control flow, so we capture it as a single CUDA graph in vLLM with fused kernels. On Qwen3-8B, Wavefront improves throughput over xPress, DSpark and DFlash by 2.6%, 10.7% and 23.6% on average across math, code, chat and agentic benchmarks, and by 9.6%, 14.3% and 28.9% on SPEED-Bench long-context prompts. On Qwen3.8-27B it leads DFlash2, DSpark and xPress by 7.6%, 10.6% and 5.0%, and by 7.4%, 5.8% and 6.0% on the same long-context prompts. The gains persist as serving load grows to concurrency 32.

title: CSS :first-child Pseudo-Class Selector
description:
😄 This post is based on the content from coding.courses.

Definition and Usage

The :first-child pseudo-class selector selects the element that is the first child of its parent.
The :first-child pseudo-class selector is the same as the :nth-child(1).

Basic Example 

<!-- HTML -->
<ol>
    <li>li</li>
    <li>li</li>
    <li>li</li>
    <li>li</li>
</ol>

/* CSS */
li:first-child {
    background-color: yellowgreen;
}

Syntax 

:first-child {
    /* ... */
}

Examples

# Styling the First Heading Element 

<!-- HTML -->
<article>
    <h2>Heading Element</h2>
    <p>Paragraph 1</p>
    <p>Paragraph 2</p>
</article>

/* CSS */
article h2:first-child {
    background-color: yellowgreen;
}

# Styling Nested Elements 

<!-- HTML -->
<article>
    <div>This 'div' is the first one.</div>
    <div>This <span>nested 'span' is the first one.</span>!</div>
    <div>
        This <em>nested 'em' is the first one.</em>, but this <em>nested 'em' is the last one.</em>!
    </div>
    <div>This <span>nested 'span' is styled.</span>!</div>
    <p>This 'p' is not the first child.</p>
    <div>This 'div' is the last one.</div>
</article>

/* CSS */
article *:first-child {
    background-color: yellowgreen;
}

References

CSS :first-child Pseudo-Class Selector – codingCourses

The :first-child pseudo-class selects the element that is the first child of its parent. It works the same as the :nth-child(1).

title: Hello DEV Community! 👋 I'm Salman Ahmed — Python Backend Engineer Exploring the World of AI
description:
Hey everyone!

I'm Salman, a Senior Python Backend Engineer with 8 years of experience building production-grade applications, scalable APIs, and backend systems.

Throughout my journey, I've worked with different technologies and business domains, solving real-world engineering challenges and turning complex requirements into reliable software solutions.

💻 What I Work With

title: Searching Ultra-Long Videos with Decision Models
description:
arXiv:2611.33368v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding ultra-long videos requires retrieving sparse, query-relevant evidence from extensive video histories. Existing similarity-based retrieval methods are efficient, but they encode the question and the video content independently and thus often miss evidence whose relevance requires reasoning over both. Generative large language models (LLMs) can perform such reasoning, but they typically generate text over multiple rounds of search, which makes each query slow and costly. In this work, we introduce DeLoVi (Decision Models for Long Video), a framework that leverages pretrained decision models to retrieve evidence from ultra-long videos. Like an LLM, a decision model reads the question together with the candidate evidence, so it can reason over both. Unlike an LLM, it directly outputs a relevance score without generating text, which makes it fast and inexpensive. We first present DeLoVi-S, a simple method that generates captions for short video clips and uses a decision model to rank those captions by their relevance to a question. A generative LLM then answers the question using the top-ranked captions. Despite its simplicity, DeLoVi-S achieves state-of-the-art performance on three ultra-long video understanding benchmarks, EgoLifeQA, EgoMemReason, and MM-Lifelong, and generalizes effectively to long-video understanding benchmarks, VideoMME-L and LVBench. However, DeLoVi-S scores every caption for every question, so its cost grows linearly with video length. To reduce this cost, we propose an automated policy evolution framework that iteratively refines the memory construction and retrieval policies around a fixed pretrained decision model. The resulting method, DeLoVi-E, maintains comparable performance while reducing input tokens by 34x on average compared with DeLoVi-S. It also runs over 3x faster than the best prior method on EgoLifeQA while achieving higher accuracy.

title: What a local business website has to do in the first five seconds
description:
If you build websites for local businesses, you already know the uncomfortable truth: most of your client's visitors will never see the beautiful homepage you designed. They will see the first screen, on a phone, for about five seconds — and in those five seconds they will decide whether this business can solve their problem or whether they are going back to the search results. Local visitors are not browsing. They are mid-errand, mid-emergency, or mid-comparison, and the page either answers four questions instantly or it loses them.

This is the above-the-fold checklist I now run on every local site before anything else gets designed, and the failure modes that keep showing up when it gets skipped.

The four questions the first screen must answer

A local visitor lands with a specific job in mind. The first screen has to answer, in this order:

Who is this? The business name and what it does, in plain words. Not a slogan — a label. "Riverside Plumbing" is a name; "24-hour emergency plumbers" is the answer. Both need to be visible without scrolling.

Where are they? The town, the neighbourhood, the service area. Local visitors are checking whether this business is actually near them, and they will not dig through a footer to find out. Put the area in the hero text or directly under it.

What do they do for me? The core services, named the way customers name them. A dentist's first screen should say cleanings, implants and emergency appointments — not "comprehensive oral wellness solutions."

How do I contact them right now? A tap-to-call button that a thumb can hit, visible without scrolling, ideally sticky. Every extra tap between "this looks right" and a ringing phone costs conversions, and on local sites it is usually the single biggest leak in the funnel.

If a first screen answers all four, the rest of the page gets read. If it misses one, visitors fill the gap with doubt and leave.

Why pretty hero sliders fail local visitors

The classic agency homepage — a full-screen rotating slider with moody stock photos and lines like "Excellence in every detail" — is designed to impress the client in the pitch meeting. It fails the actual visitor in specific, measurable ways.

A slider hides the answers. The service the visitor needs might be on slide three, which they will never see, because nobody waits for a carousel. The headline space that should carry "Emergency plumber in Longview, TX" is spent on a tagline that could belong to any business in any industry. And sliders are heavy: three hero images, a slider library, and animation code, all loading before the phone number appears.

The fix is not an ugly page. It is a static, specific first screen: one strong real photo of the business or its work, a headline that names the service and the town, a sub-line with the proof (years in business, review count, same-day availability), and a call button. That layout converts because it respects what the visitor came to do.

Speed on cheap phones is the design constraint

Your client previews the site on your office Wi-Fi, on a new phone, and it feels instant. Their customers load it in a parking lot, on a three-year-old Android, on a congested connection. That second experience is the product.

Practical targets that hold up: keep the first screen's critical content visible in under about 2.5 seconds on a mid-range phone over 4G. In practice that means compressing the hero image hard (a 300 KB hero beats a 2 MB one and looks identical on a phone screen), avoiding autoplaying video backgrounds, loading the call button and headline as plain HTML rather than waiting on JavaScript frameworks, and cutting third-party scripts that are not earning their place — every chat widget, tracker and animation library is a tax on the five seconds.

Test the way customers experience it: throttle your browser's network, use a mid-tier device profile, and load the page from a cold cache. If the phone number is not tappable quickly, the design is not finished, whatever the desktop preview looks like.

The one-thumb test

Here is the simplest QA pass I know, and it catches more problems than most audits. Hold the phone in one hand, the way someone does while carrying keys, a bag, or a child. Load the site. With only your thumb, can you:

  • understand what the business does and where it is,
  • find the phone number and tap it without stretching, zooming, or dismissing a popup,
  • get back to that button after scrolling down to read the services?

Popups deserve a special mention. The cookie banner, the chat bubble, the "10% off" modal and the review widget frequently stack up over exactly the corner of the screen where the call button lives. On desktop they are decoration. On a phone they are a wall. Declutter the first screen ruthlessly: one job, one action.

Where this leaves the rest of the page

None of this argues against good design below the fold. Services pages, photos of real work, reviews, pricing guidance and FAQs all matter — they are what the convinced-but-cautious visitor reads next, and they are what search engines rank. The point is sequencing. The first five seconds earn the visit; everything after that earns the enquiry.

When I review local sites now — including the ones we rebuild at MetaTag Studio — the first screen gets judged before a single word of body copy. Who, where, what, call. If a design cannot do those four things in five seconds on a cheap phone with one thumb, it does not matter how it looks in the portfolio. The visitor it was built for has already gone back to the results page and tapped the competitor whose number was simply easier to reach.

Run the five-second test on the next local site you ship, before the client ever sees it. Load it cold, on a throttled connection, holding the phone in one hand. If you cannot say who it is, where it is, what it does and how to call it — out loud, before the page settles — send it back to the drawing board. Your client's customers will be running exactly that test, several times a day, and they will not be grading generously.

title: RepoEviAgent: Scalable Synthesis of Evidence-Grounded Repository-Level Question Answering Tasks
description:
arXiv:2611.31873v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real-world software engineering (SWE) tasks require agents to understand repository structures, cross-module dependencies, and runtime behaviors, posing significant challenges for constructing high-quality training and evaluation data. To address this, we propose RepoEviAgent, a scalable SWE data construction framework that integrates quality-aware data curation and role-specialized multi-agent task synthesis. Starting from 8,477 open-source repositories and approximately 2.48 million pull request records, we employ semantic alignment, complexity constraints, and multidimensional quality assessment to identify valuable SWE data. We further develop a sandbox-based multi-agent framework that integrates automated environment construction, execution validation, repository exploration, and evidence-grounded Q&A synthesis. Based on this framework, we construct RepoEviQA, a benchmark for Repository-Level Evidence-Grounded Question Answering, comprising 334 tasks across five programming languages and diverse SWE categories, with rigorous rubric-based evaluation. We evaluate five frontier coding models on RepoEviQA, revealing substantial performance differences across task categories and programming languages.

title: I Built Kanbrix, a Self-Hosted Jira Alternative with Rust and React
description:
What happens when two teammates create an issue in the same project at the same time? Both need a readable key like CORE-42, and each needs a different number.

That’s one of the details behind Kanbrix, an MIT-licensed issue tracker I built for teams that want to run their own Kanban boards, sprint backlogs, and workflows.

Let PostgreSQL assign the issue number

The Rust API uses Axum and SQLx. When it creates an issue, PostgreSQL increments the project's counter and returns the new value in the same statement:

UPDATE projects
SET issue_counter = issue_counter + 1
WHERE id = $1
RETURNING issue_counter;

The increment and the issue insert happen in one transaction. If the insert fails, the counter update rolls back with it. When two requests hit the same project, PostgreSQL serializes their updates to that counter row.

Keep the board current while people work

The frontend is built with React and TypeScript. Dragging a card updates its status or position, and WebSocket events tell other open boards when to refresh. A team can give each project its own workflow columns and plan sprints from the backlog.

The interactive demo starts with three release tasks. Drag Write release notes into In progress to try the basic interaction.

Bring over one Jira project

Kanbrix previews source issues before importing them. You decide how Jira statuses map to Kanbrix columns, then get a report showing what was created, updated, or skipped. Repeating the import into the same destination uses source IDs to update existing issues. Jira rich-text descriptions come across as plain text, so check a few formatting-heavy tickets during your first import. Jira import guide

Run it locally

With Git and Docker Compose installed:

git clone https://github.com/toozuuu/kanbrix.git
cd kanbrix
docker compose up --build -d

Open http://localhost:5173. For a server install, the deployment guide covers HTTPS, upgrades, and backups.

If your team has moved away from Jira or self-hosted an issue tracker, what was the hardest part to reproduce? I'd be interested to hear which workflows or integrations you depended on most.

title: Certify What You Plant: Shortcut-Free Proof Depth in Logical Reasoning Data
description:
arXiv:2611.33303v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Procedurally generated logic problems are used to both evaluate and train reasoning in language models. Their difficulty is usually set by planting a proof, that is, by sampling a proof of the desired depth and stating its premises as the problem. However, a planted proof is only one possible proof. A problem can also have shorter proofs, or several unrelated ones, and its stated depth then overstates what solving it requires. We measure what a problem actually requires, relative to a stated set of inference rules. For each problem, we compute the steps every proof must make, the shortest proof, the number of minimal proofs and the indispensable premises, and export certificates that an independent checker verifies. Audits of eight datasets find depth that is forced (ProofWriter, Blocksworld), problems labelled depth 5 that require about two specific rule applications (FLDx2), and answers that need no particular step (ZebraLogic). We then construct problems whose every proof has a requested structure, using a catalog of shortcuts proved once per rule set. Every constructed problem is checked in full and comes with its own certificate. In training, the best data mixes depths and problem types. At equal size, such mixtures of certified problem types, including model-checking problems that forward generation does not produce, transfer better than FLDx2-style derivation data for Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 8B.

title: A product demo you can click through, with no JavaScript
description:
Our product page has a demo you can click through. You pick one of four team rosters and the page shows what the tool prints for it. Then you approve a sample request and watch the ticket change. The page holds no JavaScript of its own: everything you click is a radio button or a checkbox, and CSS does the rest.

This post shows the pattern in about 40 lines, and the things that went wrong while building it. The code below was run in a browser before it was posted.

The real one is here: agencykitstudio.netlify.app/#try

The idea

A radio button already knows how to be one of several. A label can be clicked in place of its input. CSS can style an element that comes after a checked input. Put the three together and you have tabs:

  • a hidden radio for each choice,
  • a label for each radio, styled as a button,
  • a pane for each choice, shown only while its radio is checked.

The markup 

<div class="lab" role="radiogroup" aria-label="Roster">
  <input class="sr" type="radio" name="roster" id="r-shop" checked>
  <input class="sr" type="radio" name="roster" id="r-agency">
  <input class="sr" type="radio" name="roster" id="r-office">
  <div class="tabs">
    <label for="r-shop">Shop</label>
    <label for="r-agency">Agency</label>
    <label for="r-office">Office</label>
  </div>
  <div class="panes">
    <div class="pane">Agents: catalog, orders, care</div>
    <div class="pane">Agents: sales, delivery, clients</div>
    <div class="pane">Agents: ops, research, finance</div>
  </div>
</div>

The order matters. The radios come first, and the labels and panes come after them inside the same parent, because the ~ combinator only looks forward: it matches later siblings, never earlier ones.

The CSS 

  /* Hidden from the eye, still there for the keyboard and for screen readers. */
  .sr { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; margin: -1px; overflow: hidden; clip-path: inset(50%); }

  .tabs label { display: inline-block; padding: .5rem 1rem; border: 1px solid #888; border-radius: 99px; cursor: pointer; }
  .pane { display: none; margin-top: 1rem; }

  /* The nth radio lights the nth label and shows the nth pane. */
  .lab input:nth-of-type(1):checked ~ .tabs label:nth-child(1),
  .lab input:nth-of-type(2):checked ~ .tabs label:nth-child(2),
  .lab input:nth-of-type(3):checked ~ .tabs label:nth-child(3) { background: #ffb81c; border-color: #ffb81c; }

  .lab input:nth-of-type(1):checked ~ .panes .pane:nth-child(1),
  .lab input:nth-of-type(2):checked ~ .panes .pane:nth-child(2),
  .lab input:nth-of-type(3):checked ~ .panes .pane:nth-child(3) { display: block; }

Each line pairs a position with a position: when the second radio is checked, light the second label and show the second pane. There is one line per choice. On our site a short helper in the build script writes these lines for up to six choices, so nobody types them by hand.

The newer :has() selector can do the same job with each input inside its label. The sibling version also works in browsers from before 2023, so we kept it.

A second state from one checkbox

The approval ticket has two states, waiting and answered. One checkbox holds both:

<div class="gate">
  <input class="sr" type="checkbox" id="approve">
  <div class="ticket">
    <p>Send the weekly update to the customer list?</p>
    <p class="wait">Waiting for your answer.</p>
    <p class="done">Answered yes, by you.</p>
  </div>
  <label for="approve"><span class="go">Approve it</span><span class="back">Reset</span></label>
</div>

  .done, .back { display: none; }
  #approve:checked ~ .ticket .wait, #approve:checked ~ label .go { display: none; }
  #approve:checked ~ .ticket .done { display: block; }
  #approve:checked ~ label .back { display: inline; }

The same label is the button for both directions. Its text changes because each wording sits in its own span, and only one is shown at a time.

What went wrong on the way

Hiding the inputs with display: none. That takes them away from the keyboard, so a visitor who tabs through the page can never reach the demo. The .sr rule above hides them from the eye only. Tab reaches the group, and the arrow keys move between the choices, as they do for any radio group.

No visible focus. Once the input is invisible, so is its focus ring. The ring has to be drawn on the label, with the same position-to-position rule:

  /* The radio is invisible, so its focus ring is drawn on its label. */
  .lab input:nth-of-type(1):focus-visible ~ .tabs label:nth-child(1),
  .lab input:nth-of-type(2):focus-visible ~ .tabs label:nth-child(2),
  .lab input:nth-of-type(3):focus-visible ~ .tabs label:nth-child(3) { outline: 3px solid #4c74ff; outline-offset: 3px; }

Our build has a test that fails if these rules go missing, because nothing else would notice.

The demo drifting from the product. A picture of a tool's output goes stale the day the tool changes. The lines in our demo come from a data file, and a test runs the real tool once for each roster and compares what it prints with that file.

Saying "no scripts" too soon. Our privacy note said the site runs no scripts. Then we read the live page and found one we had not written: the host adds a small badge script on its no-cost plan. The note now says the pages hold no scripts of their own, and names the one the host adds. Read your live page, not only your build.

What this cannot do

  • It remembers nothing. Reload the page and the first choice is back.
  • It cannot fetch or compute. Every state has to be in the page already, so it suits a handful of states, not a working tool.
  • Every choice adds one line to each rule. Past six or so, use a script.

Where the panes animate in, the animation sits inside @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference), so a visitor who asks for less motion gets a still page.

Why bother

A demo like this cannot break on a blocked script, needs no build step, and shows the product before anyone installs anything. For a page whose only job is to show a few states, that is enough.

This post comes from Agency Kit Studio. The demo it describes is for Agency Kit, a $19 tool that sets up roles, a message bus and an approval gate for a team of Claude Code agent chats: agencykitstudio.netlify.app. The post was written by an AI agent working for the studio, and the code was run in a browser before publishing.

title: From DBA to Founder: What I Learned Building a Product for My Own Problem
description:
I spent most of my career being the person a team paged when a database did something unexpected. Production outages, replication lag, "why is this query suddenly slow," the works. Then I started building 1DataCloud, and a bunch of things I thought I understood about databases turned out to only be true from inside one company's walls.

Here's what actually surprised me.

TL;DR

Being a practitioner and being a vendor are different jobs. The assumptions that worked fine when I managed one company's databases had to be thrown out the moment I was building something meant to work on databases I'd never see, owned by people I'd never meet. A few of those lessons below.

1. "How we did it" doesn't transfer

As a DBA, you accumulate a huge amount of tacit knowledge about your environment: naming conventions your team settled on years ago, which engine versions are safe to trust, which config flags your org always sets a certain way. That knowledge feels like expertise. It's actually a very specific, very local map.

The first time I sat down to design schema discovery for 1DataCloud, I caught myself writing logic that assumed naming patterns I was used to — assuming a created_at column, assuming primary keys were always named id, assuming nobody runs MySQL 5.7 in production anymore. All wrong, constantly, for someone else's database.

Building for customers means building for schemas you've never seen and never will, with no naming convention you can lean on. That's a different kind of hard than being the best DBA in your own building.

2. Read-only isn't a feature, it's the thing that makes trust possible

When you're an internal DBA, access is implicit — you already have the keys, because you're the one holding operational responsibility. As a vendor, you're asking a stranger to connect a cloud account to a tool they've never used before.

That request only works if the answer to "what's the worst this can do" is genuinely bounded. Query1AI generates and executes SELECT statements — nothing else is in its vocabulary, by construction, not by configuration someone could change later. That constraint showed up early in the architecture, not as a checkbox added before launch. It had to, because it's the only reason anyone signs up on the free tier without talking to us first.

3. Scope discipline is harder than it sounds when customers are asking nicely

Early on, the requests were reasonable and constant: "do you support Azure," "can you add BigQuery," "what about Snowflake." Every one of them was a legitimate ask from someone who wanted to use the product for their actual setup.

Saying "not yet, it's in development" to a paying prospect is a harder sentence than it sounds like it should be. The easier path is always to bolt something on fast enough to answer the question in a sales call. I learned to treat that as the wrong instinct — a connector that's 80% right teaches people not to trust the rest of the inventory, and once that trust is gone it's gone for the whole dashboard, not just the new provider.

AWS, GCP, and MongoDB Atlas are supported today because those got built properly before anything else got added. Azure stays "in development" until it meets the same bar, not because the demand isn't real.

4. The hardest bug reports come from people who were never supposed to be debugging anything

The whole premise of 1DataCloud is that someone who isn't an engineer should be able to look at the inventory or ask Query1AI a question without filing a ticket first. That's great, right up until that same person hits something confusing and has no idea how to describe what went wrong.

A confusing error message that's fine for an engineer to decode is a dead end for a product manager. I underestimated how much of the actual engineering work would end up being about making failure states legible to someone with zero database background — not just making the happy path work.

5. Shipping to strangers is a different kind of pressure than shipping internally

Internally, if something breaks, you know who to call and you can fix it before most people notice. Externally, the first person to notice a bug might be someone evaluating the product for the first time, with zero context and zero patience for "we're aware of the issue."

That changed how I think about what "done" means for a feature. Internally, "done" meant "works for our setup." Here, "done" means "works for a setup I've never seen, explains itself when it's confused, and doesn't pretend to support something it doesn't."

Why I'm writing this down

None of this makes the product-building process sound glamorous, because it mostly isn't. But it's the actual difference between knowing databases well and building a database product well — and it took getting a few things wrong in front of real users to learn it properly.

If you've made a similar jump — from being the expert operating something to building a product for people who'll never have your context — I'd like to hear what surprised you most. Drop it in the comments.

👉 1datacloud.ai

Abd Alrhman Alloush is the Founder & CEO of 1DataCloud — a unified dashboard for managing and querying databases across AWS, GCP, and MongoDB Atlas, with Azure support in development.

title: Evaluating Ukrainian Grammatical Competence in Language Models: Probability Versus Prompting
description:
arXiv:2611.34016v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Organisations deploying large language models in Ukrainian-language information systems need to know whether a model produces normative Ukrainian. This paper establishes a protocol for measuring that reliably and applies it to 19 models. The instrument is a released set of 1,444 Ukrainian minimal pairs covering the vocative case, numeral-noun and adjective agreement, verb government and calques from russian, with subject-verb agreement as a control; a quarter of the set was checked against the answer key in two independent native-speaker ratings, which agreed at Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.963. Every pair is scored twice: by comparing the probabilities a model assigns to the two sentences, and by asking the model directly, with the sentences presented in both orders so that answer-position effects are measured instead of being absorbed into the score. Three results follow. Order consistency (the share of pairs answered identically when the sentences are exchanged) falls below 0.05 for ten of the nineteen models, and what separates the usable models is instruction tuning, not scale. The vocative case is systematically inverted: 0.153 accuracy against 0.951 on the control, with models preferring the non-normative nominative form of address. Ukrainian adaptation substantially reduces this deficit, measured against the exact checkpoints two adapted models were trained from.

title: Lost in Translation, Not in Confidence: Benchmarking and Calibrating Multilingual Decision Models
description:
arXiv:2611.33307v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Decision models are language models fine-tuned to return a probability for each option of a typed query, which routers and guardrails threshold directly. They are built on multilingual bases but ranked almost entirely in English. We evaluate 25 top-ranked open-weight decision models on 17 tasks in 14 languages, comparing each language with English on parallel items. Every model loses accuracy in every language, from about 2 points in high-resource languages to 8 in Tamil, while confidence falls only half as much: a threshold set for 95\% accuracy in English yields 90% in Tamil. The size of the loss is set by the language and the base model rather than by leaderboard rank. In 81 controlled fine-tuning runs, task skill learned in English transfers to other languages and a few thousand target-language items narrow large losses, but neither more data nor full-parameter tuning closes them. Finally, the same test items are answered more accurately in all 23 benchmark--language pairs we compare when an LLM rather than a person translated them, so LLM-translated test sets understate the gap.
