title: Scraping Workday Career Sites Without a Browser: Notes on the wday/cxs JSON API
description:
Every time a hiring-data pipeline hits a Fortune 500 careers page, the URL ends in myworkdayjobs.com and the initial HTML is an empty shell. Most teams immediately reach for Playwright, burn 500MB of RAM per tab, and spend the next afternoon fighting infinite-scroll timers.

You do not need a browser for Workday listings. Every modern Workday careers portal pulls its job list from the same undocumented internal POST endpoint:

POST https://<tenant>.wd<N>.myworkdayjobs.com/wday/cxs/<tenant>/<site>/jobs

If you open DevTools on almost any myworkdayjobs.com site and watch the XHR tab while paging through jobs, you will see that exact call fire with a tiny JSON body.

The request shape (and the 20-item ceiling)

Here is the minimal request that works across wd1 through wd5 tenants:

curl -sS -X POST "https://acme.wd5.myworkdayjobs.com/wday/cxs/acme/External/jobs" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" \
  -d '{"appliedFacets":{},"limit":20,"offset":0,"searchText":""}'

The response comes back flat and predictable:

{
  "total": 142,
  "jobPostings": [
    {
      "title": "Senior Backend Engineer",
      "externalPath": "/job/San-Francisco/Senior-Backend-Engineer_R-10492",
      "locationsText": "San Francisco, CA",
      "postedOn": "Posted 4 Days Ago",
      "bulletFields": ["R-10492"],
      "remoteType": "Hybrid"
    }
  ]
}

Two things trip people up right away when paginating this:

  1. Stick to limit: 20. Some tenants silently clamp larger limits back down to 20, and a few return 400 if you ask for 100. Paginating in 20-row steps with offset += len(payload.JobPostings) is boring, but it does not break.
  2. Pace multi-page loops per host. Firing 15 concurrent POSTs at the same wd5 host gets you 429 pretty quickly. In our Go fetcher we keep a 120ms per-host delay on pages after offset == 0, and if a later page fails after we already collected rows, we stop and return partial results instead of discarding the whole company.

Here is the core pagination loop in Go:

const pageSize = 20
offset := 0
var jobs []WorkdayPosting

for len(jobs) < maxJobs {
    if offset > 0 {
        time.Sleep(120 * time.Millisecond)
    }
    body, _ := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
        "appliedFacets": map[string]any{},
        "limit":         pageSize,
        "offset":        offset,
        "searchText":    "",
    })
    resp, err := postJSON(ctx, apiURL, body)
    if err != nil {
        if len(jobs) > 0 {
            break
        }
        return nil, err
    }
    if len(resp.JobPostings) == 0 {
        break
    }
    jobs = append(jobs, resp.JobPostings...)
    offset += len(resp.JobPostings)
    if (resp.Total > 0 && offset >= resp.Total) || len(resp.JobPostings) < pageSize {
        break
    }
}

Four annoying quirks in the Workday payload

Once the POST works, the actual headaches are in normalizing the fields:

1. Tenant + shard + site discovery is harder than the scrape

Unlike Greenhouse (boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/<slug>/jobs) or Ashby (api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/<slug>), Workday needs three pieces of information: the tenant slug (acme), the cluster shard (wd1, wd3, wd5, etc.), and the external site name (External, Careers, GlobalCareers, or sometimes a localized path). Guessing them blindly does not scale. The reliable path is to fetch the company's /careers page (following redirects), scan for myworkdayjobs.com links, and parse host + first path segment directly from the redirect or HTML.

2. postedOn is fuzzy English text, not a timestamp

Workday does not give you an ISO-8601 publishedAt in the list endpoint. You get strings like:

  • "Posted Today"
  • "Posted Yesterday"
  • "Posted 6 Days Ago"
  • "Posted 30+ Days Ago"

Converting "today", "yesterday", and (\d+)\+?\s+days?\s+ago into approximate YYYY-MM-DD dates is easy enough:

var workdayDaysAgoRe = regexp.MustCompile(`(?i)(\d+)\+?\s+days?\s+ago`)

func parseWorkdayPostedOn(postedOn string, now time.Time) string {
    s := strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(postedOn))
    switch {
    case strings.Contains(s, "today"):
        return now.Format("2006-01-02")
    case strings.Contains(s, "yesterday"):
        return now.AddDate(0, 0, -1).Format("2006-01-02")
    }
    if m := workdayDaysAgoRe.FindStringSubmatch(s); len(m) == 2 {
        if days, err := strconv.Atoi(m[1]); err == nil {
            return now.AddDate(0, 0, -days).Format("2006-01-02")
        }
    }
    return ""
}

The catch is "Posted 30+ Days Ago". You cannot tell from the list endpoint whether a posting is 31 days old or a 9-month evergreen listing. If freshness matters for your pipeline, treat anything matching 30+ as an upper-bound unknown (aged_90d / stale candidate) rather than pretending it was posted exactly 30 days ago.

3. Requisition IDs move around

Most tenants put the req ID in bulletFields[0] (e.g., R-10492), while some leave bulletFields empty and suffix externalPath after an underscore (.../Senior-Backend-Engineer_JR10492). Falling back from bulletFields[0] to the substring after the last _ in externalPath gives a stable dedupe key for incremental runs.

4. Full descriptions require a second GET

The /jobs list endpoint only gives title, location text, remote type, and externalPath. If you need the full job description text or salary bands buried at the bottom of the JD, you have to GET:

GET https://<tenant>.wd<N>.myworkdayjobs.com/wday/cxs/<tenant>/<site><externalPath>

Skip that second call if you only need hiring velocity, department headcount, or title/location screening. It cuts request count by 20x.

Note: If you would rather not maintain Workday tenant detection and pagination yourself, I packaged this Go parser into a standalone Apify Actor (Workday Jobs Scraper) and a unified 6-ATS MCP server (ats-jobs-hiring-intel-mcp on GitHub).

title: ContextLure: Exploiting Benign Conversation History for Indirect Prompt Injection
description:
arXiv:2611.31424v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As LLMs become more capable, agents can perform more complex tasks with tools and maintain longer interactions with users. These benign conversations contain evidence on task results, user concerns, and operational constraints. The risk is that attackers who can observe benign conversations (evidence) may construct stronger indirect prompt injections without increasing the attackers' control over prior turns or the later injection. However, we still lack a clear study of how effectively attackers can select and use this evidence. To address this gap, we introduce ContextLure, a red-teaming framework in which an attacker silently observes an existing benign conversation, extracts evidence, and constructs an injection. The challenges are twofold: (a) selecting useful evidence and (b) presenting it as reasons for an unauthorized action, without changing the prior benign conversation. To efficiently exploit (a) the effect of evidence on attack success, our framework selects evidence across 2 dimensions: User/System Preferences with 3 selection policies. And to enhance (b) the process of turning the selected information into the malicious request, we introduce an Urgency/Priority matrix with 4 rewriting strategies. Across the evaluated conditions, we reach 67.4% ASR on AgentDojo and 87.3% on InjecAgent. These results show that attackers can use benign interaction evidence in later attacks without first poisoning the benign conversation.

title: Sequentially Acquiring Concept Knowledge to Guide Continual Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.33399v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The goal of continual learning (CL) is to adapt to new data (plasticity) while retaining the knowledge acquired from old data (stability). Existing methods are explicitly designed to focus on balancing stability and plasticity to mitigate the challenge of catastrophic forgetting while promoting learning. However, the impact of order and nature of samples from the new data that the network is trained on remains an under explored factor. We argue that a CL algorithm should have the ability to rank incoming samples in terms of their relationship with prior data and their effect on the learning process. In this work, we investigate if scoring and prioritizing incoming data based on their semantic relationships with the model's current knowledge can benefit CL. We propose SACK, short for Sequentially Acquiring Concept Knowledge, a plug and play technique for continual learning methods. SACK dissects categorical knowledge of the model into fine-grained concepts, computes the relationships between previously learned concepts and new concepts in each experience, and uses this relationship knowledge for prioritizing new samples. Experiments across several types of CL methods (regularization, replay, and prompt based) in class incremental and task incremental settings demonstrate that integration of SACK not only improves accuracy and reduces forgetting but also handles long tail distribution, helps focus on semantically interpretable regions, and yields better calibrated and robust models compared to prior approaches.

title: ArtTet: Watertight Part Meshes of Articulated Objects from Rigid-Body Rules and Partitioned Marching Tetrahedra
description:
arXiv:2611.33382v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present ArtTet, a method that reconstructs an articulated object from multi-view observations of two articulation states and outputs one watertight mesh per rigid part together with the joints that move them. Mesh splatting gives explicit triangles, but it treats the object as one scene. It extracts a single global surface and cannot keep the triangles of different parts apart; the mesh it exports is layered, self-intersecting, and full of holes. ArtTet follows a divide-and-conquer strategy instead. We first divide the object into rigid parts with dynamic- and geometric-constrained articulation and ownership inference. A multibody registration of the two states recovers the parts and their screw joints. Rigid-body rules on attachment, contact, and swept motion then correct joint types and part labels without any part annotation. We then divide space into part cells with an articulated tetrahedral partition, and conquer each cell with its own differentiable signed distance field on a shared tetrahedral grid. In these partitioned marching tetrahedra the fields are mutually exclusive by construction, so the extracted part meshes are closed and never overlap. All part meshes are optimized jointly from the images of both states through the recovered joints. On Articulate-100, ArtTet gives the most accurate axis directions, part motions, and part geometry over all objects among methods that use no part masks, and its part meshes have virtually no open boundary edges. We also show reconstructions of real captures from the SplArt dataset.

title: A daily puzzle needs more than a local midnight check
description:
I maintain a small group of independent browser games. A recurring product question is what a player means by “another round.” Sometimes it is a new shared daily edition. Sometimes it is practice, a replay, or simply a continuation of a local save.

Those distinctions need to be visible in the interface before they become boolean flags in the code.

Begin with the mode, not the timer

These are the projects behind the examples below; I maintain all five:

  • Poople unlimited is word-ladder practice, separate from the shared daily puzzle and dated archive.
  • Movie Krillion has a free seven-prompt daily film round. A valid credit and a rarity score are different checks.
  • MedRare.app separates daily medical trivia, ended-edition replays and free mixed practice. Its scores describe answer recall, not disease prevalence or medical advice.
  • Every Last Grain is an independent sand-digging game. Its ongoing adventure save and fixed-setup time trial are different state contexts, rather than daily editions of one result.
  • I Know Your Age is a nostalgia quiz with a final entertainment-only age guess. It should not acquire a daily streak merely because the other products have one.

The common implementation model should leave room for these differences. “All games reset at midnight” would be a poor abstraction.

A small calendar boundary example

The following is a standalone model for discussion, not a claim that these five production sites share this exact implementation. Montreal is an example edition time zone. Choose the actual product’s calendar explicitly.

const assert = require('node:assert/strict');
function dayKey(now, timeZone) {
  const parts = new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-CA', {
    timeZone, year: 'numeric', month: '2-digit', day: '2-digit'
  }).formatToParts(now);
  const value = key => parts.find(p => p.type === key).value;
  return `${value('year')}-${value('month')}-${value('day')}`;
}
function mayReveal({ mode, editionEnded, cardSubmitted }) {
  return mode === 'practice' || editionEnded || cardSubmitted;
}
const zone = 'America/Montreal';
assert.equal(dayKey(new Date('2026-11-26T04:59:59Z'), zone), '2026-11-25');
assert.equal(dayKey(new Date('2026-11-26T05:00:00Z'), zone), '2026-11-26');
assert.equal(dayKey(new Date('2026-07-01T03:59:59Z'), zone), '2026-06-30');
assert.equal(dayKey(new Date('2026-07-01T04:00:00Z'), zone), '2026-07-01');
assert.equal(mayReveal({mode:'daily',editionEnded:false,cardSubmitted:false}),false);
assert.equal(mayReveal({mode:'daily',editionEnded:false,cardSubmitted:true}),true);
assert.equal(mayReveal({mode:'daily',editionEnded:true,cardSubmitted:false}),true);
assert.equal(mayReveal({mode:'practice',editionEnded:false,cardSubmitted:false}),true);
console.log('8 assertions passed');

I ran this snippet with Node: all eight assertions passed. The four calendar checks cover the minute boundary on a winter date and a summer date. A fixed “subtract five hours” expression would be wrong for the summer pair.

formatToParts also avoids assuming that a date’s displayed punctuation or component order is suitable as a storage key. The key is deliberately assembled as year-month-day.

A calendar key is not a security boundary

A browser can use the edition key to label a result or decide which explanation to display. It cannot make an unreleased answer secret. If the answer is already in a downloaded script, hiding an HTML panel does not protect it.

For a scored daily game, the server should decide which edition is active and what can be returned. Likewise, a competitive timer cannot depend only on a tab’s animation loop: background tabs and changed device clocks are normal conditions to account for. This small snippet intentionally does not implement those server responsibilities.

The mayReveal example is a product-policy sketch. It distinguishes a completed card from an ended edition and from practice. A real application also needs to decide who is allowed to request that card, whether an attempt was actually submitted, and which explanatory fields belong in the response. Do not trust a client-supplied cardSubmitted: true as proof.

Keep score semantics out of the calendar helper

A film answer can be valid without being the highest-scoring answer. A medical-trivia rarity tier is not a clinical probability. A time-trial record is not an adventure completion percentage. These meanings should stay in their own product rules.

The calendar helper should answer one narrow question: which edition date does this instant belong to? Keeping it small makes it easier to test and harder to mistake for answer validation or anti-cheat logic.

Design the return visit

Before publishing a new mode, I would check three situations: someone returns after the edition changes; someone opens a past result; someone chooses practice after finishing today’s round. The labels, answer policy and saved result should still agree in each case.

The useful abstraction is an explicit mode plus an explicit edition boundary—not a timer pasted onto every browser game.

title: Yet Another Concept Drift Benchmark? A Principled Framework for Evaluating Drift Detectors
description:
arXiv:2611.33424v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Concept drift detection is a fundamental component of data stream learning, yet its empirical evaluation remains based on loosely defined protocols, ambiguous alarm semantics, and inconsistent metrics. We propose a principled benchmark grounded in an explicit formulation of drift observability and alarm semantics. Our framework introduces finite detection windows and repeated alarms, enabling a clear separation between detection accuracy, timeliness, and stability, and employs a reproducible observer to provide a controlled and interpretable performance signal. Building on this formulation, we define normalized evaluation metrics and a composite score addressing limitations of existing measures. We validate the framework through a large-scale stress-testing evaluation of 10 detectors across 9 learner configurations and 16 datasets.

title: Monitorable-by-design architectures for a post-Astra world: a compartmentalization-based approach
description:
arXiv:2611.31610v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Frontier models like GPT-6 Astra are increasingly able to do substantial reasoning without a monitorable chain of thought, chains of thought are becoming less legible, and are often monitored asynchronously to reduce cost. With the future of chain of thought monitoring unclear, it may be necessary to design LLMs with monitorability in mind. We propose a modification to existing LLM architectures based on GRAM, SGTM, DEMix, BTS, and similar methods to compartmentalize dangerous capabilities so that their use, especially in combination with dangerous reasoning types that may indicate strategic adversarial use, can be monitored more cheaply than chain of thought in a way that might outlast monitorable chain of thought. We propose several variants of this architecture designed to balance tradeoffs and discuss other benefits, such as capability removal.

title: UGREEN DXP4800PLUS NAS로 유튜브 쇼츠 자동화 시스템 구축기 (Docker · FastAPI · PostgreSQL · Edge-TTS)
description:
집에 NAS가 있다면 유튜브 쇼츠 자동화 시스템을 직접 구축할 수 있습니다. UGREEN DXP4800PLUS NAS에서 쇼츠 자동화 파이프라인을 구축한 과정을 살펴봅니다.

운영 상태를 확인할 항목

  • 수집 영상과 저장 스냅샷 수: 같은 조회 시각을 기록하고 집계
  • 성장률 계산: 비교 스냅샷이 없는 영상과 계산 실패를 구분
  • 콘텐츠 분류: 표본과 분류 조건을 함께 기록
  • 영상 생성: 대본·음성·자막의 결과를 단계별로 확인

수집 규모나 성공률을 인용하려면 집계 시각·질의·출력 원문을 함께 보관해야 합니다. 이 글에서는 근거를 함께 제시할 수 없는 수치 대신 구성과 확인 절차를 설명합니다. 다른 NAS 모델이나 버전에서는 동작을 별도로 확인하세요.

단순 성공 사례가 아닙니다. FastAPI 404 오류, 분류기 정확도 문제, 영상 생성 실패까지 실제 겪은 삽질과 해결 과정을 함께 담았습니다.

전체 파이프라인 구조

NAS에서는 YouTube API 수집부터 PostgreSQL 저장, 성장률·콘텐츠 분류, 대본·음성·영상 생성, drafts 저장까지를 독립된 서비스로 운영했습니다. Python 구현과 단계별 코드는 유튜브 쇼츠를 Python으로 자동 생성하는 방법에 정리했습니다. 같은 구현을 반복하기보다 DXP4800PLUS에서 확인한 운영 상태와 장애 해결에 초점을 맞춥니다.

FastAPI app.mount("/") 사용 시 API 404 오류 해결 방법

FastAPI에서 정적 파일을 루트(/)에 mount한 뒤 API가 404로 응답하는 문제를 실제로 겪었습니다. 원인은 루트 마운트가 뒤에 선언된 경로보다 먼저 요청을 가로채는 라우팅 순서였습니다. API 라우트를 먼저 등록하고 정적 파일 mount를 마지막에 두는 방식으로 해결했습니다. 재현 코드와 최소 예시는 FastAPI app.mount 사용 후 API가 404가 되는 이유와 해결 방법에 따로 정리했습니다.

YouTube 트렌드 수집기에서 AI 콘텐츠가 안 잡히는 이유

AI_AUTOMATION 클러스터에 필요한 영상이 충분히 수집되는지 먼저 확인합니다.

원인이 두 가지였습니다.

첫째, 수집 소스가 한국 급상승 위주였습니다. 한국 유튜브 급상승은 드라마, 연예, 뉴스가 압도적입니다. AI/IT 콘텐츠가 애초에 없었습니다.

아래 함수 이름은 수집 범위의 차이를 설명하기 위한 개념 예시이며 그대로 실행하는 완성 코드가 아닙니다.

# 기존: 한국 급상승과 쇼츠 검색
collect_popular(region="KR")  # 한국 급상승
collect_shorts_search(q="쇼츠")  # 한국 쇼츠

# 개선: 글로벌 키워드 + 채널 추가

collect_global_keywords(["ChatGPT shorts", "Claude AI", "n8n automation"])
collect_global_channels(["MKBHD", "Techquickie", "Linus Tech Tips"])

둘째, 분류기가 영어 키워드를 잡지 못했습니다. IT_DEVICE 클러스터를 새로 만들고 영어 키워드를 대폭 추가했습니다.

수집 범위를 바꾼 뒤에는 같은 집계 조건으로 분류별 영상 수를 비교하고, 실제로 관련 있는 영상인지 표본을 확인합니다.

왜 드라마 쇼츠는 자동화가 어렵고 IT 쇼츠는 쉬운가

자동 영상 생성을 처음 돌렸을 때 결과물이 처참했습니다. 트렌드 1위 드라마 쇼츠 대본으로 영상을 만들었는데, 배경에 여자 눈 클로즈업이 무한 루프로 돌아가고 자막은 음성과 전혀 맞지 않았습니다.

여기서 중요한 걸 배웠습니다.

자동화 가능 자동화 어려움
IT 제품 스펙 비교 드라마/감정 연출
AI 도구 소개 연예/셀럽 가십
랭킹/차트 정보 스토리텔링
앱 사용법 가이드 반전/충격 연출

드라마는 배우 표정, 타이밍, 감정선이 핵심이라 당시 구성에서는 자동화가 어려웠습니다. IT 제품은 이미지와 스펙 텍스트 중심으로 구성하기가 상대적으로 쉬웠습니다. 당시 IT_DEVICE와 AI_AUTOMATION 클러스터만 영상 자동 생성 대상으로 제한했습니다.

사용 기술 스택

  • 하드웨어: UGREEN DXP4800PLUS (Intel Pentium Gold 8505, 5코어 / 8GB DDR5)
  • 컨테이너: Docker + Docker Compose
  • 백엔드: FastAPI + Python 3.11
  • DB: PostgreSQL 15
  • 수집: YouTube Data API v3
  • AI: OpenRouter (AI 언어 모델)
  • TTS: Edge-TTS (한국어 음성)
  • 영상: FFmpeg 5.1

title: Deterministic Routing Over Chatty Swarms: How Lean Agent Pipelines Cut Latency and Token Burn in Half
description:
Early multi-agent architectures often mistook conversation for intelligence. Spinning up a planner, a writer, two critics, and a supervisor to debate every small output looks impressive in demos—until you measure latency, API burn, and failure modes in production. In 2026, resilient autonomous studios are shifting toward deterministic routing: reserving LLM reasoning strictly for creative synthesis while handing validation, media pipelines, and state tracking to lean Python code.

“Every unnecessary agent-to-agent round trip is a tax on latency, context clarity, and creative momentum.”

— Luca Automated Studio Notes

01 · THE HIDDEN COST OF FOUR-EYES AGENT LOOPS

Where Conversational Swarms Stall

When three autonomous agents critique each other in natural language, prompt context balloons exponentially with every iteration. Worse, critique agents rarely share identical grounded state: they invent stylistic nitpicks, trigger redundant retries, and burn thousands of tokens verifying facts that a five-line Python assertion could prove in two milliseconds.

During the rollout of our recent publishing infrastructure—documented in Autonomous Studio Publishing in 2026—eliminating synthetic QA round trips cut end-to-end deployment time dramatically while keeping editorial quality under direct human review.

02 · SEPARATING REASONING FROM DETERMINISTIC EXECUTION

The Two-Layer Studio Pattern

A high-leverage agent network divides work along a clean boundary: probabilistic language models draft original narratives, alt descriptions, and semantic taxonomy, while deterministic scripts handle I/O, image transcoding, HTTP retries, and schema serialization.

  • Idempotent Manifests: Store published IDs, slugs, and asset hashes in local JSON manifests so re-runs never duplicate posts or media uploads.
  • Zero-Token Validation: Verify image dimensions, WebP byte budgets, HTTP 200 status codes, and JSON-LD parseability via standard Python libraries.
  • Single-Hop Tool Execution: Pass structured payloads directly to publisher helpers instead of serializing intermediate prose between wrapper agents.
  • Direct Escalation: When a genuine creative or visual judgment call arises—such as curating motion studies like The Moment Everything Changes or Built for Open Skies—route directly to the human operator rather than a consensus bot. 03 · STATE MACHINE CONTRACT FOR MEDIA & EDITORIAL WORKFLOWS

Predictable Pipelines Under Real Hardware Limits

Whether orchestrating local GPU inference or syncing gallery upgrades like Florentine Projector Beam: Overhead 35mm Palazzo Portrait Study, explicit state transitions eliminate silent half-published failures.

DETERMINISTIC PIPELINE CONTRACT (PYTHON)

1. FETCH_RECENT   -> Query WP REST API (last 40 titles/slugs) to enforce topic uniqueness
2. SELECT_ASSET   -> Filter local studio directory against existing media filenames
3. TRANSCODE_WEBP -> Resize <= 1600px width, WebP quality=86, attach alt/caption metadata
4. PUBLISH_POST   -> Inject Article + FAQPage JSON-LD & internal links, status='publish'
5. PING_INDEXNOW  -> Submit new URLs + homepage in one batched HTTP POST

04 · MEASURING SYSTEM HEALTH BY SHIPPED ASSETS

Why Lean Architectures Scale Better

The best metric for an autonomous network is not how many messages its agents exchange, but how reliably verified work reaches production per unit of compute. By pairing deterministic Python orchestration with clean editorial interfaces, a single lean pipeline can publish weekly four-pillar updates, refresh gallery alt text, and notify search crawlers without babysitting. Browse additional architecture blueprints in Agent Networks.

FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS

Key Studio Takeaways

What is deterministic routing in an AI agent network?

Deterministic routing means using explicit code and state machines to control workflow steps, file I/O, and API validation, calling language models only where creative synthesis or semantic judgment is genuinely needed.

Why avoid multi-agent QA loops for routine publishing tasks?

Synthetic QA loops multiply token consumption and wall-clock latency while still missing deterministic issues like broken URLs or invalid JSON-LD that simple Python assertions catch instantly.

How do idempotent manifests prevent duplicate WordPress posts?

By recording source filenames, generated slugs, and returned post IDs in a structured JSON manifest after each step, retry runs can skip completed assets safely.

When is a human-in-the-loop better than another critique agent?

Whenever brand taste, emotional tone, or visual composition is at stake. Direct operator review after deterministic execution is faster, cheaper, and produces far more cohesive creative work.

Originally published at Luca Automated. Explore Luca Labs (Quant Models, Market Probabilities & Agent Setups).

title: BreathSplat: Grounding One Smooth Motion in the Breathing Phase for 4D Cone-Beam CT
description:
arXiv:2611.33392v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Four-dimensional cone-beam computed tomography (4D-CBCT) images the anatomy of a breathing patient, but sees each breathing phase from only a few angles. Breathing, however, is a smooth motion that repeats; it has a phase. Existing methods exploit this either by reconstructing the anatomy as a function of the breathing phase, often through bins, or by estimating smooth dynamic motions in time. Yet none of these grounds one smooth motion in the phase. We thus propose to share projections across breathing phases with splines. Specifically, we represent the 4D volume with dynamic Gaussians whose motion uses B-splines in space and time. We ground the motion state in the respiratory phase, which we read from well-studied conventional surrogates. Projections at the same phase in different breathing cycles then constrain the same anatomy and motion. On simulated lung scans, our method, BreathSplat, outperforms recent dynamic methods in reconstruction and motion accuracy, including those given the ground-truth phase. We further show qualitatively, on two real patient scans, that our method provides clearer reconstructions than the state of the art.

title: I built one UI component library that works in HTML, React, Vue and Svelte, with 8 styles
description:
Every time I started a new project, I hit the same wall with component libraries.

The good ones were tied to one framework. If I built a marketing page in plain HTML and the app in Vue, I needed two libraries that looked nothing alike. And almost all of them had one look. You could change the colours, but a "shadcn-style" site still looked like every other shadcn-style site.

So I built VinUI: one set of components, eight complete visual styles, any accent colour, light and dark. It works in plain HTML, React, Vue and Svelte, and every framework renders the same markup.

It's free, MIT licensed, and launching on Product Hunt today.

Try it in 10 seconds 

npx @vinish/ui init
npx @vinish/ui add button

The CLI reads your framework from package.json, writes the component files into your project and records them in vin.json. There's no runtime package to install or keep updated. The code is yours, so you can change anything.

Using plain HTML? Add one stylesheet, copy the markup, and include vinui.js for the interactive parts.

One component, eight looks

Each style is a set of design tokens, not a separate theme you bolt on. The CSS is generated from those tokens, so every component reads the same token names in every style:

  • Precision: crisp hairlines, for dev tools and SaaS
  • Tactile: physical, pressable buttons, for productivity apps
  • Clay: puffy and friendly, for onboarding and education
  • Tonal: colour-led pill shapes, for consumer and mobile-first apps
  • Editorial: typographic and airy, for blogs and portfolios
  • Terminal: monospace and developer-native, for CLI docs
  • Paper: warm and hand-made, for personal sites
  • Bento: calm, layered and borderless, for product sites

The whole theme lives on one element, usually <html>:

<html data-vin-style="tactile" data-vin-mode="dark" data-vin-radius="lg" style="--vin-accent: #0d9488">

Change data-vin-style and every component on the page follows. On the docs site you can pick a style in the header and watch the whole site change with it.

The same markup in every framework

This was the part I cared about most. Every component has one API spec (spec/<name>.json). The HTML snippets are checked against it, and the React, Vue and Svelte versions are tested to render the same markup as the HTML.

Here's the same button and input in all four:

HTML

<button class="vin-btn vin-btn--outline">Save</button>

<label class="vin-label" for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" class="vin-input" type="email">

React

import { Button } from "@/components/vin/button";
import { Input } from "@/components/vin/input";

<Button variant="outline">Save</Button>
<Input label="Email" type="email" />

Vue

<script setup>
import Button from "@/components/vin/button.vue";
import Input from "@/components/vin/input.vue";
</script>

<Button variant="outline">Save</Button>
<Input label="Email" type="email" />

Svelte

<script>
  import Button from "$lib/components/vin/button.svelte";
  import Input from "$lib/components/vin/input.svelte";
</script>

<Button variant="outline">Save</Button>
<Input label="Email" type="email" />

Because the output is identical, styles, screenshots and accessibility behave the same everywhere. Only the syntax changes.

What's included

63 components across actions, forms, data display, feedback, layout, navigation and overlays. That covers the usual (Button, Dialog, Tabs, Select, Toast) and the harder ones: Combobox, Date Picker, Data Table, Command menu, Sidebar, Resizable panels, Carousel and Chart.

There are also 7 AI chat components: Message, Bubble, Message Scroller, Attachment, Marker, Questionnaire and Trace. These are handy if you're building a chat UI.

On top of the components:

  • 13 blocks: whole sections you can paste in, such as sign-in, sign-up, a dashboard, settings, pricing, FAQ, contact and 404. For example: npx @vinish/ui add dashboard-01
  • 16 charts: area, bar, line, pie and donut, in plain SVG with no chart library. They have tooltips, keyboard support and a data table for screen readers.

Accessibility and progressive enhancement

Every component has keyboard support, focus handling and ARIA, and is checked against WCAG 2.2 AA in all 8 styles, in light and dark. The test suite uses Playwright to take screenshots and run axe in every style and mode.

In plain HTML, only components with keyboard or pointer behaviour need vinui.js, which is one small script with no dependencies. The rest need no JavaScript. Dialog, Alert Dialog, Sheet and Drawer use the browser's native <dialog>. Even without the script, the Carousel still swipes, the Chart still draws and the Data Table still shows its first page.

No Tailwind required

VinUI ships its own small CSS files, so you don't need Tailwind or any other CSS framework. If your project already uses Tailwind, VinUI can run alongside it.

Built for AI coding tools too

Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Copilot can run the same npx @vinish/ui add <name> command you do. They add real components in your framework and your style instead of guessing at markup. There's also an llms.txt (and llms-full.txt) at https://vinish.dev/ui/llms.txt, plus a JSON registry for each framework.

Updating without losing your edits

Because the files live in your project, you can edit them freely. When I ship an update, npx @vinish/ui diff shows what changed upstream, and your own changes are kept.

Try it and tell me what you think

  • Docs and live demo: vinish.dev/ui
  • GitHub: github.com/devvinish/vin-ui
  • Product Hunt: producthunt.com/posts/vinui

If VinUI looks useful, an upvote or a comment on Product Hunt today would mean a lot. I'd also love to know which of the 8 styles you'd pick, and what component you'd want next. Leave a comment here and I'll reply.

title: What survives a terrain bake from Houdini to Three.js?
description:
Full desktop experiment and runnable lab · 中文原文

I baked one procedural terrain and one Houdini heightfield to GLB, then reopened the results in Three.js r187 on an RTX 5070 Ti. Three details mattered:

  • Runtime and asset compatibility are separate. The Procedural Terrains 2.1.0 runtime generated terrain with WebGL2 in the desktop probe. The WebGPU renderer was initialized, but the library rejected it at terrain creation. The baked GLBs loaded on both r187 backends.
  • Check the signed range. The default heightfield bake flattened 4,477 elevations below zero. Baking with an eight-unit offset and undoing it on readback preserved them, with a mean absolute error of 0.00396 world units.
  • Validate the native export. The raw Houdini GLB opened in the viewer but had two out-of-range indices. Rebuilding the affected triangles from the native geometry produced a GLB with zero validator errors and warnings.

The original includes export settings, matching desktop tests, 480 GPU timing samples, and a runnable reproduction package. Codex assisted with testing and writing.

title: Stranded Compute in AI Inference Workloads: Recovering Value Through Demand Aggregation
description:
arXiv:2611.31654v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI inference infrastructure is commonly analyzed as an energy business. Under full total cost accounting it is not: in the reference deployment modeled here, capital recovery is 87.3% of fully loaded cost per token and electricity 3.7%. Because capital accrues per unit time irrespective of use, accelerator value is destroyed by non-utilization rather than by consumption. Yet, SLO qualified goodput reaches only 59.6% of nameplate throughput, and the decomposition of the loss chain shows that 25.2 of the 40.4 lost percentage points arise from scheduling idleness and stranded burst reserve. Both are properties of a tenant's demand portfolio rather than of its silicon, and neither is diversifiable by a single tenant acting alone. Modelling reserve and idle capacity as diversifiable risk, pooling demand across eight imperfectly correlated tenants (rho = 0.3) recovers 7.3 pp of goodput, approximately $0.75M per annum per megawatt of IT capacity, or between 2.8x and 4.9x the entire annual interconnection spend of the deployment that produced it. The implication for neutral colocation and interconnection providers is that the switching and interconnection layer aggregating tenant demand functions as an instrument of capital productivity while being priced as transport.

title: Your HttpClient Retry Policy Probably Never Retried a Hung Request
description:
A phone is ringing, and your service has a couple of seconds to look the caller up in the CRM so the agent sees a name instead of a bare number. The CRM's first request hangs. You have a retry policy with three retries and exponential backoff, so you expect the second attempt to save you. It never runs. The call is answered with no context, and the logs show one TaskCanceledException.

I found this pattern in my own public template, dotnet-integration-api-template. It sets http.Timeout = 10s on a typed HttpClient and adds a Polly retry with AddPolicyHandler. The retries work fine for fast failures (a 503, a refused connection). For a request that hangs, the whole 10 seconds goes to attempt one, and the retry loop is cancelled with it.

So I built a small lab to measure exactly what each common wiring does.

The setup

Every scenario uses the same fake upstream: attempt 1 hangs (30 s), and attempt 2 onwards answers 200 immediately. Every scenario has the same budget: 2 s for the whole call, 500 ms per attempt where a per-attempt timeout exists, 3 retries, 200 ms base backoff.

The fake upstream is a primary HttpMessageHandler that logs every attempt, so the tests can count what really went over the "wire":

protected override async Task<HttpResponseMessage> SendAsync(HttpRequestMessage request, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var n = Interlocked.Increment(ref _attempts);
    if (n <= HangingAttempts)
        await Task.Delay(HangFor, ct);   // hang until cancelled
    return new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK);
}

These are the four wirings:

// A: the common one. HttpClient.Timeout + retry handler
b.ConfigureHttpClient(c => c.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2));
b.AddPolicyHandler(retry);

// B: a Polly timeout, but registered BEFORE the retry
b.AddPolicyHandler(Policy.TimeoutAsync<HttpResponseMessage>(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2)));
b.AddPolicyHandler(retry);

// C: retry first, per-attempt timeout second, HttpClient.Timeout as the total budget
b.ConfigureHttpClient(c => c.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2));
b.AddPolicyHandler(retry);   // retry also handles TimeoutRejectedException
b.AddPolicyHandler(Policy.TimeoutAsync<HttpResponseMessage>(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(500)));

// D: Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience
b.AddStandardResilienceHandler(o =>
{
    o.TotalRequestTimeout.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2);
    o.AttemptTimeout.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(500);
    o.Retry.Delay = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(200);
});

The results

This is one real run on my Linux x64 dev box with .NET 8.0.34. The exact milliseconds will vary on your machine. The attempt counts won't.

Scenario Outcome Attempts Elapsed
A: HttpClient.Timeout + retry TaskCanceledException 1 2006 ms
B: timeout policy outside retry TimeoutRejectedException 1 2000 ms
C: retry outside per-attempt timeout 200 OK 2 705 ms
D: AddStandardResilienceHandler 200 OK 2 742 ms

All four have the same retry policy, and only two of them ever retry. Here is the per-attempt timeline from the same run:

Why A fails: HttpClient.Timeout wraps the whole pipeline

HttpClient.Timeout is not a socket timeout. HttpClient creates a cancellation token linked to that timeout and passes it into the entire DelegatingHandler chain that IHttpClientFactory built. That chain includes your Polly handler. Retries happen inside that token's lifetime.

When attempt one hangs, nothing fails fast. The token fires at 2 s, the in-flight attempt is cancelled, and the retry handler sees a cancellation rather than a transient failure. The template's retry uses HandleTransientHttpError(), which handles HttpRequestException, 5xx and 408, but not cancellation.

The obvious "fix" is to also handle TaskCanceledException. I added that as a separate test (A2), and it still makes exactly one attempt. The token that HttpClient passed down is already cancelled, so there is nothing left to retry with. The default HttpClient.Timeout is 100 seconds, which is why many apps never notice: they just wait a very long time.

Why B fails: handler order is outermost-first

With IHttpClientFactory, handlers run in the order you register them, and the first one registered is the outermost. Registering the timeout before the retry gives one timeout around all attempts. That makes it a total-budget timeout, not a per-attempt one. Polly's own guidance for HttpClientFactory says the same thing: put the per-try timeout inside the retry (Polly wiki: Polly and HttpClientFactory).

Why C and D work

In C, the retry is the outer handler, and each attempt gets its own 500 ms timeout. Attempt one is cut at ~500 ms with a TimeoutRejectedException, which the retry handles. After a 200 ms backoff, attempt two returns 200 at ~705 ms. HttpClient.Timeout is still there, but now it means what it should: the total budget for the call.

D is the same shape, packaged. According to the Microsoft Learn docs, the standard handler chains rate limiter â†’ total timeout â†’ retry â†’ circuit breaker â†’ attempt timeout, outermost to innermost. The defaults are a 30 s total, a 10 s per attempt, and 3 retries with a 2 s exponential base delay and jitter. The retry handles TimeoutRejectedException by default.

I also tested the worst case, where the upstream hangs on every attempt. Both C and D stop at the 2 s total budget after 2â€“4 attempts instead of blowing past it.

Gotchas I hit along the way

  • Leave HttpClient.Timeout above the pipeline's total timeout. With D, I set it to the total plus one second. If it is lower, it fires first, and you are back in scenario A with a cancellation instead of the pipeline's own TimeoutRejectedException.
  • Polly v7 and Polly v8 collide. Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Polly (v7) and Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience (Polly.Core v8) both define Polly.Timeout.TimeoutRejectedException. Referencing both in one project gives CS0433. The lab uses an extern alias so it can compare them side by side. In a real app, pick one stack.
  • Retries and POST don't mix by default. The standard handler retries all HTTP methods. Retrying a POST that creates a record can create it twice unless the endpoint is idempotent. The docs show options.Retry.DisableFor(HttpMethod.Post, ...).
  • Test attempt counts, not just outcomes. A test that only asserts "eventually got an exception" passes for A and B. The useful assertion is Assert.Equal(2, upstream.Attempts).

The takeaway

A retry policy only retries what it is allowed to see. If your only timeout is HttpClient.Timeout, or a Polly timeout registered before the retry, a hung upstream uses up the whole budget on attempt one, and your retries are decoration.

Give every call two numbers: a per-attempt timeout inside the retry and a total budget outside it. For anything with a human waiting on the other end, such as a ringing phone, a checkout or a chat reply, choose those numbers from how long that human will wait, not from the 100-second default.

My template has the same issue, so updating its wiring is my next change.

Code: github.com/AhmedElbashier/httpclient-timeout-retry-lab has the four scenarios, 7 xUnit tests, the raw run output and the chart script. Run it with dotnet test -c Release.

I'm Ahmed, a full-stack and integrations engineer (.NET, Next.js, VoIP/WebRTC). More of my work is on GitHub and my portfolio.

title: Why your date shows 1970: Unix timestamp bugs in JavaScript
description:
You fetch a record from an API, pass its created_at to new Date(), and the page says January 21, 1970. Or a scheduled job runs five and a half hours early. Or a date picker shows yesterday.

Almost every one of these comes from a handful of timestamp mix-ups. Here they are, with the fix for each.

1. Seconds vs milliseconds (the 1970 bug)

A Unix timestamp counts time since 1 January 1970, 00:00 UTC. The catch is the unit:

  • Most backends, databases and JWTs use seconds: 1795686000 (10 digits today)
  • JavaScript's Date uses milliseconds: 1795686000000 (13 digits)

Pass seconds to new Date() and JavaScript reads them as milliseconds, which is only about 20 days after the epoch:

new Date(1795686000);        // 1970-01-21...  wrong
new Date(1795686000 * 1000); // 2026-11-26...  right

The opposite mistake sends seconds-based APIs a 13-digit number, which lands tens of thousands of years in the future.

A small helper that guesses the unit by size:

function toDate(ts) {
  const n = Number(ts);
  // Below 1e11 it's almost certainly seconds (1e11 ms is only 1973)
  return new Date(n < 1e11 ? n * 1000 : n);
}

And the reverse, for sending a timestamp to an API that expects seconds:

const nowSeconds = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);

Use Math.floor, not Math.round. Rounding up can create a time slightly in the future, which some APIs reject.

2. Timestamps have no time zone. Your display does.

A timestamp is a single moment, the same everywhere. Time zones only appear when you turn it into text:

const d = new Date(1795686000 * 1000);
d.toISOString();     // always UTC, ends in "Z"
d.toLocaleString();  // the viewer's local time
d.toLocaleString('en-IN', { timeZone: 'Asia/Kolkata' }); // a fixed zone

If your server logs show UTC and your users see IST, a "5:30 hour bug" is usually just two correct times in two zones. Store and send timestamps (or ISO strings with Z), and convert to local time only at the very end, in the UI.

3. The date-only string trap

This one surprises even experienced developers:

new Date('2026-11-26');        // parsed as UTC midnight
new Date('2026-11-26T00:00');  // parsed as LOCAL midnight

A date-only ISO string is treated as UTC, but a date-time string without an offset is treated as local time. For someone in the US, the first line is still the evening of 25 November in local time, so a calendar shows the wrong day.

If you mean a calendar date (a birthday, a due date), keep it as the string '2026-11-26' and don't turn it into a Date at all. If you need a Date, add the time and offset explicitly.

4. The year 2038

Systems that store seconds in a signed 32-bit integer overflow on 19 January 2038 at 03:14:07 UTC. JavaScript itself is fine, since Date uses 64-bit floating point milliseconds. But if your data passes through an old database column, an embedded device or a C library, check the column type now. Use a 64-bit integer or a proper timestamp type.

Quick checklist

  • Count the digits: 10 means seconds, 13 means milliseconds.
  • Multiply by 1000 going into Date, divide (and floor) coming out.
  • Store and transmit in UTC; format to local time only for display.
  • Don't parse date-only strings into Date unless you mean UTC.

Try it

When I'm debugging, I paste the number into SnipFerry's timestamp converter to see the date it really points to. It runs in the browser, so nothing gets sent anywhere.

What's the worst date bug you've shipped?

title: Evaluating Large Language Models on conversational African American English: Feature classification and next-turn generation
description:
arXiv:2611.33499v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to misinterpret and misrepresent regional and social varieties of English other than Mainstream American English (MAE), such as African American English (AAE), yet most evaluations of these biases have relied on synthetic, stylized or decontextualized data. This paper instead evaluates LLMs on authentic, conversational AAE to more closely reflect how such models may encounter AAE when deployed as chatbots. Concretely, we perform two complementary evaluation tasks on 100 six-turn segments randomly sampled from the Corpus of Regional African American Language (CORAAL; Kendall and Farrington, 2024), comparing three closed-weight LLM configurations: Gemini 2.5 Flash with and without reasoning, and GPT-4.1 mini. The first task compares the models against gold-standard manual annotations for five AAE morphosyntactic features, while the second assesses their ability to generate contextually appropriate next turns, evaluating outputs for AAE feature frequency, diversity (Self-BLEU), and pragmatic quality. Reasoning-enabled Gemini is the strongest feature detector by a clear margin (macro F1 of 0.91), outperforming both other LLMs as well as a finetuned BERT-based baseline (Masis et al., 2022). In generation, however, all LLMs underproduce AAE relative to the human speakers and produce relatively uniform continuations, with reasoning-enabled Gemini producing the least AAE and the least diverse output. We conclude that a model's ability to detect AAE does not straightforwardly translate into its spontaneous use of AAE in generation, and argue that addressing this gap requires changes upstream, in how pretraining and alignment data represent dialectal variation.

title: Agent Recovery Gone Wrong: Measuring Harm Beyond Duplicate Calls
description:
arXiv:2611.31554v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Code-executing LLM agents submit blocks of code that issue several API writes. If a block fails after some of its writes have taken effect, the agent rewrites the block and continues. It is unknown how often such a recovery harms the external state when the failure occurs naturally in the code written by the agent. In this paper, we measure it on recorded trajectories of AppWorld agents. In a stratified random sample of 200 candidate episodes across ten models, 145 are partial executions confirmed by the database state. In the sample, 30 of 143 confirmed partial executions with a determinable outcome are followed by a harmful recovery, and its violation remains at the end of the run, which gives a stratification-weighted estimate of 24.6%. Two thirds of the harmful recoveries duplicate an effect, and the rest delete user data or make a wrong first-time write, e.g., an order of a wrong product. A rule that searches for repeated calls finds 75% of duplications but only 41% of all harm. We also examine two sources of operation identity for an idempotency contract. In a small pilot (17 episodes, one local model), identifiers supplied by the model do not detectably reduce harm, because the model issues a new identifier for the same operation. Identity derived from the call content, evaluated counterfactually on the sample, would have matched every harmful write in 14 to 18 of the 30 harmful recoveries, but in none of those with a wrong first-time write, and it would also have matched writes required by the task in 30 episodes. Based on these results, we outline design requirements for safer agent recovery.

title: Federated Learning with Uncertainty Quantification on Pseudo Label Exchange
description:
arXiv:2611.33395v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this work, we investigate federated stochastic operator learning for stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs), with an emphasis on heterogeneous client data distributions and uncertainty quantification. Federated learning enables clients to collaboratively train models without exchanging their original solution data, but conventional federated averaging can suffer significant performance degradation when client distributions differ, particularly when their input function supports are disjoint. To address these challenges, we propose the Federated Stochastic Operator Network (FedSON), a two-phase framework that combines auxiliary data construction with stochastic operator learning. In the first phase, locally trained deterministic neural operators and their corresponding input functions are exchanged to generate pseudolabeled auxiliary data, enabling the federated model to learn across heterogeneous input distributions without sharing original solution trajectories. In the second phase, a stochastic operator network is trained on top of the frozen deterministic operator to characterize stochastic fluctuations and quantify uncertainty in the predicted solutions. Numerical experiments involving the heat equation, viscous Burgers' equation, and two-dimensional advection-diffusion equation demonstrate the FedSON substantially improves deterministic prediction accuracy under heterogeneous client distributions while producing uncertainty estimates comparable to those obtained through centralized training.

title: Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Sets for Incomplete Data
description:
arXiv:2611.31329v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Attribute reduction in incomplete information systems is difficult because missing values break the equivalence-class structure of rough set theory. We propose the Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Set (COFRS) model. Each object is described by its set of present attributes. The similarity of two objects is a weighted overlap on the attributes present in both, divided by the fixed number of attributes |A| instead of the size of their union, so missing values are penalised globally and are not matched as wildcards. From this similarity we define a soft dependency degree based on weighted granule consistency, and we search for reducts by greedy backward elimination in O(|U|^2 |A|^2) time. We show that the relation is symmetric and non-reflexive, that the dependency degree is not monotone, and we give a sufficient condition under which monotonicity holds. On 11 UCI benchmarks with missing rates from 0.15% to 20.46%, COFRS gives the smallest reducts on average (4.1 attributes, against 5.0-11.2 for Tolerance-RS, a range-threshold variant Tol-RS_tau, Zhou-RS and the min-aggregation variant COFRS-min). The difference is significant against Tol-RS_tau, Zhou-RS and COFRS-min (Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon p<0.01) but not against Tolerance-RS (p=0.56), and it is small against the Jensen-Shen selector (adjusted p=0.084). At equal reduct size, COFRS selects more informative attributes than random subsets. With a kNN classifier the methods do not differ significantly in accuracy, F1 or G-mean; with an RBF-SVM they do, and COFRS ranks last. The gain is therefore compactness, not predictive accuracy.

title: Teaching a Multilingual Translation Model Regional Varieties: Castilian and Latin American Spanish, Asturian, Aragonese and Aranese with MADLAD-400-3B-MT
description:
arXiv:2611.33831v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Massively multilingual translation models usually have one tag per language and no control over regional varieties, and they cover a region's smaller languages poorly or not at all. We report three fine-tunes of MADLAD-400-3B-MT, each adding target tags with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), back-translation of monolingual text and replay of the base model's own translations: <2es_ES> for Spanish as written in Spain, <2es_419> for Latin American Spanish, and one model for three Romance languages of the Iberian Peninsula, Asturian (<2ast>), Aragonese (<2an>) and Aranese (<2oc_aranes>). For the Spanish varieties we annotate the 250.9M documents of MADLAD-400's Spanish split with a domain-supervised Spain vs. Latin America classifier and select variety text with a rule that admitted no Latin American document in a 340-document reference set. The Castilian model chooses Spain's everyday vocabulary in 97% of a targeted test (base model 62%) and vosotros for informal plural address in 70% (10%), while improving chrF++ on human references. A first finding is tag collapse: with a new tag initialised from <2es>, the parent tag drifts to the new variety (84-87% identical outputs). In the Iberian model, contrastive pairs and a separate learning rate for the tag embeddings keep each tag in its own language. Trained only on publicly available data, mostly the TAN-IBE Wikipedia corpora, the Iberian model matches or beats the TAN-IBE Marian systems in four of six Spanish directions on FLORES+, is 1.9 BLEU behind in Spanish->Aranese, and is second only to SalamandraTA-7B in most directions. The exception, Spanish->Aragonese, reflects a difference of written variety between Aragonese Wikipedia and the FLORES+ reference, not model quality. All three fine-tunes lose 0.6-0.7 chrF++ on average in thirteen other FLORES-200 directions. We release the models, data and variety classifier under open licences

title: CovNovBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Time Series Foundation Models under Covariate Novelty
description:
arXiv:2611.33732v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Covariate-aware time-series foundation models (TSFMs) condition their forecasts on additional input variables, called covariates, that are supplied over the future horizon. This capability makes them appealing for interventional forecasting, in which a target is predicted under a planned action such as a new product pricing policy or a new patient treatment schedule. We refer to covariates that encode such actions as treatment covariates. Current covariate-aware TSFMs, however, are trained on observed patterns, and their behavior is unclear when future treatment covariates fall outside the range seen in the history. Examples include a numerical treatment that leaves its historical range and a categorical treatment that takes a previously unseen policy. We call this practically common setting covariate novelty, and note that it is not systematically represented in existing benchmarks. We introduce an operational definition of covariate novelty and use it to construct CovNovBench, a benchmark of 88,476 evaluation series generated or filtered from four simulator-based and real-world datasets. The benchmark spans categorical and numerical treatment covariates as well as stable and trending targets. We evaluate six covariate-aware TSFMs zero-shot using point and directional accuracy metrics. No model is consistently reliable in our benchmark: point error almost always increases under covariate novelty, directional performance changes non-uniformly, and the best observed model varies across datasets and metrics. CovNovBench provides a systematic testbed for developing TSFMs that forecast more reliably under covariate novelty.

title: A comprehensive survey of deep face verification systems adversarial attacks and defense strategies
description:
arXiv:2611.33231v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Face Verification (FV) systems have exhibited remarkable performance in verification tasks and have consequently garnered extensive adoption across various applications, from identity duplication to authentication in mobile payments. However, the surge in popularity of face verification has raised concerns about potential vulnerabilities in the face of adversarial attacks. These concerns originate from the fact that advanced FV systems, which rely on deep neural networks, have recently demonstrated susceptibility to crafted input samples known as adversarial examples. Although imperceptible to human observers, adversarial examples can deceive deep neural networks during the testing and deployment phases. These vulnerabilities raised significant concerns about the deployment of deep neural networks in safety-critical contexts, prompting extensive investigations into adversarial attacks and corresponding defense strategies. This comprehensive survey provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in deep face verification, encompassing a broad spectrum of topics such as algorithmic designs, database utilization, protocols, and application scenarios. Furthermore, we conduct an in-depth examination of state-of-the-art algorithms to generate adversarial examples and the defense mechanisms devised to mitigate such adversarial threats.

title: Stop Attaching Carpet Test Reports to the Pattern ID
description:
A hotel document-control system may look tidy while storing every fire, emissions, and acoustic PDF under one pattern name. That structure hides a basic problem. The tested object is a physical floor assembly, not the artwork used to choose its appearance.

When a project changes the backing or underlay, the pattern ID remains the same. A database built around that ID can continue to display the old report as if it covers the new specification. The better design is to bind evidence to a versioned assembly and to make every upstream change visible before batch release.

Separate artwork, construction, and evidence

Use three linked records rather than one carpet record.

PatternRevision describes the motif, scale, color placement, and drawing revision. AssemblyRevision describes the face fiber, construction, pile, primary and secondary backing, underlay, and installation method. EvidenceBinding connects a report to one exact assembly revision and records the testing body, report date, tested configuration, result, and project acceptance condition.

The link should be explicit. An evidence record that names only a product family or design collection cannot prove that the current floor stack was tested. If a backing changes, create a new assembly revision and require a new evidence review. Do not overwrite the previous revision and leave the old report attached.

ADA CARPET's zone construction guidance is useful here because it starts with the room's function and construction decision. The database should do the same. A corridor and a guestroom can share a visual palette while requiring separate assembly records.

Record standards as scoped requirements

The brand source mentions GB 8624, ASTM E648, GB 18587, CRI HT-101, ISO 10140-3, ASTM E492, and product-specific FloorScore documentation. These names are not interchangeable badges. Each requirement needs a stated purpose and a project acceptance condition.

For fire documentation, identify the required classification and the applicable testing method. For acoustic documentation, identify the floor build-up being evaluated and the result required by the project. For emissions or appearance documentation, confirm that the evidence applies to the product being supplied. The testing body, report date, tested assembly, and acceptance condition should remain visible beside the result.

Do not populate these fields with generic catalog values. If the manufacturer has not supplied matching evidence for the proposed assembly, the correct state is EVIDENCE_REQUIRED, not a copied rating from another project. The source itself cautions that performance references require the actual product-specific evidence and applicable testing conditions.

Use a review state that reflects real decisions

A four-state workflow can connect design approval to installed acceptance without pretending that every check is a software certification.

type CarpetAssembly = {
  assemblyId: string;
  revision: string;
  zoneIds: string[];
  patternRevisionId: string;
  construction: string;
  faceFiber: string;
  pile: Record<string, string | number>;
  primaryBacking: string;
  secondaryBacking?: string;
  underlay?: string;
  installationMethod: string;
};

type EvidenceBinding = {
  evidenceId: string;
  assemblyId: string;
  assemblyRevision: string;
  standard: string;
  testingBody: string;
  reportDate: string;
  testedConfiguration: string;
  reportedResult?: string;
  projectAcceptanceCondition?: string;
  reviewStatus: "required" | "submitted" | "matched" | "not-applicable";
};

An assembly becomes eligible for batch release only after the required evidence has been reviewed against the current revision. Matched should mean that a responsible reviewer confirmed the correspondence. It should not be generated merely because a PDF exists or because its filename contains the pattern name.

The sample record belongs alongside the assembly. Store the approved physical sample identifier, approval date, and the configuration it represents. If the sample and the proposed production assembly differ, flag the discrepancy. A visual approval does not erase a structural change.

Preserve the decision history

Project systems often need to answer why a specification changed. Keep an append-only event log with the actor, date, previous revision, new revision, and reason. The change may come from value engineering, a supplier substitution, or a design revision. Each reason affects which evidence and approvals must be revisited.

At site acceptance, link the delivered rolls to the released assembly and batch record. Record installation deviations instead of silently updating the specification to match what arrived. The final handover should show both the approved condition and the installed condition where they differ.

ADA FLOOR's archive for the 2018 Hilton Garden Inn Zhuhai Hengqin project records 554 m² of column-free ballroom carpet and 158 guestrooms, with discussion of structure, three sample rounds, batches, and zoning. Those records show why the review states should exist. They do not provide reusable test results for a new hotel. A new project still needs its own evidence and acceptance decision.

Test the failure paths

A useful document-control test suite should include these cases.

  1. Change the underlay after evidence approval. The current assembly must return to evidence review.
  2. Attach a report tested with a different backing. The system must show a mismatch rather than a green badge.
  3. Reuse an approved pattern in a later phase. The new assembly and batch still require review.
  4. Approve a physical sample without a product structure. Production release remains blocked.
  5. Receive rolls labeled for another batch. Site acceptance records an exception.
  6. Replace a report with a newer edition. The earlier binding remains in the audit history.

Build an acceptance package from the same records

A project reviewer should not need to reconstruct the assembly by opening unrelated files. Generate a zone summary that brings together the current pattern revision, assembly revision, approved sample, evidence bindings, batch release, and unresolved exceptions. Include the project acceptance condition next to each required result.

The summary should also distinguish supplier information from project approval. A submitted report is not a matched report. An approved sample is not a released batch. Showing those states separately helps procurement, design, and site teams discuss the same status without relying on email memory.

When a system migrates older projects, preserve uncertainty. If a legacy record contains only a pattern name and a PDF, mark the assembly correspondence as unverified instead of inferring a match from the filename. Historical records remain useful, but the migration should not manufacture evidence that was never captured.

Keep site exceptions visible

Installation can introduce deviations that were not present in the approved package. A different adhesive, an additional layer, or a local substrate repair may need review. Record the exception against the zone and identify who accepted it. If the deviation affects a tested condition, route it back through the relevant evidence check.

The site record should also identify the delivered material. Link roll or piece identifiers to the released batch and retained sample. Where a repair uses reserve stock, record which stock was consumed and from which zone it came. This keeps the installed history current for future maintenance instead of freezing it at the original handover.

These checks give the database a decision trail. Review should stop a known assembly from being presented with evidence that belongs to a different one, and give the project team a clear route back to review when the floor build-up changes.

References: ADA CARPET zone construction decision guide, Hilton Garden Inn Zhuhai Hengqin archive, and ADA FLOOR brand and process information

title: Streaming Tax: Can Streaming VLMs Replace Their Offline Parents?
description:
arXiv:2611.33474v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Most vision-language models (VLMs) specialize in offline video understanding; in contrast, their post-trained versions, streaming VLMs, can perform live interactions. We investigate whether streaming VLMs can replace their offline parent models on offline tasks. Such replacement could reduce deployment costs and improve efficiency. We propose Streaming Tax to systematically evaluate streaming VLMs on offline tasks. Our exploration spans three core dimensions: understanding, trustworthiness, and generalization across 15 benchmarks. Our findings reveal a critical gap between offline capability preservation and practical replaceability. This gap emerges at two stages: streaming adaptation can alter trustworthy behavior even when offline understanding is largely preserved, while the native streaming protocol can introduce further performance losses. Our analyses show that some of these losses arise from restricted access to historical visual evidence and failures to deliver usable responses. Importantly, regarding safety, streaming models often leave both harmful and legitimate requests unanswered rather than genuinely refusing unsafe ones. We then propose Stream++, a training-free plugin to improve streaming VLMs on offline tasks.

title: Beyond the Swipe: How 5 Companies Build Dating App Features
description:
A dating app can rank a dozen profiles in milliseconds. The harder engineering question is what the ranking should use: shared values, past choices, or interest in the same activity?

The voice-first dating app oku starts with a conversation. Users talk about themselves and what they want in a relationship. The app turns those answers into a profile and returns a shortlist of potential matches. Other teams have focused on what happens after discovery, such as verifying a profile, planning a date, or starting a video call.

Here are five companies with documented dating app work, selected for the different engineering problems their projects address.

1. Turning voice interviews into ranked matches

GeekyAnts built oku’s mobile app and matchmaking system around two AI agents. The Match Recommendation Agent conducts a voice interview and uses the answers to build a profile based on the user’s personality, values, and relationship preferences. The Personal AI Companion uses later conversations to update the profile and refresh recommendations.

The app presents 12 ranked match recommendations and encourages users to focus on one connection at a time. It also includes identity verification and in-app messaging. The published tech stack lists Expo, TypeScript, PostgreSQL with pgvector, and LiveKit.

The interesting design problem is what happens when a later conversation contradicts the original interview. If a user changes a deal-breaker, that explicit update should carry more weight than an older model inference. The oku video case study shows how voice onboarding, profile updates, and ranked recommendations fit into the same product.

2. Putting identity verification inside the conversation

STRV built the iOS and Android apps for Zoe, a dating and social networking app for lesbian, bisexual, and queer women. Its case study describes in-chat mutual verification alongside standard profile verification and AI-assisted content moderation.

That placement matters. Verification during onboarding can establish an initial signal, while in-chat verification gives matched users a way to check who they are talking to when it becomes relevant. An engineering team building a similar flow would need to define what happens when a request is ignored or declined, and how the app communicates that state to each person.

3. Ranking date ideas alongside profiles

QtaSO worked on the mobile and backend systems for Flirt, where users browse date ideas with an activity, time, and place. Users rank their preferences, receive a date confirmation, and can then chat to finalize plans. The app also supports post-date feedback and reporting.

This turns matching into a workflow that continues after two users express interest. The backend has to track whether a date is proposed, confirmed, or canceled so that chat access and notifications reflect the latest state. A late push notification for a canceled date is a small technical failure with a very visible consequence.

4. Learning from browsing behavior

Relia Software developed the mobile apps and matching system for Let’s Date. The app used location, mutual likes, and feedback from browsing to inform recommendations.

Behavioral signals can accumulate as users interact with the app, but they are often ambiguous. Passing on a profile could reflect distance, timing, or simple disinterest. A ranking system that treats each pass as strong evidence about a specific trait can narrow the pool based on an assumption the user never confirmed.

5. Adding voice and video after a match

Sendbird supplied the communications technology that helped Hinge add one-to-one voice and video calls. Matches could talk inside the app before deciding whether to share phone numbers or meet in person.

Voice solves different problems at different points in the experience. In oku, the voice interview helps generate recommendations. In Hinge, a call helps two people decide what to do after matching. Interview completion and call connection rates would tell those teams very different things about whether the feature works.

What would show that voice-first onboarding works?

Interview completion shows whether users are willing to give the app that much time. A more useful follow-up measure is the share of users who start a two-way conversation with a recommended match. Tracking both would help a team see whether the longer onboarding flow leads to an interaction users value. The oku case study describes the feature design, so that outcome remains a question for product testing.

How would a matching system handle an explicit preference that conflicts with a pattern inferred from voice interviews or browsing behavior?

title: November 05, 2026
description:
Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Announcement

Scheduled maintenance of Management/Control Plane for the Apigee Edge for Public Cloud on November 6, 2026.

Scheduled maintenance of Management/Control Plane for the Apigee Edge for Public Cloud production will take place on Friday, November 6, 2026, from 9:00 PM PT to 10:00 PM PT (Saturday, November 7, 2026, from 5:00 AM UTC to 6:00 AM UTC). This maintenance follows the monthly maintenance window schedule documented in the Apigee Edge release notes archive.

During the scheduled maintenance window, the following services will be temporarily unavailable, and attempts to access them will return a 4xx status code:

  • Management Services UI
  • Management Services APIs
  • Monetization Management APIs
  • New proxy deployments
  • DevPortal Service
  • Microgateway Services
  • Edge Query (Analytics Stats APIs)

Runtime API calls to deployed API proxies are unaffected. While access to analytics queries may be temporarily unavailable during the maintenance window, all analytics and metrics data from this period will be available once maintenance ends.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.14.10

On November 5, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.14.10.

  • For information about upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to v1.14.10.
  • For information about new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release. The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch by using the Helm chart automatically updates the images. You don't typically need to make manual image changes. For information about container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Fixed

Fixed in this release

Bug ID Description
578314600 Fixed an issue where apigee-connect-agent ignored HTTPS_PROXY and failed to establish a tether in clusters that require an HTTP forward proxy for egress; the agent now uses HTTP/2 keepalive pings on the control-plane connection while honoring HTTPS_PROXY (including proxy credentials).
576707253 Removed the compromised emSign roots and the cross-signing Comodo AAA Services root from the system and Java (cacerts) trust stores across containers.
573622417 Fixed an issue where apigee-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
571378258 The apigee-redis container now uses the Valkey engine (version 8.1.10). The RESP2 wire protocol and redis-server and redis-cli binary names are unchanged.
554114419 Fixed an issue where an AssignMessage, HTTPModifier, or RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow could not set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers and failed with an invalid-header error.
524115876 Fixed an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests under load.
449228485 Fixed an issue where podDisruptionBudget overrides configured in the Helm charts were dropped by the Kubernetes API server.
432315283 Fixed an issue where changes to a multi-certificate truststore's trust anchors required a Message Processor restart when features.truststore.multi_cert_bundle.enabled was toggled at runtime; the outbound SSLContext now rebuilds automatically.

title: Learning from Recurrence: Internalizing Depth-Induced Preferences in Looped Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.33468v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A looped language model repeatedly applies the same block to its hidden state before predicting each token. The number of passes is its recurrent depth. Increasing this depth gives the model more computation per token with the same parameters. Can the shared block learn from the predictions it makes at greater depth? Following prior work, we retrofit pretrained OLMo-2-1B with a shared recurrent block and continue mid-training over varying recurrent depths. In the four-pass model, additional passes mainly redistribute probability among tokens that already rank highly after one pass. We use the continuations generated at greater depth to train only the shared block through a single pass, without reference answers or correctness filtering. We call this transfer preference write-back. Write-back further improves one-pass and multi-pass accuracy on most tasks. At their target depths, the updated models outperform a non-recurrent control matched for mid-training data and token budget on all six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with a mean relative gain in accuracy of up to 46.2% across tasks. At four-pass inference, one-pass training outperforms full-depth training on the same targets in the model with input injection. This advantage disappears in the matched model without injection. On GSM8K, using the updated block only on passes two through four recovers nearly the entire four-pass gain, showing that an update learned in one pass can improve later applications of the same block.
