title: How Much Dependency Can a Marginal Rule See? Total Correlation in Diffusion LM Parallel Decoding
description:
arXiv:2611.31990v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: A masked diffusion language model is fast because it commits several tokens per step. Each token is sampled from its own marginal, so the dependency between the tokens is lost, and the size of that loss is the conditional total correlation C of the committed set. Most decoders choose the set from per-position marginals, which can bound C but cannot determine it. We ask how well they predict it. We estimate C for fixed candidate sets on four masked diffusion LMs from two families. On three of the four, the best marginal-only predictor is off by about one bit (0.74 to 1.17), 1.8 to 3.7 times less than a baseline that knows only the bound, and most of this accuracy comes from the bound itself. On a subset, our estimate ranks sets like the exact KL cost of a parallel commit, but sits a median 0.4 to 1.1 bits below it on prose and when the rest of the text is still masked. Dream-instruct is the exception, mainly on prose, where its conditionals are least self-consistent. Among six common marginal rules, pooling over the set beats gating on its weakest position in all 24 paired comparisons. The measurement needs a validated readout: Dream and LLaDA place a position's prediction at different logit indices, and the wrong index inflates an inconsistency diagnostic 14 to 41 times. We give three checks that measure the convention. Our results concern predicting C for a fixed set, not what a dependency-aware decoder gains.

title: Failure Broadens, Success Sharpens: Continual Adaptation of Tool-Use Agents Across Diverse Tasks with Dual-Polarity Memory
description:
arXiv:2611.33612v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model agents can self-improve over time by utilizing procedural memory derived from prior task trajectories, yet the distinct utilities of memories derived from local successes and failures remain underexplored. This work studies this question in a realistic setting with heterogeneous streams of multi-domain tool-use tasks and various environment constraints common in real-world scenarios. We develop \emph{Dual-Polarity Memory with Periodic Maintenance} (DualPM), a simple, retrieval-free memory workflow characterized by (1) customizable reflection and procedural memory generation from both local successes and failures within each trajectory, and (2) periodic memory consolidation over long task streams under a given memory capacity, preventing memory explosion. Online prequential evaluation with fine-grained metrics reveals that failure memory more strongly broadens coverage, success memory better streamlines execution, while combining both polarities effectively integrates both benefits. Further studies demonstrate that DualPM enables cross-domain memory generalization and continual memory adaptation, while external evaluation on EvoMemBench reveals the portability and effectiveness of DualPM as a general long-term procedural memory method.

title: Evaluating Frontier-Model Agent Skills with Open-Weight Models in a Science Gateway
description:
arXiv:2611.31480v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scientific analyses that span many jobs and computing sites depend on workflow management systems to run reliably, but writing a production workflow requires expertise in such a system, which many domain scientists do not have. Coding agents can supply this expertise when they are guided by skills and packaged procedures for recurring tasks. We wrote skills and specialist agents for the Pegasus workflow management system with a frontier model, and the PegasusAI Studio science gateway offers them to scientists through a chat interface. New users without frontier-model credits need an open-weight model, served at no cost on research cyberinfrastructure, but skills written for a frontier model may not work with an open-weight solution. This paper presents a method for adapting such skills. An evaluation harness drives the real gateway as a user would, scores the workflows the agent builds, and feeds recurring failures back to the frontier model that maintains the skills. We evaluated 21 open-weight models on 17 tasks. The five highest-scoring models are close in quality after one trial per task, and their median response times differ twelvefold. In repeated trials with the best of the three open-weight models, we repeated scores of 0.76 on workflow building against 0.82 for Claude. The harness led to five changes to the initial skills. We also identify challenges in evaluating agents within operational systems: evaluation failures can be mistaken for model failures, and agents can circumvent experimental controls within their privilege domain. In a controlled ablation, an initially significant effect disappeared when the restrictions were properly enforced.

title: Frequency-Conditioned Privacy Auditing of Fine-Tuned Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.31581v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly fine-tuned on sensitive data, where the same person's information may appear multiple times across records. This can cause models to memorize sensitive information, but memorization does not necessarily mean that the information can be recovered. A more serious privacy risk arises when the model begins to reproduce that information during generation. In this paper, we study how often sensitive information must appear in the fine-tuning data before it becomes recoverable. Across four language models, we vary the frequency of email addresses and phone numbers from $1\times$ to $50\times$ and compare standard fine-tuning, gradient clipping, and differentially private training. We find that the number of repetitions required before sensitive information becomes recoverable varies substantially across models. Gradient clipping can delay extraction, but it does not consistently prevent leakage at high repetition. DP-SGD at $\varepsilon=5$ produces zero observed extraction through $50\times$ repetition across all four models under the attacks we test, although the utility cost varies by model. These findings characterize how observed extraction varies across sensitive-data frequencies, model families, and training mechanisms, and highlight substantial differences in extraction behavior across models. Code and data are publicly available.

title: How to Review Single-Use Approvals in AI Agent Workflows
description:
Review the authorization verdict and the destination outcome independently. An approval record tells you what could proceed under policy. The system of record tells you whether the authorized action took effect. Keep both assertions in the design review, especially when a workflow crosses application, worker and provider boundaries.

Give the decision a reviewable contract

Name the approved operation and its material parameters. Record the requester, approver, applicable policy, time window and the destination the approval covers. Have the control owner document when approval must be valid and when it becomes unavailable for new execution. Preserve a reference to the original operation so status and reconciliation remain possible after the approval is consumed.

Use language that carries over into the report. Authorized describes the decision to permit execution. Committed describes the destination’s authoritative outcome. Awaiting reconciliation describes an accepted operation whose effect is still uncertain. Give that last state an owner and a resolution policy. Keep workflow and destination records linked through references that a reviewer can use without disclosing raw credentials or production records.

Assign an owner when the records disagree

Use synthetic evidence to agree on what the report should say if records are incomplete or inconsistent. First define what counts as a new business effect. A change to the final destination state and an additional permission to execute are separate observations.

Evidence in the review Record in the assessment Ask this owner to act
Execution authority granted more than once, one matching effect recorded Authorization defect, with the destination’s observed protection Approval control owner
One eligible execution decision, destination record unavailable Business effect unverified Destination evidence owner
Decision denies execution, destination records a new effect Failed enforcement for the reviewed action Execution control and destination owners
Destination has accepted work and its outcome is pending Open reconciliation case with the original operation reference Operations owner

Include passing evidence in the same report. A valid completed case should show the intended effect once. A declined case should show the decision and no corresponding new effect. For pending work, retain the original reference until the destination establishes what happened.

Scope the remediation and retest

Choose a consequential action and name the application enforcing approval, the components that process it, and the destination that commits the change. Include scheduled work or manual recovery if they share the same authority. In the report, state which connector, environment and recovery boundaries the assessment represents. Keep a separate record of material coverage gaps.

The business impact depends on the action. An unexpected credit affects accounting. An incorrect access grant creates a production privilege exposure. For an audit-scoped workflow, preserve the record that connects the approved action, execution decision and destination effect. Scope any evidence of operation over an audit period separately.

When one application owns approval state and the destination gives reliable outcome records, remediation can center on enforcing the original authorization and linking the evidence. Distributed processing or a third-party destination can add ownership, evidence retrieval and release coordination work. Retest the authorization and the recorded effect after a change, then retain enough context for a reviewer to understand why the action was released or held.

Read the full approval-state matrix and use it to agree on the expected outcome for your own workflow.

title: 5 Checkout Rollback Gates — Uptime Monitoring APIs With Recovery Code
description:
A marketplace checkout rollback needs a release gate that can distinguish a reachable service from a checkout attempt whose outcome is still uncertain. TL;DR: compare easy-to-integrate API services for uptime monitoring by their HTTP checks, actionable alert handoff, and CI/CD integration, then require separate checkout evidence before restoring traffic. A green dashboard cannot authorize a payment retry.

What page fired?

Consider a bounded production design exercise: a checkout attempt named checkout-A crosses a business-operation boundary under release candidate, the application cannot establish its final outcome, and the responder prepares release restored. These identifiers are synthetic example data, not a customer incident or monitoring API fields. The postmortem question is specific: could the release gate accept a healthy response while leaving that original attempt unresolved? If the answer is yes, the monitoring integration has proved less than the rollback procedure assumes.

The invariant is that restored reachability does not establish safe replay. Preserve that distinction through the comparison, the code, and the final recovery decision.

1. What page fired, and what does it establish?

Begin with a notification, not a dashboard tour. Ask the integration owner to demonstrate a failed HTTP check reaching the intended responder, carrying enough context to identify the checkout service and investigate the release. Then ask how that result reaches the deployment workflow. Straightforward HTTP requests, webhook or alert integrations, and a CI/CD handoff are useful selection criteria because each has an observable acceptance test; a collection of screenshots does not show that the handoff works.

Keep three questions separate during the exercise: can the service respond, can checkout complete, and is it safe to repeat this particular attempt? A health endpoint can answer the first question under its own contract. The application must supply evidence for the others. Public status pages and reports can help communicate availability, but they should not become an authorization signal for repeating an order or payment.

Name the uncertainty.

For checkout-A, the useful release-review record would identify the attempt, the release that handled it, the outcome the application actually knows, and the unresolved decision. These are proposed application-owned evidence fields. They are not claimed vendor response fields. Losing that distinction is a concrete integration trap: a responder sees the restored release serving requests and closes the incident even though the original checkout still needs reconciliation.

2. How should we compare uptime monitoring API services before recovery?

The shortlist should include different monitoring approaches because a marketplace can fail through an unreachable checkout endpoint, a missed scheduled reconciliation, or an investigation that lacks usable evidence. Assess the same recovery decision against each approach, while resisting the temptation to treat every service that accepts HTTP as a substitute for every other one. The table describes evaluation roles, not a benchmark or a claim that any product has passed the proposed drill.

Option Role in the checkout review Acceptance test and boundary
UptimeRobot External uptime checks Exercise the monitor and alert integration; a successful reachability check still needs application evidence before checkout replay.
Better Stack Uptime monitoring and incident response Review the failed-check-to-responder handoff alongside deployment integration; keep ownership of the checkout recovery decision explicit.
Healthchecks Heartbeats for expected scheduled work Test a missing reconciliation completion signal; a heartbeat addresses a different failure from an unavailable checkout endpoint.
Datadog Broader observability during investigation Evaluate the instrumentation and correlation work needed to connect a checkout attempt to a release; require a useful investigation, not merely another chart.

Infrai provides a unified API with 295 routes across 20 modules, so adding a backend capability means another endpoint under the same contract rather than another integration. One API key and one bill cover those capabilities: the rollback job can use a single credential for its evidence requests instead of coordinating separate service keys. Plain REST requires no SDK to install, which lets an existing HTTP client handle the evidence read. Public discovery requires no key and exposes request and response schemas, with runnable examples in 10 languages available for contract review before deployment.

The trade-off is responsibility: this combined backend approach is not a substitute for an external uptime monitor. Choose UptimeRobot for an external reachability check or Healthchecks for a scheduled-work heartbeat, and test the paging handoff separately. The limitation of a log read is precise: evidence retrieval cannot establish that checkout is reachable from outside the deployment, and a successful read cannot establish that an order may be repeated.

The selection boundary matters more than the route count. Assign external reachability checks, expected-work heartbeats, paging, and evidence retrieval to explicit owners. Require separate acceptance tests for distributed trace navigation, crash symbolication, session replay, and data lifecycle controls whenever those are requirements; the existence of searchable logs does not establish those capabilities. OpenTelemetry's logs concepts are useful here because correlation context and a complete investigation are different things.

For this scenario, favor the option whose responsibilities fit the release procedure and whose handoffs the team can demonstrate. A narrower uptime service can be a good choice when the application already owns investigation evidence; a broader observability service deserves consideration when that correlation work is part of the job. Neither choice settles an ambiguous checkout outcome on its own.

3. Put a read-only check in the preventative path

The example below is a complete Go program for the evidence-read stage of a release gate. It retrieves logs with an explicit GET request, preserves the returned body without assuming an undocumented response schema, and leaves recovery approval with the application. Save it as main.go and run go run main.go. It uses only the standard library.

Set API_BASE_URL to the service's documented HTTPS API base ending in /v1, and supply INFRAI_API_KEY through the environment. The program adds no search filters: it retrieves the response as documented rather than guessing parameter names. Its output can contain application evidence, so direct it only to a restricted incident workspace and apply the team's data-handling policy. No checkout is replayed.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "io"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(value string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if date, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if delay := time.Until(date); delay > 0 {
            return delay
        }
    }
    return time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
}

func run() error {
    base := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("API_BASE_URL"), "/")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    parsed, err := url.Parse(base)
    if err != nil || parsed.Scheme != "https" || parsed.Host == "" ||
        parsed.User != nil || parsed.RawQuery != "" || parsed.Fragment != "" ||
        parsed.Path != "/v1" || key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set the trusted HTTPS API_BASE_URL ending in /v1 and INFRAI_API_KEY")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 60*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 15 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, base+"/logs/search", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            timer := time.NewTimer(retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("evidence read returned HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, data)
        }
        if _, err := os.Stdout.Write(data); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "Evidence retrieved; checkout reconciliation still requires review")
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The client allows 4 attempts, uses a 15-second request timeout, and bounds the complete operation to 60 seconds. Those are example budgets, not measured service latency. It honors Retry-After for rate limiting and otherwise backs off exponentially; when the overall deadline expires, it returns an error instead of continuing the deployment's evidence collection indefinitely. This read-only request does not need a write idempotency key.

This code does not test external reachability, notification delivery, or checkout correctness. Those remain separate checks in the comparison. Its value is a small integration boundary that retrieves evidence without attempting recovery. Don't wire its successful exit directly to checkout replay: an actual reconciliation decision needs an authoritative application record, and a log response alone cannot supply that guarantee.

4. Rehearse the handoff across both release labels

Use candidate and restored as labels in a proposed acceptance drill, with two synthetic attempts, checkout-A and checkout-B. Make the first unresolved and the second explicitly reconciled in the exercise record. Require the responder to identify the page, the affected release, and the evidence behind each recovery decision. These are test inputs, not observations about a deployed system.

The important failure to catch is evidence being reassigned by a dashboard's current release filter: switching the displayed release must not make an unresolved attempt disappear from the recovery review. Keep the drill record available independently of the current chart view, and ask the CI/CD owner to show which check can hold approval and which result merely informs the responder. If a webhook arrives, verify that its recipient can act on it; successful delivery to an integration is weaker evidence than a completed operational handoff.

Record the decision.

Then review whether anyone had to guess an attempt's outcome from a service-level health result. That guess is the postmortem finding to fix before giving a monitor more authority over rollback.

5. Limit what the gate is allowed to decide

This advice applies when checkout recovery involves an unresolved business operation. It does not justify delaying every rollback until every historical order is reconciled, nor does it turn a synthetic probe into a payment verifier; define the affected attempts and the operation that needs approval before using a gate.

For a scheduled reconciliation that never runs, evaluate a heartbeat monitor such as Healthchecks. For a simple availability question without an ambiguous checkout side effect, an external HTTP check and a tested notification path may satisfy the requirement with less integration work. Keep the decision proportional to the failure.

A useful postmortem can explain why traffic resumed and why an individual attempt was or was not repeated. Choose monitoring integrations that preserve that explanation through a release change.

Sources

References for the monitoring approaches and log concepts discussed above; the synthetic gate and acceptance drill are proposed engineering examples.

  • OpenTelemetry, logs concepts
  • UptimeRobot API documentation
  • Better Stack uptime documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Datadog documentation

title: Migrating to Tailwind CSS v4 @theme & OKLCH Without Breaking WCAG Contrast Ratios
description:
Moving from tailwind.config.js to Tailwind CSS v4's CSS-first @theme tokens and oklch() color scales feels much cleaner—until Lighthouse flags failing WCAG AA (4.5:1) contrast in dark mode or colors clip unexpectedly on sRGB displays.

1. High-Chroma OKLCH Colors Clip Outside sRGB

An accent like oklch(0.65 0.25 260) renders vividly on Display P3 laptops, then undergoes gamut mapping on standard sRGB monitors, subtly shifting perceived lightness and dropping contrast on thin UI text.

2. Dark Mode Needs Higher Lightness, Not Just Inverted Backgrounds 

@import "tailwindcss";

@theme {
  --color-brand-500: oklch(0.58 0.19 255);
  --color-surface-bg: oklch(0.99 0.004 255);
  --color-surface-fg: oklch(0.21 0.015 255);
}

A L=0.58 brand accent easily clears 4.5:1 on white (L=0.99), but drops below 3.5:1 on a dark surface (L=0.16). Pairing dark themes with slightly lower chroma and L=0.72..0.78 keeps links legible without glowing harshly.

  • WCAG Contrast Checker (AA/AAA): https://global-utils.com/en/contrast-checker

title: Looking for an Express alternative? NestJS can now run without Express
description:
Ask anyone, human or AI, what to use instead of Express, and you'll hear two names: Fastify, because it's faster, and Hono, because it's small and runs everywhere. Nest usually isn't on that list, and there's a fair reason: Nest runs on Express by default, so "use Nest instead of Express" sounds like "use Express, with more on top".

Since Nest 12.3, it doesn't have to. The NodeAdapter runs Nest directly on Node's node:http module, with no Express underneath. It handles about 50% more requests per second than Express, within a few percent of plain Fastify, and most Express middleware still works with it.

It's opt-in for now. A new project still runs on Express until you install the adapter and pass it in main.ts, a small change shown below. In Nest 13, the Node adapter becomes the default.

This post is for anyone who's leaving Express: what the Node adapter is, the numbers, what stays compatible and what doesn't, and how to move an Express app over without stopping feature work.

Why people leave Express

Express is fine. It's also the framework most people are trying to get away from, usually for one of four reasons:

  • Speed. Express is the slowest of the common Node.js options, by a wide margin on routes that do little work.
  • Everything is your decision. Validation, authentication, configuration, folder structure, how services share a database connection, how tests replace them: Express gives you a router and middleware, and the rest is a pile of libraries someone on the team picked.
  • Async errors. Before Express 5, a rejected promise in a handler didn't reach the error handler. Express 5 fixed that, but a lot of code in the wild still has the wrappers.
  • The codebase stops having a shape. A small Express app is pleasant. At thirty routes, five developers and a queue, every app looks different, and every new developer learns that one.

Fastify answers the first point and, with its plugin system, part of the second. Hono answers the first and adds edge runtimes. Nest answers the last three, and now the first one too.

Nest on node:http

nest new still sets up a project on Express, and NestFactory.create() still picks Express when you don't pass an adapter. To switch, install the Node adapter:

npm i @nestjs/platform-node

Then pass it to NestFactory.create() in main.ts:

import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { NestNodeApplication, NodeAdapter } from '@nestjs/platform-node';
import { AppModule } from './app.module.js';

const app = await NestFactory.create<NestNodeApplication>(
  AppModule,
  new NodeAdapter(),
);
await app.listen(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);

That's the whole switch. Controllers, providers, guards, pipes, interceptors and exception filters don't know which adapter they run on, so nothing else in the app changes. NestNodeApplication gives you the adapter's own methods on app: useBodyParser(), useStaticAssets(), setViewEngine() and inject(), which sends a fake request without a listening server, as Fastify's inject() does.

In end-to-end tests, pass the adapter there too, so the tests run on what production runs:

app = moduleRef.createNestApplication<NestNodeApplication>(new NodeAdapter());

Without it, the testing module creates an Express application, so the tests exercise a different server than the one you ship.

The numbers

Requests per second on GET /, each server answering Hello world!, with wrk -t4 -c100 for 8 seconds after a 3-second warm-up, on Node.js 24.20, median of 3 rounds:

Server GET /
Fastify 57.1k
Nest on Node 55.6k
Hono on Node 53.1k
Nest on Fastify 52.6k
Express 37.0k
Nest on Express 37.0k

And a separate round on an M1 Pro, with a route parameter and a JSON body:

Server GET /users/:id POST /echo (JSON)
Express 35.6k 30.1k
Fastify 54.0k 43.5k
Nest on Express 34.5k 28.2k
Nest on Fastify 48.4k 40.2k
Nest on Node 51.0k 42.4k

So Nest on Node is about 3-6% behind plain Fastify, slightly ahead of Hono on Node, and 41-50% ahead of plain Express. It's also faster than Nest on Fastify, which surprises people: the Node adapter has its own body parsers and route matching, so no other framework sits between Nest and node:http.

The benchmark and the servers for every framework, Koa, Elysia and AdonisJS included, are in nestjs/nest#18063. Run it on your own machine: other machines give other gaps.

One caveat I'd put on any framework benchmark: these routes do almost nothing. A route that queries Postgres or calls another service spends most of its time waiting for them, so for most APIs, a few percent either way won't decide anything. What these numbers settle is that, with the Node adapter, you don't pay Express's price for using Nest.

What stays Express-compatible

The Node adapter's request and response objects extend Node's IncomingMessage and ServerResponse with the Express-style helpers that middleware and exception filters usually rely on: req.get(), req.ip, req.hostname, res.status(), res.json(), res.set(), res.cookie(), res.redirect(), res.sendFile(), res.locals and the rest of the common set. Middleware runs in an Express-style stack, with the same (req, res, next) signature.

So the middleware you already use keeps working: helmet, compression, cookie-parser, express-session, express-rate-limit, morgan, and passport with @nestjs/passport. File uploads use the same Multer-based interceptors, imported from @nestjs/platform-node.

It isn't Express, though, and it differs on purpose in a few places:

  • Routes are matched by specificity, as in Fastify, not in the order they were registered, and paths are case-sensitive.
  • A string returned from a handler is sent as text/plain, not text/html.
  • No automatic ETag, so no 304 for a conditional request, except from res.sendFile() and static assets.
  • A JSON body with a __proto__ or constructor.prototype key is rejected with a 400.
  • Route parameters are capped at 100 characters, as in Fastify. maxParamLength raises it.
  • Express settings become adapter options, such as trustProxy for trust proxy.

And some Express APIs aren't there: res.render() (use the @Render() decorator), res.download(), res.format(), req.accepts(), req.subdomains and a few others, plus mounting a whole Express application with app.use(). If your app depends on one of those, or on a package that only supports Express, stay on the Express adapter for now. The HTTP adapters chapter has the complete list.

What Express never gave you

Speed is why you'd look. It's not why I'd want you to stay. Here's an endpoint that Express leaves you to assemble, in Nest:

import { Body, Controller, Post } from '@nestjs/common';
import { CurrentUser } from '@nestjs/authentication';
import { Can } from '@nestjs/authorization';
import { z } from 'zod';
import type { User } from '../users/user.js';
import { OrderPolicy } from './order.policy.js';
import { OrdersService } from './orders.service.js';

const createOrderSchema = z.object({
  items: z
    .array(z.object({ productId: z.uuid(), quantity: z.int().min(1) }))
    .min(1),
});

@Controller('orders')
export class OrdersController {
  constructor(private readonly ordersService: OrdersService) {}

  @Post()
  @Can(OrderPolicy, 'create')
  create(
    @CurrentUser() user: User,
    @Body({ schema: createOrderSchema }) dto: z.infer<typeof createOrderSchema>,
  ) {
    return this.ordersService.place(user, dto);
  }
}

Four things happen there that you'd wire up by hand in Express:

  • The route is closed by default. With @nestjs/authentication, every route requires a signed-in user unless it's marked @Public(). You can't forget to add the auth middleware to a new router, because there's nothing to add.
  • Permission checks are declared, and also closed by default. @nestjs/authorization denies a route that declares no check, so a new route without one fails closed instead of open.
  • The body is validated before the handler runs. Zod, Valibot, ArkType or any other Standard Schema library, or class-validator if you prefer classes. An invalid body is a 400 that lists what's wrong.
  • OrdersService is injected. Nest creates it once and passes it in, with its own dependencies, so a test replaces the database or the mailer without patching imports.

And the parts around that endpoint come from first-party packages, built and released by the same team, instead of from whoever maintains the library you found:

You need Nest package
Sign-in, sessions, tokens, two-factor, API keys @nestjs/authentication
Permissions @nestjs/authorization
Configuration, validated at startup @nestjs/config
A database @nestjs/drizzle, @nestjs/typeorm, @nestjs/mongoose
Queues and scheduled jobs @nestjs/bullmq, @nestjs/schedule
Email, file storage, translations @nestjs/mail, @nestjs/storage, @nestjs/i18n
Rate limiting, caching @nestjs/throttler, @nestjs/cache-manager
Retries, timeouts, circuit breakers @nestjs/resilience
Webhooks, idempotency keys, the outbox pattern @nestjs/webhooks, @nestjs/idempotency, @nestjs/outbox
OpenAPI @nestjs/swagger
WebSockets, microservices, GraphQL @nestjs/websockets, @nestjs/microservices, @nestjs/graphql
MCP servers, language models @nestjs/mcp, @nestjs/ai

None of them is required. A Nest app starts with the core and adds what it uses.

Moving an Express app over, one route at a time

You don't have to rewrite anything to start. Nest can run on your existing Express app, with both answering on the same port:

import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { ExpressAdapter } from '@nestjs/platform-express';
import { AppModule } from './app.module.js';
import { createLegacyApp } from './legacy/app.js';

const app = await NestFactory.create(
  AppModule,
  new ExpressAdapter(createLegacyApp()),
);
await app.listen(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);

createLegacyApp() is your Express app, with its app.listen() call removed. Express's routes and middleware come first, and Nest's routes answer whatever Express doesn't. They see what the Express middleware put on the request, so a guard can check the req.user your existing auth middleware sets. New endpoints go into Nest, and an existing one moves when you next touch it: write it as a Nest route, delete it from the Express router, deploy. Nothing waits for a big switch.

Two requirements: the Express app has to be on Express 5 (npx @expressjs/codemod upgrade does most of it), and a catch-all 404 handler in the Express app has to go, or it answers Nest's routes too.

The Node adapter comes at the end. While the Express app is mounted, Nest has to run on the Express adapter, because the Node adapter can't mount an Express application. Once the last Express route has moved, switch main.ts to the NodeAdapter, and the app gets the speed-up with no other change.

If the app is small enough to review in one change, moving it all at once also works, and it's a good job for a coding agent, as long as tests pin what the app does first. The Migrating from Express page has both approaches step by step, the list of things that change without an error, and a prompt to give an agent.

Getting started 

npx @nestjs/cli new orders-api
cd orders-api
npm i @nestjs/platform-node

nest new sets the project up on Express, so switch main.ts to the NodeAdapter as above. Then run npm run start:dev, and nest g resource orders gives you a module, controller, service, DTOs and tests to compare with how you'd lay it out in Express.

The Node adapter's full reference, with the same benchmark, is in the docs: HTTP adapters. If your Express app relies on something the Node adapter doesn't do, tell me: that list is shorter every release, and it's useful to know what's on it.

title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen: a faster model for general purpose robotics
description: Google's Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings strong spatial and embodied reasoning capabilities to a fast, efficient model built specifically for robotics. To help developers put these capabilities to work, the new Robotics plugin for Google Antigravity transforms the platform into a comprehensive workbench supporting rapid hardware bring-up, MuJoCo simulation, and closed-loop control. Developers can leverage these tools to transition from an unboxed robot arm to a fully functional real-to-sim-to-real application in an afternoon using natural language prompts and day-one support in the google-genai SDKs.

API Gateway

Announcement

Negative backend deadlines are no longer deprecated

The deprecation of negative backend deadline values announced on October 23, 2026 is withdrawn. In an OpenAPI 2.0 x-google-backend extension or a gRPC BackendRule, a negative deadline continues to use the default deadline, the same as 0, and won't be rejected. OpenAPI 3.x backends still reject a negative deadline.

For more information, see OpenAPI 2.0 extensions and OpenAPI 3.x extensions.

AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Feature

Syncing data from BigQuery into AlloyDB is generally available (GA). This feature lets you copy or mirror analytical tables from BigQuery into AlloyDB for low-latency operational access using the alloydb_sync extension.

For more information, see Sync BigQuery data to AlloyDB.

Feature

Direct Apache Iceberg access in AlloyDB for PostgreSQL is available for PostgreSQL 18 and later (in Preview). This feature lets you query Iceberg tables in Cloud Storage or Lakehouse runtime catalog and accelerate analytical queries using the AlloyDB columnar engine.

For more information, see Access Apache Iceberg data from AlloyDB.

Feature

AlloyDB Express is available in Preview for PostgreSQL 18. Optimized for rapid prototyping and for workflows that use AI coding agents, this configuration provides the following features:

  • Fast provisioning
  • Scale-to-zero compute when idle
  • A monthly free tier for the first 12 months of usage
  • One-click upgrades to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

For more information, see AlloyDB Express overview.

Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Announcement

Released Edge Microgateway 3.3.12.

Edge Microgateway 3.3.12 includes the following component versions:

Component Version
microgateway 3.3.12
plugins 3.3.9
edgeauth 3.2.2

To upgrade, install version 3.3.12 of the edgemicro npm package or pull the gcr.io/apigee-microgateway/edgemicro:3.3.12 Docker image. For the npm upgrade steps, see Upgrading Edge Microgateway. For earlier Edge Microgateway releases, see Edge Microgateway release notes.

Breaking

Removed support for Node.js 20 from Edge Microgateway. Use Node.js 22, 24, or 26 instead.

Edge Microgateway 3.3.12 supports only Node.js 22, 24, and 26. Support for Node.js 26 is new in this release. Before you upgrade an npm installation of Edge Microgateway to 3.3.12, upgrade the Node.js runtime on each host to version 22, 24, or 26. The 3.3.12 Docker image is built on Node.js 24, so Docker deployments need no action for this change. For supported versions, see Supported software and supported versions.

Breaking

Removed the npm and npx command-line tools from the Edge Microgateway Docker image. Install custom plugin dependencies before you add the plugins to the container.

Starting with version 3.3.12, the Edge Microgateway Docker image doesn't include npm or npx, and commands that run either tool inside the container fail. The change doesn't affect how Edge Microgateway runs. If your custom plugins have npm dependencies, run npm install in each plugin directory before you add the plugins to the container, so that each plugin's node_modules directory is included. For the steps, see Adding a custom plugin. This change doesn't affect npm installations of Edge Microgateway.

Security

Fixed multiple security vulnerabilities in Edge Microgateway. Upgrade to Edge Microgateway 3.3.12.

Bigtable

Feature

Bigtable offers conversational analytics, which lets you query your operational data using natural language. This feature uses the Conversational Analytics API and is in Preview. For more information, see Conversational analytics for Bigtable overview.

Feature

The QueryData tool lets you query the data in your database using conversational language and build data agents. This feature is available in Preview. For more information, see QueryData tool overview.

Cloud Run

Feature

Cloud Run ephemeral disk is in General Availability (GA). Ephemeral disk allows you to mount a volume that persists only for the duration of your service, job, or worker pool instance.

Cloud SQL for SQL Server

Feature

Cloud SQL for SQL Server now supports read pool autoscaling (GA), which helps you more easily manage your application's workload needs.

This feature automates read pool scale in and scale out operations based on one or both of the following conditions:

  • Allowed CPU usage of the read pool
  • Allowed number of client connections to the read pool

Change

Cloud SQL for SQL Server supports additional metrics within the system insights dashboard (GA) related to engine memory, performance, and replication.

For a detailed list of metrics and their descriptions, see Cloud SQL for SQL Server default metrics and Cloud SQL metrics.

Cloud Storage

Feature

You can pause hard deletions for a bucket when you need more time to restore soft-deleted objects before they're permanently deleted. For more information, see Pause permanent (hard) deletions of soft-deleted objects.

Cloud Workstations

Feature

The Cloud Workstations base editor (Code OSS for Cloud Workstations) includes the Antigravity extension by default.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Switch between teams in the mobile app

You can switch between multiple teams in the Gemini Enterprise mobile app without logging out and rescanning the QR code. (Teams were previously called instances.)

When you open a team for the first time, the mobile app saves it to your teams list. Additionally, you can rename teams in the list and you can remove teams from your list.

This feature is generally available (GA). For more information, see Teams in Use the mobile app.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Provisioned Throughput support for supervised fine-tuned models (GA)

Provisioned Throughput support for supervised fine-tuned models is generally available. Burndown rates for fine-tuned model inference can include a premium that's directly proportional to the model's fine-tuned inference pricing premium.

Feature

AlphaGenome gRPC and unified HTTP serving support

AlphaGenome (alphagenome-004) now supports unified HTTP/2 gRPC streaming and chunked binary protobuf HTTP streaming on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform:

  • Streams compressed binary tensor chunks directly over gRPC on shared endpoints (PredictionService.StreamDirectRawPredict on port 8081) and chunked binary protobuf payloads (proto_b64) over HTTP on dedicated endpoints (streamRawPredict on port 8080) across all seven DnaModelService methods (predict_sequence, predict_interval, predict_variant, score_variant, score_interval, score_ism_variants, and output_metadata) and 11 genomic modalities, reducing latency for 1 MB track predictions.
  • Supports concurrent multi-variant evaluation for in silico saturation mutagenesis (score_ism_variants) without HTTP gateway timeouts.
  • Supports model fold selection (ALL_FOLDS, FOLD_0, FOLD_1, FOLD_2, and FOLD_3) across both gRPC and HTTP clients through the unified alphagenome_cloud_sdk Python SDK.
  • Retains alphagenome-003 in Model Garden for backward compatibility with existing legacy HTTP deployments.

For more information, see the AlphaGenome documentation.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware 1.35.700-gke.124 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud 1.35.700-gke.124 runs on Kubernetes v1.35.8-gke.100.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for use with GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

Feature

The following changes were added in 1.35.700-gke.124:

  • Updated system components and container base images to remove the distrusted eMudhra (emSign) and AAA Certificate Services root CAs and reject compromised eMudhra intermediate CAs.
  • Upgraded Container-Optimized OS (COS) to milestone 121 (cos-121-18867-652-7), which removes the distrusted eMudhra (emSign) and AAA Certificate Services root CAs.
  • Updated the Ubuntu 24.04 node and admin workstation base image to ubuntu-gke-op-2404-1-34-v20261024 to remove the distrusted eMudhra (emSign) root CAs (USN-8944-1).

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.35.700-gke.124:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where audit-proxy retried audit log exports indefinitely on permanent errors, generating excessive audit logging traffic.
  • Fixed an issue where the Kubernetes preflight health check scanned all namespaces in the admin cluster instead of the target cluster's namespace, causing cluster upgrades to fail if an unrelated cluster had stale reconciling resources.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal 1.35.700-gke.124 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud for bare metal 1.35.700-gke.124 runs on Kubernetes v1.35.8-gke.100.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for installations or upgrades with the GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

Feature

The following changes were added in 1.35.700-gke.124:

  • Updated system components and container base images to remove the distrusted eMudhra (emSign) and AAA Certificate Services root CAs and reject compromised eMudhra intermediate CAs.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.35.700-gke.124:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where removing a node from a cluster left behind its local PersistentVolume resources instead of garbage collecting them. This fix applies to Google Distributed Cloud for bare metal local PersistentVolume resources created after upgrading to 1.35.700-gke.124; existing orphaned PersistentVolume resources must be deleted manually.
  • Fixed an issue where resetting or removing a control plane node could remove the wrong etcd or etcd-events member if another control plane node's IP address shared the same prefix (for example, 10.201.0.2 and 10.201.0.26), causing the affected node to become NotReady and stalling cluster upgrades.
  • Improved containerd resilience against state corruption if a node reboots while unpacking container images.
  • Fixed an issue where the periodic configuration drift health check failed with a version not supported error while a cluster upgrade or rollback was in progress.
  • Fixed an issue where audit-proxy retried audit log exports indefinitely on permanent errors, generating excessive audit logging traffic.
  • Fixed an issue where the Kubernetes preflight health check scanned all namespaces in the admin cluster instead of the target cluster's namespace, causing cluster upgrades to fail if an unrelated cluster had stale reconciling resources.

Google SecOps

Announcement

[Spotlight Feature] Consolidated Settings and Navigation

The Consolidated Settings and Navigation feature is now in public preview. It replaces the separate SIEM Settings and SOAR Settings menus with a single Settings menu, grouped into Administration, Access Management, Investigation, Detection and Data Management, and also updates the left navigation menu. Each settings page is shown only to users with the correct permissions. Cloud IAM, Viewer and Editor users can now view certain SOAR settings pages in read-only mode. The Google SecOps documentation has been updated to reflect the new navigational changes.

For more information, see Navigate the Google SecOps platform.

This feature is being rolled out in waves starting Monday, November 9 and continuing through Thursday, November 12.

Knowledge Catalog

Feature

Data products in Knowledge Catalog let you request access to an access group for a Google Group or on behalf of another user, in addition to yourself or a service account. Both the requester and the requested user or Google Group receive email notifications when an access request is submitted, approved, or rejected. This feature is generally available.

For more information, see Request access to data products and Manage data product access requests.

Looker

Announcement

The latest versions in the Looker (Google Cloud core) release channels are beginning deployment as follows:

  • Latest version in the Regular channel: Looker 26.20

The latest version in the Rapid and No Channel channels remains Looker 26.22.

Note: This item was added on November 12, 2026.

title: Temporal Exposure to Byzantine Vulnerability Under Intermittent Participation in Federated Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.33168v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this paper, we study the effect of participation variability on per-round Byzantine vulnerability. We formalise Dynamic Participation Exposure (DPE), a phenomenon in which the global Byzantine fraction remains below an aggregation rule's tolerance threshold, while a participating client set violates, or approaches violation of, the assumptions required for robust aggregation. Under stochastic participation, we derive the probability of per round exposure and analyse how active-set size affects the variability of the observed Byzantine fraction. We further examine the accumulation of exposure over multiple rounds and consider adversaries that selectively participate during favourable rounds. Our analysis shows that intermittent participation does not automatically imply aggregation failure. Rather, it transforms Byzantine robustness from a static population-level property into a stochastic and temporal property. To mitigate this risk, we outline actionable design recommendations based on minimum active-set constraints, temporal monitoring, participation history, and adaptive aggregation.

title: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis in Jacobian-Space: Language and Vision Models Agree Approximately Up to a Rotation
description:
arXiv:2611.33304v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) posits that AI models converge toward a shared representation of the world, even when trained on different data modalities. Previous work has found evidence for the PRH in the activations of vision and language models. In this work, we ask whether vision and language models also converge in how they act on these representations: precisely, in how these internal representations affect the models' output. At a chosen layer of a transformer, the Jacobian lens gives every word in the vocabulary (or class in an image classifier) a vector in the hidden state: the vector that most increases the model's tendency to generate that word, at that position or later, or to predict that class. Collectively, these vectors make up what is referred to as the model's J-space. We find evidence of the PRH in J-space across vision and language models, and furthermore, we find that J-spaces mostly converge up to a rotation. That is, a single rotation, fitted on a subset of words, approximately maps one model's J-space onto another's, and so applies to words and classes it was not fitted on. A word's vector, rotated from a text-only language model's J-space into the visual patch tokens of a vision-language model, changes the object the vision-language model says is in the image (and only in the image region where it is added). Rotated into an image generator's text conditioning, a word's vector changes the object in the generated image. Rotated into an ImageNet classifier (trained without text), it raises that object's class score above almost all others, and vice versa. This suggests that models converge not only in how they represent the world, but also in how they act on it.

title: The Danger of Double Precision: Working Precision as a Hidden Constraint in Gaussian Process Maximum Likelihood
description:
arXiv:2611.33647v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Gaussian process (GP) hyperparameters are routinely fitted by maximizing the marginal likelihood in IEEE double precision, although for smooth kernels and noiseless data the covariance matrix is often more ill conditioned than double precision can resolve. For a squared-exponential kernel on a design with a Bayesian-optimization cluster, refits over a range of significand widths, judged against a high-precision reference, show that the double-precision fit is a different model and that fits converge only once the width exceeds the base-2 logarithm of the covariance condition number, about 70 bits. Cholesky failure acts as an implicit conditioning constraint, caused mostly by rounding of the kernel entries; the constrained solution predicted from the working precision alone is within 20% of the best Powell fits at five of the six precisions from 40 to 64 bits, with a local expansion proved for the idealized problem. Across 43 kernels, designs and problem settings, including negative controls that double precision already resolves, the bits needed follow the log condition number at the reference optimum plus a tolerance-dependent offset, and at the loosest tolerance double precision suffices for the Matern 1.5 kernel but not for the squared-exponential kernel on clustered designs. Double-precision hyperparameters overstate the posterior standard deviation near the design cluster and, on a quadratic objective whose likelihood heads to the flat limit, stall closed-loop active learning. Promoting the whole likelihood to 80 significand bits recovers the reference accuracy on every fixed design tested, whereas a fixed jitter trades failures for a posterior bias.

title: Extraneous Cognitive Load in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.33197v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) shows that human problem-solving is affected by both intrinsic load, arising from task difficulty, and extraneous load, arising from how task information is presented. Large language models (LLMs) show analogous effects: presentation alone can affect model performance, but these effects have not yet been systematically isolated from task difficulty. To address this gap, we introduce CogLoadBench, a controlled benchmark that varies five CLT-inspired presentation factors across three reasoning task families. Across models, we find that higher extraneous load conditions often reduce accuracy by either adding competition or complicating the reasoning path. To support diagnosis and mitigation of load-related effects, we propose the Extraneous Load Score (ELS), a prompt-time metric computed from activations that estimates a model's extraneous load, and show that it generalizes across reasoning task types and load levels. We further show that shifting model representations toward lower-load directions at inference time can improve average model performance without changing prompt content.
