title: Attributing Agentic Failure in Reasoning Vision-Language Models with Interactive 2D Environments
description:
arXiv:2611.33162v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic benchmarks report a success rate that confounds distinct causes of failure: misreading the environment, never working out how components of the environment operates, operating the components in the wrong order, and failing to recover from a mistake, each of which calls for a different fix. We present an early preview of MultiNet v2.0-Gridworld - an interactive maze environment built for attribution rather than ranking. Four different types of mechanisms, namely key-door pairs, switch-gate pairs, distractors and decoys, and ordered combinations of these mechanisms, can be added, modified, or removed independently while the renderer, the action space, and the scoring function stay fixed. A breadth-first search over the joint state of position, facing direction, inventory, and mechanism state gives every instance an exact optimal action count, which sets its difficulty and grades unfinished episodes. We fix the evaluation protocol on 15 held-out mazes over 540 episodes, then evaluate three vision-language models on 50 mazes. They solve 6 of 150 episodes, 45 of the 50 mazes were not solved by any model, and no episode containing a switch-gate mechanism was solved.

title: Cloudflare Email Service vs Resend : comparaison des tarifs, limites et API
description:
Cloudflare Email Service vs Resend : quel service choisir pour l'envoi d'e-mails ?

Comparer Cloudflare Email Service et Resend revient à répondre à deux questions : à qui devez-vous écrire, et combien de messages envoyez-vous par mois. Sur le plan gratuit Workers, Cloudflare n'envoie qu'à des adresses de destination vérifiées dans votre propre compte. C'est donc un canal d'alerte gratuit pour votre équipe, et non un moyen gratuit d'écrire à vos clients. Le plan gratuit de Resend, lui, permet d'envoyer à n'importe qui, avec une limite de 3 000 messages par mois et 100 par jour. Pour l'envoi en production, Cloudflare facture 0,35 $ par tranche de 1 000 e-mails au-delà des 3 000 inclus dans Workers Paid (5 $ minimum par mois), tandis que Resend démarre à 20 $ par mois pour 50 000 e-mails.

Essayez Apidog dès aujourd'hui

Cloudflare a intégré l'Email Sending au plan gratuit Workers le 24 novembre 2026, et une réponse à l'annonce a résumé les petites lignes : « Aux destinataires vérifiés*, pas à tout le monde. » Ce guide compare les deux services à partir de leurs pages officielles de tarifs, de limites et d'API, consultées le 26 novembre 2026.

Cloudflare Email Service vs Resend en un coup d'œil

Cloudflare Email Service Resend
Destinataires en plan gratuit Uniquement les adresses de destination vérifiées dans votre compte Tout le monde
Volume en plan gratuit Illimité vers les adresses vérifiées 3 000 par mois, 100 par jour
Offre payante d'entrée Workers Paid, 5 $ minimum par mois, 3 000 e-mails inclus Pro, 20 $ par mois pour 50 000 e-mails
Dépassement 0,35 $ par tranche de 1 000 0,90 $ par tranche de 1 000 sur Pro, jusqu'à 0,46 $ sur le palier Scale le plus élevé
Limite journalière Prudente au départ pour les nouveaux comptes, elle augmente avec la réputation 100 sur le plan gratuit, aucune sur les plans payants
Interfaces Binding Workers, API REST, SMTP API REST, SMTP, SDK officiels
Destinataires par message 50 (to, cc et bcc confondus) 50
Événements Publiés dans une Cloudflare Queue Webhooks vers votre endpoint HTTPS
Domaine Doit être un domaine de votre compte Cloudflare N'importe quel fournisseur DNS
E-mail marketing Non couvert par Email Sending Broadcasts, facturés au nombre de contacts

Ce qui a changé le 24 novembre

La note de changelog de Cloudflare annonce que les comptes du plan gratuit Workers peuvent désormais intégrer des domaines d'envoi et envoyer des e-mails à leurs adresses de destination vérifiées sans frais. Vous pouvez utiliser le binding Workers, l'API REST ou SMTP.

Trois détails comptent :

  1. Les destinataires sont restreints. Envoyez à une adresse qui n'est pas vérifiée sur un compte gratuit, et le binding renvoie E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED.
  2. Les envois vérifiés sont gratuits partout. Sur tous les plans, le courrier adressé à des adresses de destination vérifiées ne compte ni dans le quota mensuel ni dans les limites journalières.
  3. Les envois vérifiés ont changé de produit. Ils relevaient d'Email Routing ; ils sont désormais du trafic Email Sending, avec un journal d'activité, des analyses, des événements et un nouveau champ GraphQL isVerifiedRecipient.

Le plan gratuit convient donc aux alertes d'astreinte et aux rapports nocturnes destinés à votre propre équipe. Les réinitialisations de mot de passe et les reçus partent vers des inconnus, et nécessitent Workers Paid.

Tarifs de Cloudflare Email Service vs Resend

Voici ce que chaque service facture aux volumes mensuels courants, calculé à partir des deux pages officielles (tarifs Cloudflare, tarifs Resend). Le montant Cloudflare inclut le minimum de 5 $ de Workers Paid, qui couvre aussi votre usage des Workers.

E-mails par mois Cloudflare (Workers Paid) Resend
3 000 5,00 $ 0 $ (gratuit, si vous restez sous 100 par jour)
10 000 7,45 $ 20 $ (Pro)
50 000 21,45 $ 20 $ (Pro)
100 000 38,95 $ 35 $ (Pro)
500 000 178,95 $ 350 $ (Scale)
1 000 000 353,95 $ 650 $ (Scale)

Le calcul pour Cloudflare est simple : retirez les 3 000 e-mails inclus et multipliez le reste par 0,35 $ par tranche de 1 000. Pour 100 000 e-mails, cela donne 97 × 0,35 $ = 33,95 $, plus 5 $.

En dessous de 3 000 par mois, Resend Free ne coûte rien si aucun jour ne dépasse 100 envois. Juste aux paliers 50 000 et 100 000 de Resend, Resend est légèrement moins cher. Entre les paliers et à volume élevé, le tarif forfaitaire de Cloudflare l'emporte : environ 300 $ par mois d'économie à 1 million d'e-mails.

Notes de facturation : Cloudflare compte les hard bounces dans le quota, mais pas les envois rejetés au niveau de l'API, comme les adresses supprimées. Resend ne facture qu'au mois, et les dépassements nécessitent d'activer « Transactional Overages », sinon il vous est proposé de passer à une offre supérieure.

Si vous envoyez aussi des newsletters, Resend facture le marketing séparément : les Broadcasts sont limités par contacts, et non par e-mails, en démarrant à 1 000 contacts sur le plan gratuit et à 40 $ par mois pour 5 000. Les pages Email Sending de Cloudflare ne décrivent que l'envoi transactionnel, comparez donc cette ligne uniquement chez Resend.

Limites d'envoi et limites de débit

Cloudflare ne publie pas de chiffre journalier fixe. Les nouveaux comptes « démarrent avec un quota journalier prudent » qui augmente avec votre comportement d'envoi, votre délivrabilité et la santé de votre compte (page des limites). Quand vous l'atteignez, chaque interface échoue à sa manière :

Interface Réponse à la limite journalière
Binding Workers E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED
API REST HTTP 429
SMTP 451 4.7.1 à la fin de DATA

Par message : 50 destinataires, 25 MiB au total et 16 Ko d'en-têtes personnalisés. Un formulaire sur la page des limites permet de demander une limite plus élevée.

Resend publie ses chiffres. Le plan gratuit vous plafonne à 100 e-mails par jour, les plans payants n'ont pas de plafond journalier, et l'API autorise 10 requêtes par seconde et par équipe sur tous les plans (limites d'usage). Un appel par lot envoie jusqu'à 100 e-mails en une seule requête, et les en-têtes retry-after indiquent à votre client quand ralentir.

Ainsi, sur un nouveau compte Cloudflare, attendez-vous à ce qu'un pic le jour du lancement heurte une limite que vous ne pouvez pas connaître à l'avance, et gérez les trois types d'erreur. Sur Resend, concevez autour de 10 requêtes par seconde.

Forme de l'API et des SDK

Les deux API prennent les mêmes champs essentiels, donc migrer revient surtout à un chercher-remplacer.

Dans un Worker, Cloudflare vous fournit un binding. Ajoutez-le à votre configuration Wrangler :

[[send_email]]
name = "EMAIL"

Puis envoyez depuis votre handler :

await env.EMAIL.send({
  from: "alerts@yourdomain.com",
  to: "oncall@example.com",
  subject: "Disk usage above 90%",
  text: "Disk usage on db-1 is above 90%.",
});

En dehors des Workers, vous faites un POST des mêmes champs vers /accounts/{account_id}/email/sending/send sur l'API REST Cloudflare avec un token d'API, ou vous utilisez les SDK officiels Node, Python et Go. Le SDK Node de Resend ressemble à ceci :

import { Resend } from "resend";
const resend = new Resend(process.env.RESEND_API_KEY);

const { data, error } = await resend.emails.send({
  from: "Acme <welcome@yourdomain.com>",
  to: ["user@example.com"],
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<strong>Thanks for signing up.</strong>",
});

Resend ajoute une idempotencyKey, les envois planifiés, l'envoi par lot et les templates React Email. Notre guide de l'API Resend détaille chacun, et le guide des clés d'API Resend couvre la portée des clés. Si vous préférez piloter depuis un terminal, consultez comment installer et utiliser la CLI Resend.

Événements et webhooks

Cloudflare publie les événements Email Sending via des abonnements aux événements dans une Cloudflare Queue. Vous la consommez avec un Worker ou un consommateur HTTP pull. Chaque abonnement couvre un domaine d'envoi. Les événements sont message.delivered, message.deferred, message.bounced, message.failed, message.rejected et message.complained. La liste ne contient pas d'événements d'ouverture ni de clic.

Resend poste des webhooks signés vers votre endpoint HTTPS. Les événements incluent email.sent, email.delivered, email.delivery_delayed, email.bounced, email.complained, email.opened, email.clicked, email.failed, email.suppressed et email.received. Le plan gratuit autorise 1 endpoint webhook, Pro 5 et Scale 10.

Besoin du suivi des ouvertures et des clics ? Resend le propose sur tous les plans. Déjà sur Workers ? Un consommateur de Queue vous évite d'exposer une route webhook publique.

Configuration du domaine

Cloudflare intègre un domaine depuis votre compte Cloudflare et écrit les enregistrements DNS à votre place : des enregistrements MX et SPF sur un sous-domaine cf-bounce pour la gestion des bounces, un enregistrement DKIM et un enregistrement DMARC sur _dmarc. Si votre DNS est hébergé ailleurs, vous devrez d'abord transférer la zone vers Cloudflare.

Resend fonctionne avec n'importe quel fournisseur DNS : vous ajoutez les enregistrements SPF et DKIM qu'il vous fournit. Le plan gratuit inclut 3 domaines, Pro 10 et Scale 1 000, avec 100 de plus pour 20 $ par mois sur Pro et Scale.

Lequel choisir ?

  • Alertes et rapports pour votre propre équipe, budget de 0 $ : Cloudflare sur Workers Free. Vérifiez l'adresse de chaque coéquipier, et les envois sont gratuits, sans quota.
  • Un projet perso qui écrit à de vrais utilisateurs sous 100 par jour : Resend Free.
  • Une app déjà sur Workers, envoyant 200 000 messages ou plus par mois : Cloudflare sur Workers Paid. Le tarif par message est environ la moitié de celui de Resend à ce volume.
  • Besoin du suivi des ouvertures et des clics, de la planification, de React Email ou des Broadcasts marketing : Resend.
  • Votre DNS n'est pas chez Cloudflare et vous ne voulez pas le déplacer : Resend.

Certaines équipes utilisent les deux : Cloudflare pour le courrier interne, Resend pour les clients. Notre sélection d'API e-mail gratuites liste d'autres options.

Testez les deux API d'envoi avec Apidog CLI

Avant de changer de fournisseur, testez les deux avec les mêmes requêtes, y compris le comportement de votre code face à un 429. Votre agent de codage peut le faire avec Apidog CLI pendant que vous examinez le résultat.

Configurez-le une fois :

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

Donnez ensuite un seul prompt à Claude Code, Codex ou OpenCode :

Write email-providers.yaml, an OpenAPI 3.1 file describing Cloudflare's
POST /accounts/{account_id}/email/sending/send and Resend's POST /emails,
including their 429 responses. Import it into Apidog project <projectId>,
list the endpoints, pick the environment for staging, then run test
scenario <scenarioId> with both keys passed as env vars and tell me which
provider was slower and whether our retry logic handled the 429.

L'agent exécute ces commandes :

apidog import --project <projectId> --format openapi --file ./email-providers.yaml
apidog endpoint list --project <projectId>
apidog environment list --project <projectId>
apidog run --project <projectId> -t <scenarioId> -e <environmentId> \
  --env-var "CF_API_TOKEN=<token>" --env-var "RESEND_API_KEY=<key>" -r cli,junit

Faites pointer le scénario vers des adresses vérifiées sur Cloudflare et vers l'adresse de test delivered@resend.dev de Resend, pour qu'aucun test n'écrive à un client. Ajoutez --upload-report pour consulter l'exécution dans l'application ; Apidog CLI dans Claude Code couvre la configuration de l'agent.

Une fois que cela fonctionne pour un développeur, toute une équipe peut s'en servir : Sharkly est un tableau où vous assignez des tâches comme « migrer l'e-mail de réinitialisation de mot de passe vers Cloudflare et relancer les tests e-mail » à des agents de codage qui tournent sur vos propres machines avec votre propre plan Claude Code, Codex ou OpenCode, en exécutent plusieurs en parallèle, et examinent ce qu'ils livrent avant la fusion. C'est gratuit pour commencer.

FAQ

Cloudflare Email Service est-il gratuit ? L'envoi vers les adresses de destination vérifiées de votre compte est gratuit sur tous les plans, y compris Workers Free, et ne compte dans aucun quota. L'envoi vers n'importe qui d'autre nécessite Workers Paid, qui inclut 3 000 e-mails par mois puis coûte 0,35 $ par tranche de 1 000.

Cloudflare est-il moins cher que Resend ? À la plupart des volumes, oui. À 1 million d'e-mails par mois, il coûte environ 354 $ contre 650 $. Juste aux paliers Pro de 50 000 et 100 000 de Resend, Resend est quelques dollars moins cher, et en dessous de 3 000 par mois, Resend Free ne coûte rien.

Puis-je utiliser Cloudflare Email Service sans Workers ? Oui. L'API REST et SMTP fonctionnent depuis n'importe quel backend, mais votre domaine doit être dans votre compte Cloudflare.

Cloudflare Email Service suit-il les ouvertures et les clics ? Sa liste d'événements Email Sending couvre delivered, deferred, bounced, failed, rejected et complained. Elle ne contient pas d'événements d'ouverture ni de clic. Resend suit les ouvertures et les clics sur tous les plans.

Quelle est la limite du plan gratuit de Resend ? 3 000 e-mails par mois et 100 par jour, 3 domaines et 1 endpoint webhook, avec envoi vers n'importe quel destinataire.

title: Tells of a Lying Machine: Analyzing LLM-Generated Strategic Dialogue in Chinese Werewolf
description:
arXiv:2611.33747v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Social-deduction games give models opposing objectives, but they also give roles different information and speaking obligations. We analyze 5,404 public utterances from 150 Chinese Werewolf games played by 12 models, comparing ordinary wolves with ordinary villagers so that special roles are excluded. Private knowledge and goals still differ, and no utterance is verified as true or false. After model and length adjustment, wolf utterances score higher on both certainty and uncertainty (coefficients +0.074 and +0.072). Emotional intensification has the largest rank-biserial effect (r = .145), but it depends on a single degree marker and correlates weakly with human-rated affect. Three annotators' ratings of 392 utterances show higher wolf scores on four behavioral dimensions, and five LLM judges reach 60.8%-70.2% accuracy on a shared evaluation set. In a generation probe that prompts six models with a wolf identity but a villager speaking goal under fixed public context, certainty (+0.164) and emotional intensification (+0.095) increase. These findings describe role-associated language rather than verified lying, and they argue for explicit comparison groups and lexicon sensitivity checks in game-based deception evaluation. Data and code are available at https://github.com/justinchoi929/Tells-of-a-Lying-Machine

title: StyleID++: Position-Decoupled and Structure-Coherent Style Retrieval across Diffusion Architectures
description:
arXiv:2611.33323v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Attention injection offers a remarkably simple route to training-free style transfer: content queries retrieve style keys and values inside a pretrained diffusion model. We show that this operation also creates an overlooked failure mode. Position signals that are useful within one image become a spurious shared coordinate system across two spatially unrelated images, causing content tokens to favor style tokens at similar coordinates. This cross-image positional leakage appears in both convolutional U-Nets and diffusion transformers (DiTs), despite their different position mechanisms. Removing the positional shortcut exposes a second problem: unconstrained global retrieval lets related content tokens select incompatible style regions, producing fragmented appearance. We present StyleID++, a training-free framework that addresses the two problems jointly. Position-Decoupled Retrieval reduces coordinate-dependent matching through circular padding in U-Nets and injection-only RoPE removal in DiTs, while preserving native position modeling elsewhere. Affinity-Coherent Refinement then regularizes style assignments with the content self-attention graph, encouraging structurally related tokens to retrieve compatible style evidence. We quantify the leakage with a coordinate--centroid correlation and a permutation test on the style reference. The permutation error can be driven to zero in both backbones, which identifies the position mechanism as the carrier of the leakage, and StyleID++ obtains the best ArtFID of all methods we compare.

title: DiffER$^2$: Diffusion Ensembles for Retrosynthesis Prediction with SMILES Adapted Particle Guidance
description:
arXiv:2611.33557v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Computational retrosynthesis prediction has the potential to reduce development time for newly discovered drugs by automatically generating potential reactions for a target product. Data-driven approaches commonly treat this as a sequence-to-sequence generation task on SMILES strings. In this work, we construct ensembles of discrete-time and continuous-time diffusion models for molecular generation and incorporate guidance mechanisms for improved output diversity. We propose an adaptation of particle guidance to SMILES sequence generation which significantly improves the number of unique molecules generated by diffusion ensembles while increasing top-k accuracy. These results further expand the efficacy of discrete diffusion for SMILES generation, and our empirical analyses offer new insights into the capabilities of diffusion models for chemical retrosynthesis.

title: Verified Proof Refactoring with Codex and Qwen
description:
arXiv:2611.31762v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We refactor existing Lean 4 proofs to reduce source length and checking cost while preserving theorem statements and compatibility across Lean versions. A locally served Qwen model uses the open-source Codex CLI to inspect source, retrieve declarations, and test proof replacements. The host keeps a replacement only if it improves the objective and Lean accepts it on every required version. A deterministic CPU pass then refines the verified proofs. On the 60 problems in Lean Refactor Arena, model search achieves a local mean combined score of 82.07, and cleanup raises it to 82.18. The final proofs pass all 127 required proof--version checks. Our system placed first in the open-source LLM track of Lean Refactor Arena at VeriCodeGen.

title: DiCALM: Converting Autoregressive Convolution-Attention Language Models into Discrete Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.33919v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing methods for adapting autoregressive (AR) language models to diffusion generation focus mainly on full-attention architectures. More efficient hybrid architectures remain underexplored. We introduce DiCALM, a recipe for converting the hybrid convolution-attention models of the LFM2 family (LFM2 and LFM2.5) from AR to masked-diffusion generation. DiCALM progressively extends LFM2's causal gated convolution so that it captures local context in both directions. It combines this extension with a masking warm-up and joint AR--diffusion training. In controlled experiments, DiCALM performs comparably to the corresponding fine-tuned LFM2.5-based AR models and delivers consistent speedups over them at both the 350M and 1.2B scales: over 1.4x on average and up to 1.79x.

title: Making agent retries safe across timeouts and restarts
description:
Imagine an enterprise support agent ordering an approved replacement for a customer. The order goes through, but the confirmation times out. The agent retries and reports success. Two orders are now queued for fulfillment, and the support team has a duplicate to sort out.

That sequence is easy to miss if the only thing you check is whether the retry succeeded. To reproduce it, this experiment uses a small HTTP order service and a scripted tool caller. In the first timeout case, the caller gave up after about 101 ms. The order had already been committed. Retrying created another row with the same tenant, product and quantity. The caller saw one timeout followed by a successful 201 Created.

The failure sits between the tool and the service, so reproducing it does not require a model. The setup uses two SQLite databases, one for the caller's saved state and one for the service's orders. All failures are injected locally. This is a deployment exercise, not a report from a customer environment.

Across three rounds, the experiment recorded 117 scenario runs and 288 HTTP requests, keeping failed attempts alongside successful ones. Reusing a saved operation key prevented duplicates in several cases. It was not enough when the service had no record of the earlier request, whether because that record was never saved or had already been deleted.

What happens between a tool call and its result

For the replacement order in the opening example, the tool request could be as small as this:

POST /orders
Content-Type: application/json

{"sku":"keyboard","quantity":1}

The service can commit this order and lose the connection before the response reaches the caller. To make that timing reproducible, the test gives the caller a 100 ms socket timeout and makes the service hold its response for 500 ms after committing. Here is the caller's record, with unrelated fields omitted:

{
  "fault": "timeout_after_commit",
  "timeout_seconds": 0.1,
  "status": null,
  "error_type": "TimeoutError",
  "error": "timed out",
  "elapsed_ms": 100.892311
}

The exception tells us how long the caller waited. To find out whether the order exists, we have to look at the server trace and database. Raising the timeout above 500 ms would let this particular response arrive, but it would leave the connection-drop and process-crash cases unresolved.

That is why increasing timeouts or adding backoff cannot settle the duplicate-order problem on its own. As AWS explains in its guidance on timeouts and retries, a failed call can still have side effects. Once the order is committed, a retry needs a way to identify it as work already done.

Three retry strategies, the same faults

An idempotency key gives the service an identifier it can recognize when the caller retries. To check what that actually protects, the experiment runs each scenario with three ways of identifying the request:

Strategy What the caller sends
No key The same payload again, without an operation identifier
New key per attempt A new UUID for every HTTP request
Durable action key One UUID saved for the intended action before the first request, then reused

The service supports keys throughout. What changes is the caller: it either omits the key, replaces it on every attempt, or saves and reuses it. A fresh UUID on each request still makes every retry look like new work, even though the payload has not changed.

The results below count orders created in one scenario run. Counting successful responses would miss the original problem. All three repetitions produced these counts.

Injected condition No key New key per attempt Durable action key
Response arrives normally 1 1 1
Caller times out after commit 2 2 1
Connection closes after commit 2 2 1
Service exits before commit, then restarts 1 1 1
Service exits after commit, then restarts 2 2 1
Caller process dies before its completion checkpoint 2 2 1
Eight concurrent deliveries of one intended action 8 8 1
All three responses are dropped 3 3 1

Notice the difference between a service exit before and after commit. Before commit, there is no saved order, so the next attempt should create one. After commit, creating another would be a duplicate. The service needs to return the result of the original order instead.

These counts describe deliberately injected faults, not their frequency in production traffic. They establish which behavior each strategy produces. To understand why the durable key works here, we need to follow where it is stored and how the service uses it.

Keep the identity outside the model conversation

For the support workflow, the key belongs to the approved replacement order. Retrying its HTTP request does not mean the customer approved another order.

The caller therefore saves a mapping from (tenant, action) to a random UUID before making the first request. A fresh invocation looks up the same action and gets the same key. Storing that mapping in SQLite lets it survive a caller restart; keeping it in a Python variable would not.

This only works if the workflow preserves the action identifier as well. After a restart, the test resumes action-1 and retrieves its saved key. Generating a new action ID at that point would lose the protection before the next HTTP request was sent. The same applies to model-driven tool calls: an SDK retry, a workflow retry and a resumed invocation may all be attempts to complete one approved action. Their identity needs to come from saved workflow state.

Two genuinely separate orders can have identical payloads. If a customer intentionally orders two keyboards in two transactions, hashing the payload as the operation key would incorrectly collapse the second order into the first. The distinct-action control sends the same payload with two action identities and correctly creates two orders.

A payload hash is still useful, but for a different check: whether a caller has changed the request while reusing an existing key. That check belongs on the service side.

The service has to make a promise it can keep

Recognizing the key is only half the job. The service also needs to know what happened when it first received that key. It stores a replay receipt: a record of the key, request fingerprint, response status and response body. When the same key and payload arrive again, the service returns that saved response, including the original order ID.

The order and its receipt are written together:

BEGIN IMMEDIATE
  look up (tenant, operation, key)
  if a receipt exists:
    reject a different payload, or return the saved response
  otherwise:
    insert the order
    insert its replay receipt
COMMIT

Both inserts occur in one transaction. If storing the receipt fails, the order insert rolls back too. One regression test forces exactly that failure with a SQLite trigger, then verifies that a later valid request can still create the order.

For concurrent deliveries, this example acquires the write transaction before reading the receipt. SQLite allows only one writer at a time. That makes the eight-request result straightforward: one request creates the order, and the other seven replay its result.

This choice also serializes unrelated writes. It is convenient for a small reproduction, but the test says nothing about its throughput at customer scale. A different database needs its own tested locking and conflict-handling path.

There are also boundaries the service must enforce when looking up a receipt. The key is scoped to the tenant and operation, so the same UUID in another tenant must not return the first tenant's order. The local test uses a header to supply tenant identity; a deployed service would have to obtain and authorize that identity from authenticated context. Possessing a key is not permission to see its result.

Within that scope, the request fingerprint prevents a key from being reused for different work. Changing the quantity returns 409 and creates no second order. Reordering the JSON fields remains a replay, because the fingerprint is computed from canonicalized input. Invalid quantities are rejected before the key is consumed.

These are explicit service semantics. Providers may make different choices about saved errors and retention. For example, Stripe documents its own replay and parameter-matching rules; copying a header name does not copy that contract.

A key did not fix the split transaction

The transaction around both writes may look like a small implementation detail. To test whether it matters, one comparison mode commits the order first and saves the receipt in a separate transaction.

The service then exits between those writes. After restarting, it has an order but no receipt. The caller retries with the original durable key, but the service finds nothing to replay and creates another order. The saved events show where the duplicate comes from:

order_committed_without_receipt  order A
process exits
request received with same key
committed                        order B
response_sent                    201

This excerpt shortens the UUIDs for readability. The complete events retain both IDs and timestamps.

All three repetitions produced two orders, despite the stable key. The missing guarantee was atomic storage of the effect and its replay record.

AWS's article on idempotent APIs makes the same requirement explicit: recording the request token and performing the mutations need to be an atomic operation.

That boundary becomes harder when the effect belongs to another system. A local database transaction cannot roll back a payment that an external provider has already accepted. The provider needs to recognize the same operation identity, or the integration needs a way to query and reconcile the outcome. Queuing the work through an outbox can make the local handoff durable, but the receiver still has to tolerate repeated delivery.

This experiment does not implement a payment provider, an outbox or cross-service recovery. Its guarantee ends at the order service's database.

Stopping retries does not establish failure

Even with both writes in one transaction, the workflow still has a problem if confirmation never arrives. Another scenario drops every response and stops after three attempts. The durable key keeps the final database at one order, but the caller has only three connection failures to work with. Its outcome remains unknown.

Reporting that operation as failed would be misleading. Automatically starting a new action with a fresh key could create another order. A workflow needs a distinct path for an unresolved outcome: retain the original identity, reconcile through an authorized lookup or repeat request when safe, and escalate if it cannot establish what happened.

For the support team, this means the workflow should not say either “replacement failed” or “replacement confirmed” based on those responses alone. An evaluation needs to capture the same distinction. A checker that sees only tool exceptions might count three failed operations; one that sees only the database might call the workflow successful. What actually happened is more specific: one order was created, duplicates were prevented, and the caller never received confirmation.

Retry limits, backoff and a total deadline still matter. The example uses fixed attempt counts to expose correctness; it does not test a production backoff policy or retry storms. Its socket timeout is not a complete workflow deadline.

How long does the protection last?

Keeping an unresolved action for later recovery raises another question: will the service still recognize it when the workflow resumes?

A final test deletes the replay receipt after a successful request, then sends the same key again. The service creates a second order. This models lost replay history rather than testing expiry against a clock, but it exposes the dependency: retaining the key on the caller is not enough if the service has forgotten it.

The retention window therefore needs to account for how long a workflow can remain paused, not just the few seconds an HTTP library spends retrying. Before enabling automatic recovery, the deployment needs an answer for what happens when an approved action resumes outside that window.

A durable business identifier with a uniqueness rule may provide longer protection than a temporary response cache. Where that is unavailable, a late resume may need reconciliation rather than another create request.

Run it and inspect the records

The source keeps these failure modes together so you can compare them against the same service. It runs on Linux with Python 3.11 or newer, uses only the standard library, and starts local processes listening on 127.0.0.1.

git clone https://github.com/deavgprime/iac-eval-bench.git
cd iac-eval-bench
git switch --detach 5de3e73a495878377f57324e9947f2e90ca89554
python3 docs/examples/safe_retries.py run \
  --output runs/safe-retries \
  --repetitions 3
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p test_safe_retries.py -v

Use a fresh output directory each time. The driver refuses to overwrite an existing run.

The saved evidence includes every client attempt, the server events and final order/receipt snapshots. The source includes the unsafe comparison modes, so the duplicate behavior can be reproduced as well as the protected path.

The recorded run used Python 3.12.3 and SQLite 3.45.1. It completed in 29.26 seconds, with 18.53 CPU seconds across child processes. The driver and largest child each reached a reported peak RSS of about 29.4 MiB. Those are per-process peaks, not total concurrent memory. Event logging flushes to disk and affects timing, so these measurements describe the test workload rather than service performance.

The crash tests terminate processes; they do not test a host outage, disk failure or regional failover. The fault headers are test controls, not an interface to expose in a deployment.

For a tool that creates orders, the first test worth borrowing is the one that started this article: commit the write, lose its response, then retry through the real workflow. Check how many orders exist, whether the workflow kept the same action identity, and what it tells the support team. A green status after the retry is not enough to answer any of those questions.

title: LLMVC: Large Language Model-Guided Generative Video Compression
description:
arXiv:2611.33580v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent generative video methods achieve strong perceptual compression by encoding videos into compact latent representations and reconstructing them with powerful generative decoders. However, visual encoders must compress both high-level semantics and dense visual details into a unified latent space, which complicates entropy coding and decoding and may cause semantic drift under aggressive compression. In this work, we propose Large Language Model-Guided Video Compression (LLMVC), which leverages the summarization capability of frozen video large language models (Video-LLMs) to generate compact semantic tokens aligned with temporal latent slices for guiding video compression. Specifically, Hybrid Bidirectional Bimodal Attention (HBBA) enables bidirectional interactions between visual and semantic features during encoding and decoding. Semantic-Conditioned Cross-Attention (SCCA) incorporates semantic features into probability modeling during entropy coding. These semantic features provide high-level guidance throughout the pipeline, improving representation quality and encouraging semantic consistency through a transmitted text side channel. Experiments on UVG, MCL-JCV, and HEVC show that LLMVC consistently improves compression performance over traditional and recent neural video compression methods in terms of LPIPS and DISTS, while also achieving better fidelity than recent perceptual codecs.

title: EvOrderBench: When do sampled frames establish event order?
description:
arXiv:2611.33492v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are often asked which of two actions in a video happened first, given only a few sampled frames. Such frames can show that both actions occurred without showing which came first, so a reliable model should state an order only when the frames establish it. Forced-choice temporal benchmarks treat every input as answerable and reward lucky guesses, while answerability benchmarks do not separate frames that miss an action from frames that show both actions but not their order. We introduce EvOrderBench, a real-video benchmark of 579 event families. Each family fixes an episode and a question and varies only the frames: of two four-frame inputs, only one establishes the order, and two six-frame inputs extend the other one with either the frames that resolve the order or frames that do not. Every input is labeled for whether its frames establish each action and their order. Across sixteen open-weight configurations and three closed-source references, the best open models order nearly as accurately as the references when the frames establish the order, but withhold correctly on at most 83% of the inputs where they do not, against at least 90% for every reference; forced-choice accuracy cannot reveal this gap. Open models withhold mainly when the frames show neither action; once the frames show one or both, most of them commit to an order. Thinking narrows the gap, even when it is switched on within a single checkpoint, mainly by separating sufficient from insufficient evidence rather than by making models more cautious overall. Accurate ordering thus does not imply knowing when the frames fall short, and benchmarks should reward withholding alongside ordering.

title: Introducing Vercel Schedules
description:
Cron jobs are useful for work that needs to happen regularly. You can use them to do things such as back up your database on a schedule, or keep data in sync between two systems.

You define them once in code and then can update them by editing their config and redeploying. But today, agents interact with users as work evolves, and schedules need to be updated in real time.

We built Vercel Schedules to allow agents and applications to create, change, or cancel one-time and recurring schedules through code, without redeploying.

What are Vercel Schedules?

Schedules builds on the static approach used by Vercel Cron Jobs, but are designed to let users and agents decide when work should happen while your application is still running. A schedule tells Vercel when to trigger a task and where to send it. Your application provides the code that carries out the work.

You can use schedules for both static and dynamic jobs:

  • Static schedules keep the timing in vercel.json or Build Output API configuration and sync when you deploy. You can use them to call private functions or HTTP paths, or send messages to Queue topics.

  • Dynamic schedules let your app create and manage schedules through the JS SDK, CLI, or API as it runs. They support one-time and recurring work through Queue topics.

You can also test scheduled work on Preview deployments and in custom environments before running it in Production.

How Schedules works

Take this example: A user could ask an agent with web access, “Tomorrow morning, summarize the top five stories on Hacker News.” The traditional solution would be storing the request and its schedule time in a database, then using a cron job to check for work that is due.

With Schedules, an agent can create a schedule that records the request and when to run it, without a separate database and polling job. The example below defines an AI SDK tool that gives an agent this capability.

When the task is due, Vercel uses Queues to deliver the saved request to your app. Your app provides code to read that request, check the user’s current permissions, and start the agent. The agent fetches the top five Hacker News posts with a web tool, then returns a summary for your app to save for the user.

If you already build agents with fx’s JavaScript library, libfx or Pi’s agent library, you can add a similar scheduling tool. The eve agent framework uses Vercel Schedules to provide dynamic scheduling tools for production agents hosted on Vercel.

Run recurring application jobs

You can schedule recurring work with Vercel Schedules. Schedules can be created dynamically via the JS SDK, API, and CLI, or set up in your project’s configuration.

For example, to create a job that cleans up expired records every day, you could define a schedule that invokes a private function in your chosen time zone:

Vercel calls this cleanup code directly, without exposing it at a public URL. It checks that each call comes from the scheduling service, so you don’t have to add that check yourself.

If your app already uses the Nitro 3 server framework, its experimental integration lets you run the recurring jobs in your existing scheduledTasks configuration as private functions.

You can also try the agent task and cleanup locally with vercel dev, then test them on a Preview branch or in a custom environment before production. Use Run Schedule in your project’s Schedules tab to try either task without waiting, and see when past runs happened.

Get started

Vercel Schedules is now in Public Beta, and you can use it for the recurring tasks your application already runs. When a user or agent chooses when work should happen, your code can create and manage a schedule for that task.

To get started, check out the Vercel Schedules skill and read the documentation.

title: Tabla Ejecutiva, Kanban y Calendario en React 19 sobre un Índice Estático
description:
Publicado originalmente en Datalaria.

En los dos primeros artículos de esta serie demostramos cómo erradicar la desincronización entre bases de datos externas y Git (Artículo 1) y cómo blindar la calidad de los metadatos y la paridad bilingüe mediante contratos de tipado estricto en Pydantic v2 y pipelines de CI/CD (Artículo 2).

Al finalizar ese pipeline de backend disponemos de un activo de datos excepcional: el archivo public.json, un dataset normalizado, determinista y auditado que consolida el 100% de los posts técnicos, aplicaciones interactivas y kits descargables del ecosistema.

Sin embargo, los datos estructurados en disco carecen de utilidad si el equipo editorial y la dirección técnica deben inspeccionarlos leyendo código fuente o ejecutando comandos en la terminal. Para tomar decisiones estratégicas de publicación se requiere una interfaz ejecutiva de alto nivel: una consola de control (cockpit) que permita filtrar por categorías temáticas, monitorizar cuellos de botella en un flujo Kanban, visualizar los próximos lanzamientos en un calendario mensual y capturar nuevas ideas al vuelo.

En este artículo desglosamos la arquitectura frontend de Datalaria Pulse: cómo diseñamos una Single Page Application (SPA) en React 19 + TypeScript que se monta directamente sobre un índice estático, ofreciendo interactividad instantánea con latencia cero sin incurrir en costes de servidores ni depender de bases de datos lentas.

🗺️ Hoja de Ruta de la Serie Datalaria Pulse

Para entender cómo encaja cada pieza del rompecabezas de Content Ops as Code, esta serie se compone de 5 entregas estructuradas:

  1. ⚪ Parte 1: Adiós Notion: Datalaria Pulse o la Gestión Editorial que se Escribe Sola desde Git
  2. ⚪ Parte 2: Del Front Matter al Índice: Pydantic v2, Paridad Bilingüe y Automatización con CI/CD
  3. 🟢 Parte 3 (Este artículo): Tabla Ejecutiva, Tablero Kanban y Calendario Mensual en React 19 sobre un Índice Estático
  4. ⚪ Parte 4 (Dom 29/11): Google Analytics 4 y Search Console Automatizados: Cómo Medir el ROI Orgánico de Cada Post, App y Kit
  5. ⚪ Parte 5 (Mié 02/12): Gestión Editorial para Equipos de Documentación, SEO y Marketing: de Notion a Excel en 5 minutos y Fábrica con IA

0. Objetivos de la Fase y de este Artículo: Interactividad Instantánea sobre Datos Estáticos

El propósito de esta etapa en la Datalaria Pulse radica en democratizar el acceso al catálogo editorial mediante una experiencia de usuario (UX) fluida, moderna y reactiva.

Objetivos Estratégicos:

  1. Consumo de Datos con Cero Latencia: Eliminar las llamadas a bases de datos relacionales tradicionales en la navegación pública sirviendo un índice estático inmutable (public.json) alojado en la CDN.
  2. Multi-Visualización de Contenidos: Proyectar la misma fuente única de verdad (SSOT) a través de tres prismas complementarios: Tabla Ejecutiva (auditoría analítica), Tablero Kanban (ciclo de vida) y Calendario Mensual (planificación temporal).
  3. Captura Optimista Desacoplada: Permitir a cualquier autor registrar ideas o notas en local con persistencia inmediata en el navegador (localStorage), facilitando la exportación limpia a YAML para su posterior commit en Git.
  4. Fundación para el Modo Pro: Diseñar los componentes visuales de modo que puedan alternar de forma transparente entre el dataset público estático y la sincronización colaborativa en tiempo real con Supabase PostgreSQL.

Objetivos Específicos de este Artículo 3:

  • Explicar el patrón arquitectónico Static-First SPA: cómo React 19 renderiza cientos de activos en memoria sin desfase de red (network lag).
  • Desgranar la ingeniería de la Tabla Ejecutiva: búsqueda predictiva, filtros combinados por taxonomía y paginación ajustable (10, 25, 50 registros).
  • Analizar el diseño del Tablero Kanban de 5 Columnas (Idea, Borrador, En Revisión, Programado, Publicado) y su lógica de estados.
  • Presentar la rejilla del Calendario Editorial y el sistema de captura de ideas con exportación atómica a Git backlog.

1. Conexión con el Ecosistema Datalaria: De las Suites Ejecutivas al Dashboard React 19

El diseño de la interfaz de Datalaria Pulse bebe directamente de los estándares de usabilidad, estética de panel de instrumentos y rigor cuantitativo forjados en nuestras suites precedentes:

  1. La Ergonomía Visual de LifeOps: Pulse adopta la tipografía corporativa Outfit + Inter, el modo oscuro profundo (Dark Slate #080d1a a #0f172a), los resplandores neón cian y esmeralda, y la estructura de navegación segmentada flotante que desarrollamos originalmente para la gestión personal en LifeOps.
  2. Presentación Directiva de la Suite de Toma de Decisiones: La cabecera de Pulse sigue el estándar directivo C-Level: 4 Macro KPIs con bordes superiores neón (Total Activos, Publicados, Programados y Paridad Bilingüe) seguidos de métricas operativas contextuales (palabras indexadas, patrimonio de contenidos estimado y activo líder de tráfico orgánico).
  3. Taxonomía Triple de Ingeniería S&OP: Al igual que en la planificación operativa segmentamos referencias por familias y canales, Pulse implementa un selector dinámico en 3 niveles: macro-grupos del ecosistema (Artículos vs Apps vs Kits), 5 pilares temáticos del blog y categorías detalladas.
  4. Tipado de Extremo a Extremo en Spec-Driven Development (SDD): Las interfaces TypeScript en React 19 son un reflejo idéntico de los esquemas Pydantic v2 documentados en specs/apps/pulse/spec.md. No existe discrepancia en nombres de campos, tipos opcionales ni valores por defecto.

2. Arquitectura Frontend: React 19, TypeScript y Carga Optimista

La inmensa mayoría de las herramientas de gestión de contenidos cometen el error de acoplar la interfaz web a una API REST conectada a una base de datos relacional. En ese modelo tradicional, cada vez que un usuario abre el tablero Kanban, la aplicación emite una consulta SQL compleja (SELECT * FROM posts JOIN categories...), introduce spinners de carga y genera latencias perceptibles de 200 a 800 ms.

En Datalaria Pulse invertimos por completo la ecuación aplicando el patrón Static-First:

// apps/pulse/web/src/App.tsx (Extracto del ciclo de carga)
interface PublicPulseDataset {
  version: string;
  generated_at: string;
  total_assets: number;
  published_assets: number;
  scheduled_assets: number;
  ideas_count: number;
  parity_summary: Record<string, number>;
  assets: ContentAsset[];
}

export function App() {
  const [dataset, setDataset] = useState<PublicPulseDataset | null>(null);
  const [activeTab, setActiveTab] = useState<
    'dashboard' | 'table' | 'kanban' | 'calendar' | 'health' | 'channels'
  >('dashboard');

  useEffect(() => {
    // Carga atómica del índice estático compilado en build time
    fetch(`./data/public.json?t=${Date.now()}`, { cache: 'no-store' })
      .then(res => res.json())
      .then((data: PublicPulseDataset) => {
        setDataset(data);
      })
      .catch(err => console.error("Error cargando public.json:", err));
  }, []);

  // ...
}

¿Por Qué Esta Arquitectura Supera a las Bases de Datos Clásicas?

  • Latencia de 0 ms en Navegación: Una vez descargado el archivo public.json (~60 KB comprimido en gzip), todas las operaciones de búsqueda por texto, ordenación de columnas, filtrado por tags y conmutación de vistas se resuelven en memoria local en menos de 1 milisegundo.
  • Cero Coste de Servidor: No requiere instancias de Node.js, contenedores Docker ni bases de datos activas en el edge. El frontend y los datos se sirven íntegramente como activos estáticos desde cualquier CDN global.
  • Inmunidad ante Caídas: Si una API externa o un servidor de analítica sufre una interrupción, el panel de control de Datalaria Pulse continúa funcionando de forma impecable porque la fuente de verdad ya está congelada en el commit de Git.

3. Vista 1: La Tabla Ejecutiva Multifactorial

La Tabla Ejecutiva es el caballo de batalla para auditorías masivas de catálogo. Cuando un equipo gestiona más de 100 artículos técnicos, necesita responder preguntas complejas en segundos: ¿cuáles son los posts con un SEO Score inferior a 70?, ¿qué artículos superan las 3.000 palabras pero no tienen traducción al inglés?, ¿cuál es el activo líder en tráfico relativo?.

Activo / Título Tipo Estado Fecha Pub Palabras Paridad Score SEO
5 Fuerzas de Porter... POST Published 2026-10-19 4.218 pal. complete 100 / 100
DAFO Cuantitativo y CAME... POST Published 2026-10-13 4.867 pal. complete 100 / 100
Matriz BCG Dinámica... POST Published 2026-10-26 3.920 pal. complete 100 / 100

Capacidades de Ingeniería Implementadas:

  1. Filtro Multi-Criterio Combinado y Enlaces Profundos: La barra de herramientas permite filtrar simultáneamente por texto predictivo (coincidencias en título, slug y etiquetas), tipo de activo (post, app, kit, suite) y estado editorial (published, scheduled, draft, idea), soportando deep-linking por URL (?tab=table&type=app&status=published).
  2. Conmutador de Historial de Versiones (🔀): Permite alternar al instante entre la vista consolidada de activos principales y el desglose de versiones evolutivas SemVer (vX.Y.Z).
  3. Diagnóstico Interactivo de Notion CSV en 1 Clic (Operación Crisol): Botón de validación que analiza exportaciones CSV de Notion en el propio navegador, auditando campos obligatorios, fechas y categorización sin enviar datos al servidor.
  4. Ordenación Bidireccional y Paginación Inteligente: Pulsar sobre cualquier cabecera reordena al instante por fecha, volumen léxico o índice de tráfico, con conmutador de densidad (10, 25 o 50 filas).
  5. Píldoras Cromáticas de Estado y Avance Rápido en Kanban (→): Etiquetas visuales de alto contraste (complete en verde, missing_en en rojo) y botones de transición inmediata de etapa editorial en Kanban sin abrir modales.

4. Vista 2: El Tablero Kanban Editorial de 5 Columnas

title: What Is Redundant at High Resolution? Efficient Attention and Feed-Forward Design for All-in-One Image Restoration
description:
arXiv:2611.33636v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-scale architectures are widely adopted in all-in-one image restoration (AIO-IR) to capture larger-scale context at low-resolution stages and refine details at high-resolution (HR) stages. However, processing spatially large feature maps at HR stages incurs substantial computational costs and memory traffic, making efficient HR processing challenging. To address this challenge, we propose High-resolution Global-Local Restoration (HiGLR), an efficient multi-scale AIO-IR network grounded in an analysis of spatial redundancy in self-attention and convolutional feed-forward networks (ConvFFNs). Specifically, this analysis identifies three key redundancies: per-query readout at the finest-scale stage, key routing across neighboring queries at intermediate stages, and spatial mixing in the expanded feature spaces of ConvFFNs. Accordingly, HiGLR replaces costly self-attention at the finest-scale stage with a learned input-independent kernel. At intermediate stages, we propose a Block-Routed Hybrid Attention, which combines coarse-scale dense attention with fine-scale block-sparse attention over value residuals relative to coarse summaries, and shares routing indices across neighboring queries. We further introduce a Dual-Space FFN that performs spatial mixing in a compact space and pointwise nonlinear transformation in an expanded space, enabling efficient kernel fusion. Combining these designs, HiGLR achieves state-of-the-art performance while delivering up to a $4.24\times$ inference speedup over existing methods.

title: LimoBench: How Street Smart Are Large Language Models?
description:
arXiv:2611.31682v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed how humans interact with information, enabling natural-language interfaces across various domains. They are increasingly deployed for geospatial applications including map-based question answering, location-based services, and natural-language interfaces to spatial databases. But are LLMs truly location-aware, able to reliably interpret and precisely answer location queries involving real-world coordinates, points of interest (POIs), and geospatial distances? To answer this concretely, we present LimoBench, a street-level benchmark of 82 natural-language location queries over seven canonical spatial operations: geocoding, reverse geocoding, routing, directionality, range search, $k$-nearest-neighbor search, and spatial join. The queries are grounded in real map data of West Lafayette, Indiana, and are graded by location and semantic complexity. They are designed to probe LLMs' street-level spatial awareness, from simple lookups to multi-step spatial reasoning. We also present Limo, an approach based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that enhances the location awareness of LLMs. Limo grounds LLMs in PostGIS-backed spatial data through a compact set of tools. We find that ungrounded models mostly achieve single-digit accuracy (3.1% for GPT-6 Luna) across different spatial operations. In contrast, the same models achieve near-perfect accuracy (99.3% for GPT-6 Luna) when given access to Limo's spatial tools through MCP. Current LLMs thus have limited and unreliable street-level spatial knowledge, while grounding provides accurate answers at modest overhead (+0.2 s latency, 7.7$\times$ tokens, and 2.2$\times$ cost for GPT-6 Luna). We release the benchmark, Limo toolset, and evaluation code to encourage the community to evaluate their own location-aware LLM approaches.
