title: From Driving Data to Risk Scores: How Technology Shapes Auto Insurance Decisions
description:
Technology is changing how businesses collect information, identify patterns, and make decisions. The auto insurance industry is part of this transformation. Insurers increasingly use digital records, statistical models, and connected vehicle technology to evaluate potential risks and determine policy pricing.

For drivers with accidents, traffic violations, or gaps in coverage, understanding this process can be especially important. These circumstances may affect how insurers evaluate applications, but technology also gives insurance companies additional ways to analyze driving behavior and individual risk.

Understanding the relationship between driving data and high-risk auto insurance decisions helps drivers make more informed choices when comparing coverage.

1. How Insurers Turn Driving Information Into Risk Assessments

Insurance underwriting involves evaluating the likelihood and potential cost of future claims. Traditionally, insurers have relied on information such as driving records, previous claims, vehicle details, location, and insurance history.

Today, digital systems make it easier to organize and analyze these details. Information can be collected from application forms, motor vehicle records, claims databases, and other permitted sources.

For example, an applicant with several recent accidents may receive a different assessment from someone with a clean driving record. Similarly, repeated traffic violations or previous insurance cancellations may influence an insurer's decision.

These are common auto insurance risk factors, although their importance varies between insurance companies and state regulations.

Technology helps underwriting teams process this information more consistently. However, an automated assessment does not necessarily mean every applicant receives the same result. Insurers use different underwriting guidelines, rating methods, and eligibility requirements.

2. The Role of Telematics in Modern Auto Insurance

One of the most important developments in vehicle-related insurance technology is telematics.

Telematics systems collect information about vehicle usage and driving behavior through smartphone applications, connected vehicle systems, or devices installed in vehicles.

Depending on the program, collected information may include:

  • Total miles driven
  • Driving time and frequency
  • Rapid acceleration
  • Hard braking
  • Sharp cornering
  • Vehicle location

This information is often called telematics data. It can help insurers understand driving patterns beyond what appears in a traditional driving record.

For example, two drivers may have similar insurance histories but very different driving habits. One may drive short distances during daylight hours, while another regularly travels long distances late at night. A usage-based insurance program may consider these differences when evaluating driving behavior.

However, telematics is not used by every insurer or every policy. Participation requirements, data collection practices, and pricing effects depend on the specific program.

For drivers exploring high-risk auto insurance, it is worth understanding whether a particular insurer offers a usage-based program and how participation could affect premiums.

3. How Predictive Analytics Helps Identify Risk Patterns

Insurance companies work with large amounts of historical information. Predictive analytics helps them examine this information and identify patterns associated with claims and potential losses.

For example, analysts may examine relationships between accident frequency, vehicle type, driving distance, location, and previous claims. These patterns can contribute to statistical models used during underwriting and pricing.

This is where predictive analytics becomes useful.

Instead of reviewing every data point independently, analytical systems can identify combinations of factors that may indicate different levels of risk. Insurers can use these insights to improve their understanding of expected claim costs.

Some companies also use machine learning techniques to process large datasets. These systems can identify patterns that may be difficult to detect through manual analysis alone.

Nevertheless, predictive models are not perfect. Their results depend on the quality of the information supplied, the assumptions used during development, and the way insurers interpret their outputs.

A model should support responsible decision-making rather than replace appropriate oversight.

4. Understanding Risk Scores and Insurance Pricing Models

A risk score is a way of representing an assessment of potential insurance risk. It may be based on multiple factors, depending on the insurer's underwriting and rating system.

For instance, an insurer may consider driving experience, previous accidents, vehicle usage, location, and claims history when evaluating an application.

These details can be processed through statistical methods and internal risk scoring algorithms.

The resulting assessment may influence whether an application meets the insurer's eligibility guidelines and how the policy is priced.

It is important to understand that there is no single universal risk score used by every auto insurance company. Each insurer may use its own insurance pricing models, subject to applicable laws and regulatory requirements.

For someone seeking high-risk auto insurance, this explains why receiving different quotes from different insurers is possible even when the same basic information is provided.

One company may have underwriting guidelines that accommodate a particular driving history, while another may consider the same applicant outside its preferred risk category.

Comparing available options can therefore be more useful than assuming every insurer evaluates risk in exactly the same way.

5. Why Data Accuracy and Transparency Matter

Technology can improve the speed of insurance assessments, but incorrect information can still create problems.

An outdated violation, incorrectly recorded accident, or inaccurate vehicle detail may affect an application or quote. Drivers should review the information used during the insurance application process and correct errors through the appropriate reporting agency or insurer.

Accurate driving history is particularly important because previous incidents may influence underwriting decisions for a specific period, depending on state rules and company guidelines.

Insurers also need to consider data accuracy when developing automated systems. Incomplete records, inconsistent information, or poorly designed models can lead to unreliable assessments.

Privacy is another important consideration, especially with telematics programs. Before enrolling, drivers should understand what information an application or device collects, how it is used, and whether location or driving behavior is monitored.

Transparency helps consumers make informed decisions about sharing their information.

6. What Technology Means for Drivers With Challenging Records

Digital underwriting does not automatically eliminate the challenges associated with previous accidents, violations, or coverage interruptions. However, it helps explain why insurance decisions can differ between companies.

A driver looking for high-risk auto insurance should consider several practical steps:

  1. Review driving and claims records for possible errors.
  2. Provide accurate information when requesting quotes.
  3. Compare coverage limits, deductibles, and policy conditions.
  4. Ask insurers how previous incidents affect eligibility and pricing.
  5. Review available payment options and policy requirements.
  6. Maintain continuous coverage whenever possible and legally appropriate.

Drivers should also remember that the lowest quoted premium is not necessarily the best choice. A policy should provide appropriate protection and meet applicable state requirements.

Technology can make insurance comparisons and application processes more accessible, but understanding the actual policy remains essential.

Conclusion

The combination of digital records, telematics, statistical analysis, and automated underwriting is changing how insurers evaluate potential risks. These technologies help companies process information, identify patterns, and develop pricing approaches based on multiple factors.

For drivers with previous accidents, violations, or insurance interruptions, understanding these processes can make insurance decisions less confusing. Although underwriting standards differ between companies, reviewing personal records and comparing available policies can help identify suitable coverage.

Drivers who want to explore High-Risk Auto Insurance Coverage Options can compare available solutions and learn more about the factors that may influence eligibility, policy features, and premiums.

title: A production checklist for staging validation
description:
Before deployment

  • [ ] Confirm the owner and operational purpose for this signal.
  • [ ] Review configuration and middleware placement against the current integration guide.
  • [ ] Use fake secrets and representative requests to check redaction and capture behavior.
  • [ ] Confirm the intended storage, retention, and access policy.

During validation

A production observability change deserves its own staging test because it touches request handling and data retention. A representative test should cover middleware placement, route capture, redaction, persistence, access, and restart behavior. Write a short acceptance checklist for the routes that matter and run it after configuration or version changes.

After rollout

  • [ ] Ask an engineer unfamiliar with the change to find one useful event.
  • [ ] Check for noisy or missing records and adjust the policy deliberately.
  • [ ] Document the next action an on-call responder should take.

One final guardrail

Avoid enabling broad payload inspection in production until the expected data and access controls are understood. A checklist is only useful when it reflects the current version and the actual data your application handles.

Learn more: TracerNest

title: Measuring the Real Cost of a Crypto On-Ramp Quote in Python (Mercuryo Example)
description:
If your dApp or wallet has a "Buy crypto" button, there is a good chance it opens a third-party on-ramp widget such as Mercuryo. The widget handles card payments, ID checks and fraud screening, which is exactly the part you do not want to build yourself. But it also means the price your user pays is decided somewhere you do not control.

This post looks at an on-ramp quote the way a developer would: as data you can check. I wrote it after putting together a plain-language Mercuryo guide for NutshellCrypto, which covers the fees, KYC rules, limits and country availability in detail.

Why a "5% fee" is not the whole story

Mercuryo's help center (checked Nov 26, 2026) lists a fee of up to 5.5% for card, Apple Pay and Google Pay buys (minimum EUR 1), up to 3% for bank transfer (minimum EUR 2), and an extra 0.25% to 1% for non-EUR currencies. On top of that there can be:

  • a network fee for sending the coins,
  • an infrastructure fee set by the partner app (Mercuryo says typically 0% to 2%, never above 5%),
  • a spread built into the quoted price.

So the honest number is not any single fee. It is the gap between what the user pays in fiat and what the crypto they receive is worth at the market mid price. That gap is easy to compute, and it works for any provider, not just Mercuryo. If you want the bigger picture on how fees stack up, our breakdown of crypto exchange fees and spreads goes deeper.

A small Python check

The script below does three things:

  1. checks the amount against the published minimum and per-transaction limits (Mercuryo says limits include fees),
  2. computes a worst-case fee from the published "up to" rates,
  3. fetches the BTC/EUR mid price from CoinGecko's free API and measures the real all-in cost of a quote.

It uses only the standard library.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Check the all-in cost of an on-ramp quote against the market mid price.

Stdlib only. Uses CoinGecko's free simple/price endpoint for the mid price.
"""
import json
import urllib.request

# Published "up to" fees from Mercuryo's help center (checked Nov 26, 2026).
MAX_FEE = {"card": (0.055, 1.0), "bank": (0.03, 2.0)}  # (rate, minimum in EUR)

# Per-transaction limits for verified users outside the EEA (fees included).
TX_LIMIT_EUR = {"card": 15_000, "applepay": 2_000}
MIN_BUY_EUR = 25


def mid_price(coin_id: str, fiat: str = "eur") -> float:
    url = (
        "https://api.coingecko.com/api/v3/simple/price"
        f"?ids={coin_id}&vs_currencies={fiat}"
    )
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "onramp-check/1.0"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=15) as r:
        return float(json.load(r)[coin_id][fiat])


def worst_case_fee(amount_eur: float, method: str, non_eur_extra: float = 0.0) -> float:
    rate, minimum = MAX_FEE[method]
    return max(amount_eur * rate, minimum) + amount_eur * non_eur_extra


def check_limits(amount_eur: float, method: str) -> list[str]:
    problems = []
    if amount_eur < MIN_BUY_EUR:
        problems.append(f"below the EUR {MIN_BUY_EUR} minimum")
    cap = TX_LIMIT_EUR.get(method)
    if cap and amount_eur > cap:
        problems.append(f"above the EUR {cap:,} per-transaction limit")
    return problems


def all_in_cost(paid_fiat: float, crypto_received: float, mid: float) -> dict:
    market_value = crypto_received * mid
    cost = paid_fiat - market_value
    return {
        "market_value": round(market_value, 2),
        "cost": round(cost, 2),
        "cost_pct": round(100 * cost / paid_fiat, 2),
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Example: the widget says EUR 200 by card gets you 0.00344 BTC.
    paid, received, method = 200.0, 0.00344, "card"

    print("limit check:", check_limits(paid, method) or "ok")
    print("worst-case published fee: EUR", round(worst_case_fee(paid, method), 2))

    mid = mid_price("bitcoin", "eur")
    print("BTC mid price: EUR", round(mid, 2))
    print("all-in cost of this quote:", all_in_cost(paid, received, mid))

When I ran it on Nov 26, 2026 it printed:

limit check: ok
worst-case published fee: EUR 11.0
BTC mid price: EUR 55234.0
all-in cost of this quote: {'market_value': 190.0, 'cost': 10.0, 'cost_pct': 5.0}

The example quote is made up so the math is easy to follow. Swap in the real numbers from your widget's final confirmation screen. The mid price moves every minute, so your output will differ.

Two quick edge cases from the same functions:

>>> check_limits(20, "card")
['below the EUR 25 minimum']
>>> check_limits(3000, "applepay")
['above the EUR 2,000 per-transaction limit']

What to do with this as a builder

  • Show the final quote, not the headline fee. If your app offers several on-ramp providers, compare their final crypto amounts for the same fiat amount. That one number already includes fees and spread.
  • Validate the address and network before the handoff. On-chain purchases cannot be reversed. A basic format and network check saves real support tickets. Our guide to crypto wallet addresses lists what to look at.
  • Expect KYC friction. Mercuryo requires government ID and a selfie, and US users also need a driver's license or state ID plus an SSN. Users who drop off at this step are not a bug in your app. See KYC in crypto for why on-ramps ask.
  • Know who holds the coins. If users buy into a provider's own wallet, that is a custodial wallet. Sending to a wallet the user controls is a different risk profile; our self-custody guide explains the trade-off.
  • Check regional rules. Per Mercuryo's help center, it does not serve New York or Vermont, and US users cannot cash out to a card. Partner apps may also enable it only in some regions.

Wrap-up

On-ramp widgets are a great shortcut, but the price is a black box unless you measure it. A few lines of Python turn "up to 5.5%" into an exact cost for a specific quote, and that is the number users actually care about. For the full rundown on Mercuryo's fees, limits, licenses and tax notes, read the Mercuryo guide on NutshellCrypto.

This article is for education only and is not financial, tax or investment advice. Fees, limits and availability change often, so check the provider's current terms before you buy or sell.

Note: I wrote this with AI assistance, then checked the facts against Mercuryo's help center and ran the code myself.

title: Make a contact form’s success message audible without moving focus
description:
Try submitting a contact form with a screen reader while leaving keyboard focus on the Send button. The green confirmation may appear on screen while the reader says nothing. A useful fix is to put the confirmation in a status region that already exists when the page loads.

Here is a minimal example. The callback belongs in the success branch of the form handler, after the server has accepted the enquiry.

<button type="submit">Send enquiry</button>
<p id="enquiry-status" role="status"></p>

function showEnquiryReceipt(reference) {
  const status = document.getElementById('enquiry-status');
  status.textContent = 'Enquiry received. Your reference is ' + reference + '.';
}

The empty paragraph does two jobs. It gives sighted readers a stable place to find the receipt, and its status role asks assistive technology to announce changes politely. Keep it in the accessibility tree while empty. Making the paragraph with display: none and revealing it at the same moment as the text can make the announcement unreliable. The reference in this example is a fictional enquiry number such as DEMO-42.

A quick acceptance check

  1. With a screen reader on, tab to Send enquiry and activate it. Keep your hands off the keyboard until the test response arrives.
  2. For a successful test response, listen for the reference once. Confirm that the same reference is visible and that keyboard focus is still on Send enquiry.
  3. Repeat with an unsuccessful response. The success receipt must stay empty. Show a distinct, visible error and keep the entered message available so the visitor can retry.

This example covers an in-place submission. A form that navigates to a new confirmation page needs a meaningful page title and heading as well. Test the interaction with the browser and screen reader your visitors actually use.

Written by Looms VN for teams maintaining the enquiry forms on their websites.

title: Running a Node.js API and a worker together
description:
Originally published on gregale.dev. I build Gregale, so read this as a vendor's page. Competitor details come from each vendor's own docs, linked in the post.

A reliable setup for a Node.js API and a worker has four parts: both processes deploy from one repository so they never run different versions, a crash or memory leak in the worker cannot take down the API, the queue lives in a managed database with backups, and a bad release rolls back before most users see it. The cheapest version of that keeps the worker small and lets the API stop costing money while it is idle. On Gregale you describe the API and the worker in a Compose file and deploy them as one project with a managed PostgreSQL database. The API pauses between requests and is not billed while paused, and every production release reaches 1% of traffic first and rolls back on its own on errors (in beta). On raw machine price alone, Fly.io's smallest Machines cost less; the comparison below shows each option.

The API and the worker on Gregale 

# compose.yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    command: node dist/server.js
    ports: ['3000:3000']
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
  worker:
    build: .
    command: node dist/worker.js
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
  db:
    image: postgres:17

gregale deploy reads this as one project:

  • api becomes an app with a public URL. It pauses about a second after its last request and is not billed while paused.
  • worker has no ports:, so it becomes a background service that runs all the time.
  • db becomes a managed PostgreSQL database, and both services get its connection string as DATABASE_URL.
  • depends_on on api holds each new worker release until the API's release from the same deploy is live. If the API's release fails, the worker's release fails too and the current one keeps serving, so the two never run mixed versions.

To run migrations before each release, add a Compose step that the API waits for with condition: service_completed_successfully; Gregale runs it as the API's release command. A project with two or more services needs Hobby or higher. See Deploy a multi-service app and Deploy an Express app.

Where the worker gets its jobs

  • Postgres-backed, such as pg-boss or Graphile Worker: jobs live in the database you already have, covered by its backups and point-in-time restore. One less system to run, which suits most small apps.
  • Redis-backed, such as BullMQ: higher throughput, one more system to run. Gregale's managed Redis is not generally available yet, so point REDIS_URL at a Redis you run elsewhere.

Scheduled work does not need the worker either: a cron calls a path on your API on a schedule, and Gregale wakes the API for it.

gregale-dev/node-api-worker is a complete Compose project for this setup, with an Express API, a private worker and a job queue in Postgres. The worker has no polling loop: the API calls its private POST /drain after storing a job, so the worker runs only while there's work, and gregale deploy --project deploys all of it.

What two small always-on processes cost

The API and the worker each at the smallest paid size that stays on, before any database. Prices are each vendor's own, checked on November 25, 2026:

Platform API + worker, smallest always-on size Notes
Fly.io 2 × $2.19 = $4.38 a month (256 MB each) Lowest-priced regions; Fly.io Managed Postgres from $4 a month
Railway $5 a month minimum, credited toward usage Two services holding 256 MB each use about $5 of memory a month, before CPU
Gregale Gregale Hobby: $10 a month for 5 apps Includes 1 managed PostgreSQL database; the API is not billed while paused
DigitalOcean App Platform 2 × $5 = $10 a month (512 MiB each) The free tier covers static sites only
Render 2 × $7 = $14 a month (512 MB each) Workers have no free instance; Render Postgres from $6 a month
Heroku 2 × $7 = $14 a month (0.5 GB each, Basic) Eco dynos are $5 a month but sleep after 30 minutes idle

On Gregale, Hobby includes 200 GB-RAM-hours a month. A worker that runs all month at 256 MB uses most of it; an API that serves requests some of the time adds little, because paused time is not billed. Past the allowance, usage costs $0.05 per GB-RAM-hour, up to a spend cap you set, so a bill never runs past the limit you chose.

Reliability is where the platforms differ

  • Releases: Render, Railway and Heroku switch all traffic to a new version once it passes its health check, and rolling back is a manual step. Fly.io replaces Machines one at a time. Gregale sends 1% of the API's traffic first and rolls back on its own on a higher 5xx rate, crash loops or slower responses (in beta).
  • Version skew: on any platform, deploying the API and the worker separately can leave them on different versions for a while. Gregale's depends_on gate keeps them in step.
  • Database recovery: Gregale's managed PostgreSQL keeps a 7-day point-in-time restore window, and on paid plans a rollback can restore the database to the moment before a migration. A database runs in a single zone, with no high-availability promise.
  • Isolation: each Gregale app instance runs in its own Firecracker microVM, so a runaway worker cannot take memory from the API.

How to choose

  • Lowest price for two always-on processes, and you will configure Machines yourself: Fly.io.
  • Pay only for what each service uses, with Redis one click away: Railway.
  • A fixed price per instance on a familiar platform: Render or DigitalOcean App Platform.
  • A small team that wants the API and worker to release together, roll back on their own and stop billing for the API while it is idle: Gregale.

Sources

Gregale figures come from the plans and managed PostgreSQL docs. Other platforms' figures were checked against each vendor's own pages on November 25, 2026: Fly.io pricing, Fly.io Managed Postgres, Railway pricing, DigitalOcean App Platform pricing, Render pricing, Render free instances, Heroku pricing.

FAQ

What is the cheapest reliable way to run a Node.js API and a worker?

Two small processes from one repository, a queue in a managed database, and releases that keep both on the same version. On raw machine price Fly.io is cheapest, at $2.19 a month per 256 MB Machine. Gregale Hobby is $10 a month for both plus a managed PostgreSQL database, with the API unbilled while idle and automatic rollback (in beta).

Do I need Redis for a Node.js job queue?

Only for Redis-based queues such as BullMQ. pg-boss and Graphile Worker keep jobs in Postgres, so the database you already have, and its backups, cover the queue too.

Can the API and the worker deploy together on Gregale?

Yes. Describe both in a Compose file and deploy them as one project on Hobby or higher. With depends_on and condition: service_healthy, the worker's new release waits for the API's and fails with it, so the two never run mixed versions.

title: React Chat Widget: Add a Free Live Chat to a React or Next.js App
description:
A React chat widget for live support doesn't need an npm package or a chat backend you build yourself: load a hosted widget's script once at the root of your app, and drive it from your components through a small global API. This post shows how with SealReply, a hosted live chat whose Free plan has no time limit, for a Vite/CRA app and for Next.js (App Router and Pages Router).

Why a hosted widget instead of building one

Building a support chat means WebSockets, an agent dashboard, offline handling, notifications and storage. For most apps that's weeks of work that has nothing to do with the product. A hosted widget gives you all of it for one script tag, and your React code only has to do two things:

  • load the script once, so client-side navigation doesn't create a second widget;
  • talk to it from components (open it from your own button, react to new messages, tell it who's signed in).

SealReply is a good fit for this because its widget is built with single-page apps in mind: it's about 38 KB, loads async, follows route changes made with history.pushState, and exposes a small window.SealReply API. The Free plan includes 1 agent, 1 website and 300 chats a month, with no card.

Step 1: Get the embed code

Sign up, add your site's address (the widget only loads on that domain), and copy the embed code. It's one line:

<script src="https://cdn.sealreply.com/widget.js" data-site-key="sk_…" async></script>

The site key isn't a secret, so it can sit in your code or in a public env variable.

Step 2a: Plain React (Vite or CRA)

The simplest correct place is index.html, just before </body>:

<!-- index.html -->
<body>
  <div id="root"></div>
  <script type="module" src="/src/main.tsx"></script>
  <script src="https://cdn.sealreply.com/widget.js" data-site-key="sk_…" async></script>
</body>

It sits outside React, so re-renders, Strict Mode double-mounting and route changes never touch it.

Step 2b: Next.js App Router

Next.js has no HTML file, so use next/script in the root layout. Your data-* attributes are forwarded to the script element:

// app/layout.tsx
import Script from "next/script";

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        {children}
        <Script
          src="https://cdn.sealreply.com/widget.js"
          data-site-key="sk_…"
          strategy="afterInteractive"
        />
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}

Use afterInteractive to show the chat button early, or lazyOnload if your Lighthouse score matters more. A script in the root layout loads once, even as users navigate with <Link>.

Step 2c: Next.js Pages Router

Same idea, in pages/_app.tsx (not _document.tsx):

// pages/_app.tsx
import type { AppProps } from "next/app";
import Script from "next/script";

export default function App({ Component, pageProps }: AppProps) {
  return (
    <>
      <Component {...pageProps} />
      <Script src="https://cdn.sealreply.com/widget.js" data-site-key="sk_…" strategy="afterInteractive" />
    </>
  );
}

Step 3: Check there's exactly one widget

Open your deployed app, click through a few routes, then run this in the console:

document.querySelectorAll('script[src*="widget.js"]').length; // 1
window.SealReply?.version; // a version string

One tag and a version means it's loaded once and ready. Send yourself a message and answer it from the dashboard to check both ends.

Step 4: Open the chat from your own button

Add data-launcher="none" to the script tag to hide the default corner button, then open the chat from any component. The script is async, so guard with optional chaining:

"use client";

export function ContactButton() {
  return (
    <button type="button" onClick={() => window.SealReply?.open()}>
      Chat with us
    </button>
  );
}

Step 5: Show an unread count

The widget fires a sealreply:ready event on window when it's ready, and lets you subscribe to new messages:

"use client";
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

export function ChatButton() {
  const [unread, setUnread] = useState(0);

  useEffect(() => {
    const onMessage = () => setUnread((n) => n + 1);
    const subscribe = () => window.SealReply?.on("message", onMessage);
    if (window.SealReply) subscribe();
    else window.addEventListener("sealreply:ready", subscribe, { once: true });
    return () => {
      window.removeEventListener("sealreply:ready", subscribe);
      window.SealReply?.off("message", onMessage);
    };
  }, []);

  return (
    <button type="button" onClick={() => window.SealReply?.open()}>
      Chat with us{unread > 0 ? ` (${unread})` : ""}
    </button>
  );
}

The cleanup matters: without off, every remount adds another listener.

Step 6: Tell the chat who's signed in (safely)

Passing a plain user ID to a chat widget lets anyone change it in DevTools and chat as someone else. SealReply avoids this by checking an HMAC-SHA256 signature of the ID that your server makes with a secret from the dashboard. In a SPA, call identify after sign-in and reset on sign-out:

// identityHash comes from your backend, never computed in the browser
window.SealReply?.identify({
  external_id: String(user.id), // sign and send the exact same string
  identity_hash: identityHash,
  name: user.name,
  email: user.email,
});

// on sign-out
window.SealReply?.reset();

Agents then see a verified customer with one history across devices. A missing or wrong signature never breaks the chat; the visitor just stays anonymous.

Wrapping up

For a React app, live chat comes down to: one script loaded once at the root, a couple of guarded calls from client components, and a server-signed identity if you have accounts. You can use SealReply free with no card and no time limit. The full Next.js write-up, including TypeScript types for window.SealReply, is here: How to add live chat to Next.js.

Disclosure: the Gingertool team also works on SealReply. This post was written with AI assistance.

title: How Many Samples Is RL Worth? Best-of-N versus RL Post-Training for Text-to-Image Models
description:
arXiv:2611.33232v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) on a reward that can be checked automatically has become a common last step in the training of text-to-image models. A simpler way to get more correct images is best-of-N: draw N images from the base model and keep the one that a picker prefers. We ask how many base model samples one RL sample is worth, and call this number the exchange rate. We measure it for Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium and its public Flow-GRPO checkpoint on 398 new prompts in the style of GenEval, the benchmark behind the RL reward, with human labels on every prompt and two automatic judges other than the reward. The answer depends on the prompt. Four fifths of the prompts do not ask for a position (for example, one object left of another). On these, the base model catches up: best-of-16 with an off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) as the picker is about as good as one RL image. A person who looks through up to 3 base images finds a correct one as often as one RL image is correct. On the prompts that ask for a position, RL is far ahead: a person finds a correct image among 8 base images for only 52% of the prompts, against 92% for one RL image. Over all prompts, our primary test, which we fixed in advance, finds best-of-16 with the VLM picker 9.3 points behind one RL image when both automatic judges must pass an image. People see a smaller gap, 5.5 and 6.5 points in two checks. FLUX.1-dev shows a similar gap in the same test. RL also solves 20 prompts that the base model misses in 128 tries, and 1,024 tries recover half of them. The automatic judges are wrong in opposite directions: a detector-based judge like the reward, as used in our primary test, reports a larger gap than people see, and VLM judges report little or none. Comparisons of RL with best-of-N should therefore check the selected images by hand.

title: Fixing the Outlook Duplicate VML Button Bug, Gmail's 102 KB Clip, and 4 ESP Packaging Traps
description:
It is 4:40 PM on a Friday. The launch email goes out Monday at 9:00 AM.

Three QA screenshots hit Slack in ten minutes. Classic Outlook on Windows is rendering two stacked "Claim Offer" buttons. Gmail clipped the footer right above the unsubscribe link with [Message clipped] View entire message. And Klaviyo just bounced the single .zip exported from Figma.

If you hand-code emails or convert Figma frames for Klaviyo, Braze, Mailchimp, or HubSpot, you have probably fought these exact bugs. Here is why each one happens, the copy-pasteable fix, and how to catch them locally before opening an ESP uploader.

1. The Outlook Duplicate Button VML Fix (Classic vs. New Outlook)

Outlook is now two completely different rendering engines behind one icon.

Classic Outlook for Windows (2016 to 2021 and Microsoft 365, supported through 2029) uses Microsoft Word. It ignores CSS border-radius and anchor padding, so rounded buttons still need VML (<v:roundrect>). New Outlook for Windows and Outlook on the Web run Chromium (WebView2). They render normal CSS and ignore <!--[if mso]> comments.

That split is why legacy VML button generators now break enterprise inboxes. Older snippets wrap <v:roundrect> inside <!--[if mso]>, then drop the modern HTML <a> button right after <![endif]--> with mso-hide:all; inline. Inside nested tables or forwarded threads, Classic Outlook frequently ignores mso-hide:all; and paints both the VML shape and the HTML link. You get two stacked buttons.

Leave <v:roundrect> outside <!--[if mso]> or mismatch a closing tag, and you get the mirror bug: raw VML leaking into Chromium and Gmail.

Step A: Declare VML namespaces and lock 96 DPI

Classic Outlook silently skips <v:roundrect> unless <html> declares Microsoft's VML and Office namespaces. On Windows laptops set to 125% or 150% display scaling, buttons also stretch unless <head> pins PixelsPerInch to 96:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
  xmlns:v="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:vml"
  xmlns:o="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:office:office">
<head>
  <!--[if gte mso 9]>
  <xml>
    <o:OfficeDocumentSettings>
      <o:AllowPNG/>
      <o:PixelsPerInch>96</o:PixelsPerInch>
    </o:OfficeDocumentSettings>
  </xml>
  <![endif]-->
</head>

Step B: Strictly isolate both buttons (mso vs. !mso)

Skip mso-hide:all. Put the VML button strictly inside <!--[if mso]> ... <![endif]-->, and put the HTML <a> button strictly inside <!--[if !mso]><!--> ... <!--<![endif]-->. Watch those extra <!--> and <!-- markers: Classic Outlook treats the entire !mso block as a comment, while New Outlook, Gmail, Apple Mail, and Yahoo render the <a> tag normally.

<table role="presentation" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0" align="center"
  style="border-collapse:collapse;mso-table-lspace:0pt;mso-table-rspace:0pt;">
  <tr>
    <td align="center" style="padding:0;">
      <!--[if mso]>
      <v:roundrect xmlns:v="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:vml"
        xmlns:w="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:office:word"
        href="https://example.com/offer"
        style="height:46px;v-text-anchor:middle;width:220px;"
        arcsize="17%" stroke="f" fillcolor="#0d99ff">
        <w:anchorlock/>
        <center style="color:#ffffff;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:15px;font-weight:700;">
          Claim Offer
        </center>
      </v:roundrect>
      <![endif]-->
      <!--[if !mso]><!-->
      <a href="https://example.com/offer" target="_blank"
        style="display:inline-block;background-color:#0d99ff;color:#ffffff;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size:15px;font-weight:700;line-height:1.2;text-align:center;text-decoration:none;border-radius:8px;padding:14px 24px;min-width:172px;border:0;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;">
        Claim Offer
      </a>
      <!--<![endif]-->
    </td>
  </tr>
</table>

Two small details that trip people up:

  • Keep <w:anchorlock/> inside <v:roundrect>. Without it, Word lets recipients click and resize the button box instead of following the link.
  • VML arcsize is a percentage of button height, not pixels: Math.min(50, Math.max(0, Math.round((radius / height) * 100))). An 8px radius on a 46px button is 17%; a full pill caps at 50%.

To catch regressions in CI, tokenize <!--[if mso]>, <![endif]-->, <!--[if !mso]><!-->, <!--<![endif]-->, and <v:roundrect> in order. Fail the build if any <v:roundrect> appears when msoDepth <= 0, or if an <a tag follows </v:roundrect><![endif]--> without <!--[if !mso]><!-->.

2. Gmail's 102 KB Clipping Fix (Stop Crushing Your Hero Images)

When Gmail clips a campaign, most teams open TinyPNG, squash their hero JPEG from 320 KB down to 55 KB, send a test, and watch Gmail clip it in the exact same spot.

Gmail clips at 102 KB (104,448 UTF-8 bytes) of raw HTML MIME. External images fetched over HTTPS do not count against that limit.

What actually pushes a template past 104,448 bytes is markup bloat. Raw Figma-to-HTML exports often nest a single heading inside five wrapper tables and repeat 600 bytes of inline style resets on every <td>. Unpurged Tailwind or framework <style> blocks burn another 15 to 30 KB in <head> before any copy loads. Worse, inlining data:image/... base64 images adds a ~33% text tax to your HTML AND Gmail strips data: URIs on <img> anyway, leaving you with a clipped message and a broken image box.

Keep your local HTML under 92 KB (94,208 UTF-8 bytes). At send time, your ESP wraps every link in a long click-tracking redirect, adds open pixels, and appends MIME headers. That easily eats another 6 to 10 KB.

3. The 4 ESP Packaging Traps (Zero Universal ZIP)

Even lean HTML bounces on upload when packaged for the wrong ESP:

ESP Package Format Limit Required Unsubscribe Tag Classic Gotcha
Mailchimp Single flat-root .zip (no images/ folder) < 1 MB `* UNSUB
Klaviyo Twin-file: {% raw %}template.html + separate images.zip < 10 MB/img {% unsubscribe %} Single combined ZIP fails; images.zip paths are case-sensitive (images/hero.png)
Braze Single flat-root .zip (no subdirectories) < 5 MB {{${set_user_to_unsubscribed_url}}} Zipping the parent folder buries index.html one level deep
HubSpot Standalone HTML + external HTTPS CDN (no ZIP) CDN hosted {{ unsubscribe_link }} + {{ site_settings.company_name }} Relative <img src> or <v:fill src> breaks; every URL must be https://

Watch out for OS zip quirks too: macOS Finder's Compress injects __MACOSX/ and .DS_Store junk into flat-root ZIPs, and older Windows tools write \ backslashes instead of POSIX / paths.

4. When to Skip VML (And 3 Free Browser-Local Tools)

You do not always need VML or raw HTML imports. If 95% of your subscribers are on consumer Gmail or Apple Mail and square corners in Classic Outlook are fine, use a padded <td> link and save ~400 bytes per button. And if non-technical marketers edit copy every week, build native blocks inside Klaviyo or Mailchimp instead of importing HTML.

If you do ship Figma-to-HTML or custom ESP templates and want to test your own email HTML locally without uploading client templates to a random server, these three free zero-login tools run completely client-side:

  • Free Dual-Outlook Bulletproof VML Button Generator to compute arcsize and copy isolated <!--[if mso]> / <!--[if !mso]><!--> button HTML.
  • Free 0-Upload Gmail 102 KB + Dual-Outlook VML Preflight Checker to inspect exact UTF-8 byte weight, unpaired VML, base64 images, and Mailchimp/Klaviyo/Braze/HubSpot packaging locally in your browser.
  • Free 600px Auto-Layout Figma Email Starter Kit on Figma Community for clean 600px Auto-Layout frames.

Candid note: MailPack HTML (our local Figma plugin built on this engine) is queued behind AdPack HTML5 in Figma Community review, so there is zero charge today, and early access is open on the site if you want a heads-up when it ships.

title: Executive Table, Kanban Board, and Monthly Calendar in React 19 Over Static Data
description:
Originally published at Datalaria.

In the first two articles of this series, we demonstrated how to eliminate synchronization drift between external databases and Git (Article 1) and how to bulletproof metadata quality and bilingual parity through strict Pydantic v2 data contracts and CI/CD pipelines (Article 2).

At the conclusion of that backend pipeline, we produce an exceptional data asset: public.json, a normalized, deterministic, and fully audited dataset consolidating 100% of the ecosystem's technical articles, interactive applications, and downloadable product suites.

However, structured data on disk remains inaccessible if technical editors and engineering leaders must inspect it by reading raw code or running CLI commands. Making strategic publication decisions demands a high-level executive cockpit: an operations center capable of filtering by taxonomy, identifying workflow bottlenecks in a Kanban pipeline, scheduling future releases on a monthly calendar, and capturing spontaneous ideas on the fly.

In this article, we break down the frontend engineering behind Datalaria Pulse: how we architected a Single Page Application (SPA) in React 19 + TypeScript that mounts directly over a static index, delivering instantaneous interactivity with zero network latency without server overhead or sluggish database queries.

🗺️ Datalaria Pulse Series Roadmap

To understand how each piece of the Content Ops as Code architecture fits together, this series consists of 5 structured installments:

  1. ⚪ Part 1: Goodbye Notion: Datalaria Pulse and Editorial Governance that Writes Itself from Git
  2. ⚪ Part 2: From Front Matter to Index: Pydantic v2, Bilingual Parity, and CI/CD Automation
  3. 🟢 Part 3 (This article): Executive Table, Kanban Board, and Monthly Calendar in React 19 over a Static Index
  4. ⚪ Part 4 (Sun Nov 29): Automated Google Analytics 4 and Search Console: Measuring the Organic ROI of Every Post, App, and Kit
  5. ⚪ Part 5 (Wed Dec 02): Editorial Operations for Docs, SEO, and Marketing Teams: From Notion to Excel in 5 Minutes and AI Agent Factory

0. Phase Objectives and Article Scope: Instant Interactivity over Static Data

The core objective of this stage in Datalaria Pulse is to democratize access to the editorial catalog through a fluid, modern, and reactive user experience (UX).

Strategic Objectives:

  1. Zero-Latency Data Consumption: Eliminate traditional relational database roundtrips in the public interface by serving an immutable, CDN-cached static dataset (public.json).
  2. Multi-View Content Projection: Present the single source of truth (SSOT) through three complementary perspectives: Executive Table (analytical auditing), Kanban Board (lifecycle stages), and Monthly Calendar (release cadence).
  3. Decoupled Optimistic Capture: Enable authors to draft ideas and notes locally with instant browser persistence (localStorage), offering one-click YAML export for subsequent Git commits.
  4. Foundation for Pro Mode: Design modular components capable of switching seamlessly between the static public dataset and real-time collaborative synchronization via Supabase PostgreSQL.

Specific Objectives for this Article 3:

  • Explain the Static-First SPA architectural pattern: how React 19 parses and filters hundreds of assets in client memory with zero network lag.
  • Detail the engineering behind the Executive Table: predictive search, combined multi-taxonomy filters, and flexible pagination (10, 25, 50 rows).
  • Analyze the mechanics of the 5-Stage Kanban Board (Idea, Draft, In Review, Scheduled, Published) and its state transitions.
  • Present the Editorial Calendar Grid and the local idea capture workflow with atomic Git backlog export.

1. Connecting with the Datalaria Ecosystem: From Executive Suites to the React 19 Cockpit

The interface design of Datalaria Pulse directly inherits the ergonomics, boardroom aesthetic, and quantitative rigor established in our earlier suites:

  1. The Visual Ergonomics of LifeOps: Pulse adopts the Outfit + Inter corporate typography, deep dark slate styling (#080d1a to #0f172a), neon cyan/emerald atmospheric accents, and the floating segmented navigation deck originally developed for our LifeOps platform.
  2. C-Level Executive Presentation from the Decision Suite: The Pulse navbar follows executive boardroom standards: 4 Macro KPIs highlighted by neon top borders (Total Assets, Published, Scheduled, and Bilingual Parity), complemented by contextual operational metrics (indexed words, estimated content equity, and top organic traffic driver).
  3. Triple Taxonomy from S&OP Engineering: Just as supply chain planners segment inventory by family and channel, Pulse incorporates a dynamic 3-level taxonomy selector: macro ecosystem tiers (Articles vs Apps vs Kits), official 5-pillar blog themes, and granular category breakdowns.
  4. End-to-End Type Safety under Spec-Driven Development (SDD): TypeScript interfaces in React 19 mirror the exact Pydantic v2 contracts specified in specs/apps/pulse/spec.md. There is zero divergence in field naming, optionality, or default structures.

2. Frontend Architecture: React 19, TypeScript, and Zero-Latency State

Most content management tools make the architectural mistake of tightly coupling their web UI to a dynamic REST or GraphQL API backed by a remote database. Under that traditional paradigm, every time a user opens a Kanban board, the client executes heavy database queries (SELECT * FROM posts JOIN categories...), displays loading spinners, and introduces 200 to 800 ms of latency.

In Datalaria Pulse, we invert this model using the Static-First paradigm:

// apps/pulse/web/src/App.tsx (Data Loading Lifecycle Extract)
interface PublicPulseDataset {
  version: string;
  generated_at: string;
  total_assets: number;
  published_assets: number;
  scheduled_assets: number;
  ideas_count: number;
  parity_summary: Record<string, number>;
  assets: ContentAsset[];
}

export function App() {
  const [dataset, setDataset] = useState<PublicPulseDataset | null>(null);
  const [activeTab, setActiveTab] = useState<
    'dashboard' | 'table' | 'kanban' | 'calendar' | 'health' | 'channels'
  >('dashboard');

  useEffect(() => {
    // Atomic fetch of precompiled static build index
    fetch(`./data/public.json?t=${Date.now()}`, { cache: 'no-store' })
      .then(res => res.json())
      .then((data: PublicPulseDataset) => {
        setDataset(data);
      })
      .catch(err => console.error("Error loading public.json:", err));
  }, []);

  // ...
}

Why This Architecture Outperforms Traditional Web Databases:

  • 0 ms Navigation Latency: Once the lightweight public.json bundle (~60 KB gzipped) is loaded into browser memory, all search queries, column sorting, tag filtering, and view transitions execute in under 1 millisecond.
  • Zero Server Costs: The application requires no Node.js servers, Docker containers, or edge workers. Both frontend code and dataset assets are delivered entirely through static CDN edge nodes.
  • Outage Resilience: Even if external analytics APIs or database services experience downtime, the Datalaria Pulse cockpit functions without degradation because its data is immutably version-controlled inside the Git commit.

3. View 1: The Multi-Criteria Executive Table

The Executive Table serves as the primary instrument for deep catalog auditing. When an organization manages over 100 technical articles, editorial leaders must answer complex questions in seconds: which articles score below 70 in SEO audit?, which long-form guides exceed 3,000 words but lack English translations?, which asset leads organic search traffic?.

Activo / Title Type Status Pub Date Words Parity SEO Score
Porter's Five Forces... POST Published 2026-10-19 4,218 w. complete 100 / 100
Quantitative SWOT & CAME... POST Published 2026-10-13 4,867 w. complete 100 / 100
Dynamic BCG Matrix... POST Published 2026-10-26 3,920 w. complete 100 / 100

Key Engineering Features:

  1. Multi-Criteria Filtering & URL Deep-Linking: The control bar enables simultaneous filtering by predictive text (fuzzy matches across titles, slugs, and tags), asset class (post, app, kit, suite), and editorial state (published, scheduled, draft, idea), supporting URL deep linking (?tab=table&type=app&status=published).
  2. Version History Switcher (🔀): Instantly toggles between consolidated parent assets and granular SemVer release histories (vX.Y.Z).
  3. 1-Click Interactive Notion CSV Diagnostics (Operation Crucible): Client-side validation button that parses Notion CSV exports in browser memory, auditing mandatory columns, dates, and taxonomy without sending data to servers.
  4. Bi-Directional Sorting and Adaptive Pagination: Clicking any header instantly reorders the catalog alphabetically, chronologically, by word count, or by relative traffic index, with configurable density (10, 25, or 50 rows).
  5. High-Contrast Parity Badges and Quick-Advance Kanban (→): Clear chromatic indicators (complete in emerald green, missing_en in rose pink) and 1-click stage transition buttons in Kanban without opening modal dialogs.

4. View 2: The 5-Stage Editorial Kanban Board

While the table specializes in analytical auditing, the Kanban Board manages the day-to-day workflow of technical writing and peer review. We structure the editorial lifecycle into 5 immutable stages:

Card Architecture in the Kanban Grid:

Each card in the board functions as an autonomous component displaying:

  • Asset Type and Timestamp: Category badge (POST, APP, KIT) and target release date.
  • Full Title & Link: Direct link to inspect the asset in localhost or live production.
  • Taxonomy Pillar: Official content category assignment (Strategy & Operations, AI, Engineering & Projects, Startups, Pioneers & Icons, Tech Culture & Media).
  • Quality Score: SEO Score badge (0 to 100) color-coded via a traffic light system (green $\ge 80$, amber $\ge 60$, red $< 60$).

With 192 consolidated assets distributed across these 5 stages (127 bilingual articles, 44 SemVer application releases 🚀 APP / ⚡ APP vX.Y, and 21 B2B Kit editions 📦 KIT, with 180 public assets exposed under invariants INV-PULSE-1..8), engineering managers instantly identify review bottlenecks or verify whether upcoming scheduled releases satisfy weekly publishing quotas.

5. View 3: The Monthly Calendar and Rapid Idea Capture

An editorial calendar is not merely a list of dates; it is an instrument of strategic rhythm. The Monthly Calendar view in Datalaria Pulse projects upcoming releases on an interactive chronological timeline:

Date Asset Title Type
2026-11-18 Goodbye Notion: Datalaria Pulse and Editorial Ops from Git POST
2026-11-22 From Front Matter to Index: Pydantic v2 & GitHub Actions POST
2026-11-25 Executive Table, Kanban Board, and Monthly Calendar in React 19 POST
2026-11-29 Automated GA4 and Search Console: Measuring Organic ROI of the Blog POST
2026-12-02 Editorial Operations for SEO and Marketing Teams: From Notion to Excel in 5 Minutes POST

Rapid Idea Capture with Local Persistence:

To maintain creative flow while authors research or code, we engineered the + New Idea modal:

  1. Quick-Entry Modal: Enables technical writers to record working titles, assign categories, tag relevant technologies, and write briefing notes.
  2. Optimistic In-Memory Merging: Saving an idea writes it instantly to browser localStorage and optimistically merges it with the in-memory public.json array, updating the Idea Kanban column and top-level KPIs in zero milliseconds.
  3. Atomic Git Export (YAML): The top navbar includes a dedicated YAML (N) button that formats all local ideas into valid YAML ready to commit directly into data/editorial/backlog.yaml. This bridges the web interface into Git without manual data entry.

🚀 Official Datalaria App: Datalaria Pulse — Try Live Demo

6. Key Takeaways and Next Steps

Implementing this React 19 frontend proves that speed and visual sophistication do not require abandoning the simplicity of static architectures:

  • Instantaneous UX: Search, filtering, and Kanban view shifts operate in sub-millisecond speeds over an in-memory dataset.
  • Complete Lifecycle Governance: From the first captured idea to production SEO audits, every editorial stage is visible in a unified dashboard.
  • Foundation for Scale: This identical frontend architecture powers the real-time cloud synchronization of Pulse Pro when teams connect their Supabase accounts.

Experience the Cockpit and Get the Kit:

  • Switch between the Executive Table, Kanban Board, and Calendar directly in our live Datalaria Pulse Cockpit.
  • Get the master Excel tracker, Notion migration scripts, and automation suite in the Datalaria Pulse Kit.

Coming Up in Part 4/5:

Automated Google Analytics 4 and Search Console: Measuring real organic ROI, content equity, and freshness scoring without exposing private metrics.

Questions or feedback on this implementation? Join the discussion in the original article on Datalaria.

title: A Quiet Hero Video Still Needs a Motion Preference
description:
A white backdrop can make a looping hero video feel subtle and restrained, almost like a static illustration. Yet the movement is still movement. Visitors who configure their device to reduce animation should still get a clear, usable page without that constant loop.

Start with a still state

Design the hero around a poster image and real text before wiring up playback. Your headline, value proposition, and primary call to action should stand on their own while the video is paused, buffering, or unavailable.

When preparing a clip on a light canvas, white background video can help keep the visual frame clean. However, asset styling does not answer whether the clip should autoplay in your UI. Treat autoplay as a separate product decision driven by user intent and accessibility.

Apply the preference to playback

Read the MDN reduced-motion reference to map the prefers-reduced-motion media query to a restrained default state—and then make sure your <video> element actually honors it. Tweaking a CSS @media rule alone will not stop an already playing HTML video element.

Expose a visible play/pause toggle whenever ongoing motion stays in the layout. If a visitor explicitly starts playback, persist or respect that choice instead of clobbering it on unrelated component re-renders.

Test without the happy path

Enable reduced motion at the OS or browser level before loading the page. Inspect initial render, throttled network conditions, and failed media requests. Your poster frame should stay anchored with the headline and CTA rather than collapsing into an empty box while waiting for media.

Verify keyboard navigation and focus states on the playback control as well. Calm visual styling helps, but runtime behavior is what makes motion preferences meaningful. The page should feel complete even when decorative motion stays frozen.

During design and code review, treat the static state as a first-class UI state—not a random frame grabbed mid-motion. Give the still composition intentional framing, contrast, and hierarchy from the start.

title: TOTP in Node with no packages: four steps, each checked against RFC 6238
description:
When an authenticator code is rejected, the fault sits in one of four steps: decoding the secret, turning the clock into a counter, the HMAC, or the truncation to six digits. Writing those four steps yourself is the quickest way to know which one to look at. Here they are in Node with no packages, each with a known answer to check against.

The known answer is the test vector from RFC 6238. Its secret is the ASCII text 12345678901234567890, which an authenticator app takes in Base32 as GEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQGEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQ. At 59 seconds after 1 January 1970 the 8-digit SHA-1 code is 94287082, and the 6-digit code is its last six digits, 287082. A function that prints those two is right.

Step 1: the Base32 secret becomes bytes

The setup key printed under a QR code is Base32: the letters A to Z and the digits 2 to 7, each character carrying 5 bits. Spaces, padding and lower case do not matter, so strip them first.

const ALPHABET = 'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ234567';

function base32Decode(input) {
  const clean = input.toUpperCase().replace(/[\s=]/g, '');
  let bits = 0, value = 0;
  const out = [];
  for (const ch of clean) {
    const idx = ALPHABET.indexOf(ch);
    if (idx === -1) throw new Error(`not Base32: ${ch}`);
    value = (value << 5) | idx;
    bits += 5;
    if (bits >= 8) {
      out.push((value >>> (bits - 8)) & 0xff);
      bits -= 8;
    }
  }
  return Buffer.from(out);
}

Check: the Base32 decoder, set to Decode and Base32, turns the test secret into 12345678901234567890 and reports 20 bytes. That size is normal: most services use 20 random bytes, 160 bits, which is 32 Base32 characters.

Step 2: the clock becomes a counter

Unix time in seconds, divided by the period and rounded down. The period is 30 seconds unless the service says otherwise. The counter is then written as 8 bytes, big-endian.

const counter = Math.floor(time / period);  // 59 / 30 -> 1
const msg = Buffer.alloc(8);
msg.writeBigUInt64BE(BigInt(counter));      // 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 01

For a real date: at 12:00:10 UTC on 8 November 2026 the counter is 59804640. That step runs from 12:00:00 to 12:00:30, so the code on screen then has 20 seconds left.

Step 3: HMAC-SHA1 of those 8 bytes 

const mac = crypto.createHmac('sha1', base32Decode(secret)).update(msg).digest();

For the test key and counter 1 this is 20 bytes:

75a48a19d4cbe100644e8ac1397eea747a2d33ab

You can check this step on its own. The counter bytes are not printable, so a text box cannot hold them, but a file can:

printf '\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x01' > counter.bin
openssl dgst -sha1 -hmac 12345678901234567890 counter.bin

The HMAC generator with SHA-1, the key typed as Text and the message switched to File gives the same hex for counter.bin. If your own value differs here, look at how the counter was encoded: the text "1" and the 8-byte number 1 are different messages.

Step 4: truncate to digits

The low 4 bits of the last byte pick an offset. The 4 bytes starting there, with the top bit cleared, make a number, and the code is its last 6 or 8 digits.

const offset = mac[mac.length - 1] & 0x0f;          // 0xab & 0x0f = 11
const bin = mac.readUInt32BE(offset) & 0x7fffffff;  // 0xc1397eea -> 0x41397eea
return String(bin % 10 ** digits).padStart(digits, '0');

0x41397eea is 1094287082. The last 8 digits are 94287082 and the last 6 are 287082. Keep the padStart: a code whose number begins with zeros still has to be six characters long.

Steps 2 to 4 as one function 

const crypto = require('node:crypto');

function totp(secret, { time = Date.now() / 1000, period = 30, digits = 6, algo = 'sha1' } = {}) {
  const counter = Math.floor(time / period);
  const msg = Buffer.alloc(8);
  msg.writeBigUInt64BE(BigInt(counter));
  const mac = crypto.createHmac(algo, base32Decode(secret)).update(msg).digest();
  const offset = mac[mac.length - 1] & 0x0f;
  const bin = mac.readUInt32BE(offset) & 0x7fffffff;
  return String(bin % 10 ** digits).padStart(digits, '0');
}

const secret = 'GEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQGEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQ';
console.log(totp(secret, { time: 59, digits: 8 }));  // 94287082
console.log(totp(secret, { time: 59 }));             // 287082

Both lines print the RFC values on Node 24. For a live check I pasted the same secret into a TOTP generator this afternoon. At 14:09 IST it showed step 59856079 with 713 395 as the previous code, 827 335 as the current one and 749 271 as the next; totp() for steps 59856078, 59856079 and 59856080 printed the same three.

Checking a code someone typed

Servers usually accept a code from one step before or after the current one, so a code typed a few seconds late still works. Returning which step matched also tells you roughly how far off the user's clock is.

function verify(secret, code, { window = 1, period = 30, ...opts } = {}) {
  const now = Date.now() / 1000;
  for (let step = -window; step <= window; step++) {
    const expected = totp(secret, { ...opts, period, time: now + step * period });
    if (expected.length === code.length &&
        crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(expected), Buffer.from(code))) {
      return step; // 0 on time, -1 one step late, +1 one step early
    }
  }
  return null;
}

timingSafeEqual is there for a reason: an ordinary string comparison stops at the first different character, so its timing leaks how much of a guess was right. A constant-time comparison checks every byte every time.

When the phone and the server still disagree

  • The clock. A code that only works one step early or late means a clock about 30 seconds off.
  • Settings the app ignores. Google Authenticator historically used SHA-1, six digits and 30 seconds whatever the otpauth link asked for. Keep those defaults unless you control both sides.
  • The secret. One wrong character in the Base32 key, or a different algorithm, digit count or period on the server, changes every code.

The same example is worked through by hand in the TOTP guide. I wrote this with AI help; the test values come from the linked pages as they read on 26 November 2026, and every output above is from running the code.

title: Pretraining for Forecasting in Relational Databases
description:
arXiv:2611.33645v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real-world forecasting increasingly relies on asynchronous transaction logs in relational databases rather than uniformly sampled arrays. While relational deep learning (RDL) models can forecast from these complex histories, they are typically trained separately for each specific target and root entity type. We introduce Query-Conditioned Relational pretraining (QCRP), a self-supervised framework that enables a standard RDL backbone to act as a universal forecaster across a database. QCRP generates diverse forecasting objectives using a structured temporal query grammar and interleaves them through a shared conditional predictor. This produces a robust, frozen encoder reusable for downstream tasks via lightweight predictors or a zero-shot interface. Evaluated on large-scale RelBench databases, QCRP learns frozen representations that support competitive forecasting across tasks and entity types. Furthermore, a single unified QCRP model checkpoint is competitive with isolated, entity-specific specialists. We demonstrate promising results for reusing the learned representations from standard RDL backbones for forecasting tasks in relational databases.

title: How to Center a Div in CSS: 5 Simple Methods That Actually Work
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

Yes, you can center a div in CSS. The simplest reliable way is to make the parent a flex container with display: flex, justify-content: center and align-items: center. This article tries that and four other solid methods on the same small profile card.

<div class="card">
  <div class="avatar">L</div>
  <h2>Lavkush Kumar</h2>
  <p>Full stack developer who builds websites, games and tutorials.</p>
  <button type="button">Say Hello</button>
</div>

That is our card: a circle with the letter L, a name, one line of text and a button. With no centering yet, the browser parks it in the top left corner. Every method below starts from this card. Only the CSS changes.

Meet the Card Before We Move It

The card needs its own styling, which stays the same through all five methods: a 300 pixel wide card with soft corners and a gentle shadow, an 84 pixel teal avatar circle with a white L, and simple sizing rules for the name, paragraph and button.

.card {
  width: 300px;
  padding: 28px 24px;
  background: #ffffff;
  border: 1px solid #dfe4e8;
  border-radius: 14px;
  text-align: center;
  box-shadow: 0 6px 24px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.10);
}
.avatar {
  width: 84px;
  height: 84px;
  margin: 0 auto 14px;
  border-radius: 50%;
  background: #0f766e;
  color: #ffffff;
  font-size: 36px;
  font-weight: bold;
  line-height: 84px;
}

Spot one detail: margin: 0 auto 14px in the avatar rule. The auto margins split the spare space evenly, so the circle sits in the middle of the card, a preview of method 3. If you are still sorting out which language does what, our guide to HTML vs CSS vs JavaScript and what each one does explains it in plain words.

Method 1: Flexbox, the One to Learn First

Flexbox is the method most developers reach for. Put three lines on the parent, here the body:

body {
  margin: 0;
  min-height: 100vh;
  display: flex;
  justify-content: center;
  align-items: center;
}

margin: 0 removes the browser's default page gap, and min-height: 100vh makes the body as tall as the window, because vertical centering needs a parent tall enough to have a middle. display: flex turns the body into a flex container, then justify-content: center and align-items: center center the card horizontally and vertically. I checked this in a real browser: at 1280 by 800 the card starts 490 pixels from the left and 256 from the top.

Use Flexbox when centering one item, or a row of items, inside a parent. The MDN guide to centering an element shows the same recipe as its first example, and our CSS Flexbox explained with examples guide walks through it step by step.

Method 2: Grid, One Line Does the Job

Grid is the newer layout system in CSS, and for pure centering it is even shorter:

body {
  margin: 0;
  min-height: 100vh;
  display: grid;
  place-items: center;
}

display: grid turns the body into a grid container, and place-items: center centers the item both ways in one go. The card looks identical.

Use Grid when the section is already a grid, or when you plan to center several items, like a gallery of cards. For a single card it is a tie with Flexbox. Our guide to CSS Grid explained with examples shows how grid rows and columns work.

The MDN guide to centring an element with CSS.

Method 3: Margin Auto, the Classic Horizontal Fix

This is the oldest method on the list, and it still works for one job: centering a block element left to right.

.card {
  width: 300px;
  margin: 0 auto;
}

When a block element is narrower than its parent, the browser has spare space on the sides. Setting the left and right margins to auto splits that space equally, which puts the card in the middle. It now sits in the horizontal center, but it stays at the top.

Use it when you only need horizontal centering, like a blog article column or a form. The element must be a block element with a set width. Without a width, the div stretches to fill the parent and there is no spare space to split.

Method 4: Absolute Positioning Plus Transform

This method is two steps: pull the card to the middle of the page, then nudge it back by half its own size so its center sits on the middle point.

.card {
  position: absolute;
  top: 50%;
  left: 50%;
  transform: translate(-50%, -50%);
}

position: absolute takes the card out of the normal flow. top: 50% and left: 50% move its top left corner to the exact middle of its positioned parent, the page itself when no closer positioned ancestor exists. Now the card sits too far down and right, so transform: translate(-50%, -50%) shifts it back by half its own size. The percentages refer to the card itself, so this works at any card size.

Use this method to center something on top of other content, like a popup or a loading spinner. It is not for normal page layout, because an absolutely positioned element stops taking up space, so content below it can slide underneath.

Method 5: Text Align, for Inline Content Inside the Card

The last method does not center the card at all. It centers the things inside the card:

.card {
  text-align: center;
}

text-align: center centers inline content, like text, images and a button, inside their parent. That is why the name, paragraph and button line up neatly in the middle of the card. It works on the card's children, not on the card itself, so putting it on the body moves nothing, because the card is a block element.

Use it inside a card, a header or a footer whenever you want a heading or a line of text centered in its box. It is the simplest method of the five, and the most misunderstood, because beginners try it on the wrong element. Remember: text-align centers what is inside, Flexbox and Grid center the box itself.

When the Card Refuses to Move

Almost every stuck card is one of four mistakes. First, the parent has no height: if you use Flexbox or Grid and the parent is only as tall as the card, there is no middle to center in, so add min-height: 100vh to the parent. Second, you centered the wrong element: for Flexbox and Grid, the rules go on the parent, not on the card. Third, margin: auto did nothing because the card has no width. Fourth, the browser's default 8 pixel body margin throws the card off by a few pixels.

One more check: open the browser developer tools and look at the box model, which shows the card's real width, padding and margins. The MDN guide to aligning items is worth a bookmark too.

Questions Beginners Actually Ask

Why is my div not centering even though I used margin auto?

Almost always because the div has no set width. Without one, the div fills its parent, so there is no spare space for the auto margins to split. Add width: 300px and keep margin: 0 auto.

Should I use Flexbox or Grid to center a div?

For one item, either works and the result looks the same. Pick Flexbox for a row or column layout, and Grid if the section is already built with grid. Learn Flexbox first.

How do I center a div both horizontally and vertically?

Use Flexbox with justify-content: center and align-items: center on the parent, or Grid with place-items: center. Both need a tall parent, so add min-height: 100vh.

Does text align center work on a div?

No, not on the div itself. text-align: center centers the inline content inside an element, like text and images, but it does not move a block element. To move the div, use one of the four methods above.

Which Method When

Method Centers Best for Watch out for
Flexbox Both ways One item, or a row of items Parent needs height for vertical centering
Grid Both ways Sections already built with grid Overkill for one row
Margin auto Horizontal only Article columns and forms Needs a width, horizontal only
Absolute plus transform Both ways Popups, modals and overlays Leaves the page flow
Text align Content inside Headings, text and buttons in a card Does not move the block itself

Your Turn: Two Small Challenges

First, center the card vertically as well using only margin: auto on the card and Flexbox on the body, then remove the Flexbox lines and get the same result with Grid. Second, add a teammate card beside the first one, with a different letter and name, and center the pair with gap: 20px on the body.

A Short Ending

Centering a div feels hard only while the methods are a mixed up list in your head. Once each one is tied to a job, the choice gets easy: Flexbox for most days, Grid when the layout is already a grid, margin auto for a horizontal fix, absolute positioning for overlays, and text align for the words inside.

title: CypherMAS: Benchmarking Routing Reliability in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.33242v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) distribute reasoning across specialized agents that must exchange messages and invoke tools reliably. Existing evaluations typically couple communication with open domain tasks, making it difficult to determine whether a failure arises from reasoning, malformed tool use, lost messages, or forgotten requests. Prior benchmarks do not isolate communication execution or measure routing redundancy against a known optimal path. We introduce CypherMAS, a synthetic benchmark that isolates communication and routing in fixed multi-agent graphs. Agents in chain, star, bipartite, or ring graphs route cyphered messages to remote peers holding the matching decoders; since the optimal route is known, redundant LLM calls can be measured and routing failures may be easily tracked. Across eleven open-weight models from 4B to 753B, small models fail at routing and tool use, dense models above 27B degrade with diameter, and successful runs exceed minimum LLM calls. These findings identify communication reliability as a distinct scaling bottleneck for multi-agent systems and provide a controlled diagnostic for complex multi-agent systems. The source code is freely available: https://github.com/Andoree/CypherMAS.

title: Agent Evaluation Without Ground Truth: A Null Proportion Perspective
description:
arXiv:2611.31539v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The correctness of actions taken by agents is typically evaluated against known, externally verified ground truth labels, such as whether a proof is correct or whether code compiles and passes unit tests. However, as coding and science agents are entrusted with more end-to-end autonomy -- proposing interventions, running experiments, and deciding what to deploy and investigate next -- whether an agent's actions genuinely improve an outcome must be inferred from noisy, often inconclusive experiments. To evaluate agents in this setting, we define agent quality as a weighted sum of correct decisions along its trajectory, using sequences of $e$-values as statistical evidence regarding correctness in place of ground-truth labels. Our framework accommodates arbitrarily dependent decisions, data-dependent trajectory termination, dynamically generated hypotheses, and quality measures defined after the trajectory concludes. We construct upper and lower bound estimators and confidence sets for agent quality with statistical guarantees that hold uniformly over agent trajectory distributions and establish instance-wise sharpness of our estimator class. We demonstrate our methods with a case study comparing the success of Claude Opus and Claude Haiku in improving the runtime of an open-source Python package.

title: DoseSteer: Steering diffusion-based dose prediction models towards clinical targets via Dual-Response Guidance
description:
arXiv:2611.33577v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI dose-prediction models generate patient-specific 3D dose distributions from patient anatomy. Yet these predictions can still miss structure-level clinical dose targets. Once deployed, most existing predictors offer no direct mechanism to correct such deviations, deferring target enforcement to downstream plan optimization. We introduce DoseSteer, an inference-time framework that steers frozen diffusion-based dose prediction models towards specified clinical targets without retraining. To meet clinical targets while preserving overall dose prediction quality, we propose Dual-Response Guidance (DRG), a structure-centric algorithm that probes the model's responses to perturbations in each structure's noisy dose and context and jointly solves for per-structure steering strengths. Across five dataset-model configurations spanning three diffusion architectures and three datasets, DRG outperforms 12 training-free baselines under identical reference-derived target proxies, removing at least 97% of the target error, reducing the official dose error by 7.8% on average, and improving dose fidelity outside the steered structures. DoseSteer reconciles learned anatomical dose priors with explicit structure-level targets at test time, establishing a principled, training-free mechanism to refine AI dose predictions prior to plan optimization. Code is available at https://github.com/csp2002/DoseSteer.
