title: SplatWAM: Splatting World Action Models for Real-Time 3D Imagination
description:
arXiv:2611.33467v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: World models typically predict future observations in pixel or latent space, limiting their ability to directly represent true 3D scene evolution. We present SplatWAM (Splatting World Action Model), a generative world model that learns action-conditioned dynamics directly over compact 3D Gaussian primitives. A tokenizer SplatWAM-T first encodes a variable number of unposed views into a fixed budget of Gaussian tokens. A dynamics model SplatWAM-D then predicts future Gaussian states in a single forward pass per action, using log-Euclidean covariance coordinates and differentiable rendering supervision to facilitate learning in an explicit 3D space. Each predicted state can be rasterized from arbitrary viewpoints, enforcing a shared 3D representation across views by construction. On OGBench Scene, SplatWAM renders novel views 12x faster than video world models (~80 FPS on an RTX 5090) with up to 2.0 dB higher PSNR. We further introduce SplatWAM-P, a lightweight flow-matching policy head jointly trained with the dynamics model. Across 8 task suites, model-free Gaussian-token policies outperform pixel-based counterparts by up to 24.8 percentage points. SplatWAM-P improves over Latent Particle World Model (LPWM) by 12 percentage points and matches HIQL without a learned value function. On LIBERO, our ~1B model outperforms WorldVLA (~7B) and the robot-pretrained OpenVLA (~7B), while matching OpenVLA-OFT when both are trained without large-scale robot pretraining. Code and checkpoints will be released.

title: How Developers Can Prototype Better Empty States Before the Final Design Is Ready
description:
Empty states are easy to ignore during development.

A dashboard usually looks good when it contains data.

A project list looks complete when several projects already exist.

An analytics page feels useful when charts are filled with numbers.

But new users often see something very different.

No projects.

No files.

No messages.

No reports.

No saved searches.

No activity.

That first empty screen can become one of the most important moments in the product.

Unfortunately, empty states are often implemented at the end of development with:

a gray icon

one sentence

and a button.

A better approach is to prototype them earlier, even before the final visual design is ready.

Why Empty States Matter

An empty state is not simply missing content.

It is a product state.

The interface should explain:

what this area is for

why nothing appears yet

what the user can do next

what will happen after they take action

Consider a project dashboard.

Weak empty state:

No projects found.

Better empty state:

You have not created a project yet.

Create your first project to organize tasks, files, and team activity.

Create Project

The second version does more than report database state.

It teaches the product.

There Are Different Types of Empty States

Not every empty screen means the same thing.

Developers should identify the state before designing the visual.

A first-use empty state means:

The user has never created anything.

A cleared state means:

Content existed, but the user deleted or completed it.

A no-results state means:

A search or filter returned nothing.

An error-related empty state means:

The application expected content but could not load it.

A permission state means:

The user cannot access the content.

Each case requires different messaging.

First-Use Empty States Should Teach

A first-use screen is an onboarding opportunity.

Imagine an API monitoring dashboard with no monitors.

Instead of:

No monitors.

Try:

Create your first monitor.

Track an endpoint and receive alerts when availability or response time changes.

Add Monitor

Now the interface explains both:

what to do

and

why to do it.

No-Results States Should Help Recovery

Search results require a different strategy.

If someone searches:

production-auth-service

and receives no results, a large onboarding illustration is probably unnecessary.

The interface should help the user recover.

For example:

No results for “production-auth-service.”

Try:

removing filters

checking spelling

searching a shorter term

viewing all services

The best visual may be much simpler.

Do Not Confuse Empty States With Errors

Suppose an API request fails.

Displaying:

No data yet.

would be misleading.

The user may think they have no records when the actual problem is:

network failure

authentication failure

server error

timeout

Developers should model these states separately.

For example:

loading

loaded_empty

loaded_with_data

error

permission_denied

This makes the UI much easier to reason about.

Design the State Machine First

Before drawing anything, define the application state.

A simple component might support:

Loading

Empty

Populated

Error

Unauthorized

The visual layer should respond to those states.

Do not use:

if items.length === 0

as the only empty-state rule.

If the request failed and items is also empty, the application may accidentally show the wrong message.

Write the Message Before Creating the Illustration

A useful empty state begins with copy.

Before designing the visual, answer:

What happened?

Why does it matter?

What should the user do next?

For example:

What happened?

No deployment environments exist.

Why does it matter?

Environments allow the user to separate development, staging, and production configuration.

What should happen next?

Create an environment.

Now write:

No environments yet.

Create an environment to separate development, staging, and production settings.

Create Environment

The illustration should support this message rather than determine it.

Keep the Illustration Secondary

Empty-state illustrations can improve personality and comprehension.

But the visual should not compete with the action.

The hierarchy should usually remain:

Headline

Short explanation

Primary action

Illustration

The exact order may change depending on layout.

The important point is that users should never need to understand the drawing before understanding what to do.

Prototype With Rough Visuals First

Final illustrations can take time.

Early product development does not need polished artwork.

A rough concept is enough to answer questions such as:

Does the page feel too empty?

How much vertical space should the illustration use?

Should the CTA sit above or below the visual?

Does the illustration distract from the headline?

Does the layout still work on mobile?

At this stage, speed matters more than visual perfection.

Use Simple Shapes

Developers do not need to become illustrators to prototype useful empty states.

Many concepts can be represented with:

rectangles

circles

arrows

folders

documents

small icons

simple characters

browser-window shapes

For example, an empty API dashboard might show:

a small browser window

an endpoint line

a disconnected status indicator

That is enough to communicate the idea.

Match the Illustration to the Task

Avoid using a generic rocket illustration everywhere simply because it looks attractive.

The visual should relate to the user action.

Examples:

No files

Illustration:
empty folder

No API keys

Illustration:
key outline

No deployments

Illustration:
server or deployment pipeline

No saved searches

Illustration:
search icon with empty result cards

No team members

Illustration:
empty avatar group

The visual becomes more useful when it reinforces meaning.

Do Not Show a Failure Image for a Normal State

A first-use empty state is not an error.

Avoid visual language such as:

warning symbols

broken objects

red colors

sad faces

unless something actually failed.

The user simply has not created content yet.

The design should feel inviting, not alarming.

Build a Reusable Empty-State Component

Once several screens need empty states, create a shared component.

Conceptually, it may accept:

illustration

title

description

primary action

secondary action

size

For example:

EmptyState

Title:
No projects yet

Description:
Create your first project to begin organizing your work.

Primary action:
Create project

Illustration:
projects-empty

Now different product teams can use one consistent pattern.

Separate Layout From Illustration

Do not build the entire page as one large image.

The illustration should be an asset inside a responsive layout.

Keep:

title

description

buttons

links

as real interface elements.

Benefits include:

accessibility

responsive behavior

translation

analytics

easier content updates

better SEO where relevant

The image should decorate or explain.

It should not contain essential interface text.

Think About Dark Mode

An illustration that looks good on a white background may fail completely in dark mode.

Common problems include:

dark outlines disappearing

white backgrounds creating visible rectangles

low-contrast colors

shadows becoming distracting

Test illustrations against both themes.

Transparent backgrounds are often easier to reuse.

Prefer Vector Assets When Appropriate

Simple UI illustrations often work well as SVG.

Advantages include:

small file size

sharp rendering

easy scaling

CSS control in some implementations

good performance

However, do not automatically embed extremely complex generated SVG files containing thousands of paths.

Inspect and optimize assets before shipping them.

Optimize Raster Assets

If the illustration is PNG, WebP, or AVIF:

resize it appropriately

compress it

avoid exporting at unnecessarily large dimensions

provide responsive sizes when needed

An empty state should not add several megabytes to the first page a new user sees.

Lazy Loading Is Not Always Correct

Developers often apply lazy loading automatically.

But the empty-state illustration may appear above the fold and be immediately visible.

If so, excessive lazy loading can create:

layout shifts

delayed visuals

visible loading flashes

Treat the asset according to its actual position in the interface.

Reserve the Layout Space

If an image loads after text, reserve the expected dimensions.

Otherwise:

content appears

image loads

CTA suddenly moves downward

This creates layout shift.

Define width and height or use a stable aspect-ratio container.

Test Mobile Early

Desktop mockups often have large amounts of empty space.

Mobile screens do not.

A desktop layout might contain:

illustration on the left

content on the right

On mobile, stack them.

You may also reduce:

illustration size

spacing

secondary text

The main action should remain visible without excessive scrolling.

Do Not Make the Illustration Too Tall

A common empty-state mistake is allowing the artwork to push the CTA below the fold.

Remember the primary job:

help the user move forward.

If the illustration consumes 60 percent of the screen, it may be visually attractive but functionally harmful.

Test the page at realistic viewport heights.

Prototype Before the Design Team Is Available

Small teams often face a timing problem.

Engineering has already built the feature.

The final visual design will not arrive until later.

The choice should not be:

block development

or

ship an unfinished screen.

Create a temporary visual prototype.

When experimenting with simple sketches and concepts, a free online drawing application can help developers explore rough visual directions before a final illustration is handed off or created.

The prototype does not need to become the production asset.

Its purpose is to validate the interface structure.

Name Temporary Assets Clearly

If a placeholder enters the repository, make its status obvious.

Avoid:

empty-state-final.svg

when the asset is temporary.

Use:

empty-projects-placeholder.svg

or:

prototype-empty-dashboard.svg

This reduces the chance that a temporary drawing accidentally survives for two years.

Track Placeholder Debt

Temporary assets tend to become permanent.

If the team plans to replace them, create an issue.

For example:

Replace prototype empty-state illustrations with final design assets.

Include:

affected routes

asset filenames

design owner

target milestone

Visual debt deserves the same visibility as technical debt.

Test With Real Copy

Do not prototype using:

Lorem ipsum

The actual message affects layout.

A short heading:

No projects yet

behaves differently from:

You haven't created any monitoring projects yet

Localization may make the text even longer.

Use realistic copy early.

Plan for Translation

If the product supports multiple languages, empty states need flexible layouts.

Buttons may become longer.

Descriptions may wrap differently.

Headings may occupy two or three lines.

Avoid fixed-height containers built around English text.

Do Not Put Text Inside the Illustration

If translated text is baked into an SVG or PNG, localization becomes much harder.

It also creates accessibility problems.

Keep meaningful text in HTML or native UI components.

Consider Reduced Motion

Animated empty states can be engaging.

For example:

subtle floating shapes

small loading loops

gentle character movement

But animation should not be required to understand the interface.

Respect reduced-motion preferences.

Animation should enhance the state, not define it.

Use Animation Sparingly

A bouncing illustration beside a button can quickly become distracting.

Ask:

Does this animation explain something?

Does it guide attention?

Or is it simply moving because it can?

For most empty states, still graphics are perfectly sufficient.

Measure the CTA

An empty state has a measurable job.

For example:

No projects → Create Project

Track:

empty-state impressions

CTA clicks

successful project creation

abandonment

If users see the screen repeatedly but rarely continue, the issue may be:

unclear copy

weak CTA

poor positioning

missing explanation

not the illustration.

Compare First-Time and Returning Users

The same empty state may need different messaging.

First-time user:

You haven't created a project yet.

Returning user after deleting everything:

You currently have no projects.

Those experiences have different contexts.

Product state can be more precise than simply checking for an empty array.

Use Secondary Actions Carefully

Some empty states need more than one path.

For example:

Create Project

or

Import Existing Project

Choose one clear primary action.

The second option should remain visually secondary.

Too many buttons turn a guidance screen into another decision problem.

Consider Example Content

Sometimes the best empty state is not empty.

An analytics product might display:

sample dashboard

example chart

demo report

The user can understand the outcome before creating real data.

This works especially well when the value of the product is difficult to imagine from an illustration alone.

Allow Demo Data to Be Removed

If you use example content, label it clearly.

Users should understand:

this is sample data

not their real data.

Provide an easy transition to real content.

Create an Empty-State Inventory

As the product grows, list every empty state.

For example:

Projects

Deployments

API keys

Team members

Reports

Search results

Notifications

Integrations

Saved filters

Then record:

state type

headline

CTA

illustration

component used

This prevents each team from reinventing the pattern.

Create Illustration Families

If every screen uses a completely different visual style, the product begins to feel inconsistent.

Define a simple illustration language.

For example:

same stroke width

same color palette

same corner radius

same level of detail

same perspective

same background treatment

Individual illustrations can vary while still feeling like one system.

Final Artwork Can Arrive Later

The development workflow can be:

Define state

Write copy

Build reusable component

Create rough placeholder

Test layout

Implement behavior

Validate mobile

Receive final design

Replace placeholder asset

Run visual review

This allows engineering and design to work in parallel.

The Placeholder Should Still Be Good Enough

Temporary does not mean careless.

Even a prototype asset should:

match the concept

be reasonably sized

not contain copyrighted material you cannot use

avoid misleading information

have appropriate contrast

fit the layout

A placeholder should support development without creating new problems.

Review Empty States During QA

QA plans often focus on populated screens.

Include empty states explicitly.

Test:

brand-new account

zero results

deleted content

expired permissions

failed request

slow loading

empty filtered view

These states are often where UI bugs hide.

Empty States Reveal Product Architecture

An empty screen can expose unclear product thinking.

If the team cannot answer:

What should the user do here?

the problem may not be visual design.

It may mean the workflow itself is unclear.

Empty-state design forces the team to explain the next step.

Final Thought

Empty states deserve more attention than they usually receive.

They are often the first interface a new user encounters.

They can teach the product.

Guide the next action.

Explain missing content.

Recover from searches.

And make unfinished areas feel intentional.

Developers do not need final illustrations before they can build these experiences.

Start with the state model.

Write the message.

Define the action.

Prototype a simple visual.

Build a reusable component.

Then replace the placeholder when final design assets are ready.

A good empty state is not decoration around an empty database result.

It is part of the product experience.

title: What People Ask Before Spending $3,000 Over WhatsApp
description:
We do not have a checkout. Orders go through WhatsApp: the customer sends a message from a product page, we confirm availability, they pay, we ship. It is an unusual setup for a store with 27,000 listings, and it has one accidental benefit — every pre-purchase question is written down.

After nine months, about 4,000 conversations, I went through a sample of 600 and tagged them. The distribution was not what I expected.

The questions, by category

What they ask Share of conversations
Exact dimensions / will it fit my thing 31%
Is this the real photo of the item I will receive 22%
Shipping time to my country, and duty 18%
Condition details (scratches, wear, box, papers) 14%
Payment method and buyer protection 9%
Everything else 6%

Two things stand out. First, dimensions beat every other question by a wide margin. Second, nobody asks "is it authentic" as a standalone question. They ask for more photos, and the authenticity question lives inside that request.

Dimensions: the question a size chart cannot answer

The single most common message is a variant of "what fits inside." A 25 cm bag has an exterior width, an interior width, a base depth, and a strap drop, and none of those four numbers answers whether a phone, a cardholder and a pair of sunglasses will go in together.

What actually works, in our experience:

  • Interior dimensions, measured at the widest usable point, not the exterior shell
  • Strap drop, because a bag that will not go over a coat shoulder is a return
  • Base depth, which determines whether the bag stands up when set down
  • Weight empty, which nobody lists and everybody cares about

When we started putting these on the listing, the dimension questions did not disappear — they got shorter. People stopped asking "how big is it" and started asking "will a 15-inch laptop fit," which is a question we can answer in one line.

Photos: the real authenticity question

"As in picture?" is the phrase. What it means is: are these stock images from a brand site, or photos of the actual unit?

For a resale business this is the whole trust problem in three words. Our answer is a short video taken on the day of the enquiry, plus close-ups of the areas a counterfeit gets wrong — hardware engraving, stitching density at the corner, the interior label. It costs ten minutes per serious buyer and converts most of them.

Shipping and duty: the part that loses sales

18% of conversations are about delivery time and import charges. The honest answer is 5–13 working days, and duty depends on the destination and the declared value. Buyers who have been burned before by a "free shipping" listing that arrived with a customs bill are suspicious of anything vague, so we state the range and the Incoterms plainly.

The conversations that die are almost always here. Someone asks "how long to Germany," gets a range, and goes quiet. We have not solved that. A live delivery estimate per country would probably help, and it is on the list.

Payment: the smallest category, the biggest objection

Only 9% ask directly. But the ones who do are usually the highest-value buyers, and they want to know what happens if the item never arrives. We answer with the payment method's own dispute process rather than our promise, because a promise from an unknown shop is worth nothing.

What I would tell someone building the same thing

WhatsApp ordering removes checkout friction and adds trust work. If your catalog is small and your average order is high, that trade is worth it. If your average order is $40, you will drown.

The operational cost is real: someone has to answer within an hour, in the buyer's timezone, with accurate measurements at hand. That last part is why we put measurements in the database in the first place — so the answer is a lookup, not a walk to the stockroom.

If you want to see what a listing with these fields looks like, the watch category is the densest one we have, and a single two-tone Submariner is a reasonable example. Bags are the same idea with different fields — a Birkin 30 needs interior volume, a Neverfull MM needs strap drop.

We are Superwander, an independent shop for watches, bags, shoes and apparel, shipping worldwide in 5–13 working days. If you are running conversational commerce at any scale, I would like to compare notes on response-time tolerance — that number is the one we still do not know.

title: Recovering What Matters, Transferring Only What Is Reliable: Toward Precise Reference-Based Super-Resolution
description:
arXiv:2611.33455v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reference-based super-resolution (RefSR) aims to recover missing details from high-quality references. However, existing methods face two fundamental challenges. First, perceptual plausibility does not guarantee content fidelity. Existing methods often produce visually convincing details without faithfully recovering reference-specific information, such as text, codes, and identity cues. Second, faithful reference reading does not guarantee reliable information transfer. Increasing reference utilization also exposes the restoration process to misleading content, as global semantic relevance does not necessarily imply local correspondence consistency. To address these challenges, we propose PreciseRef, a reference-aware generative framework for faithful and reliable RefSR. At its core, Asymmetric Twin-Attention (ATA) allows target and reference images to participate in a unified attention space while the reference keeps its own shape. By letting their image tokens interact directly through joint attention, ATA facilitates fine-grained reference information retrieval without explicit image alignment. To ensure reliable information transfer, we introduce Dual-Scale Reference Gating (DRG), which combines Semantic Relevance Gating (SRG) to filter globally irrelevant reference context and Bidirectional Consistency Gating (BCG) to suppress unreliable local correspondences. Furthermore, we establish VeriRef, a benchmark evaluating exact reference-dependent content recovery and robustness to mismatched references. Extensive experiments show that our method achieves 85.6% character accuracy and 76.3% exact code decoding, compared with 17.4% and 0% for existing methods, while effectively suppressing erroneous reference transfer. It also achieves state-of-the-art perceptual quality on CUFED5 and WR-SR.

title: BRAG: Bayesian Retrieval Augmented Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.31656v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) ranks memory chunks by semantic similarity to the query. Many methods improve on this by learning from feedback on what was retrieved, but each is a separate heuristic, with no account of when it is the right choice. We introduce BRAG, a generative model of retrieval with use. Each chunk generates the queries it answers from a mixture of von Mises-Fisher components anchored at its original embedding, and each chunk has a latent utility that drifts over time. The model gives the optimal inference, a closed-form filter that stores a few keys and two scalars per chunk and updates them online from the labels of a curator, and it frames retrieval as a control problem. It also shows when existing methods are optimal. Query averaging, Rocchio-style feedback and frequency reranking are special cases with fixed parameters, NUDGE is the case of one key per chunk with no dynamics, and LADER the limit of one key per past query. On two public long-term memory benchmarks, BRAG matches these methods on queries asked before, as expected, because when nothing changes over time the assumptions behind these special cases hold. On harder problems, where a new chunk makes an old one obsolete, BRAG outscores them. They all stay at plain-search level (Recall@5 0.67-0.71), while BRAG retrieves the new chunk 0.80-0.86 of the time. We also ran BRAG on three of NUDGE's seven text benchmarks, and it matches or beats NUDGE on all three. On nine months of a personal agent's memory (20,640 chunks), BRAG raises Recall@5 on held-out queries from 0.75 to 0.98 and Recall@1 from 0.44 to 0.97, with little change on chunks never queried.

title: PatientFlowSynth: Evaluating FHIR Agents with Matched Patient Charts
description:
arXiv:2611.31521v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agents that search patient charts must classify claims from retrieved records, including cases with missing or conflicting evidence. In Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR), status fields can change how those records should be interpreted. PatientFlowSynth provides 18,000 tasks from 225 synthetic patients and 18 templates that hold the patient, question, and retrieval program fixed across chart variants representing four evidence states. Re-executing the program verifies each variant's reference answer, evidence sets, and search requirements. Strict success requires a completed response with correct labels and citations exactly matching an accepted evidence set retrieved during the episode. Where required, a tool response must also show a complete search at the specified scope. In a study using GPT-5.6 Luna and 225 synthetic patients (3,600 matched pairs), explicit Encounter-status guidance increased strict success from 40.7% to 51.3% (+10.6 percentage points; 95% patient-bootstrap confidence interval, 8.4 to 12.8). Among cases whose primary reference label was insufficient evidence, label agreement fell from 49.2% to 29.3%. A prespecified two-model replication reproduced both changes. Failed retrieval can mask interpretation errors by producing a correct insufficient-evidence label without examining the relevant records. Additional model comparisons showed that the benefit of guidance was model-dependent. Retrieval, citation, and classification should be evaluated separately.

title: Confidence scores for gated automation of large language models
description:
arXiv:2611.33394v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong capabilities in automated decision-making. However, LLMs may produce incorrect answers with high confidence, limiting their applicability in decisions that affect individuals and organizations. Reliable confidence scores are necessary to gate such decisions, and existing estimates are frequently unavailable or too coarse to support effective gating. This work uses supervised learning to train models to predict the correctness of LLM-generated answers, enabling automated confident responses and routing uncertain ones for human review. A linear confidence score head is fitted to the final-layer hidden state of the frozen LLM backbone, and text-only metamodels are trained as an alternative for closed models. All results come from a single 2B-parameter backbone, on graded answers that are about 98% SQuAD and the remainder TruthfulQA. Against multiple baselines, the confidence score head outperforms all baselines and metamodels, automating the largest fraction of the workload at high accuracy targets. Prompted confidence scores can appear well calibrated yet lack the resolution needed for thresholding. Although transferability to unseen datasets is modest, the confidence score head remains the most robust approach. The proposed confidence scoring framework enhances the safety of automating LLM-based agents and can be adapted to gate other properties, including safety or compliance.

title: Modeling Event-Conditioned Emotional Expression Response with LLM Agents in a Synthetic Social Simulation
description:
arXiv:2611.31851v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Emotions are central drivers of human behavior, yet most behavioral models fail to capture their role in shaping perception, decision-making, and collective action. Application areas such as emergency response and public health are especially constrained by the lack of emotion-aware modeling. While large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into agent-based models (ABMs), little work has examined how to endow LLM agents with emotional reasoning or validated their ability to reproduce empirically observed emotional patterns. This study addresses this gap by introducing a hierarchical prompting framework that conditions LLM agents with demographic, psychological, and contextual cues to generate event-conditioned emotional responses to real-world events. We validate the resulting event-conditioned emotional responses against large-scale social media reaction data derived from the Social Science One Facebook URL Shares Dataset, complemented by demographic and personality benchmarks. Our simulation results reproduce both polarized and consensus-driven emotional patterns with significant fidelity, supporting the application of LLM agents for emotion-aware modeling in behavioral simulations. We also find, however, that systematic gaps in emotional expression of LLM agents and human populations exist, such as the underexpression of anger relative to human baselines. As such, these findings highlight the need for continued calibration if LLM agents are to serve as proxies for human populations in behavioral modeling. By quantifying their divergence from human populations in terms of emotional expression, we hope that our methods can aid in this effort.

title: Do Not Let the Prior Heal the Anomaly: Selective Anchoring for Detection from Incomplete Measurements
description:
arXiv:2611.33331v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative priors can recover anatomical detail from incomplete medical measurements, but may erase the very lesions that imaging aims to detect, even when the measurements contain evidence of them. We introduce selective anchoring that protects reliably measured image components from prior-driven changes, while allowing expressive generative models to reconstruct unresolved structure. Acquisition uncertainty in the protected components is either added deterministically to the downstream test or carried by the ensemble through stochastic perturbations of the readings. We implement this principle as a wrapper for pretrained diffusion and flow samplers and as AnchoredFM, a fast constrained flow model. Under a linear-Gaussian measurement model, the protected coefficients are unbiased in expectation and achieve nominal interval coverage across repeated acquisitions, independently of the learned prior. Across sparse-view CT, accelerated brain MRI, and photoacoustic tomography, selective anchoring improves lesion contrast preservation and uncertainty reliability, and can reduce reconstruction error within lesions. For tumor detection in accelerated MRI, with a healthy reference estimated from the measurements alone, deterministic anchoring raises mean AUROC across eight samplers from 78.4% to 84.6% and lesion sensitivity at 0.25 false-positive marks per slice from 38.8% to 47.5%, with gains in all four predefined tumor-size groups. At thresholds frozen on healthy validation data, mean sensitivity rises from 20.2% to 44.1% (37.6% with stochastic anchoring). These findings show how expressive generative priors can reconstruct unresolved anatomy without healing away the abnormalities that the measurements support.

title: Don't let your agents' dreams turn into nightmares. Let them daydream.
description:
Agent memory had a busy year. The newest trick is dreaming: a background job that, between sessions, reads back through an agent's logs and rewrites its memory. It merges duplicates, corrects notes it thinks are wrong, and promotes the important ones into the context the next session starts with. Anthropic described it this month as offline reflection on logs, named after the way the hippocampus replays the day while you sleep (https://anthropic.com/research/components-of-agent-memory).
I build OmniMem (https://github.com/richarvey/OmniMem), an open source memory server for AI agents, written in Rust and served over MCP. Dreaming tackles the problem I care about most: agents that never learn from their own sessions. But the way it's usually built, unattended and in the background, runs straight into something we learned the hard way with production systems. State that changes without a gate eventually changes in a way you didn't want.
This post is the argument for manual gates on agent memory, what OmniMem already gates, and how 7.2 adds learning from session transcripts, which I'm calling daydreaming, without giving up any of them.

The criticism, and the gate that answers it

In August The New Stack collected practitioners' reactions to dreaming (https://thenewstack.io/anthropic-agent-memory-dreaming/). In fairness, Anthropic's own talk sent proposed updates to a human for review. The critics' point was that this isn't enough on its own. Here's what they raised, paraphrased, with what OmniMem does about each.

  • Repeated mistakes get promoted to permanent policy, and review becomes a rubber stamp at fleet scale (Jayakumar Ramalingam). In OmniMem nothing becomes a skill or a believed memory without a person accepting it, one item at a time, and proposals carry the memories they came from.- "The right instinct aimed at the wrong evidence", and a store that drifts towards whatever happened lately (Vladimir Beskorovainyi). Daydream's reinforcement gate counts sessions across the whole history, not the latest batch.- Transcripts hold content the agent never wrote, so an automated writer reading them is an attack surface (Viktor Bulanek). The detectors are deterministic pattern matchers, not a model. Transcripts pass the scrub gate first, and every finding waits for a person.- A persisted hallucination becomes infrastructure; provenance matters, and sometimes forgetting is the safe move (Berk Yilmaz). Every memory carries provenance and validity dates, there are tools to end a fact's validity or forget it, and contradiction resolution keeps the losing side for audit.- Dreaming isn't cheap or deterministic like garbage collection; it's repeated paid model runs (Kerstin Frailey). Detection and the skill compiler are deterministic and local. An LLM is optional and only rewords a proposal.The common thread: memory is state that agents act on, so every change to it needs evidence, an owner and a way back. ## What OmniMem already gates (7.0.x, today) None of this is new for 7.2. It's the foundation daydreaming sits on, and it's why I didn't want to bolt on an unattended loop.
  • Skills: propose, then a person accepts. compile_skill in propose mode turns accumulated experience into a SKILL.md draft and returns a diff. Write mode is only a request: by default (HUMAN_APPROVAL=human) OmniMem asks the person through MCP elicitation, or parks the proposal in the settings panel's Pending list when the client can't ask. The compiler is deterministic, so the same sources render a byte-identical skill and a diff only ever shows a real change.- Trust: only a person moves it. Every memory has a trust state: candidate, accepted, disputed, superseded or rejected. Facts the enrichment worker extracts start as candidates. Confirming or rejecting goes through the panel or the CLI, and there is deliberately no MCP tool that can do it. Restoring a backup never raises trust either, so a doctored backup can't promote anything.- Contradictions: resolved, never deleted. check_contradictions links memories that disagree. Its resolve mode records the outcome on both sides and goes through the same human approval as skills. The loser is kept with the reason, and the decision can be reopened.- Provenance and licence on every memory. Retrieved (an outside source), concluded (the system's own reasoning) or asserted (you said it), decided at write time and never scored on.- Time. Memories carry valid_from and valid_to, end_validity closes a fact that stopped being true, and recall accepts valid_at and known_at, so you can ask what was true in March and what OmniMem believed at the time.- Audit. The store writes the audit log in the same transaction as the change. Below the full level no row holds memory text, and a forget scrubs earlier rows for that memory too.- The graveyard. record_experience and log_abandoned record approaches that failed and why. A PreToolUse hook (Claude Code, OpenCode, the Mistral Vibe CLI and Kiro) refuses a tool call that repeats a known dead end. On my dead-end benchmark that hook was the difference: agents with the answer already in the store made no memory calls on their own.## Daydream: learning from transcripts, with you in the room The gap all those gates left: OmniMem only learned from what an agent chose to remember, and agents mostly don't choose. The session transcript is the best record of what really happened, and OmniMem never read it. 7.2 changes that, and it's in development now on the v7.2.x branch. When it runs. Only when a person is there: importing a log, a session-end hook firing, or pressing Daydream now. There is no scheduler. Where the logs come from. Five routes feed one pipeline: the desktop app (local discovery and a local scan), the settings panel's new Logs page (browser upload), omnimem logs import on the CLI, session-end hooks, and a new MCP tool, submit_session_log, for clients that keep no transcripts locally. That's the 50th tool. Day one covers every client OmniMem has a guide for:
  • Read from disk: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor, GitHub Copilot (VS Code), Kiro, Mistral Vibe CLI, OpenCode- Account export upload: claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Mistral Vibe on the web (formerly Le Chat)- Agent submits its own session: GitLab Duo, Lumo, Open Design*What it looks for.* Seven deterministic detectors: tool_error, retry_loop, user_correction, revert, abandoned, recovery and guard_hit. A failure followed by a recovery becomes a proposed piece of experience: the approach that failed, and the fix that worked. Repeated failure with no recovery becomes a proposed dead end. Repeated corrections on one topic become a candidate preference, in your own words. When it proposes. A signal has to recur in at least two distinct sessions, counted across the whole history, before anything is proposed. A pattern seen in one client only stays scoped to that client, which is also the evidence the model-routing work planned for 7.3 will need. Where it lands. As a candidate, with the client, the model and references back to the sessions and turns it came from. It goes into the Pending list. Nothing daydreamed is ever accepted without a person. The defaults change nothing until you import a log: DAYDREAM=manual, DAYDREAM_MIN_SESSIONS=2, DAYDREAM_LLM=off and TRANSCRIPT_RETENTION=none. ## The scrub gate: no secrets reach an LLM Transcripts are where credentials leak: the .env an agent prints, the token in a curl command, the connection string in a stack trace. A memory store is the worst place for one, because recall will put it straight back into a later session's context, and from there into a model provider's request log. ### Where 7.0 was 7.0's Claude Code session-end hook already redacted its session record with a redact() function: seven regexes, compiled on every call. It caught OpenAI-style sk- keys, GitHub tokens, AWS access key IDs, bearer tokens, password= style assignments, PEM private keys and JWTs. It missed GitLab and Slack tokens, Google keys, Tailscale keys and passwords inside database URLs. And nothing stopped a future code path skipping it. ### What 7.2 does instead A new crate, omnimem-scrub, sits in front of everything, and the core idea is to make skipping it impossible to compile. Text straight from a transcript is a RawText: no Display, no Serialize, and a Debug that prints a placeholder. The only way to get a CleanText is Scrubber::scan(), which fails closed. The store, the embedder, the LLM client and the queue take CleanText only. Forgetting to scan stops being a bug you find in production and becomes a build that won't compile. The rules run in layers:
  • Known formats: provider and platform tokens (Anthropic, OpenAI, AWS, GitHub, GitLab, Slack, Stripe, Google, Tailscale, Cloudflare, Hugging Face, npm, PyPI), PEM keys, JWTs, and OmniMem's own bearer and OAuth secrets- Credentials in structure: passwords in URLs, Authorization and Cookie headers, .env blocks, password flags- Keyword plus entropy: a high-entropy value next to secret, token or api_key, the way gitleaks does it, which catches formats nobody listed- Your own secrets by fingerprint: register a token or a config file and OmniMem keeps a salted SHA-256 and a length, never the value- Personal data, opt-in: emails, phone numbers, private IPs, tailnet hostnamesThe built-in pack is written in gitleaks' TOML rule format, so you can drop in an existing gitleaks.toml. A hit becomes a typed placeholder carrying a short keyed hash, so the same secret gets the same placeholder throughout a session and "the key that failed" still makes sense to a detector, but the value is never recoverable. Rules marked as blocking, like private keys, drop the whole turn, and too many in one session quarantine it for review. The crate also builds for WebAssembly, so the settings panel scans a log in your browser before upload, and the server scans it again on arrival. The findings report holds counts and offsets, never values. With the default retention, no transcript text is stored at all. The tests are the part I'll hold the release on. A canary test plants fake secrets of every rule type in every adapter's fixtures, runs a full import and daydream, then byte-searches the database, the WAL, the audit log, captured tracing output, the embedder's inputs and a mocked LLM's request log. One hit fails the build. ## Follow along, or pick something up Dreaming will mature, and plenty of the people building it care about these problems. My position is simple: memory that agents act on should only change when a person says so, with the evidence attached and a way back. Let your agents daydream. Keep the nightmares out. All of 7.2 is public:
  • Milestone 7.2.0, 18 issues starting with the scrub gate: https://github.com/richarvey/OmniMem/milestone/6- Milestone 7.2.1, the follow-ups: https://github.com/richarvey/OmniMem/milestone/7- The scrub gate issue, with the type design: https://github.com/richarvey/OmniMem/issues/44- The spec: https://github.com/richarvey/OmniMem/blob/v7.2.x/docs/daydream-spec.mdIf you know one of these clients' log formats better than its docs do, the adapter issues are a good place to start. And if you think a gate is still too thin, I'd rather hear it now than after release. Reply here, open an issue, or find me on Mastodon at https://mastodon.squarecows.com/@ric

title: Constructive Causal Abstraction and a Case Study in Mechanistic Interpretability
description:
arXiv:2611.31795v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing frameworks in causal abstraction first propose a high-level causal model, and then verify whether its interventional effects agree with those of a given micro-level model - the two models are declared causally consistent when the discrepancy is zero. However, proposing a consistent macro causal model is difficult, because macro causal relations are almost never well-defined, since distinct micro-level interventions associated with the same apparent macro intervention can produce different effects. Our central insight is that causally consistent macro-level models can be obtained constructively: ill-defined macro interventions can be interpreted as missing variables on the macro level, and can be accounted for by introducing a complementary variable q that retains omitted causally relevant state. In the linear case, q has a unique form and we provide sufficient conditions for valid implementations to exist; in the nonlinear case, we provide an ODE-based algorithm for constructing implementations. We call this framework Constructive Causal Abstraction (CCA), and use CCA to formulate the difference between machine-learning model auditing and editing. With the Bias-in-Bios biographies dataset, we demonstrate that CCA allows practitioners to articulate assumptions when detecting the model's gender bias. Finally, CCA resolves a well-known paradox known as "interpretability illusion" which points to a mismatch between the subspace for editing and the one where the model implements a signal-to-output pathway.

title: A Generative AI Agent to Emulate Interactive Human-driven Vehicles for Automated Driving Testing in Urban Areas
description:
arXiv:2611.31797v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Realistic modeling of human-driven vehicle (HDV) interactions is essential for automated driving safety testing in urban areas. Existing methods struggle to reproduce realistic safety-critical interactions involving high collision risk for the following reasons: they often assume full observability, overlooking interactions arising from occlusion. Driving styles are mainly characterized by vehicle maneuvers, limiting the diversity of safety-critical interaction behaviors. Moreover, learning signals from safety-critical interactions can be diluted by non-critical driving behaviors. To address these issues, we propose a generative AI agent to emulate interactive HDVs. The agent incorporates field-of-view modeling to account for driver visibility under occlusion and characterizes the interaction process using five metrics spanning its initial, intermediate, and final stages. It automatically learns diverse interaction styles through a dynamic mixture-of-experts network. Through residual reinforcement learning, the agent further refines generated trajectories to match the real-world distributions of safety-critical interaction characteristics. Experiments on the INTERACTION dataset show that our method reduces Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD) by 39.9\%--87.1\% across five interaction characteristics compared with a state-of-the-art baseline. Our method achieves greater improvements of up to 87.1\% in final-stage interaction metrics, suggesting that it can reduce error accumulation in long-horizon trajectory generation. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each proposed component, particularly highlighting the importance of residual refinement. Generalization experiments show that our method approaches the performance of full training on unseen intersections with only one epoch of fine-tuning.

title: Beyond Random Starts: Amortized Initialization for Adversarial Attacks on Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.33414v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Gradient-based transferable adversarial attacks achieve state-of-the-art attack success rates against black-box vision-language models (VLMs). However, they require hundreds of costly optimization steps for each image pair. One possible reason is that these attacks typically start from random perturbations that contain no information about the source or target image. In this work, we study whether amortized adversarial generation can provide better initializations for gradient-based attacks. By learning across many image pairs, amortization allows a generator to produce adversarial perturbations for new inputs without optimizing each perturbation from scratch. We introduce SPARK, a lightweight looped perturbation generator conditioned on both the source and target images. SPARK repeatedly applies the same network to refine a perturbation, producing effective adversarial attacks in a few forward passes without requiring gradients through surrogate vision encoders at inference time. We show that these perturbations provide effective warm starts for existing gradient-based attacks, substantially improving attack success rates while reducing the number of optimization steps required. These improvements generalize across different attack methods, VLMs, and unseen image categories. SPARK also produces effective standalone attacks at a fraction of the computational cost of gradient-based optimization. Code and model weights are available at https://github.com/Patchwork53/SPARK.

title: PINN-Slicer: Exploiting Rotational Symmetry to Solve the Photon Orbit Equation Around a Black Hole
description:
arXiv:2611.33953v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) typically struggle with long-horizon domains, often requiring the network to be retrained as the domain grows. We present PINN-Slicer, a method for second-order autonomous ordinary differential equations, $\ddot{u} = G(u, \dot{u})$, which exploits the invariance of this class of equations under translations of the independent variable. A single PINN, embedded within a solution ansatz that enforces the initial conditions explicitly, is trained on a thin slice of the independent variable using Sobol-sampled initial conditions. The PINN is then deployed recursively, slice-by-slice, across the full domain. We demonstrate PINN-Slicer on the nonlinear equation that describes photon orbits around a black hole, and reach a point-by-point root-mean-square error (RMSE) below $10^{-3}$ in $u = r_s/r$ (the inverse radial coordinate in units of the Schwarzschild radius) relative to a finite-difference reference solution. A key advantage of PINN-Slicer is that a single trained network generalizes to any orbital initial condition within the training range, without retraining. In addition, PINN-Slicer can cope with solution domains that may not be known a priori.

title: VersionGS: Compact and Motion-Robust Dynamic Gaussian Splatting via Versioned Gaussians
description:
arXiv:2611.33374v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent dynamic Gaussian splatting methods encode temporal change, either as smooth functions of time or as constrained updates between frames. We observe that their reconstruction quality degrades significantly under fast motion. In challenging dance sequences, their PSNR drops by 1.1-4.0 dB on high-motion frames compared to low-motion frames. To overcome this limitation, we propose VersionGS, a method that directly encodes per-frame Gaussian states and uses motion estimation only to guide reconstruction. Within each group of frames, unchanged Gaussians keep their current versions in a shared dictionary, while modified Gaussians are appended as new versions. To maximize version reuse, we introduce selective sequential construction, which refines the Gaussians selected by optical flow, photograph differences or rendering errors and leaves the others unchanged. The dictionary is then pruned, fine-tuned with simulated quantization and encoded as images. Adjusting the pruning ratio trades off storage and quality without rebuilding the dictionary. On the fast dance sequences of DanceNet3D, VersionGS improves foreground PSNR by 2.7 dB over the best baseline, and its PSNR decreases by less than 0.3 dB on the highest-motion frames. On N3DV and Technicolor, it requires 6.0x and 5.7x less storage than TAD-GS, the strongest baseline overall, while achieving even higher PSNR. Finally, playback is fast and requires no motion model or neural network, only a 3DGS rasterizer.

title: FlowersBench: A FluidFlower-Inspired Dataset for Benchmarking Carbon Storage Surrogates Across Geological Structures
description:
arXiv:2611.33335v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Machine learning surrogates are emerging as a computationally efficient tool for uncertainty quantification in geological carbon storage (GCS). Geological structure constitutes a major source of uncertainty; however, existing benchmark simulation datasets predominantly vary petrophysical and operational parameters within a fixed geological setting. Generalisation to unseen geological structures therefore remains largely unexplored. We introduce FlowersBench, a benchmark dataset of 5,000 two-dimensional, reservoir-scale CO$_2$ storage simulations across 244 structural geometries. The geometries are sampled from an in-house structural generator inspired by the FluidFlower experiments and Case B of the 11th Society of Petroleum Engineers Comparative Solution Project (SPE11B). Each simulation is run with Open Porous Media (OPM) Flow over a 50-year injection period and a 500-year post-injection monitoring period. Test geometries are withheld from training to assess generalisation to unseen structural geometries. Two additional subsets support evaluation under structural shift. The first extends the parameter ranges of the structural generator beyond those used for training, and the second introduces an unseen topology of multiple parallel faults. A baseline U-Net surrogate is trained to predict CO$_2$ gas saturation. In representative test cases, the surrogate recovers the main migration pathways, including lateral spreading beneath low-permeability layers and upward flow along fault damage zones, with errors concentrated near the plume boundary. Under both structural shifts, prediction error exceeds that on the held-out geometries, and the increase in relative error is greater for the unseen fault topology. FlowersBench is publicly available and provides a common basis for evaluating GCS surrogates across geological structures.

title: Parts search starts from the bike, not the part number
description:
A buyer who needs a spare part rarely knows its number. They know their machine: a road bike, 11-speed, disc brakes, a 12x142 rear axle. So parts search has to start there, and the hard part is not matching words but deciding what fits. I built search that starts from the machine on a commercial parts platform; that code is not mine to publish, so here is the same idea on an open-source reference store with an invented catalog, where every number below can be rerun: mcp-commerce-evals (Rust, MIT).

Compatibility is data, with dimensions

The store's catalog has 500 parts, and each one lists what it fits as tags in five dimensions: drivetrain speed, bike type, wheel size, brake type and axle standard. One rule decides whether a part fits a bike:

pub fn is_compatible(fits: &[String], required: &[String]) -> bool {
    required.iter().all(|req| match dimension_of(req) {
        Some(dim) => {
            let constrained = fits.iter().any(|t| dim.contains(&t.as_str()));
            !constrained || fits.contains(req)
        }
        None => fits.contains(req),
    })
}

A part that lists no tag in a dimension does not care about it: a saddle fits any drivetrain. A part that lists some tags in a dimension fits only a bike with one of them: an 11-speed chain does not fit a 12-speed bike. Before the rule runs, what the buyer typed is made canonical, so 11 speed becomes 11-speed, Disc Brakes becomes disc-brake, 29er becomes 29in and MTB becomes mountain.

Filter, do not only match words

The tags are also indexed as text, so a sentence works on its own: "a chain that fits my 11-speed road bike" drops the filler words and searches for chain, 11speed and road. But a long sentence mixes words about the part with words about the bike, and the bike words can win.

"rear hub for a 12x142 thru axle frame with an 11-speed disc brake setup", sent as text only, returns five thru axles first. "Thru axle" and "12x142" are in their titles; the first expected hub is 9th. The same need sent as query: "rear hub", category: "hub" and fits: ["12x142", "11-speed", "disc-brake"] returns five hubs, all of them right.

The filters have their own trap. "11-speed chain, in stock, under $30" with fits: ["11-speed"], stock and price filters but no category returns chain lube first. Lube lists no compatibility tags, so by the rule above it fits every bike and passes every fit filter, and the word "chain" is in its title. Add category: "chain" and the search returns exactly the three expected chains. Universal parts are correct for the rule and noise for the buyer: a fit filter needs a category next to it.

That is why the store's search_products tool takes free text plus brand, category, fits, in_stock_only and max_price_usd, and its description tells the assistant what fits looks like. The hub query shows what it is worth when the assistant turns "my bike" into filters instead of pasting the sentence.

The eval marked a good question wrong

The repo measures the store twice: tool-level, by calling the search tool directly, and assistant-level, by letting a model shop through the tools and scoring the part id it commits to. On the 8 compatibility queries the tool-level hit@1 is 0.88 (95% interval 0.53 to 0.98); the one miss is the hub query above. With an assistant on top, Claude Haiku (3 trials per query) and Claude Sonnet (1 trial) both scored 0.88 on the same kind.

The misses were not retrieval failures. On "disc rotor that works on my e-bike" twelve rotors fit by tag: five centerlock and seven 6-bolt, in 180 or 203 mm. Both models listed rotors and asked two questions: is the hub 6-bolt or centerlock, and which diameter. Haiku did that in all three trials and committed nothing; Sonnet committed none.

Both questions are right. A rotor has to match the hub's mount, and the frame or fork caps the diameter, as Sonnet's reply added. In this catalog the hub and the rotor both record their mount, but as plain attributes: mount is not one of the five dimensions, so no fit filter can use it. And the catalog has no frames or forks, so nothing records a maximum rotor size. The scorer rewards committing to a part, so asking back counts as a miss.

"skewer for my road bike" shows the other way to handle a missing fact. In one of three trials Haiku asked whether the bike is quick-release or thru-axle and committed nothing. Sonnet wrote "I'm assuming your bike has quick-release dropouts", named the 12x142 and 12x100 thru axles it would offer otherwise, and committed to a skewer. Same uncertainty, but the buyer gets an answer and a way to correct it.

Three things I take from it:

  • The assistant found holes in the compatibility model before any buyer did: brake mount should be a dimension that constrains both rotors and hubs, and the maximum rotor size belongs to the frame and fork.
  • "Asked a fair question" should be its own outcome in an eval, not a failure. Otherwise the score pushes you toward an assistant that guesses.
  • When one answer is far more likely, "assume it, say so, commit" serves the buyer better than a list of questions. The tool description is the place to ask for that.

What I would not claim

Eight compatibility queries is a small sample, and the interval runs from 0.53 to 0.98. I wrote the catalog and the queries myself, so this shows that compatibility can be modelled and measured, not how well any real store does. The model runs had no fixed temperature, so a rerun will differ.

The rule, the tags and the eval are in the repo: github.com/Vladimir-Pirotskiy/mcp-commerce-evals. The first post, on what the evals measured overall: I measured how well an AI assistant shops through MCP. More of my work: pirotskiy.com.

title: A Lazy-Loading Vertical Video Grid in Plain JavaScript
description:
Profile pages on short-video sites are long grids of 9:16 thumbnails, often hundreds of them. Rendering every image and preview at once makes the page slow, especially on phones. This post builds a small vertical-video grid in plain JavaScript that loads thumbnails only when they approach the viewport, plays a muted preview on hover, and keeps layout stable while images load.

Markup and layout 

<ul class="grid" id="grid"></ul>

.grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(140px, 1fr));
  gap: 8px;
  list-style: none;
  padding: 0;
}
.tile {
  position: relative;
  aspect-ratio: 9 / 16;      /* reserves space, no layout shift */
  background: #222;
  border-radius: 8px;
  overflow: hidden;
}
.tile img, .tile video {
  width: 100%;
  height: 100%;
  object-fit: cover;
  display: block;
}
.tile .views {
  position: absolute;
  left: 6px;
  bottom: 6px;
  color: #fff;
  font: 600 12px/1 system-ui, sans-serif;
  text-shadow: 0 1px 2px rgba(0, 0, 0, .6);
}

aspect-ratio: 9 / 16 is the important line. Each tile has its final size before the image arrives, so the grid never jumps.

Creating tiles without loading images

Store the real URL in a data attribute and leave src empty:

function createTile({ thumb, preview, views }) {
  const li = document.createElement("li");
  li.className = "tile";
  li.innerHTML = `
    <img alt="" data-src="${thumb}" decoding="async">
    <span class="views">${views}</span>`;
  li.dataset.preview = preview || "";
  return li;
}

Lazy loading with IntersectionObserver 

const io = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
  for (const entry of entries) {
    if (!entry.isIntersecting) continue;
    const img = entry.target.querySelector("img[data-src]");
    if (img) {
      img.src = img.dataset.src;
      img.removeAttribute("data-src");
    }
    io.unobserve(entry.target);
  }
}, { rootMargin: "400px 0px" }); // start loading a bit before tiles appear

A rootMargin of a few hundred pixels hides the loading from users who scroll at a normal speed. Native loading="lazy" also works for images, but the observer gives you one place to hook in previews, analytics or placeholders.

Hover previews that do not pile up

Creating a <video> element for every tile is expensive. Create one on hover and remove it on leave:

function attachPreview(tile) {
  let video = null;
  tile.addEventListener("mouseenter", () => {
    if (!tile.dataset.preview) return;
    video = document.createElement("video");
    Object.assign(video, { src: tile.dataset.preview, muted: true, loop: true, playsInline: true });
    tile.appendChild(video);
    video.play().catch(() => {}); // autoplay can still be blocked
  });
  tile.addEventListener("mouseleave", () => {
    if (video) { video.pause(); video.remove(); video = null; }
  });
}

Muted, inline playback is what browsers allow without a user gesture. On touch devices skip previews entirely; matchMedia("(hover: hover)") tells you whether hover exists.

Rendering in batches 

const grid = document.getElementById("grid");
const canHover = matchMedia("(hover: hover)").matches;

function render(items) {
  const frag = document.createDocumentFragment();
  for (const item of items) {
    const tile = createTile(item);
    if (canHover) attachPreview(tile);
    io.observe(tile);
    frag.appendChild(tile);
  }
  grid.appendChild(frag);
}

For very long lists, fetch the next page when a sentinel element at the end of the grid intersects, and call render again.

Seeing the pattern in practice

If you want to see how a real public profile grid behaves, with hundreds of tiles and view counts on each, a public TikTok profile viewer shows that layout in a normal browser tab. Watching the network panel while scrolling one is a quick way to compare a production grid with your own implementation.

Summary

  • Reserve space with aspect-ratio to avoid layout shift.
  • Load thumbnails with IntersectionObserver and a generous rootMargin.
  • Create preview videos on demand and destroy them on leave.
  • Append tiles in batches with a DocumentFragment.

title: Decision-1.1 now available on AI Gateway
description:
Decision-1.1 from Microsoft AI is now available on AI Gateway. It is more accurate, better calibrated, and faster than Decision-1.

The decision model returns structured answers instead of free-form text for tasks such as routing support requests, choosing which model should handle a request, selecting the next step in a workflow, or grading AI responses.

  • Boolean: the probability that a condition is true

  • Choice: a selected category and probabilities for each option

  • Score: a numerical rating on a scale you define

Multiple questions can share the same input in one request. Better calibration means the model's probabilities track how often it is right, so your application can set thresholds for when to act, flag a case for review, or escalate.

Decision-1.1 accepts the same request format as Decision-1. To switch, change the model ID to microsoft/decision-1.1.

Call it through the AI SDK, the OpenAI-compatible Decisions API, or the AI CLI. The examples below require ai 7.0.128 or later for TypeScript, or the OpenAI Python SDK 3.26.0 or later for Python.

Decision requests appear in request logs, count toward budgets, and support decision fallbacks.

Try Decision-1.1 in the model playground, or see the decision models documentation for request formats and question types.

Read more
