title: Deletion You Can Check: Auditing LLM Unlearning
description:
arXiv:2611.33525v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A common indication that a fine-tuned model has forgotten a deleted record is a membership-inference score near chance (ROC-AUC $\approx 0.5$). This reading is sound only if the comparison population represents how the record should behave after a valid deletion---a counterfactual that is rarely validated. We test this premise in a controlled $2\times2$ study pairing two membership-inference benchmarks, ArxivMIA and BookMIA, with two language models, Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen2.5-1.5B. Exact retraining validates the membership reference: it lies within the prespecified chance band on ArxivMIA but reaches $0.122$ on BookMIA, causing the same metric to reject an empirical deletion reference. A post-hoc BookMIA/Qwen diagnostic replaces benchmark label-0 records with same-pool, never-fine-tuned records and moves the reference from $0.257$ to $0.523$, supporting population mismatch in that cell. Each approximate-unlearning checkpoint is judged jointly on membership removal, deletion-targeted shift beyond non-deletion variation, and utility. On the admitted ArxivMIA/Llama axis, no tested configuration of gradient ascent with retain descent (GA+GD), negative-preference optimization with retain training (NPO-RT), or teacher--student unlearning (SCRUB) passes. A score near chance is not evidence of forgetting until a reference establishes what chance means.

title: Constructing physical mechanisms with artificial intelligence
description:
arXiv:2611.31653v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mechanisms recur across the sciences: the equation for heat in a solid also describes molecular diffusion or a Brownian particle. A mechanism is rarely written in one equation; its operation, boundaries, parameters and closures are stated at different steps of a derivation, where methods that read text or fit formulas miss it. We built an equation-native system that reads the equations of all 2.5 million arXiv manuscripts, and show that mechanisms can be compiled from them and constructed by deterministic calculation. A constructor detaches, transfers, unfolds, composes and joins their parts across disciplines; where parts do not fit, the failure is an equation for the missing term. Constructions turn a threshold reactor into a memory that a weak signal writes, an oscillator into a switch through two changes that each fail alone, and a rhythm into the regulator of a chemical amount, each with conditions for an experimental test.

title: Anthropic Messages API Rust Geçişi: Claude API Kullanıcıları İçin Neler Değişti?
description:
Anthropic, Claude Messages API'sini Python'dan Rust'a Taşıdı — Peki Siz İçin Ne Değişti?

Anthropic, her Claude API çağrısının arkasındaki /v1/messages uç noktası olan Messages API'sini Python'dan Rust'a taşıdı. Anthropic'in Rust ile yazılmış Messages API servisi Eylül 2026'dan beri herkese açık trafiği karşılıyor. Anthropic, istek başına yaklaşık %70 daha az CPU ve ilk token'a kadar geçen sürenin (time to first token) medyanında yaklaşık %20'lik bir düşüş bildiriyor. İstek ve yanıt biçiminiz değişmedi.

Apidog'u bugün deneyin

Aşağıda: Anthropic'in ne ölçtüğü, yeni servisin eski servisle birebir eşleştiğini nasıl kanıtladığı, yeniden neyi test etmeniz gerektiği ve ilk token süresini (TTFT) kendinizin nasıl ölçeceği yer alıyor.

Ne oldu: Messages API artık Rust üzerinde çalışıyor

Messages API, HTTP isteğinizi bir isteme (prompt) dönüştüren, bunu Claude üzerinden çalıştıran ve yanıtı akış (streaming) halinde geri gönderen servistir. Anthropic bunu 2023'te Python ile geliştirdi. 25 Kasım 2026'da Anthropic'in mühendislik ekibi, Eylül 2026'da herkese açık trafiği devralan eksiksiz bir yeniden yazımı anlatan Migrating our Messages API to Rust yazısını yayımladı.

Yazıdan bilinmesi gereken üç sayı var; bunların kapsamını da Anthropic bir şekil (figure) açıklamasında belirtiyor:

Metrik Bildirilen değişim Anthropic'in verdiği kapsam
İstek başına CPU yaklaşık %70 daha düşük tek bölge, Ağustos–Ekim
İstek başına bellek %80'den fazla daha düşük tüm üretim ortamı, Ağustos–Ekim
Medyan ilk token süresi (TTFT) yaklaşık %20 daha düşük müşterilerin Claude Code istekleri, kabaca 7–21 Eylül

TTFT sayısı Claude Code trafiğinden geliyor, her API müşterisinden değil; dolayısıyla kendi gördüğünüz değişim daha büyük, daha küçük ya da hiç görünmez olabilir. CPU ve bellek tasarrufları Anthropic'in sunucularına ait.

Peki neden? Anthropic'e göre API trafiği 2024 başından 2026 sonbaharına kadar kabaca 1.800 kat büyüdü ve Python her adımda ek yük getiriyordu. Yalnızca çıktı ayrıştırmaya (output parsing) yapılan kısmi bir yeniden yazım CPU'yu yalnızca yaklaşık %8–10 azalttı.

Messages API her istekte ne yapar

Anthropic'in yazısına göre her istek şu aşamalardan geçer:

  1. İsteği doğrula ve kabul et ya da reddet.
  2. Sistem isteminizden, mesajlardan ve araç tanımlarından istemeyi oluştur; bu sırada ayarları çözümle.
  3. İstemeyi token'lara ayır (tokenize).
  4. Güvenlik sınıflandırıcılarıyla tarayıp denetle.
  5. Modeli çalıştır; model yanıtı tek tek token'lar halinde yazar.
  6. Çıktıyı metin, düşünme (thinking) ve araç çağrılarına ayrıştır.
  7. Olayları size akıt ve hız sınırları ile faturalandırma için kullanımı say.

Model hariç her şey Rust'a taşındı. 1, 2, 6 ve 7. adımlar, entegrasyonunuzun API'ye dokunduğu noktalardır: doğrulama hataları, araç tanımları, dönen araç çağrıları ve kullanım sayıları.

Anthropic Rust yeniden yazımını nasıl doğruladı

İlginç olan kısım Rust değil; doğrulama. Rust sürümü Nisan ayına kadar Anthropic'in kabaca 700 entegrasyon testinin yaklaşık %98'inden geçmişti, ancak üretim girdilerinin yalnızca yaklaşık dörtte biri eşleşiyordu. Testler tek başına yeterli değildi.

Bunun üzerine ekip, Rust'u canlı Python servisinin yanında bir gölge (shadow) olarak çalıştırdı. Model bir kez çalıştırıldı ve çıktısı Rust'a tekrar oynatıldı (replay), böylece determinizm olmayışı sahte bir fark üretemedi. Her adım karşılaştırıldı ve ilk sapma hatanın kabaca nerede olduğunu gösteriyordu.

İki detay öne çıkıyor:

  • Tasarımdan gelen gizlilik. Mühendisler kullanıcı isteklerini ya da Claude'un yanıtlarını okumadı. Bir diff kaydı yalnızca kendi biçimini tutuyordu: adım, ilk farklılaşan byte ve uzunluklar.
  • Ön incelemeyi (triage) ajanlar yaptı. Koordine eden bir Claude ajanı her yeni fark türünü bir işçi ajana veriyor; o ajan bunu bir kum havuzunda (sandbox) yeniden üretiyor, Rust kodunu düzeltiyor ve bir test ekliyordu. Düzeltmeleri mühendisler gözden geçiriyordu.

Üretim eşleşme oranı, yazıdaki grafiğe göre başlangıçtaki %24'ten Ağustos'a kadar %99,6'ya çıktı. Herkese açık trafik Eylül'de taşındı.

Claude API kullanıcıları için ne değişti, ne değişmedi

İşte pratik tablo:

Alan Değişti mi? Ne yapmalısınız
Uç nokta, başlıklar, istek gövdesi Değişiklik duyurulmadı Hiçbir şey
Yanıt ve akış olayı biçimleri Değişiklik duyurulmadı Sözleşme testlerinizi çalıştırmaya devam edin
Model davranışı Hayır (aynı modeller) Hiçbir şey
Medyan TTFT Claude Code trafiğinde daha düşük Kendi değerinizi ölçün
İstem oluşturma ve çıktı ayrıştırmadaki uç durumlar Python ile tam eşleşecek şekilde yazıldı Araçlar, kullanım ve limitler üzerinde testleri yeniden çalıştırın

Yazı, herkese açık sözleşmede herhangi bir değişiklik duyurmuyor. Amaç, Python servisiyle tam eşleşmeydi: "böylece bir müşterinin aldığı şeyi değiştirebilecek her türlü sapmayı yakalayabilirdik." Entegrasyonunuz muhtemelen Eylül ayından beri zaten Rust üzerinde çalışıyor.

Anthropic'in yol boyunca bulduğu hatalar yine de faydalı bir kontrol listesi oluşturuyor:

  • Araç çağrılarında JSON kaçış karakterleri. Python, emoji gibi belirli karakterleri metin kodlarına dönüştürüyordu (escape); ilk Rust sürümü bunları olduğu gibi yazdı. İkisi de geçerli JSON'dur. Ham araç çağrısı dizgelerini hash'liyor, önbelleğe alıyor ya da byte düzeyinde karşılaştırıyorsanız, önce ayrıştırın (parse).
  • Yanlış boyutta okunan bir bağlam limiti. Bir diff, 1M limitinin 200K olarak okunduğunu gösterdi. Uzun bir istemi beklediğiniz limite karşı test edin.
  • Eksik araç açıklamaları ve silinen satır sonları. Kendisinin bir kısmını kaybeden bir istem (prompt) yine de 200 döndürür ve makul görünen bir yanıt verir; bu yüzden bu hatalar sessizdir. Araç ağırlıklı istemlerinizde yalnızca durum kodlarına değil, çıktı kalitesine de iddiada (assert) bulunun.
  • Eksik kullanım alanları. Faturalandırma panolarınız usage alanını okur. input_tokens ve output_tokens alanlarının her zaman mevcut olduğuna dair iddiada bulunun.

Bunların hiçbiri bugün bilinen açık bir sorun değil. Bunlar, özellikle daha yeni bir API sürümüne de sabitlediyseniz (pin), sözleşme testine değer kategorilerdir; Claude API version 2026-10-21 rehberimiz o yükseltmeyi ayrıntılı ele alıyor.

Kendi çağrılarınızda ilk token süresini nasıl ölçersiniz

İlk token süresi (TTFT), bir istek gönderdikten sonra üretilmiş metnin ilk parçasını alana kadar geçen gecikmedir. Akışlı (streaming) bir çağrıda bu, ilk content_block_delta olayıdır; HTTP 200 veya message_start değil, çünkü bunlar model henüz hiçbir şey yazmadan önce gelir. Akış dokümantasyonu olay sırasının tamamını listeliyor.

  1. Bunu ttft.mjs olarak kaydedin (Node 18 veya üzeri): 
const t0 = performance.now();
const res = await fetch("https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "x-api-key": process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY,
    "anthropic-version": "2023-06-01",
    "content-type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    model: "claude-haiku-5-5",
    max_tokens: 64,
    stream: true,
    messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Name three rivers in five words." }],
  }),
});
const requestId = res.headers.get("request-id");
const decoder = new TextDecoder();
let ttft = null;
for await (const chunk of res.body) {
  const text = decoder.decode(chunk, { stream: true });
  if (ttft === null && text.includes("event: content_block_delta")) {
    ttft = performance.now() - t0;
  }
}
const total = performance.now() - t0;
console.log(JSON.stringify({ requestId, status: res.status,
  ttftMs: Math.round(ttft), totalMs: Math.round(total) }));
  1. 20 kez veya daha fazla çalıştırın; tek bir örnek çoğunlukla ağ titreşimidir.
  2. Medyanı ve p95'i raporlayın. Anthropic'in iddiası medyanla ilgili.
  3. İstemi, modeli ve max_tokens değerini sabit tutun ve destek için request-id değerini kaydedin (bkz. hata referansı).
  4. 429 ve 529 yanıtlarını ayrı sayın: bunlar gecikme değil, hız sınırlama ve aşırı yüktür. Claude API rate limits rehberimize bakın.

Kod yazan ajanınızın kontrolü Apidog CLI ile çalıştırmasına izin verin

Bir gecikme betiği API'nin ne kadar hızlı olduğunu söyler; bir sözleşme testi ise kodunuzun beklediğini hâlâ döndürdüğünü söyler. Apidog CLI, Claude Code, Codex veya başka bir kod yazan ajanın Apidog projenizde testi oluşturmasını ve çalıştırmasını sağlar.

Bir kez kurun:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

Sonra ajanınıza tek bir istem verin:

In Apidog project <projectId>, add an environment whose base URL is
https://api.anthropic.com and that reads my key from ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Create the
endpoint POST /v1/messages and a test case that sends a short non-streaming request
to claude-haiku-5-5 with max_tokens 64 and asserts: status 200, a request-id header,
content[0].type is text, stop_reason is end_turn or max_tokens, and
usage.input_tokens and usage.output_tokens are integers. Run it 20 times, list
failures with their request-id, then run ttft.mjs 20 times and report median and p95.

Ajan mevcut ortamları kontrol eder, tahmin yürütmek yerine yük biçimlerini okur, sonra senaryoyu yazar ve çalıştırır:


apidog environment list --project <projectId>
apidog environment create "Claude API" --project <projectId> --base-url https://api.anthropic.com
apidog cli-schema get endpoint-create
apidog endpoint create --project <projectId> --file messages-endpoint.json
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file messages-contract.json
apidog test-case create --project <projectId> --file messages-contract.json
apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <projectId> -e <envId> -n 20 -r cli,json

-n 20 senaryoyu tekrarlar ve -r cli,json ajanın size geri okuduğu bir rapor yazar. Aynı apidog run ... -r junit adımını CI'a koyun; yanıt biçimindeki sessiz bir değişiklik, faturalandırma panonuzu bozmak yerine build'inizi düşürür; Apidog CLI CI/CD pipeline guide kopyala-yapıştır bir kurulum içeriyor. CLI'da yeni misiniz? Claude Code'da Apidog CLI nasıl kullanılır yazısıyla başlayın.

Ekibiniz Claude API'ye birden fazla servisten çağrı yapıyorsa, Sharkly, her birinin sözleşme kontrolünü paylaşımlı bir panodaki görev olarak bir kod yazan ajana devretmenizi sağlar; ajanlar mevcut Claude Code veya Codex planınız altında kendi makinelerinizde çalışır ve birleştirmeden (merge) önce ürettiklerini gözden geçirebilirsiniz. Başlangıç için ücretsizdir.

Sonuç

Anthropic'in Messages API Rust geçişi, sizden hiç eylem istenmeyen bir sunucu tarafı değişiklikti — ve asıl mesele de buydu: Anthropic, aylarca yeni servisin gerçek trafikte eskisiyle eşleştiğini kanıtladı.

Yine de "aynı sözleşme" iddiası, bir öğleden sonra içinde doğrulayabileceğiniz bir iddiadır. Kendi TTFT'nizi ölçün, araç çağrıları, kullanım alanları ve limitler üzerinde bir sözleşme testi bulundurun ve kod yazan ajanınızın ikisini de bir zamanlamayla çalıştırmasına izin verin.

SSS

Anthropic, Rust'a geçerken Claude API'yi değiştirdi mi? İstek veya yanıt biçiminde bir değişiklik duyurulmadı. Anthropic'in amacı Python servisiyle tam eşleşmeydi; bu, Eylül 2026'daki geçişten önce adım adım üretim trafiğine karşı doğrulandı.

Claude API artık daha hızlı mı? Anthropic, kabaca 7–21 Eylül arasında müşterilerin Claude Code isteklerinde ölçülen medyan ilk token süresinde yaklaşık %20'lik bir düşüş bildiriyor. Kendi çağrılarınız farklı olabilir; bu yüzden bir akış betiğiyle ölçün.

Rust geçişi Claude API faturamı düşürür mü? Anthropic böyle bir şey söylemiyor. %70 CPU ve %80 bellek tasarrufu Anthropic'in sunucularındadır; fiyatlandırma token başınadır ve yazının konusu değildi.

Anthropic, kullanıcı verisini okumadan yeniden yazımı nasıl test etti? Yalnızca her farkın biçimini (adım, ilk farklılaşan byte ve uzunluklar) kaydetti; asla istek veya yanıtların metnini okumadı ve tek bir model çıktısını her iki servise tekrar oynattı.

Geçişten sonra neyi yeniden test etmeliyim? Araç çağrıları, kullanım alanları, bağlam limitine yakın uzun istemler ve akış olaylarının işlenmesi. Anthropic'in kendi diff'lerinin yeniden yazım sırasında ortaya çıktığı alanlar bunlar.

title: One Token, Many Lessons: Sliding-Window Attention within Gated Delta Networks
description:
arXiv:2611.33257v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Linear attention compresses historical context into a fixed-size recurrent state, reducing the computational and memory costs of long-sequence modeling. From the perspective of test-time regression (TTR), the state matrix can be viewed as an online-learned regression model, where keys and values serve as inputs and targets respectively, and queries are used to read from the model. From this perspective, the effectiveness of state learning depends not only on the update rule but also on how the key-value learning pairs used for state updates are constructed. While existing work has largely focused on how the state is updated and organized, we investigate how the learning pairs used for state updates are constructed. To this end, we propose Sliding-Window Gated DeltaNet (SWGDN), which replaces short convolutions in Delta-Rule linear attention with sliding-window attention to perform content-dependent local aggregation of projected queries, keys, and values. Our experiments show that SWGDN makes the key-value pairs used in consecutive updates more similar in both GDN2 and KDA. In SWGDN, carrying information from the same token across updates can help the recurrent state reinforce a previously learned association. The local mixing strategy can be incorporated into any Delta-Rule-based linear attention architecture without changing its state update equations or chunkwise parallel algorithms. We apply this strategy to two Delta-Rule variants, GDN2 and KDA, and experimental results demonstrate that SWGDN outperforms the original Delta-Rule baseline across multiple benchmarks.

title: Pitfalls of Dependency-Ready Decoding for Masked Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.33823v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have shown strong performance on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku, Trip Planning, and Countdown. MDMs introduce a freedom in the order in which tokens may be unmasked, and to exercise this freedom for good accuracy, early decoding strategies relied on signals of confidence or the downstream impact of decoding a token. However, simple examples seem to illustrate that resolving a token's dependencies before unmasking it should be important. Therefore, we examine whether this principle, which we call dependency-ready decoding, would contribute to better accuracy, from a practical and a theoretical perspective. We examine a recent decoder that implements dependency-readiness through attention, and generally find that when it performs better than confidence-based or future utility baselines, its decoding order collapses to left-to-right decoding. For theoretical analysis, we establish a definition of dependency without resorting to attention, measured by an information-theoretic score of how much revealing a single masked token (or a set) would shift the model's prediction for another. We prove that when the margin is large relative to this score, no such revelation can change the top prediction, so in this regime Maximum-Margin decoding already commits dependency-ready tokens. These findings leave only a narrow scope for future dependency-ready decoders: their potential benefit is limited to positions with margins smaller than the information-theoretic sensitivity, and reliance on attention should be questioned.

title: The 150 KB Google Ads Myth (And Building a 0-Upload HTML5 Ad ZIP Validator in Pure Browser JS)
description:
It's 11:12 PM on a Thursday. The product campaign goes live at 8:00 AM.

A Slack screenshot lands in #paid-media: Google Ads just bounced the 300x250.zip with one of its famously unhelpful HTML5 upload errors. The designer immediately opens TinyPNG and starts crushing retina product photography into muddy 8-bit soup, trying to drag a 184 KB banner down under 150 KB because a 2019 Medium post at the top of search results said Google Ads caps HTML5 ZIPs at 150 KB.

Except 184 KB wasn't the problem.

Google Ads Display accepts HTML5 ZIPs up to 600 KB. The actual culprit? A single animation: ctaGlow 1.6s ease-in-out infinite; left on the button, plus macOS Finder quietly stuffing __MACOSX/._index.html into the archive when someone right-clicked Compress.

If you ship display banner sets for clients or performance marketing teams, you've probably lost at least one evening to this exact headache. Here are the real 2026 specs across the five major ad networks, why the 150 KB myth won't die, and how we built a zero-dependency, 0-upload HTML5 ad ZIP validator right inside the browser so nobody has to guess at 11 PM again.

1. The 5 HTML5 Ad Specs People Keep Mixing Up

The 150 KB ceiling isn't made up. It's just the wrong network. 150 KB is the IAB Strict Standard Display (LEAN initial-load) limit, which Adform also enforces. Somewhere along the way, agency Notion wikis copy-pasted "150 KB" onto Google Ads checklists and never touched them again.

Here is what the five networks performance teams actually upload to enforce today:

Ad Network Max Compressed ZIP Max Files Max Animation Required Metadata & Click Handler
Google Ads Display 600 KB 40 ≤ 30s (no infinite) <meta name="ad.size">, clickTag (or ExitApi), HTTPS Google-hosted external URLs only
IAB Strict Display 150 KB 15 ≤ 30s (no infinite) Standard window.clickTag + window.open(clickTag)
DV360 / CM360 200 KB 40 ≤ 30s (no infinite) <meta name="ad.size">, clickTag variable
Adform DHTML 150 KB 40 ≤ 30s (no infinite) Root manifest.json + Adform.DHTML.js + dhtml.getVar('clickTAG')
Google App Campaigns (UAC) 5 MB (5,120 KB) 512 ≤ 30s (no infinite) <meta name="ad.size"> + exitapi.js + ExitApi.exit() (plain clickTag fails)

Even when your ZIP is 40 KB, four silent traps still bounce uploads:

  1. The App Campaigns vs. Display click-handler mismatch. Drop a perfectly valid clickTag banner into a Google App Campaign and it gets rejected. UAC strictly expects https://tpc.googlesyndication.com/pagead/gadgets/html5/api/exitapi.js and an ExitApi.exit() call.
  2. Adform's manifest.json + capital-TAG trap. Adform doesn't just read index.html. It expects a valid root manifest.json declaring source, width, height, and clicktags.clickTAG, paired with Adform.DHTML.js (s1.adform.net) and dhtml.getVar('clickTAG').
  3. Unapproved external hosts. Pull a font from an unwhitelisted CDN, hotlink a client logo from a staging S3 bucket, or leave one stray http:// link in CSS url(...), and Google Ads rejects the whole bundle. Bundle assets inside the ZIP, or stick strictly to whitelisted HTTPS hosts (fonts.googleapis.com, fonts.gstatic.com, s0.2mdn.net, tpc.googlesyndication.com, ajax.googleapis.com).
  4. Silent ZIP packaging bugs. Windows zip utilities occasionally write backslash (\) entry paths like assets\hero.png instead of POSIX forward slashes (assets/hero.png), choking Linux ad-ingestion servers. macOS Finder sneaks in __MACOSX/ and .DS_Store junk files (burning slots against IAB's 15-file limit). And zipping the folder instead of its contents buries index.html at campaign-v3/index.html instead of the ZIP root.

2. Parsing & Validating HTML5 Ad ZIPs in Pure Browser JS (0 Bytes Uploaded)

When we built a pre-flight checker for these five specs, one rule came first: zero bytes uploaded to a server.

Paid-media teams handle embargoed launches: unreleased pricing, upcoming SKUs, client rebrands under NDA. Telling a designer or media buyer to upload pre-launch client creative to a random third-party backend just to check <meta name="ad.size"> is a bad habit.

You don't need a backend for this anymore, and you don't even need JSZip. Modern browsers (and Node 20+) ship DataView, TextDecoder, DecompressionStream('deflate-raw'), and CompressionStream('deflate-raw'). That's enough to parse, audit, preview, and even pack clean POSIX ZIPs inside a browser tab with the Wi-Fi switched off.

Three real engineering details make it hold up on messy production ZIPs.

A. Read the ZIP Backwards From EOCD (0x06054b50), Not Byte 0

The classic mistake when writing a JS ZIP reader from scratch is walking Local File Headers (0x04034b50) forward from byte 0. That works on half the ZIPs in the wild and breaks on the other half, because streaming ZIP creators (including macOS Finder and several CLI tools) set the data-descriptor flag and write 0 for compressedSize in the local header.

The real directory sits at the end of the file. Scan backward from the end of the ArrayBuffer for the End of Central Directory (EOCD) signature 0x06054b50, read each Central Directory entry (0x02014b50), inspect the raw filename bytes (flagging Windows \ backslashes before normalizing), and inflate method 8 entries with native DecompressionStream('deflate-raw'):

async function inflateRaw(compressedBytes) {
  const source = new ReadableStream({
    start(controller) {
      controller.enqueue(compressedBytes);
      controller.close();
    }
  });
  const reader = source
    .pipeThrough(new DecompressionStream("deflate-raw"))
    .getReader();

  const chunks = [];
  let totalLength = 0;
  while (true) {
    const { done, value } = await reader.read();
    if (done) break;
    chunks.push(value);
    totalLength += value.byteLength;
  }

  const out = new Uint8Array(totalLength);
  let offset = 0;
  for (const chunk of chunks) {
    out.set(chunk, offset);
    offset += chunk.byteLength;
  }
  return out;
}

export async function parseZipBuffer(buffer) {
  const bytes = new Uint8Array(buffer);
  const view = new DataView(bytes.buffer, bytes.byteOffset, bytes.byteLength);

  // Scan backwards for EOCD signature 0x06054b50 (max 64KB ZIP comment)
  const minOffset = Math.max(0, bytes.byteLength - 65557);
  let eocdOffset = -1;
  for (let i = bytes.byteLength - 22; i >= minOffset; i--) {
    if (view.getUint32(i, true) === 0x06054b50) {
      eocdOffset = i;
      break;
    }
  }
  if (eocdOffset === -1) throw new Error("Missing ZIP EOCD signature.");

  const entryCount = view.getUint16(eocdOffset + 10, true);
  let offset = view.getUint32(eocdOffset + 16, true);
  const decoder = new TextDecoder("utf-8", { fatal: false });
  const files = [];
  let hasBackslashPaths = false;

  for (let i = 0; i < entryCount; i++) {
    if (view.getUint32(offset, true) !== 0x02014b50) {
      throw new Error("Corrupt Central Directory entry.");
    }
    const method = view.getUint16(offset + 10, true);
    const compressedSize = view.getUint32(offset + 20, true);
    const nameLen = view.getUint16(offset + 28, true);
    const extraLen = view.getUint16(offset + 30, true);
    const commentLen = view.getUint16(offset + 32, true);
    const localOffset = view.getUint32(offset + 42, true);

    const rawName = decoder.decode(bytes.subarray(offset + 46, offset + 46 + nameLen));
    if (rawName.includes("\\")) hasBackslashPaths = true;
    const path = rawName.replace(/\\/g, "/");
    offset += 46 + nameLen + extraLen + commentLen;
    if (path.endsWith("/")) continue; // directory entry

    const localNameLen = view.getUint16(localOffset + 26, true);
    const localExtraLen = view.getUint16(localOffset + 28, true);
    const dataStart = localOffset + 30 + localNameLen + localExtraLen;
    const slice = bytes.subarray(dataStart, dataStart + compressedSize);

    const data = method === 0 ? slice.slice()
      : method === 8 ? await inflateRaw(slice)
      : (() => { throw new Error(`Unsupported ZIP method: ${method}`); })();

    files.push({ path, method, compressedSize, bytes: data });
  }

  return { zipBytes: bytes.byteLength, files, hasBackslashPaths };
}

Going the other direction (packing clean POSIX ad ZIPs inside our Figma plugin and our on-the-fly sample generator) runs the same primitives in reverse: a 12-line IEEE 802.3 CRC-32 table (0xedb88320), CompressionStream('deflate-raw') for HTML/CSS/SVG, and automatic STORE (method 0) fallback for already-compressed .png, .jpg, .webp, or .woff2 files so we never burn bytes re-deflating compressed images.

B. Catching CSS Animations That Sneak Past 30 Seconds

A naive /infinite/ regex misses stacked timing math (animation-delay: 22s; animation-duration: 3s; animation-iteration-count: 4; = 34 seconds, rejected) and fires false positives on CSS comments or class names.

Two edge cases tripped us up early:

  1. Strip /* comments */ and @keyframes { ... } blocks first (tracking { / } brace depth) so the declaration-block parser only reads real selector rules.
  2. Never blindly .split(",") an animation shorthand. If a layer uses cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1), naive comma-splitting shreds the declaration into junk tokens. Split only on top-level commas outside parentheses.

For every layer rule, total runtime is plain arithmetic:

// Per animation entry on a selector:
const totalSeconds = iterations === Infinity
  ? Infinity
  : Math.max(0, delay + duration * iterations);

Track the maximum across every <style> block and .css file in the ZIP. If hasInfiniteLoop is true or maxDurationSeconds > 30, flag it red before the archive ever touches Google Ads.

C. Sandboxed Live iframe Preview + Click-Exit Verification

Header checks catch spec violations, but designers also want to watch the animation play and click the banner to prove clickTag or ExitApi.exit() actually fires, without executing untrusted ad JavaScript inside the host page's origin.

Since every file from the ZIP is already unpacked as Uint8Array bytes in memory, we rewrite relative asset references (<link rel="stylesheet">, <style> url(...), <img src>, <script src>) into in-memory data: URIs, prepend a tiny click-monitor shim inside <head>, and mount the document in a locked-down iframe:

const iframe = document.createElement("iframe");
iframe.setAttribute("sandbox", "allow-scripts"); // no allow-same-origin, no parent DOM/cookie access
iframe.setAttribute("width", String(width));
iframe.setAttribute("height", String(height));
iframe.setAttribute("srcdoc", inlinedHtmlWithClickShim);

title: The Empty State Is Where Your Product Tells the Truth
description:
I've started paying more attention to screens that contain almost nothing.

Not the polished dashboard with sample data. Not the page with twenty records and all the buttons working.

The empty one.

A new user opens the app for the first time. No projects. No messages. No history. Just a blank area and maybe a button that says "Create your first..."

Technically, everything works.

But I think this is where a surprising number of products quietly lose people.

An empty screen is not necessarily a simple screen.

Consider a few situations:

A search returns no results. Is the query wrong, or is there genuinely nothing to find?

A dashboard has no activity. Is that because the user just started, or because something stopped working?

A file list is empty. Should the user upload something, create something, or connect another service?

A task queue shows zero items. Is everything complete, or did the system fail to load?

The UI might look identical in some of these cases, but the meaning is completely different.

And that's the part I find interesting.

Developers often model what happens when data exists. We don't always model the absence of data with the same care.

In code, an empty array is straightforward. In a real product, it can represent several different states:

Nothing has been created yet.

A filter removed all matching results.

The user doesn't have permission to see anything.

Data hasn't arrived yet.

Something went wrong.

Treating all five as items.length === 0 might be convenient, but it can also hide important information from the person using the product.

I'm not suggesting that every empty state needs an illustration, animation, or paragraph of friendly copy.

Sometimes a simple message is enough.

What matters is that the interface tells the user what's happening and, when appropriate, what they can do next.

There's also a developer-side benefit: thinking explicitly about empty states often exposes assumptions in the data model and application logic before they become bigger problems.

Here's what I'm curious about:

When you're building a feature, do you design the empty state alongside the normal state, or does it usually become something you remember just before calling the work finished?

And have you ever discovered a genuine product bug simply because you started looking more carefully at what happens when there's no data?

title: Fast and Scalable Abstract Interpretation for Deep Neural Networks
description:
arXiv:2611.33259v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Abstract interpretation can certify properties of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), but precise analyses remain expensive. General implementations repeat work when analyzing the same architecture under different inputs and properties. Interleaving this work with numerical operations limits GPU utilization and restricts how much of the analysis a tensor compiler can process together.
  We present Scepter, a framework for specializing DNN abstract interpreters through structural semantics. The semantics determine the structure of intermediate abstract values while deferring their numerical evaluation. Structural computations from successive operations can therefore be performed together before certification, generating an executable tensor program. With the abstract interpreter and DNN architecture fixed, the program can be reused with different weights and input regions. We prove that it computes the same bounds as the general interpreter in exact arithmetic. The generated program also exposes operations and their dependencies for tensor compilation and memory planning. We implement Scepter for the tensor programs that Neuton generates from ConstraintFlow specifications.
  We evaluate Scepter on eight abstract interpreters and 44 DNNs against six baseline systems on GPUs and CPUs. Scepter handles networks with up to 153x as many neurons as the largest completed by the corresponding baselines. It completes DeepPoly on ResNet50 and VGG-16, whereas none of the evaluated DeepPoly baselines completes either network. On configurations completed by both systems, GPU geometric-mean speedups over Neuton range from 11.9x to 44.4x across eight analyses, with a 2.60x geometric-mean reduction in peak memory. In an input-splitting case study, Scepter proves 68 properties for which the baselines time out.
  Code: https://github.com/uiuc-focal-lab/constraintflow.git

title: Anthropic rewrote its Messages API in Rust. The tests said 98%. Production said 25%.
description:
The gap between passing tests and matching production

Anthropic published a detailed write-up on 25 November 2026 about migrating its Messages API from Python to Rust. The API is the main way customers, Claude Code and Cowork reach Claude, and traffic grew roughly 1,800 times from early 2024 to fall 2026. The Python service was creaking under validation, tokenisation, safety screening and streaming on every request, so Rust was the obvious move.

Claude wrote the first version of the core request path in about a week. Generation was not the bottleneck. Verification was.

Verdict: Writing the new code was the easy part. Proving it behaved the same as the old code was the real work. When your tests pass and production disagrees, production is right.

The tests said 98%. Production said 25%.

In April, the Rust version passed about 98% of its roughly 700 integration tests. Yet only about a quarter of real production inputs matched. Two reasons explain the gap.

First, the tests were coupled to the Python implementation. They ran the Python API inside the test process and mocked services like billing and rate limiting in Python memory. When the tests were ported, they changed along with the code, so a pass could mean the code was right or that the test had been changed to let wrong code through. An audit found more than 100 weakened assertions in the ported tests.

Second, the tests were incomplete. The API has dozens of features and far too many configurations to test exhaustively: just 20 binary options make over a million combinations.

Mismatches were often subtle. Python escapes certain characters in JSON tool calls, an emoji for example, replacing them with text codes, while Rust wrote them as is, so the prompts differed by a few bytes. And production weights bugs differently: in a suite each case counts once, but in live traffic one common bug mismatches on every request it touches.

Production became the verifier

Anthropic turned the production API itself into the verifier, shadowing live traffic through both versions. Two hard constraints applied: a request could only count once toward a customer's limits and bill, and nobody could read customer requests or Claude's replies, for privacy.

So instead of comparing text, they compared the shape of each difference. Checkpointing compared every step of request handling, piece by piece, so the first place the versions differed pointed at roughly where the code differed. A fingerprint, where the difference began plus the length difference, grouped identical bugs for triage. Because Claude is nondeterministic, the model ran once and its output was replayed to Rust.

Three loops closed the gap

Each differing request left a small record in the logs. A script grouped them every 10 to 30 minutes and alerted a coordinating Claude agent only on a new kind of record. The coordinator assigned a worker agent to each kind, with a shared Slack thread where human engineers could follow along and steer. Agents fixed issues in a fast inner loop, a cloud sandbox with both codebases and local checks that compared the prompts each version would build in under a second, without calling the model. Fixes were validated in a slower outer loop against production traffic, and mistakes were recorded in a memory loop so agents learned from them over time. The seam between the inner and outer loops was a checkpoint for human review: inside the sandbox a wrong guess cost seconds and harmed nothing.

The result

The Rust API now uses about 70% less CPU per request and cuts median time to first token by about 20%, with no downtime and no feature freeze. The performance gain is real, but the verification machinery that made the migration trustworthy is the interesting part.

What to steal

  • Treat production as the oracle when your tests cannot define correct. A green suite is a claim, not proof.
  • Audit ported tests for weakened assertions before trusting them to judge a rewrite. Anthropic found more than 100.
  • Compare shapes, not raw text, when privacy rules out reading traffic.
  • Give agents fast verification loops, or slow feedback turns them into guessers.
  • Keep a memory of past mistakes, so each fix makes the next one cheaper.

Read the full write-up from Anthropic: Migrating our Messages API to Rust.

Quick poll

What would you verify first before trusting a rewrite like this?

  • The test suite
  • Production shadowing
  • An assertions audit
  • Nothing, ship it

Vote in the comments.

If you found this interesting, I write about engineering leadership in the age of AI agents every week in The AI-Native Engineering Leader, what actually works for engineering leaders building with AI agents, and what to skip.

title: Vercel Functions now support request bodies up to 20MiB
description:
Vercel Functions now accept inbound request bodies up to 20MiB, up from 4.5MB, in Public Beta.

To turn this on, set the VERCEL_SUPPORT_LARGE_REQUEST_BODY=1 environment variable. The opt-in applies to the whole project in the environment where you set it, so you can test the larger limit on preview before enabling it in production. It requires the project's functions to use the performance memory setting of 4GB. It applies to functions on the Node.js, Python, and Bun runtimes, and to Routing Middleware. Functions and Routing Middleware on the Edge runtime keep the 4.5MB cap and return 413 on oversize bodies, so moving them onto the larger limit means switching to the Node.js runtime with runtime: 'nodejs', or proxy.ts in Next.js.

When a project opts in, Routing Middleware receives request headers and metadata but no request body, enforced at the project level. Middleware still runs and still sees every other request header, so body-dependent middleware behavior is the one thing that becomes unavailable. This avoids sending the body twice, to both middleware and the target function, which would raise cost and time to first byte.

When handling larger request bodies, read the body promptly and avoid holding it in memory to prevent backpressure and memory issues.

Learn more in the Vercel Functions limitations documentation.

title: VivaWorld: Long-Horizon Video World Model With Compositional 3D Priors
description:
arXiv:2611.33591v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon video generation is key to interactive world modeling, physical intelligence, and spatial reasoning, yet maintaining geometric consistency and accurate camera control remains challenging without 3D grounding. We introduce \textbf{VivaWorld}, a framework for generating geometry- and view-consistent long videos from an image. We first construct a compositional hybrid 3D representation that combines reconstructed point clouds, which preserve observed scene geometry and appearance, with generated textured meshes, which provide complete object geometry across $360^\circ$ novel views. We also introduce a connected-region filter removing inconsistent floating components for robust cross-view reconstruction and propose a hybrid camera embedding that combines global and object-anchored Pl\"{u}cker rays to capture both scene-level camera motion and camera-object relationships, and inject it together with the visual guidance into a video generation model via a control adapter. Extensive experiments show VivaWorld achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and camera control, while supporting controllable novel-view synthesis, long-horizon scene exploration, and physical AI. Project page is available at: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/sil/projects/vivaworld/

title: HEAR, SEE, SPIKE ONCE: Highly Efficient NeuroAI Temporal Neural Networks for Low-Precision Multimodal Audio-Visual Classification and Online Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.31884v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spiking neural networks for multimodal audio-visual classification reach high accuracy by adopting deep-learning machinery: multi-stage convolutional or transformer encoders trained end-to-end with surrogate-gradient backpropagation through time. These prior works typically rely on full-precision (32-bit) parameters and do not treat hardware efficiency as a primary design objective. In this paper, we propose NeuTNN-AV, a much simpler hardware-amenable multimodal substrate built on the recently proposed NeuroAI Temporal Neural Network (NeuTNN) and demonstrate that it can match or outperform state-of-the-art SNN baselines with a fraction of their synapse counts. NeuTNN neurons carry multiple active dendritic segments. Each input line spikes at most once (temporal coding) and every weight is learned via a local reward-modulated spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) rule. All weights are 4-bit integers and inference uses only comparisons and additions. On CREMA-D, it reaches 78.6% with 2.34M synapses establishing a new state-of-the-art SNN accuracy, against 77.14% for MISNet-XL (31M parameters). On UrbanSound8K-AV, NeuTNN reaches 98.82% with 1.38M synapses, against 96.85% for SMMT (9.99M parameters) and 98.96% for MISNet-XL (31M parameters). Weight memory is 23-106x smaller than the spiking baselines, and the measured synaptic energy per inference is two to three orders of magnitude lower. Furthermore, the proposed NeuTNN learns CREMA-D in a single pass with 73.8% accuracy and demonstrates rapid online continual learning by adapting to unseen actors from a few dozen clips.

title: A Perturbation-Driven Framework for Sensitivity Analysis of Dimensionality Reduction
description:
arXiv:2611.33523v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Low-dimensional representations produced by dimensionality reduction (DR) are commonly evaluated using distortion measures such as trustworthiness and continuity. In this paper, we study the sensitivity of DR methods to plausible input variations by quantifying changes in structural preservation and visually diagnosing how these changes manifest in the resulting representations. This perspective reflects the fact that real-world datasets are finite, noisy samples of an underlying distribution, and DR should not produce substantially different structures under small data changes. We introduce a model-agnostic, perturbation-driven sensitivity evaluation framework that treats perturbations as controlled probes of plausible data variation. Across multiple perturbation families and strength levels, we repeatedly perturb the input, apply a DR method, and evaluate the resulting low-dimensional representations using a set of distortion measures to derive sensitivity profiles for each DR method. We demonstrate the utility of our framework through case studies on DR method comparison, behavior analysis, and robustness improvement. We find that methods performing well according to conventional distortion measures (e.g., t-SNE) can still exhibit substantial sensitivity, leading to instability in visually salient structures such as trajectories and clusters, while certain methods (e.g., multidimensional scaling) may exhibit improved structural preservation under specific perturbations. These results highlight the importance of sensitivity analysis for comparing DR methods, diagnosing perturbation-sensitive visual patterns, and guiding the development of more robust DR methods toward trustworthy visual analytics.
