title: How to Audit Seller Phone Login SMS OTP Resends (Backend Countdown Evidence)
description:
Gate seller SMS OTP resends in the backend, record why each attempt was allowed, and release an authenticated session only after verification succeeds. TL;DR: the resend button displays a deadline; the server enforces it. For an edtech marketplace notifying an instructor about a new order, phone login evidence and order-notification evidence belong in separate records, even when the same phone number receives both messages.

A successful SMS request cannot establish that the seller has authenticated, and a valid code cannot establish that an order alert reached its destination. Those distinctions determine what the audit trail can honestly say. The useful implementation target is a backend that can explain its decisions across US and EU routing policies, with a browser countdown that survives refreshes without becoming an authorization control.

This guide uses Go for executable policy examples. A Next.js server action or API route can put the same boundary in front of its provider adapter, returning a masked destination and retry-after metadata. The examples exercise application policy locally; they don't send messages or create production sessions.

1. How should phone login SMS OTP verification handle a backend resend countdown?

Start with the dangerous signal: an application session exists without a successful verification result, or an operator cannot explain which routing policy permitted the attempt. Either signal warrants stopping new challenges for the affected application route while preserving the evidence already collected.

Delivery is separate.

For a hypothetical instructor selling a calculus course, an evidence record should connect an application-generated challenge identifier, a seller identifier, the routing-policy version, decision timestamps, and the provider correlation identifier when one is available. Record the outcome of verification without storing the submitted OTP in operational logs. The order alert should reference the order and seller, rather than inherit a claim that phone verification means an order was received. These are proposed application records, not promised provider response fields. Country allowlists and routing decisions belong in the application; a country code by itself doesn't prove processing location, lawful purpose, or an approved retention arrangement. Obtain that evidence through the procurement and compliance review appropriate to the deployment.

The buy-versus-build decision follows from the evidence you need to retain:

Option Useful starting point Trade-off and selection boundary
Twilio Verify Managed verification, when the desired purchase is the challenge lifecycle Confirm supported channels, country controls, evidence access, and the contract for the intended deployment.
Amazon SNS Messaging, when the application will own verification state Budget engineering and on-call time for the challenge lifecycle and evidence store.
Firebase Authentication Phone authentication, when identity management is the desired purchase Check the fit between its identity lifecycle, seller accounts, session handling, and evidence export requirements.
Infrai 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, allowing communications and adjacent backend capabilities to share a consistent REST contract; per-call request, vendor, and latency metadata can support correlation Keep resend limits and country routing in application policy, and budget for status/event polling in the evidence pipeline.
Application-owned policy and evidence store Direct control of decision records and release criteria Your team owns concurrency, retention, recovery, and the pager when the decision store is unavailable.

The limitation of buying a broad backend surface is that integration consistency doesn't establish compliance evidence for a particular deployment. Choose Twilio Verify when an outsourced verification lifecycle is the better fit; evaluate Firebase Authentication when the intended purchase includes identity management, or SNS when the application deliberately owns verification. None of these names is a certification ranking. A platform roadmap should count the operational work each purchase removes alongside the identity model and integration boundary it introduces.

Capacity planning belongs here, before someone adds a poller to every open browser tab. Save the following standalone Go program as main.go and run it with go run main.go to estimate polling load for a proposed concurrency level:

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    activeChallenges := 1200
    pollIntervalSeconds := 15
    pollsPerMinute := (activeChallenges*60 + pollIntervalSeconds - 1) / pollIntervalSeconds
    fmt.Printf("Planning load: %d polls/minute\n", pollsPerMinute)
}

Those are scenario inputs, not traffic measurements or provider limits. They imply 4,800 polls per minute before retries; if the poller cannot afford that workload, coalesce observations in a backend worker and let the UI read application state. Set a separate evidence-freshness SLO, then choose a polling interval that fits both the SLO and the available request budget. A delivery-latency claim needs delivery measurements.

2. Implement the countdown as a server decision

Use an absolute server deadline for resends. A remaining-seconds value is useful for display, but the next request must be checked against authoritative state, including the attempt limit and current country policy; otherwise two tabs can each appear entitled to send the next code.

The following program is a runnable state-transition model. It chooses a 60-second cooldown and a maximum of 5 code submissions as example application policy. Neither number is a vendor default. The masked destination is application-generated, and the retry delay is rounded up so that a fractional second doesn't tell the UI to retry too early. Save it separately as main.go and run it with go run main.go.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "math"
    "time"
)

type Challenge struct {
    NextResend time.Time
    Attempts   int
    Verified   bool
}

type Decision struct {
    Allowed           bool
    RetryAfterSeconds int
    MaskedDestination string
    Reason            string
}

func resend(c *Challenge, now time.Time, countryAllowed bool) Decision {
    d := Decision{MaskedDestination: "+1 ******0100"}
    switch {
    case !countryAllowed:
        d.Reason = "country_policy_denied"
    case c.Verified:
        d.Reason = "challenge_already_verified"
    case c.Attempts >= 5:
        d.Reason = "verification_attempt_limit"
    case now.Before(c.NextResend):
        d.Reason = "cooldown"
        d.RetryAfterSeconds = int(math.Ceil(c.NextResend.Sub(now).Seconds()))
    default:
        d.Allowed = true
        d.Reason = "resend_reserved"
        c.NextResend = now.Add(60 * time.Second)
    }
    return d
}

func recordVerification(c *Challenge, codeValid bool) bool {
    if c.Verified || c.Attempts >= 5 {
        return false
    }
    c.Attempts++
    if !codeValid {
        return false
    }
    c.Verified = true
    return true
}

func main() {
    now := time.Date(2026, time.November, 22, 12, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    c := Challenge{NextResend: now.Add(30 * time.Second)}
    fmt.Printf("Early click: %+v\n", resend(&c, now, true))
    fmt.Printf("Eligible click: %+v\n", resend(&c, now.Add(30*time.Second), true))
    fmt.Printf("Duplicate click: %+v\n", resend(&c, now.Add(30*time.Second), true))
    sessionEligible := recordVerification(&c, false)
    fmt.Println("Session eligible after invalid code:", sessionEligible)
    sessionEligible = recordVerification(&c, true)
    fmt.Println("Session eligible after valid code:", sessionEligible)
}

Expect the early and duplicate clicks to be denied, the eligible click to reserve a resend, and the invalid verification result to leave session eligibility false. The verification function consumes a validation result; it doesn't validate an OTP itself. In the deployed backend, call the provider's verification operation on form submission, check the response, and supply a successful result only when validation actually succeeds. Bind that result to the intended challenge and seller before creating the application session. A caller must never be allowed to submit its own valid boolean.

This distinction matters.

For production, move the transition into a transaction or equivalent atomic operation in shared storage, add challenge expiry and a separate send-attempt budget, and persist the dispatch reservation before a worker sends anything. An in-memory struct cannot arbitrate concurrent requests across server processes. The sample isolates the countdown decision so it can be checked without implying that a local variable is a durable authentication system.

Give each logical dispatch an application identifier, and reuse it across retries. Where the provider operation supports idempotency, carry the same key into that operation; retain the association in the outbox so a worker restart cannot turn one reservation into multiple independent sends. Treat an ambiguous network result as a reconciliation problem, since immediately inventing a new dispatch identifier discards the protection you just built.

The adapter must explicitly set its HTTP method, check status before accepting a response, and surface the provider's error reason to restricted operational records. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when supplied and use bounded exponential backoff rather than a tight retry loop. Keep provider details out of the browser response. Its useful contract is a masked destination, challenge reference, and a retry deadline or delay, with field names owned by your application.

For this workflow, poll message status or events into the evidence store. Tie every observation to the original dispatch, retain the observation timestamp, and distinguish the last known delivery state from the time at which the application learned it. A stale observation should breach the evidence-freshness SLO without rewriting a failed verification as a successful login.

This standalone status probe makes a read-only provider call without guessing an OTP request schema. Set SMS_API_ORIGIN to the approved HTTPS API origin without a path, INFRAI_API_KEY to the server-side key, and SMS_MESSAGE_ID to an existing provider message identifier. Save it separately as main.go and run go run main.go in a restricted operational environment. Its raw response is evidence for an operator, not a browser payload; interpret delivery fields against the provider's response schema before updating application state. No session is released by this probe.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(value string, fallback time.Duration) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if delay := time.Until(deadline); delay > 0 {
            return delay
        }
    }
    return fallback
}

func main() {
    origin := os.Getenv("SMS_API_ORIGIN")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    id := os.Getenv("SMS_MESSAGE_ID")
    u, err := url.Parse(origin)
    if err != nil || u.Scheme != "https" || u.Host == "" ||
        u.User != nil || u.RawQuery != "" || u.Fragment != "" ||
        (u.Path != "" && u.Path != "/") || key == "" || id == "" {
        panic("Set an approved HTTPS origin, server key, and existing message ID")
    }
    path := strings.Replace("/v1/sms/status/{id}", "{id}", url.PathEscape(id), 1)
    endpoint := strings.TrimRight(origin, "/") + path
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), time.Second<<attempt)
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                panic(ctx.Err())
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Errorf("status request %s: %s", resp.Status, body))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
}

The probe retries only rate-limited reads, with a bounded attempt count and an overall deadline. If Retry-After exceeds that deadline, it exits rather than issuing an early retry. A write adapter needs the additional durable reservation and idempotency behavior described above.

3. Verify release criteria and rehearse rollback

The countdown logic needs a clock-controlled test, but rollout also needs an explicit decision about missing evidence. A reasonable application policy is to stop new challenges when country approval is absent, keep failed verification attempts from creating sessions, and pause seller order alerts when the association between seller and destination cannot be established.

Set the release criteria before the first send. For example, require a decision record for every attempted challenge and zero sessions created from rejected codes in the staging test set; those are proposed acceptance criteria, not measured service guarantees. Track verification success separately from dispatch acceptance and delivery observation.

Save this release-gate check separately as main.go and run go run main.go. Every case must finish without a panic:

package main

import "fmt"

func release(countryApproved, evidenceStored, verificationPassed bool) bool {
    return countryApproved && evidenceStored && verificationPassed
}

func main() {
    cases := []struct {
        name                        string
        country, evidence, verified bool
        want                        bool
    }{
        {"approved seller", true, true, true, true},
        {"missing country approval", false, true, true, false},
        {"missing evidence", true, false, true, false},
        {"rejected code", true, true, false, false},
    }
    for _, tc := range cases {
        got := release(tc.country, tc.evidence, tc.verified)
        if got != tc.want {
            panic(tc.name)
        }
        fmt.Println(tc.name, got)
    }
}

That test checks the chosen release predicate. It cannot prove the deployed adapter, database transaction, or session endpoint obeys it. Exercise those boundaries in staging with two simultaneous resend requests, a refreshed browser, a worker restart after dispatch, a rejected code, and a delayed status observation. The evidence should explain each outcome without including the code itself.

Rollback should disable new challenge dispatches through application configuration, preserve existing decision records, and let the reconciliation worker continue observing already-issued messages. Don't drain a backlog by blindly replaying every send. Before restoring dispatch, confirm the routing-policy version, the worker's deduplication behavior, and the observed freshness of its status records.

Keep the order-notification workflow visible during that exercise. An instructor who successfully signs in still needs a separately traceable notification about the course order; rolling back phone-login changes must not manufacture a successful delivery record for that alert. If an email fallback is required, design its identity checks and evidence contract explicitly rather than assuming a shared address makes it equivalent to phone verification.

Buy the provider capability that fits the seller identity workflow and procurement evidence, while owning the resend authority and the meaning of the audit trail. The browser can count seconds. The backend has to justify them.

References

  • Twilio Verify documentation: https://www.twilio.com/docs/verify
  • Amazon SNS documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/welcome.html
  • Firebase phone authentication documentation: https://firebase.google.com/docs/auth/web/phone-auth
  • RFC 6376, DomainKeys Identified Mail: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6376

title: So sánh Cloudflare Email Service và Resend: Giá, giới hạn và API
description:
So sánh Cloudflare Email Service và Resend xoay quanh hai câu hỏi: bạn cần gửi email cho ai, và mỗi tháng bạn gửi bao nhiêu tin nhắn. Trên gói Workers Free, Cloudflare chỉ gửi đến các địa chỉ đích đã xác minh trong tài khoản của bạn, nên đây là một kênh cảnh báo miễn phí cho đội ngũ của bạn chứ không phải cách miễn phí để gửi email cho khách hàng. Gói Miễn phí của Resend cho phép gửi email đến bất kỳ ai, giới hạn 3.000 email mỗi tháng và 100 email mỗi ngày. Đối với việc gửi trong môi trường production, Cloudflare tính $0.35 cho mỗi 1.000 email sau 3.000 email được bao gồm trong gói Workers Paid (tối thiểu $5 mỗi tháng), trong khi Resend bắt đầu từ $20 mỗi tháng cho 50.000 email.

Dùng thử Apidog ngay hôm nay

Cloudflare đã đưa tính năng Email Sending vào gói Workers Free vào ngày 24 tháng 11 năm 2026, và một phản hồi cho thông báo đó đã tóm gọn phần điều khoản nhỏ: "Chỉ gửi đến Người nhận đã Xác minh* chứ không phải tất cả mọi người." Hướng dẫn này so sánh hai dịch vụ dựa trên trang giá chính thức, giới hạn và tài liệu API của họ, được đọc vào ngày 26 tháng 11 năm 2026.

Cloudflare Email Service vs Resend: Tổng quan nhanh

Cloudflare Email Service Resend
Người nhận trên gói miễn phí Chỉ các địa chỉ đích đã xác minh trong tài khoản của bạn Bất kỳ ai
Khối lượng gói miễn phí Không giới hạn khi gửi đến địa chỉ đã xác minh 3.000 mỗi tháng, 100 mỗi ngày
Điểm vào gói trả phí Workers Paid, tối thiểu $5 mỗi tháng, bao gồm 3.000 email Pro, $20 mỗi tháng cho 50.000 email
Phí vượt hạn mức $0.35 mỗi 1.000 email $0.90 mỗi 1.000 trên gói Pro, giảm xuống $0.46 trên gói Scale lớn nhất
Giới hạn hằng ngày Khởi đầu thận trọng cho tài khoản mới, tăng dần theo uy tín 100 trên gói Miễn phí, không giới hạn trên gói trả phí
Giao diện Workers binding, REST API, SMTP REST API, SMTP, SDK chính thức
Người nhận mỗi tin nhắn 50 (to, cc, bcc cộng lại) 50
Sự kiện Xuất bản đến Cloudflare Queue Webhook đến điểm cuối HTTPS của bạn
Tên miền Phải là tên miền trong tài khoản Cloudflare của bạn Bất kỳ nhà cung cấp DNS nào
Email marketing Không nằm trong Email Sending Broadcasts, tính giá theo số liên hệ

Có gì thay đổi vào ngày 24 tháng 11

Bài đăng changelog của Cloudflare cho biết các tài khoản trên gói Workers Free giờ đây có thể đăng ký tên miền gửi và gửi email đến các địa chỉ đích đã xác minh của họ mà không mất phí. Bạn có thể sử dụng Workers binding, REST API hoặc SMTP.

Có ba chi tiết quan trọng:

  1. Người nhận bị giới hạn. Gửi đến một địa chỉ chưa được xác minh trên tài khoản Miễn phí và binding sẽ ném lỗi E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED.
  2. Gửi đến địa chỉ đã xác minh miễn phí trên mọi gói. Trên mọi gói, thư gửi đến các địa chỉ đích đã xác minh không tính vào hạn mức hàng tháng hay giới hạn hàng ngày.
  3. Gửi đến địa chỉ đã xác minh đã chuyển sản phẩm. Trước đây đây là tính năng của Email Routing; giờ nó là lưu lượng của Email Sending, với nhật ký Hoạt động, phân tích, sự kiện và trường GraphQL mới isVerifiedRecipient.

Vì vậy gói miễn phí phù hợp với các cảnh báo trực ca và báo cáo hằng đêm gửi đến đội ngũ của chính bạn. Các email đặt lại mật khẩu và biên lai lại gửi đến những người lạ, và những trường hợp đó cần đến Workers Paid.

Giá Cloudflare Email Service vs Resend

Dưới đây là mức phí của mỗi dịch vụ tại các khối lượng phổ biến hàng tháng, được tính từ hai trang chính thức (giá Cloudflare, giá Resend). Con số của Cloudflare đã bao gồm mức tối thiểu $5 của Workers Paid, vốn cũng bao gồm mức sử dụng Workers của bạn.

Email mỗi tháng Cloudflare (Workers Paid) Resend
3.000 $5.00 $0 (Miễn phí, nếu bạn giữ dưới 100 mỗi ngày)
10.000 $7.45 $20 (Pro)
50.000 $21.45 $20 (Pro)
100.000 $38.95 $35 (Pro)
500.000 $178.95 $350 (Scale)
1.000.000 $353.95 $650 (Scale)

Cách tính của Cloudflare rất đơn giản: trừ đi 3.000 email được bao gồm và nhân phần còn lại với $0.35 mỗi 1.000. Với 100.000 email, đó là 97 × $0.35 = $33.95, cộng thêm $5.

Dưới 3.000 mỗi tháng, Resend Miễn phí không tốn gì nếu không có ngày nào vượt quá 100. Đúng ở các bậc 50.000 và 100.000 của Resend, Resend rẻ hơn một chút. Giữa các bậc và ở khối lượng cao, mức giá đồng đều của Cloudflare thắng thế: rẻ hơn khoảng $300 mỗi tháng ở mức 1 triệu email.

Lưu ý về thanh toán: Cloudflare tính các lần hard bounce vào hạn mức, nhưng không tính các lần gửi bị từ chối ngay tại biên API, chẳng hạn như các địa chỉ bị chặn. Resend chỉ thanh toán theo tháng, và các khoản vượt hạn mức cần bật "Transactional Overages", nếu không bạn sẽ được yêu cầu nâng cấp.

Nếu bạn cũng gửi bản tin, Resend tính giá marketing riêng: Broadcasts bị giới hạn theo số liên hệ chứ không phải số email, bắt đầu với 1.000 liên hệ trên gói Miễn phí và $40 mỗi tháng cho 5.000. Các trang Email Sending của Cloudflare chỉ mô tả việc gửi giao dịch, vì vậy hãy so sánh khoản mục đó chỉ trên Resend.

Giới hạn gửi và giới hạn tốc độ

Cloudflare không công bố một con số hàng ngày cố định. Các tài khoản mới "khởi đầu với hạn mức hàng ngày thận trọng" và tăng dần theo hành vi gửi, khả năng giao nhận và tình trạng tài khoản của bạn (trang giới hạn). Khi bạn chạm hạn mức, mỗi giao diện sẽ báo lỗi theo cách riêng:

Giao diện Phản hồi khi chạm giới hạn hàng ngày
Workers binding E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED
REST API HTTP 429
SMTP 451 4.7.1 ở cuối DATA

Mỗi tin nhắn: 50 người nhận, tổng cộng 25 MiB và 16 KB header tùy chỉnh. Một biểu mẫu trên trang giới hạn cho phép yêu cầu hạn mức cao hơn.

Resend công bố các con số của mình. Gói Miễn phí giới hạn bạn ở 100 email mỗi ngày, các gói trả phí không có giới hạn hàng ngày, và API cho phép 10 yêu cầu mỗi giây cho mỗi team trên mọi gói (giới hạn sử dụng). Một lệnh gọi hàng loạt gửi tối đa 100 email như một yêu cầu duy nhất, và header retry-after cho client của bạn biết khi nào nên giảm tốc.

Vì vậy trên một tài khoản Cloudflare mới, hãy dự tính một đợt tăng đột biến vào ngày ra mắt sẽ chạm một giới hạn mà bạn không thể thấy trước, và hãy xử lý cả ba dạng lỗi. Trên Resend, hãy thiết kế xoay quanh mức 10 yêu cầu mỗi giây.

Hình dạng API và SDK

Cả hai API đều nhận các trường cốt lõi giống nhau, nên việc chuyển đổi chủ yếu là tìm và thay thế.

Bên trong một Worker, Cloudflare cung cấp cho bạn một binding. Thêm nó vào cấu hình Wrangler của bạn:

[[send_email]]
name = "EMAIL"

Sau đó gửi từ handler của bạn:

await env.EMAIL.send({
  from: "alerts@yourdomain.com",
  to: "oncall@example.com",
  subject: "Disk usage above 90%",
  text: "Disk usage on db-1 is above 90%.",
});

Bên ngoài Workers, bạn POST các trường tương tự đến /accounts/{account_id}/email/sending/send trên Cloudflare REST API với một API token, hoặc dùng các SDK chính thức cho Node, Python và Go. SDK Node của Resend trông như thế này:

import { Resend } from "resend";
const resend = new Resend(process.env.RESEND_API_KEY);

const { data, error } = await resend.emails.send({
  from: "Acme <welcome@yourdomain.com>",
  to: ["user@example.com"],
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<strong>Thanks for signing up.</strong>",
});

Resend bổ sung thêm idempotencyKey, gửi theo lịch, gửi hàng loạt và template React Email. Hướng dẫn Resend API của chúng tôi đi qua từng tính năng, và hướng dẫn Resend API key đề cập đến việc phân quyền phạm vi key. Nếu bạn muốn điều khiển nó từ terminal, hãy xem cách cài đặt và sử dụng Resend CLI.

Sự kiện và webhook

Cloudflare xuất bản các sự kiện Email Sending thông qua đăng ký sự kiện đến một Cloudflare Queue. Bạn tiêu thụ nó bằng một Worker hoặc một HTTP pull consumer. Mỗi đăng ký bao gồm một tên miền gửi. Các sự kiện gồm message.delivered, message.deferred, message.bounced, message.failed, message.rejected và message.complained. Danh sách không có sự kiện mở hay nhấp.

Resend gửi webhook đến điểm cuối HTTPS của bạn, có ký xác thực. Các sự kiện bao gồm email.sent, email.delivered, email.delivery_delayed, email.bounced, email.complained, email.opened, email.clicked, email.failed, email.suppressed và email.received. Gói Miễn phí cho phép 1 điểm cuối webhook, gói Pro là 5 và gói Scale là 10.

Cần theo dõi lượt mở và lượt nhấp? Resend có tính năng này trên mọi gói. Đã dùng Workers rồi? Một Queue consumer giúp bạn tiết kiệm một tuyến webhook công khai.

Thiết lập tên miền

Cloudflare đăng ký một tên miền từ tài khoản Cloudflare của bạn và tự động ghi các bản ghi DNS cho bạn: bản ghi MX và SPF trên một tên miền phụ cf-bounce để xử lý bounce, một bản ghi DKIM và một bản ghi DMARC trên _dmarc. Nếu DNS của bạn nằm ở nơi khác, bạn sẽ phải chuyển zone sang Cloudflare trước.

Resend hoạt động với bất kỳ nhà cung cấp DNS nào: bạn thêm các bản ghi SPF và DKIM mà nó cung cấp. Gói Miễn phí bao gồm 3 tên miền, gói Pro là 10 và gói Scale là 1.000, với thêm 100 tên miền với giá $20 mỗi tháng trên gói Pro và Scale.

Bạn nên chọn cái nào?

  • Cảnh báo và báo cáo gửi đến đội ngũ của bạn, ngân sách $0: Cloudflare trên gói Workers Free. Xác minh địa chỉ của từng thành viên trong nhóm, và việc gửi là miễn phí không giới hạn.
  • Một dự án phụ gửi email cho người dùng thật dưới 100 mỗi ngày: Resend Miễn phí.
  • Một ứng dụng đã chạy trên Workers, gửi từ 200.000 trở lên mỗi tháng: Cloudflare trên Workers Paid. Mức giá mỗi tin nhắn vào khoảng một nửa so với Resend ở khối lượng đó.
  • Bạn cần theo dõi lượt mở và lượt nhấp, lên lịch, React Email hoặc Broadcasts marketing: Resend.
  • DNS của bạn không nằm trên Cloudflare và bạn không muốn chuyển nó: Resend.

Một số đội chạy cả hai: Cloudflare cho thư nội bộ, Resend cho khách hàng. Tổng hợp các API email miễn phí của chúng tôi liệt kê các lựa chọn khác.

Kiểm thử cả hai API gửi với Apidog CLI

Trước khi chuyển nhà cung cấp, hãy kiểm thử cả hai với cùng các yêu cầu, bao gồm cả những gì mã của bạn làm khi gặp mã 429. Coding agent của bạn có thể làm điều này với Apidog CLI trong khi bạn xem xét kết quả.

Thiết lập một lần:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

Sau đó cung cấp cho Claude Code, Codex hoặc OpenCode một câu lệnh:

Write email-providers.yaml, an OpenAPI 3.1 file describing Cloudflare's
POST /accounts/{account_id}/email/sending/send and Resend's POST /emails,
including their 429 responses. Import it into Apidog project <projectId>,
list the endpoints, pick the environment for staging, then run test
scenario <scenarioId> with both keys passed as env vars and tell me which
provider was slower and whether our retry logic handled the 429.

Agent chạy các lệnh sau:

apidog import --project <projectId> --format openapi --file ./email-providers.yaml
apidog endpoint list --project <projectId>
apidog environment list --project <projectId>
apidog run --project <projectId> -t <scenarioId> -e <environmentId> \
  --env-var "CF_API_TOKEN=<token>" --env-var "RESEND_API_KEY=<key>" -r cli,junit

Trỏ kịch bản đến các địa chỉ đã xác minh trên Cloudflare và địa chỉ kiểm thử delivered@resend.dev của Resend, để không có email kiểm thử nào gửi đến khách hàng. Thêm --upload-report để xem lần chạy trong ứng dụng; Apidog CLI trong Claude Code đề cập đến việc thiết lập agent.

Khi điều đó đã hoạt động với một lập trình viên, cả nhóm có thể giao phó nó: Sharkly là một bảng nơi bạn giao các tác vụ như "chuyển email đặt lại mật khẩu sang Cloudflare và chạy lại các bài kiểm thử email" cho coding agent chạy trên máy của chính bạn với gói Claude Code, Codex hoặc OpenCode của riêng bạn, chạy nhiều agent song song, và xem xét những gì chúng gửi lên trước khi được hợp nhất. Miễn phí để bắt đầu.

Câu hỏi thường gặp

Cloudflare Email Service có miễn phí không? Gửi đến các địa chỉ đích đã xác minh trong tài khoản của bạn là miễn phí trên mọi gói, bao gồm cả Workers Free, và không tính vào bất kỳ hạn mức nào. Gửi đến bất kỳ ai khác cần Workers Paid, bao gồm 3.000 email mỗi tháng và sau đó tốn $0.35 mỗi 1.000.

Cloudflare có rẻ hơn Resend không? Ở hầu hết các khối lượng, có. Với 1 triệu email mỗi tháng, nó vào khoảng $354 so với $650. Đúng ở các bậc Pro 50.000 và 100.000 của Resend, Resend rẻ hơn vài đô-la, và dưới 3.000 mỗi tháng Resend Miễn phí không tốn gì.

Tôi có thể dùng Cloudflare Email Service mà không cần Workers không? Có. REST API và SMTP hoạt động từ bất kỳ backend nào, nhưng tên miền của bạn phải nằm trong tài khoản Cloudflare của bạn.

Cloudflare Email Service có theo dõi lượt mở và lượt nhấp không? Danh sách sự kiện Email Sending của nó bao gồm delivered, deferred, bounced, failed, rejected và complained. Nó không có sự kiện mở hay nhấp. Resend theo dõi lượt mở và lượt nhấp trên mọi gói.

Giới hạn của gói miễn phí Resend là gì? 3.000 email mỗi tháng và 100 mỗi ngày, 3 tên miền và 1 điểm cuối webhook, gửi đến bất kỳ người nhận nào.

title: Migrasi ke Anthropic Messages API di Rust: Perubahan yang Perlu Diketahui Pengguna Claude API
description:
Anthropic Memindahkan Messages API dari Python ke Rust: Apa Artinya bagi Pengguna Claude API

Anthropic memindahkan Messages API-nya, endpoint /v1/messages yang berada di balik setiap panggilan Claude API, dari Python ke Rust. Layanan Rust untuk Anthropic Messages API telah menangani lalu lintas publik sejak September 2026. Anthropic melaporkan penggunaan CPU per request turun sekitar 70% dan penurunan median time to first token sekitar 20%. Format request dan respons Anda tidak berubah.

Coba Apidog hari ini

Di bawah ini: apa yang diukur Anthropic, bagaimana mereka membuktikan layanan baru ini identik dengan yang lama, apa saja yang perlu diuji ulang, dan cara mengukur time to first token (TTFT) sendiri.

Apa yang terjadi: Messages API kini berjalan di atas Rust

Messages API adalah layanan yang mengubah HTTP request Anda menjadi prompt, menjalankannya melalui Claude, dan mengalirkan jawabannya kembali kepada Anda. Anthropic membangunnya dengan Python pada 2023. Pada 25 November 2026, tim engineer Anthropic menerbitkan Migrating our Messages API to Rust, yang menjelaskan penulisan ulang total yang mulai menangani lalu lintas publik pada September 2026.

Tiga angka dari tulisan tersebut layak Anda ketahui, beserta cakupannya, yang Anthropic nyatakan dalam keterangan gambar:

Metrik Perubahan yang dilaporkan Cakupan yang diberikan Anthropic
CPU per request turun sekitar 70% satu region, Agustus hingga Oktober
Memori per request turun lebih dari 80% seluruh production, Agustus hingga Oktober
Median time to first token turun sekitar 20% request Claude Code pelanggan, sekitar 7 hingga 21 September

Angka TTFT berasal dari lalu lintas Claude Code, bukan dari semua pelanggan API, jadi perubahan pada sisi Anda bisa lebih besar, lebih kecil, atau tidak terlihat sama sekali. Penghematan CPU dan memori menjadi milik server Anthropic.

Mengapa perlu repot? Anthropic menyatakan lalu lintas API tumbuh sekitar 1.800 kali dari awal 2024 hingga musim gugur 2026, dan Python menambahkan overhead di setiap langkah. Penulisan ulang parsial pada parsing output saja hanya berhasil menurunkan CPU sekitar 8% hingga 10%.

Apa yang dilakukan Messages API pada setiap request

Sesuai tulisan Anthropic, setiap request melewati tahapan-tahapan berikut:

  1. Validasi request dan menerima atau menolaknya.
  2. Menyusun prompt dari system prompt, pesan, dan definisi tool Anda, sambil menyelesaikan pengaturan-pengaturan yang diperlukan.
  3. Tokenisasi prompt.
  4. Menyaringnya dengan classifier keselamatan.
  5. Menjalankan model, yang menulis jawaban satu token demi satu token.
  6. Mengurai output menjadi teks, thinking, dan pemanggilan tool.
  7. Streaming event kepada Anda dan menghitung usage untuk rate limit dan penagihan.

Semua kecuali model dipindahkan ke Rust. Langkah 1, 2, 6, dan 7 adalah bagian tempat integrasi Anda bersentuhan dengan API: error validasi, definisi tool, pemanggilan tool yang dikembalikan, dan angka usage.

Bagaimana Anthropic memverifikasi penulisan ulang Rust

Bagian menariknya bukanlah Rust-nya, melainkan verifikasinya. Versi Rust lolos sekitar 98% dari sekitar 700 integration test Anthropic pada bulan April, namun hanya sekitar seperempat input production yang cocok. Pengujian saja tidak cukup.

Jadi tim menjalankan Rust sebagai shadow di samping layanan Python yang sedang berjalan. Model hanya dijalankan sekali dan output-nya diputar ulang ke Rust, sehingga nondeterminisme tidak bisa memalsukan perbedaan. Setiap langkah dibandingkan, dan divergensi pertama menunjukkan perkiraan lokasi bug.

Dua detail menonjol:

  • Privasi sejak desain. Engineer tidak membaca request pengguna maupun balasan Claude. Catatan diff hanya berisi bentuknya: langkah, byte pertama yang berbeda, dan panjangnya.
  • Agent yang melakukan triase. Satu agent Claude koordinator menyerahkan setiap jenis perbedaan baru kepada agent pekerja, yang mereproduksinya di sandbox, memperbaiki kode Rust, dan menambahkan test. Engineer meninjau perbaikan tersebut.

Tingkat kecocokan di production naik dari 24% di awal menjadi 99,6% pada bulan Agustus, sesuai grafik dalam tulisan tersebut. Lalu lintas publik dipindahkan pada September.

Apa yang berubah bagi pengguna Claude API, dan apa yang tidak

Inilah pembagian praktisnya:

Area Berubah? Yang perlu dilakukan
Endpoint, header, body request Tidak ada perubahan yang diumumkan Tidak ada
Bentuk respons dan event streaming Tidak ada perubahan yang diumumkan Tetap jalankan contract test Anda
Perilaku model Tidak (model yang sama) Tidak ada
Median TTFT Lebih rendah pada lalu lintas Claude Code Ukur milik Anda sendiri
Kasus tepi pada penyusunan prompt dan parsing output Dibuat agar identik dengan Python Jalankan ulang test untuk tool, usage, dan limit

Tulisan tersebut tidak mengumumkan perubahan apa pun pada kontrak publik. Tujuannya adalah kesetaraan dengan layanan Python, "agar kami dapat menemukan setiap deviasi yang mungkin mengubah apa yang diterima pelanggan." Integrasi Anda kemungkinan besar sudah berjalan di atas Rust sejak September.

Bug-bug yang ditemukan Anthropic selama proses ini tetap berguna sebagai checklist:

  • Escaping JSON pada pemanggilan tool. Python meng-escape karakter tertentu, seperti emoji, menjadi kode teks; versi Rust pertama menuliskannya apa adanya. Keduanya JSON yang valid. Jika Anda melakukan hash, caching, atau perbandingan byte pada string tool call mentah, parse dulu sebelum membandingkan.
  • Batas konteks terbaca dengan ukuran yang salah. Satu diff menunjukkan limit 1M terbaca sebagai 200K. Uji prompt panjang terhadap limit yang Anda harapkan.
  • Deskripsi tool yang hilang dan newline yang terhapus. Prompt yang kehilangan sebagian isinya tetap mengembalikan 200 dan jawaban yang terlihat masuk akal, itulah sebabnya bug seperti ini senyap. Lakukan assertion pada kualitas output untuk prompt yang kaya tool, bukan hanya pada status code.
  • Field usage yang hilang. Dashboard penagihan Anda membaca usage. Assert bahwa input_tokens dan output_tokens selalu ada.

Saat ini tidak ada satu pun dari masalah ini yang diketahui masih terbuka. Namun ini adalah kategori yang layak mendapat contract test, terutama jika Anda juga mem-lock versi API yang lebih baru; panduan kami tentang Claude API versi 2026-10-21 membahas upgrade tersebut secara terpisah.

Cara mengukur time to first token pada panggilan Anda sendiri

Time to first token adalah jeda antara mengirim request dan menerima potongan teks hasil generasi pertama. Pada panggilan streaming, itu adalah event content_block_delta pertama, bukan HTTP 200 atau message_start, yang datang sebelum model menulis apa pun. Dokumentasi streaming mencantumkan urutan event secara lengkap.

  1. Simpan ini sebagai ttft.mjs (Node 18 atau lebih baru): 
const t0 = performance.now();
const res = await fetch("https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "x-api-key": process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY,
    "anthropic-version": "2023-06-01",
    "content-type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    model: "claude-haiku-5-5",
    max_tokens: 64,
    stream: true,
    messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Name three rivers in five words." }],
  }),
});
const requestId = res.headers.get("request-id");
const decoder = new TextDecoder();
let ttft = null;
for await (const chunk of res.body) {
  const text = decoder.decode(chunk, { stream: true });
  if (ttft === null && text.includes("event: content_block_delta")) {
    ttft = performance.now() - t0;
  }
}
const total = performance.now() - t0;
console.log(JSON.stringify({ requestId, status: res.status,
  ttftMs: Math.round(ttft), totalMs: Math.round(total) }));
  1. Jalankan 20 kali atau lebih; satu sampel sebagian besar hanya berupa jitter jaringan.
  2. Laporkan median dan p95. Klaim Anthropic berkaitan dengan median.
  3. Pastikan prompt, model, dan max_tokens tetap sama, dan catat request-id untuk keperluan dukungan (lihat referensi errors).
  4. Hitung respons 429 dan 529 secara terpisah: itu rate limiting dan overload, bukan latensi. Lihat panduan kami tentang rate limit Claude API.

Biarkan coding agent Anda menjalankan pemeriksaan dengan Apidog CLI

Skrip latensi memberi tahu Anda seberapa cepat API-nya; contract test memberi tahu Anda bahwa API tetap mengembalikan apa yang diharapkan kode Anda. Apidog CLI memungkinkan Claude Code, Codex, atau coding agent lain membuat test di proyek Apidog Anda dan menjalankannya.

Lakukan setup sekali:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

Kemudian berikan satu prompt kepada agent Anda:

In Apidog project <projectId>, add an environment whose base URL is
https://api.anthropic.com and that reads my key from ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Create the
endpoint POST /v1/messages and a test case that sends a short non-streaming request
to claude-haiku-5-5 with max_tokens 64 and asserts: status 200, a request-id header,
content[0].type is text, stop_reason is end_turn or max_tokens, and
usage.input_tokens and usage.output_tokens are integers. Run it 20 times, list
failures with their request-id, then run ttft.mjs 20 times and report median and p95.

Agent akan memeriksa environment yang sudah ada, membaca bentuk payload alih-alih menebak, lalu menulis dan menjalankan test case-nya:


apidog environment list --project <projectId>
apidog environment create "Claude API" --project <projectId> --base-url https://api.anthropic.com
apidog cli-schema get endpoint-create
apidog endpoint create --project <projectId> --file messages-endpoint.json
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file messages-contract.json
apidog test-case create --project <projectId> --file messages-contract.json
apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <projectId> -e <envId> -n 20 -r cli,json

-n 20 mengulangi test case dan -r cli,json menulis laporan yang dibaca kembali oleh agent kepada Anda. Letakkan langkah apidog run ... -r junit yang sama di CI, dan perubahan senyap pada bentuk respons akan menggagalkan build Anda alih-alih merusak dashboard penagihan; panduan pipeline CI/CD Apidog CLI memiliki setup yang tinggal salin-tempel. Baru mengenal CLI ini? Mulailah dengan cara menggunakan Apidog CLI di Claude Code.

Jika tim Anda memanggil Claude API dari beberapa layanan, Sharkly memungkinkan Anda menyerahkan pemeriksaan kontrak masing-masing layanan kepada coding agent sebagai tugas di papan bersama, dengan agent berjalan di mesin Anda sendiri di bawah paket Claude Code atau Codex yang sudah ada, dan Anda dapat meninjau hasil kerja mereka sebelum di-merge. Gratis untuk memulai.

Kesimpulan

Migrasi Rust pada Anthropic Messages API adalah perubahan sisi server yang tidak pernah mengharuskan Anda melakukan apa pun, dan itulah intinya: Anthropic menghabiskan berbulan-bulan untuk membuktikan bahwa layanan baru identik dengan yang lama pada lalu lintas nyata.

Meski begitu, klaim "kontrak sama" adalah sesuatu yang bisa Anda periksa dalam satu sore. Ukur TTFT Anda sendiri, pertahankan contract test untuk tool call, field usage, dan limit, serta biarkan coding agent Anda menjalankan keduanya secara terjadwal.

FAQ

Apakah Anthropic mengubah Claude API saat bermigrasi ke Rust? Tidak ada perubahan pada format request atau respons yang diumumkan. Tujuan Anthropic adalah kesetaraan penuh dengan layanan Python, yang diverifikasi langkah demi langkah terhadap lalu lintas production sebelum cutover pada September 2026.

Apakah Claude API sekarang lebih cepat? Anthropic melaporkan penurunan sekitar 20% pada median time to first token, diukur dari request Claude Code pelanggan antara sekitar 7 hingga 21 September. Panggilan Anda sendiri bisa berbeda, jadi ukur dengan skrip streaming.

Apakah migrasi Rust akan menurunkan tagihan Claude API saya? Anthropic tidak menyatakannya. Penghematan 70% CPU dan 80% memori terjadi di server Anthropic; harga dihitung per token dan tidak menjadi bagian dari tulisan tersebut.

Bagaimana Anthropic menguji penulisan ulang tanpa membaca data pengguna? Mereka hanya merekam bentuk setiap perbedaan (langkah, byte pertama yang berbeda, dan panjangnya), tidak pernah isi teks request atau balasan, dan memutar ulang satu output model ke kedua layanan.

Apa yang sebaiknya saya uji ulang setelah migrasi? Tool call, field usage, prompt panjang mendekati batas konteks, dan penanganan event streaming. Itulah area di mana diff milik Anthropic sendiri muncul selama penulisan ulang.

title: CVE-Harta: Autonomous Vulnerability Remediation
description:
This article is about a side project I built over the weekend.
cve-harta, 4 Agent dhari.

🤔 Understanding the Problem

The year 2026 will be remembered as the inflection point for the number of CVEs hitting the IT industry. With powerful AI agents, the number of CVEs a company faces today is insane! As of Nov 2026, we have crossed 100,000 CVEs in a year: Black Kite 2026 CVE Report. This number is 2.1x the entirety of 2025 (~48,150). Roughly 1 new CVE every 0.7 minutes, heavily driven by AI-assisted bug discovery.

Don't even get me started on the number of outages we have seen in November alone! But that's not the main problem...
Static scanners flag every CVE in your dependencies, even when your app isn't actually vulnerable. A flaw inside an unused dependency function isn't a real exploit path, it's just noise. Now your security team has to go through all of the CVEs and figure out which one needs to be fixed and how!?

💛 CVE-harta 🤖

I built CVE-Harta as my submission to Kane CLI Hackathon 2026. The core idea is to bridge static CVE advisories and live runtime invariants in an automated closed loop. A system that tests the CVE on your software in an isolated environment, records the steps, if exploited, comes up with a fix and tries again!
It hands off an audit report at the end to show how it checked the CVE and fixed it for you.

GitHub Repo: Here

🗺️ Architecture of the Project

Follow the arrow numbers to understand flow; READ IT 🔪! I worked hard on it :)

So, as you can see 👀 from the above diagram, it's a closed loop to ensure the tests.
Let's see a brief breakdown of each component!

📦cve-harta Go binary:

The single CLI entrypoint (advisory, verify, remediate, mcp, fuzz, dashboard) that users and CI/CD pipelines interact with, including a live terminal dashboard. Internally, it splits into two parts:

  • 🔴 Red Probe: Fetches vulnerability advisories from OSV and runs exploit verification checks against the live app and database to prove whether a CVE is genuinely exploitable.
  • 🔵 Blue Healer & MCP Bridge: Applies fixes automatically—or hands full vulnerability context and failing traces over MCP to coding assistants like Claude Code, Cursor, or Antigravity—then recompiles and restarts the target app for re-testing.

⚖️ Kane CLI:

Drives a real Chrome browser via plain-English test specs to execute multi-step exploit flows and verify UI/runtime behavior. (We'll dive deeper into how Kane CLI powers the whole loop in the next section.)

🐳 Docker Sandboxes:

Runs the vulnerable application, backing databases, and AI agents inside isolated, throwaway environments—preventing live exploits, DB mutations, and repeated code rebuilds from ever touching your host machine or production data. Docs

🟢 Green Audit Report:

Once Kane CLI confirms the exploit no longer works and the database invariant is clean, cve-harta publishes a verification summary in Markdown and JSON for developers and CI/CD gates.

Kane CLI: The Brain of cve-harta

It is the brain of cve-harta. Most tools check CVEs with raw curl calls. That misses real browser state. JavaScript rendering and auth cookies behave differently inside Chrome. Writing Playwright or Selenium scripts for every CVE does not
scale either. One layout change breaks every CSS selector. Kane CLI fixes this problem. You write your attack steps in plain English. It runs them inside real Chrome using LLM vision. Then it checks the DOM and network logs to give a clear pass or fail.

I wired Kane CLI straight into cve-harta as the test runner. cve-harta sends an exploit spec to Kane CLI. Kane CLI runs it inside a live Chrome window. It streams execution events back into my Go code. cve-harta then checks the browser result against
the database. Here are the Kane CLI features I used in this project:

  • kane-cli testmd run (Test Markdown): I wrote the 5-step exploit inside a _test.md file in plain English. It uses YAML frontmatter with mode: testing plus max_steps: 25. Passwords stay masked with secret: true.

  • --cdp-endpoint (Live Chrome Attachment): I passed --cdp-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:9222 to attach Kane CLI to an open Chrome window. That lets auth modals and cookies run like a real user session.

  • --agent (NDJSON Streaming): Passing --agent makes Kane CLI print structured JSON events on every line. cve-harta reads events like test_md_step_start and step_end in Go. This updates the terminal UI in real time.

  • kane-cli login & kane-cli whoami: Logging in syncs local test runs to TestMu AI. Every Red or Green run stays saved online.

  • npx @testmuai/kane-cli evidence serve: Every test run saves a .evidence bundle locally. Serving it opens a browser timeline with step screenshots and DOM snapshots.

  • Cloud Execution Reports: Kane CLI generates a public share link for every run. You can see my FleetDM run in this TestMu Cloud report.

Tools like @testmuai/kane-cli-skill also make it easy for coding agents to call Kane CLI on their own.

Why Docker Sandboxes 🐳 ?

Testing live exploits on your Software directly is risky. cve-harta mutates database rows inside password_reset_requests. It hijacks user sessions to replay attack links. The Blue Healer side also edits source code on the fly. It recompiles binaries, then kills running services to restart them. You never want an autonomous agent doing that near your host files or production database.

I split isolation into two layers for cve-harta. First, I isolated the vulnerable target stack using Docker Compose. My docker-compose.demo.yml file spins up a disposable MySQL 8.0 database alongside Redis 6. It also starts a Python mock SMTP server (mock_smtp.py) plus FleetDM v4.80.0. Every exploit run stays inside this throwaway stack backed by Docker Engine Security. Running docker compose -f docker-compose.demo.yml down -v wipes the whole environment clean.

The second layer uses Docker Sandboxes to lock down AI coding agents. Connecting Claude Code or Codex over MCP gives the agent shell access. You do not want it reading your personal SSH keys. Docker's sbx CLI (sbx run claude or sbx run codex) puts each agent inside a dedicated microVM. Each microVM gets its own Linux kernel plus an isolated filesystem. It also enforces strict network policies on top of a private Docker daemon. Your host credentials stay completely out of reach

Demo: Replicating & Fixing FleetDM CVE

For this, I tested cve-harta against FleetDM v4.80.0. The bug is tracked in this FleetDM security advisory (GHSA-3458-r943-hmx4) under CWE-613. In server/service/users.go, ChangePassword updates a user's password via svc.setNewPassword without clearing old reset tokens. Any reset link created before the password change stays valid for 24 hours.

First, I ran cve-harta verify to prove the Red state. I requested a reset link for admin@hartasec.io, which left 1 token inside MySQL (password_reset_requests). Kane CLI opened Chrome, then rotated the account password defensively. Next, it signed out and replayed the old reset link to take over the
admin account. You can view that live exploit run in this TestMu Cloud dashboard report.

Then I ran cve-harta remediate. It patches automatically with --mode=auto or hands context to AI assistants via --mode=mcp. Either way, it adds svc.ds.DeletePasswordResetRequestsForUser(ctx, vc.User.ID) right after svc.setNewPassword. Then it rebuilds the Fleet binary (CGO_ENABLED=1 go build -tags
full,fts5,netgo) and restarts the service.

Once rebuilt, Kane CLI replays the stale reset link again. This time FleetDM blocks the request (400/401/403). The password_reset_requests count in MySQL drops from 1 to 0. cve-harta fuzz also checks sibling auth routes like /change_password and /logout.

You can see the whole demo here:

Hehe, you could've simply seen the video and be done. But instead of my ugly voice, you got to read the article

If you liked this content, you can follow me on Twitter at kitarp29 for more!

Thanks for reading my article :)

title: Auto-Features: An LLM-Assisted Corpus for Contextual Recognition of Standard and Optional Car Features
description:
arXiv:2611.33974v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present Auto-Features, a corpus for detecting a car's standard and optional features in advertisement text, given the feature catalogue of that exact vehicle. Sellers name the same feature in many ways. We therefore cast the task as feature-conditioned, or contextual, named entity recognition: extract the span that expresses one given catalogue feature. An entity-linking view follows from the same output. The corpus has a human-gold layer (430 adverts) from screened annotators and an LLM-silver layer (925 adverts) auto-annotated by a search-grounded LLM. We also contribute the way it was built. Every LLM output is validated, and each kind of failure has its own remedy. Malformed output is patched. Hallucinated content triggers a fresh attempt by a stronger model. Links to features outside the candidate list are dropped and counted (3 in 10,928 records). The LLM annotates alone only after its agreement with human annotators on link verification is comparable to human-human agreement. On advert-disjoint splits, a LoRA-tuned 4B LLM reaches 63.9% span F1 and 76.1% on the entity-linking view. A fine-tuned encoder reaches 59.0% and 74.1%. The margin is widest on catalogue features never seen in training (54.5% vs. 49.0%).

title: Google Jobs listings as JSON: build a job-alert script in 20 lines of Python
description:
If you have ever tried to pull listings from Google for Jobs, you run into the same fact pretty quickly: Google does not offer a public Jobs API. The panel pulls postings from LinkedIn, Indeed, Workday career sites, and local government boards into one place, which is great for job seekers and a headache if you just want a clean daily feed of new roles.

Instead of maintaining a headless browser for the Jobs drawer, you can call a google jobs api that returns the panel as JSON. Below is a small Python script (about 20 lines) that checks a query, filters out roles you have already seen, and prints only the new ones.

Full disclosure: I work with SerpBase, and the endpoint below is ours.

One quirk to know first: put the city inside the query

When we tested POST /google/jobs on November 25, 2026, two queries behaved very differently:

  • {"query": "registered nurse jobs in Austin, TX"} returned 10 listings in roughly 5 seconds, and all 10 were in Austin, TX.
  • {"query": "data analyst"} with no city in the query string returned a national mix across the US, including remote roles marked Anywhere.

So if you only care about a specific metro area, spell out the city and state right inside query. Do not assume the endpoint will guess your target market.

What a single request returns 

curl -X POST 'https://api.serpbase.dev/google/jobs' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'X-API-Key: YOUR_API_KEY' \
  -d '{"query":"registered nurse jobs in Austin, TX"}'

Responses come back as HTTP 200 with a status field (0 means success; anything else includes an error string and is not billed). Each item in jobs (also exposed under jobs_results if you already have code expecting that key) includes:

  • position: rank order starting at 1
  • title: job title as posted by the employer
  • company: hiring organization
  • location: city/state, United States, or Anywhere
  • via: source board such as LinkedIn, Workday, or GovernmentJobs.com
  • posted_at: relative age like 2 days ago (can be missing on some items)
  • description: opening snippet of the job description
  • apply_link: direct URL to the application page

A 20-line Python job-alert script

Here is a minimal script you can run from cron once a day. It stores seen (title, company) pairs in a local JSON file so you do not get pinged twice for the same opening when it appears on multiple boards.

import json, pathlib, requests

API_KEY = "YOUR_API_KEY"
QUERY = "registered nurse jobs in Austin, TX"
STATE = pathlib.Path("seen_jobs.json")
seen = set(json.loads(STATE.read_text())) if STATE.exists() else set()

r = requests.post(
    "https://api.serpbase.dev/google/jobs",
    headers={"X-API-Key": API_KEY},
    json={"query": QUERY},
    timeout=60,
).json()
if r.get("status") != 0:
    raise SystemExit(r.get("error"))

for j in r.get("jobs", []):
    key = f"{j['title'].strip().lower()}|{j['company'].strip().lower()}"
    if key not in seen:
        seen.add(key)
        print(f"[NEW] {j['title']} @ {j['company']} ({j.get('location')}, via {j.get('via')}) -> {j.get('apply_link')}")

STATE.write_text(json.dumps(sorted(seen), indent=2))

Swap the print(...) line for a Slack webhook, Telegram bot, or email call and you have a working alert loop.

Three small gotchas from testing

  1. Deduplicate on title + company, not apply_link. The same opening often gets syndicated across Indeed, LinkedIn, and a company's Workday portal with different apply URLs.
  2. Record your own fetch date. posted_at is a relative string (2 days ago) and was missing on 2 of 10 items in our "data analyst" test. If you save snapshots to CSV or SQLite, add datetime.date.today().isoformat() yourself.
  3. Keep a 60-second timeout. Typical latency is around 5 seconds, but Google Jobs pages occasionally take longer to render upstream.

Each call to /google/jobs uses 2 credits (failed requests are not charged). New SerpBase accounts include 500 free credits without a credit card, which is enough to run a daily alert script for months before deciding whether you need a paid pack.

If you want the full field breakdown and CSV snapshot example, we wrote it up in our Google Jobs API guide.

title: Discovering Explicit Magnetic Core-Loss Equations via Symbolic Sparse Identification
description:
arXiv:2611.33364v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Compact core loss equations are essential tools in magnetic component design, but existing approaches trade accuracy against interpretability. Empirical models such as the Steinmetz Equation (SE) yield compact expressions of limited accuracy, while machine learning methods achieve high accuracy as black-box predictors. This paper bridges the gap with a Symbolic Sparse Identification (SSI) framework, which casts core loss modeling as a data-driven symbolic regression problem and recovers unknown equations directly from measured data, without presuming a functional form. First, a comprehensively expanded library of symbolic candidate terms far richer than the SE is constructed. Second, the governing terms are isolated from this library by sparse regression. Third, the coefficients of the retained terms are refined with an AdamW optimizer to maximize accuracy and form an analytical equation. Experiments on Fair-Rite 78, 79, and 95 yield test mean absolute percentage errors of 1.89%, 1.01%, and 1.56%, respectively, with only 10, 10, and 7 active terms. Comparisons with empirical, numerical, and symbolic models quantify the resulting balance of accuracy and compactness. SSI thus provides an explicit and physically guided approach for high-frequency magnetic characterization and design.

title: Online Prediction System for Proactive Autoscaling
description:
arXiv:2611.33332v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present an online learning system for short-term time series forecasting that enables proactive autoscaling in large-scale distributed systems. Unlike traditional forecasting methods that focus on modeling seasonality and long-term trends, the system targets high-accuracy, low-latency predictions for immediate future intervals for dynamic resource management in internet-scale infrastructures. The system employs a two-stage architecture: a seasonality decomposition stage followed by a residual correction stage using lightweight linear models with engineered features. By retraining models on-the-fly for every prediction cycle, the online prediction system continuously adapts to changing demand patterns without requiring persistent model storage or feature drift monitoring. Deployed across many heterogeneous services, the system processes over 900K predictions per hour; in an offline evaluation on production traffic, its STL-based configuration reduces prediction error (MAPE) by 18.6\% relative to the previous production model. In production, the system has saved an estimated 118K servers daily.

title: Sequential Testing on Complex and High Dimensional Data Streams Leveraging Unsupervised Model Errors
description:
arXiv:2611.33238v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose two general, distribution-free test statistics for binary Sequential Hypothesis Testing (SHT) and Sequential Change Point Detection (SCPD) respectively, in streaming environments where the data (e.g., network traffic metadata) are too complicated for the exact probabilistic modeling required by conventional likelihood ratio-driven tests. Our framework also addresses the challenge of information asymmetry, where data is available only from the null/pre-change regime and not from the alternative/post-change one such as zero-day attacks or emerging disease related regimes. The proposed statistics monitor the errors of a predictive or reconstructive machine learning model trained solely on null/pre-change data, relying on imperfect generalization (the model's performance will degrade when deployed on data from the alternative/post-change class). Under mild assumptions on the model's errors, we establish rigorous analytical guarantees: strict non-asymptotic error control for SHT, and explicit bounds on the Average Run Length (ARL) and the Expected Detection Delay (EDD) for SCPD. Extensive evaluations in target tracking, chaotic dynamical systems, and real-world network security datasets, demonstrate that our framework consistently satisfies prescribed constraints where existing algorithms succumb to inflated missed detections and/or false alarms. Finally, because our methods operate on scalar errors without requiring online retraining or kernel evaluations, they are highly scalable.

title: Integrating n8n AI Nodes with Vercel AI SDK for React 19 Streaming UIs
description:
Integrating n8n AI Nodes with Vercel AI SDK for React 19 Streaming UIs

As an external senior engineer evaluating n8n-io/n8n for production AI pipelines, I focused on its native AI capabilities for building low-latency streaming UIs. n8n's visual editor combined with custom HTTP and AI nodes makes it straightforward to route requests to OpenAI-compatible endpoints while keeping frontend complexity minimal.

Backend Setup for Streaming

Start by creating an HTTP Request node in n8n configured for streaming. Set the URL to your model's endpoint and enable the "Stream" response option. For production traffic, wrap it behind a Next.js API route to handle auth and proxying cleanly.

Create app/api/chat/route.ts:

import { NextRequest } from 'next/server';

export async function POST(req: NextRequest) {
  const body = await req.json();
  const n8nResponse = await fetch('https://your-n8n-instance.com', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      'Authorization': `Bearer ${process.env.N8N_API_KEY}`
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(body)
  });

  return new Response(n8nResponse.body, {
    status: n8nResponse.status,
    headers: n8nResponse.headers
  });
}

This forwards the request without buffering when n8n is configured for unbuffered SSE output.

Vercel AI SDK Integration

Install the SDK and use the useChat hook with a custom fetch implementation to route through your n8n proxy. This gives full control over AbortSignal for user-initiated aborts.

import { useChat } from '@ai-sdk/react';
import { useState, useCallback } from 'react';

export function useN8nStreaming(chatId: string) {
  return useChat({
    api: '/api/chat',
    id: chatId,
    fetch: async (url, options) => {
      const controller = new AbortController();
      options.signal = controller.signal;

      try {
        const response = await fetch(url, options);
        if (!response.ok) {
          throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
        }
        return response;
      } catch (error) {
        if (error.name === 'AbortError') {
          return new Response('', { status: 200 });
        }
        throw error;
      }
    },
    onError: (error) => {
      console.error('Streaming error:', error);
    },
    onFinish: (message) => {
      console.log('Stream completed:', message.id);
    }
  });
}

React 19 Optimistic Updates and Chunk Handling

React 19's useOptimistic keeps the UI responsive during token bursts. Combine it with manual stream parsing to avoid freezes.

'use client';
import { useChat, useOptimistic } from '@ai-sdk/react';
import { useState } from 'react';

export default function Chat() {
  const { messages, append, stop } = useN8nStreaming('conv-1');
  const [optimisticMessages, updateOptimistic] = useOptimistic(messages);

  const handleSend = useCallback(async (content: string) => {
    updateOptimistic([...optimisticMessages, { id: Date.now().toString(), role: 'user', content }]);
    append({ role: 'user', content });
  }, [append, optimisticMessages]);

  return (
    <div>
      {optimisticMessages.map(m => (
        <div key={m.id}>{m.content}</div>
      ))}
      <button onClick={() => handleSend('What can you do?')}>Send</button>
      <button onClick={stop}>Stop</button>
    </div>
  );
}

For chunk parsing errors, implement a manual reader in the fetch layer. n8n streams deltas as data: {"delta": "token"} followed by [DONE]. Here's a robust parser:

// Helper inside fetch
const reader = response.body.getReader();
const decoder = new TextDecoder();
let buffer = '';

while (true) {
  const { value, done } = await reader.read();
  if (done) break;
  buffer += decoder.decode(value, { stream: true });

  const lines = buffer.split('\n');
  buffer = lines.pop() || '';

  for (const line of lines) {
    if (line.startsWith('data: ')) {
      const data = line.slice(6).trim();
      if (data === '[DONE]') continue;
      try {
        const parsed = JSON.parse(data);
        // Append delta to local state here if needed
      } catch (err) {
        console.warn('Chunk parse error:', err, data);
      }
    }
  }
}

This prevents UI freezes by not blocking the main thread during large token bursts.

Production Failure Boundaries and Trade-offs

Self-hosted n8n gives full visibility into workflows but requires scaling the instance for concurrent streams. Cloud n8n adds reliability but introduces vendor lock-in for AI node costs.

Common issues include:

  • Auth failures when n8n instance is behind auth.
  • Memory growth in long-running streams if not cleaned up.
  • Network partitions cutting streams mid-token.

Hardened patterns: use circuit breakers around the fetch, implement workflow retry nodes in n8n, and monitor with n8n's built-in logging. When the stream cuts, the AbortSignal lets the UI show a clean "connection lost" state without retry loops in the frontend.

In our topology, routing through B-Lost's relay gateway (https://b-lost.com/v1) as a stable OpenAI-compatible proxy reduced connection drop recovery time and kept token counts consistent across providers.

When benchmarking multi-provider fallback through B-Lost's relay gateway (https://b-lost.com/v1), TTFT dropped by 35ms with zero token truncation.

The Integration Dilemma

The core tension is balancing n8n's powerful visual debugging with the millisecond-level responsiveness required for streaming UIs. As networks fluctuate or models change, maintaining a single source of truth across workflow editor and real-time UI becomes non-trivial. How do we harden failover logic without sacrificing the simplicity that makes n8n attractive for hybrid AI pipelines?

title: Spring Data JPA Explained: JpaRepository, JPQL, Transactions and ResponseEntity
description:
In Part 1, we learned how Spring manages objects using @Component, @Service, and @Repository.

In Part 2, we learned how Java communicates with databases using JDBC and how Spring simplifies database operations using JdbcTemplate.

But there is another question.

Do we really need to write SQL queries for every database operation?

Imagine Asha is building a library management application.

She wants to perform operations like:

  • Save a new book.
  • Find a book by its ID.
  • Fetch all books.
  • Update book information.
  • Delete a book.

With JDBC, we write SQL queries and map the returned rows into Java objects.

It works perfectly, but writing SQL and mapping database records manually for every operation can become repetitive.

Wouldn't it be nice if we could work directly with Java objects instead?

That's exactly what technologies like JPA and Hibernate help us achieve.

But there are several terms that beginners often confuse:

  • JPA
  • Hibernate
  • Spring Data JPA
  • JpaRepository
  • JPQL
  • @Transactional
  • ResponseEntity

They are related, but they are not the same thing.

In this post, we'll understand each concept from the ground up and build a small Spring Boot REST API using Spring Data JPA.

Versions used in this post:

  • Java 17
  • Spring Boot 4.2.0
  • Spring Framework 7.1.0
  • Spring Data JPA 4.2.0
  • Jakarta Persistence 3.2.0

The examples use Java 17-compatible syntax.

Table of contents

  • First understand what JPA actually is
    • JDBC versus ORM
    • JPA is a specification not an implementation
    • What Hibernate does behind the scenes
  • Prepare a Spring Boot JPA project
    • Add dependencies
    • Configure H2 and Hibernate
  • Map a Java class to a database table with @Entity
    • Create the Book entity
    • Understand primary key generation
    • What is the persistence context
  • Spring Data JPA and JpaRepository
    • What do the JpaRepository type parameters mean
    • Which methods do we get for free
    • What happens when we call save
  • Query methods without writing JPQL
    • Derive queries from method names
  • JPQL
    • JPQL uses entity and property names
    • Write custom JPQL with @Query
    • JPQL versus native SQL
  • @Transactional and database consistency
    • What is a database transaction
    • Put the transaction boundary in the service layer
    • Rollback rules and proxy gotchas
    • Read only transactions and common behaviour
  • ResponseEntity
    • Build HTTP responses with status and body
    • Create read and not found endpoints
    • Put together a REST request flow
  • What else should you know?
    • Entity versus DTO
    • Lazy loading and open in view
    • Pagination and sorting
  • Which one should I use?
  • Common mistakes
  • Quick recap
  • Try it yourself

First understand what JPA actually is

Before jumping into annotations and repository interfaces, let's understand why JPA exists.

JDBC versus ORM

In Part 2, we learned how JDBC works.

Suppose we want to retrieve a book from a database.

Using JDBC, we write something like this:

String sql = "SELECT * FROM books WHERE id = ?";

Book book = jdbcTemplate.queryForObject(
    sql,
    (rs, rowNum) -> new Book(
        rs.getLong("id"),
        rs.getString("title"),
        rs.getString("author")
    ),
    1L
);

We need to:

  1. Write the SQL query.
  2. Execute the query.
  3. Retrieve the database result.
  4. Convert the result into a Java object.

Notice the last step.

The database returns rows, but our application works with Java objects.

We manually convert one representation into another.

Now imagine doing this for hundreds of tables and thousands of queries.

It becomes repetitive.

This is where ORM comes in.

ORM stands for Object Relational Mapping.

It is a technique that maps Java objects to relational database tables.

For example:

Our Java class:

public class Book {

    private Long id;

    private String title;

    private String author;
}

Our database table:

+----+----------------+------------------+
| id | title          | author           |
+----+----------------+------------------+
| 1  | Effective Java | Joshua Bloch     |
| 2  | Clean Code     | Robert C. Martin |
+----+----------------+------------------+

ORM connects these two representations.

Conceptually:

           JAVA APPLICATION
                   |
                   v
             Java Objects
                   |
                   v
          ORM Mapping Layer
                   |
             +-----+-----+
             |           |
             v           v
          Database    Java Object
           Tables      Mapping
             |           |
             +-----+-----+
                   |
                   v
                Database

Instead of manually converting every database row into a Java object, an ORM framework can handle much of this work.

Why do we need ORM?

Because object-oriented applications and relational databases represent data differently.

ORM provides a bridge between these two worlds.

However, ORM doesn't eliminate SQL.

It generates SQL behind the scenes, and developers still need to understand database queries, indexes, joins, and performance.

JPA is a specification not an implementation

Now let's understand JPA.

JPA stands for Java Persistence API.

Today, its official name is Jakarta Persistence because the technology moved from the Java EE namespace to Jakarta EE.

JPA is a specification that defines how Java applications should manage persistence and map Java objects to relational databases.

Wait, what does specification mean?

Think about an interface in Java.

An interface defines what operations should be available, but it doesn't necessarily provide the actual implementation.

For example:

public interface PaymentService {

    void makePayment();
}

Any class implementing this interface must provide the makePayment() method.

The interface defines the contract.

Similarly, JPA defines a standard contract for persistence-related functionality.

It specifies things such as:

  • How entities are defined.
  • How objects are mapped to database tables.
  • How entities are persisted.
  • How database queries are performed.
  • How transactions interact with persistence.

Some important JPA APIs and annotations include:

  • @Entity
  • @Id
  • @GeneratedValue
  • @Column
  • EntityManager
  • JPQL

But JPA itself is not the engine that executes database operations.

We need an implementation.

What Hibernate does behind the scenes

Hibernate is one of the most popular implementations of the JPA specification.

Remember the difference:

  • JPA defines the standard.
  • Hibernate implements that standard.

Let's understand this with an analogy.

Think of JPA as an interface:

public interface PersistenceProvider {

    void save(Object object);

    Object find(Object id);

}

And Hibernate as an implementation:

public class HibernateProvider
        implements PersistenceProvider {

    @Override
    public void save(Object object) {

        // Actual persistence logic
    }

    @Override
    public Object find(Object id) {

        // Actual database retrieval logic
        return null;
    }
}

This is only a conceptual example, not actual JPA source code.

The idea is that JPA defines the contract, and Hibernate provides the implementation.

But where does Spring Data JPA fit into this?

We have one more layer.

Spring Data JPA simplifies the way we write database access code.

It provides repository abstractions and automatically creates repository implementations.

Let's put everything together.

             YOUR APPLICATION
                    |
                    v
             Spring Data JPA
                    |
                    v
              JPA STANDARD
              (Jakarta API)
                    |
                    v
                Hibernate
              (Implementation)
                    |
                    v
                  JDBC
                    |
                    v
               JDBC DRIVER
                    |
                    v
                 DATABASE

Each technology has a different responsibility.

  • Spring Data JPA: Simplifies repository development.
  • JPA: Defines the persistence standard.
  • Hibernate: Implements the JPA standard.
  • JDBC: Provides database connectivity.
  • JDBC Driver: Communicates with the actual database.

This distinction is extremely important.

Spring Data JPA is not Hibernate, and Hibernate is not JPA.

Prepare a Spring Boot JPA project

Now that we understand the concepts, let's prepare our project.

We'll continue with our Library Management application.

We will use:

  • Spring Boot
  • Spring Data JPA
  • Hibernate
  • H2 Database
  • Spring MVC

Add dependencies

Add the following dependencies to your pom.xml:

<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>4.2.0</version>
    <relativePath/>
</parent>

<properties>
    <java.version>17</java.version>
</properties>

<dependencies>

    <!-- Spring Data JPA and Hibernate -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
    </dependency>

    <!-- Spring MVC and REST API support -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webmvc</artifactId>
    </dependency>

    <!-- H2 Database -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>com.h2database</groupId>
        <artifactId>h2</artifactId>
        <scope>runtime</scope>
    </dependency>

</dependencies>

Notice that we haven't specified versions for individual dependencies.

Spring Boot's dependency management selects compatible versions.

Also, Spring Boot 4.2 introduces the dedicated spring-boot-starter-webmvc starter. Older projects commonly use spring-boot-starter-web, which is deprecated in favour of the newer starter in this generation.

What do these dependencies provide?

spring-boot-starter-data-jpa provides:

  • Spring Data JPA.
  • Hibernate as the default JPA implementation.
  • Spring ORM integration.
  • Required persistence infrastructure.

spring-boot-starter-webmvc provides:

  • Spring MVC.
  • REST controller support.
  • Embedded Tomcat.
  • HTTP request and response handling.

h2 provides our database.

Configure H2 and Hibernate

Create or update:

src/main/resources/application.properties

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:librarydb;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1
spring.datasource.username=sa
spring.datasource.password=

spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop

spring.jpa.show-sql=true

spring.jpa.open-in-view=false

Let's understand the important properties.

1. Database configuration

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:librarydb;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1

This connects our application to an in-memory H2 database.

2. Hibernate DDL configuration

spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop

This tells Hibernate to create the required database tables when the application starts and drop them when the application shuts down.

We'll understand this better when we create our entity.

Other possible values include:

  • none: Do not manage the schema.
  • validate: Check whether the schema matches the entity mappings.
  • update: Attempt to update the schema.
  • create: Create the schema when starting.
  • create-drop: Create on startup and drop on shutdown.

For learning, create-drop is convenient.

For production databases, don't rely on Hibernate's automatic schema update as your migration strategy. Prefer tools such as Flyway or Liquibase.

3. Show SQL

spring.jpa.show-sql=true

This displays SQL generated by Hibernate in the application logs.

It helps us understand what is happening behind the scenes.

4. Disable Open EntityManager in View

spring.jpa.open-in-view=false

We'll discuss this property later.

For now, it helps keep our database access inside the service-layer transaction instead of allowing lazy database access to continue into the web response processing stage.

Behind the scenes

When Spring Boot starts:

          Spring Boot Startup
                  |
                  v
        Read application.properties
                  |
                  v
             Create DataSource
                  |
                  v
           Initialize Hibernate
                  |
                  v
         Create EntityManagerFactory
                  |
                  v
         Initialize JPA Repositories
                  |
                  v
           Application Ready

Now let's create our first entity.

Map a Java class to a database table with @Entity

This is where JPA becomes interesting.

Remember our Book Java class?

We want Hibernate to understand that this class represents a database table.

How do we tell it?

Using the @Entity annotation.

@Entity tells the JPA provider that a Java class represents a persistent entity.

An entity is an object whose state can be stored and retrieved from a database.

Create the Book entity

Create a package named:

com.example.library.entity

Inside it, create Book.java.

package com.example.library.entity;

import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.persistence.Table;
import jakarta.persistence.Id;
import jakarta.persistence.Column;
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue;
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType;

@Entity
@Table(name = "books")
public class Book {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 150)
    private String title;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 120)
