    private String author;

    // Required by JPA
    protected Book() {
    }

    public Book(String title, String author) {

        this.title = title;
        this.author = author;
    }

    public Long getId() {
        return id;
    }

    public String getTitle() {
        return title;
    }

    public void setTitle(String title) {
        this.title = title;
    }

    public String getAuthor() {
        return author;
    }

    public void setAuthor(String author) {
        this.author = author;
    }
}

Let's understand the annotations one by one.

1. @Entity

@Entity
public class Book {
}

Marks the class as an entity.

Hibernate recognizes it and manages its persistence.

2. @Table

@Table(name = "books")

Specifies the database table name.

Our Java class is named Book, but we want the table name to be books.

That's why we use @Table.

3. @Id

@Id
private Long id;

Every entity must have a primary key.

A primary key uniquely identifies an entity record.

Here, the id field is our primary key.

4. @Column

@Column(nullable = false, length = 150)
private String title;

Specifies mapping details for the database column.

Here:

  • nullable = false means the column should not accept NULL values.
  • length = 150 specifies the column's length.

5. No-argument constructor

protected Book() {
}

JPA requires an accessible public or protected no-argument constructor for entity instantiation.

That is why we included it.

Also, a JPA entity should not be a Java record or a final class under the Jakarta Persistence entity-class rules.

Behind the scenes

When Hibernate discovers our Book entity, it understands the mapping:

             JAVA CLASS
                 |
                 v
             @Entity
                 |
                 v
           Book.java
                 |
       +---------+---------+
       |         |         |
       v         v         v
      id       title     author
       |         |         |
       v         v         v
  PRIMARY KEY  COLUMN    COLUMN
       |         |         |
       +---------+---------+
                 |
                 v
            BOOKS TABLE

The entity mapping provides the information Hibernate needs to work with the database table.

Understand primary key generation

You might have noticed this annotation:

@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)

Why do we need it?

Imagine inserting a book.

Without automatic ID generation, we would have to assign a unique ID manually every time.

For example:

Book book = new Book("Effective Java", "Joshua Bloch");

Where does the ID come from?

GenerationType.IDENTITY tells the persistence provider to use a database identity column for generating primary keys.

In our H2 database, the database generates the ID automatically.

Other generation strategies include:

  • IDENTITY: Uses a database identity column.
  • SEQUENCE: Uses a database sequence.
  • TABLE: Uses a database table to manage generated identifiers.
  • AUTO: Lets the persistence provider choose an appropriate strategy.

For this example, we'll use IDENTITY.

What is the persistence context

Now let's understand one of the most important JPA concepts.

Suppose we retrieve a book from the database:

Book book = repository.findById(1L).orElseThrow();

Now imagine updating its title:

book.setTitle("Updated Effective Java");

Wait!

We didn't execute an UPDATE query.

We didn't call jdbcTemplate.update().

We didn't even call repository.save().

So how does the database know that the title changed?

This is where the Persistence Context comes in.

A persistence context is an environment that manages entity instances and tracks their changes.

For a given entity identity, the persistence context maintains a unique managed entity instance.

Think of it as a tracking area for Java objects that are currently managed by JPA.

Behind the scenes

             Persistence Context
                     |
              +------+------+
              |             |
              v             v
           Book 1         Book 2
              |             |
              v             v
          ID = 1         ID = 2
           Title         Title
              |             |
              +------+------+
                     |
                     v
              Change Tracking
                     |
                     v
               Database Sync

Let's understand what happens.

  1. Hibernate retrieves a book from the database.
  2. The entity becomes managed by the persistence context.
  3. We change the book's title.
  4. Hibernate notices the change.
  5. At flush or transaction commit, Hibernate synchronizes the changes with the database.

This automatic change detection is called Dirty Checking.

Let's see a practical example:

@Transactional
public void renameBook(Long id) {

    Book book = repository.findById(id).orElseThrow();

    book.setTitle("Updated Effective Java");

}

The entity is managed inside the transaction.

When the transaction commits, Hibernate detects the changed field and generates an UPDATE statement.

Expected SQL (illustrative):

UPDATE books
SET title = ?
WHERE id = ?;

Output after retrieving the book again:

Updated Effective Java

This is one of the major advantages of JPA.

We can work with Java objects, and Hibernate handles the synchronization with the database.

Spring Data JPA and JpaRepository

Now we understand JPA and Hibernate.

But there is still one problem.

Do we need to write EntityManager code for every database operation?

Not necessarily.

Spring Data JPA makes this much easier.

It provides repository interfaces that allow us to perform common database operations without manually writing their implementations.

This is where JpaRepository comes in.

What do the JpaRepository type parameters mean

You might have seen code like this:

public interface BookRepository
        extends JpaRepository<Book, Long> {
}

What exactly does JpaRepository<Book, Long> mean?

JpaRepository is a generic interface.

It accepts two important type parameters:

JpaRepository<T, ID>

Where:

  • T represents the entity type.
  • ID represents the primary key type.

In our example:

JpaRepository<Book, Long>

Means:

  • Book is our entity.
  • Long is the type of its primary key.

Why Long?

Because our entity contains:

private Long id;

If our entity had an Integer ID, we would use:

JpaRepository<Book, Integer>

If it had a String ID:

JpaRepository<Book, String>

The second generic parameter must match the entity's identifier type.

Which methods do we get for free

This is the interesting part.

Consider our repository interface:

package com.example.library.repository;

import com.example.library.entity.Book;

import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;

public interface BookRepository
        extends JpaRepository<Book, Long> {

}

We haven't implemented a single method.

We haven't written SQL queries.

We haven't used EntityManager.

Yet we can perform several database operations.

For example:

1. Save a book

Book book = new Book(
    "Effective Java",
    "Joshua Bloch"
);

bookRepository.save(book);

2. Find a book by ID

Optional<Book> book = bookRepository.findById(1L);

3. Fetch all books

List<Book> books = bookRepository.findAll();

4. Delete a book

bookRepository.deleteById(1L);

5. Count books

long count = bookRepository.count();

6. Check whether a book exists

boolean exists = bookRepository.existsById(1L);

Some commonly used inherited operations are:

  • save()
  • saveAll()
  • findById()
  • findAll()
  • existsById()
  • count()
  • deleteById()
  • delete()
  • flush()

We get these operations through the repository abstraction.

How does this work when we haven't implemented anything?

Spring Data JPA creates the repository implementation automatically at runtime.

A commonly used implementation is SimpleJpaRepository.

Conceptually:

       BookRepository Interface
                 |
                 v
       Spring Data JPA
                 |
                 v
       Repository Proxy Created
                 |
                 v
         SimpleJpaRepository
                 |
                 v
             EntityManager
                 |
                 v
              Hibernate
                 |
                 v
              Database

When we inject BookRepository, Spring provides the generated repository implementation.

That's why we don't need to write the implementation ourselves.

One important point:

BookRepository does not need @Repository explicitly.

Spring Data JPA detects repository interfaces and registers their implementations automatically.

What happens when we call save

Let's understand what actually happens when we execute:

Book book = new Book(
    "Clean Code",
    "Robert C. Martin"
);

Book savedBook = bookRepository.save(book);

Does save() directly execute an SQL INSERT?

Not necessarily at the exact moment you call it.

Spring Data JPA delegates the operation to its repository implementation.

Depending on whether the entity is considered new or existing, it typically calls either:

  • EntityManager.persist()
  • EntityManager.merge()

For a newly created book with a null ID, Spring Data JPA normally treats it as a new entity and uses persist().

For an existing detached entity, it can use merge().

Behind the scenes

          bookRepository.save(book)
                       |
                       v
               SimpleJpaRepository
                       |
                       v
             Is the entity new?
                       |
                 +-----+-----+
                 |           |
                Yes          No
                 |           |
                 v           v
              persist()    merge()
                 |           |
                 +-----+-----+
                       |
                       v
                Persistence Context
                       |
                       v
                  Hibernate
                       |
                       v
                 Generate SQL
                       |
                       v
                    Database

For new entities, Hibernate may execute the INSERT during save() or later during flush/transaction commit, depending on the identifier strategy and execution context.

The important thing is that calling save() does not mean SQL must always be executed immediately.

Also, always use the returned entity:

Book savedBook = bookRepository.save(book);

This matters particularly when JPA uses merge(), because the returned instance is the managed instance.

Query methods without writing JPQL

So far, we have used methods that Spring Data JPA provides automatically.

But what if we want to find books based on their author?

For example:

  • Find books by author.
  • Find books by title.
  • Find books containing a particular word.
  • Find books written after a particular date.

Do we need to write queries for every operation?

Not always.

Spring Data JPA supports Derived Query Methods.

Derive queries from method names

A derived query is a database query that Spring Data JPA generates by analyzing the repository method name.

For example:

List<Book> findByAuthor(String author);

What does this method name tell Spring?

  • find: We want to retrieve records.
  • By: We are specifying a condition.
  • Author: The condition is based on the entity's author property.

Spring Data JPA understands the method name and generates the corresponding query.

Let's add a few methods to our repository:

public interface BookRepository
        extends JpaRepository<Book, Long> {

    List<Book> findByAuthor(String author);

    List<Book> findByAuthorIgnoreCase(String author);

    List<Book> findByTitleContainingIgnoreCase(String keyword);

    List<Book> findByAuthorAndTitle(
        String author,
        String title
    );
}

Let's understand each method.

1. Find books by author

findByAuthor("Joshua Bloch");

Equivalent query conceptually:

SELECT *
FROM books
WHERE author = 'Joshua Bloch';

2. Ignore case while comparing author

findByAuthorIgnoreCase("joshua bloch");

This performs a case-insensitive comparison according to the query and database semantics.

3. Find books containing a particular word

findByTitleContainingIgnoreCase("java");

This searches for books whose titles contain the word java, ignoring case.

4. Combine multiple conditions

findByAuthorAndTitle(
    "Joshua Bloch",
    "Effective Java"
);

Conceptually:

SELECT *
FROM books
WHERE author = 'Joshua Bloch'
AND title = 'Effective Java';

Let's understand some commonly used keywords.

  • And: Combines two conditions.
  • Or: Combines alternative conditions.
  • Between: Checks a range.
  • LessThan: Checks whether a value is smaller.
  • GreaterThan: Checks whether a value is greater.
  • Containing: Searches for a matching substring.
  • StartingWith: Matches values beginning with a particular string.
  • EndingWith: Matches values ending with a particular string.
  • IgnoreCase: Ignores case differences for supported string comparisons.
  • IsNull: Checks for NULL values.

Behind the scenes

When Spring Data JPA discovers your repository interface, it analyzes the method names and prepares query implementations.

        Repository Interface
                  |
                  v
        findByAuthorIgnoreCase()
                  |
                  v
       Parse Method Name
                  |
                  v
       Identify Entity Property
                  |
                  v
          Generate Query
                  |
                  v
              JPQL
                  |
                  v
             Hibernate
                  |
                  v
              SQL Query
                  |
                  v
              Database

This is useful when queries are relatively simple.

But what happens when we need more control?

That's where JPQL becomes useful.

JPQL

JPQL stands for Java Persistence Query Language.

It is a query language defined by Jakarta Persistence.

It allows us to query entities and their properties rather than directly querying database tables and columns.

This is an important difference between JPQL and SQL.

JPQL uses entity and property names

Consider our Java entity:

@Entity
@Table(name = "books")
public class Book {

    @Id
    private Long id;

    private String title;

    private String author;
}

Our database table is named:

books

But our entity is named:

Book

Now suppose we want to fetch all books written by Joshua Bloch.

In SQL, we would write:

SELECT *
FROM books
WHERE author = 'Joshua Bloch';

In JPQL, we write:

SELECT b
FROM Book b
WHERE b.author = 'Joshua Bloch';

Notice the difference.

SQL uses:

  • Table name: books
  • Column name: author

JPQL uses:

  • Entity name: Book
  • Java property: author

Why?

Because JPQL operates on the object model rather than directly on the database schema.

Behind the scenes

             JPQL QUERY
                  |
                  v
      SELECT b FROM Book b
      WHERE b.author = ?
                  |
                  v
             JPA Provider
                  |
                  v
               Hibernate
                  |
                  v
           Translate JPQL
                  |
                  v
             Generate SQL
                  |
                  v
             Execute Query
                  |
                  v
               Database

Hibernate translates the JPQL query into SQL suitable for the configured database.

Write custom JPQL with @Query

Spring Data JPA allows us to write custom JPQL queries using the @Query annotation.

For example:

@Query(
    "SELECT b FROM Book b WHERE b.author = :author"
)
List<Book> findBooksByAuthor(
    @Param("author") String author
);

Let's understand the annotations.

@Query tells Spring Data JPA which query should execute when the repository method is called.

@Param connects the Java method parameter with the named parameter in the JPQL query.

Here:

:author

is the named parameter.

And:

@Param("author") String author

provides its value.

We can also write case-insensitive queries:

@Query("""
    SELECT b
    FROM Book b
    WHERE LOWER(b.author) = LOWER(:author)
""")
List<Book> findBooksByAuthorIgnoreCase(
    @Param("author") String author
);

Example:

List<Book> books =
    bookRepository.findBooksByAuthorIgnoreCase("joshua bloch");

books.forEach(book ->
    System.out.println(book.getTitle())
);

Output:

Effective Java

Why would we use @Query when derived query methods already exist?

Because some queries become difficult to express through method names.

Imagine queries involving:

  • Multiple conditions.
  • Joins between entities.
  • Aggregation.
  • Subqueries.
  • Complex filtering.

Writing JPQL gives you more control over the query.

JPQL versus native SQL

Sometimes JPQL is not enough.

You might need a database-specific function or a query that takes advantage of a particular database feature.

Spring Data JPA allows native SQL queries through @Query.

Example:

@Query(
    value = "SELECT * FROM books WHERE author = :author",
    nativeQuery = true
)
List<Book> findBooksUsingNativeSQL(
    @Param("author") String author
);

Notice the difference.

JPQL:

SELECT b FROM Book b WHERE b.author = :author

Native SQL:

SELECT * FROM books WHERE author = :author

JPQL works with entities and Java properties.

Native SQL works directly with database tables and columns.

Which one should you choose?

Prefer JPQL when you want database-independent queries based on your entity model.

Use native SQL when you need database-specific SQL features or when a complex SQL query is more appropriate.

Remember that native SQL can make your application more dependent on a particular database.

@Transactional and database consistency

Now let's understand another important annotation.

@Transactional.

You will see this annotation frequently in Spring Boot service classes.

But why do we need it?

Suppose Asha's library application allows users to borrow books.

When a user borrows a book, the application might need to:

  1. Check whether the book is available.
  2. Create a borrowing record.
  3. Update the book's availability.

What happens if the first operation succeeds, the second operation succeeds, but the third operation fails?

The database might end up in an inconsistent state.

We need a way to make sure related database operations succeed or fail together.

This is where transactions come in.

What is a database transaction

A transaction is a group of database operations treated as one logical unit of work.

A transaction follows the well-known ACID properties.

  • Atomicity: All operations succeed together or are rolled back together.
  • Consistency: A transaction should preserve database rules and constraints.
  • Isolation: Concurrent transactions should not interfere with one another beyond the configured isolation guarantees.
  • Durability: Once committed, changes should persist according to the database's durability guarantees.

Let's take a simple example.

A user transfers ₹500 from Account A to Account B.

Two operations are needed:

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 500
WHERE id = 1;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + 500
WHERE id = 2;

What if the first UPDATE succeeds but the second fails?

We don't want ₹500 to disappear.

Both operations must belong to one transaction.

Conceptually:

             BEGIN TRANSACTION
                     |
                     v
            Deduct ₹500 from A
                     |
                     v
             Add ₹500 to B
                     |
                     v
              Both successful?
                /       \
              Yes        No
               |          |
               v          v
            COMMIT     ROLLBACK
               |          |
               v          v
          Save changes  Undo changes

This is the problem @Transactional helps solve in Spring.

Put the transaction boundary in the service layer

Spring provides the @Transactional annotation to define transaction boundaries.

Example:

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Service
public class BookService {

    private final BookRepository bookRepository;

    public BookService(BookRepository bookRepository) {

        this.bookRepository = bookRepository;
    }

    @Transactional
    public void renameBook(Long id, String newTitle) {

        Book book = bookRepository
            .findById(id)
            .orElseThrow();

        book.setTitle(newTitle);

    }
}

What does @Transactional do here?

It tells Spring that this method should execute within a transaction.

When the method starts, Spring's transaction infrastructure begins or joins an appropriate transaction.

When the method completes successfully, the transaction can commit.

If an applicable exception occurs, the transaction can roll back.

Notice that we didn't call:

bookRepository.save(book);

Why?

Because we loaded the book inside a transaction.

The book is managed by the JPA persistence context.

When we modify its title, Hibernate detects the change through dirty checking and synchronizes it with the database during flush or commit.

Behind the scenes

       Controller Calls Service
                  |
                  v
          Spring Transaction
              Begins
                  |
                  v
         Find Book From Database
                  |
                  v
          Entity Becomes Managed
                  |
                  v
          Update Book Object
                  |
                  v
           Method Completes
                  |
                  v
           Hibernate Flush
                  |
                  v
            Commit Transaction
                  |
                  v
          Database Updated

Why do we usually put @Transactional on service methods?

Because the service layer represents a business operation.

A single business operation might involve multiple repository calls.

We want all those operations to participate in the same transaction.

For example, borrowing a book could involve:

  • Updating the book.
  • Creating a borrowing record.
  • Updating a user's borrowing count.

These operations should belong to one logical unit of work.

Putting the transaction boundary at the service layer makes that intention clear.

Rollback rules and proxy gotchas

Let's understand rollback behaviour.

Consider this example:

@Transactional
public void updateBook(Long id) {

    Book book = bookRepository
        .findById(id)
        .orElseThrow();

    book.setTitle("Temporary Title");

    throw new IllegalStateException(
        "Something went wrong!"
    );
}

What happens?

The book's title is changed in memory.

But before the method completes, an exception occurs.

IllegalStateException is an unchecked exception.

By default, Spring rolls back transactions when unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and its subclasses) or Error escape the transactional method.

The transaction is rolled back.

Expected exception:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: Something went wrong!

After the rollback, the old book title remains in the database.

What about checked exceptions?

By default, checked exceptions do not trigger rollback.

For example, IOException.

When you need a checked exception to trigger rollback, configure it explicitly:

@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)
public void updateBook(Long id) throws Exception {

    // Database operations

    throw new Exception("Something failed");
}

There is another interesting behaviour beginners should know.

Self-invocation problem

Spring's default transaction management uses proxies.

A proxy is an object that sits between the caller and the actual service implementation.

When another bean calls a transactional method through the Spring-managed service, the proxy can apply transaction behaviour.

But consider:

@Service
public class BookService {

    public void processBook() {

        updateBook();
    }

    @Transactional
    public void updateBook() {

        // Database operations
    }
}

Here, processBook() calls updateBook() directly using this.

The call does not go through the Spring proxy.

Therefore, the transaction annotation on updateBook() is not applied through the default proxy mechanism for this self-invocation.

A better approach is to put the transactional operation in a separate Spring-managed service or call it from another bean through the proxy.

Behind the scenes

        Another Spring Bean
                 |
                 v
          Spring Proxy
                 |
        Apply Transaction
                 |
                 v
          Actual Service
                 |
                 v
         Execute Method

But when a method calls another method inside the same object:

          Actual Service
                 |
                 v
          this.updateBook()
                 |
                 v
          Direct Method Call
                 |
                 v
        Proxy Is Bypassed

Keep this in mind when debugging transactions that seem to be ignored.

Read only transactions and common behaviour

Not every operation modifies data.

For example, fetching all books is a read operation.

We can mark such methods as read-only:

@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public List<Book> getAllBooks() {

    return bookRepository.findAll();
}

Why use readOnly = true?

It communicates that the transaction is intended for reading.

Depending on the persistence provider and database, this can enable useful optimizations.

For example, Hibernate can adjust its flush behaviour to avoid unnecessary dirty checking in suitable read-only transactions.

But remember something important.

readOnly = true is generally a hint for the underlying transaction infrastructure and persistence provider.

It is not a universal security mechanism that guarantees write operations are impossible.

A good default:

  • Use @Transactional(readOnly = true) for read-oriented service methods.
  • Use @Transactional for methods that modify data.
  • Put transaction boundaries around complete business operations.

Spring Data JPA also provides transactional behaviour for inherited repository CRUD methods.

However, declared query methods do not automatically receive transaction configuration in every case.

That's another reason why service-level transaction boundaries are useful.

ResponseEntity

Until now, we have focused on database operations.

But how does our backend send the result to the client?

Suppose Ravi sends an HTTP request:

GET /api/books/1

Our application retrieves the book from the database.

Now we need to send the result back.

Should we return a Java object directly?

We can.

But what if we want to control:

  • HTTP status code.
  • Response headers.
  • Response body.

This is where ResponseEntity comes in.

ResponseEntity is a Spring class that represents an entire HTTP response, including its status code, headers, and body.

Build HTTP responses with status and body

Consider a simple REST controller:

@RestController
public class BookController {

    @GetMapping("/books")
    public String getBooks() {

        return "Fetching all books";
    }
}

Output:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Response body:

Fetching all books

The controller returns a value, and Spring MVC writes it into the HTTP response body.

But what if we want more control?

We can use ResponseEntity.

@GetMapping("/books")
public ResponseEntity<String> getBooks() {

    return ResponseEntity.ok("Fetching all books");
}

Output:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Response body:

Fetching all books

Let's look at some commonly used methods.

1. Return HTTP 200 OK

return ResponseEntity.ok("Success");

2. Return HTTP 201 Created

return ResponseEntity
    .status(HttpStatus.CREATED)
    .body("Book created");

3. Return HTTP 404 Not Found

return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();

4. Return HTTP 204 No Content

return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();

5. Return an HTTP response with a custom header

return ResponseEntity
    .ok()
    .header("X-Application", "Library")
    .body("Success");

Why do we need this?

Because HTTP responses contain more than just data.

A good REST API should communicate the correct status of an operation to its clients.

Behind the scenes

           Controller Method
                  |
                  v
              ResponseEntity
                  |
         +--------+--------+
         |        |        |
         v        v        v
       Status   Headers   Body
         |        |        |
         +--------+--------+
                  |
                  v
          Spring MVC Response
                  |
                  v
                Client

Spring MVC uses HTTP message converters to convert Java response objects into HTTP representations such as JSON.

Create read and not found endpoints

Let's make this more practical.

Suppose our API needs three operations:

  • Fetch all books.
  • Fetch one book by ID.
  • Create a new book.

First, let's create a response DTO.

A DTO is a Data Transfer Object.

We'll discuss it in more detail later.

Create BookResponse.java:

package com.example.library.dto;

public record BookResponse(
    Long id,
    String title,
    String author
) {}

Now create a request DTO:

CreateBookRequest.java

package com.example.library.dto;

public record CreateBookRequest(
    String title,
    String author
) {}

Now create the service:

BookService.java

package com.example.library.service;

import com.example.library.dto.BookResponse;
import com.example.library.dto.CreateBookRequest;
import com.example.library.entity.Book;
import com.example.library.repository.BookRepository;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;

@Service
public class BookService {

    private final BookRepository bookRepository;

    public BookService(BookRepository bookRepository) {

        this.bookRepository = bookRepository;
    }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public List<BookResponse> getAllBooks() {

        return bookRepository.findAll()
            .stream()
            .map(this::toResponse)
            .toList();
    }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public Optional<BookResponse> getBookById(Long id) {

        return bookRepository.findById(id)
            .map(this::toResponse);
    }

    @Transactional
    public BookResponse createBook(CreateBookRequest request) {

        Book book = new Book(
            request.title(),
            request.author()
        );

        Book savedBook = bookRepository.save(book);

        return toResponse(savedBook);
    }

    private BookResponse toResponse(Book book) {

        return new BookResponse(
            book.getId(),
            book.getTitle(),
            book.getAuthor()
        );
    }
}

Notice that the service does not know anything about HTTP status codes.

Its responsibility is to handle business operations.

Now let's create our controller.

BookController.java

package com.example.library.controller;

import com.example.library.dto.BookResponse;
import com.example.library.dto.CreateBookRequest;
import com.example.library.service.BookService;

import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/books")
public class BookController {

    private final BookService bookService;

    public BookController(BookService bookService) {

        this.bookService = bookService;
    }

    // Fetch all books
    @GetMapping
    public ResponseEntity<List<BookResponse>> getAllBooks() {

        return ResponseEntity.ok(
            bookService.getAllBooks()
        );
    }

    // Fetch book by ID
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<BookResponse> getBookById(
        @PathVariable Long id
    ) {

        Optional<BookResponse> book =
            bookService.getBookById(id);

        if (book.isEmpty()) {

            return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
        }

        return ResponseEntity.ok(book.get());
    }

    // Create a new book
    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<BookResponse> createBook(
        @RequestBody CreateBookRequest request
    ) {

        BookResponse savedBook =
            bookService.createBook(request);

        return ResponseEntity
            .status(HttpStatus.CREATED)
            .body(savedBook);
    }
}

Let's understand the important annotations:

  • @RestController: Marks the class as a REST controller.
  • @RequestMapping: Defines the common URL prefix.
  • @GetMapping: Handles HTTP GET requests.
  • @PostMapping: Handles HTTP POST requests.
  • @PathVariable: Extracts values from the URL.
  • @RequestBody: Converts the incoming JSON request body into a Java object.

The important part is the return type:

ResponseEntity<BookResponse>

This means our controller returns an HTTP response with a BookResponse body.

Put together a REST request flow

Let's prepare some initial data.

Update your main application class:

LibraryApplication.java

package com.example.library;

import com.example.library.entity.Book;
import com.example.library.repository.BookRepository;

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;

import java.util.List;

@SpringBootApplication
public class LibraryApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        SpringApplication.run(
            LibraryApplication.class,
            args
        );
    }

    @Bean
    CommandLineRunner loadData(BookRepository repository) {

        return args -> {

            if (repository.count() == 0) {

                repository.saveAll(
                    List.of(
                        new Book(
                            "Effective Java",
                            "Joshua Bloch"
                        ),
                        new Book(
                            "Clean Code",
                            "Robert C. Martin"
                        )
                    )
                );
            }
        };
    }
}

Our package structure now looks like this:

com.example.library
|
+-- LibraryApplication.java
|
+-- controller
|   +-- BookController.java
|
+-- service
|   +-- BookService.java
|
+-- repository
|   +-- BookRepository.java
|
+-- entity
|   +-- Book.java
|
+-- dto
    +-- BookResponse.java
    +-- CreateBookRequest.java

Now start the application.

Let's send some requests.

1. Fetch all books

Request:

curl -i http://localhost:8080/api/books

Expected response:

HTTP/1.1 200
Content-Type: application/json

Response body:

[
    {
        "id": 1,
        "title": "Effective Java",
        "author": "Joshua Bloch"
    },
    {
        "id": 2,
        "title": "Clean Code",
        "author": "Robert C. Martin"
    }
]

2. Fetch a book by ID

Request:

curl -i http://localhost:8080/api/books/1

Expected response:

HTTP/1.1 200
Content-Type: application/json

Response body:

{
    "id": 1,
    "title": "Effective Java",
    "author": "Joshua Bloch"
}

3. Fetch a book that doesn't exist

Request:

curl -i http://localhost:8080/api/books/999

Expected response:

HTTP/1.1 404

There is no response body.

Why?

Because our controller explicitly returns:

ResponseEntity.notFound().build();

4. Create a new book

Request:

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/books \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{"title":"Head First Java","author":"Kathy Sierra"}'

Expected response:

HTTP/1.1 201
Content-Type: application/json

Response body:

{
    "id": 3,
    "title": "Head First Java",
    "author": "Kathy Sierra"
}

We returned HTTP 201 because a new resource was created.

Notice how all the concepts we learned are working together.

Complete request flow

                 CLIENT
                    |
                    v
           HTTP Request (JSON)
                    |
                    v
              CONTROLLER
                    |
                    v
               SERVICE
                    |
            @Transactional
                    |
                    v
              REPOSITORY
                    |
                    v
              JpaRepository
                    |
                    v
                Hibernate
                    |
                    v
                 JDBC
                    |
                    v
                DATABASE
                    |
                    v
             Query / Result
                    |
                    v
              SERVICE
                    |
                    v
              BookResponse
                    |
                    v
              ResponseEntity
                    |
                    v
                 CLIENT

This is a typical Spring Boot backend request lifecycle.

What else should you know?

We have covered the main topics, but there are a few related concepts that are important when building real-world applications.

Entity versus DTO

One thing you'll notice in our application is that we don't directly return the Book entity from the controller.

Instead, we return:

BookResponse

Why?

Because an Entity and a DTO serve different purposes.

Entity

An entity represents persistent data.

It is mapped to a database table.

Example:

@Entity
public class Book {

    @Id
    private Long id;

    private String title;

    private String author;
}

DTO

A DTO is used to transfer data between application boundaries.

Example:

public record BookResponse(
    Long id,
    String title
) {}

Notice that the DTO doesn't contain the author field.

Maybe our API should expose only the ID and title.

Using a DTO gives us control over what data is returned.

Why should we avoid directly returning entities?

  • It prevents unnecessary exposure of database fields.
  • It separates the API structure from the database structure.
  • It helps avoid JSON serialization problems with entity relationships.
  • It makes API changes easier.

A simple rule:

Use entities for persistence and DTOs for API communication.

Lazy loading and open in view

Consider a different application with two entities:

  • Department
  • Employee

One department can have many employees.

We might define a relationship like this:

@OneToMany(mappedBy = "department")
private List<Employee> employees;

Now imagine fetching one department.

Should Hibernate immediately retrieve every employee belonging to it?

Not necessarily.

This is where Lazy Loading comes in.

Lazy loading means related data is loaded only when it is accessed, provided the mapping uses lazy fetching and the persistence context is still available.

For example:

Department department =
    departmentRepository.findById(1L).orElseThrow();

// Access employees later
List<Employee> employees = department.getEmployees();

The employee collection might be loaded only when the application accesses it.

This can save unnecessary database queries.

However, if the persistence context is already closed when we access the lazy relationship, Hibernate may throw:

org.hibernate.LazyInitializationException:
could not initialize proxy - no Session

Another problem is the N+1 query problem.

For example, you fetch 10 departments using one query.

Then, while iterating over them, you access the employees of each department.

Hibernate might execute another query for each department.

Instead of one query, you end up executing 11 queries.

That's why we need to understand:

  • Lazy loading.
  • Eager loading.
  • Fetch joins.
  • Entity graphs.
  • DTO projections.

Also, in our application, we configured:

spring.jpa.open-in-view=false

This prevents Spring Boot's Open EntityManager in View mechanism from keeping the JPA EntityManager open across the whole web request.

It encourages fetching the data required by the API within the service-layer transaction.

Pagination and sorting

Imagine our library application has 100,000 books.

Should we fetch all 100,000 records whenever the client requests /api/books?

Definitely not.

We need pagination.

Pagination means dividing a large result set into smaller pages.

Spring Data JPA supports pagination through Pageable.

Example:

Pageable pageable = PageRequest.of(0, 10);

Page<Book> books = bookRepository.findAll(pageable);

What do these values mean?

PageRequest.of(0, 10)
  • 0: First page.
  • 10: Number of records per page.

The result is a Page<Book>.

It gives us access to:

  • Page content.
  • Total number of elements.
  • Total number of pages.
  • Current page number.
  • Whether another page exists.

We can also add sorting:

Pageable pageable = PageRequest.of(
    0,
    10,
    Sort.by("title").ascending()
);

Page<Book> books = bookRepository.findAll(pageable);

This retrieves the first 10 books sorted by title.

Why does this matter?

Because fetching only the records required by the client improves efficiency and reduces unnecessary database work.

Which one should I use?

Now let's summarize when to use each technology.

JDBC

Choose JDBC when:

  • You want low-level database control.
  • You want to write SQL manually.
  • You need to understand database connectivity.

JdbcTemplate

Choose JdbcTemplate when:

  • You want to write custom SQL.
  • You want Spring to manage JDBC boilerplate.
  • You want more direct control over SQL execution.

Spring Data JPA

Choose Spring Data JPA when:

  • Your application works primarily with Java entities.
  • You need common CRUD operations.
  • You want repository interfaces.
  • You want automatic query generation.

JpaRepository

Choose JpaRepository when:

  • Your repository needs standard CRUD operations.
  • You need pagination and sorting.
  • You want JPA-specific repository functionality.

JPQL

Choose JPQL when:

  • You need custom queries based on entity properties.
  • Derived query methods become difficult to read.
  • You want object-oriented queries instead of direct database SQL.

Native SQL

Choose native SQL when:

  • You need database-specific features.
  • Your query is easier to express in SQL.
  • You need direct access to database-specific functionality.

@Transactional

Use it when:

  • Multiple database operations belong to one business operation.
  • You need atomic database operations.
  • You need predictable transaction boundaries.

ResponseEntity

Use it when:

  • You need to control HTTP status codes.
  • You need to add response headers.
  • You need different response formats based on the operation result.

My recommendation:

For most typical Spring Boot backend applications, start with:

  • Spring Data JPA for persistence.
  • JpaRepository for common CRUD operations.
  • JPQL for custom entity-based queries.
  • @Transactional at service boundaries.
  • DTOs for API request and response objects.
  • ResponseEntity when controlling HTTP responses.

However, don't assume JPA is always better than JDBC.

For complex reporting, bulk operations, or database-specific queries, JdbcTemplate or native SQL can be a better fit.

Common mistakes

Let's look at six mistakes beginners frequently make.

1. Thinking JPA and Hibernate are the same thing

JPA is a persistence specification, while Hibernate is an implementation of that specification.

Understand the difference before working with JPA annotations.

2. Confusing JpaRepository generic parameters

The first parameter is the entity type, and the second is the primary key type.

For example:

JpaRepository<Book, Long>

Make sure the second type matches your entity's ID field.

3. Writing SQL table names inside JPQL queries

JPQL works with entity names and Java properties, not directly with database table and column names.

Use Book and author in JPQL, not books and author as table/column references.

4. Assuming save() always executes SQL immediately

JPA manages persistence operations through its persistence context.

Changes may be synchronized during flush or transaction commit.

Understand dirty checking and the entity lifecycle.

5. Putting @Transactional on a method called only through self-invocation

Spring's default proxy-based transaction management intercepts external calls through the proxy.

A direct method call inside the same class bypasses that proxy.

Move transactional work into another Spring-managed bean when appropriate.

6. Returning JPA entities directly from every REST controller

Entities represent database persistence structures, while DTOs represent API data.

Use DTOs to control what your API exposes and avoid serialization issues involving entity relationships.

Quick recap

Let's revise everything we learned.

  • ORM maps Java objects to relational database tables.
  • JPA, now Jakarta Persistence, is a persistence specification.
  • Hibernate is a popular JPA implementation.
  • Spring Data JPA simplifies repository development.
  • @Entity marks a Java class as a persistent entity.
  • @Id defines the primary key.
  • @GeneratedValue configures primary key generation.
  • The persistence context manages entity instances.
  • Dirty checking automatically detects changes to managed entities.
  • JpaRepository<T, ID> provides common persistence operations.
  • Spring Data JPA generates repository implementations automatically.
  • Derived query methods generate queries from method names.
  • JPQL queries entities and Java properties instead of database tables and columns.
  • @Query allows us to define custom JPQL or native SQL queries.
  • @Transactional defines transaction boundaries.
  • Unchecked exceptions and errors trigger rollback by default.
  • readOnly = true provides a read-only transaction hint and optimization opportunity.
  • Spring's default proxy-based transaction mechanism does not intercept self-invocation.
  • ResponseEntity controls HTTP status codes, headers, and response bodies.
  • DTOs separate API data from database entities.
  • Pagination helps retrieve large datasets efficiently.

Try it yourself

Practice idea:

Extend the Library Management application.

Implement the following operations:

  • Fetch all books.
  • Fetch a book by ID.
  • Add a new book.
  • Update a book's title.
  • Delete a book.
  • Find books by author.
  • Find books containing a particular keyword.
  • Fetch books using pagination and sorting.

Use the following structure:

Controller
    |
    v
Service
    |
    v
Repository
    |
    v
Database

Use JpaRepository for CRUD operations, derived queries for simple searches, and JPQL for custom queries.

Use ResponseEntity to return appropriate HTTP status codes.

Bonus experiment:

Build the same Library Management application twice.

First, use JdbcTemplate.

Then, replace the persistence layer with Spring Data JPA.

Compare:

  • Amount of code.
  • SQL query handling.
  • Object mapping.
  • CRUD operations.
  • Transaction management.

Try to understand what Spring Data JPA and Hibernate are doing for you behind the scenes.

If this helped, or if you spotted something I should fix, tell me in the comments. I'm still learning too.

title: Who Attributes a Mind to Whom? Mutual Theory of Mind in Simulated User-Assistant Conversation
description:
arXiv:2611.33327v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When users assume that an AI chatbot has mental states, they are more likely to develop over-reliance, emotional dependence, and in extreme cases, psychological harm or self-harm. However, how these mind attributions arise in conversations and how human or AI factors influence this is still unknown. We study how users attribute minds using a minimal framework: a simulated user with different characteristics chats with assistants that differ in social style and memory. We also introduce a message-level measure of who attributes a mind to whom in four directions, checked with trained coders and applied by a fine-tuned encoder that reproduces an LLM judge. Our results show that, on average, nine out of thirteen characteristics raised simulated users' attribution to the assistant. We found that relational needs such as attachment anxiety raised it as theory predicts, some general personality traits raised it as well, and AI-specific characteristics the least. By contrast, the assistant's social style barely changed simulated users' mind attribution. Instead, sycophantic instructions raised the assistant's attribution to itself. Memory raised users' attribution only with some user models. The model playing the user changed overall attribution and the effects of characteristics, style, and memory. Our framework measures how persona descriptions affect mind attribution in simulation. It gives concrete hypotheses for human studies and shows the need for more consistent user simulators.

title: Safe Autoformalization: Sufficiency and Necessity with Entailment Graphs
description:
arXiv:2611.31571v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autoformalization translates a natural-language statement into a formula that captures its intent, which depends on the statement's context: the background that disambiguates it. LLMs make autoformalization practical, but their probabilistic output carries no formal guarantees. We propose techniques for safe autoformalization that certify one-sided logical adequacy: a formula sufficient for the intent is safe to enforce, and a formula necessary for it is safe to rely on. We use LLMs to generate candidate formulas and order them by logical strength in an Entailment Graph (EG), an ordering a solver decides. Each edge carries a residual and a co-residual, the two adjoints of the entailment order, all fixed by the candidate pool alone. In a context, two searches return the sufficient frontier, the weakest candidates that entail the statement, and the necessary frontier, the strongest candidates the statement entails; each step is one local check against an edge's residual or co-residual. The frontiers bracket the statement and yield the ambiguity residue, which holds exactly of the situations the candidates certify neither as satisfying nor as violating it; the statement is ambiguous precisely when the residue is satisfiable. For natural-language statements and contexts, an LLM entailment oracle decides the checks; it is sound if it accepts only checks that hold, and complete if it accepts every check that holds. We prove that a sound oracle makes the search safe regardless of pool quality, and that a complete one makes the frontiers tight. On security-critical AWS properties, EGs are safe in all 20 cases of an expert-adjudicated study, where majority vote over equivalence clusters and Universal Self-Consistency are unsafe in 25% and 10%. An ablation with the same oracle but no graph is unsafe in 25% and rejects every candidate in another 30%. We machine-checked our proofs in Lean.

title: Export Excel Charts as Images in Java: Single Charts, Multiple Charts, and Chart Sheets
description:
Charts in Excel are often useful beyond the workbook itself. You might want to add a sales chart to a presentation, include a trend line in a report, or display a chart on a web page. Taking screenshots works for the occasional chart, but it becomes tedious when a workbook contains several charts, and the results may require extra cropping.

With Java, you can export existing Excel charts directly as PNG images without recreating the charts or capturing the entire worksheet. This tutorial covers three cases: exporting a specific chart, saving every chart in a worksheet, and exporting a standalone chart sheet.

Set Up the Java Project

Add the following repository and dependency to your Maven project's pom.xml:

<repositories>
    <repository>
        <id>com.e-iceblue</id>
        <url>https://repo.e-iceblue.com/nexus/content/groups/public/</url>
    </repository>
</repositories>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>e-iceblue</groupId>
        <artifactId>spire.xls.free</artifactId>
        <version>16.3.1</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

If your pom.xml already contains <repositories> or <dependencies>, add the entries to the existing sections rather than creating duplicate top-level elements.

Prepare a Sample Excel Workbook

The examples use a workbook named sales_report.xlsx with the following sheets:

  • Sales Summary — a regular worksheet containing a quarterly sales column chart and a sales trend line chart.
  • Regional Sales — a regular worksheet with a pie chart showing sales by region.
  • Annual Sales Share — a standalone chart sheet, rather than a chart embedded in a cell-based worksheet.

Save sales_report.xlsx in the program's working directory. Each example loads the same workbook independently and creates its own output files.

1. Export a Specific Excel Chart as a PNG Image

If you need just one chart—say, the quarterly sales chart—you can select it by its index in the worksheet instead of exporting the entire sheet.

The Workbook.saveChartAsImage(Worksheet, int) method returns a BufferedImage for the specified chart. Chart indexes are zero-based, so 0 refers to the first chart in that worksheet. Java's ImageIO.write() can then save the returned image as a PNG file.

Complete Java code:

import com.spire.xls.Workbook;
import com.spire.xls.Worksheet;

import javax.imageio.ImageIO;
import java.awt.image.BufferedImage;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.nio.file.Paths;

public class ExportSingleExcelChart {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Workbook workbook = new Workbook();

        try {
            workbook.loadFromFile("sales_report.xlsx");
            Worksheet sheet = workbook.getWorksheets().get(0);

            if (sheet.getCharts().getCount() == 0) {
                System.out.println("No charts found in the worksheet.");
                return;
            }

            // Export the first embedded chart
            BufferedImage image = workbook.saveChartAsImage(sheet, 0);

            Path outputDir = Paths.get("output/single_chart");
            Files.createDirectories(outputDir);

            ImageIO.write(image, "png",
                    outputDir.resolve("quarterly_sales.png").toFile());

            System.out.println("Chart exported.");
        } finally {
            workbook.dispose();
        }
    }
}

The program saves the first chart as output/single_chart/quarterly_sales.png. To export another chart from the same worksheet, change the index to 1, 2, and so on, provided that the chart exists.

2. Export All Charts from an Excel Worksheet

A worksheet may contain several charts that you want to reuse in a report or dashboard. Instead of exporting them one by one, you can get them all in a single call.

Workbook.saveChartAsImage(Worksheet) returns a BufferedImage[] containing the images of the charts in that worksheet. The following program loops through the array and saves each image with a sequential filename.

Complete Java code:

import com.spire.xls.Workbook;
import com.spire.xls.Worksheet;

import javax.imageio.ImageIO;
import java.awt.image.BufferedImage;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.nio.file.Paths;

public class ExportAllExcelCharts {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Workbook workbook = new Workbook();

        try {
            workbook.loadFromFile("sales_report.xlsx");
            Worksheet sheet = workbook.getWorksheets().get(0);

            if (sheet.getCharts().getCount() == 0) {
                System.out.println("No charts found in the worksheet.");
                return;
            }

            // Render every embedded chart in the worksheet
            BufferedImage[] images = workbook.saveChartAsImage(sheet);

            Path outputDir = Paths.get("output/all_charts");
            Files.createDirectories(outputDir);

            for (int i = 0; i < images.length; i++) {
                Path outputFile = outputDir.resolve("chart_" + (i + 1) + ".png");
                ImageIO.write(images[i], "png", outputFile.toFile());
            }

            System.out.println("Exported " + images.length + " charts.");
        } finally {
            workbook.dispose();
        }
    }
}

If the first worksheet contains two charts, the output folder will look like this:

output/
└── all_charts/
    ├── chart_1.png
    └── chart_2.png

This method handles charts on the selected worksheet only. If your charts are distributed across several worksheets, iterate over the worksheets and export each sheet's charts separately.

3. Export an Excel Chart Sheet as an Image

Excel also supports chart sheets, where a chart occupies its own sheet instead of appearing within a regular worksheet. These are different from embedded charts, so they use a different overload.

You can access a chart sheet through Workbook.getChartsheets() and pass it to Workbook.saveChartAsImage(ChartSheet). The following example exports the first chart sheet to PNG. Notice the explicit cast: the Java API documents getChartsheets() as returning a raw ArrayList.

Complete Java code:

import com.spire.xls.Workbook;
import com.spire.xls.ChartSheet;

import javax.imageio.ImageIO;
import java.awt.image.BufferedImage;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.nio.file.Paths;

public class ExportExcelChartSheet {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Workbook workbook = new Workbook();

        try {
            workbook.loadFromFile("sales_report.xlsx");

            if (workbook.getChartsheets().isEmpty()) {
                System.out.println("No chart sheets found in the workbook.");
                return;
            }

            // Access the first standalone chart sheet
            ChartSheet chartSheet = (ChartSheet) workbook.getChartsheets().get(0);
            BufferedImage image = workbook.saveChartAsImage(chartSheet);

            Path outputDir = Paths.get("output/chart_sheet");
            Files.createDirectories(outputDir);

            ImageIO.write(image, "png",
                    outputDir.resolve("annual_sales_share.png").toFile());

            System.out.println("Chart sheet exported.");
        } finally {
            workbook.dispose();
        }
    }
}

The exported image is saved as output/chart_sheet/annual_sales_share.png. If a workbook contains several chart sheets, you can select the one you need rather than assuming the first is always the right one.

Common Questions

1. What is the difference between exporting a chart and exporting a worksheet?

saveChartAsImage() exports the chart itself. It does not include the surrounding cell grid or values outside the chart. If you need an image of the entire worksheet, use a worksheet-to-image method such as Worksheet.saveToImage() instead.

2. Why doesn't the program find my chart?

First, check whether the object in Excel is an actual chart or just a pasted picture. Then confirm that the code targets the worksheet containing that chart. A standalone chart sheet is handled separately and won't appear in the ordinary worksheet's embedded-chart collection.

3. Can I edit the exported chart in Excel?

The PNG is a static image: you cannot change its data series or axes as you would in Excel. Exporting does not modify the original chart in the workbook, however, so you can edit the original and generate a new image whenever the data changes.

4. Why does the exported chart look slightly different from Excel?

Chart images are rendered outside Excel, so font availability and support for particular chart features can affect the output. This is especially noticeable when a workbook uses custom fonts or complex chart types. Check a representative image before exporting a large batch.

5. Can I export charts as JPEG instead of PNG?

You can use Java's ImageIO to write a JPEG, but JPEG does not support transparency. If the rendered image has an alpha channel, convert it to an RGB image first. For charts with labels, gridlines, and fine lines, PNG is usually a better default because it avoids JPEG compression artifacts.

Conclusion

If you already have charts in an Excel workbook, exporting them as images is often easier than recreating them or taking screenshots. Use the chart index when you need one chart, the worksheet overload to export all embedded charts, or the chart-sheet overload for a standalone chart sheet. The resulting PNG files can then be reused in presentations, reports, and web pages.

title: Vercel completes ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification
description:
Vercel has completed its ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification, meeting the international standard for AI management systems.

This certification gives our customers confidence to ship fast with agents on Vercel, demonstrating how Vercel designs, builds, operates, and governs our AI products.

Our AI management system covers Vercel’s underlying infrastructure and core AI products, including AI Gateway, Vercel Agent, v0, AI-based open source software and frameworks, as well as the people and processes behind them.

Vercel’s certificate is available here, and additional audit documentation is available through our Trust Center.

What is ISO 42001?

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is the international standard for AI management systems and applies to any organization that develops, provides, or uses AI.

An AI management system is the set of policies, roles, processes, and controls through which an organization consistently governs AI activities. The standard includes requirements for leadership accountability, AI risk assessment, lifecycle management, data governance, transparency, and continual improvement.

The requirement that makes ISO 42001 distinct from security standards is the AI system impact assessment. Security frameworks cover how an organization protects information, but ISO 42001 covers how it builds and uses AI, including the assessment of how an AI system impacts the people it touches, and the benefits and harms that would result when that system materially changes.

To obtain the certification, we underwent a two-stage audit performed by an independent, accredited certification body, which evaluated whether our AI management system is designed correctly and operates effectively. The certificate is valid for three years, with annual surveillance audits in between.

“Enterprises want agents in production, but no one should have to choose between moving fast with AI and governing it well,” said Talha Tariq, CTO for Security. “We built our AI governance to run as continuously as we ship, and ISO 42001 is the independent check that it works.”

What this means for customers

AI moved into the critical path of how software gets built faster than the governance around it did. Teams are shipping agents, assistants, and model-backed features on Vercel every day, and the questions that follow are no longer hypothetical:

  • Who is accountable when a model behaves unexpectedly?

  • What data reached a model?

  • How is the system monitored once it’s live?

  • Who decided the system was ready?

We pursued ISO 42001 because we are committed to providing enterprise-grade AI products. This certification attests that we run deliberate, auditable AI systems.

How we govern AI at Vercel

There are three primary ways AI is governed at Vercel.

Impact assessments

Vercel conducts AI system impact assessments which cover foreseeable benefits, harms, failures, and misuse. We reassess these risks and benefits when the system materially changes.

Evaluations before release

We maintain evals for our AI systems covering performance, safety, and security, with human review for material changes.

Clear data commitments

Where it is not the default option based on pricing plan, we provide customers the ability to set their data handling preferences ranging from zero data retention (ZDR) to training opt-out. Our AI policy is available at v0.app/policy.

Ship fast, with confidence

We are committed to helping teams ship fast with confidence in the way AI is built and governed at Vercel. ISO 42001 is proof of that commitment, giving our customers:

  • Confidence in agentic infrastructure: Vercel’s AI systems have been audited, which means customers using our AI products start from a reviewed foundation instead of an unexamined one.

  • Governance can ship at the speed of the product: Agents now drive the development and deployment of applications. Governance and oversight that occurs quarterly can’t govern software that changes hourly, so we built a system that reviews AI as continuously as we ship it.

  • Simplified and accelerated assurance: Customers and partners can rely on this certification, alongside our other compliance attestations, to meet AI governance diligence requirements for faster third-party vendor onboarding.

  • Clear lines of responsibility: ISO 42001 requires that responsibilities be allocated across the AI supply chain. Our documentation outlines what Vercel is accountable for and what remains yours, the same shared-responsibility model we use for security.

  • Discipline that holds over time: Annual surveillance audits mean this isn’t a one-time claim. As our AI products change, the system that governs them stays under independent review.

AI is changing what people build on Vercel, and we intend for the governance around it to keep pace. We’ll continue to expand the scope of our certifications as our products grow.

title: XRL4T1D: A Post-hoc Explainability Framework for Reinforcement Learning in Type 1 Diabetes Management
description:
arXiv:2611.31498v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) requires lifelong insulin therapy, and reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promise for automated dosing in the UVA/Padova simulator. However, the decisions of RL controllers remain difficult to interpret. We present XRL4T1D, a post-hoc explainability framework for evaluating pretrained insulin-dosing policies without retraining. Each policy uses 60 minutes of continuous glucose monitor (CGM) and administered-insulin history, sampled every 5 minutes, to recommend insulin. We use SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to compare the importance of CGM and insulin-history inputs and summarize insulin-history attributions over three 20-minute windows motivated by insulin-on-board. We assess whether these attributions correspond to policy-output sensitivity through targeted input replacement and compare temporal rankings with TimeSHAP. In all 80 patient-policy-mask-size cases, replacing the highest-attribution inputs changes the normalized insulin recommendation more than replacing the lowest-attribution or random inputs. The highest-attribution insulin-history window is also the most output-sensitive in 115 of 120 patient-policy-scenario configurations, and KernelSHAP and TimeSHAP select the same top window in 111 of 120. Applying XRL4T1D to PPO and G2P2C across 20 virtual patients, we find that both controllers rely predominantly on CGM history, especially G2P2C. However, the distribution of insulin-history importance across recent, middle, and older windows varies by cohort, explainer, and analysis settings, without a consistent separation between controllers. Global feature-attribution rankings remain stable under the tested observation corruptions. These results show why attribution fidelity, temporal reproducibility, and controller-comparison robustness should be assessed separately.

title: Express without magic: what each piece does
description:
Yesterday you wrote an HTTP server in twenty lines. Today you install Express and it tells you this:

added 65 packages in 2s

Sixty-five packages for a layer that is, underneath, a queue of functions. It's worth knowing what's inside those sixty-five before handing them your API. And one piece sums it up better than any diagram: you send a 200 KB body and get a 413 Payload Too Large that you never wrote. A middleware you didn't know about decided it.

Install it and look at what it brings 

npm install express

With Express 5, the install leaves 65 packages, and the first thing the server does is tell the world it uses Express:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-Powered-By: Express
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 5
ETag: W/"5-Y7v+qCuIgO0zzbdiqhH6tyKpCiQ"

That X-Powered-By is free information for anyone hunting known vulnerabilities. It's one line to remove, and in production you always remove it:

app.disable("x-powered-by");

Notice the ETag and the Content-Type too. You wrote neither: Express adds them. And the Content-Type is text/html for a string that was plain text, which is the first sign that res.send does more than it looks.

What Express adds to req and res

res.send picks the type, computes Content-Length and adds an ETag. res.json does the same with JSON and the right Content-Type. res.status chains:

app.get("/", (req, res) => {
  res.send("hello\n");
});

app.get("/books/:id", (req, res) => {
  res.json({ id: req.params.id, sort: req.query.sort ?? "title" });
});

curl -s "http://localhost:3211/books/42?sort=date"

{"id":"42","sort":"date"}

Two new things compared to the http module: route parameters (:id) that arrive in req.params, and req.query already parsed. In the previous lesson that was a Map keyed by "GET /books/:id" that didn't exist, and a hand-rolled new URL(). Here it's a string with a colon and a property.

And req.params is always strings: id is "42", not 42. If you need a number, convert it and validate.

express.json(): the middleware you didn't write

This is what the plan asked to look inside, and three requests show it.

app.post("/echo", express.json(), (req, res) => {
  res.json({ received: req.body });
});

With Content-Type: application/json:

curl -s -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"book":"Emma"}' http://localhost:3211/echo

{"received":{"book":"Emma"}}

Without that header:

curl -s -X POST -d '{"book":"Emma"}' http://localhost:3211/echo

{}

The body is ignored and req.body stays empty. No error, no warning: the middleware only acts when the Content-Type matches. It's the most common integration failure with clients that don't send the header, and you diagnose it by looking at req.headers["content-type"].

With 200 KB:

HTTP/1.1 413 Payload Too Large
X-Powered-By: Express
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'

The default limit is 100 KB (limit: "100kb") and the same middleware enforces it. That's the 413 you never wrote: the first time you see it you search your code and it isn't there. It's in Express, in an option you change when the API takes images or documents:

app.use(express.json({ limit: "1mb" }));

Underneath, express.json() does what you did by hand in the previous lesson: read the stream, accumulate, check the limit, parse. With one thing you didn't have: if the JSON is broken, it answers 400 with a syntax error instead of letting your route's catch decide.

The missing sibling: forms

An HTML <form> doesn't send JSON: it sends application/x-www-form-urlencoded. Mount only express.json() and that body is ignored too, with req.body back to {}.

app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: false }));

curl -s -X POST -d "name=ada&role=admin" http://localhost:3222/form

{"body":{"name":"ada","role":"admin"}}

extended: false uses the simple query-string parser; true adds nested structures through qs. For flat forms, false is enough and less surprising.

That's the pattern that repeats across Express: one middleware, one content type. express.json() for JSON, express.urlencoded() for forms, multer for multipart/form-data. What you don't mount isn't parsed, and nothing warns you.

Middleware: a queue of functions

A middleware is a function with three arguments: req, res and next. It runs in the order it was registered, and next() passes the turn along.

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  console.log("1 · before the route:", req.method, req.url);
  next();
});

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  const t0 = Date.now();
  res.on("finish", () => console.log("3 · finished in", Date.now() - t0, "ms"));
  next();
});

1 · before the route: GET /boom
3 · finished in 6 ms

Two things there: the order is registration order, not the order you care about; and res.on("finish") lets you measure the end of a request without wrapping the route. That's how a logger or a latency gauge gets built in three lines.

And the part that costs an hour of debugging: if a middleware calls neither next() nor a response method, the request hangs. No error, no default framework timeout: the client just waits.

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} after %{time_total}s\n" --max-time 3 http://localhost:3211/hang

000 after 3.001259s

000 is curl saying "no response", and its exit code is 28. When it happens, look for the middleware that forgot next().

Errors: the four-argument middleware

A route that throws doesn't take the server down: Express catches it and looks for a middleware with four arguments.

app.get("/boom", () => {
  throw new Error("exploded");
});

app.use((error, req, res, next) => {
  console.log("4 · error caught:", error.message);
  res.status(500).json({ error: "something broke" });
});

HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

The four arguments aren't optional to Express: that's how it tells an error handler from a normal middleware. Write three and your handler never runs, with no warning at all. It's one of the cruellest signatures in the ecosystem.

In Express 5 this also works with async functions: a rejected promise goes to the same handler. In Express 4 you had to wrap it by hand. The next lesson goes deep on that.

And a trap worth knowing now: if your handler answers 500 no matter what, you destroy the status the framework had already chosen. A body over the limit arrives as a 413, and my handler above turned it into a 500 — measured, in the server log: 4 · error caught: request entity too large. Express attaches status to those errors; read it before deciding the code.

Third-party: cors and morgan

Each is one line to install and each replaces code you'd write worse.

app.use(morgan("dev"));
app.use(cors());

morgan leaves one line per request on standard output:

GET /public/data.txt 200 5.979 ms - 19

Method, path, status, duration and bytes. It's what you'd have written by hand with res.on("finish") in the previous lesson, colours included.

And cors() answers the preflight with considerably more judgement than the three headers you wrote by hand:

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET,HEAD,PUT,PATCH,POST,DELETE
Vary: Access-Control-Request-Headers

Five methods against the three you declared, and a Vary header that stops a cache from serving the wrong response to another origin. That Vary is exactly the kind of detail you don't write until it bites you.

express.static and the router

express.static serves a whole directory with cache headers, ranges and Last-Modified:

app.use("/public", express.static("public"));

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Accept-Ranges: bytes
Cache-Control: public, max-age=0
Last-Modified: Sat, 14 Nov 2026 22:33:33 GMT

And express.Router() is what the Map router was missing: an object that groups routes and gets mounted under a prefix.

const users = express.Router();
users.get("/", (req, res) => res.json([{ id: 1, name: "ada" }]));
users.get("/:id", (req, res) => res.json({ id: req.params.id }));

app.use("/api/users", users);

curl -s http://localhost:3211/api/users
curl -s http://localhost:3211/api/users/7

[{"id":1,"name":"ada"}]
{"id":"7"}

The prefix composes: inside the router the path is / and /:id, outside it's mounted at /api/users. That lets you keep routes/users.js with its own routes and app.js with five lines of mounting. And when the project grows, the next step is the factory pattern: a function that takes dependencies and returns the app, so it can be tested without opening a port.

What Express solves by itself, and what it doesn't

One thing you wrote by hand in the previous lesson and get for free here: OPTIONS.

curl -s -i -X OPTIONS http://localhost:3222/get-only

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Allow: GET, HEAD

Express answers on its own, with the Allow header and the methods that route accepts. It saves a branch and, more importantly, saves you from getting it wrong.

But 405 still doesn't exist. A PUT to a route that only accepts GET returns 404, exactly like your Map router did.

404

Still the wrong answer according to the protocol, and still what the framework does by default. If you want to tell "doesn't exist" from "not that method", you write it yourself. It's one of those things you assume the framework already does and it doesn't.

Common problems

req.body is empty

express.json() is missing, or the client isn't sending Content-Type: application/json. Without the header, the middleware doesn't touch the body.

413 Payload Too Large and I don't know where it comes from

From the limit on express.json, 100 KB by default. Raise it on the route that needs it, not across the whole app.

The request hangs with no response

A middleware called neither next() nor a response method. Find the last one that ran before the silence.

My error handler never runs

It has three arguments. Express needs four to recognise it, even if you never use next.

req.params.id isn't a number

Everything arriving through the URL is a string. Convert and validate, and return 400 when it isn't.

A string's Content-Type is text/html

res.send("hello") assumes HTML. For plain text, call res.type("text/plain") first, or res.json if it's data.

What you take from this lesson

  • Express is a queue of functions: middleware in order, and next() to pass the turn.
  • res.send and res.json fill in type, length and ETag for you; X-Powered-By is always removed.
  • req.params and req.query exist; parameters are strings.
  • express.json() only acts on Content-Type: application/json, has a 100 KB limit and answers 413 when you pass it.
  • A middleware that doesn't call next() leaves the request hanging with no warning.
  • The error handler needs four arguments, and in Express 5 it also catches async ones.
  • cors and morgan replace your own code with something better thought out.
  • express.Router() groups routes and is mounted under a prefix.
  • The application factory (createApp(deps)) is what makes all of this testable.

You have the framework taken apart. What comes next is what turns a pile of routes into a service you can maintain: centralised error handling, validation at the boundary, a layered structure, logs and an orderly shutdown.

Never stop coding!
