title: How a Rust civ sim stays deterministic with WebAssembly SIMD and threads
description:
I'm building The Human Box, a civilization sim that runs in the browser. People wander, find food, form tribes, fight, and eventually build towns. The engine is Rust, compiled to WebAssembly, and it's MIT on GitHub: 1homsi/thehumanbox.

I wrote earlier about how tribes invent their own words. This is about the other question I get: how the same engine ticks in a tab without the world changing when SIMD or threads turn on.

The hosted browser world is deliberately small. DEFAULT_MAX_POPULATION is 350. The engine's hard cap, MAX_POPULATION_LIMIT, is 5,000, which the desktop build can opt into. So this is not a 10,000-person demo. It is a tick that has to stay cheap at a few hundred people, and stay correct if someone later opens a much larger world.

One tick

Simulation::tick lives in crates/sim-core/src/sim/simulation/tick.rs. A tick is not "run every person." It is a fixed sequence: bookkeeping and strategy objectives, lineage aggregates, the civilisation pass, seasons and physics, droughts and weather, farms, animals, then the people.

Some of that work is on a cadence, not every tick. Physics steps every 5 ticks. The civilisation pass builds a spatial index with 8-tile buckets only every 500 ticks, for cross-lineage contact. Slow world evolution runs every 300 ticks. A day is DAY_LENGTH 600 ticks. A season is 3,000.

When it is time for the people, the code copies hot fields into columns, builds two spatial indexes with 10-tile buckets (people and animals), separates crowds, then takes each living person's turn.

That turn is split on purpose. The comment in tick.rs is the short version: everyone looks at once (reads of the world, on all cores), then each is written in order from what they saw. Then everyone chooses at once, from the world as choosing begins, and each acts on their choice, in order.

Looking and choosing go through sim/par.rs. Acting writes positions, needs, births and deaths on the struct, in index order. If a tribe splits mid-pass, only the people after the founder have their looks redone, because those are the only ones the split can change.

Hot fields in columns

A person is a large struct: memories, trust, names, inventory, a Q-table. The passes that walk everyone (rebuild the spatial grid, separate a crowd, scan neighbours, smooth velocity) only need a few words of that. Pulling the whole struct through cache for x and y is wasteful.

So next to Vec<Organism> there is OrganismColumns in crates/sim-core/src/organism/columns.rs. Slot i is organisms[i]. The columns hold position, previous position, velocity, needs, a lineage id, age, a flag word, and an alive byte:

pub struct OrganismColumns {
    ready: bool,
    pub x: Vec<f32>,
    pub y: Vec<f32>,
    // prev_*, vx, vy, energy, hydration, health ...
    /// `1` living, `0` dead. A byte, not `bool`, so a SIMD load is a lane.
    pub alive: Vec<u8>,
    pub lineage: Vec<Sym>,
    pub age: Vec<u32>,
    pub flags: Vec<u32>,
}

Columns are a cache, not the save image. sync_from copies the hot words off the structs and marks them ready. Anything that writes a hot field through the struct calls invalidate. After people choose and act, the columns are invalid until the next sync. Velocity smoothing at the end of the tick writes back through smooth_velocity.

Pairing still uses the live structs. It runs after that person's own step, and the people before them have already aged, moved, partnered or died. A snapshot taken at the start of the turn would answer a different question.

There is a small example, crates/sim-core/examples/soa_columns.rs, that walks a 4,000-person crowd the old way and the new way. When this landed in #1158, that pass went from 423.7 µs to 396.7 µs, about 1.07x. Not a headline speedup. It is what the SIMD kernels and the spatial rebuild actually read.

A spatial grid on those columns

Neighbour scans do not compare every living pair. SpatialIndex in crates/sim-core/src/sim/spatial.rs drops people into buckets. The organism pass uses a bucket size of 10 tiles. The occasional civilisation contact pass uses 8.

The build walks the alive, x and y columns four at a time and calls simd::bucket4. If the world would need more than 65,536 buckets (MAX_DENSE_BUCKETS), the index switches from a dense grid to a sparse map. A comment in the file notes that a 600 by 300 tile map in 10-tile buckets is only 1,800 buckets, so almost every real world stays dense.

Queries reuse a caller-owned Vec. query_into clears it and fills it, instead of allocating a fresh one per person per look. Perception of nearby animals, for example, queries radius 8 into a scratch buffer, then measures distances four lanes at a time.

Four lanes, three backends, one answer

The numeric kernels live in crates/sim-core/src/simd/. They cover movement integration, Manhattan and hypot distance, and the bucket coordinates above. Each kernel runs four lanes (LANES = 4).

Native builds use SSE2 or NEON. The wasm SIMD module (feature = "wasm-simd") uses simd128. Everything else, including a wasm build without that feature, runs the same operations one lane at a time.

The important part is not the width. It is that every kernel has to match the scalar path bit for bit: no fused multiply-add, no reassociation, and hypot follows DetMath::det_hypot (the f64 product inside libm::hypotf, then sqrt). The tests compare edges and random bit patterns against that scalar definition. If SIMD rounded differently, two browsers would diverge on the same seed.

The page never assumes the browser can run SIMD. apps/web/src/simulation/wasmSimd.ts keeps a one-instruction wasm module (v128.const) taken from the wasm-feature-detect probe. WebAssembly.validate accepts it only when the engine can run SIMD. If it does, the worker loads the SIMD build. If it does not, it loads the scalar build. Both export the same Sim API and tick the same world.

Threads, but only when the page can share memory

The first worker-thread change (#1159) ran read-only passes on Rayon and left the web build single-threaded. That is still the fallback. The web client can now also load a third module, the wasm-threads build, which turns the parallel feature on through wasm-bindgen-rayon (scripts/build-wasm-threads.sh).

apps/web/src/simulation/wasmEngine.ts decides which one to start. Threads are only requested when the page is cross-origin isolated and SharedArrayBuffer exists. Those come from the Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp headers in apps/web/public/_headers. Mobile WebKit skips the threaded build. Elsewhere, the worker tries the threaded module first.

The threaded module is about 5 MB, so a hung compile used to hold the splash screen for the full 30 second module timeout plus the 10 second pool timeout, 40 seconds, before the single-thread engine even began (#923). Now the threaded start gets a 3 second head start (THREADS_HEAD_START_MS). If it is still going, the single-thread engine starts beside it, and whichever is ready first runs the world. A fast threaded start never downloads the second module.

Thread count is navigator.hardwareConcurrency minus 2 cores reserved for the page and the renderer, capped at MAX_SIM_THREADS (6). WebKit desktop is capped at 4, and the start reserves a 640 MB heap before the pool comes up.

The rule that keeps this from changing the world when you change the core count is in crates/sim-core/src/sim/par.rs:

//! The rule that keeps worlds reproducible: work handed to these helpers reads the world and returns a
//! value; it never writes to the world or draws from the world's random numbers. Results come back in index
//! order, so a run gives the same world whatever the number of cores, and the same world with the
//! `parallel` feature off (the web build), where the same work runs on one thread.

perceive_all and choose_all are the obvious callers. Choosing does not draw from the world RNG on the workers. The tick draws one tick_seed on the main thread, and each person gets choice_rng(tick_seed, index). Writes, including births, deaths and every later use of self.rng, stay in the original order.

When #1159 landed, a 2,000-person test went from 21.75 ms to 19.98 ms a tick on 4 threads. Same story as the column bench: a modest win, measured, and only accepted because a save stayed byte-identical at 1, 4 and 6 threads.

What I am not claiming

I am not claiming the browser runs 5,000 people at 60 frames a second. The default hosted cap is 350. The 4,000 and 2,000 figures above are benchmark crowds, not the world you get when you open the site.

CI still has a performance gate (make perf-gate): three seeds at 8,000 ticks, plus one 25,000-tick run, checking max, p99 and mean time per tick, memory, and a checksum of the printed history. The gate is there because a slower tick on a bigger world is not the same as a slower tick.

There is also a calm-town path (town_lod.rs) that can step a quiet region every 8, 16, 32 or 64 ticks instead of every tick. That does change how a given seed plays out, so it is a behaviour change, not a transparent speedup. I am leaving that for another write-up.

The renderer is a separate problem. The map runs on xipjs in a WebGL2 stack, on the main thread, while the sim ticks in a Web Worker (apps/web/src/simulation/wasmWorker.ts). Paused worlds do not keep asking for frames.

If you want to read the code, start at tick.rs, then organism/columns.rs, sim/spatial.rs, simd/mod.rs, sim/par.rs, and apps/web/src/simulation/wasmEngine.ts.

I use AI-assisted coding tools on this project. They helped with parts of the code, and an AI assistant helped draft this write-up.

The code is at github.com/1homsi/thehumanbox, and you can play it at thehumanbox.com.

title: November 20, 2026
description:
Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.17.5

On November 20, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.17.5.

  • For information about upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to v1.17.5.
  • For information about new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release. The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch by using the Helm chart automatically updates the images. You don't typically need to make manual image changes. For information about container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Security

Bug ID Description
N/A Security fixes for apigee-hybrid-cassandra.

App Engine flexible environment Java

Security

The following runtime language contains important security updates:

  • Java 17 and later: 17.0.21.1+2, 21.0.13.1+2, 25.0.5.1+2

Take immediate action by rebuilding and redeploying your applications to pick up the patched Java runtime, and then remove any temporary JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS mitigation flags.

For more information, see security bulletin GCP-2026-082.

App Engine standard environment Java

Security

The following runtime language contains important security updates:

  • Java 17 and later: 17.0.21.1+2, 21.0.13.1+2, 25.0.5.1+2

Applications receive the patched runtime automatically with no action required.

To refresh warm instances immediately, redeploy your application.

If you added a temporary JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS mitigation flag in app.yaml or appengine-web.xml, remove it and redeploy.

For more information, see security bulletin GCP-2026-082.

Buildpacks

Security

The following runtime language contains important security updates:

  • Java 17 and later: 17.0.21.1+2, 21.0.13.1+2, 25.0.5.1+2

Take immediate action by rebuilding and redeploying your applications to pick up the patched Java runtime, and then remove any temporary JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS mitigation flags.

For more information, see security bulletin GCP-2026-082.

Cloud Run

Security

The following runtime language contains important security updates:

  • Java 17 and later: 17.0.21.1+2, 21.0.13.1+2, 25.0.5.1+2

Workloads with automatic base image updates enabled receive the patched runtime automatically with no action required. To refresh warm instances immediately, redeploy your workload.

For custom containers, Cloud Run jobs and worker pools, and deployments without automatic base image updates, rebuild and redeploy your workloads with a patched JDK or base image, and then remove any temporary JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS mitigation flags.

For more information, see security bulletin GCP-2026-082.

Cloud Run functions

Security

The following runtime language contains important security updates:

  • Java 17 and later: 17.0.21.1+2, 21.0.13.1+2, 25.0.5.1+2

Functions with automatic base image updates enabled receive the patched runtime automatically with no action required. To refresh warm instances immediately, redeploy your function.

For functions without automatic base image updates, redeploy your functions to pick up the patched runtime, and then remove any temporary JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS mitigation flags.

For more information, see security bulletin GCP-2026-082.

Cloud Scheduler

Feature

Cloud Scheduler support for customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) is generally available (GA). You can use symmetric keys that you manage in Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) to protect HTTP and Pub/Sub job data at rest.

Cloud Storage

Feature

In buckets with hierarchical namespace enabled, you can now use the JSON API folders.deleteRecursive method to delete a non-empty folder and all its contents in a single long-running operation. For more information, see Delete a folder.

Config Connector

Announcement

Config Connector version 1.162.0 is now available.

Feature

New Alpha Resources (Direct Reconciler):

  • AIPlatformContext: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform metadata contexts for grouping lineage and metadata artifacts in metadata stores.
  • APIHubAPI: Apigee API hub APIs for registering and tracking APIs in API hub.
  • APIHubAttribute: Apigee API hub attributes for defining custom metadata attributes and attaching them to resources in API hub.
  • APIHubCuration: Apigee API hub curations for configuring curation endpoints that process API metadata.
  • BigQueryReservationReservationGroup: BigQuery reservation groups for grouping and organizing BigQuery reservations.
  • CCInsightsPhraseMatcher: Customer Experience Insights phrase matchers for matching phrases and words in conversation transcripts.
  • CCInsightsQAScorecard: Customer Experience Insights QA scorecards for defining collections of questions to score conversations during quality analysis.
  • CloudBuildConnection: Cloud Build connections for connecting source code management systems such as GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket.
  • ConfigDeliveryFleetPackage: Config Sync fleet packages for packaging and deploying Kubernetes configurations across fleets of clusters.
  • DatabaseMigrationConversionWorkspace: Database Migration Service conversion workspaces for converting database schemas and code during migrations.
  • DataformFolder: Dataform folders for organizing files and folders with hierarchical access controls.
  • DataformReleaseConfig: Dataform release configurations for compiling Dataform repositories into release compilation results.
  • DataformTeamFolder: Dataform team folders for organizing Dataform repositories and folders at the project level with hierarchical access controls.
  • DataformWorkflowConfig: Dataform workflow configurations for scheduling and executing Dataform workflow invocations.
  • DataplexAsset: Knowledge Catalog assets for managing Cloud Storage buckets and BigQuery datasets within zones in a lake.
  • DataplexDataAsset: Knowledge Catalog data assets for packaging and sharing BigQuery datasets and tables in data products.
  • DataplexDataScan: Knowledge Catalog data scans for running data quality checks and data profiling jobs on data sources.
  • DataplexGlossary: Knowledge Catalog glossaries for organizing business glossary categories and terms.
  • DevConnectAccountConnector: Developer Connect account connectors for configuring OAuth provider connections to external developer tools.
  • DeviceStreamingSession: Device Streaming device sessions for allocating remote physical Android devices for interactive streaming.
  • DialogflowConversationDataset: Dialogflow ES conversation datasets for importing conversation data to train conversation models.
  • DiscoveryEngineControl: Agent Search controls for conditioning search and recommendation serving behavior.
  • DiscoveryEngineSampleQuerySet: Agent Search sample query sets for grouping sample queries used to evaluate search quality.
  • NetworkSecurityAddressGroup: Cloud Next Generation Firewall address groups for defining reusable IP address and domain collections in firewall policies.
  • NetworkSecurityBackendAuthenticationConfig: Cloud Load Balancing backend authentication configurations for configuring TLS trust and backend authentication settings on load balancers.
  • NetworkSecurityGatewaySecurityPolicy: Secure Web Proxy gateway security policies for defining security policy rules on Secure Web Proxy gateways.
  • NetworkSecurityInterceptDeployment: Network Security Integration intercept deployments for deploying zonal packet-intercept backends for network traffic inspection.
  • SaaSServiceMgmtUnitKind: App Lifecycle Manager unit kinds for defining shared release models and rollout templates for SaaS deployment units.
  • VertexAIFeatureOnlineStore: Feature Store on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform feature online stores for serving machine learning features and embedding indexes at low latency.
  • WebSecurityScannerScanConfig: Security Command Center Web Security Scanner scan configurations for configuring automated vulnerability scans of web applications.

Feature

New Fields:

  • MemorystoreInstance (#15095)
    • Added support for the spec.endpoints[].connections[].pscAutoConnection.ipVersion and status.observedState.endpoints[].connections[].pscAutoConnection.ipVersion fields.

Change

Reconciliation Improvements:

Added support for direct reconciliation to an additional resource, with opt-in behavior. The API is unchanged. To use the direct reconciler, add the alpha.cnrm.cloud.google.com/reconciler: direct annotation to the corresponding Config Connector object. The following resource now has direct reconciliation support:

  • DialogflowCXAgent

The following resources now use the direct reconciler by default:

  • AccessContextManagerGCPUserAccessBinding
  • ApigeeAddonsConfig
  • ApigeeNATAddress
  • ApigeeSyncAuthorization
  • AppEngineFirewallRule
  • AppEngineFlexibleAppVersion
  • AppEngineServiceSplitTraffic
  • AppEngineStandardAppVersion
  • BigQueryDatasetAccess
  • ComputeMachineImage
  • ComputeNetworkEndpoint
  • ComputeRegionPerInstanceConfig
  • DocumentAIProcessorDefaultVersion
  • FirebaseProject
  • HealthcareConsentStore
  • KMSCryptoKeyVersion
  • KMSKeyRingImportJob
  • KMSSecretCiphertext
  • NetworkServicesEdgeCacheService

Feature

title: Neighbor Crowding Predicts Feature Stability in Sparse Autoencoders
description:
arXiv:2611.33182v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) offer an approach to identify language model representations by breaking apart polysemantic features into more sparse, interpretable ones. Yet, it is challenging to identify which of the learned features are actually stable, rather than artifacts of initialization. One approach is to train multiple SAE seeds, and compare the learned features across seeds by cosine similarity, but this is notably costly. This raises the question of whether stable features can be identified without the computational expense of training multiple seeds. In this work, we examine cross-seed feature stability across differing levels of training tokens, and demonstrate that in TopK SAEs, it is highly predictable using six computationally cheap statistics derived from a single training run. Neighbor crowding, a geometric property of the dictionary, is the strongest single predictor, with features that sit in dense regions of the unit sphere more likely to be stable than isolated ones.

title: Fast Muscle-Driven Whole-Body Motion Tracking with a Differentiable World Model
description:
arXiv:2611.33460v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tracking motion capture with a whole-body musculoskeletal model means coordinating hundreds of muscles through contact, and current controllers take hours to days of GPU time to train, so every tuning decision is expensive. SuperMimic trains a tracking policy by backpropagating through the rollouts of a learned world model. We extend it to MS-Human-700 (700 muscles) and MyoFullBody (354 muscles), with MuJoCo's activation dynamics inside the world model. To make its training fast, our recipe takes the speedups developed for the Unitree G1, replaces three of their settings that fail on muscles, and adds four changes of our own: observations without muscle geometry, data collection concurrent with the updates, Beta exploration noise that keeps every excitation in $[0,1]$, and 50 Hz control. On one RTX 5090 it trains MS-Human-700 in 6.3 minutes to the held-out return that SuperMimic's published hyperparameters reach in 3.9 hours, 37$\times$ sooner, and in 20 minutes to lower tracking errors than theirs after 10 hours. It trains MyoFullBody 34$\times$ sooner without retuning. Ablations show what is specific to muscles: a higher policy learning rate stalls half of the runs, and clipped Gaussian noise adds a tonic co-contraction that Beta noise avoids. Finally, refining the policy's actions through the world model at test time lowers the position error by a further 26% with no held-out clip failing, and reaches the same return after 5.1 instead of 6.3 minutes of training. Code, the training recipe and videos are on the project page https://muscle-supermimic.beanpow.top.

title: A practical guide to staging validation in Node.js
description:
Start with the question

A production observability change deserves its own staging test because it touches request handling and data retention. A representative test should cover middleware placement, route capture, redaction, persistence, access, and restart behavior. The goal is not to collect more fields; it is to shorten the path from symptom to a testable explanation.

Put it into practice

Write a short acceptance checklist for the routes that matter and run it after configuration or version changes. Start in a non-production environment, inspect a normal request and an edge case, and record what you would change before enabling the same configuration more broadly.

Make the result actionable

Write down where the signal appears, who can see it, and what the next debugging step should be. If an engineer cannot make a decision from the captured event, revise the signal or its context.

Keep the boundary clear

Avoid enabling broad payload inspection in production until the expected data and access controls are understood. Recheck the current TracerNest documentation for version-specific configuration, then adapt the example to your service rather than copying a setting without understanding its effect.

Learn more: TracerNest

title: Model a Bespoke Rug Brief So Surface, Structure and Sample Approval Cannot Be Confused
description:
A custom rug brief often begins as an email and ends as several attachments. One message describes the color, another carries a scaled plan, and a later sample photograph introduces a new fiber note. The risk is not merely untidy documentation. The production ticket can combine a current drawing with an obsolete sample approval.

ADAHANDMADE's commission records suggest a cleaner data boundary. Face yarns, surface technique, contour, backing, edge finishing, pad scope, furniture overlay and sample identification are separate decisions. A schema can enforce that separation without pretending to replace design review.

The model below is an illustrative implementation for a project tool. It is not an official ADAHANDMADE schema, and it contains no invented manufacturing tolerances.

Keep the Reference Design and the Commission Snapshot Separate

The 41-piece archive records a material, technique, shape, main color and reference dimensions for each named design. Those fields describe the reference. A custom commission may change dimensions, shape, palette, material or arrangement.

Store the reference slug independently from the approved commission snapshot. That lets a buyer begin with Paeonia or Jasminum without freezing every custom decision to the catalog record. It also makes later changes visible.

A second separation is equally important. Relief carving and high-low cut pile describe the face surface. They do not describe the backing material, whether an anti-slip pad is included, or how the edge is finished. These belong in different objects.

An Illustrative JSON Schema

The following Draft 2020-12 schema requires the main evidence groups while leaving project-specific dimensions and construction details to the approved order.

{
  "title": "IllustrativeHandTuftedRugCommission",
  "type": "object",
  "required": [
    "commission_id",
    "reference_design",
    "room_brief",
    "commission_snapshot",
    "surface",
    "backing_and_edge",
    "sample_review",
    "approval_link"
  ],
  "properties": {
    "commission_id": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
    "reference_design": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": ["slug", "archive_revision"],
      "properties": {
        "slug": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
        "archive_revision": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 }
      }
    },
    "room_brief": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": [
        "unit",
        "room_dimensions",
        "fixed_openings",
        "furniture_plan_revision",
        "furniture_overlay_scale",
        "circulation_notes",
        "lighting_notes"
      ],
      "properties": {
        "unit": { "const": "cm" },
        "room_dimensions": {
          "type": "object",
          "required": ["length", "width"],
          "properties": {
            "length": { "type": "number", "exclusiveMinimum": 0 },
            "width": { "type": "number", "exclusiveMinimum": 0 }
          }
        },
        "fixed_openings": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string" } },
        "furniture_plan_revision": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
        "furniture_overlay_scale": {
          "type": "string",
          "pattern": "^[1-9][0-9]*:[1-9][0-9]*$",
          "examples": ["1:20"]
        },
        "circulation_notes": { "type": "string" },
        "lighting_notes": { "type": "string" }
      }
    },
    "commission_snapshot": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": [
        "snapshot_revision",
        "shape",
        "finished_dimensions",
        "palette_reference",
        "motif_direction",
        "furniture_coverage_intent"
      ],
      "properties": {
        "snapshot_revision": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
        "shape": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
        "finished_dimensions": {
          "type": "object",
          "required": ["width", "length"],
          "properties": {
            "width": { "type": "number", "exclusiveMinimum": 0 },
            "length": { "type": "number", "exclusiveMinimum": 0 }
          }
        },
        "palette_reference": { "type": "string" },
        "motif_direction": { "type": "string" },
        "furniture_coverage_intent": { "type": "string" }
      }
    },
    "surface": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": ["face_yarns", "technique", "nap_direction"],
      "properties": {
        "face_yarns": {
          "type": "array",
          "minItems": 1,
          "items": {
            "type": "object",
            "required": ["fiber", "structure_role"],
            "properties": {
              "fiber": {
                "enum": [
                  "wool",
                  "fine_wool",
                  "worsted_wool",
                  "coarse_wool",
                  "wool_loop",
                  "felted_wool",
                  "viscose",
                  "lyocell",
                  "silk"
                ]
              },
              "structure_role": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
              "ratio_percent": {
                "type": "number",
                "minimum": 0,
                "maximum": 100
              }
            }
          }
        },
        "technique": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
        "nap_direction": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 }
      }
    },
    "backing_and_edge": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": ["backing_material", "edge_finish", "pad_included", "floor_protection_notes"],
      "properties": {
        "backing_material": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
        "edge_finish": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
        "approved_edge_width_mm": { "type": "number", "exclusiveMinimum": 0 },
        "pad_included": { "type": "boolean" },
        "floor_protection_notes": { "type": "string" }
      }
    },
    "sample_review": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": ["sample_id", "status", "daylight_checked", "night_lighting_checked", "nap_views_checked"],
      "properties": {
        "sample_id": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
        "status": { "enum": ["pending", "approved", "invalidated"] },
        "daylight_checked": { "type": "boolean" },
        "night_lighting_checked": { "type": "boolean" },
        "nap_views_checked": { "type": "boolean" },
        "review_notes": { "type": "string" }
      }
    },
    "approval_link": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": ["drawing_revision", "drawing_overlay_scale", "sample_id", "quotation_reference"],
      "properties": {
        "drawing_revision": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
        "drawing_overlay_scale": {
          "type": "string",
          "pattern": "^[1-9][0-9]*:[1-9][0-9]*$",
          "examples": ["1:20"]
        },
        "sample_id": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
        "quotation_reference": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 }
      }
    }
  }
}

The scale fields accept any recorded positive integer ratio. 1:20 appears only as an example. The application check compares the brief and drawing ratios mathematically. The schema deliberately allows project-specific surface and edge descriptions. A viscose relief-carved reference and a wool-and-lyocell high-low reference should not be forced into one generic construction label. The fiber enum reflects categories documented in the ADAHANDMADE archive, but an approved custom material note still needs human verification.

Reject Ambiguous Briefs Early

The first useful validation is not a visual render. It is a missing-field check. A brief that names a wool rug but places viscose in the free-text notes has no controlled material decision. A request for an oval rug without a complete contour has no controlled shape. The schema should return those gaps before a sample is presented for approval.

The same rule applies to coordinates and dimensions. Store the source unit beside every measurement, then convert only in a derived view. Keep the client's approved dimensions separate from catalog reference dimensions. If a model mixes them, the interface may display a confident outline that has never been approved for production.

These checks do not decide whether a design is beautiful. They make the brief reviewable. Once the required records exist, the team can discuss color, scale and furniture visibility without guessing which version of the brief is current.

Add Application Rules for Cross-Field Consistency

JSON Schema checks structure. It does not know whether two sample IDs refer to the same physical object or whether a change has invalidated an earlier review. Those checks belong in application logic.

Before release, verify that the sample ID in sample_review equals the sample ID in approval_link. Verify that the drawing revision exists, that its furniture plan matches the room brief, and that the recorded overlay scale matches the scale stated on the drawing. An approved status should also require completed daylight, nighttime and nap-direction checks.

A change to face yarns, palette or surface technique should invalidate the sample approval and open a new review. A change to contour or furniture coverage should create a new drawing revision. A change only to transport notes may leave the material sample and geometry untouched, but the order record still needs a traceable update.

import re

_SCALE_PATTERN = re.compile(r"^([1-9][0-9]*):([1-9][0-9]*)$")

def parse_scale(value):
    if not isinstance(value, str):
        return None
    match = _SCALE_PATTERN.fullmatch(value)
    if match is None:
        return None
    return tuple(map(int, match.groups()))

def overlay_scales_match(record):
    brief_scale = parse_scale(record["room_brief"]["furniture_overlay_scale"])
    drawing_scale = parse_scale(record["approval_link"]["drawing_overlay_scale"])
    return (
        brief_scale is not None
        and drawing_scale is not None
        and brief_scale[0] * drawing_scale[1] == drawing_scale[0] * brief_scale[1]
    )

def material_signature(surface):
    yarns = sorted(
        (y["fiber"], y["structure_role"], y.get("ratio_percent", -1))
        for y in surface["face_yarns"]
    )
    return (tuple(yarns), surface["technique"])

def requires_new_sample(previous, current):
    return (
        material_signature(previous["surface"]) != material_signature(current["surface"])
        or previous["commission_snapshot"]["palette_reference"]
        != current["commission_snapshot"]["palette_reference"]
    )

This comparison is a review trigger, not a chemical or performance test. It simply prevents a new material description from inheriting an old sample approval silently.

Keep Care and Installation Bound to the Same Version

The approved record should carry the care reference and installation notes for the actual composition. The materials and care guidance asks for the design name, material, room type, traffic and cleaning equipment. Those inputs are more useful than a generic product label.

Backing, pad inclusion and floor protection should remain visible in the production and handover records. Door movement and total installed thickness are site checks, not values that can be inferred from the surface technique. The specification guide provides the framework for these order details.

The result is a modest but important improvement. Instead of one overloaded rug specification, the tool keeps distinct evidence groups and links them through explicit revisions. The archive supplies the reference, the room plan supplies the geometry, the sample supplies the material review, and the approval record states which versions belong to the order.

title: Catch missing feature flags before they reach production
description:
Vercel Flags can now block a deployment from reaching production if you’ve declared a flag in code but haven’t created it in your project. Without that definition, your app can silently fall back to the flag’s default value, even if that turns on a feature you meant to keep off.

The Flag Definitions Present Deployment Check runs when a deployment is ready. If any flags are missing, the check fails and lists them in the results, where you can create each one before redeploying.

The check reads your Flags SDK discovery endpoint. With flags@4.5.0 or later on Vercel, it works without FLAGS_SECRET; earlier versions still require the secret.

To turn on blocking, teams on all plans can enable the check in their project’s Build and Deployment settings and mark it as required. See the Deployment Checks documentation for setup details.

title: How Professional Web Design, UX/UI, and SEO Services Help Businesses Grow in Dharamshala
description:
As a business owner in Dharamshala you are aware that customers now use the internet to find businesses in your local area. Whether they are looking for accommodation, food, travel companies or professional services a large amount of research will be done online.
By having web design UX/UI and SEO services your business can reach more people, give customers a great experience and grow.
Here is how these services can help your business grow.

1. All Dharamshala Businesses Should Have a Professional Website

There are different types of businesses in Dharamshala including tourism, hospitality, education, retail, healthcare and professional services. Customers will often look online to find businesses.
Without a website or an outdated website customers are likely to go with competitors who have a professional website.

A professional website can:

- Show your products/services in a manner.

  • Help build trust with potential customers.
  • Provide information about your business.
  • Allow you to receive inquiries.
  • Reach customers outside of your area.
  • Provide a base for digital marketing.

2. Professional Web Design Creates Trust

Customers will often have an impression of your business when they find your website for the first time online. Many customers will form opinions based on your website’s appearance. Whether it is easy to understand.
Professional web design focuses on ensuring your website looks like your brand. This includes layout, colours, fonts, images, navigation and overall appearance.
For example if you have a hotel business then your website should have images of your property, information about rooms, facilities, location and booking. If you are a service provider then your website should have clear information about your service.

3. UX/UI Design Can Help You Grow

Even if you have a website, if customers cannot find the information they need or find it difficult to navigate around your website they may leave without getting in touch.
UX and UI design are important aspects of modern website design.

Understanding UX (User Experience)

User Experience focuses on how easy your website is for people to use. It takes into consideration what customers need, what they expect to see, what they browse and how they search for information.
UX design can help make this simple and easy.

Understanding UI (User Interface)

User Interface focuses on the look of your website. This includes buttons, menus, fonts, colours, images, icons and overall layout.
Having a planned out interface will make your website look professional and organised. It will also help keep your website throughout.

UX and UI are closely linked together. UX ensures that your website is easy to use while UI ensures that your website is easy to understand
By having planned UX and UI design your customers will be able to find the information they need, understand what your business offers and perform actions such as submitting an inquiry.
For businesses in Dharamshala this can help create an online experience for your customers from local and from other parts of India or abroad.

4. SEO Can Increase Your Customer Base

Having a professional website is a start. However people also need to be able to find your website. SEO can help increase your visibility in search engines when people search for something

Customers may search for services in your area such as:

- Best hotel in Dharamshala

  • Web designing company in Dharamshala
  • Taxi service in Dharamshala
  • Restaurants near McLeod Ganj
  • Digital marketing services in Himachal Pradesh

If your website has relevant and helpful information about your services and is well optimised your website has a great chance of appearing for searches.

SEO includes:

- On-page SEO

– Optimising page titles, meta descriptions, headings, content, internal links and keywords.

- SEO

– Improving the speed of your website making it mobile friendly, crawlable indexable, improving site structure and much more.

- Off-page SEO

– Increasing the authority of your website by having relevant backlinks, genuine business listings and much more.

- Local SEO

– Improving the visibility of your business by providing accurate business information, local content and a well maintained Google Business Profile.

SEO is a long term process. You will not see results immediately. This depends on the competition, the quality of your website, content and many other factors. However by performing SEO you can help your business gain relevant traffic.

5. Mobile Friendly Website Design

Many people use their smartphones to search for products, services and businesses. This is especially important for tourism related businesses in Dharamshala. Customers will often search for hotels, restaurants, transport and local attractions.
If your website is not easy to use on a device then customers may struggle to read information, click on buttons and fill in inquiry forms.
Responsive Web Design can help. This means the layout of your website will adapt to the size of the screen.

A mobile friendly website should have:

- Easy to read text without needing to zoom in.

title: KiRA: Kronecker Input-Gated Rank Adaptation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Pretrained Models
description:
arXiv:2611.33236v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Full fine-tuning of large pretrained models is expensive, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is the standard alternative. Most PEFT methods use low-rank updates, whose rank lies far below that of full fine-tuning and is the same for every input. Input-adaptive variants vary the capacity per input but remain within the low-rank bottleneck, and whether a task benefits from input conditioning is not known before training. This paper introduces Kronecker input-gated rank adaptation (KiRA). Instead of the conventional low-rank product, the update $\Delta W$ is the Kronecker product of a frozen random $p\times p$ matrix $A$ and a trainable factor $M(x)$, which overcomes the rank ceiling: because rank is multiplicative under this product, $A$ multiplies the rank of $M(x)$ by $p$ without adding trainable parameters. The factor $M(x)$ is further decomposed as $B_1\,\mathrm{diag}(g(x))\,B_2$, where the input gate $g(x)$, computed once per sample by a network shared across all adapted layers, adjusts the rank of the update to each input in steps of $p$. Where input conditioning is unnecessary, the gate is folded into $B_1$ at deployment. Because the gate changes the rank only in discrete steps, the benefit of input conditioning can be predicted before training from a few hundred labeled inputs. Across six medical imaging and language benchmarks, KiRA attains the highest mean score against five published baselines with 8.7--9.7 times fewer trainable parameters than low-rank adaptation, and the pre-training criterion agrees with the measured benefit of input conditioning on all six tasks.

title: Reproducing History Is Not Enough: Intervention-Level Assurance for LLM-Generated Simulators
description:
arXiv:2611.31736v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models can now write simulation programs of operational processes and workflows. These programs can be reused to answer what-if questions on new records and policies. However, a program that reproduces recorded history can still give wrong answers to what-if questions; requested changes may be applied wrongly, or they may be applied to records other than the ones the question is about, or the program may stop being valid once its policy is revised. Current checks return a pass-or-fail verdict for the whole program, which says little about whether any single answer can be trusted. We propose Vouch, a library that judges whether an answer from a generated simulator can be trusted for the change being asked about. Each what-if question is turned into a structured change, which is checked against the program and the current records. The library also keeps a record of the kinds of change each program has passed or failed, and repeats the relevant tests whenever the program is reused. We apply it to three program-generation platforms, with programs built by five language models, across four domains: manufacturing, IT operations, and pharmacy and loan-application workflows, using independently checked reference answers. Our baselines are the platforms' own checks where such checks exist, an LLM-as-a-judge, and a ReAct agent that can run the program. We measure how many correct answers are trusted, how many are wrongly rejected, how many wrong answers are accepted, and what the checking costs.
  On programs written by Haiku and Sonnet in one platform, Vouch removes 97.6% of the wrong answers, while still trusting 80.1% of all answers. At equal coverage, it accepts fewer wrong answers than LLM judges built on Claude Haiku. We disclose code and results for reproducibility.

title: Typical Angina, Reversed: A Long-Standing Documentation Error in the UCI Heart Disease Data
description:
arXiv:2611.33248v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The UCI Heart Disease data are a widely used machine-learning benchmark. We show that their chest-pain variable is stored in reverse of its documentation. At all four sites, the code documented as "asymptomatic" (4) marks patients with typical angina, and the code documented as "typical angina" (1) marks patients with almost none of the classical angina features (at Cleveland, no chest pain).
  Two complementary checks establish this: (i) the chest-pain table and regression coefficients of the original 1986 Cleveland study are reproduced only under the corrected reading; (ii) in the Budapest, Switzerland and Long Beach files, 93-96% of patients coded 4 have all three classical angina features. A 1990 word-labeled Cleveland file already uses the documented labels, and Statlog (Heart), a Cleveland subset, stores the same codes. OpenML, PMLB and two highly voted Kaggle copies that name the categories use the same documented labels (about 400,000 downloads combined).
  We audited a seeded random sample of 150 records from a pre-specified Scholar query for SHAP studies of these data mentioning asymptomatic chest pain (124 readable). Of 32 papers that state a direction for a named category, 25 (78%; 95% CI 61-89%) state one inconsistent with the corrected category identities; 22 (69%; 51-82%; post hoc) are attributable to the documentation error, and nine of these explain it clinically. None of the 124 readable papers identifies the reversal.
  Conventional models are essentially unaffected, one reason the error went unnoticed. Interpretations that attach the documented names to model effects are reversed, and zero-shot language-model classifiers that read the labels are misled: with the documented labels, three open-weight models lose 0.12-0.33 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) given age, sex and chest-pain type. We give the corrected mapping, evidence and code.

title: Go SMS Provider Migration — Expiring Security Notifications and OTP Fallback
description:
A password-reset message has to arrive while its challenge is useful. For a media publisher serving readers in the US and EU, that constraint should drive the choice of a simple transactional SMS API for security notifications. An accepted send is only the beginning.

Short answer: Keep the reset deadline and recovery state in the application. Choose a basic SMS provider for alerts and bounded OTP flows; evaluate a verification specialist when managed authentication and prompt channel coordination determine success. Keep delivery adapters replaceable, and never let a provider switch silently extend a challenge's lifetime.

Consider a design exercise: a reader requests a reset during a breaking-news subscription campaign. Give the challenge an illustrative five-minute lifetime. At minute four, a queued delivery attempt becomes eligible to run. In that review, I would ask whether the remaining minute is useful before asking which provider should receive the request. These are proposed operating parameters, not delivery measurements or a reported incident.

Time is gone.

The invariant is that every retry, resend, and fallback must fit inside the same recovery deadline. Provider acceptance cannot establish that a reader received a message, and receipt cannot establish that a password reset was authorized. Those are separate transitions. Keeping them separate makes a provider migration easier to reason about.

How should an SMS provider handle security notifications and OTP fallback during migration?

Start with an application-owned recovery record: an opaque reset identifier, an absolute expiry, the current challenge generation, and the verification outcome. Keep the recipient and any secret out of ordinary job logs. A delivery attempt should reference this record instead of carrying enough stale state to authorize a reset on its own.

Media teams should try Infrai for the SMS alert and basic code-delivery portion when one key and one bill across backend services reduce credential administration and invoice reconciliation. Its self-describing API provides public discovery with request and response schemas, giving the team a concrete contract to inspect before writing a replaceable adapter. This removes schema guesswork during integration; it doesn't prove that another provider accepts the same requests.

The replacement boundary needs to be specific. Let application code request delivery for a recovery attempt, then let an adapter translate that intent into provider fields. Store the external message identifier alongside the adapter that issued it. Verification identifiers belong to that adapter too: a flow started with one provider cannot be assumed to continue with another. During migration, finish existing flows with their original adapter or explicitly invalidate them before issuing replacement challenges. The application contract survives; provider payloads still need translation.

This costs state. It buys a controlled exit.

Infrai offers a plain REST API with no SDK required. Its documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages, including Go, so a team migrating this worker can inspect the schema and start from a language-specific example instead of translating an unfamiliar SDK. The standard HTTP client shown below keeps that dependency outside recovery logic. This is an integration convenience, not a claim of wire compatibility between messaging providers.

The shared API supports ordinary SMS sending, code issuance and verification, and resending. Its platform documents an Idempotency-Key convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window, but discovery marks idempotency per capability. Inspect that declaration before relying on provider deduplication for a particular write. A five-minute application expiry and a 24-hour deduplication window answer different questions: one controls authorization lifetime; the other controls repeat application of a request.

Compare the recovery responsibility, then the API

Include Twilio Verify, Vonage Verify, and Resend in the comparison. They address different portions of the recovery chain. The table defines evaluation boundaries rather than promising equal coverage or measured delivery performance.

Option Role to evaluate Boundary to settle before adoption
Twilio Verify Verification specialist candidate for delegating the code lifecycle Check expiry, resend semantics, and the requirements for the intended US/EU destinations against its verification documentation.
Vonage Verify Alternative specialist candidate for a managed verification flow Evaluate its lifecycle independently; challenge identifiers and status meanings aren't a portable application contract.
Resend Email-side candidate for a recovery fallback Assess the email integration separately from the SMS verification decision; retain application recovery state.
Infrai Shared backend API for alerts and basic SMS code flows Shared credentials and discovery reduce integration work; recovery orchestration remains an application responsibility.

The deciding test is whether a reset remains recoverable within its expiry under retries and delayed status observation. There is no measured fastest-provider ranking here. Test actual destination countries and message types before making delivery judgments. A country label in a requirements document isn't delivery evidence.

Choose a verification specialist when its documented lifecycle better matches the responsibility you want to delegate. Choose a direct messaging integration with an appropriate event model when prompt channel coordination determines success. Infrai's messaging status is pull-based, so the application must budget for status observation; email-code fallback needs application-owned code handling. It is better suited to alerting and basic code flows than a complete multi-channel authentication system.

Inspect the contract before dispatching work

Keep two checks separate: inspect the adapter's declared contract during integration, then enforce the recovery deadline before each delivery attempt. The Go program below demonstrates both boundaries without sending a reset message. Save it as main.go and run it with go run main.go. Discovery is public and requires no key; the request deliberately carries no credential. It retrieves the schema for inspection rather than inventing an SMS payload.

The network call is read-only. On rate limiting, it honors Retry-After in seconds or HTTP-date form and otherwise uses exponential backoff. Its context bounds the inspection operation; a longer server-requested wait ends through that deadline instead of causing an early retry. The 45-second delivery reserve is an illustrative application policy, not a latency guarantee.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func inspect(ctx context.Context) error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/sms.batch.send", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if until, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
                delay = time.Until(until)
                if delay < 0 {
                    delay = 0
                }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery rate-limit retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    start := time.Date(2026, time.November, 21, 12, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    expires := start.Add(5 * time.Minute)
    for _, elapsed := range []time.Duration{time.Minute, 270 * time.Second} {
        remaining := expires.Sub(start.Add(elapsed))
        fmt.Println("elapsed:", elapsed, "eligible:", remaining > 45*time.Second)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    if err := inspect(ctx); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The first simulated delivery passes; the later one stops because only 30 seconds remain. Discard late work under that policy and give the reader a clear way to request a new challenge. A longer reserve protects against stale messages but rejects more work. Set it deliberately, then revisit it using production observations.

The example isn't a durable worker. In production, atomically coordinate the generation check and dispatch claim through durable state. Reject replaced challenges and already verified recoveries. Persist a logical attempt key before sending and reuse it after an uncertain response. A retry repeats one logical write; a resend is a deliberate new delivery decision, still bounded by the original expiry. Provider deduplication, where documented, adds another layer. A process-local map cannot settle an ambiguous network outcome after a restart.

Recheck expiry after any backoff. Preserve response status and actionable error information with secrets removed. Don't turn every failure into another message.

Run the cutover as a recovery-state change

Migrate new challenges first. Keep old verification identifiers attached to their original provider until those challenges expire. If rollback is necessary, route subsequent new challenges back through the previous adapter; avoid replaying the pending queue into another provider. An ambiguous acceptance followed by a cross-provider replay can produce two deliveries even when each provider deduplicates its own requests correctly. This is the migration trap an adapter alone cannot prevent.

The runbook should track challenge creation, dispatch acceptance, last status observation, verification outcome, and expiration as separate evidence. Start a fallback decision from recovery state and a deadline. A quiet polling interval isn't proof that the first channel failed. For the email branch, validate the application-owned challenge and invalidate superseded generations.

Apply destination-country policy and abuse controls before dispatch. With this shared API, geographic restrictions and country-based spending circuit breakers belong in application logic. Shared credentials reduce administrative work; they do not supply recovery policy.

Where does this approach stop fitting?

This design fits a media site sending password-reset notifications and basic security codes while retaining orchestration. Its main trade-off is application-owned expiry, fallback, and migration state. Infrai is not a fit for a team requiring a complete managed multi-channel authentication system; evaluate Twilio Verify or Vonage Verify for that verification responsibility instead. That's a meaningful limitation, even with a small API integration.

If prompt event-driven coordination is central, prioritize a messaging stack with a suitable documented event model. If the team wants managed verification, evaluate Twilio Verify and Vonage Verify directly. If a required recovery channel is voice, WhatsApp, or RCS, Infrai's email/SMS surface doesn't cover that requirement. A replaceable adapter helps move delivery code; it cannot supply missing workflow semantics.

Keep the deadline authoritative, make retries identifiable, and choose the provider whose responsibility matches the part of recovery you intend to delegate. A reset message is useful only while the application can safely honor it.

Sources

References for evaluating the contracts and workflow boundaries:

  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Vonage Verify documentation
  • Resend documentation

If the shared API boundary fits your recovery design, start with the schemas and conventions in the Infrai documentation.

title: Semantic Density Does Not Predict Agent-Memory Collapse
description:
arXiv:2611.33184v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Persistent textual memory can improve LLM agents, but repeated updates can erode task performance. We ask whether memory-store statistics warn before held-out accuracy declines. We registered mean pairwise cosine similarity ($\rho$) and 13 additional geometry, retrieval, and graph statistics on 805 snapshots from 13 memory methods across ALFWorld, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, and two ARC-AGI settings. These methods store trajectories, rules, workflows, strategies, or linked records, using selective retrieval or whole-store prompting. No such statistic reliably predicted early signs of task accuracy decline, and $\rho$ had zero median lead. With the checkpoint after peak accuracy as a secondary decline point, measures of highly similar pairs and nearest-neighbor crowding changed earlier but did not consistently outperform stored-item count. We trained classifiers on this corpus and applied them unchanged to PropWorld runs of up to 5,000 crafting tasks. They falsely flagged 56.9% of checkpoints from size-limited stores with stable accuracy and detected only 18% of checkpoints after task success fell to zero. Thus, global semantic density did not provide a reliable warning, while local crowding did not transfer consistently across memory designs. In these long-horizon runs, size-limited stores remained stable, while the sole failure arose when unbounded whole-store prompting exceeded model input capacity, which token growth predicted directly.

title: JHealthBench-L: Clinician-Reviewed Localization of HealthBench for Rubric-Based Medical LLM Evaluation in Japan
description:
arXiv:2611.34024v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Rubric-based benchmarks such as HealthBench evaluate large language models (LLMs) on open-ended health consultations using case-specific physician criteria, many of which presuppose the healthcare institutions, medications, and care pathways of their source region. Under machine translation alone, these regional assumptions remain in the rubric, leaving responses appropriate in Japan uncredited or falsely penalized under foreign clinical rules. To adapt established clinical evaluation perspectives to Japan without authoring rubrics from scratch, we construct JHealthBench-L (79 patient-facing consultations, 1,022 criteria) through source-cited LLM drafting, single-specialist selection and revision, independent dual-physician review, and meta-review. Specialists rewrote only 4.4% of criteria from scratch, and independent reviewers approved 93.6% of Stage-2 criteria without issue. Comparing JHealthBench-L with a machine-translated baseline across 18 LLMs reveals that translation-only evaluation preserves coarse model rankings ($\tau = 0.817$, mean shift +0.027) yet flips verdicts on 17.7% of modified criteria (vs. 7.3% re-grading noise) and reduces false penalties on Japan-adapted negative criteria by 7.1 percentage points, masking item-level clinical mismeasurement behind stable leaderboards. Axis-level and paired analyses further show that context awareness and Japan-specific clinical criteria remain primary bottlenecks, whereas Japanese continual pretraining and reasoning post-training substantially improve locally grounded performance. Datasets, physician revision logs, and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/horshohei/JHealthBench-L.

title: Top 10 Tailwind CSS Secrets Every Developer Should Know (Shortcuts Most People Ignore)
description:
You write w-10 h-10 for the hundredth time. You copy a color, add /50 by guessing, and hope it works. Then you open a teammate's code and see something like size-10 or has-[:checked]:bg-orange-50, and you think: wait, you can do that? 👀

Most of us learn Tailwind CSS the same way: a few utility classes, a few tutorials, and then we stop exploring. The framework has plenty of small shortcuts that quietly make your code shorter and cleaner.

So, how many of these Tailwind CSS tips and tricks do you already use? Let's find out. This post focuses on Tailwind CSS v4. 🚀

What Are Tailwind CSS Secrets?

Tailwind CSS is a utility-first CSS framework. Instead of writing a custom class like .card in a CSS file, you build your design with small classes right in your HTML: p-4, rounded-lg, bg-white.

Think of it like LEGO. Each utility class is one brick. Once you know the special bricks, you build faster.

These "secrets" aren't hidden or illegal magic. They are real features from the official docs that many developers skip because the basics already work. They're shortcuts you didn't know you had. 😊

Why These Shortcuts Matter

  • Less typing. Shorter class lists are easier to read and review.
  • Fewer bugs. Built-in features beat hand-written workarounds.
  • Less custom CSS. You stay inside Tailwind instead of jumping between files.
  • Better teamwork. Clean utilities are easier for others to understand.

Small habits add up across a whole project.

The 10 Tailwind CSS Secrets (With Real Examples)

1. size-* sets width and height together ✅

Instead of this:

<img class="w-12 h-12 rounded-full" src="avatar.jpg" alt="Avatar" />

Write this:

<img class="size-12 rounded-full" src="avatar.jpg" alt="Avatar" />

Perfect for avatars, icons, and square buttons. It's half the typing for the same result.

2. The slash trick controls color opacity

Add / and a number to any color:

<div class="bg-black/50 text-white/80">Semi-transparent overlay</div>

No extra opacity classes and no custom CSS. Great for image overlays and soft backgrounds.

3. Spacing values aren't limited to a fixed list (v4)

In v4, spacing-based utilities work from a base spacing value, so numbers you may have thought didn't exist can work:

<div class="w-17 mt-13 grid grid-cols-15">...</div>

No more reaching for w-[68px] just because w-17 wasn't in your old config. 💡

4. Named groups stop hover chaos

You probably know group-hover. But what happens when groups are nested and the wrong parent triggers the hover?

Name them:

<div class="group/card">
  <div class="group/title">
    <h3 class="group-hover/card:text-orange-500 group-hover/title:underline">
      Hello
    </h3>
  </div>
</div>

Each child now knows exactly which parent it listens to. The same idea works with peer.

5. has-* styles a parent based on its children

CSS now has a :has() selector, and Tailwind gives you a variant for it:

<label class="has-[:checked]:bg-orange-50 has-[:checked]:border-orange-400 border p-4">
  <input type="radio" name="plan" />
  Pro plan
</label>

When the radio inside is checked, the whole card changes style. No JavaScript, no extra state. Handy for selectable cards and form groups.

6. Container queries are built in (v4)

Media queries look at the screen. Container queries look at the parent's size, which is ideal for reusable components.

<div class="@container">
  <div class="grid grid-cols-1 @md:grid-cols-2 gap-4">
    ...
  </div>
</div>

The same card can now adapt when it's in a sidebar versus a wide page. 🔧

7. Arbitrary values and properties are your escape hatch

Need something that isn't in the scale? Use square brackets:

<div class="w-[calc(100%-2rem)] grid-cols-[1fr_2fr] top-[117px]">...</div>

Notice the underscore. Tailwind turns _ into a space, so 1fr_2fr becomes 1fr 2fr.

You can even write a whole CSS property:

<div class="[mask-type:luminance]">...</div>

Use this when needed, but don't let it replace the design scale (more on that below).

8. starting: animates elements when they first appear

Animating an element as it enters the page used to need JavaScript or tricky CSS. The starting: variant targets the style an element begins with:

<div popover id="menu"
  class="opacity-0 open:opacity-100 starting:open:opacity-0 transition-discrete transition-opacity">
  Menu content
</div>

It relies on modern browser features, so check browser support before using it in production.

9. @theme turns your design tokens into utilities

In v4, configuration lives in your CSS file. Define a token once:

@import "tailwindcss";

@theme {
  --color-brand: #fd6e4e;
}

Now bg-brand, text-brand, and border-brand just work, and the value is also available as a CSS variable. One source of truth for your brand colors. ⚡

10. data-* and aria-* variants style real states

Instead of toggling extra classes in JavaScript, style the attributes you already have:

<button aria-disabled="true" class="aria-disabled:opacity-50">Save</button>

<div data-state="open" class="data-[state=open]:rotate-180">▼</div>

Your accessibility attributes now double as styling hooks. This also pairs nicely with component libraries that set data-state for you.

Comparison: The Long Way vs The Shortcut

Task Long way Shortcut
Square element w-10 h-10 size-10
Faded color custom CSS or extra wrapper bg-black/50
Checked card JS + extra class has-[:checked]:bg-orange-50
Responsive component screen media queries @container + @md:
Brand color repeated hex codes @theme + bg-brand

The shortcuts aren't always "better," but they're often shorter, safer, and easier to maintain.

Best Tips: Do's & Don'ts

Do:

  • ✅ Define repeated colors and fonts in @theme instead of copying hex values.
  • ✅ Use size-* and the slash opacity trick as daily habits.
  • ✅ Check the official docs when you're unsure. Tailwind v4 changed some things from v3.
  • ✅ Test newer features like starting: in the browsers your users actually use.

Don't:

  • ❌ Don't use arbitrary values for everything. If you write w-[68px] ten times, make it a token.
  • ❌ Don't copy v3 config advice into a v4 project without checking.
  • ❌ Don't build class names by joining strings (like `bg-${color}-500`). Tailwind scans for complete class names, so write them in full.

Common Mistakes People Make

1. Mixing v3 and v4 instructions.
Tutorials online often mix versions. In v4, setup and configuration moved to CSS. When something doesn't work, check which version the tutorial was written for.

2. Overusing arbitrary values.
They feel fast, but they scatter random numbers across your project. A theme token is cleaner.

3. Building dynamic class names.
Writing `text-${color}-500` looks smart, but Tailwind can't detect classes that never appear as full strings. Map your options to complete class names instead.

4. Forgetting browser support.
Newer CSS features are great, but your audience decides what's safe. A quick check saves a surprise bug report.

5. Never reading the docs after the basics.
The docs are full of small wins. Ten minutes of scrolling can improve your habits for months. 😊

Conclusion

The best Tailwind CSS secrets aren't complicated. They're small shortcuts: size-*, opacity slashes, named groups, has-*, container queries, @theme, and state variants. Together they mean cleaner code and less custom CSS.

Pick two or three and use them in your next component. That's enough to feel the difference.

If this helped, read more developer posts on hamidrazadev.com, share it with a friend who loves Tailwind, and tell me in the comments: which shortcut was new to you? 🚀

title: Anthropic Rewrote Its Messages API in Rust — and the Hard Part Wasn't Writing the Code
description:
Anthropic just published one of the most honest engineering stories of the year: how it moved its Messages API — the route every Claude API call, Claude Code session, and Cowork task travels — from Python to Rust. The new version uses about 70% less CPU per request and cuts median time to first token by about 20%, with zero downtime and no freeze on feature development.

The surprising part isn't the rewrite. Claude wrote the first version of the API's core request path in about a week. The surprising part is what Anthropic says actually consumed the effort: proving the new code behaved exactly like the old one.

The generator–verifier gap comes to production

Anthropic frames the problem as a generator–verifier gap. It's often far easier to verify a solution than to produce one — checking a Sudoku solution is trivial, finding it is not. Many of Claude's most ambitious projects have relied on that gap: a proof assistant can check each step of a mathematical proof, and a test suite can judge a codebase migration.

But live systems break the pattern. Users rely on edge cases and quirks that fall outside the test suite, and "correct" is hard to define exhaustively. Generating the Rust code was the easy part. Verifying it was the project.

The numbers explain why a rewrite became unavoidable. The Messages API started in 2023 as what one engineer called "basically a request forwarder" — a thin Python service passing requests to the model. By late 2025, every request had to be validated, converted into a prompt, tokenized, and screened by safety classifiers, while replies had to be sorted into text, thinking, and tool calls. Python added overhead to every one of those steps. Meanwhile, traffic grew roughly 1,800 times from early 2024 to fall 2026.

The incremental fix that didn't pay

The team did what the standard advice says: rewrite only the slow parts. They rewrote the model-output parsing code in Rust and called it from Python. CPU usage fell about 8% to 10% — but each token now crossed between Python and Rust three times, adding complexity and new overhead. The gains didn't justify the cost.

What changed the calculus was Claude itself. By May 2026, Claude was writing more than 80% of the code Anthropic merged. The effort of a full rewrite was dropping fast. The question became: could Claude also help capture every behavior and fix in the production system — and how would anyone verify that?

Why 700 tests weren't enough

The team started with its existing suite of about 700 integration tests. Two problems limited how much they could trust it.

First, the tests were coupled to the Python implementation. They ran the Python API inside the test process and mocked services like billing and rate limiting in Python's memory. The tests had to change along with the code, and Claude helped with both — so a "pass" could mean the code was right, or that the test had been weakened to let wrong code through. An audit found more than 100 weakened assertions.

Second, the tests were incomplete. The API has dozens of features, and the combinations explode: just 20 binary options make over a million combinations — 12 days of tests at a second each, for one model, before varying the prompts. In practice, engineers test a subset that approximates production. It inevitably misses cases.

The gap showed up in the numbers. In April, the Rust API passed about 98% of its tests — yet only about a quarter of inputs matched on production traffic. One example: when Python writes JSON tool calls, it escapes certain characters (like an emoji) by replacing them with text codes. Rust wrote those characters as-is, so the two prompts differed by a few bytes. Production also weights bugs differently than a test suite: each case counts once in tests, but a single common bug in live traffic fires on every request it touches.

Turning production into the verifier

With tests insufficient, Anthropic used the existing system as an oracle — shadowing. Requests ran through both the old and new code, and the results were compared. Standard shadowing tools assume a request can safely run twice and that the service is deterministic. Neither held: a request had to count only once toward a customer's limits and bill, and Claude's replies are nondeterministic.

The fix: run the model once and replay its output to the Rust version. With both versions working from the same model output, every stage before and after the model call had to match exactly — because Claude accepts almost any prompt, even a small deviation can change its reply without triggering an error.

There was also a privacy constraint. The team worked without reading user requests or Claude's replies, so it couldn't just look at where the two versions diverged. Instead it recorded the shape of each difference:

  • Checkpointing. Both versions handle a request in the same steps — accept or reject it, resolve settings, build the prompt. Comparing step by step, and piece by piece within the prompt, located roughly where the migration code differed.
  • Fingerprinting. Once the rough location was known, the team recorded where each difference began in the prompt plus the length difference. One bug tends to leave the same fingerprint on every request it affects, so errors could be grouped and triaged by fingerprint.

Three loops, and a human at the seam

Each differing request left a record in the logs, and a single bug could produce hundreds of thousands of nearly identical records. A script ran every 10 to 30 minutes, grouped records by which fields differed, and alerted a coordinating Claude agent only when it saw a new kind of record. The coordinator assigned a worker agent to each new kind and opened a thread in a shared Slack channel where engineers could follow along.

From there, three loops did the work:

  • The inner loop ran in a cloud sandbox where agents could test hypotheses in seconds. The input check built the prompt each version would send — without calling the model, so a comparison took under a second. The output check ran both versions against a scripted reply. Agents had to reproduce each difference themselves, since they could only see the fingerprint, not the request behind it. A wrong guess cost seconds and harmed nobody.
  • The outer loop validated fixes against shadowed production traffic, comparing deployments with and without each fix. It caught what the sandbox missed, since the local verifier wasn't always configured exactly like production.
  • The memory loop recorded what came out of reviews and applied it to every agent that followed. When an engineer rejected a shortcut — an agent had proposed copying a web-search tool description into files instead of having Rust call the internal service — the decision, the reason, and the correct fix were saved as a note. Later agents recognized the same bug from new fingerprints and linked it to the note instead of writing another workaround. In June, an agent went through about 60 review comments, grouped the recurring problems, and proposed rules that an engineer edited and approved for the team's CLAUDE.md.

Human review sat at the seam between the inner and outer loops. A verifier can tell an agent whether outputs matched, Anthropic notes, but not whether a fix is good enough to ship. Engineers reviewed proposed fixes, decided whether a difference was a bug or a deliberate change, and increasingly moved to the edge — writing the rules and checks the agents worked within.

The lesson that generalizes

Anthropic closes with a metaphor: migration is usually like rebuilding the Ship of Theseus plank by plank while it sails, and changing too many planks at once means coming into dock. Claude made it possible to build an identically functioning ship alongside the first — even as the first kept sailing and having its planks replaced — and move the passengers over a few at a time.

The takeaway the team states plainly: verification is the new bottleneck. Writing code is no longer the constraint; how quickly you can verify results is. Ambition can increase as long as there's a way to verify correctness — and when tests and formal checks aren't enough, a production system itself can be the verifier. The work is in designing the verification signal: checkpoints that locate a difference in the code, fingerprints that tell one bug from another, and loops simple enough to scale as the model gets more capable.

For anyone planning their own rewrite, the message is uncomfortable but useful: if your migration plan is mostly about generating the new code, you've planned the easy half.

Source: Anthropic, "Migrating our Messages API to Rust" (November 25, 2026) — https://www.anthropic.com/research/migrating-api-to-rust
