title: Residual Cross-Model Narrative Convergence under Shared Prompts: Auditing Prompt Controls and Narrative Measurement
description:
arXiv:2611.34015v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Stories created by LLMs based on the same prompts can be narratively similar to one another. This similarity may reflect constraints imposed by the prompts as well as the models' writing tendencies. The current research analyzes 51,240 stories created by five models in the StoryScope corpus based on 10,248 common prompts. It uses 213 narrative features in seven dimensions to compare cross-model distances between stories generated from the same prompts with distances between stories generated from different but semantically matched prompts. To assess the relationship between narrative features and prompt content, a semantic relevance mask was evaluated against 420 author-annotated prompt-feature judgments (F1 = .813; near-threshold accuracy = .621). The equally weighted mean Residual Convergence Index (RCI) was .409 without masking and .406 with masking. These findings indicate measurable cross-model narrative convergence relative to a semantically matched-prompt baseline, with little change following semantic relevance masking.

title: Transférer un site sans une minute de coupure : le déroulé heure par heure
description:
Copier les fichiers et la base de données est la partie facile d'une migration. Ce qui casse un transfert, c'est le moment de bascule : pendant quelques heures, une partie de vos visiteurs atterrit sur l'ancien serveur, l'autre sur le nouveau. Si les deux sont vivants et acceptent des données, vous perdez des commandes et des messages sans jamais le savoir.

La méthode ci-dessous supprime ce trou. Elle repose entièrement sur le TTL, et elle se prépare la veille.

J moins 2 : abaisser le TTL

C'est l'étape que tout le monde saute, et la seule qui rende la bascule instantanée.

Dans la zone DNS actuelle, passez le TTL des enregistrements concernés (A, AAAA, les CNAME du site, et les MX si le courrier bouge aussi) à 300 secondes.

Ne changez rien d'autre. Puis attendez la durée de l'ancien TTL, en entier. Si votre TTL était à 86400, il faut vraiment attendre une journée : les caches détiennent encore l'ancienne valeur avec l'ancienne durée, et rien ne peut accélérer ça.

À la fin de cette attente, tous les résolveurs du monde savent qu'ils doivent revérifier votre domaine toutes les cinq minutes. Vous avez acheté votre bascule instantanée.

J moins 1 : monter le nouveau site et le tester par l'IP

Installez fichiers et base sur le nouvel hébergeur, sans toucher au DNS.

Pour le tester avant la bascule, modifiez le fichier hosts de votre machine : il court-circuite le DNS pour vous seul.

# Windows : C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts
# macOS et Linux : /etc/hosts
203.0.113.10   votredomaine.fr www.votredomaine.fr

Vous naviguez alors sur le nouveau serveur avec le vrai nom de domaine, pendant que le reste du monde reste sur l'ancien. C'est le seul moyen de vérifier les liens absolus, les certificats et les chemins d'images sans rien casser.

Testez le formulaire de contact et le tunnel de commande à ce moment-là. Une base migrée dont les identifiants sont restés ceux de l'ancien serveur ne se voit qu'en essayant d'écrire dedans.

Jour J : passer l'ancien serveur en lecture seule

Avant de toucher au DNS, empêchez l'ancien site d'accepter la moindre écriture. Sinon, pendant la période de bascule, une commande passée par un visiteur encore dirigé vers l'ancien serveur atterrira dans une base que vous n'emporterez pas.

Selon la plateforme : mode maintenance, désactivation du tunnel de commande, ou fermeture des formulaires. Puis faites la dernière synchronisation de la base, celle qui compte.

Jour J : la bascule

Changez l'enregistrement A vers la nouvelle IP. Avec un TTL à 300, la modification est visible partout en cinq minutes.

Vérifiez sans attendre, en interrogeant deux résolveurs publics :

nslookup votredomaine.fr 1.1.1.1
nslookup votredomaine.fr 8.8.8.8

S'ils rendent tous deux la nouvelle adresse, c'est fait.

Jour J plus 1 : le certificat, puis le TTL

Le certificat HTTPS se génère après la bascule, jamais avant : l'autorité de certification vérifie que le domaine pointe bien vers le serveur qui demande le certificat. Tant que le DNS n'a pas basculé, la demande échoue, et c'est normal.

Une fois le site stable, remontez le TTL à 3600 ou plus.

Ne débranchez pas l'ancien serveur tout de suite

Gardez-le allumé une semaine, en lecture seule. Deux raisons concrètes : quelques caches exotiques traînent au-delà de toute logique, et surtout, c'est votre porte de retour si un problème apparaît au troisième jour.

Un ancien serveur résilié le soir même est la décision qu'on regrette le plus.

L'ordre, en une ligne

TTL bas, site monté et testé par hosts, ancien site en lecture seule, dernière synchro, bascule DNS, certificat, TTL remonté, ancien serveur gardé une semaine.

Chaque étape sautée se paie en données perdues, pas en temps gagné. Si vous préférez confier la bascule, c'est ce que je fais à partir de 59 €, sans coupure et avec le retour arrière préparé.

Article publié à l'origine sur creebs.fr. Creebs dépanne les sites WordPress et PrestaShop en panne, chaque solution testée en labo avant d'être écrite.

title: Casper: A Projection-Based Neurosymbolic Layer for Scalable & Guaranteed Constraint Satisfaction
description:
arXiv:2611.33527v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many real-world problems demand exact constraint satisfaction to be meaningfully solved, yet existing neurosymbolic methods face a stark trade-off: those that guarantee satisfaction fail to scale, while those that scale must resort to approximation. Meanwhile, traditional deep learning approaches offer no satisfaction guarantees at all. In this paper, we propose Casper, a neurosymbolic layer that simultaneously (i) guarantees constraint satisfaction, (ii) scales at inference time, (iii) is fully automated, requiring no problem-specific engineering, and (iv) is fully differentiable, making it composable with any neural predictor both at training and at inference time. Casper casts constraint satisfaction as a closed-form Euclidean projection onto the constraint-feasible region, computable in a single forward pass. Experiments across MNIST arithmetic (up to 1024 digits), Sudoku solving, and Warcraft pathfinding show that Casper is the only method that produces guaranteed-valid outputs at scale: on $30\times30$ Warcraft grids, exact baselines time out and approximate ones produce valid paths less than 7% of the time, while Casper produces them 100% of the time.

title: How I Built a Free MCP Server for Decoding 2,375 Cosmetic & Perfume Batch Codes
description:
Every bottle of Dior, Chanel, CeraVe, or COSRX has a short alphanumeric string engraved on the glass or crimped into the tube — a batch code (like 4B01 or 38Z401). Under EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) 1223/2009, products with a shelf life over 30 months don't have to print an expiration date; consumers and second-hand buyers have to decode that batch code instead.

While building CosmeScan (a free batch code decoder and recall checker covering 2,375 cosmetic, skincare, K-Beauty, and perfume brands), I noticed a growing pattern in our traffic: a significant share of users were coming directly from AI assistants like ChatGPT and Claude asking "When was Dior batch 4B01 made?" — and LLMs frequently hallucinated the manufacturing year because cosmetic conglomerates reuse 10-year cyclic codes and proprietary calendars.

To give AI agents deterministic, verified answers instead of guesses, I built and published cosmescan-mcp — a free, read-only, zero-API-key Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on npm and Glama.

Here is how it works and how you can wire it into Claude Desktop, Cursor, or any MCP-compatible client in 30 seconds.

Why LLMs Struggle with Cosmetic Batch Codes

Cosmetic batch codes are deceptively tricky for language models:

  • 10-year repeating cycles: LVMH (6B01 = Feb 2026 or Feb 2016), Estée Lauder (A66 = June 2026 or June 2016), and L'Oréal (38Z401) recycle year identifiers every decade.
  • Sequential registries: Chanel uses a rolling 4-digit monthly counter (~8-year cycle) that cannot be guessed from arithmetic alone.
  • Conglomerate M&A drift: Acquired brands (like Byredo under Puig, Maison Francis Kurkdjian under LVMH, or Aesop under L'Oréal) have two or three different historical encoding schemes depending on the production year.
  • Cloned counterfeit lots: On secondary marketplaces (Vinted, eBay, Depop), counterfeiters reuse valid vintage batch codes (for example, 19280 on Baccarat Rouge 540 or 19S01 on Creed Aventus). A naive date decoder tells the buyer "Valid date!" even though the code is a known counterfeit signature.

Architecture: Thin Stdio MCP Client + Edge REST API

I wanted cosmescan-mcp to have zero secrets, zero local database bloat, and instant npx startup:

Claude Desktop / Cursor / MCP Host
        │  (stdio JSON-RPC 2.0)
        ▼
cosmescan-mcp (Node.js + @modelcontextprotocol/sdk)
        │  (HTTPS GET, read-only, no API key)
        ▼
CosmeScan Public API (Cloudflare Worker + static JSON catalog)
  ├── /v1/decode?brand=dior&code=4B01
  ├── /v1/brands?q=cerave
  └── /v1/brand/dior

The package is just ~4.2 kB unpacked, uses @modelcontextprotocol/sdk over StdioServerTransport, and exposes 3 deterministic, read-only tools:

Tool Purpose
decode_batch_code Decodes manufacturing date, product age, PAO shelf-life status, cloned counterfeit lot warnings, and EU Safety Gate / US FDA recall alerts
search_brands Searches across all 2,375 supported cosmetic, skincare, K-Beauty, and fragrance brands
get_brand_info Returns brand metadata, parent conglomerate, batch format hints, and direct decoder URL

You can also inspect the underlying public REST endpoints directly in the CosmeScan Open API Docs.

Quick Setup (Claude Desktop / Cursor / Windsurf)

No account or API key is required. Add this block to your claude_desktop_config.json or .cursor/mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "cosmescan": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "cosmescan-mcp"]
    }
  }
}

Once connected, you can ask your assistant:

"Check Christian Dior batch code 4B01 — when was it manufactured, is it fresh, and are there any recalls or counterfeit warnings?"

The agent calls decode_batch_code({ brand: "dior", code: "4B01" }) and receives structured JSON with the exact manufacturing date (2024-02), formula age, EU PAO freshness status, and whether the lot matches any active EU Safety Gate (RAPEX), US FDA, or RappelConso recall — or any of the 306 known cloned counterfeit batch codes documented in our 2026 Counterfeit & Recall Observatory.

Passing Glama Introspection & awesome-mcp-servers Checks

A quick tip if you're publishing your own Node.js MCP server to directories like Glama or punkpeye/awesome-mcp-servers:

  1. Include a minimal Dockerfile (node:22-alpine, npm install --omit=dev, ENTRYPOINT ["node", "index.js"]) so automated registries can spin up your server in a container and run initialize + tools/list introspection.
  2. Write a fast end-to-end stdio smoke test spawning node index.js and piping real JSON-RPC frames (initialize → notifications/initialized → tools/list → tools/call) before publishing to npm.
  3. Never write logs to stdout — stdout is strictly reserved for JSON-RPC messages in stdio MCP servers; send all diagnostics to stderr.

Links & Open Resources

  • GitHub Repository (MIT): https://github.com/guillaumefric0-del/cosmescan-mcp
  • npm Package: https://www.npmjs.com/package/cosmescan-mcp
  • Glama Verified Listing: https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/guillaumefric0-del/cosmescan-mcp
  • Web App & Open API Docs: https://cosmescan.com/api-docs/
  • 2026 Counterfeit & Recall Open Study: https://cosmescan.com/observatory-2026/

Feedback, PRs, and new brand decoding rules are always welcome!

title: Understanding Mode Collapse in Diffusion Models under Classifier-Free Guidance
description:
arXiv:2611.33719v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The use of classifier-free guidance in diffusion and flow models has proven critical to their empirical success, as it allows for the controllable generation of lower-temperature and higher-fidelity samples. Despite its widespread use, classifier-free guidance remains both empirically and theoretically poorly understood, owing to the difficulty of solving the associated transport equations for arbitrary normalizing flows. In this paper, we observe that the effects of classifier-free guidance arise from a mismatch between the representation capabilities of the conditional and unconditional distributions, wherein the conditional distribution exhibits higher complexity and fidelity. We propose an analytical model to capture this observation: the conditional distribution is a Gaussian mixture whose means lie on an ellipsoid, and the unconditional distribution is a single Gaussian approximating the mixture. The flows arising from this mixture are closed under scaling, enabling us to derive analytic closed-form solutions for the guided distribution at all noise scales and guidance levels. Our analytic solution shows that classifier-free guidance induces (a) a shift along a mean-axis direction and (b) a persistent skew toward, and concentration around, a singular point corresponding to the conditional sample starting from zero noise. We validate our theoretical predictions on pretrained, large-scale image diffusion models.

title: Off-the-Shelf Autonomous Agents for Game Playtesting
description:
arXiv:2611.31570v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In playtesting games, a human operator is typically required to test most gameplay elements. In this work we present Buddy, an autonomous game solving agent which can solve long time horizon objectives in an unseen 3D role-playing game using off-the-shelf language model systems. Buddy will take actions, receive feedback on those actions, and pursue a goal across many turns. No written walkthrough or model training of any kind is required, and we show that this paradigm holds in a novel environment where the agent must discover solutions via exploration rather than recalling them from pretraining. We demonstrate three downstream capabilities: game solving with no provided walkthrough, logging bug tickets for encountered difficulties, and conversion of successful agent traces into scripted hierarchical task networks for regression testing. Unlike existing playtesting solutions, our framework is fully modular: language models and harnesses can be easily swapped out as capabilities improve over time.

title: AI-human hybrid conversations: Can AI Agents Improve Discourse Quality?
description:
arXiv:2611.33459v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conversations are central to how people exchange information, share experiences, and develop collective understanding. Yet, across conversational settings, discussions often suffer from uneven participation, unanswered contributions, and a narrow range of perspectives. As generative AI agents increasingly participate alongside humans, hybrid human-AI conversations present a new opportunity to address these challenges. We investigate whether AI agents can serve as catalysts for human interaction, improving conversational engagement and broadening collective discourse. We develop a framework for introducing generic and persona-conditioned AI agents into evolving discussions and evaluate it through two complementary studies. First, using agent-based simulations grounded in Reddit discussions across four domains, we find that AI-generated conversations are more positive and less toxic than human conversations, but substantially less semantically diverse. Persona conditioning produces more human-like contributions and narrows this diversity gap, while increasing the representation of underrepresented personas can shift which perspectives emerge without necessarily increasing overall diversity. Second, we conduct a pre-registered experiment with 221 participants across nine discussion threads, comparing human-only conversations with those involving generic or persona-conditioned AI agents. We find that AI participation increases responsiveness, reduces unanswered contributions, and broadens the range of ideas expressed by human participants, even though the AI agents themselves do not fully reproduce human conversational diversity. These findings suggest that the value of hybrid human-AI conversations lies not simply in the content AI agents generate, but also in their potential to stimulate more responsive and diverse interactions among humans.

title: One Step, Four Clocks: How GUI Agents Fall Out of Step
description:
arXiv:2611.31522v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: GUI agents can choose correct actions yet fail as interfaces change during deliberation. Latency alone cannot explain these failures because actions may become invalid at different interaction stages. We model four events: environment change, observation availability, decision commitment, and action receipt (EODA). We introduce ChronotopeGym to study these failures under Paused, Replay, and Live execution. Across five tasks, agents can fail in Live despite succeeding when responses remain valid, even when actions meet deadlines. On Moving Balloon, updating a pending click raises success from 0% to 100% without changing response time. Our accelerator-resident GUI controller, Chronotope, maintains compact interaction history and selectively keeps, updates, or redecides pending actions. Compared with Agent S3, Chronotope reduces median end-to-end latency by 85.5% for a 27B model, expanding its performance envelope to 100% Live success at an 8-second deadline versus 0%. Chronotope enables real-time GUI control through compact interaction history, knowing when to preserve, revise, or replace actions, and an overall efficient architectural design that obviates verbose reflection, reasoning, and grounding calls.

title: A Semantics-First Approach to Multimodal Video Captioning with Frozen Encoders and Stabilized Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.33409v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose the Audio-Visual Query Transformer (AVQFormer), a highly efficient architecture built upon a 2.7B parameter LLM featuring a fixed-length $K=16$ semantic alignment module, stabilized via Adaptive Self-Critical Sequence Training (ASCST) with Entropy Regularization. Multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) often rely on global audio representations to compensate for inefficient, frame-based visual encoders. While our Phase 1 prompted evaluations demonstrate that the Multimodal Base Model achieves strong deep semantic alignment (scoring 0.889 on BERTScore F1), optimizing this architecture for legacy metrics reveals a performance gap. We explore this gap as a hypothesis we term temporal alignment friction: a conflict where global audio representations disrupt the chronological sequence of visual frames, leading to penalties under visually-focused evaluation metrics. Consequently, by stripping away the audio, our Video-Only ablation conforms more closely to this rigid syntax, achieving 63.0 CIDEr. While trailing larger models such as Qwen2.5-VL (67.4 CIDEr), this establishes a strong baseline for sub-3B parameter LLM-based models. This indicates that CIDEr, as applied to datasets such as MSR-VTT, may exhibit a bias toward visually grounded syntax, limiting its ability to fully capture multimodal semantic richness.

title: Better code, fewer tokens: The benefits of Code Connect in MCP
description: When going from design to code, agents lack the context of your production components. With Code Connect in Figma’s MCP, they get that context. We measured its impact on token usage, task duration, and code quality.

title: Large-scale Model Merging via Recovery-aware Task Weighting
description:
arXiv:2611.33315v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Model merging combines multiple task-specific expert models into a single model. However, merging preserves expert capabilities unevenly across tasks. This imbalance is particularly pronounced in large-scale settings, where some tasks can suffer severe capability losses even when average accuracy remains high. To address this imbalance, we introduce Recovery-aware Task Weighting (RaTW), a model merging framework that assigns larger weights to tasks whose expert capabilities are poorly retained by an initial merged model. We quantify these recovery opportunities as the fraction of a task's labeled validation samples that its expert predicts correctly but the initial merged model gets wrong, and use the resulting task weights to re-merge the experts. To evaluate merging at large scale, we construct CLIPMerge-100, a 100-task benchmark with task-specific experts on CLIP ViT-L/14 and ViT-B/32. Across eleven merging methods with 20, 50, and 100 tasks on two CLIP backbones, RaTW improves both mean accuracy and tail20 (the mean expert-normalized accuracy of the 20% worst-retained tasks) in all 33 ViT-L/14 settings and 32 of 33 ViT-B/32 settings. We further introduce ReForge++, which combines RaTW with iterative model refinement and outperforms all evaluated baselines, including a matched-budget control, in both mean accuracy and tail20 across all settings.

title: Priority Projects now in public beta
description:
Priority Projects are now in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. This optional upgrade for individual Vercel projects adds bot and traffic-source signals, Page Integrity for monitoring and controlling client-side scripts and connections, and additional Firewall controls and alerts.

Bot signals

Bot protection is free on all plans. You can enable it to challenge non-browser traffic while allowing verified bots. Priority adds more detailed bot signals: categories, verification status, and names where available. Use these signals in:

  • Firewall rules: Match on bot_name, bot_category, bot_status, and bot_protection in the dashboard or with vercel firewall rules add.

  • Application code: Read x-vercel-bot-category, x-vercel-bot-name, and x-vercel-verified-bot from request headers in Routing Middleware and Vercel Functions. See the header reference for verified and claimed bot names.

  • Logs and Observability: Logs show the Firewall action on all plans. Priority adds the matched rule and bot details where available. In Firewall Observability, Priority adds botCategory for unverified traffic. Log Drains also include bot classifications.

Traffic Sources

Priority adds Traffic Sources labels for requests from Tor exit nodes, VPNs, open or anonymizing proxies, and residential proxies. It also labels traffic flagged by abuse blocklists.

Use these labels in custom Firewall rules, analyze them in Firewall Observability, or read them from the x-vercel-waf-source request header in your application. A request can have multiple labels.

Use the Traffic Sources managed ruleset to log, challenge, or block traffic by source category. Review matching traffic before enabling blocking, since these categories can also include legitimate users.

To enable the Traffic Sources managed ruleset from the CLI, run vercel firewall managed-rulesets enable traffic-sources. This stages the change; review it with vercel firewall diff, then apply it with vercel firewall publish.

Page Integrity

Priority Projects get access to Page Integrity to monitor client-side scripts and connections, receive alerts when new scripts or connections are detected, and block unapproved resources.

Page Integrity maintains a resource inventory and uses Content Security Policy (CSP) for discovery and enforcement, without adding client-side JavaScript.

It operates in three stages:

  • Detect: Discover scripts using report-only CSP headers on sampled requests.

  • Review: Approve or reject scripts and record business justifications.

  • Block: Enforce a CSP that blocks scripts outside the approved inventory.

Page Integrity must be enabled separately. Configure monitoring and review resources in the dashboard; the CLI can also show its resource inventory:

Firewall controls and alerts

Anomaly alerts

DDoS alerts are available on all plans. Priority adds anomaly alerts for bot traffic and requests matching system or custom Firewall rules. Use these alerts to investigate potential attacks and unusual traffic patterns.

Configure notifications in your team’s Settings > Alerts, with delivery options including email, Slack, and webhooks.

View recent alerts with vercel alerts --since 24h. To manage alert configuration from the CLI, see vercel monitors.

OWASP Core Ruleset

On Pro, Priority lets you enable the OWASP Core Ruleset to protect against common web application attacks. Enterprise projects can already enable it without Priority.

Add it as a team default from Security > Rules, or enable it for a linked project via the CLI with vercel firewall managed-rulesets enable owasp --yes followed by vercel firewall publish. OWASP inspection is billed separately per inspected request and GB of inspected payload.

Response-based rate limiting

Priority adds response conditions to the rate-limit rules available on all plans. Count requests toward a limit only when their responses match specified HTTP status codes or response headers. For example, count 401 responses from failed login attempts or 404 responses for missing pages, rather than every matching request.

Higher Firewall limits

Priority increases the following per-project limits (shown as standard → with Priority):

Get started

Priority costs $200 per project per month. Enable it from your project’s Firewall or Settings page, or with the CLI.

For the CLI, update to the latest version with vercel upgrade, then enable Priority for the project you want to upgrade:

Page Integrity usage is billed separately. Its standard rate is $2 per 1,000 monitored page views, with each view covering up to 100 scripts.

Learn more in the Priority Projects documentation.

title: Why Read-Only Database Access Matters More Than You Think
description:
Why Read-Only Database Access Matters More Than You Think

The first question every engineering lead asks when someone proposes letting non-technical teammates query a production database is some version of: what happens if they break something?

It's the right question. And it's the one that decides whether a self-service data tool ever gets turned on for anyone outside engineering.

TL;DR

Read-only enforcement is what makes natural-language database querying safe to hand to non-engineers. Query1AI generates and executes SELECT statements only — write operations aren't a configuration someone could disable, they're simply not in the execution path. Try it free →

The Real Risk Isn't Bad Questions — It's Write Access

Someone who doesn't know SQL asking a confusing question isn't actually dangerous. Worst case, they get an answer that doesn't match what they meant, and they ask again more precisely. That's a UX problem, not a safety problem.

The actual risk shows up the moment a tool sitting between a person and a production database is capable of more than reading. A natural-language interface that can also run UPDATE, DELETE, or DDL statements turns every ambiguous question into a potential incident — not because anyone intended harm, but because a misread intent plus write access is how rows get modified or dropped by accident.

This is also the reason most teams never seriously consider giving broader database access to non-engineers in the first place. It isn't that the questions aren't reasonable. It's that the access model doesn't give anyone confidence nothing will go wrong.

Read-Only Has to Be Structural, Not a Setting

There's a meaningful difference between a tool that's configured to avoid write operations and one that's incapable of them.

A configuration is a setting someone could change, a permission someone could misconfigure, or a default that quietly shifts in a future update. It depends on someone remembering it's there.

An architectural constraint doesn't depend on anyone remembering anything. If the query execution layer only knows how to run SELECT statements — if INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and DDL simply aren't operations the system is able to send to the database — then there's no scenario where a misinterpreted question becomes a destructive one. Not because it's discouraged. Because it isn't possible.

How This Shows Up in Query1AI

1DataCloud's Query1AI is built around exactly this constraint. It takes a plain-English question, reads the schema metadata the Unified Dashboard already mapped for that database — table names, column names, data types, relationships — and turns the question into SQL. That SQL is read-only by construction: Query1AI generates and executes SELECT statements, and nothing else is in its vocabulary.

That means a sales rep asking "which customers haven't logged in for 30 days" and a product manager asking a question that gets parsed in a way they didn't expect both land in the same place: a query that reads data and returns it. Neither one can accidentally trigger a write, because the path from question to query never passes through write operations at all.

The generated SQL is also visible before and after it runs. If a result looks off, the actual query is right there to check — nothing about how the answer was produced is hidden from the person who asked.

Why This Changes What's Possible for a Team

Once read-only is a structural guarantee rather than a policy, the conversation about who gets database access changes shape entirely.

Engineers stop being the only safe option. When write access was on the table, restricting database access to engineers was the responsible choice. When it isn't on the table, that restriction is solving a problem that no longer exists.

Self-service stops being a risk tradeoff. Letting a product manager or a sales lead query a database directly isn't "convenience traded against safety" anymore — the safety constraint doesn't loosen just because more people have access.

Mistakes stay cheap. A confusing question produces a confusing answer, which gets refined and asked again. It never produces a changed row, a dropped table, or a corrupted dataset.

What Read-Only Doesn't Mean

Worth being precise here: read-only means the query execution path can only read data — it doesn't mean every table or column is automatically appropriate for every person to see. Query1AI works from the schema metadata connected to a given database; whether a particular teammate should be looking at a particular database at all is still a question of who your organization has given access to in the first place, managed through 1DataCloud's organization and role settings. Read-only access answers "can this break something," not "who should see this" — those are two different questions, and read-only enforcement only answers the first one.

A Couple of Things Worth Clarifying

Can Query1AI ever run an UPDATE or DELETE if someone asks it to? No. The execution layer doesn't support write operations, so there's no configuration to bypass and no scenario where a write gets sent to the database through this path.

If the generated SQL is wrong, can someone see it before trusting the result? Yes. The SQL Query1AI generates is visible alongside the result, so if an answer looks unexpected, the actual query is right there to check.

Summary

Read-only access is the detail that makes natural-language database querying safe to hand to people who aren't engineers. Not because the questions they ask are more careful, but because the system answering them was never given the ability to write in the first place.

👉 1datacloud.ai

Does your team let non-engineers query production data today? What's the access model — read replicas, a BI layer, something else entirely? Curious how other teams have drawn this line.

Abd Alrhman Alloush is the Founder & CEO of 1DataCloud — a unified dashboard for managing and querying databases across AWS, GCP, and MongoDB Atlas.

title: Vercel Blob now supports TTLs for automatic deletion
description:
Vercel Blob can now delete blobs automatically. Pass ttlDays when you write a blob and it is deleted that many days after upload, from 1 to 730 days. The TTL counts from the blob's upload date.

Use TTLs for blobs you would otherwise delete yourself, such as session transcripts, exports, and temporary uploads.

ttlDays works on put(), copy(), putImage(), multipart uploads, and presigned upload URLs. Every write result and head() response now includes expiresAt, so you know when a blob is due for deletion.

setTtl() changes or removes the TTL of blobs you already have, one URL or up to 1,000 at a time, without re-uploading them.

In Vercel CLI 65.16.0 and later, pass --ttl-days to vercel blob put, put-image, copy or presign, and use vercel blob set-ttl on existing blobs.

Setting a TTL costs one Advanced Operation per started 60 days, on top of the write. A 7-day TTL costs one, and the 730-day maximum costs 13. Clearing a TTL and the deletions themselves are free. You can track TTL operations in the Blob section of the Observability tab.

npm install @vercel/blob@2.9.0

Learn more in the Vercel Blob documentation.

title: แก้ไขข้อผิดพลาดอีเมล Cloudflare: E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED, E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED และ 429
description:
ข้อผิดพลาดของ Cloudflare Email เริ่มปรากฏใน log มากขึ้นเมื่อวันที่ 24 พฤศจิกายน 2026 เมื่อ Cloudflare เปิดให้ Email Sending ใช้งานได้บนแผน Workers Free โดยมีเงื่อนไขสำคัญอยู่บรรทัดเดียวใน changelog นั่นคือ บนแผน Free คุณจะส่งอีเมลได้เฉพาะไปยังที่อยู่ปลายทางที่ยืนยันแล้วในบัญชีของคุณเท่านั้น

ลองใช้ Apidog วันนี้

คำตอบสั้นๆ: E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED หมายความว่าคุณใช้ Workers Free และผู้รับไม่ใช่ที่อยู่ปลายทางที่ยืนยันแล้ว ให้ยืนยันที่อยู่หรืออัปเกรดเป็น Workers Paid และห้าม retry เด็ดขาด E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED (Workers binding), HTTP 429 (REST API) และ 451 4.7.1 (SMTP) หมายความว่าคุณส่งถึงขีดจำกัดต่อวันของบัญชีแล้ว ให้จัดคิวข้อความและ retry ภายหลัง หรือขอเพิ่มขีดจำกัด

ความหมายของข้อผิดพลาด Cloudflare Email

Cloudflare Email Service รายงานปัญหาเดียวกันในสามรูปแบบ คือ Workers binding จะโยน code แบบ string, REST API จะส่งกลับ HTTP status พร้อมรหัสตัวเลข และ SMTP จะตอบกลับด้วย reply code ทั้งสามแบบใช้ชุดขีดจำกัดของบัญชีเดียวกัน

ปัญหา Workers binding REST API SMTP Retry?
ผู้รับไม่ได้รับอนุญาตบนแผนของคุณ E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED 403, code 10208 550 5.7.1 ที่ RCPT TO ไม่
ถึงขีดจำกัดการส่งต่อวันแล้ว E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED 429 451 4.7.1 ภายหลัง
ถึงขีดจำกัดอัตราการส่งหรือ concurrency E_RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED 429, code 10004 451 4.7.1 ได้ พร้อม backoff
ผู้รับอยู่ใน suppression list E_RECIPIENT_SUPPRESSED 400 ข้อความถูกปฏิเสธ ไม่
บัญชีถูกระงับชั่วคราวเพราะ repute E_ACCOUNT_SUSPENDED 403, code 10207 ไม่ระบุ ไม่

แหล่งที่มา: หน้า Limits ของ Cloudflare, รหัสข้อผิดพลาดของ Workers API และ รหัสการตอบกลับ SMTP ตรวจสอบเมื่อวันที่ 26 พฤศจิกายน 2026

ประเด็นสำคัญคือ ตารางข้อผิดพลาดของ REST มีเพียงรายการเดียวสำหรับ 429 คือ 10004 (email.sending.error.throttled) และ SMTP ใช้ 451 4.7.1 ทั้งสำหรับ rate limit และ daily limit มีเพียง binding เท่านั้นที่บอกคุณได้ว่าคุณชนขีดจำกัดตัวไหน

แก้ไข E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED บน Workers Free

E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED เป็นกฎของแผน ไม่ใช่ความล้มเหลวชั่วคราว บน Workers Free นั้น Email Sending จะรับเฉพาะที่อยู่ปลายทางที่ยืนยันแล้วในบัญชีของคุณเท่านั้น ที่อยู่อื่นใดจะล้มเหลวแบบเดียวกันทุกครั้งที่ลอง ดังนั้นห้าม retry เด็ดขาด

คุณมีทางออกสามทาง:

  1. ยืนยันที่อยู่ ใน dashboard ไปที่ Compute > Email Service > Email Routing > Destination Addresses เพิ่มที่อยู่แล้วคลิกลิงก์ในอีเมลยืนยันของ Cloudflare หนึ่งบัญชีสามารถเก็บที่อยู่ปลายทางได้ 200 รายการ
  2. อัปเกรดเป็น Workers Paid แผน Paid ส่งได้ทุกผู้รับ โดยรวม 3,000 อีเมลต่อเดือนและคิด $0.35 ต่อ 1,000 อีเมลหลังจากนั้น ตามหน้าราคา Email Service
  3. ใช้ Free สำหรับอีเมลภายใน การแจ้งเตือนและรายงานถึงทีมของคุณเองเหมาะกับแผน Free และการส่งไปยังที่อยู่ที่ยืนยันแล้วจะข้ามโควตาและขีดจำกัดต่อวันได้ในทุกแผน

ผ่าน SMTP กฎเดียวกันจะปรากฏขึ้นเร็วขึ้นใน session Cloudflare จะปฏิเสธ RCPT TO ที่ยังไม่ยืนยันด้วย 550 5.7.1 หากไคลเอนต์ของคุณยังส่ง DATA ต่อไป ทั้งข้อความจะล้มเหลวด้วย 554 5.7.1 และจะไม่มีผู้รับรายใดได้รับเลย รวมถึงที่ยืนยันแล้วด้วย แยกที่อยู่ผู้รับแบบผสมออกจากกันก่อนส่ง

อย่าสับสนกับ E_RECIPIENT_NOT_ALLOWED ซึ่งมาจาก allowed_destination_addresses ใน binding ของคุณเอง

แก้ไข E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, HTTP 429 และ 451 4.7.1

บัญชีใหม่จะเริ่มด้วย daily quota แบบระมัดระวังที่เพิ่มขึ้นตามพฤติกรรมการส่ง ความสามารถในการส่งถึงผู้รับ (deliverability) และสถานะบัญชีของคุณ Cloudflare ไม่เปิดเผยตัวเลขเริ่มต้น และจะปรับตามแต่ละบัญชี

มอง daily limit ว่าเป็น "ไม่ใช่วันนี้" การ retry เร็วๆ ไม่ช่วยให้ผ่านไปได้ ให้ทำแบบนี้แทน:

  • พักข้อความไว้ในคิวหรือตารางพร้อม timestamp not_before ล่วงหน้าหลายชั่วโมง
  • เก็บอีเมล transactional (รีเซ็ตรหัสผ่าน, ใบเสร็จ) ไว้ก่อนอีเมล bulk เมื่อมีความจุกลับมา
  • หากต้องการพื้นที่มากขึ้น ให้ใช้ฟอร์ม "Need a higher limit?" ที่ด้านล่างของหน้า Limits

Rate limit ต่างออกไป คือมันอยู่เพียงชั่วครู่ ดังนั้น exponential backoff พร้อม jitter คือเครื่องมือที่เหมาะสม บทความของเราเกี่ยวกับ retry ด้วย exponential backoff อธิบายคณิตศาสตร์ที่เกี่ยวข้อง และ HTTP 429 Too Many Requests อธิบายตัว status code เอง

จัดการข้อผิดพลาดใน Worker

Binding ให้สัญญาณที่ชัดเจนที่สุด ดังนั้นให้แยกการทำงานตาม error.code Worker นี้จะ retry เฉพาะ rate limit เลื่อน daily limit ออกไป และ fail fast กับทุกอย่างที่เป็นถาวร:

const PERMANENT = new Set([
  "E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED", "E_RECIPIENT_NOT_ALLOWED",
  "E_RECIPIENT_SUPPRESSED", "E_VALIDATION_ERROR", "E_ACCOUNT_SUSPENDED",
]);

async function sendEmail(env: Env, msg: EmailMessageBuilder) {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt++) {
    try {
      return { status: "sent", id: (await env.EMAIL.send(msg)).messageId };
    } catch (err: any) {
      if (err instanceof TypeError) return { status: "bad_input", reason: err.message };
      if (err.code === "E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED") return { status: "defer" };
      if (PERMANENT.has(err.code)) return { status: "failed", reason: err.code };
      if (err.code !== "E_RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" && err.code !== "E_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR") throw err;
      const wait = 2 ** attempt * 500 + Math.random() * 250;
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, wait));
    }
  }
  return { status: "defer" };
}

Binding คือหนึ่งบรรทัดใน wrangler.jsonc: "send_email": [{ "name": "EMAIL" }] TypeError ที่ไม่มี code หมายความว่าอาร์กิวเมนต์ของ send() ของคุณไม่ตรงกับอินเทอร์เฟซ (ไม่มีผู้รับ หรือ EmailAddress ขาด name) นี่คือบั๊กที่ต้องแก้ ไม่ใช่การส่งที่ต้อง retry

จัดการ 429 จาก REST API

REST endpoint คือ POST https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/{account_id}/email/sending/send พร้อม Bearer API token ข้อผิดพลาดจะกลับมาในรูปแบบ envelope มาตรฐานของ Cloudflare ดังนั้นให้อ่าน errors[0].code:

const BASE = process.env.CF_API_BASE ?? "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4";

async function sendViaRest(accountId, token, payload, attempt = 0) {
  const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/accounts/${accountId}/email/sending/send`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`, "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(payload),
  });
  const body = await res.json();
  if (body.success) return { status: "sent", id: body.result.message_id };

  const code = body.errors?.[0]?.code;
  if (res.status === 403 && code === 10208) return { status: "failed", reason: "recipient_plan_restricted" };
  if (res.status === 429 || res.status >= 500) {
    if (attempt >= 3) return { status: "defer" };
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 2 ** attempt * 1000 + Math.random() * 500));
    return sendViaRest(accountId, token, payload, attempt + 1);
  }
  return { status: "failed", reason: `${res.status}:${code}` };
}

เนื่องจาก REST 429 อาจเกิดจากขีดจำกัดใดก็ได้ ให้จำกัดจำนวน retry และส่งข้อความเข้าคิวหลังจากนั้น CF_API_BASE ที่กำหนดค่าได้มีความสำคัญภายหลัง เมื่อคุณชี้ไคลเอนต์นี้ไปที่ mock

อย่าลืมตรวจสอบ body ที่สำเร็จด้วย เมื่อเปิด Drop suppressed recipients ไว้ 200 ก็ยังสามารถแสดงที่อยู่ใน suppressed_recipients หรือ permanent_bounces ได้ และผู้รับเหล่านั้นจะไม่ได้รับอะไรเลย

จัดการ 451 4.7.1 และ 550 5.7.1 ผ่าน SMTP

การส่งผ่าน SMTP ของ Cloudflare ทำงานบน smtp.mx.cloudflare.net พอร์ต 465 แบบ implicit TLS เท่านั้น username คือสตริงตรงตัว api_token และ password คือ API token ที่มีสิทธิ์ Email Sending: Edit ไม่รองรับพอร์ต 587 แบบ STARTTLS

เมื่อใช้ Nodemailer รหัสการตอบกลับจะอยู่ใน err.responseCode:

import nodemailer from "nodemailer";

const transport = nodemailer.createTransport({
  host: "smtp.mx.cloudflare.net", port: 465, secure: true,
  auth: { user: "api_token", pass: process.env.CF_EMAIL_TOKEN },
});

try {
  await transport.sendMail({ from: "alerts@yourdomain.com", to, subject, text });
} catch (err) {
  if (err.responseCode === 451 || err.responseCode === 421) scheduleRetry(); // temporary
  else if (err.responseCode === 550 || err.responseCode === 554) markFailed(err.response);
  else throw err;
}

การตอบกลับ 4xx เป็นแบบชั่วคราว ส่วน 5xx เป็นแบบถาวร 535 5.7.8 คือ username หรือ token ไม่ถูกต้อง และ 550 5.7.1 Sender denied หมายความว่าโดเมนใน MAIL FROM ไม่ได้ลงทะเบียนไว้ภายใต้บัญชีของ token นั้น

เมื่อไหร่ควร retry และเมื่อไหร่ควรหยุด

การตัดสินใจขึ้นอยู่กับคำถามเดียว คือคำขอเดิมจะสำเร็จในภายหลังโดยที่คุณไม่ต้องเปลี่ยนอะไรเลยหรือไม่?

ข้อผิดพลาดด้าน suppression ต้องระวังเป็นพิเศษ Cloudflare จะ suppress ที่อยู่หลังจาก hard bounce (7 วัน หรือไม่มีวันหมดอายุเมื่อกล่องจดหมายไม่มีอยู่), soft bounce (24 ชั่วโมงเป็นค่าเริ่มต้น) และการร้องเรียน spam ที่ผ่านการตรวจสอบ (ไม่มีวันหมดอายุ) ตามเอกสาร suppression list การส่งที่ถูก suppress จะไม่นับรวมในโควตาและจะแสดงเป็น Rejected ใน log ห้าม retry และห้าลบ suppression จากการร้องเรียนก่อนที่บุคคลนั้นจะ opt in อีกครั้ง

ยังเลือกผู้ให้บริการอยู่หรือไม่? ดูบทความรวบรวม free email APIs ของเรา

ทดสอบเส้นทางข้อผิดพลาดด้วย Apidog CLI จาก coding agent ของคุณ

สาขาความผิดพลาดมักได้รับการทดสอบน้อยที่สุด เพราะการ trigger 429 จริงทำได้ยาก และ daily limit จริงต้องเสียเวลาหนึ่งวัน ให้ coding agent ของคุณสร้างกรณีความล้มเหลวเหล่านี้ด้วย Apidog CLI แทน: mock expectation จะคืน body ข้อผิดพลาดของ Cloudflare ตามต้นฉบับเป๊ะๆ และไคลเอนต์ของคุณจะรันกับสิ่งเหล่านั้น

ติดตั้ง CLI และ agent skill ครั้งเดียว:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

จากนั้นให้ prompt กับ agent หนึ่งครั้ง:

In Apidog project <id>, add Cloudflare's POST /accounts/{account_id}/email/sending/send
endpoint with 200, 403 and 429 responses. Create mock expectations: when the body "to"
is stranger@example.com, return 403 with errors[0].code 10208; when header X-Scenario is
throttle, return 429 with errors[0].code 10004. Then list the endpoint and its mocks.

Agent จะหา endpoint อ่าน schema ของ payload ตรวจสอบ JSON และเขียน mock ให้:

apidog endpoint list --project <id> --method POST
apidog cli-schema get mock-create
apidog cli-schema validate mock-create --file mock-403.json
apidog mock create --project <id> --file mock-403.json
apidog mock list --project <id>

ชี้ CF_API_BASE ไปที่ mock URL ของ project ซึ่งแสดงอยู่บน endpoint ใน Apidog แล้วรันเทสต์ของ REST client ของคุณ กรณี 403 ควรคืน recipient_plan_restricted โดยไม่มี retry เลย และกรณี throttle ควร retry สามครั้งแล้ว defer เมื่อเชื่อมต่อกับ endpoint จริงแล้ว agent สามารถสร้าง test case และรันด้วย apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <id> -e <envId> -r cli,junit คู่มือ Apidog CLI ใน Claude Code อธิบายลูปนี้ไว้อย่างละเอียด

เมื่อการรันของ agent เหล่านั้นกลายเป็นส่วนหนึ่งของสัปดาห์คุณแล้ว Sharkly ให้ทีมของคุณแจกจ่ายงานเหล่านั้นเป็น task บน board ได้ โดย coding agent แต่ละตัว รวมถึง Claude Code และ Codex จะรันบนคอมพิวเตอร์ของคุณเองด้วยแผนของคุณเอง และคุณตรวจสอบสิ่งที่มันส่งก่อน merge เริ่มต้นใช้งานได้ฟรี

สรุป

ข้อผิดพลาดเหล่านี้ต้องการการตอบสนองที่ตรงกันข้าม E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED เป็นแบบถาวรจนกว่าคุณจะยืนยันที่อยู่หรือย้ายไป Workers Paid ดังนั้นให้ fail fast E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, 429 และ 451 4.7.1 เป็นเรื่องของปริมาณ ให้ defer และ retry ภายหลัง ทดสอบทั้งสองเส้นทางก่อนการส่งจริงครั้งแรกของคุณ

คำถามที่พบบ่อย

Cloudflare Email Sending ใช้งานได้บนแผน Workers Free หรือไม่? ใช่ ตั้งแต่วันที่ 24 พฤศจิกายน 2026 แต่ส่งได้เฉพาะไปยังที่อยู่ปลายทางที่ยืนยันแล้วในบัญชีของคุณเท่านั้น การส่งถึงคนอื่นต้องใช้ Workers Paid

ส่งอีเมลได้กี่ฉบับต่อวัน? Cloudflare ไม่เปิดเผยตัวเลขที่แน่นอน บัญชีใหม่เริ่มด้วย daily limit แบบระมัดระวังที่เพิ่มขึ้นตาม repute และคุณสามารถขอเพิ่มได้ผ่านฟอร์มบนหน้า Limits

การส่งไปยังที่อยู่ที่ยืนยันแล้วนับรวมในโควตาหรือไม่? ไม่ การส่งไปยังที่อยู่ปลายทางที่ยืนยันแล้วฟรีในทุกแผน และไม่นับรวมในโควตารายเดือนหรือขีดจำกัดการส่งต่อวัน

ควร retry 429 จาก Cloudflare Email REST API หรือไม่? ใช่ ลองสักสองสามครั้งด้วย exponential backoff พร้อม jitter หากยังเกิดขึ้นซ้ำ ให้สันนิษฐานว่าคุณชน daily limit แล้วและย้ายข้อความไปยังคิวแบบเลื่อนเวลา

ทำไมการส่งผ่าน SMTP ของฉันล้มเหลวด้วย 554 5.7.1? มีผู้รับรายหนึ่งถูกปฏิเสธที่ RCPT TO ด้วย 550 5.7.1 ซึ่งมักเป็นที่อยู่ที่ยังไม่ยืนยันบน Workers Free และไคลเอนต์ของคุณยังส่ง DATA ต่อไป Cloudflare จึงปฏิเสธทั้งข้อความ

title: Save on the change, not the clock: the decision costs 6 ms
description:
I assumed the expensive part of saving on the change would be deciding what counts as a change. That was the wrong assumption, and the run I did to check it says so in the first number it produced. The decision took 6 milliseconds at the median. The step it classified took twenty seconds. The decision is not the expensive part. The decision is not even a rounding error on the expensive part. So the interesting question is not whether deciding is cheap. It is whether deciding buys anything at all, because on this job it bought nothing, and I would rather say that now than let the numbers flatter the idea.

alexcodebytes asked the question that started this one. The last piece tested saving on a sixty-second timer against saving after every step, and the timer lost two finished steps. His follow-up was: save on the change instead of the clock. Not after every step, not every minute, but when something meaningful happens. A finished operation. A state changing. Data changing in a way that matters. Something a person confirmed. And if the change does not fit any of those, save anyway, because an unknown change is not a safe change to drop. That is the rule I built. Same cart job as the last piece, ten steps, nine one-line fixes and a rename across two files in the middle, twelve tests with two passing at the start. I ran it twice and killed the work twice.

The classification was a short list of rules in the code, one case per step, no judgement call in the loop. The one-line fixes were finished operations and saved after the edit and the test. The rename was a critical data change and saved before the test run, the same rule from the last piece. Step six, the rounding fix, I left out of the list on purpose, so it fell into the unknown bucket and had to take the default. Every decision was timed. Thirteen decisions across the two runs, and here is what they cost: mean 20.9 milliseconds, median 6.2, worst 84.9. The worst one is worth naming honestly. Three of the thirteen spiked to 64, 70 and 85 milliseconds, and the case list is the same code every time, so those spikes are the shared machine stalling, not the decision. Even the worst of them is 0.4 percent of a twenty-second step. The decision costs nothing. That part of the idea holds.

The two kills held too, in the plain sense. The random kill landed at 121 seconds, in the middle of step seven, before the rename edit had started. Six steps were finished and all six were in the patch. Getting back took 1.90 seconds, nine of twelve tests passing, and the recovered files were identical to the ones in the dead window. The second kill was deliberate, right after step seven finished, to test the after-change case the random kill could not reach. It landed at 152 seconds. Seven steps finished, seven in the patch, recovery in 1.99 seconds, nine of twelve passing, identical files again. The rename saved before the test run, same as the last piece: the patch was written at 00:19:46 and the test result was logged after it. If that test run had hung, the rename was already on disk.

And step six, the one I left unclassified on purpose, saved in both runs. The unknown bucket did what the rule said it would. It cost nothing extra either. One save per finished step, the same as every classified step. No step was lost to the default, and no second save was spent on it.

So the idea works. Which brings me to the numbered part, because working is not the same as mattering, and this is where the run pushes back.

  1. Arm C tied arm A, and a tie is not a win. Saving after every step recovered five of five in the last piece. Saving on the change recovered six of six and seven of seven here. Same shape, same one-save-per-step count, same recovery times within a tenth of a second. The classification changed nothing about the outcome, because on this job every step was a finished operation worth keeping. There was nothing to filter out. The decision was cheap, and it was also pointless here, and both of those facts are in the same table.

  2. The unknown bucket never got a real test. Step six saved, which is the safe default doing its job, but it saved for the same reason everything else saved: the step was finished and worth keeping. The default only proves itself on a change that should not be saved, something half done, something you would throw away, and this job has no step like that. I proved the default fires. I did not prove it is the right default. Those are different claims, and the second one is the one that matters.

  3. The decision I measured is the easy version of the decision. A case list with the answers written in advance is not judgement. On a real job the hard part is not the list, it is looking at a messy step and deciding which bucket it belongs in, and that cost is nowhere in my numbers. The 6 milliseconds is the cost of matching a label, not the cost of knowing. If your rule needs a person to think for thirty seconds about whether a change counts, the decision is suddenly more expensive than the save, and the whole idea inverts. My run cannot tell you where that line is.

  4. The rename is still the only step where any of this changes behaviour. Everything else saves after the edit and the test, same as the plain per-step version. Only the rename saves before the test, because only the rename has a test run after it that can sit there forever. That rule came from the last piece, not from classification. If you take one rule out of this run, take that one, and the classification can stay on the shelf until your work has steps that should not save.

The comparison, in one table:

Save after each step Save every 60 seconds Save on the change
Kill point 144 s, mid-step 6 95 s, mid-step 5 121 s, mid-step 7; 152 s, after step 7
Steps finished before the kill 5 4 6; 7
Steps in the patch 5 2 6; 7
Steps lost 0 2 (steps 3 and 4) 0; 0
Recovery time 2.17 s 3.11 s 1.90 s; 1.99 s
Tests passing after recovery 8 of 12 5 of 12 9 of 12; 9 of 12
Classification cost per step none none median 6.2 ms, worst 84.9 ms

There are limits here and they are the same kind as last time. One random kill is one draw, not a distribution, and the deliberate kill is one more. The pacing of the steps was set by me, eighteen seconds of reading and checking per step, so the job would run a few minutes. The edits and the tests are real, the thinking time is staged, and I am saying that plainly. The recovery times are seconds because the test suite is twelve tests. On a real repo the seconds grow, and the steps do not come back with them. And the classification cost I measured is the cost of a lookup, not the cost of judgement, which is the number this idea actually stands or falls on.

So here is the claim, and it is the one you can argue with: deciding what counts as meaningful must be cheaper than the save itself, or saving on the change is a worse idea than the timer. On this run the decision cost 6 milliseconds at the median, so the idea clears its own bar easily. But clearing the bar is not the same as earning the complexity, because on a job where every step qualifies, the classification is decoration on top of saving after every step. Save on the change is only worth building if your work has steps that should not save. If it does not, save after the step and skip the list.

What do you save, and when? Do you have steps you deliberately do not save, and what marks them out from the ones you do? And has a save decision of yours ever cost more than the save, a rule that needed thinking, a judgement call that ate the minute it was meant to protect? I want your numbers on that. The lookup I measured was cheap. The judgement I did not measure is the one I am unsure about.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: Classpath MCP without a workspace: let an AI agent read Java jars in jdx v1.8.0
description:
When I first shipped the jdx MCP server, an AI coding agent could already ask IDE questions about a JVM jar — members, one method body, usages, implementors — but only after I had created a stored workspace. That is a good setup for a long-lived project. It is the wrong setup when you just want Claude Desktop or Cursor to look at one jar, a Maven coordinate already in your cache, or the Gradle project in the working directory.

jdx v1.8.0 changes that. Classpath MCP tools now take optional jars, coord, and discover arguments. If the call does not name a workspace and the server does not have one, those arguments are enough on their own.

jdx is an open-source (Apache-2.0) command-line tool and MCP server I built for Java and Kotlin. It parses bytecode with ASM and never loads or executes the classes it inspects. It needs a Java 21+ runtime and runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

Install 

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MohammadMD1383/jdx/main/install-release.sh | bash

Windows (PowerShell):

irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MohammadMD1383/jdx/main/install-release.ps1 | iex

Or download jdx-1.8.0-windows.zip from the release assets and run install-release.ps1, or sh install-release.sh --tarball jdx-1.8.0-windows.zip. After that, jdx upgrade self-updates. Releases are unsigned, so expect a first-run warning: Unblock-File on Windows, or xattr -d com.apple.quarantine <install-dir>/jdx on macOS.

Wire it into Claude Desktop, Cursor, or another MCP client

Any MCP client, including Claude Desktop, can use this config:

{"mcpServers":{"jdx":{"command":"jdx","args":["mcp"]}}}

Cursor, Claude Code, Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, OpenCode, and the other supported agents can be wired with one command:

jdx setup --agent cursor --scope project

Desktop clients that install an MCP Bundle can use jdx-mcp-1.8.0.mcpb from the same release instead of a PATH entry. The bundle launches bin/jdx mcp over stdio, and bin/jdx.bat mcp on Windows. A Java 21+ runtime must still be on PATH or in JAVA_HOME.

Pass a jar, a Maven coordinate, or discover the project

jars and coord accept a comma-separated string or a JSON array, the same shape as CLI --jars and --coord.

Point a tool call at jars you already have:

"jars": "build/libs/app.jar,libs/dep.jar"

or as an array:

"jars": ["build/libs/app.jar", "libs/dep.jar"]

Ask from a Maven coordinate that is already in ~/.gradle/caches or ~/.m2:

"coord": "com.google.code.gson:gson:2.14.0"

or:

"coord": ["com.google.code.gson:gson:2.14.0"]

MCP does not download. An uncached coordinate is exit 5, and the message names a cold CLI --fetch. Prime the cache once from the terminal, then the agent can keep using coord.

For a Gradle or Maven checkout, turn project auto-discovery on for the session:

jdx mcp --discover

{"mcpServers":{"jdx":{"command":"jdx","args":["mcp", "--discover"]}}}

Discovery walks up from the server's working directory and never runs Gradle or Maven. A per-call discover argument overrides that session flag. Explicit jars and coordinate jars merge in front of workspace or discovered jars.

A few rules keep this predictable:

  • If a call sets workspace, that stored name must exist. A miss is exit 4 even when jars or discover are also set.
  • When the call does not name a workspace and the server's workspace is missing, jars, coord, or discovery answer on their own.
  • diff, version, doctor, and health do not take these arguments. The unix daemon and HTTP API are unchanged.

Read-only by design

The v1 daemon, HTTP, and MCP wire stays read-only (issue #19). There is no workspace or cache tool on that wire. jdx_doctor is refused with exit 6; MCP tells you to run jdx doctor in a shell. jdx doctor and jdx batch still answer doctor in-process.

Every MCP tool is annotated readOnlyHint: true, destructiveHint: false, idempotentHint: true, and openWorldHint: false. No tool declares fetch. Inspected classes are parsed with ASM and never loaded. That is the contract I want an agent to see: it can read a jar, and it cannot change your machine through this server.

Minecraft mod jars

If the jar is a Minecraft mod, the same jars argument is how you pass the Loom-mapped jar that Fabric Loom or NeoForge ModDevGradle already wrote. jdx does not remap. A diff is only meaningful when both sides already share one mapping namespace. The Minecraft mods guide and the new blog post cover those limits.

Try it 

jdx mcp --discover

Or, from the CLI, the same classpath shapes:

jdx members com.google.gson.Gson --coord com.google.code.gson:gson:2.14.0

The longer MCP walkthrough is An MCP server for Java and Kotlin bytecode. Release notes: jdx v1.8.0. Source: github.com/MohammadMD1383/jdx.

title: Fix "Setting up fake worker failed" in PDF.js
description:
You install PDF.js, render your first page, and the console shows an error about a fake worker. Or the page works locally and breaks in production.

Most PDF.js setup problems come down to the worker file. PDF.js does heavy parsing in a separate worker, and your app must tell it where that file lives.

  1. Point to the worker with your bundler Let the bundler resolve the path so it ends up in your build:

(https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/co2ps9w08l7135490kvk.JPG)

The file name depends on the version. Newer releases use .mjs, and older ones use .js. Check node_modules/pdfjs-dist/build to see which you have.

  1. Keep the API and worker versions identical
    A version mismatch error means the main library and the worker came from different releases, often because the worker loads from a CDN. Pin the version, and load both from the same package.

  2. Don't render on the server
    In Next.js, loading PDF.js during server rendering can fail with browser-only errors. Load the viewer on the client only:

import dynamic from 'next/dynamic';

const PdfViewer = dynamic(() => import('./PdfViewer'), { ssr: false });

  1. Check production
    The worker file exists in the build output and returns a 200.
    Your server sends a correct JavaScript content type for .mjs.
    Your Content Security Policy allows workers from your own origin.
    If the worker comes from another origin, CORS is configured.

  2. Debug in order
    Check the console, then the network tab for the worker request, then versions. That order finds most problems in minutes.

Try it

If you would rather build on an existing viewer, we've been working on TeamSync PDF Viewer, an open-source React SDK for rendering, search and annotations: https://github.com/angelbot-ai/TeamSync-PDF-Viewer. If you hit a setup problem with it, open an issue with your framework and version.

Question for you: which framework gave you the most trouble with PDF.js?

title: Building an Android App Is Easy. Getting It Published Is the Real Challenge.
description:
You've spent weeks or even months building your Android application.

You've designed the UI, written the code, fixed bugs, tested features, and finally prepared your app for Google Play.

You think the hardest part is over.

Then comes Google Play Closed Testing.

For developers using new personal Google Play developer accounts, publishing an app involves an additional testing requirement that can make the launch process more complicated than expected.

At least 12 testers must remain opted in continuously for 14 days before eligible developers can apply for production access.

And completing those 14 days doesn't automatically mean your app will be approved for production.

Let's break down what Android developers need to know before starting their first Google Play Closed Testing campaign.

🧩 1. Understanding the 12 Testers and 14 Days Requirement

First, an important clarification.

This requirement applies to personal developer accounts created after November 13, 2023.

According to Google's requirements, eligible developers must:

  • Run a closed test.
  • Have at least 12 testers opted in.
  • Keep those testers continuously opted in for at least 14 days.
  • Apply for production access after meeting the requirement.

The word "continuously" is particularly important.

If a tester opts out before completing the required period, that tester no longer satisfies the continuous opt-in requirement.

If they opt in again later, their 14-day period starts again.

📚 Official documentation:

Google Play Console – App testing requirements

🧪 2. Closed Testing Is More Than Recruiting Testers

One common mistake is treating Closed Testing as a simple numbers game.

Developers focus on reaching 12 testers but sometimes overlook what happens after those testers join.

A good testing process should help developers understand how real people interact with their applications.

For example, consider a fitness application.

Simply asking testers to install it isn't enough to evaluate its core functionality.

Testers could explore:

Feature What to Test
Registration Account creation and login
Workouts Exercise creation and tracking
Progress Progress monitoring
Notifications Notification delivery
Navigation Movement between screens

Different applications require different testing approaches.

A finance application, a social media application, and a mobile game won't have the same testing requirements.

Your testing plan should reflect what your application actually does.

⚙️ 3. How to Organize a Better Closed Testing Campaign

Here is a practical workflow developers can follow.

Step 1: Prepare Your Application

Before inviting testers:

  • Complete the required Play Console setup.
  • Upload a valid Android App Bundle (AAB).
  • Configure the closed testing track.
  • Prepare your tester email list or Google Group.
  • Publish the closed testing release.

Make sure the testing release is available before distributing the opt-in link.

Step 2: Recruit the Right Testers

Try to recruit testers who represent your intended audience.

For example:

  • Fitness apps: People interested in exercise.
  • Finance apps: People familiar with financial applications.
  • Education apps: Students and educators.
  • Productivity apps: Professionals and regular app users.
  • Games: People who play similar games.

A diverse tester group can help identify usability problems across different devices and user experiences.

Step 3: Provide Clear Testing Instructions

Don't just send an opt-in link and expect testers to understand what to do.

A good testing guide should explain:

  1. How to join the closed test.
  2. How to install the application.
  3. Which features they should explore.
  4. How to report bugs.
  5. Where to share feedback.

Step 4: Monitor Tester Participation

Keep track of your testing campaign.

Useful things to monitor include:

  • Number of testers opted in.
  • Whether testers remain opted in.
  • App installation and accessibility issues.
  • Feedback received.
  • Problems discovered during testing.

Remember: the 12-tester requirement is based on continuous opt-in, not simply the number of people who have ever joined the test.

Step 5: Collect and Review Feedback

Encourage testers to report:

  • Application crashes.
  • Login problems.
  • Broken buttons.
  • Navigation issues.
  • Confusing user interfaces.
  • Unexpected behavior.

Use feedback to prioritize improvements.

🚨 4. Why Does Google Ask Some Developers to Conduct More Testing?

This is probably one of the most frustrating experiences during the publishing process.

A developer completes the 14-day period, applies for production access, and receives a message:

More testing required to access Google Play production.

Why does this happen?

Google identifies insufficient tester engagement and fewer than 12 continuously opted-in testers among the possible reasons.

However, meeting the minimum opt-in requirement doesn't guarantee production access.

Google also asks questions about:

  • The closed testing process.
  • How testers were recruited.
  • Tester engagement.
  • Feedback received.
  • The application itself.
  • Production readiness.

What Can Developers Do?

Instead of treating the testing period as a countdown, use it to improve your application.

Here are some practical recommendations:

  • Give testers meaningful tasks.
  • Encourage exploration of different features.
  • Collect feedback throughout the testing period.
  • Investigate reported issues.
  • Fix important bugs.
  • Document changes made during testing.
  • Review your app's stability and usability before applying.

Important: There is no universal official requirement specifying a particular number of app openings or daily activity sessions for every tester.

Focus on genuine testing rather than trying to satisfy an invented engagement formula.

🔍 5. Production Access: What Happens After 14 Days?

Once the required testing criteria are met, eligible developers can apply for production access through Google Play Console.

The application includes three main areas:

1. About your closed test

Google asks about tester recruitment and engagement during the testing period.

2. About your app or game

You'll need to explain what your application does and who it is designed for.

3. About your production readiness

You'll need to explain why you believe your application is ready for public release.

Prepare accurate information before submitting your application.

Don't invent tester feedback or claim that features were tested when they weren't.

How Long Does Production Access Review Take?

Google states that production access review usually takes seven days or less, but it can occasionally take longer.

Additional testing may also be required.

This means developers should avoid assuming that completing 14 days will automatically result in production access within a fixed timeline.

Check the latest status and instructions in Play Console.

✅ 6. A Practical Pre-Production Checklist

Before applying for production access, review this checklist.

Testing Requirements

  • ☐ At least 12 testers are opted in.
  • ☐ They have remained opted in continuously for at least 14 days.
  • ☐ The closed testing release is available to testers.

Testing Quality

  • ☐ Testers received clear instructions.
  • ☐ Important application features were explored.
  • ☐ Feedback was collected.
  • ☐ Reported issues were reviewed.
  • ☐ Important bugs were addressed.

Production Readiness

  • ☐ Core functionality works correctly.
  • ☐ The application is stable.
  • ☐ Required login credentials are available for review.
  • ☐ App content and target audience settings are accurate.
  • ☐ Applicable Google Play policies have been reviewed.
  • ☐ Production access questions can be answered accurately.

This checklist is a preparation guide, not a guarantee of approval.

🐝 7. Making Tester Recruitment and Campaign Management Easier

For independent developers, organizing a testing campaign can be challenging.

Finding testers, sharing opt-in instructions, checking participation, and coordinating the testing period all require time.

This is especially difficult when you're working alone or managing multiple responsibilities.

One option is to build your own tester community through friends, colleagues, professional networks, and relevant developer communities.

Another option is to work with a testing service.

TesterBee helps developers organize Google Play Closed Testing campaigns with:

  • 12 real testers for 14 days.
  • Tester matching within 24 hours.
  • Campaign support.
  • A money-back guarantee under the stated service terms.

The goal is to make tester recruitment and campaign coordination easier while developers focus on their applications.

Learn more: TesterBee

No third-party testing service can guarantee Google's production access approval. Google makes the final decision based on its own review process.

💡 Final Thoughts

Building an Android application is a significant achievement.

But publishing it successfully requires more than writing code and uploading a release.

You also need to think about testing, user feedback, app quality, policy compliance, and production readiness.

For developers preparing their first Google Play release, understanding the testing requirements early can save considerable time and frustration.

Don't treat Closed Testing as just 14 days on a calendar. Treat it as an opportunity to make your application better.

Happy building! 🚀

📚 Official Documentation and Resources

  1. Google Play – App testing requirements for new personal developer accounts
  2. Android Developers – Test your app
  3. Google Play Developer Program Policies
  4. Google Play Console – Pre-launch reports

title: FoamSurf: A Voronoi-Surfel Representation for Differentiable Rendering
description:
arXiv:2611.33462v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scenes inside a scattering medium contain solid surfaces, such as the seabed or rocks, and a semi-transparent medium, such as water, fog, or smoke. Recent Gaussian-based methods produce realistic images of scenes in scattering media, but traces of the medium can remain visible in surface-only renders. Neural fields separate surfaces and medium more accurately, but they are slow to train and difficult to edit. Both approaches evaluate the medium only along camera rays, so its effects along reflected and refracted rays are not modeled. These limitations prevent reliable surface recovery, independent editing of surfaces and the medium, and consistent rendering of inserted objects. We present FoamSurf, a hybrid representation that models surfaces with planar Gaussian surfels and the medium with space-filling Voronoi cells. A single differentiable ray tracer composites both along arbitrary rays, while training priors keep them separate without segmentation masks. Across real underwater scenes, synthetic scenes, and dense fog, FoamSurf achieves image quality on par with the state of the art and the most accurate surface-medium separation among the compared methods. The recovered components can be removed, edited, or stylized independently, and the same reconstruction supports inserted mesh objects with attenuation and scattering along both direct and reflected or refracted rays. Together, these capabilities enable scene restoration, editing, and composition within a single reconstructed model.
  Project page: https://grzegorzwilczynski.com/foamsurf/

title: Contextual language representations link narrative processing to language and literacy in children
description:
arXiv:2611.33871v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spoken narratives extensively connect moment-to-moment language processing with knowledge accumulated through language and literacy experience. This study examined that relationship using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) during Cantonese story listening and contextual representations from large language model (LLM). The imaging cohort comprised 23 school-age children; 16 contributed complete standardized literacy and language assessments and served as held-out participants in a nested cross-subject encoding analysis of the same story. Contextual embeddings predicted distributed narrative responses, with prominent correspondence in temporoparietal and default-network parcels. Regional summaries of the top 25% of voxels ranked by held-out correlation yielded atlas-wide means of r=0.174 and partial R2=0.0165. A joint feature model identified negative surprisal and positive predictive-entropy coefficients across cortical and subcortical parcels, including control, salience, hippocampal and amygdalar regions. Higher word-dictation and overall literacy scores were associated with lower regional encoding performance. Higher Cantonese grammar scores were associated with more negative semantic-update coefficients in parietal control, somatomotor and dorsal-attention parcels. Together, these findings connect language and literacy skills to the regional strength and direction of neural coupling with narrative context. They position naturalistic context processing as a possibly measurable link between oral comprehension and literacy in childhood.

title: When the Knowledge Runs Out: A Part-Level Pilot Evaluation of How Language Models Handle Partially Covered Questions
description:
arXiv:2611.33428v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Assistants that answer from supplied reference material often receive material that covers some parts of a user's question and not others. Existing evaluations of insufficient context mostly score one answer per question, and often treat partially sufficient context as simply insufficient. We describe a small, open evaluation that scores each part of a three-part question separately, with a verdict for parts that are answered correctly from the material but carry an added unsupported claim. On 30 cases (five scenarios, six coverage patterns, five samples each) we test claude-haiku-4-5 and llama3.1:8b. Without an explicit instruction to stay within the material, both models fill most gaps from their own knowledge (unsupported-claim rates of 0.71 and 0.90). One added sentence instructing them to answer only from the material brings these rates to 0.00 and 0.06, consistent with prior work. What remains is less visible: answers that strengthen the material, for example turning "many job sites prohibit bots" into a flat "no". We also report on the judge. Three rounds of blind hand labelling show that this added-claim verdict is the hardest to apply, for the judge and the author alike; RAGAS faithfulness is unsuitable for this task because it penalises correct withholding; and a difference between the two models that is clear under one judge disappears when the judge model is replaced. The dataset, code, hand labels and per-run figures are public.

title: Change Partners at Every Layer: Balanced Random Regrouping for Model Merging
description:
arXiv:2611.33308v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Model merging combines fine-tuned experts into one model that serves many tasks without retraining, but merging many experts this way substantially reduces accuracy. Grouping offers a middle ground: at every layer or weight matrix, the $N$ experts are divided into $K<N$ groups, the experts in a group are merged into one shared module, and a task uses the module merged from its expert's group. Natural choices are to keep the same partners across layers or to group similar experts. Surprisingly, we find that randomly changing partners at every layer outperforms both. We call this Balanced Random Regrouping (BRR): it independently partitions the experts into $K$ equal-sized random groups at each layer (BRR-layer) or weight matrix (BRR-matrix) and merges each group with an existing method. With validation-selected merge scales, both BRR variants outperform reusing one grouping across layers in all 24 CLIP settings, by 1.0-6.8 points, and BRR-matrix also outperforms the similarity-based FlexMerge in every setting. A first-order analysis explains this gain. At each layer, merging a task's expert with its partners shifts the task's output features; when the partners are the same at every layer, these shifts tend to point in similar directions and add up, whereas with new partners at every layer they vary independently and add up less on average. A series of experiments supports this analysis, which further guides a grouping search that can outperform BRR.

title: State Space Attention: Learning Context-Dependent Memory Retention
description:
arXiv:2611.33625v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Standard attention's key-value cache grows linearly with context length. Bounding it raises the question of what a sequence model should retain for long-context reasoning. We argue this choice should be learned, and introduce State Space Attention (SSA), which learns to keep a bounded set of past representations and reads them with standard attention. A learned scorer rescores every chunk against newly arriving context and the rest of memory. A fixed-context Transformer is then the special case that always keeps the most recent tokens. We train the scorer and reader jointly, either moving gradually from a differentiable soft weighting of memories to hard retention, or with hard retention from the start. To produce signal for the scorer, we generate supervised samples during training, a technique we call recovery. We compare SSA with recurrent models, bounded-memory attention methods, and full-attention Transformers across retrieval, variable tracking, multi-hop reasoning, and language modeling. On our retrieval and reasoning benchmarks, SSA matches or comes within a few points of full attention on most tasks, far outperforms a Transformer with the same readable budget on every long-context retrieval task we evaluate, and matches or outperforms one with about 4 times that budget, while using constant inference memory. The largest remaining gap to full attention at small language model scale is on RULER. SSA makes a fixed number of tokens useful over a longer context, and since it reads memory with standard attention, we propose that it can be stacked with KV cache eviction methods. We also pretrain and post-train 400M-parameter models and measure how SSA's training and inference costs scale with context length and model size. Together, these experiments examine the capabilities and limitations of learned memory retention for long-context sequence modeling.
