title: E2SIM: Long-Horizon Simulation of Everyday Human Behavior with Evolving States
description:
arXiv:2611.31641v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents are increasingly expected to support users over long periods, across work, and daily life. This requires modeling not only who users are, but also how their goals, interests, activities, and interactions evolve over time. A challenge in longitudinal user simulation is maintaining consistency between these evolving states and the consequences of actions in a shared environment. We introduce E2SIM, a longitudinal user simulation framework that jointly models evolving actor states and a dynamic shared environment. E2SIM connects actor-state updates with shared-world changes through a feedback loop linking immediate actions, delayed outcomes, and actor-specific observations across work and life. This allows the consequences of earlier actions to shape later behavior, while preserving differences in what each actor knows. We further propose a suite of longitudinal trajectory diagnostics, measuring dynamic consistency, coherent event progression and collaboration, and non-degenerate trajectory development rather than static consistency alone. In one 60-day simulation, E2SIM produced more extracted event threads judged meaningful by our evaluator and fewer near-duplicate actions than four direct-generation baselines. The framework and evaluation methods provide a basis for studying longitudinal user simulation, with potential applications in training and evaluating AI agents that assist users over extended periods.

title: Sparse Adaptation for In-Context Learning on Data Streams
description:
arXiv:2611.33325v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) generates massive data streams, making edge computing essential for low-latency applications and 5G networks. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) enable adaptation through in-context examples rather than parameter updates, but evolving streams challenge context relevance and computational efficiency. This work introduces SAIL, a framework for sparse adaptation of TFMs that reuses the model's key--value cache between adaptation events. SAIL reconstructs its support set only when drifts in stream structure indicate potential context inadequacy, while the structural representation itself is updated by changes in predictive performance. SAIL combines prequential error monitoring with online, class-specific micro-clustering to detect changes in cluster mass, class separability, and feature-space coverage. Upon adaptation, a context budget is allocated proportionally to class mass, and the most recently updated micro-clusters provide representative observations for refitting. This limits context redundancy and computational cost while preserving recent structural information.

title: Building and Adapting Next.js Templates with Lovable: A Practical Guide
description:
AI-assisted coding environments have transformed how developers prototype landing pages and web applications. Lovable allows developers to describe complex interfaces in plain English, generating functional, component-driven layouts in seconds. However, if your target production stack is Next.js, bridging the gap between browser-based AI generation and the Next.js App Router requires deliberate architecture and prompt planning.

In this guide, we will walk through how to prompt Lovable to generate Next.js-ready structures, handle client versus server boundaries, and cleanly export templates into an existing Next.js codebase.

1. Structuring Prompts for Next.js Architecture

By default, browser-based AI editors often produce single-page React applications bundled with Vite or similar setups. If you plan to drop the generated code into a Next.js App Router project, your prompts must explicitly specify architectural conventions up front.

When writing a prompt for Lovable to produce a template, include these constraints:

  • Client vs. Server Components: Specify that interactive widgets (such as dropdowns, carousels, or dark-mode toggles) should include the 'use client'; directive at the top of their respective component files.
  • Routing Conventions: Direct the model to isolate page shells from reusable UI widgets so that screens easily map to app/page.tsx or app/(routes)/[slug]/page.tsx.
  • Styling Standards: Request standard Tailwind CSS classes instead of CSS-in-JS or custom global stylesheets, which makes importing components into Next.js straightforward.
  • Asset Handling: Ask for standard next/image patterns or placeholders that match Next.js image optimization conventions rather than raw HTML <img> tags.

Example Scaffold Prompt 

Create a modern SaaS landing page template using TypeScript and Tailwind CSS.
Structure the code modularly so it fits the Next.js App Router:
- Separate the layout into modular sections: Navbar, HeroSection, FeatureGrid, PricingTable, and Footer.
- Add 'use client'; to any component requiring state, such as the mobile navigation drawer and interactive pricing toggle.
- Use Lucide icons and avoid external runtime animation libraries that require Node-specific packages.
- Ensure all image tags follow standard Next.js Image component attributes (src, alt, width, height).

2. Navigating Common Conversion Pitfalls

Even when the generated code looks complete, moving templates from an AI workspace into Next.js can trigger common build errors. Watching for these early will save significant debugging time:

Directive Missing on Interactive Elements

Next.js App Router defaults all files in the app/ directory to React Server Components. If Lovable generates hooks like useState, useEffect, or custom hooks inside a component without 'use client';, Next.js will throw a build failure. Review each generated file that imports React hooks and confirm the directive is placed at line 1.

Navigation Hooks

AI builders often default to react-router-dom methods (like useNavigate or Link from react-router-dom). In Next.js, replace these imports with:

import Link from 'next/link';
import { useRouter } from 'next/navigation';

Window and Document Access

Code that accesses window.innerWidth or document.cookie during the initial render will fail during Next.js server-side rendering (SSR). Wrap browser-only evaluations inside useEffect blocks or guard them with checks such as typeof window !== 'undefined'.

3. Workflow: Exporting Lovable Output into Next.js

Once you have generated your interface within Lovable, use the following step-by-step workflow to integrate it cleanly into your project.

Step 1: Initialize Your Target Next.js Project

If you do not already have a project, create one using the official starter:

npx create-next-app@latest my-app --typescript --tailwind --app --eslint

Step 2: Establish the Component Hierarchy

Organize your repository to mirror standard Next.js patterns:

my-app/
├── app/
│   ├── layout.tsx
│   └── page.tsx
├── components/
│   ├── sections/
│   │   ├── hero.tsx
│   │   ├── features.tsx
│   │   └── pricing.tsx
│   └── ui/
│       ├── button.tsx
│       └── card.tsx
└── lib/
    └── utils.ts

Developers who prefer starting with ready-to-use component foundations can explore typescript templates engineered for modern AI tools like Lovable and Cursor, which provide clean React code tailored for fast imports.

Step 3: Copy UI Primitives and Utility Helpers

Most modern templates rely on small utility functions like cn() (combining clsx and tailwind-merge). Ensure these dependencies are installed:

npm install clsx tailwind-merge lucide-react

Add lib/utils.ts:

import { type ClassValue, clsx } from "clsx";
import { twMerge } from "tailwind-merge";

export function cn(...inputs: ClassValue[]) {
  return twMerge(clsx(inputs));
}

Step 4: Assemble the Landing Page

Finally, import your modular sections into app/page.tsx:

import { HeroSection } from '@/components/sections/hero';
import { FeatureGrid } from '@/components/sections/features';
import { PricingTable } from '@/components/sections/pricing';
import { Footer } from '@/components/sections/footer';

export default function HomePage() {
  return (
    <main className="flex min-h-screen flex-col bg-slate-950 text-slate-50">
      <HeroSection />
      <FeatureGrid />
      <PricingTable />
      <Footer />
    </main>
  );
}

4. Checklist for Production Readiness

Before shipping your newly integrated template to production, run through this quick checklist:

  • [ ] Type Safety: Run npx tsc --noEmit to ensure TypeScript interfaces and component props contain no implicit any errors.
  • [ ] Metadata: Add dynamic or static metadata objects in layout.tsx or page.tsx using Next.js Metadata types for SEO and OpenGraph cards.
  • [ ] Image Optimization: Replace static paths with Next.js <Image /> tags specifying explicit widths, heights, or fill with appropriate aspect ratios.
  • [ ] Linting & Formatting: Execute npm run lint to catch broken links, unescaped entities, or unhandled hooks before building.

Disclosure: published by the official PromptedSite account (promptedsite.com); drafted with AI assistance.

title: Your API Works. Your Tests Pass. So Why Did the Mobile App Break?
description:
Imagine this.

It's Friday afternoon. Your backend team has just deployed a small API update. Nothing major. Just a simple field rename.

The developer changes:

{
  "user_name": "John"
}

to:

{
  "username": "John"
}

All unit tests pass. The CI pipeline is green. The deployment is successful.

Then your support channel starts exploding.

📱 The mobile app can't display user profiles.

💻 The frontend team reports unexpected errors.

🚨 The QA team discovers that an API response has changed.

And suddenly, what looked like a harmless code improvement becomes a production incident.

The real problem? Nobody checked whether the API provider and its consumers still agreed on the contract.

This is exactly the problem API Contract Testing is designed to solve.

Let's explore why it matters, how it works, and how development teams can prevent these surprises before they reach production.

First, What Exactly Is an API Contract?

Think of an API contract as an agreement between two teams.

One team builds an API (the provider).

Another team consumes that API (the consumer).

The agreement defines:

  • Which endpoints are available.
  • What request parameters are expected.
  • Which fields must be included in responses.
  • What data types are supported.
  • Which HTTP status codes can be returned.
  • How errors should be structured.

For example, imagine your order service returns:

{
  "id": "ORD-101",
  "status": "shipped",
  "total": 499.99
}

Your mobile application expects these three fields.

If a developer removes total, changes its type, or renames status, the mobile application might stop working.

An API contract makes these expectations explicit and machine-readable.

Common contract formats include:

  • OpenAPI for REST APIs.
  • Pact files for consumer-driven contracts.
  • GraphQL SDL for GraphQL APIs.
  • WSDL and XSD for SOAP services.
  • AsyncAPI for event-driven architectures.

Why Traditional Testing Sometimes Misses the Problem

Here's something interesting.

Your application can have:

  • 100% passing unit tests.
  • Successful integration tests.
  • A green deployment pipeline.

And still break its consumers.

Why?

Because different testing approaches answer different questions.

Testing approach What does it verify?
Unit Testing Does an individual function work?
Functional API Testing Does the API behave correctly?
Integration Testing Do connected components work together?
Contract Testing Do the provider and consumer still agree?
End-to-End Testing Does the complete user journey work?

Contract testing focuses on the communication boundary between services.

It doesn't replace functional or integration testing. It complements them.

And because contract checks can run independently of a full production-like environment, they provide fast feedback during development.

Let's See API Contract Testing in Action

Consider an e-commerce application.

It has:

  • An Order Service.
  • A Payment Service.
  • A Customer Service.
  • A Mobile Application.

The mobile application calls:

GET /orders/123

The backend promises to return:

{
  "id": "123",
  "status": "paid",
  "total": 499.99
}

Let's define a simplified OpenAPI response contract:

paths:
  /orders/{id}:
    get:
      responses:
        "200":
          description: Order found
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                required:
                  - id
                  - status
                  - total
                properties:
                  id:
                    type: string
                  status:
                    type: string
                    enum:
                      - pending
                      - paid
                      - shipped
                      - cancelled
                  total:
                    type: number
                    minimum: 0

Now imagine a developer changes the response:

{
  "id": "123",
  "status": "paid",
  "amount": 499.99
}

The total field has been renamed to amount.

The contract test detects that the required total property is missing.

Instead of discovering the problem after deployment, the team gets an immediate failure in the pull request.

That's the real value of contract testing: catching breaking changes before customers experience them.

Three Approaches to API Contract Testing

Not every application needs the same contract testing strategy.

Here are three commonly used approaches.

  1. Schema-First Contract Testing

In this approach, the API specification is the source of truth.

The provider defines its API contract using OpenAPI.

Automated tests validate whether actual API requests and responses follow that specification.

OpenAPI Specification
        ↓
Automated Contract Tests
        ↓
API Provider
        ↓
Validate Response
        ↓
   Pass / Fail

Best for:

  • Teams maintaining OpenAPI specifications.
  • Public APIs.
  • APIs with multiple unknown consumers.
  • Teams adopting spec-first development.

Popular tools include Schemathesis, Dredd, Specmatic, and other OpenAPI-based testing platforms.

  1. Consumer-Driven Contract Testing

Sometimes, the provider doesn't know exactly what every consumer needs.

This is where consumer-driven contract testing becomes useful.

Each consumer defines its expectations, and the provider verifies that it can satisfy them.

For example:

The mobile app needs id, status, and total.

The reporting service needs id and total.

Both consumers publish their expectations through contracts.

The provider verifies those expectations before releasing changes.

One popular tool for this approach is Pact.

Best for:

  • Microservices architectures.
  • Independently deployed services.
  • Multiple teams consuming the same API.
  • Applications with complex service dependencies.
  1. Snapshot-Based Contract Testing

This approach captures an API response and compares future responses against the saved version.

For example:

First execution:

{
  "id": 101,
  "name": "John"
}

Later execution:

{
  "id": 101,
  "username": "John"
}

The snapshot comparison detects the difference.

Snapshots are easy to introduce, but they can be sensitive to harmless changes. They should complement explicit contracts rather than replace them.

How to Integrate API Contract Testing into CI/CD

Contract testing becomes much more powerful when it runs automatically.

Imagine the following workflow:

Step 1: Developer Creates a Pull Request

A developer submits changes to an API.

Step 2: Validate the API Specification

Check whether the OpenAPI specification is valid and follows your team's standards.

Step 3: Run Contract Tests

Validate API responses against the published contract. For consumer-driven testing, verify the relevant consumer expectations.

Step 4: Detect Breaking Changes

Compare the updated API specification with the previous version.

Examples of potentially breaking changes:

  • Removing a required response field.
  • Renaming an existing field.
  • Changing a field's data type.
  • Removing a documented response code.
  • Adding a new required request parameter.

Step 5: Apply Quality Gates

If a breaking change is detected, fail the pipeline unless the change has been explicitly reviewed and approved as part of a versioning or migration strategy.

Step 6: Merge and Release

Only approved changes move forward.

The result?

Fewer unexpected API compatibility issues and faster feedback for development teams.

Tools That Make API Contract Testing Easier

Here are some tools worth exploring:

Tool Main purpose
Pact Consumer-driven contract testing
Schemathesis Automated tests from OpenAPI
Specmatic Spec-driven contract testing
Dredd Validating APIs against API descriptions
Spectral OpenAPI linting
oasdiff Detecting OpenAPI breaking changes
Postman API response and schema validation

You don't need to adopt every tool.

Start with your existing API specification and choose the testing approach that fits your architecture.

5 Common Contract Testing Mistakes

Even teams that understand contract testing can make these mistakes.

  1. Writing API Specifications After Development

If your specification is always updated after implementation, it can end up documenting accidental behavior rather than the intended contract.

Treat your contract as code and review changes alongside implementation changes.

  1. Testing Only Successful Responses

A contract also includes error responses.

Validate documented 400, 401, 403, 404, and other relevant responses.

  1. Ignoring Breaking Changes

A renamed field might look harmless to the backend developer but can break multiple consumers.

Introduce specification comparison and review breaking changes before merging.

  1. Relying Only on End-to-End Testing

End-to-end tests are valuable, but they can be slower and require complex environments.

Contract tests provide a faster way to validate service boundaries independently.

  1. Treating Every API Change as Breaking

Adding an optional response field is generally compatible with tolerant consumers, while removing a required field is usually breaking.

Understand the difference before blocking every specification update.

Where Shift-Left Testing Changes the Game

Here's where things become interesting.

Traditional testing often discovers compatibility problems late in the development lifecycle.

Shift-left testing changes that approach.

Instead of asking, "Did the API break after deployment?"

We ask, "Can we detect the breaking change before the code is merged?"

With a shift-left API testing strategy:

  • API specifications become part of development.
  • Contract checks run during pull requests.
  • Schema changes are reviewed early.
  • Breaking changes are identified automatically.
  • Developers receive feedback before deployment.
  • QA teams spend less time discovering preventable interface issues.

The objective isn't simply to write more tests.

It's to make API quality everyone's responsibility.

At Total Shift Left, this is the kind of development workflow we're passionate about: bringing API testing closer to the code changes that can introduce defects.

Final Thoughts: Your API Is Only as Reliable as Its Contract

Modern applications depend on communication between dozens, sometimes hundreds, of services.

A small API change can create a big problem when consumers aren't prepared for it.

API contract testing helps teams protect these communication boundaries, detect breaking changes early, and build more reliable distributed systems.

Remember:

A successful API response doesn't always mean a successful API integration.

The real question is whether the API is delivering what it promised to its consumers.

Want to explore API contract testing in more detail?

Read our complete guide:

API Contract Testing: What It Is, How It Works and Tools – Total Shift Left.

You'll find deeper explanations, practical OpenAPI and Pact examples, testing approaches, tools, CI workflows, and best practices.

Let's Talk, Developers!

I have a question for everyone working with APIs and microservices:

Have you ever experienced a production bug caused by an unexpected API change?

Was it a renamed field, a missing response property, an incompatible data type, or something else?

And more importantly, how did your team catch it?

Share your experience below. Your story might help another developer avoid the same Friday-evening production incident!

title: CloudWatch Omni Collects Azure Telemetry and Brings Different Metric Models Into One Space
description:
TL;DR

  • CloudWatch Omni is the part of Amazon CloudWatch that holds logs, metrics and traces from several providers in one workspace, and it now collects four kinds of telemetry from Microsoft Azure.
  • The four kinds are Azure resource logs, Azure Monitor platform metrics, virtual network flow logs, and traces from Application Insights, all landed in CloudWatch and visible in Omni spaces.
  • Setup runs through a Microsoft Entra ID tenant connected to an AWS account and Region, and the collector is scoped by telemetry type, subscription, Azure Region, resource type and tag.
  • Collection is available from all Azure Public Regions and can be ingested into every Region where CloudWatch Omni runs, so the footprint follows the two providers' Region lists.
  • Azure platform metrics arrive at a one-minute collection frequency, are stored 93 days, and can be charted over 30 days at most on a single chart, so the retention a team sees in one console still follows each provider's rules.
  • Microsoft documents that pre-aggregated platform metrics and raw Prometheus metrics can report different values for the same sample time until latency settles and granularity matches, which is the reason thresholds need re-baselining after a migration.
  • The Entra tenant connection is a cross-cloud identity path, and it deserves a review of its own: who can change the connector, which subscriptions it can reach, and what it can read.

CloudWatch Omni now collects Azure resource logs, Azure Monitor platform metrics, virtual network flow logs and Application Insights traces. The announcement on 21 November 2026 frames the benefit simply: teams that run workloads on both clouds no longer need separate monitoring tools or custom pipelines to see their whole environment, and during an incident a slow request can be followed from an Azure-hosted service to its AWS dependencies without switching consoles.

That framing is accurate and it stops where the hard part begins. Bringing telemetry into one place simplifies collection and incident navigation. Microsoft's documentation describes the aggregation, granularity and latency that teams need to account for when comparing data and defining alerts.

The announcement page, which is where the telemetry types and the Entra ID tenant step are stated. Source: aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/11/amazon-cloudwatch-omni-microsoft-azure, captured 22 November 2026.

What the connector collects and what you choose

The list of collected signals is short enough to plan against: resource logs, platform metrics, flow logs from virtual networks, and traces from Application Insights.

The choices sit in the connector configuration. Connecting a tenant to an AWS account and Region opens a scope decision, and the post names the dimensions that scope it: telemetry types, subscriptions, Azure Regions, resource types and tags. Each of those is a filter that lets the team limit collection before enabling the connector.

Tags are the lever worth using first. A tag that already marks production workloads, cost centres or data classification turns the connector into a scoped collector and limits which Azure resources feed telemetry into CloudWatch.

The scope decision also sets the incident path. A connector limited to two subscriptions produces a dashboard that answers questions about those two, and the first incident that touches a third subscription will send someone back to the console to widen it under pressure. Writing that boundary down next to the alert rules is cheaper than discovering it at 3am.

Netics editorial visual, 22 November 2026: what the Azure-native view exposes on one side, and what the Omni space receives on the other.

Azure platform metrics are pre-aggregated in Azure Monitor and collected at one-minute frequency

Azure resources produce platform metrics without any configuration, and Microsoft documents the collection frequency as one minute unless a specific metric definition says otherwise. That frequency is the finest resolution a consumer of those metrics can rely on.

The frequency figure is worth carrying into the connector design. A dashboard that aggregates five-minute buckets on the AWS side and one-minute samples on the Azure side compares two different things, and the difference is invisible once both series are drawn on the same axis.

Azure Monitor stores platform metrics in pre-aggregated form. Platform metrics are pre-aggregated and stored in a time-series database, and Azure Monitor collects them at one-minute frequency unless a metric definition states otherwise. A team that assumes it is reading raw samples will compare it against a source that does report raw samples and find a mismatch that looks like an incident.

Microsoft's diagram of how metrics reach Azure Monitor and where they are read back: separate paths, separate query surfaces, one subscription's worth of resources. Source: learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/essentials/data-platform-metrics, retrieved 22 November 2026.

A 93-day store with a 30-day chart window

Retention follows the source as well. Microsoft stores platform and custom metrics for 93 days, and its documentation adds a detail that matters for trend work: a single metrics chart can query at most 30 days of data, whatever the store holds.

Longer history needs a different path. The same documentation points at sending platform metrics to a Log Analytics workspace for long-term trending, which is a deliberate act with its own cost. Application Insights is a separate case again: log-based metrics inherit the retention of the underlying logs, described as 31 days to two years, while Application Insights logs are stored 90 days.

A cross-cloud dashboard inherits all of this. A quarter-over-quarter capacity comparison built on Azure platform metrics needs a workspace export, whatever console displays it.

Netics editorial visual, 22 November 2026: the four numbers that decide what a cross-cloud comparison can honestly claim.

Two metric models in one space

The clearest warning in Microsoft's documentation is about sources. Metrics from different sources and collection methods can use different aggregations, and differences in aggregation and latency can lead to different metric values for a specific sample time. The same page says the differences disappear over time once latency stops being an issue and the comparison happens at the same granularity.

That single paragraph describes the working method for anyone assembling a cross-cloud view. Compare at the same granularity, allow for the ingest delay, and record which aggregation each alert depends on. Latency expectations for platform metrics exported through diagnostic settings are documented separately, so teams should review them before defining alert timing.

Dimensions add a second variable. Azure describes a namespace as a category for a metric and dimensions as name and value pairs that carry context, such as a disk-space metric whose Drive dimension separates C: from D:. Dimension names and values are case-insensitive. A cross-cloud query that groups by a dimension has to know which dimension names exist on the Azure side, since the equivalent in an AWS namespace is a different string even when the concept is identical.

The Azure Monitor metrics documentation, the page that carries the one-minute frequency, the 93-day store and the aggregation warning quoted here. Source: learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/essentials/data-platform-metrics, captured 22 November 2026.

Re-baselining thresholds before the first alert

Every threshold that arrives with an existing alert rule was tuned against one source's aggregation and one source's latency. Evaluating the same threshold in a shared space requires checking its aggregation, granularity and latency first.

The practical order is short. List the alerts that will read cross-cloud data. For each, write down the source metric, its aggregation, and its granularity. Then re-derive the threshold from a period that includes a normal week and a deploy, and only then point the alert at the new space. Keep the remaining alerts on their source platform and schedule their recalculation.

Microsoft's Metrics explorer screenshot shows multiple metrics over time; the documentation separately warns that sources and collection methods may use different aggregations.

The Metrics explorer with an aggregation chosen per metric, which is the control that makes two charts comparable or not. Source: learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/essentials/data-platform-metrics, retrieved 22 November 2026.

The Entra tenant connection as a trust path to review

Connecting a Microsoft Entra ID tenant to an AWS account and Region creates a relationship that outlives the project that motivated it. It is also the part of this feature a security review should read first.

Three questions belong in that review. Which identity in the AWS account can create, modify or remove the connector, since that identity now controls what telemetry crosses the boundary. Which subscriptions the connector can reach, because a wide scope reads more than the incident that started the work. And what the collected data contains, since resource logs and flow logs carry IP addresses, resource names and, depending on the workload, more than an operations team expects.

The review prevents a risky cross-cloud observability pattern: one connector, created during a pilot, with an unchanged scope, feeding a dashboard that becomes the shared view of both clouds. Teams that already run monitoring built around incidents will recognise the shape, and the fix is the same discipline applied to a new data source.

Originally published on the Netics blog.

title: What People Choose Not to Say: A Multimodal Benchmark for Fine-Grained Information Manipulation in Conversations
description:
arXiv:2611.31346v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances in MLLMs have improved social understanding, enabling models to recognize emotions and distinguish truthful from deceptive behaviors. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on coarse-grained emotion recognition or binary truth-deception detection, overlooking the diverse ways people manipulate information in conversations, such as withholding, leakage, fabrication, evasion, and defensive counterclaim. Understanding these behaviors requires reasoning about underlying facts, participant knowledge, and conversational context, making them difficult to evaluate reliably. To address this gap, we introduce InfoCon, a multimodal benchmark for fine-grained information manipulation in conversations. InfoCon identifies six fine-grained strategies and derives a coarse consistency label from their factual and interactional relations. We develop an evidence-grounded multi-agent annotation framework to construct and verify reliable labels from rich contextual evidence. We benchmark representative multimodal models and systematically analyze their fine-grained information manipulation understanding, providing a testbed beyond binary truth-deception judgments.

title: Compilation is not correctness: 301 PLC tasks, 11.92 points of LLM code that compiles and misbehaves
description:
A shift register, written in Structured Text. The reference implementation assigns the bits in reverse order, which preserves the old values. The model-generated one assigns them forward, starting with Q0 := D0. Both compile. Both run. Both end with the same output.

At scan 11 the set branch drives the register to 1111. At scan 12, a shift with D0 = 0 produces 0111 in the reference and 0000 in the candidate — the new value walked across all four bits. At scan 14 the reset branch makes them agree again.

If your acceptance test is "imports with 0 compile errors", this program passes. If it's "check a few properties", it depends on which property. If it's "look at the final outputs", it passes too. Only a per-scan comparison catches it.

That's the whole argument of a 2026 paper from Beihang University — Compilation Is Not Correctness: Scan-by-Scan Evaluation of LLM-Generated PLC Programs (arXiv:2610.28675) — and the numbers are worse than the anecdote suggests.

What they built

CycleBench: 301 Structured Text tasks (287 function blocks + 14 programs), 684 scenarios, 61,424 scans. Each task ships with a reviewed public spec (behaviour requirements, POU identity, I/O interface, initial values, parameters), a hidden reference implementation, hidden input scenarios, and the expected per-scan output trace.

The evaluator compiles both sides with a pinned Matiec → C → GCC pipeline, drives reference and candidate in fresh sessions with identical inputs, identical public initial values and a virtual clock advanced one scan interval at a time, then compares every declared output and inout after every scan. No trajectory alignment. The first scan counts. All tasks stay in the denominator — missing candidates, interface violations, build failures and runtime failures are all failures, classified by stage.

The gap: 11.92 points

Across 8 LLMs × 4 baseline methods = 9,632 results:

Compiles Passes execution
All baseline results 83.99% 72.07%
Best method (CycleGen) 94.89% 83.31%

That's 11.92 points (95% bootstrap CI [9.63, 14.43]) of programs that build and then behave wrong. The gap exists in every model–method combination, including combinations with a compile rate above 99%.

It also gets worse with size: grouping by reference length, the gap is 3.67 points for 1–20 line programs and 24.07 points for programs over 80 lines. Longer, more stateful programs are exactly where compilation stops telling you anything.

Why it hides: transient mismatches and sampling phase

The failures don't usually sit at the end of the trace. 144 of 157 audited behavioural failures re-converge inside the scenario, and in 115 of 157 no mismatch run lasts more than 5 consecutive scans.

So the natural habit — "check every Nth scan" — is a sampling problem, not a coverage problem:

Observation policy Behavioural failures missed (of 157)
Every scan 0
Every 2 scans 11 (7.01%)
Every 5 scans 34 (21.66%)
Every 10 scans 47 (29.94%)
Last scan only 98 (62.42%)

Even with scenario endpoints always checked. And the phase matters: shifting which scans you look at — same programs, same inputs — moves the miss rate for stride 5 between 12.10% and 28.03%. No fixed phase finds everything.

The paper's second example is a timer, which is the version PLC engineers will recognise instantly:

(* candidate: uses the previous scan's input *)
TOF0(IN := pir_active, PT := T#20s);
(* ... manual override update ... *)
pir_active := stairs_pir_sensor AND NOT lights_buttons_state;
stairs_light := lights_buttons_state OR TOF0.Q;

The off-delay timer is called before pir_active is assigned, so it consumes the value from the previous scan. The lamp is wrong at scan 7 and correct again at scans 8–9. Look at the later scans and you will never know.

Where the failures cluster (use this as a checklist)

Of the 157 audited behavioural failures:

Category Share
Public output update 27.4%
Arithmetic / boundary logic 22.3%
Timing / call order 15.9%
Reset / priority 9.6%
State retention / overwrite 8.9%
Edge detection 8.3%
Initialisation 5.7%

The first three categories are 65.6% of behavioural failures. Note what dominates: not fancy algorithms, but when a value is written, which boundary condition was missed, and whether a stateful block was called before its inputs were current. Compile errors, by contrast, are boring: 53.42% of them are malformed statements or declarations — the compiler already tells you about those.

Generation can improve, but it doesn't close the gap

The authors then built CycleGen: generate k candidates, repair compile errors with bounded compiler feedback, write runtime self-tests in a separate model context, and pick the candidate that passes the most self-tests.

Execution pass rate goes 74.63% → 83.31% (+8.68 points). The ablation is the interesting part, because it prices each piece:

Configuration Compiles Executes Avg tokens
Direct, 1 candidate 84.93% 74.63% 1,929
5 candidates, take first valid 92.23% 79.94% 9,740
+ compiler-guided repair 94.85% 81.69% 11,922
+ self-test selection 94.89% 83.31% 18,197

Two things worth internalising:

  • Diminishing returns are brutal. k=5 → k=8 buys 0.87 points going in… and then loses 4 passes while spending 38.8% more tokens. The observed k=5 dominates its own extensions.
  • Model-written tests are a signal, not an oracle. Only 54.35% of self-test suites accepted all bound reference cases; mutation detection was 73.33%; only 43 of 192 suite slots caught any mutant. Using them to rank candidates is useful. Using them to declare correctness is not.

And the gap persists at the top: CycleGen still leaves 11.59 points between compiling and behaving.

What this means if you're shipping generated PLC code

Three layers, and the paper's 11.92-point gap is the cost of skipping the middle one:

  1. Structural validation — parse, interface check, compile. Fast, cheap, and provably insufficient on its own.
  2. Per-scan behavioural regression — same inputs, same initialisation, same logical clock, compare every declared output on every scan. This is the layer that catches the shift register and the timer.
  3. Full-machine and on-hardware verification — PLCSIM Advanced or the real controller, when you care about communication, motion, I/O channels and scan jitter.

We build for layers 2 and 3. TiaLink drives a local TIA Portal over Openness (V17–V21): it indexes the project into a knowledge graph — call relations, cross-references, DB member reads and writes, dangling references — so a change's blast radius is visible before you write, and LAD blocks go through a LadDoc schema check before import and compile. Our cloud simulator handles the per-scan execution side with deterministic scan semantics, timer ticks injected via tickMs.

Boundaries (what we did not do)

  • We did not run CycleBench. We did not reproduce its scores. This is our reading of the paper, with the tables re-checked against the PDF.
  • Deterministic scan semantics is not physical real time. Injected scan intervals make regression repeatable; they do not reproduce scan jitter, communication timing or hardware response.
  • Our simulation path covers a subset of IEC 61131-3 (IF/CASE/FOR/WHILE, arrays and structs, timers, edges), not the whole language, and not communication, technology objects, motion control, safety programs or hardware channels.
  • Passing the benchmark means "matches a reference on the provided finite scenarios" — not functional correctness, termination, or physical safety. The authors say this themselves, and it's worth repeating because it is the most common way this kind of result gets over-read.

Paper: Jinyun Chen, Juntao Hu, Haochen Li, Wentao Song, Ningbo Gu, Jianwei Niu, Qing Gao, Rui Wang. Compilation Is Not Correctness: Scan-by-Scan Evaluation of LLM-Generated PLC Programs. arXiv:2610.28675, October 2026.

If you're evaluating LLM-generated PLC code today, the cheapest thing you can steal from this paper is the acceptance rule: a task passes only if every declared output matches on every scan. Everything else — properties, sampled scans, final values — is a filter that lets a known class of bug through.

title: A Hierarchy of Risk Certificates for Representation-Based Prediction
description:
arXiv:2611.33333v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Representation-based prediction underlies many machine-learning systems. Yet a fitted predictor's failure to meet an accuracy requirement does not establish that its representation-decoder class cannot meet it. We study optimal population mean squared error (MSE) over Lipschitz decoders acting on a fixed representation. For blocks of $b\geq2$ independent and identically distributed (iid) observations, we minimize total squared error (normalized by $b-1$) under pairwise Lipschitz constraints. We prove that expected block scores form nondecreasing lower bounds on optimal class risk and converge to that risk on compact metric feature spaces, although no fixed block size provides a uniform relative guarantee. Verified dual lower bounds and iid calibration observations independent of model development, with bounded targets and predictions, yield simultaneous lower confidence bounds on optimal class risk and upper confidence bounds on fitted-predictor risk. These bounds can establish that every admissible decoder exceeds a prescribed MSE threshold or that an admissible fitted predictor meets it. Controlled experiments illustrate population-risk certification; fixed PTB-XL and Bike Sharing experiments provide deterministic empirical-risk conclusions. The results support principled assessment and selection of representation-decoder configurations. Efficient certification at scale and extensions to dependent observations remain open problems.

title: Trigger-Invariant Contrastive Unlearning for Backdoor Removal
description:
arXiv:2611.33571v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Backdoor attacks pose a severe threat to modern NLP models by embedding hidden triggers that induce malicious behavior at inference time. Recent unlearning methods such as gradient ascent (GA) attempt to remove backdoors by maximizing the loss on poisoned samples; however, these methods can suffer from a critical limitation: they may shift the trigger's influence to other classes rather than eliminating it. In this work, we propose Trigger-Invariant Contrastive Unlearning (TICU), a framework for mitigating textual backdoor behavior by enforcing prediction and representation invariance to trigger insertion. TICU constructs clean and trigger-inserted counterfactual pairs, then fine-tunes the model so that both inputs produce consistent output distributions and aligned hidden representations. To preserve clean-task performance, TICU also retains the supervised classification loss on clean data and constrains parameter drift from the original model. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets, model architectures, and attack settings show that TICU improves triggered accuracy and reduces trigger-induced prediction shifts compared with existing baselines, while maintaining competitive label-flipping performance and limiting clean-task degradation.

title: Learning What vs. Learning How: Decomposing Task and Interface Competence in Agentic Training
description:
arXiv:2611.31427v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents operate through harnesses that define system prompts, action formats, feedback loops, and resource constraints. A model may possess the knowledge needed to solve a task yet fail to express that knowledge through a particular harness. This raises a basic question: when a policy fails under a given harness, is it missing task knowledge or the competence to operate the interface? We distinguish two components of agentic competence: task competence, the knowledge and reasoning needed to solve a task, and interface competence, the ability to act on that knowledge through a given harness. Across four reasoning and agentic benchmarks, we show that harness-conditioned training yields vastly different outcomes depending on how these interact. Multi-harness distillation aggregates task knowledge from trajectories collected through different harnesses into a shared policy, but this knowledge is realised only when training preserves or improves competence on the inference-time interface. Otherwise, single-harness training can induce interference in interface competence, sometimes catastrophically collapsing performance on a held-out harness despite improvements in underlying task knowledge. To disentangle task and interface supervision, we introduce harness rehearsal: distillation on traces that carry minimal task knowledge while exercising the target interface. Cross-harness task supervision or rehearsal alone yields little gain, but their combination yields gains far larger than either: on BFCL V3 multi-turn with Qwen3-4B, they achieve 8.5% and 32.5% respectively, versus 58.8% together. Finally, on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) is more robust than distillation to single-harness training: it does not substantially degrade performance on other harnesses, and interface competence acquired through multi-harness distillation persists through subsequent RL.

title: Building a Unified Inline Code Editing Model for GitHub Copilot
description:
arXiv:2611.33314v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: AI-assisted coding ranges from fully agentic coding to inline code suggestions in the editor. Inline suggestions require predicting a developer's most likely next edit from an editing session. The next edit may lie at the cursor, in nearby lines, or farther away, and one editing intent can span several of these. The preceding system queries separate completion, nearby edit, and long-distance edit models, each with its own output format, in a fixed sequence; it thus cannot express intents spanning distant locations in one response, can require several sequential model calls per suggestion, and prioritizes completion even when a correction would serve better. We present a unified model that predicts all three edit types in one output space: a sequence of anchored diff patches specifying locations, deleted lines, and added lines. This representation permits multiple edits per response, so the client can serve later edits from a cache without further model calls. We train this model in two phases, first unifying next edit and long-distance edit prediction, then adding code completion. We synthesize multi-edit supervision from single-edit data via model pseudolabeling and edit history playback. We use a binary LLM-graded reward, a patch validity taxonomy shared by data filtering, reward, and evaluation, and grader boosting for targeted failure modes. Phase 2 also adapts how the client processes and presents model outputs. In controlled online A/B experiments in GitHub Copilot, Phase 1 significantly reduces time to display by 6.77% and output tokens by 58.93% relative to the three-model baseline. In Phase 2, the 3-in-1 model and client adaptations reduce dismissed suggestions per user by 10.06% relative to the 2-in-1 model paired with the completion model. Throughout this report, we also share our methodology and learnings in evaluation, training, and end-to-end model and system design.

title: The Bundesrat corpus: A dataset of political discourse in the German Federal Council
description:
arXiv:2611.33173v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Bundesrat is Germany's second legislative chamber and a constitutional veto player within its political system. The members of the Bundesrat are delegates of state governments. Tracing the political discourse in the Bundesrat is challenging as it has a limited machine-readable corpus available. To address this issue, we present a speaker-attributed corpus of 1,067 Bundesrat plenary sessions from the chamber's first session on 7 September 1949 to 10 July 2026. In this period, a total of 53,362 speeches by 2,473 individuals were delivered in the chamber, including written statements. Each speech includes a speech ID, the full German text, the speaker's name, the date and location of the session, the federal state that the speaker represents, the speaker's role (if applicable), the type of contribution, and the speaker's gender. The dataset provides interdisciplinary research opportunities across computational political science, legislative studies, and parliamentary discourse analysis, coupled with discourse from the Bundestag.

title: Headlong: a complete agent harness written in Bash
description:
Headlong

Most coding agents wake up when you message them, do a job, then stop. Headlong takes the opposite approach. It is a complete agent harness written in Bash, built around shellm, a recursive language model loop that keeps thinking between conversations. Your team's Slack messages arrive as observations in that stream, and the agent decides whether to answer. Each step rebuilds context from an append-only log, recent entries in full and older ones summarised in tiers, so a long-running agent loses nothing to compaction. It is small, readable end to end, and easy to modify. As of 26 November 2026 it has 1,313 stars on GitHub, is Apache-2.0 licensed, and has no GitHub release yet. The repo is now under Laude Institute.

Repo: https://github.com/laude-institute/headlong

What you get

  • A recursive language model loop (shellm) that keeps thinking between conversations, instead of waking up per message
  • Slack messages delivered as observations in the stream, with the agent deciding whether to answer
  • Context rebuilt each step from an append-only log: recent entries in full, older ones summarised in tiers
  • A small Bash codebase, readable end to end and easy to modify

The test for Headlong is a long-running job: does the agent still know what happened last week?

Quick poll

What would you use Headlong for first?

  • Letting it watch a Slack channel

title: Synchronizing Cameras via 3D Object Relationships
description:
arXiv:2611.33387v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this paper, we synchronize multiple videos of the same dynamic event through object relationships. Driven by dynamic reconstruction and novel view synthesis, many recent synchronization methods rely on pixel-level evidence, such as point correspondences across views or the photometric losses of a reconstructed scene. In dynamic scenes, however, fast motion and occlusions make the moving regions that carry much of the timing information hard to match across views. We thus propose to bring back the traditional wisdom that objects are reliable cues for global reasoning about cameras. Measured in 3D, the relationships between objects, such as the distance between two people, are stable across all views up to scale; they can serve as cues for alignment. To compare these relationships across cameras, we only need the identity of each object in every view, as the cues are relational. We obtain these identities by giving a vision-language model a few frames of every camera and prompting it to identify the objects in the scene. We then segment and track each identified object through every video with an open-vocabulary segmentor. To obtain the 3D locations of objects, we use a pretrained depth estimator. Where depth or segmentation fails, we complement these 3D cues with 2D motion from point tracks. Finally, we synchronize the cameras by finding the temporal offsets at which the cues of different cameras agree best, first for each camera pair and then for all cameras jointly with robust optimization. We evaluate our method on four standard benchmarks, outperforming the state of the art.

title: Two Timescales of Forgetting in Fine-tuning of Language Models: Fast Behavioral Suppression and Slow Representational Drift
description:
arXiv:2611.33302v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Today, a core pipeline of artificial intelligence systems is pretraining on a broad range of text corpora and then fine-tuning on specific tasks or desired behaviors. Yet we still have limited understanding of how fine-tuning on a restricted data distribution modifies representations acquired during pretraining. In particular, it remains unclear whether surface behavioral suppression happens together with the erasure of latent representations that support it. In this work, we study supervised fine-tuning (SFT) by pretraining transformers on a controlled context-free grammar with hierarchical latent structure, the Random Hierarchy Model (RHM), and fine-tuning with a restricted subset of its generative rules. While during pretraining the model's ability to generate with the correct grammar rules coincides with building the internal representations of the corresponding latent, we find that SFT exhibits a very different dynamics: (i) the generation of deleted rules changes on a fast timescale inversely proportional to the magnitude of the token-latent correlation; meanwhile, their corresponding representations stay intact; (ii) the hidden representations of the deleted rules become forgotten on a much longer timescale, associated with a slow drift of the network parameters. Finally, we observe analogous results in a realistic setup with natural language, suggesting that this timescale separation in forgetting is a more general phenomenon of fine-tuning language models.

title: NORMCRAFT: Cultural Norm Generation for Context-Aware Language Model Alignment
description:
arXiv:2611.33726v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cultural alignment requires large language models (LLMs) to infer often-implicit social norms from a scenario and its cultural context. Existing approaches typically adapt individual models or supply external cultural knowledge, while learning norm inference independently of downstream response generation remains underexplored. We introduce NORMCRAFT, a modular framework that decouples norm inference from response generation. Through norm-centric multi-view supervision, we train an LLM as a norm generator to recover shared norms from prospective, adherence, and violation scenarios without downstream response labels. The generated norms guide a separate, frozen LLM (the responder). With Qwen3.5-4B as the responder, NORMCRAFT outperforms prompting and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baselines on four of five downstream metrics. On SafeWorld, its responses reflect the reference norms more often (Coverage) and more precisely (Faithfulness), exceeding Responder SFT by 18.0 and 14.1 percentage points, respectively. Direct norm evaluation also shows higher norm quality than the base and few-shot generators. The same trained generator improves cultural alignment on SafeWorld across fourteen frozen LLMs spanning five families and 0.8B to 27B parameters, with the largest gains for the smallest models.

title: AWS Savings Plans for startups: how much to commit and which plan
description:
In short:

  • Compute Savings Plans give up to 66% off EC2, Fargate and Lambda; EC2 Instance Savings Plans up to 72% off one instance family; Database Savings Plans up to 35% off managed databases.
  • Commit to about 70 to 80% of your lowest steady hourly spend, not your average. Unused commitment is money you pay for nothing.
  • Fix waste first, then commit. A Savings Plan on an oversized server locks in the oversize.

A Savings Plan is the biggest single discount on AWS that needs no engineering work. You promise to spend a fixed amount per hour for one or three years, and AWS bills the matching usage at a lower rate. For a startup with a steady base of servers, that is often 25 to 40% off the biggest line of the bill.

It is also the easiest way to waste money on AWS. A commitment cannot be cancelled. Commit too much, or commit before you clean up, and you pay for capacity you do not use, every hour, for a year.

This post covers which plan to buy, how to size the commitment from your own data, and the order to do it in.

The three kinds of Savings Plans

Plan Covers Maximum discount Flexibility
Compute Savings Plans EC2 (any family, size, region, OS), Fargate, Lambda up to 66% High: follows you if you change instance types or move to containers
EC2 Instance Savings Plans One instance family in one region, e.g. m7g in us-east-1 up to 72% Low: tied to that family
Database Savings Plans Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, DocumentDB, Neptune, Keyspaces, Timestream, DMS up to 35% Medium: any of these services, 1-year only

Sources: Compute and EC2 Instance Savings Plans and the Database Savings Plans announcement (December 2025).

The "maximum" numbers are for 3-year, all-upfront plans on specific instance types. A 1-year, no-upfront Compute Savings Plan typically lands around 25 to 30% off on-demand for common instances. For example, an m8gn.large in us-east-1 lists at about $0.146 an hour on-demand and about $0.106 with a 1-year no-upfront Compute Savings Plan, roughly 27% less (Holori price data).

Database Savings Plans are the new one. Before them, the only discount for RDS was a Reserved Instance tied to one engine, size and region. The new plan follows your database spend across services and sizes, which suits a startup that may resize or move from RDS to Aurora during the year.

Step 1: clean up before you commit

A Savings Plan discounts what you run. If what you run is oversized, you lock in the oversize for a year. Before buying, do the free fixes:

  • Delete idle resources and old environments: see 3 hidden AWS charges.
  • Right-size servers whose CPU sits below 20%.
  • Move what you can to Graviton, which is about 20% cheaper on its own: see moving to AWS Graviton.
  • Schedule dev and staging to stop at night and at weekends.

Then wait two to four weeks for usage to settle. The new, lower baseline is what you commit to.

Step 2: find your steady hourly floor

Savings Plans are bought in dollars per hour of discounted usage. The safe size comes from the lowest level your compute spend reaches, not the average.

The quickest way to see it is in Cost Explorer: filter to EC2 compute, Fargate and Lambda, set granularity to Hourly (it covers the last 14 days), and look for the floor of the line, usually at night or at weekends. If the floor is $4.00 an hour on-demand, that is your starting point.

AWS also recommends a commitment from your history:

aws ce get-savings-plans-purchase-recommendation \
  --savings-plans-type COMPUTE_SP \
  --term-in-years ONE_YEAR \
  --payment-option NO_UPFRONT \
  --lookback-period-in-days THIRTY_DAYS \
  --query 'SavingsPlansPurchaseRecommendation.SavingsPlansPurchaseRecommendationDetails[0].[HourlyCommitmentToPurchase,EstimatedMonthlySavingsAmount,EstimatedAverageUtilization]'

Treat that number as an upper limit. The recommendation assumes the next year looks like the last 30 days. For a startup, it often does not.

Step 3: size the commitment

A rule that works for most startups: commit to 70 to 80% of the steady floor, in on-demand terms, converted to the discounted rate.

Example: the floor is $4.00 an hour on-demand, and the plan saves about 28%.

  • 75% of the floor is $3.00 an hour of on-demand usage.
  • At 28% off, that usage costs $2.16 an hour under the plan. That is the commitment.
  • Monthly: $2.16 × 730 hours = about $1,577, covering usage that would have cost $2,190 on-demand. Saving: about $613 a month, $7,350 a year.

Everything above $3.00 an hour of usage stays on-demand. That is not waste; it is the flexibility to shrink, change architecture, or move to Graviton later without paying for nothing.

If your usage grows, buy a second plan later. Several small plans bought over time are safer than one big plan bought at the start.

Step 4: pick the plan for each part of the bill

Situation Plan
EC2, ECS on Fargate or Lambda, still changing Compute Savings Plan, 1 year, no upfront
A big, stable EC2 fleet on one family you will not change EC2 Instance Savings Plan, for that family only
RDS or Aurora running all the time Database Savings Plan, 1 year
A database you plan to replace or shut down within a year Nothing yet, stay on-demand

Two things to check with databases:

  • Existing RDS Reserved Instances keep applying until they expire. Plan the Database Savings Plan for when they end, not on top of them.
  • Serverless databases (Aurora Serverless, DynamoDB on-demand) are covered too, so steady serverless spend can be committed like provisioned instances.

Step 5: watch utilisation every month

After buying, two numbers in Cost Explorer > Savings Plans tell you whether it was the right size:

  • Utilisation: how much of your commitment you used. Below about 95% means you committed too much.
  • Coverage: how much of your eligible usage the plans covered. Low coverage with high utilisation means there is room for another small plan.

Add a budget alert so a drop shows up the week it happens, not at the end of the year. In AWS Budgets, choose Create budget, then Savings Plans budget, then Utilization, set the threshold to 95% and add your email. It takes two minutes and needs no code.

You can also read both numbers from the command line for last month:

aws ce get-savings-plans-utilization \
  --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-11-01 \
  --query 'Total.Utilization.UtilizationPercentage'

aws ce get-savings-plans-coverage \
  --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-11-01 \
  --query 'SavingsPlansCoverages[].Coverage.CoveragePercentage'

Mistakes that waste money

  • Committing to the average, not the floor. Every quiet hour below the commitment is paid for and unused.
  • Buying 3 years because the discount is bigger. For a startup, the risk of change is bigger than the extra discount.
  • Buying an EC2 Instance Savings Plan, then moving to Graviton or containers. The plan stays on the old family.
  • Buying before cleaning up. The commitment locks in today's waste.
  • Forgetting the end date. When a plan expires, usage goes back to on-demand prices silently. Put the renewal date in a calendar.

Savings Plans checklist

  1. Clean up idle resources, right-size and move to Graviton first.
  2. Wait for usage to settle, then find the steady hourly floor.
  3. Commit to 70 to 80% of the floor, 1 year, no upfront.
  4. Use Compute Savings Plans for changing compute, Database Savings Plans for steady databases.
  5. Check utilisation and coverage monthly, and set a utilisation budget alert.
  6. Add small plans over time instead of one big one.

Want a rough idea of the total saving first? Try the AWS savings estimator. If you would like someone to size the commitment from your real usage, the AWS cost optimization review does exactly that, or start with a Free AWS Review.

Discount figures are from the AWS Savings Plans pricing page and the Database Savings Plans announcement, checked in November 2026. This is general information, not financial advice for your company.

Common questions

Which AWS Savings Plan is best for a startup?

Usually a 1-year, no-upfront Compute Savings Plan. It applies to EC2 in any family and region, Fargate and Lambda, so it keeps working when your architecture changes. The extra discount of an EC2 Instance Savings Plan only pays off if you are sure of the instance family for the whole term.

How much should I commit to?

Look at your hourly compute spend over the last 30 to 60 days and find the steady floor, the level you never go below. Commit to about 70 to 80% of that floor. Anything above it stays on-demand, which is fine.

What are Database Savings Plans?

A Savings Plan launched in December 2025 that gives up to 35% off Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, DocumentDB, Neptune, Keyspaces, Timestream and DMS for a 1-year commitment with no upfront payment. Unlike Reserved Instances, it is not tied to one instance size or engine.

Can I cancel or sell a Savings Plan?

No. You pay the hourly commitment for the whole term, whether you use it or not. That is why the commitment should be smaller than your steady usage.

Should I pick 1 year or 3 years?

Most startups should pick 1 year. Three years gives a bigger discount, but your product, team and architecture will probably look very different in three years.

Originally published on DevOps with Umar. Free tool for this: the Savings Plans vs On-Demand calculator. More in the tools list.

title: A production checklist for dependency footprint
description:
Before deployment

  • [ ] Confirm the owner and operational purpose for this signal.
  • [ ] Review configuration and middleware placement against the current integration guide.
  • [ ] Use fake secrets and representative requests to check redaction and capture behavior.
  • [ ] Confirm the intended storage, retention, and access policy.

During validation

A small runtime dependency footprint can simplify review, but it does not replace checking what the application actually runs. TracerNest is described as a zero-runtime-dependency npm package, which can reduce the number of transitive runtime packages it introduces. Inspect the installed package, lockfile changes, supported Node versions, and update policy as part of normal dependency review.

After rollout

  • [ ] Ask an engineer unfamiliar with the change to find one useful event.
  • [ ] Check for noisy or missing records and adjust the policy deliberately.
  • [ ] Document the next action an on-call responder should take.

One final guardrail

Treat package claims as version-specific and keep reviewing release notes and security advisories. A checklist is only useful when it reflects the current version and the actual data your application handles.

title: Multi-agent System for Automatic Discovery of Pareto-optimal Meta-solvers for PDEs
description:
arXiv:2611.31611v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Designing linear solvers for discretized partial differential equations requires problem-specific expertise. We present a multi-agent framework, in which language-model agents propose, critique, implement, and evaluate solver configurations assembled from Krylov methods, preconditioners, block factorizations, and neural operators. Inside the proposing agent, a non-dominated sorting genetic evolutionary algorithm evolves the population of meta-solvers toward the Pareto front of six measured quantities, so that one run returns a front of trade-offs rather than a single tuned solver. The system runs on small open-weight language models served on a single laptop, and we compare it with a single agent on four problems. For three-dimensional acoustic scattering and elasticity, it delivers 47 and 48 convergent hybrid solvers out of 60 candidates. Relative to the Jacobi-preconditioned Krylov baselines, the best of the discovered solvers reduce the iteration counts by factors of 4.7 and 60 and the online solve time by factors of 2.3 and 3.0, whereas the single agent produces no executable plan. For coupled dynamic thermoelasticity in two and three dimensions, where the baselines fail, it completes 98 of 100 transient candidates and, compared with the single agent, reaches a given accuracy 15 times faster in two dimensions and a displacement error 20 times lower in three dimensions.
