title: Not All Interpretation Methods Are Created Equal: Tiered Evaluation of AI Interpretability
description:
arXiv:2611.31833v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As AI transitions to sociotechnical deployments, uninterpretable models pose serious threats to reliability, public trust and contestability. However, not all interpretation methods are created equal: for interpretability to enhance deployment safety and effectiveness, interpretation methods must be evaluated in a tiered system to differentiate evidence levels of trustworthiness, rather than validated through isolated interpretation instances. Our core vision is that elevating the evaluation of interpretation methods to a core AI assessment metric will drive robust knowledge discovery from data (KDD) and ensure safe, contestable sociotechnical deployments of AI. To this end, we propose TRUST, a tiered evaluation framework that builds upon the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) principles for Veridical Data Science (VDS) and the Predictive, Descriptive and Relevant (PDR) foundations. To differentiate interpretation methods effectively and systematically, TRUST grades interpretation across five tiers: Task-Aligned PDR Foundations, Rigorous Epistemic Grounding, Unifying Semantic Understanding, Scope Transferability, and Targeted Prospective Validation. We present a start-to-finish case study of the iterative Random Forest (iRF) family under TRUST and contrast it with other LLM interpretation methods that struggle to clear specific tiers. Finally, we conclude with brief initial thoughts on how TRUST principles can extend in autonomous agentic frameworks. Ultimately, the TRUST framework fosters contestability and epistemic grounding as foundational evaluation principles for human-machine workflows and, eventually, autonomous agentic workflows.

title: Build a video view counter that ignores autoplay, refreshes and bots
description:
TL;DR

Counting play events counts muted autoplay, refreshes and bots as viewers. We'll build a tracker that counts a view only when the player is at least 50% on screen, playing, in a visible tab, for 2 continuous seconds (the MRC video viewability floor), plus a Node server that dedupes per viewer and drops bots with isbot. In a scripted test, the naive counter said 5 and the real one said 1.

Why play is the wrong event 🎥

There's no universal definition to copy. YouTube doesn't publish its organic threshold, Shorts counts every start since March 2025, Facebook reports "Views" and 3-second plays separately, and LinkedIn ads use 2 continuous seconds at 50% visible. (Swydo, updated Nov 2026, Blck Alpaca)

So we'll pick a definition on purpose. The MRC viewable impression guideline for video ads (50% of pixels, 2 continuous seconds) is a sensible floor:

Condition How we detect it
At least 50% on screen IntersectionObserver with a 0.5 threshold
Actually playing playing / pause / waiting / ended events
Tab is visible document.visibilityState
2 continuous seconds timer that resets if any condition breaks
Not a repeat server dedupe per viewer + video + 30 min window
Not a bot isbot on the user agent, server-side

Stack: Node 22, isbot 5.2.4, no framework. Tested in Chromium 158 with Playwright.

1. The client tracker 

// public/view-tracker.js
// A "view" = the player was >= 50% on screen, actually playing, in a visible tab,
// for QUALIFY_MS of continuous time. One view per element per page load.
const QUALIFY_MS = 2000;

export function trackViews(video, { videoId, endpoint = '/api/view' }) {
  let onScreen = false, playing = false, counted = false;
  let streakStart = null, timer = null;

  const pageVisible = () => document.visibilityState === 'visible';
  const qualifying = () => onScreen && playing && pageVisible();

  function update() {
    if (counted) return;
    if (qualifying() && streakStart === null) {
      streakStart = performance.now();
      timer = setTimeout(fire, QUALIFY_MS);
    } else if (!qualifying() && streakStart !== null) {
      clearTimeout(timer);           // streak broken: MRC-style "continuous"
      streakStart = null;
    }
  }

  function fire() {
    counted = true;
    const body = JSON.stringify({ videoId, viewerId: viewerId(), ts: Date.now() });
    navigator.sendBeacon(endpoint, new Blob([body], { type: 'application/json' }));
  }

  new IntersectionObserver(([e]) => { onScreen = e.intersectionRatio >= 0.5; update(); },
    { threshold: [0, 0.5, 1] }).observe(video);
  video.addEventListener('playing', () => { playing = true; update(); });
  for (const ev of ['pause', 'waiting', 'ended', 'emptied'])
    video.addEventListener(ev, () => { playing = false; update(); });
  document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', update);
}

function viewerId() {
  try {
    let id = localStorage.getItem('vid_viewer');
    if (!id) { id = crypto.randomUUID(); localStorage.setItem('vid_viewer', id); }
    return id;
  } catch { return 'anon'; }
}

A few choices worth calling out:

  • playing, not play. play fires when playback is requested; playing fires when frames are actually moving. A stall (waiting) breaks the streak.
  • The streak resets. Scroll away at 1.9 s and you start again from zero. That's what "continuous" means.
  • sendBeacon survives the page unloading, so a view that qualifies right before navigation still arrives.

💡 Tip: for long-form content, consider a second, higher-threshold event (say "engaged view" at 30 s). Keep names distinct so nobody mixes them up on a dashboard.

2. The server: dedupe and bots 🛠️ 

npm i isbot

// server.mjs
import http from 'node:http';
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { isbot } from 'isbot';

const DEDUPE_MS = 30 * 60 * 1000;          // one view per viewer per video per 30 min
const lastCounted = new Map();             // `${viewerId}:${videoId}` -> ts (use Redis in prod)
export const stats = { received: 0, bot: 0, duplicate: 0, counted: 0, naivePlays: 0 };

const server = http.createServer(async (req, res) => {
  if (req.method === 'POST' && req.url === '/api/view') {
    let raw = ''; for await (const c of req) raw += c;
    stats.received++;
    const ua = req.headers['user-agent'] ?? '';
    if (isbot(ua)) { stats.bot++; return res.writeHead(204).end(); }
    const { videoId, viewerId } = JSON.parse(raw);
    const key = `${viewerId}:${videoId}`, now = Date.now();
    if (now - (lastCounted.get(key) ?? 0) < DEDUPE_MS) { stats.duplicate++; return res.writeHead(204).end(); }
    lastCounted.set(key, now); stats.counted++;
    return res.writeHead(204).end();
  }
  if (req.method === 'POST' && req.url === '/api/naive-play') { stats.naivePlays++; return res.writeHead(204).end(); }
  if (req.url === '/stats') return res.writeHead(200, {'content-type':'application/json'}).end(JSON.stringify(stats));
  const path = req.url === '/' ? '/feed.html' : req.url;
  try {
    const body = await readFile('public' + path);
    const type = path.endsWith('.js') ? 'text/javascript' : path.endsWith('.mp4') ? 'video/mp4' : 'text/html';
    res.writeHead(200, { 'content-type': type }).end(body);
  } catch { res.writeHead(404).end(); }
});
server.listen(3000, () => console.log('listening on :3000'));

⚠️ Note: the static file handler is demo-only (no path sanitizing). Don't ship it. In production, the dedupe map belongs in Redis with a TTL, and viewerId should come from your auth session when you have one.

3. A feed page that runs both counters

Three muted autoplaying videos: two at the top, one far below the fold. Each gets the real tracker and a naive play counter so we can compare.

<!-- public/feed.html -->
<!doctype html><meta name=viewport content="width=device-width">
<style>video{display:block;width:480px;height:270px;margin:0 0 40px}.spacer{height:3000px}</style>
<video id=a src="/long.mp4" muted autoplay playsinline loop></video>
<video id=b src="/long.mp4" muted autoplay playsinline loop></video>
<div class=spacer></div>
<video id=c src="/long.mp4" muted autoplay playsinline loop></video>
<script type=module>
import { trackViews } from '/view-tracker.js';
for (const v of document.querySelectorAll('video')) {
  trackViews(v, { videoId: v.id });
  v.addEventListener('play', () => navigator.sendBeacon('/api/naive-play'), { once: true });
}
</script>

4. Simulate real traffic with Playwright

Scenario: a viewer loads the feed, scrolls 300 px after 1 s (video a leaves the screen), refreshes, and then a headless bot visits.

// run.js
const { chromium } = require('playwright');
const stats = async p => (await (await p.request.get('http://localhost:3000/stats')).json());
(async () => {
  const b = await chromium.launch();
  const human = await b.newContext({ userAgent: 'Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/142.0.0.0 Safari/537.36', viewport:{width:1280,height:720} });
  const p = await human.newPage();
  await p.goto('http://localhost:3000/');
  await p.waitForTimeout(1000);
  await p.evaluate(() => window.scrollTo(0, 300));      // video "a" drops below 50% visible after 1s
  await p.waitForTimeout(3000);
  console.log('after first visit  ', JSON.stringify(await stats(p)));
  await p.reload(); await p.waitForTimeout(3000);
  console.log('after reload       ', JSON.stringify(await stats(p)));
  const bot = await (await b.newContext()).newPage();   // default HeadlessChrome UA
  await bot.goto('http://localhost:3000/'); await bot.waitForTimeout(3000);
  console.log('after headless UA  ', JSON.stringify(await stats(bot)));
  console.log('default UA was:', await bot.evaluate(() => navigator.userAgent));
  await b.close();
})();

$ node server.mjs &
listening on :3000
$ node run.js
after first visit   {"received":1,"bot":0,"duplicate":0,"counted":1,"naivePlays":2}
after reload        {"received":2,"bot":0,"duplicate":1,"counted":1,"naivePlays":3}
after headless UA   {"received":4,"bot":2,"duplicate":1,"counted":1,"naivePlays":5}
default UA was: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) HeadlessChrome/158.0.8127.36 Safari/537.36

5. Reading the results 📊

Scenario Naive play Qualified views
First visit +2 (a and b started) +1 (b only; a was on screen ~1 s)
Reload +1 +0 (arrived, rejected as duplicate)
Headless bot +2 +0 (2 arrived, rejected by isbot)
Total 5 1

Two things I didn't expect:

  1. Video c never started. Chromium didn't autoplay the muted video while it was 3000 px offscreen, so even the naive counter skipped it. That's browser behavior you shouldn't rely on; a taller viewport or a different browser could start it.
  2. My own test harness is a bot. Playwright's default UA contains HeadlessChrome, which isbot flags. If your synthetic monitoring hits pages with view tracking, it's either inflating your counts (naive) or silently filtered (this setup). Set a real UA in tests that need to count, and know which one you're doing.

Things to know

  • Keep both numbers. Rename the naive count to "starts" and keep it. The gap between starts and views tells you how much of your autoplay gets real attention.
  • UA filtering is the floor. It catches honest automation. If views affect payouts, add rate limits per IP/viewer and anomaly checks.
  • Not tested here: the visibilitychange path (background tabs), Safari, mobile. The harness is headless Chromium 158 on one machine.

What's next

  • Send videoId, viewerId and a session id with every beacon into a real events table, then compute views in SQL so you can change the definition later and backfill.
  • Add an "engaged view" at a longer threshold and plot it next to views per video. The videos where the two diverge most are the ones worth a look.

title: Driving Windows Apps Without Sending 10 Screenshots per Task (turbo-desktop-mcp)
description:
Most desktop computer-use agents work by taking a full screenshot after every click. On a 1280x720 desktop capture, one image costs 1,229 input tokens under Anthropic's width * height / 750 formula. A 6-step form fill burns 7,374 vision tokens before the model writes a single word.

I just released turbo-desktop-mcp v0.1.0 on PyPI (uvx turbo-desktop-mcp), a standalone Windows 10/11 MCP server that drives native desktop apps through Windows UI Automation (UIA) first and only falls back to real input or Windows OCR when a control has no UIA pattern.

GitHub: https://github.com/Tthanh2k6/turbo-desktop
PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/turbo-desktop-mcp/

How the control tree and deltas work

Instead of returning raw XML or PNGs, inspect_compact flattens a window into one line per interactive control:

<<<SCREEN_CONTENT w1 TurboFixture>>>
[w1:e1] <Edit> "Full name" = ""
[w1:e2] <ComboBox> "Country" = "Vietnam"
[w1:e3] <CheckBox> "I agree to terms" [unchecked]
[w1:e4] <Button> "Submit"
<<<END_SCREEN_CONTENT>>>

Refs stay stable across calls. On subsequent calls, onlyChanged=true returns only added (*), changed (~), and removed (-) lines. Multi-step sequences run inside batch_actions and stop on the first error.

When an app exposes no UIA tree (custom-drawn canvases, games), inspect_compact sets treeEmpty: true and runs Windows built-in WinRT OCR, returning clickable lines like [w1:o3] text "Save" @412,230.

Measured numbers: UIA deltas vs screenshots

I ran a reproducible 4-task benchmark (desktop-mcp/tests/field/bench_uia_vs_screenshot.py) on Windows 11 against three native C# WinForms fixtures (turbo_fixture.exe, turbo_editor.exe, turbo_canvas.exe). UIA text tokens were counted with tiktoken (o200k_base). Screenshot baselines captured real PNGs on the same windows and measured both exact window crops (460x420 to 620x440) and standard 1280x720 desktop captures.

Task turbo-desktop-mcp (UIA + delta) Window-crop PNGs 1280x720 desktop PNGs Payload bytes (UIA vs PNG)
1. WinForms form fill (3 fields + Submit + verify) 760 tok (4 calls) 1,548 tok (6 shots) 7,374 tok 2.1 KB vs 55.2 KB
2. 5-step stateful UI loop (click + delta diff) 862 tok (12 calls) 1,548 tok (6 shots) 7,374 tok 2.5 KB vs 40.5 KB
3. Native editor multi-line Unicode write + readback 456 tok (4 calls) 1,092 tok (3 shots) 3,687 tok 1.3 KB vs 17.4 KB
4. Custom-drawn canvas (empty UIA tree, WinRT OCR) 235 tok (2 calls) 125 tok (1 shot) 1,229 tok 0.7 KB vs 3.4 KB
Total (4 tasks) 2,313 tok 4,313 tok 19,664 tok 6.5 KB vs 116.4 KB

Two honest takeaways from that table:

  1. On standard WinForms controls (tasks 1 to 3), UIA + deltas cut token usage by 8.1x to 9.7x compared to 720p full-desktop captures, and by 1.8x to 2.4x even against tiny tightly cropped fixture windows.
  2. On Task 4 (360x260 custom canvas with no UIA tree), a cropped PNG (125 tokens) is smaller than the WinRT OCR text output (235 tokens). OCR still helps if you want clickable coordinates without passing images to a vision model, or if the full screen is large.

In an earlier 30-task field run with claude -p --model haiku driving the real MCP server, 29 of 30 tasks passed (173 calls, 203 turns, $0.2513 total). The single failure was UWP Calculator on an isolated exebox desktop where Windows forces UWP activation onto WinSta0\Default.

Things that broke on real Windows before v0.1.0

Three Windows quirks bit me during testing:

  • WinForms modal dialogs hang UIA Invoke. Calling UIA Invoke on a WinForms menu item like File -> Save As... blocks the UIA call until the modal dialog closes. turbo-desktop-mcp returns pending: true / blocked: true instead of hanging, and recommends sending press_keys (Ctrl+S) whenever a shortcut exists.
  • UIPI blocks input to elevated windows. If a normal-privilege server tries to click an admin window, Windows drops the input silently. turbo-desktop-mcp checks process elevation against its own token (is_elevated_above_us) and marks those windows elevated: true, actionable: false.
  • Sharing a live PC with an agent. When falling back to real mouse/keyboard input, turbo-desktop-mcp waits until you stop moving the mouse, holds a low-level hook (WH_KEYBOARD_LL / WH_MOUSE_LL) during the action, draws an orange edge glow around the monitor, and releases immediately on Esc x3 or emergency Ctrl+Alt+Shift+K. Windows with titles matching .env, secret, token, password, or password managers are always hidden and denied.

Quick start (Windows 10/11, Python 3.12+) 

claude mcp add turbo-desktop -e PYTHONUTF8=1 -- uvx turbo-desktop-mcp

Or install directly:

pip install turbo-desktop-mcp

The standalone MCP server (desktop-mcp) is MIT-licensed and has 245+ automated Windows tests running on GitHub Actions. If you test it against Electron, WPF, or Qt apps and hit weird UIA trees, open an issue on the repo.

title: Agents can now find Vercel CLI commands by describing the task
description:
Coding agents can now use vercel help search to find Vercel CLI commands by describing a task in plain language.

The search returns a list of matching commands. Add --with-help to include the help page for the first result in the same call. For example, vercel help search "roll back production" --with-help returns the options and examples for vercel rollback.

Search also supports:

  • API endpoints: When a Vercel API endpoint matches the task, search returns a vercel api command with the request path and placeholders for every required input. The agent can fill in the values without guessing the path.

  • JSON output: Use --json to return search results as JSON. Combine it with --with-help to include usage instructions, options, and examples for the first result.

Search recognizes common wording, such as “show” instead of “list,” and handles minor spelling mistakes.

The CLI also includes a skill that tells coding agents to start with vercel help search when looking for a command. Vercel doesn't log your search text.

Update to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade.

Read more

title: Quantum Machine Learning for Signature Forgery Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.33163v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Offline handwritten signatures remain a primary behavioural biometric in legal and financial documents. Detecting skilled forgeries from a static raster image is hard because pen pressure, timing and stroke order are missing. This work studies a family of quantum machine learning pipelines for offline signature forgery detection on a public Kaggle corpus of images split into two classes. We pair a ZZ feature map quantum kernel with three classical learners: K-Nearest Neighbours, Support Vector Machine and Random Forest. We then propose a deeper hybrid that uses EfficientNetB0 as a frozen feature extractor, reduces the resulting 1280 dimensional representation to a qubit register sized subspace through a quantum compatible principal component projection and decides class membership with a nearest neighbour rule. On a single held out test fold the proposed hybrid reaches 92.62 percent accuracy. On stratified five fold cross validation the same pipeline yields a mean accuracy of 91.26 percent with a standard deviation of 1.13 percent. The pipeline keeps a quantum embedding step that is portable to NISQ hardware. We report a controlled ablation across six quantum variants, confusion matrices, a t SNE projection and per class precision, recall and F1 score.

title: Geophysics-informed invertible operator network for Bayesian geophysical inversion
description:
arXiv:2611.33178v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Geophysical inverse problems are inherently ill-posed because of sparse observations and measurement noise. Classical sampling-based Bayesian inference methods, such as Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), are computationally prohibitive because they require many forward simulations. Data-driven machine-learning methods often struggle to produce physically consistent solutions when training data are limited. To address these issues, we propose a geophysics-informed invertible operator network (GI-ION) that integrates an invertible neural network (INN) within a deep operator-learning framework for efficient Bayesian geophysical inversion. The INN serves as the branch network and transforms the model parameters into branch coefficients that represent the forward solution and a latent variable that captures uncertainty in the inverse problem. By learning the forward operator and enforcing statistical independence between the branch coefficients and the latent variable, GI-ION enables efficient sampling from a learned conditional approximation, even with sparse boundary observations. We validated GI-ION on three representative cases: 1D surface-wave dispersion and travel-time tomography for a 2D synthetic random-field model and a seismic-slice model. Numerical experiments demonstrate robust performance across diverse problem settings and efficient conditional sampling.

title: Blocking malicious npm packages before and during installation
description:
Vercel now checks for blocked npm packages before and during dependency installation in builds, helping prevent malicious install scripts from running.

The checks use a blocklist of specific package versions selected for blocking because of malware or security vulnerabilities, with new rules typically reaching new builds within minutes.

  • Before installation, Vercel checks supported lockfiles, including when dependencies are restored from the build cache.

  • During installation, Vercel blocks affected public npm downloads.

Existing checks of installed dependencies and function outputs continue before deployment.

These protections apply automatically to new builds on all plans, with no configuration required.

If a blocked dependency is detected, Vercel fails the deployment, identifies the package and version in the error, and attempts to invalidate the affected build cache. Update the dependency to a safe version and update the lockfile, then redeploy.

title: Logging in Java: SLF4J, Log4j2 and Spring Boot Explained
description:
Imagine you are building a Spring Boot application.

Everything works perfectly on your machine. You register users, authenticate them, save data to the database, and return responses.

But one day, something goes wrong in production.

A user reports that registration is failing. Another user says the application is responding slowly. You check the application, but you have no idea what happened when those requests were processed.

How would you investigate?

You could add System.out.println() statements everywhere:

System.out.println("User registration started");

System.out.println("Checking username");

System.out.println("Saving user");

System.out.println("Registration completed");

This might work for a small program, but it becomes difficult to manage in a real application.

You need something better.

You need a way to record application events, understand what happened, identify errors, and investigate problems even after they occur.

This is where logging comes in.

In this blog, we'll understand logging from scratch, explore its components, learn about logging levels, and finally configure SLF4J and Log4j2 in a Spring Boot application.

Table of contents

  • Start with the problem: why do we need logging?
    • Why System.out.println() is not enough
    • What is a log message?
    • Where can log messages go?
  • Understand the three main logging components
    • What is a Logger?
    • Create a Logger in Java
    • What is an Appender?
    • Common appenders
    • What is a Layout?
    • How the components work together
  • Understand logging levels
    • TRACE
    • DEBUG
    • INFO
    • WARN
    • ERROR
    • FATAL and OFF
  • SLF4J: the logging facade
    • Why do we need SLF4J?
    • SLF4J vs Log4j2
    • How SLF4J and Log4j2 work together
  • Use SLF4J in a Spring Boot application
    • Enable debug logging in Spring Boot
    • Configure logging in application.properties
    • Write logs to a file
  • Use Log4j2 instead of the default Logback
    • Configure Log4j2 with log4j2-spring.xml
    • Example: console and rolling file appenders
    • Database and email appenders
  • Logging best practices
  • Which one should I use?
  • Common mistakes
  • Quick recap
  • Try it yourself

Start with the problem: why do we need logging?

Let's start with a simple example.

Suppose we have a user registration method:

public void registerUser(User user) {

    // Validate user

    // Save user

    // Return response
}

Now imagine the registration fails.

Where did it fail?

  • Did username validation fail?
  • Did the database connection fail?
  • Did saving the user fail?
  • Was there an unexpected exception?

Without useful records of what happened, debugging becomes difficult.

Logging solves this problem by recording important events that happen while your application is running.

For example:

2026-11-26 10:00:01 INFO  User registration started
2026-11-26 10:00:02 INFO  Username validation completed
2026-11-26 10:00:03 INFO  User saved successfully
2026-11-26 10:00:03 INFO  User registration completed

Now we have a timeline of what happened.

If something fails, we can inspect the logs and understand where the problem occurred.

Why System.out.println() is not enough

You might be thinking:

"Why do we need a logging framework? Can't we just use System.out.println()?"

Let's compare them.

1. No logging levels

With System.out.println(), every message is just printed.

You cannot naturally distinguish between:

  • Normal application information.
  • Debugging information.
  • Warnings.
  • Errors.

You can manually add labels, but you would still need to build the filtering and configuration mechanisms yourself.

2. Difficult to control output

Suppose you want to print debugging messages only during development.

With System.out.println(), you may have to search for and remove or comment out many statements.

With a logging framework, you can configure the logging level without changing your logging statements.

3. No built-in destination management

You may want logs to go to:

  • Console.
  • Files.
  • A database.
  • A remote logging system.

A logging framework provides configurable destinations through appenders.

4. Difficult to maintain

A real application can contain hundreds of classes.

A proper logging framework gives you a consistent way to create, filter, format, and manage log messages.

So, instead of:

System.out.println("User registered");

We can write:

logger.info("User registered");

Much cleaner.

What is a log message?

A log message is a record of an event that happened inside an application.

For example:

INFO  User registered successfully
WARN  Password reset link is about to expire
ERROR Database connection failed

A log event can contain more than just the message.

It may contain:

  • Timestamp.
  • Logging level.
  • Logger name.
  • Thread name.
  • Message.
  • Exception information.
  • Additional context.

For example:

2026-11-26 10:15:20 ERROR
com.example.service.UserService
User registration failed

The logging framework collects this information and sends it to the configured destination.

One important distinction:

A successful operation is not a separate logging level.

For example:

logger.info("User registered successfully");

A warning is also not necessarily a failed operation:

logger.warn("Password reset link is about to expire");

And a failure is commonly recorded using:

logger.error("User registration failed");

The level tells us the severity or importance of the event. The message explains what happened.

Where can log messages go?

Once an application creates a log message, where should it be stored?

There are several possibilities.

1. Console

The log message is printed in the terminal or IDE console.

Example:

INFO User registered successfully

This is useful during local development because you can immediately see what your application is doing.

2. File

The log message is written to a file, commonly with a .log extension.

Example:

logs/application.log

This is useful when you need to inspect application activity after it has happened.

3. Database

The log message is inserted into a database table.

For example:

+--------------------------------------+
|              application_logs       |
+--------------------------------------+
| id | level | message       | time    |
+--------------------------------------+
| 1  | INFO  | User created  | 10:00   |
| 2  | ERROR | DB failed     | 10:05   |
+--------------------------------------+

This can be useful in specific systems where logs need to be queried using application-specific database operations.

However, storing every application log in your main database is not always a good idea. It can create unnecessary database load and complicate retention.

4. Email

Some logging configurations can send notifications through SMTP.

For example, you may configure an email appender to send an email when a serious error occurs.

ERROR: Payment processing failed

Application: Payment Service
Time: 10:15 AM

This can be useful for selected critical events, but sending an email for every log message would quickly become noisy.

Understand the three main logging components

Now let's understand how a logging framework manages these operations.

Three important components are:

  1. Logger
  2. Appender
  3. Layout

Think of them like a newspaper publishing process.

  • Logger: Decides which event needs to be recorded.
  • Appender: Decides where the record should go.
  • Layout: Decides how the record should look.

Let's understand them one by one.

What is a Logger?

A logger is the object through which your application creates log messages.

Whenever a class needs to write logs, it obtains a logger and uses it.

For example:

logger.info("User registered");
logger.warn("Invalid request received");
logger.error("Database connection failed");

The logger is the entry point of the logging process.

It also has a name, which is commonly the fully qualified name of the class that created it.

For example:

com.example.service.UserService

Why is the logger name useful?

Imagine you have 100 classes in your application.

You may want to enable DEBUG logs only for:

com.example.service.UserService

You don't necessarily want debugging messages from every other class.

Logger names and package hierarchies make this possible.

Create a Logger in Java

Let's create a simple Java class using SLF4J.

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

public class UserService {

    private static final Logger logger =
            LoggerFactory.getLogger(UserService.class);

    public void registerUser() {

        logger.info("User registration started");

        logger.debug("Validating username");

        logger.info("User registered successfully");
    }
}

Let's understand the important line:

private static final Logger logger =
        LoggerFactory.getLogger(UserService.class);

Logger

Logger

This is the logging interface provided by SLF4J.

LoggerFactory

LoggerFactory

It is responsible for providing a logger instance.

UserService.class

UserService.class

This tells the factory which class is requesting the logger.

The resulting logger is associated with the UserService class name.

Why static final?

  • static: One logger reference is shared by instances of the class.
  • final: The reference cannot be reassigned.

You can use this logger throughout the class.

What is an Appender?

We have created a logger and written:

logger.info("User registered successfully");

But where does this message go?

Does the logger itself write directly to the console?

Not necessarily.

This is where an Appender comes in.

An appender decides where a log event should be delivered.

For example:

Logger
  |
  v
Appender
  |
  v
Console

Or:

Logger
  |
  v
Appender
  |
  v
application.log

You can configure multiple appenders for a logger.

For example, the same log event can be sent to both the console and a file.

Common appenders

Let's understand some common Log4j2 appenders.

1. ConsoleAppender

Writes log messages to the console.

Logger
   |
   v
ConsoleAppender
   |
   v
Terminal

Useful during local development.

2. FileAppender

Writes log messages to a file.

Logger
   |
   v
FileAppender
   |
   v
application.log

Useful when you want to preserve log output.

3. RollingFileAppender

Writes logs to a file and can rotate the file when configured size or time conditions are met.

For example:

logs/
    application.log
    application-2026-11-25.log
    application-2026-11-24.log

This prevents one log file from growing indefinitely.

4. JDBCAppender

Writes log events to a relational database using JDBC.

For example:

Logger
   |
   v
JDBCAppender
   |
   v
Database
   |
   v
application_logs table

You need to configure the database connection and the SQL statement used to insert log events.

5. SMTPAppender

Can send log events through email using SMTP.

For example, you could configure it to send an email for ERROR-level events.

Important: These are different destinations supported by logging implementations. You do not need to configure every appender in every application.

What is a Layout?

We now know:

  • Logger creates log events.
  • Appender sends them to a destination.

But how should the message look?

For example, should it look like this?

INFO User registered

Or this?

2026-11-26 10:15:20 INFO
com.example.service.UserService
User registered

This is where a Layout comes in.

A layout controls how a log event is formatted before it is written by an appender.

For example, a Pattern Layout lets you define a pattern.

%d %-5level %c - %msg%n

Let's understand the pattern:

  • %d: Date and time.
  • %-5level: Logging level, aligned to five characters.
  • %c: Logger name.
  • %msg: Log message.
  • %n: New line.

Example output:

2026-11-26 10:15:20 INFO  com.example.UserService - User registered

You can also use different layouts.

For example:

  • Pattern Layout: Human-readable text.
  • JSON Template Layout: Structured JSON.
  • XML Layout: XML-formatted output.

JSON logs are especially useful when logs are collected by centralized logging platforms because machines can parse the fields easily.

How the components work together

Now let's connect everything.

Suppose your code executes:

logger.error("Payment processing failed");

What happens?

+----------------------------+
|          Logger            |
|                            |
| logger.error(message)      |
+----------------------------+
              |
              v
+----------------------------+
|          Appender          |
|                            |
| Decide destination         |
+----------------------------+
              |
              v
+----------------------------+
|           Layout           |
|                            |
| Format the log event       |
+----------------------------+
              |
              v
+----------------------------+
|         Destination        |
|                            |
| Console / File / DB / SMTP |
+----------------------------+

The exact internal pipeline can include filters, logger configurations, and other components. But this is the basic mental model.

Remember:

  • Logger: Who creates the log event?
  • Appender: Where should the event go?
  • Layout: How should the event be formatted?

Understand logging levels

Not every event in an application has the same importance.

For example:

Application started
User logged in
Cache miss occurred
Database connection failed

Should all these messages have the same priority?

No.

Logging frameworks provide different logging levels to classify messages based on their severity.

The common Log4j2 levels, ordered from least severe to most severe, are:

TRACE
  |
  v
DEBUG
  |
  v
INFO
  |
  v
WARN
  |
  v
ERROR
  |
  v
FATAL

OFF is used to disable logging.

Let's understand each level.

TRACE

TRACE is used for very detailed information about application execution.

For example:

logger.trace("Entering validateUser() method");

logger.trace("Checking username length");

logger.trace("Exiting validateUser() method");

When would you use it?

Suppose a method contains multiple conditions and you need to understand exactly which path the application follows.

TRACE can help you inspect those details.

It is usually too detailed for normal production logging.

DEBUG

DEBUG is used for information that helps developers investigate application behavior.

Example:

logger.debug("User ID received: {}", userId);

logger.debug("Fetched {} records from database", users.size());

You might use DEBUG when:

  • Investigating an issue.
  • Understanding a method's execution.
  • Checking intermediate values.
  • Debugging a database query or service call.

It is commonly enabled during development or temporarily when troubleshooting production issues.

Be careful not to log passwords, tokens, or other sensitive values.

INFO

INFO is used for normal application events.

For example:

logger.info("Application started");

logger.info("User registered successfully");

logger.info("Payment processed successfully");

These messages help you understand the application's normal operation.

For many applications, INFO is a reasonable default logging level.

WARN

WARN is used when something unexpected happens, but the application can still continue.

Example:

logger.warn("Password reset link is about to expire");

logger.warn("Cache is unavailable, falling back to database");

A warning does not always mean that an operation failed.

It tells us that something deserves attention.

ERROR

ERROR is used when an operation fails or an important problem occurs.

Example:

logger.error("Database connection failed");

You can also log an exception with its stack trace:

try {
    userRepository.save(user);
} catch (Exception exception) {

    logger.error("Failed to save user", exception);
}

The exception object allows the logging framework to include useful diagnostic information, such as the exception type and stack trace.

Don't swallow exceptions just because you logged them. Your application still needs to handle or propagate the failure appropriately.

FATAL and OFF

FATAL

Log4j2 provides a FATAL level for very severe events that may cause the application to stop working.

Example:

logger.fatal("Application cannot initialize critical configuration");

However, not all logging frameworks support FATAL.

For example, SLF4J's standard Logger API does not expose a fatal() method. In SLF4J applications, such events are commonly logged using error().

OFF

OFF disables logging at the configured level.

For example, a logger configured with OFF will not emit normal log events.

Now, how does a logging level actually work?

Suppose we configure:

Root logging level: INFO

The logger accepts messages at INFO and more severe levels.

So:

TRACE  -> Not logged
DEBUG  -> Not logged
INFO   -> Logged
WARN   -> Logged
ERROR  -> Logged

Why?

Because INFO is the minimum severity that we want to record.

This is called the logging threshold.

SLF4J: the logging facade

Now let's discuss another name you will frequently see in Java applications: SLF4J.

SLF4J stands for Simple Logging Facade for Java.

It provides a common logging API that your application can use without depending directly on one particular logging implementation.

But why do we need another logging library when Log4j2 already exists?

Let's understand the problem.

Why do we need SLF4J?

Imagine you are developing an application using Log4j2.

Your code directly imports Log4j2 classes:

import org.apache.logging.log4j.LogManager;
import org.apache.logging.log4j.Logger;

Now suppose your team decides to switch from Log4j2 to Logback.

You may need to change logging imports and code across multiple classes.

That creates unnecessary coupling between your application code and the logging implementation.

SLF4J solves this by providing a common API.

Instead of writing code directly against Log4j2, you write:

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

Your application uses SLF4J.

A compatible logging provider handles the actual logging.

This separates:

  • The API used by application code.
  • The implementation that performs logging.

SLF4J vs Log4j2

This is one of the most common points of confusion.

Are SLF4J and Log4j2 competitors?

Not exactly.

They serve different roles.

SLF4J

SLF4J is a logging facade.

It provides interfaces such as:

Logger
LoggerFactory

It defines how your application writes log messages.

It does not provide the complete logging implementation and configuration system by itself.

Log4j2

Log4j2 is a logging framework.

It provides the actual logging implementation through its API and Log4j Core.

It supports:

  • Loggers.
  • Appenders.
  • Layouts.
  • Logging levels.
  • Filters.
  • Configuration files.

A simple comparison:

+--------------------------------+
|             SLF4J              |
|                                |
|     Common Logging API         |
+--------------------------------+
                |
                v
+--------------------------------+
|       Logging Provider         |
|                                |
|          Log4j2                |
+--------------------------------+
                |
                v
+--------------------------------+
|          Log4j Core            |
|                                |
|  Loggers / Appenders / Layouts |
+--------------------------------+
                |
                v
       Console / File / DB

You can use SLF4J with Log4j2.

You can also use SLF4J with other compatible logging implementations, such as Logback.

How SLF4J and Log4j2 work together

Let's see the actual code.

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

public class PaymentService {

    private static final Logger logger =
            LoggerFactory.getLogger(PaymentService.class);

    public void processPayment() {

        logger.info("Payment processing started");

        logger.debug("Validating payment details");

        logger.info("Payment processed successfully");
    }
}

Notice that we imported:

org.slf4j.Logger
org.slf4j.LoggerFactory

We did not import Log4j2 classes.

If Log4j2 is configured as the SLF4J provider, these calls are handled by Log4j2.

If Logback is configured as the provider, the same SLF4J logging code can work with Logback.

This is the main benefit of SLF4J.

Your application code remains independent of the underlying logging implementation.

Use SLF4J in a Spring Boot application

Now let's move to Spring Boot.

Suppose you create a Spring Boot application using the standard starters.

Do you need to manually install a logging framework?

Usually, no.

Spring Boot provides logging support automatically through its starter dependencies.

By default, Spring Boot uses Logback when the standard logging starter is present.

This means you can start using SLF4J directly.

For example:

package com.example.service;

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class UserService {

    private static final Logger logger =
            LoggerFactory.getLogger(UserService.class);

    public void registerUser() {

        logger.info("User registration started");

        logger.debug("Validating user details");

        logger.info("User registered successfully");
    }
}

You don't need to manually configure a logger for every class in an XML file.

The logger can be obtained using LoggerFactory.

Enable debug logging in Spring Boot

Suppose your application contains:

logger.debug("Validating user details");

But you don't see the message in the console.

Why?

Because Spring Boot's default logging level is INFO.

DEBUG messages are below the INFO threshold, so they are filtered out.

How do we enable them?

There are multiple ways.

Option 1: Enable debug mode when starting the application

java -jar myapp.jar --debug

You can also use:

debug=true

But be careful.

Spring Boot's debug mode enables additional DEBUG-level output for selected core loggers. It does not enable DEBUG logging for every logger in your application.

Option 2: Enable DEBUG for your application package

In application.properties:

logging.level.com.example=DEBUG

Now DEBUG messages from loggers under com.example can be recorded.

Option 3: Enable DEBUG for one class

logging.level.com.example.service.UserService=DEBUG

This is useful when you are investigating one specific class.

Option 4: Enable DEBUG globally

logging.level.root=DEBUG

This enables DEBUG logging for the root logger and can produce a lot of output, including messages from framework libraries.

Use it carefully.

Configure logging in application.properties

Spring Boot provides convenient logging properties.

Let's look at some common configurations.

Set the root logging level

logging.level.root=INFO

Enable DEBUG for your application

logging.level.com.example=DEBUG

Enable TRACE for a specific package

logging.level.com.example.service=TRACE

Reduce Spring Web logs

logging.level.org.springframework.web=WARN

Enable SQL logging

For Hibernate SQL statements, you can configure:

logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG

To inspect SQL parameter binding, the exact logger depends on the Hibernate version. For Hibernate 6, a commonly used logger is:

logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=TRACE

Be careful with SQL parameter logging in production because it can expose sensitive data.

Write logs to a file

By default, Spring Boot logs to the console.

What if we also want a file?

We can configure:

logging.file.name=logs/application.log

Now Spring Boot writes logs to:

logs/
    application.log

You can also specify a directory:

logging.file.path=logs

When only the path is configured, Spring Boot uses the default file name spring.log.

If both logging.file.name and logging.file.path are configured, the file name property takes precedence.

Spring Boot also supports log file rotation through the underlying logging system.

For standard Logback configurations, you can customize rotation properties using logging.logback.rollingpolicy.*.

For more advanced configuration, use the native configuration file of your selected logging implementation.

Use Log4j2 instead of the default Logback

Now let's say you specifically want to use Log4j2 in your Spring Boot application.

Remember:

Spring Boot uses Logback by default when the standard logging starter is present.

To switch to Log4j2, we need to replace the default logging implementation.

Configure Log4j2 with log4j2-spring.xml

If you use Maven, exclude the default logging starter and add the Log4j2 starter.

For example, if you are using spring-boot-starter-web, configure it like this:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-logging</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-log4j2</artifactId>
</dependency>

Make sure you use the Spring Boot dependency management or parent POM so that the dependency versions remain compatible.

You should also check that another dependency has not brought the default logging implementation back onto the classpath.

Why do we exclude spring-boot-starter-logging?

Because that starter brings the default Logback-based logging setup.

We want Log4j2 to be the actual logging implementation.

Once configured, create this file:

src/
  main/
    resources/
      log4j2-spring.xml

Why log4j2-spring.xml instead of log4j2.xml?

Spring Boot provides additional Log4j2 configuration extensions.

The -spring variant allows those extensions to be used during configuration.

Configure Log4j2 with log4j2-spring.xml

Let's create a basic configuration.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>

<Configuration status="WARN">

    <Appenders>

        <Console name="Console" target="SYSTEM_OUT">

            <PatternLayout
                pattern="%d{yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss} %-5level %c - %msg%n"/>

        </Console>

    </Appenders>

    <Loggers>

        <Root level="info">
            <AppenderRef ref="Console"/>
        </Root>

    </Loggers>

</Configuration>

Let's understand it.

Configuration

<Configuration status="WARN">

This is the main configuration element.

Appenders

<Appenders>

This section defines where log events should go.

We created a console appender:

<Console name="Console" target="SYSTEM_OUT">

PatternLayout

<PatternLayout
    pattern="%d{yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss} %-5level %c - %msg%n"/>

This defines how the log message should look.

Loggers

<Loggers>

This section defines logger configurations.

Root logger

<Root level="info">

The root logger acts as the parent logger for application loggers that don't have a more specific configuration.

We connected it to the console appender:

<AppenderRef ref="Console"/>

Now log messages at INFO level and above can be printed on the console.

Example:

2026-11-26 10:15:20 INFO  com.example.UserService - User registered
2026-11-26 10:15:21 WARN  com.example.UserService - Cache unavailable
2026-11-26 10:15:22 ERROR com.example.UserService - Database failed

Example: console and rolling file appenders

Let's make the configuration a little more practical.

We want:

  • INFO and above messages on the console.
  • DEBUG and above messages in a file.
  • Automatic file rotation.

Example:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>

<Configuration status="WARN">

    <Appenders>

        <Console name="Console" target="SYSTEM_OUT">
            <PatternLayout
                pattern="%d{yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss} %-5level %c - %msg%n"/>
        </Console>

        <RollingFile
            name="File"
            fileName="logs/application.log"
            filePattern="logs/application-%d{yyyy-MM-dd}-%i.log.gz">

            <PatternLayout
                pattern="%d{yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss} %-5level %c - %msg%n"/>

            <Policies>
                <SizeBasedTriggeringPolicy size="10 MB"/>
            </Policies>

            <DefaultRolloverStrategy max="10"/>

        </RollingFile>

    </Appenders>

    <Loggers>

        <Root level="info">

            <AppenderRef ref="Console"/>

            <AppenderRef
                ref="File"
                level="debug"/>

        </Root>

    </Loggers>

</Configuration>

Here we created two appenders.

Console appender

<Console name="Console" target="SYSTEM_OUT">

Writes log messages to the console.

Rolling file appender

<RollingFile
    name="File"
    fileName="logs/application.log"
    filePattern="logs/application-%d{yyyy-MM-dd}-%i.log.gz">

Writes logs to application.log and defines a naming pattern for archived files.

Size-based policy

<SizeBasedTriggeringPolicy size="10 MB"/>

When the file reaches the configured size, Log4j2 can roll over the file.

Maximum archives

<DefaultRolloverStrategy max="10"/>

Configures the maximum number of rollover files for this strategy.

The exact rollover behavior depends on the configured policies and strategy.

Appender reference

<AppenderRef ref="Console"/>
<AppenderRef ref="File" level="debug"/>

We connect both appenders to the root logger.

This means a DEBUG event can be sent to the file appender, while the console appender only receives events at its configured INFO threshold.

This is useful when you want more detailed information in files without flooding the console.

Database and email appenders

We discussed JDBCAppender and SMTPAppender earlier.

Let's understand where they fit.

JDBCAppender

A JDBCAppender can write log events into a database.

Conceptually:

Logger
   |
   v
JDBCAppender
   |
   v
Database connection
   |
   v
INSERT INTO application_logs ...

You need to configure:

  • JDBC connection details.
  • A connection source.
  • A table.
  • An appropriate SQL statement.
  • The layout or message mapping required by the configuration.

For example, a log table might contain:

+--------------------------------------+
|           application_logs           |
+--------------------------------------+
| id                                   |
| log_level                            |
| logger_name                          |
| message                              |
| created_at                           |
+--------------------------------------+

But remember: database logging is not automatically the best option.

A busy application can generate thousands of log events. Writing each event to the main application database can create additional load.

For many production systems, logs are written to files or standard output and then collected by a centralized logging platform.

SMTPAppender

An SMTPAppender can send log events through an SMTP server.

Conceptually:

Logger
   |
   v
SMTPAppender
   |
   v
SMTP Server
   |
   v
Email notification

For example, you may configure selected ERROR events to trigger email notifications.

This requires suitable mail dependencies and SMTP configuration.

Avoid sending an email for every log message. It can create excessive notifications and make important failures harder to notice.

Logging best practices

Before finishing, let's look at some practices worth following in real projects.

1. Use meaningful messages

Avoid:

logger.info("Here");

Prefer:

logger.info("User registration completed");

A useful log message should explain what happened.

2. Use the correct logging level

Don't log every message using ERROR.

For example:

logger.info("User logged in");

logger.warn("Payment retry limit is almost reached");

logger.error("Payment processing failed");

3. Use parameterized logging

Avoid unnecessary string concatenation:

logger.debug("User ID: " + userId);

Prefer:

logger.debug("User ID: {}", userId);

Parameterized logging can avoid unnecessary message construction when the level is disabled.

4. Never log sensitive information

Avoid logging:

  • Passwords.
  • Access tokens.
  • Refresh tokens.
  • API keys.
  • Database credentials.
  • Sensitive personal information.

Logs can be accessible to more people and systems than the application database itself.

5. Include exceptions when useful

Avoid:

logger.error("Something failed");

Prefer:

logger.error("Failed to save user", exception);

This allows the logging framework to record exception details and stack traces.

6. Avoid excessive logging

Logging every variable and every method call at INFO level makes production logs difficult to understand.

Use DEBUG or TRACE for detailed diagnostic information.

7. Configure log rotation

A log file that grows indefinitely can consume all available disk space.

Use a suitable rolling policy and retention period.

8. Use structured logging when needed

For distributed applications, JSON logs can be easier for centralized logging systems to parse and search.

9. Use correlation IDs

When a request passes through multiple services, a correlation ID helps you connect related log events.

For example:

Request ID: req-123

API Gateway       -> req-123
User Service      -> req-123
Payment Service   -> req-123

This makes debugging distributed applications much easier.

Which one should I use?

Let's connect everything.

SLF4J

Use it as the logging API in your application code.

It keeps your code independent of the underlying logging implementation.

Logback

A common default choice in Spring Boot applications.

You generally don't need to replace it unless you have a specific requirement.

Log4j2

Choose it when you need its features, configuration capabilities, or when your organization standardizes on it.

ConsoleAppender

Useful for local development and container environments where standard output is collected by the platform.

FileAppender / RollingFileAppender

Useful when you need local log files and controlled file rotation.

JDBCAppender

Useful for selected scenarios where writing log events to a relational database is required.

SMTPAppender

Useful for selected email notifications, usually for serious events rather than routine logging.

For a typical Spring Boot application, a sensible starting point is:

Application Code
       |
       v
      SLF4J
       |
       v
    Logback
       |
       +----------+
       |          |
       v          v
    Console     File

If your project requires Log4j2, you can replace Logback with Log4j2 while keeping SLF4J in your application code.

Common mistakes

  1. Using System.out.println() for application logging: It does not provide the same level filtering, destination management, and configuration capabilities as a logging framework. Use a logger instead.

  2. Confusing SLF4J with Log4j2: SLF4J is a logging facade, while Log4j2 is a logging implementation and framework. Understand their different responsibilities.

  3. Using ERROR for every message: ERROR should represent an actual error condition. Use INFO for normal events, WARN for concerning situations, and DEBUG or TRACE for diagnostic details.

  4. Expecting DEBUG messages at the default INFO level: DEBUG is below INFO, so it is filtered out. Configure the appropriate logger level in Spring Boot.

  5. Assuming the Logger writes directly to a file: The logger creates log events, while appenders deliver them to destinations. Layouts format those events.

  6. Logging passwords and tokens: Logs can expose sensitive information. Never record authentication credentials, access tokens, or secrets in plain text.

Quick recap

  • Logging records important events that happen inside an application.
  • System.out.println() is not a replacement for a proper logging framework.
  • A log event contains information such as level, logger name, timestamp, message, and exception details.
  • Log messages can be sent to console, files, databases, or email.
  • Logger creates log events.
  • Appender decides where log events are delivered.
  • Layout decides how log events are formatted.
  • Common appenders include ConsoleAppender, FileAppender, RollingFileAppender, JDBCAppender, and SMTPAppender.
  • Logging levels include TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, and FATAL.
  • SLF4J is a logging facade.
  • Log4j2 is a logging framework and implementation.
  • Spring Boot uses Logback by default with its standard logging starter.
  • You can enable DEBUG logging using logging.level properties.
  • You can configure file output using logging.file.name.
  • You can replace the default Logback implementation with Log4j2 using spring-boot-starter-log4j2.
  • log4j2-spring.xml is used for advanced Log4j2 configuration in Spring Boot.

Try it yourself

Don't just read these concepts. Try them in a Spring Boot project.

Practice 1: Create a Logger

Create a UserService class.

Create a logger using LoggerFactory.

Print messages using:

  • trace()
  • debug()
  • info()
  • warn()
  • error()

Observe which messages appear with the default logging level.

Practice 2: Enable DEBUG logging

Add this to application.properties:

logging.level.com.example=DEBUG

Run your application again.

Observe the difference.

Practice 3: Write logs to a file

Add:

logging.file.name=logs/application.log

Run your application and check whether the log file is created.

Practice 4: Understand Log4j2 components

Create a log4j2-spring.xml configuration.

Configure:

  • One ConsoleAppender.
  • One RollingFileAppender.
  • One PatternLayout.
  • One Root logger.

Generate log messages and observe where they appear.

Bonus challenge

Create a small Spring Boot application with a user registration endpoint.

Log these events:

INFO  - Registration request received
DEBUG - Validating username
INFO  - Username validation completed
INFO  - Saving user
ERROR - Registration failed

Configure the application so that:

  • INFO and above messages appear on the console.
  • DEBUG and above messages are written to a file.
  • Log files rotate when they reach 10 MB.

If this helped, or if you spotted something I should fix, tell me in the comments. I'm still learning too.

title: Look Before You Commit: Visual-Evidence-Guided Decoding for Multimodal Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.31677v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion multimodal large language models rely on confidence to decide when to commit candidate tokens during generation. In multimodal tasks, however, confidence cannot distinguish whether a candidate originates from image evidence or the language prior. We perform paired forward ablation and find that nearly nine out of ten high-confidence commits are insensitive to the image, while degenerate and hallucination samples exhibit significant increases in the entropy of deep-layer attention organization. Based on this diagnosis, we propose CD-APC, a training-free decoding method. CD-APC performs evidence-adjusted scoring within a base-supported pool and uses dual gating based on model acceptability and contrastive concentration to decide whether to commit, together with an inverse-window mechanism that adapts to inter-step difficulty. Across two backbones and five benchmarks, CD-APC consistently improves performance, indicating that stable visual evidence improves model outputs.
