title: How Brigadahub and Range AI take a guest from question to paid booking
description:
Brigadahub is the public booking and payments platform for Brigada Hub in General Santos City, a venue with a 30-bay golf driving range, pickleball court rental and open play, and a kids playground. Guests use it to reserve and pay for range bays, courts and play sessions in a few taps, while staff manage everything from one live admin panel. Range AI is the assistant behind the website chat and Facebook Messenger, answering guests in English, Tagalog, Taglish or Bisaya and able to carry a conversation from a first question to a completed payment.

A guest starts by asking a question in chat, often about prices, availability or how open play works. Range AI classifies the message with word and character TF-IDF features into a calibrated LinearSVC covering about 94 intents, so it can tell a pricing question from a booking request or a waiver question. When the intent is a booking, the assistant moves the guest into the flow rather than just replying with text.

Inside the chat, Range AI presents live slot chips for available bays and courts, then walks the guest through the waiver, a quote and payment without leaving the conversation. The same booking path is available on the Brigadahub site as a five-step checkout with live bay and court availability and PayMongo checkout. For open play, the platform runs a live queue, digital waivers and QR check-in so guests and staff work from the same state.

The assistant never invents a price. Management-approved replies are reworded by Gemini Flash only behind a fact guard that blocks any changed price, link or amount, so the model can make an answer sound natural without altering the facts. When the system cannot resolve a request, it hands off to staff and sends email alerts. Accuracy on real guest messages was raised from 55% to 71%, which reflects the gap between clean test phrases and how guests actually type.

Behind the interface, the stack is React 19 and TypeScript on the front end, Express 5 and Supabase for the API and data, PayMongo for payments, and Python with FastAPI and scikit-learn for the intent classifier. Gemini is reached through OpenRouter, and Messenger is integrated through the Messenger API so the same assistant answers on Facebook at any hour. Staff use a role-based admin panel to run the venue, manage the open-play queue and handle check-ins.

The system was built to solve three connected problems: let guests book and pay in a few taps, keep staff on one live admin panel instead of scattered tools, and answer the same questions on Messenger at any hour without ever inventing a price. Range AI and Brigadahub are two views of the same booking state, which is why a guest can ask a question in chat and end up with a paid reservation that staff can see immediately.

Brigadahub + Range LLM is a system built by Jonald Penpillo, a software developer and AI engineer in the Philippines.

Read the case study: Brigadahub + Range LLM

Originally published at penpillo-jonald.online. Written with AI from the project's case study notes and published automatically.

title: Verified experience improves materials prediction with large language models
description:
arXiv:2611.33195v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Materials discovery is an iterative loop: experiments and calculations verify predictions, and each outcome can inform the next. Yet most predictors are specialized single-task models fixed after training. Large language models have recently emerged as predictors across heterogeneous tasks but generally underperform specialized models, and retrieval-augmented variants discard their own outcomes. Benchmarks also score queries in isolation, leaving improvement from outcomes untested. Here we construct MatMemBench, a sequential benchmark of 22 materials tasks that reveals outcomes only after prediction and tests online adaptation, memory retention and cross-task transfer. We present MatRecall, a framework that lets large language models store verified predictions, with evidence, outcome and error, as episodes and recall them without retraining. MatRecall improved median performance by 62% over a memory-free model, exceeded specialized models on 11 tasks, remained useful after feedback stopped and transferred between related tasks. Verified experience could become a reusable resource for self-improving discovery loops.

title: Rethinking Knowledge Distillation for Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.33670v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Knowledge distillation has recently proven highly effective for improving autoregressive models, but its applicability to DLMs remains poorly understood. We present the first systematic study of KD for DLMs and uncover two non-intuitive failures of classical forward-KL (FKL) distillation: (i) student perplexity does not improve monotonically with more teacher-generated data, and (ii) on the same teacher-generated corpus, FKL distillation underperforms simply training the student with the original DLM denoising objective. To address them, we propose a unified, data-free distillation framework for masked DLMs. First, the framework runs an off-policy distillation phase that absorbs general knowledge from a static set of teacher-generated data. Then, the framework employs on-policy distillation which consists of three techniques: a trajectory loss along the student's own reverse process, confidence reweighting that down-weights tokens where the teacher is unsure, and a trust-region anchor that stabilizes the moving target. On MDLM, the resulting student attains a GPT-2 perplexity of $24.75$, surpassing the teacher's $27.04$; on Dream-7B distillation to a 93M student model, the framework reduces Qwen-2.5 perplexity from the FKL-distilled baseline of $25.23$ to $19.83$ while preserving performance on zero-shot general capability benchmarks.

title: When Rerankers Work Together: Better and Faster Reranking without Joint Training
description:
arXiv:2611.33844v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Standalone reranker quality does not determine its value in a multistage RAG pipeline. We systematically study heterogeneous rerankers composed without joint training, spanning lexical, single-vector, late-interaction, and joint query-context scoring. Two lightweight semantic coarse scorers, Cache-Pointwise and Cache-Shapley, learn from passage relevance labels and share cacheable representations and linear-time singleton inference. Under matched candidates and budgets, we compare cascades with stage-removal references to measure evidence retention, repair and breakage, reader accuracy, and online pruning cost. On NoLiMa 32K with Gemma, inserting these scorers before CrossEncoder or Provence improves answer accuracy by 4.02-9.43 percentage points while accelerating online pruning by 1.57-1.88x relative to the corresponding reranker alone. Cache-Pointwise composed with ColBERTv2 through reciprocal rank fusion improves accuracy by 4.60 points at 1.36x speedup over direct ColBERTv2. The stage-removal comparisons reveal an asymmetry: a cascade can outperform its final reranker alone while underperforming its coarse selector alone. Two readers, a second multi-hop dataset, and three-stage extensions show that the gains depend on the reader, reranker pairing, and stage configuration. These findings demonstrate a practical route to better and faster reranking without joint training and motivate studying stage order, candidate budgets, and rank fusion as determinants of composition quality.

title: Cloudflare Email Service vs Resend: comparativa de precios, límites y API
description:
Cloudflare Email Service frente a Resend: cuándo el plan gratuito es suficiente

Cloudflare Email Service frente a Resend se reduce a dos preguntas: a quién necesitas enviar correos y cuántos mensajes envías al mes. En el plan Workers Free, Cloudflare solo envía a direcciones de destino verificadas de tu propia cuenta, así que es un canal de alertas gratuito para tu equipo, no una forma gratuita de enviar correos a clientes. El plan Free de Resend permite enviar a cualquiera, con un límite de 3.000 al mes y 100 al día. Para envíos en producción, Cloudflare cobra 0,35 $ por cada 1.000 correos a partir de los 3.000 incluidos en Workers Paid (mínimo de 5 $ al mes), mientras que Resend empieza en 20 $ al mes por 50.000.

Prueba Apidog hoy

Cloudflare incorporó Email Sending al plan Workers Free el 24 de noviembre de 2026, y una respuesta al anuncio resumió la letra pequeña: «Solo a destinatarios verificados*, no a todo el mundo». Esta guía compara ambos servicios usando sus páginas oficiales de precios, límites y API, consultadas el 26 de noviembre de 2026.

Cloudflare Email Service frente a Resend de un vistazo

Cloudflare Email Service Resend
Destinatarios en el plan Free Solo direcciones de destino verificadas en tu cuenta Cualquiera
Volumen en el plan Free Sin límite para direcciones verificadas 3.000 al mes, 100 al día
Punto de entrada de pago Workers Paid, mínimo de 5 $ al mes, 3.000 correos incluidos Pro, 20 $ al mes por 50.000 correos
Exceso 0,35 $ por cada 1.000 0,90 $ por cada 1.000 en Pro, baja a 0,46 $ en el nivel Scale más alto
Límite diario Empieza de forma conservadora para cuentas nuevas, crece con la reputación 100 en Free, ninguno en los planes de pago
Interfaces Binding de Workers, API REST, SMTP API REST, SMTP, SDK oficiales
Destinatarios por mensaje 50 (para, cc y bcc combinados) 50
Eventos Se publican en una Cloudflare Queue Webhooks a tu endpoint HTTPS
Dominio Debe ser un dominio en tu cuenta de Cloudflare Cualquier proveedor de DNS
Email marketing No cubierto por Email Sending Broadcasts, con precio según contactos

Qué cambió el 24 de noviembre

La entrada del changelog de Cloudflare indica que las cuentas del plan Workers Free ahora pueden incorporar dominios de envío y enviar correos a sus direcciones de destino verificadas sin coste. Puedes usar el binding de Workers, la API REST o SMTP.

Tres detalles importan:

  1. Los destinatarios están restringidos. Si envías a una dirección que no está verificada en una cuenta Free, el binding lanza E_RECIPIENT_PLAN_RESTRICTED.
  2. Los envíos verificados son gratuitos en todos los planes. En cualquier plan, el correo a direcciones de destino verificadas no cuenta para la cuota mensual ni para los límites diarios.
  3. Los envíos verificados cambiaron de producto. Antes eran una función de Email Routing; ahora son tráfico de Email Sending, con registro de actividad, analíticas, eventos y un nuevo campo GraphQL isVerifiedRecipient.

Así que el plan gratuito encaja en alertas de guardia e informes nocturnos para tu propio equipo. Los restablecimientos de contraseña y los recibos van a desconocidos, y esos necesitan Workers Paid.

Precios de Cloudflare Email Service frente a Resend

Esto es lo que cobra cada servicio en volúmenes mensuales habituales, calculado a partir de las dos páginas oficiales (precios de Cloudflare, precios de Resend). La cifra de Cloudflare incluye el mínimo de 5 $ de Workers Paid, que también cubre tu uso de Workers.

Correos al mes Cloudflare (Workers Paid) Resend
3.000 5,00 $ 0 $ (Free, si no superas los 100 al día)
10.000 7,45 $ 20 $ (Pro)
50.000 21,45 $ 20 $ (Pro)
100.000 38,95 $ 35 $ (Pro)
500.000 178,95 $ 350 $ (Scale)
1.000.000 353,95 $ 650 $ (Scale)

El cálculo de Cloudflare es sencillo: resta los 3.000 correos incluidos y multiplica el resto por 0,35 $ por cada 1.000. Con 100.000 correos son 97 × 0,35 $ = 33,95 $, más 5 $.

Por debajo de 3.000 al mes, Resend Free no cuesta nada si ningún día superas los 100. Justo en los niveles de 50.000 y 100.000 de Resend, Resend es algo más barato. Entre niveles y en volúmenes altos, la tarifa plana de Cloudflare gana: unos 300 $ al mes más barato con 1 millón de correos.

Notas sobre la facturación: Cloudflare cuenta los rebotes duros para la cuota, pero no los envíos rechazados en el límite de la API, como las direcciones suprimidas. Resend factura solo mensualmente, y los excesos requieren activar «Transactional Overages»; de lo contrario, se te pedirá que actualices.

Si también envías newsletters, Resend fija el precio del marketing por separado: los Broadcasts están limitados por contactos, no por correos, empezando con 1.000 contactos en Free y 40 $ al mes por 5.000. Las páginas de Email Sending de Cloudflare describen solo envíos transaccionales, así que compara esa partida solo en Resend.

Límites de envío y de velocidad

Cloudflare no publica una cifra diaria fija. Las cuentas nuevas «empiezan con una cuota diaria conservadora» que crece con tu comportamiento de envío, la entregabilidad y el estado de la cuenta (página de límites). Cuando la alcanzas, cada interfaz falla a su manera:

Interfaz Respuesta al alcanzar el límite diario
Binding de Workers E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED
API REST HTTP 429
SMTP 451 4.7.1 al final de DATA

Por mensaje: 50 destinatarios, 25 MiB en total y 16 KB de cabeceras personalizadas. Un formulario en la página de límites permite solicitar un límite mayor.

Resend publica sus cifras. Free te limita a 100 correos al día, los planes de pago no tienen límite diario, y la API permite 10 solicitudes por segundo por equipo en todos los planes (límites de uso). Una llamada por lotes envía hasta 100 correos como una sola solicitud, y las cabeceras retry-after indican a tu cliente cuándo retroceder.

Así que en una cuenta nueva de Cloudflare, espera que un pico el día del lanzamiento alcance un límite que no puedes prever, y gestiona las tres formas de error. En Resend, diseña en torno a las 10 solicitudes por segundo.

Estructura de la API y los SDK

Ambas API aceptan los mismos campos principales, así que cambiar de una a otra es sobre todo buscar y reemplazar.

Dentro de un Worker, Cloudflare te da un binding. Añádelo a tu configuración de Wrangler:

[[send_email]]
name = "EMAIL"

Luego envía desde tu handler:

await env.EMAIL.send({
  from: "alerts@yourdomain.com",
  to: "oncall@example.com",
  subject: "Disk usage above 90%",
  text: "Disk usage on db-1 is above 90%.",
});

Fuera de Workers, haces un POST con los mismos campos a /accounts/{account_id}/email/sending/send en la API REST de Cloudflare con un token de API, o usas los SDK oficiales para Node, Python y Go. El SDK de Node de Resend tiene este aspecto:

import { Resend } from "resend";
const resend = new Resend(process.env.RESEND_API_KEY);

const { data, error } = await resend.emails.send({
  from: "Acme <welcome@yourdomain.com>",
  to: ["user@example.com"],
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<strong>Thanks for signing up.</strong>",
});

Resend añade un idempotencyKey, envíos programados, envío por lotes y plantillas de React Email. Nuestra guía de la API de Resend recorre cada una, y la guía de la clave de API de Resend cubre el ámbito de las claves. Si prefieres manejarlo desde una terminal, consulta cómo instalar y usar la CLI de Resend.

Eventos y webhooks

Cloudflare publica eventos de Email Sending mediante suscripciones a eventos en una Cloudflare Queue. Los consumes con un Worker o con un consumidor de extracción HTTP. Cada suscripción cubre un dominio de envío. Los eventos son message.delivered, message.deferred, message.bounced, message.failed, message.rejected y message.complained. La lista no incluye eventos de apertura o clic.

Resend envía webhooks firmados a tu endpoint HTTPS. Los eventos incluyen email.sent, email.delivered, email.delivery_delayed, email.bounced, email.complained, email.opened, email.clicked, email.failed, email.suppressed y email.received. El plan Free permite 1 endpoint de webhook, Pro 5 y Scale 10.

¿Necesitas seguimiento de aperturas y clics? Resend lo tiene en todos los planes. ¿Ya estás en Workers? Un consumidor de Queue te ahorra una ruta de webhook pública.

Configuración del dominio

Cloudflare incorpora un dominio de tu cuenta de Cloudflare y escribe los registros DNS por ti: registros MX y SPF en un subdominio cf-bounce para la gestión de rebotes, un registro DKIM y un registro DMARC en _dmarc. Si tu DNS está en otro sitio, primero tendrías que mover la zona a Cloudflare.

Resend funciona con cualquier proveedor de DNS: añades los registros SPF y DKIM que te proporciona. Free incluye 3 dominios, Pro 10 y Scale 1.000, con 100 más por 20 $ al mes en Pro y Scale.

¿Cuál deberías elegir?

  • Alertas e informes para tu propio equipo, con presupuesto de 0 $: Cloudflare en Workers Free. Verifica la dirección de cada compañero y los envíos son gratuitos sin cuota.
  • Un proyecto paralelo que envía correos a usuarios reales por debajo de 100 al día: Resend Free.
  • Una app que ya está en Workers y envía 200.000 o más al mes: Cloudflare en Workers Paid. La tarifa por mensaje es aproximadamente la mitad que la de Resend en ese volumen.
  • Necesitas seguimiento de aperturas y clics, programación, React Email o Broadcasts de marketing: Resend.
  • Tu DNS no está en Cloudflare y no quieres moverlo: Resend.

Algunos equipos usan ambos: Cloudflare para el correo interno y Resend para los clientes. Nuestro recopilatorio de API de correo gratuitas incluye otras opciones.

Prueba ambas API de envío con Apidog CLI

Antes de cambiar de proveedor, prueba las dos con las mismas solicitudes, incluido lo que hace tu código ante un 429. Tu agente de programación puede hacerlo con Apidog CLI mientras tú revisas el resultado.

Configúralo una vez:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick your agent when prompted

Luego dale a Claude Code, Codex u OpenCode un único prompt:

Write email-providers.yaml, an OpenAPI 3.1 file describing Cloudflare's
POST /accounts/{account_id}/email/sending/send and Resend's POST /emails,
including their 429 responses. Import it into Apidog project <projectId>,
list the endpoints, pick the environment for staging, then run test
scenario <scenarioId> with both keys passed as env vars and tell me which
provider was slower and whether our retry logic handled the 429.

El agente ejecuta estos comandos:

apidog import --project <projectId> --format openapi --file ./email-providers.yaml
apidog endpoint list --project <projectId>
apidog environment list --project <projectId>
apidog run --project <projectId> -t <scenarioId> -e <environmentId> \
  --env-var "CF_API_TOKEN=<token>" --env-var "RESEND_API_KEY=<key>" -r cli,junit

Dirige el escenario a direcciones verificadas en Cloudflare y a la dirección de prueba delivered@resend.dev de Resend, para que ningún correo de prueba llegue a un cliente. Añade --upload-report para ver la ejecución en la app; Apidog CLI en Claude Code cubre la configuración del agente.

Una vez que funcione para un desarrollador, un equipo puede repartirlo: Sharkly es un tablero donde asignas tareas como «migra el correo de restablecimiento de contraseña a Cloudflare y vuelve a ejecutar las pruebas de correo» a agentes de programación que se ejecutan en tus propias máquinas con tu propio plan de Claude Code, Codex u OpenCode, ejecutas varios en paralelo y revisas lo que entregan antes de que se fusionen. Es gratis para empezar.

Preguntas frecuentes

¿Cloudflare Email Service es gratis? Enviar a direcciones de destino verificadas en tu cuenta es gratis en todos los planes, incluido Workers Free, y no cuenta para ninguna cuota. Enviar a cualquier otra persona requiere Workers Paid, que incluye 3.000 correos al mes y luego cuesta 0,35 $ por cada 1.000.

¿Cloudflare es más barato que Resend? En la mayoría de volúmenes, sí. Con 1 millón de correos al mes son unos 354 $ frente a 650 $. Justo en los niveles Pro de 50.000 y 100.000 de Resend, Resend es unos pocos dólares más barato, y por debajo de 3.000 al mes Resend Free no cuesta nada.

¿Puedo usar Cloudflare Email Service sin Workers? Sí. La API REST y SMTP funcionan desde cualquier backend, pero tu dominio debe estar en tu cuenta de Cloudflare.

¿Cloudflare Email Service hace seguimiento de aperturas y clics? Su lista de eventos de Email Sending cubre delivered, deferred, bounced, failed, rejected y complained. No tiene eventos de apertura ni de clic. Resend hace seguimiento de aperturas y clics en todos los planes.

¿Cuál es el límite del plan gratis de Resend? 3.000 correos al mes y 100 al día, 3 dominios y 1 endpoint de webhook, enviando a cualquier destinatario.

title: Multimodal Safety Evaluation of Vision-Language Models in Japanese
description:
arXiv:2611.33789v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed in Japanese-language settings, yet multimodal safety evaluation has been largely English-centric. We extend the Multimodal Safety Test Suite (MSTS) of R\"ottger et al. (2025) to Japanese as the 12th language, contributing 320 machine-translated and post-edited cases with reference answers plus 82 culturally localized Japanese images. We introduce an evaluation framework that (i) extends MSTS's 3-class safety grouping with a 5-point scale that also rewards useful (not just safe) responses, and (ii) separates image recognition from safety judgment to isolate recognition errors. Using this framework, we evaluate five modern Japanese VLMs (Gemini-3-Flash, GPT-5, InternVL3, LLM-JP-4-VL, Qwen3-VL) against human evaluation, and find substantial variance in the safety readiness across the models. Finally, we evaluate two LLM-as-a-Judge models and find that providing a reference answer improves agreement with human safety judgments, though recall for detecting unsafe responses remains limited, underscoring the difficulty of automating multimodal safety evaluation. The dataset created for our study will be released upon publication.

title: ChemDeduce: Benchmarking LLMs for Unknown Chemical Identification through Interactive Simulated Experiments
description:
arXiv:2611.33848v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance in chemical knowledge and reasoning, yet it remains unclear whether they can solve problems whose answers must be discovered through experimentation. We investigate this question through Unknown Chemical Identification, where a model must actively design experiments, interpret observations, update hypotheses, and ultimately identify a hidden substance. We introduce ChemDeduce, an interactive evaluation framework for assessing LLMs through simulated experiments. ChemDeduce formulates chemical identification as a sequential decision process and provides a stateful simulated laboratory with explicit instrument and operational constraints, enabling scalable and reproducible evaluation of iterative experimental reasoning. We benchmark eight frontier LLMs on 200 chemicals, yielding 1600 model--target pairs and 4800 episodes over three independent repetitions, and evaluate identification accuracy, operational compliance, interaction efficiency, and trajectory-level reasoning quality. Despite generating seemingly plausible experimental plans, current models achieve an average identification accuracy ranging from 23.83% to 67.33%, revealing substantial limitations in experiment selection, evidence interpretation, and sequential hypothesis refinement.

title: Self-Improving Long-Horizon Reasoning by Learning Summaries from Local Continuations
description:
arXiv:2611.31621v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reasoning models degrade as their context grows, so longer reasoning traces do not by themselves give longer effective horizons. One way to extend the horizon is to compress the reasoning history into a compact state from time to time and continue from the state. Existing methods train the state with the final-answer reward or distill it from a stronger model. Neither signal is tailored to measure the contribution of the state alone. We observe that a reasoning model that degrades over long trajectories still behaves reliably in short contexts. We aim to preserve this short-context behavior when compressing the reasoning history. Motivated by this, we train a separate summarizer with Delta-KL, a reward computed from the frozen reasoning model's token-level predictions on sampled continuations, and run inference by truncating the trace, summarizing it, and continuing from the summary (TruSuCo). Training uses a few thousand questions with 4k-token reasoning prefixes and does not need answers or external teachers. Under a fixed 32k-token budget, the trained summarizer improves on vanilla reasoning and on an untrained summarizer in all nine settings across mathematical benchmarks and Reasoning Gym puzzles, by up to 7.7 points and 12 points, respectively. The improvement over vanilla reasoning grows with the budget. At 128k tokens, our method outperforms it by 10 points on AIME 2024--2026. Analyses show that truncation prevents the collapse of vanilla reasoning and that the trained summaries retain more of the reasoning history.

title: CriticalScenes: Scalable Photorealistic Critical-Scenario Generation for Closed-Loop Driving Adaptation
description:
arXiv:2611.33255v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Safety-critical interactions are rare in recorded driving data, leaving end-to-end driving planners with limited exposure to evasive behaviour during training. This lack of critical supervision can lead to unsafe behaviour and, in rare instances, collisions. To address this gap, we introduce CriticalScenes, a reconstruction-based framework that transforms ordinary recorded driving scenes into photorealistic safety-critical interactions with corresponding collision-avoidance supervision. Across 53 reconstructed source scenes, 979 of 1,060 attempted interactions yield feasible threat trajectories (92.4\%), while the inserted threat actors remain detectable in more than 95\% of non-occluded observations within 5--35\,m. Experiments with two structurally different end-to-end planners show that the generated supervision improves critical-scenario planning, while closed-loop transfer varies across planner architectures. SparseDrive achieves a 46.5\% relative reduction in collision rate on an independent photorealistic closed-loop benchmark, whereas UniAD shows only a modest closed-loop improvement despite substantial open-loop gains. The results further highlight the importance of closed-loop evaluation, as improvements in open-loop trajectory prediction do not necessarily translate into equivalent safety gains.

title: Sightlines issue no.2: What leaders need to know about building agents
description: Agentic products pose a unique set of design challenges. How do you build a tool that’s powerful and knowledgeable enough to be a true partner, while keeping trust and security at the core? Here’s what we’ve heard from leaders.

title: Evaluation and Restoration of Safety in Reasoning-Tuned LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.33515v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Open-source LLMs that are optimized for reasoning, such as VibeThinker, aim to democratize AI by bringing high-capability models to users with limited resources. They are broadly available but lack regulation and external guardrails; therefore, in order to integrate them safely into human society, it is critical that they perform in a safe manner. There are popular and intuitive arguments for why improved reasoning should improve safety, but recent evidence suggests that, in fact, the opposite may be true. This paper aims to characterize and mitigate this issue. First, it develops a metric for evaluating LLMs optimized for reasoning, and shows that increasing reasoning across multiple model families increases the unsafe rate in all cases. Second, it proposes a method for restoring safety by combining evolution strategies with a post-training guardrail (ESPG). Compared to alternative methods for safety post-training such as GRPO, ESPG is simple to implement, requires no GPU memory beyond that of inference, and works with remarkably few training samples (e.g.\ 30), yet makes the model significantly safer. The study thus establishes a path towards safe post-training of open-source AI models.

title: Self-supervised Clipped-objective Reinforcement Leaning Framework for Risk-aware Portfolio Management
description:
arXiv:2611.33652v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Portfolio management involves balancing diverse financial assets, a critical yet challenging task in quantitative trading. Although deep reinforcement learning has emerged as an active research domain for solving complex sequential decision-making problems over the past decade, deploying reinforcement learning frameworks in non-stationary financial markets raises formidable difficulties. Most existing reinforcement learning-based portfolio management models fail to account for tick-level intraday market dynamics (e.g., order flow imbalances and liquidity fluctuations), which reflect rapid capital movements. Simultaneously, these models suffer from unstable learning processes due to reinforcement learning's inherent high variance. This paper presents a Self-supervised Clipped-objective Portfolio management framework (SCP), which addresses these limitations through a two-phase architecture. Market feature integration phase (application contribution) integrates micro-level market microstructure patterns with macro-level financial indicators to enhance sensitivity to intraday asset trend dynamics. Policy optimization Phase (AI contribution) employs intermediate asset state representations to derive optimal portfolio allocations via a self-supervised clipped-objective policy-learner, ensuring both effectiveness and computational efficiency. Extensive evaluations on three major index datasets from China's A-share market demonstrate that SCP's superior performance in balancing risk-return trade-offs compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Exploratory and ablation studies further validate the contributions of SCP's key components.

title: Compressible Representations: Functional Spines in Deep Neural Networks
description:
arXiv:2611.31817v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep networks embed inputs in high-dimensional representations, but how much of this capacity actually drives behavior? We introduce a framework for identifying, at each layer, the subspace of the representation that is functionally sensitive to the task. Using a matrix analogous to the Fisher information but defined over the hidden representation, we rank directions by their influence on downstream computation and project onto the most task-sensitive subspace. Across pretrained vision networks, representations are remarkably compressible: a small fraction of the task-sensitive subspace preserves most performance, often requiring far fewer dimensions than geometric alternatives. We find that this compressed representation is also more robust to adversarial attacks generated on the full network. We additionally show that this decomposition recovers functionally distinct subspaces within the same representation: on cue-conflict stimuli, shape-sensitive and texture-sensitive directions are largely non-overlapping, and ablating one selectively impairs the corresponding task while leaving the other intact. Task-sensitive subspaces also provide a principled foundation for continual learning: constraining gradient updates to lie orthogonal to the task-sensitive subspaces of prior tasks outperforms standard variance-based gradient projection methods. Finally, restricting representational comparisons to task-sensitive subspaces reveals that inter-model alignment is higher in task-sensitive directions than in task-insensitive directions at later layers, and that conditioning on different tasks over the same stimuli uncovers asymmetries that full-space similarity measures cannot detect. Together, these results establish that deep networks compute through a low-dimensional functional spine embedded within a much larger representational space.

title: Resource-Efficient Multimodal Fusion for Early Rice Blast Forecasting in Sustainable Agriculture
description:
arXiv:2611.33237v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Resource-efficient artificial intelligence has become increasingly important for sustainable agriculture, where timely disease forecasting must be achieved under computational and energy constraints. Early estimation of rice blast can enhance food security by optimizing crop management practices while reducing excessive pesticide use. However, existing frameworks often suffer from high computational overhead and limited capability to model the complex spectral-temporal dependencies present in heterogeneous meteorological and remote sensing data. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a lightweight multimodal fusion framework comprising an attentive positional encoding-based Transformer and a convolutional neural network (CNN)-embedded gated recurrent unit (GRU) for efficient spectral-temporal representation learning. The attention-enhanced positional encoding assigns adaptive importance to sequential meteorological tokens, enabling effective modelling of temporal characteristics. In parallel, the lightweight CNN extracts discriminative spectral features, while the GRU captures temporal dynamics from remote sensing imagery acquired over two time-instances. A multimodal fusion layer integrates these heterogeneous representations to forecast rice blast risk 5-10 days before symptom manifestation across diverse agro-climatic zones. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a validation accuracy of 96.93% and an F1-score of 95.79%. In addition to its predictive performance, the lightweight multimodal architecture substantially reduces computational complexity, inference latency, and carbon emissions, making it an energy-efficient solution for large-scale disease forecasting. The proposed framework provides a practical foundation for resource-efficient artificial intelligence in sustainable agriculture.

title: Confidence-Based Adaptive Retrieval Fails Where It Matters Most: A Paradox in Biomedical Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2611.33210v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for biomedical question answering, but plausible incorrect answers remain a safety risk in clinical settings. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can ground responses in medical literature, while confidence-based adaptive RAG retrieves only when the model appears uncertain. We evaluate this routing strategy on three biomedical QA benchmarks of increasing difficulty and compare models across a broad range of parameter scales. The results reveal a paradox: confidence is well calibrated (AUROC 0.78--0.89) on standard medical exam questions where retrieval adds little value (+2.4\% to -1.4\%), yet becomes \emph{near-random} (AUROC 0.506) on specialist-level questions where retrieval helps most (+11.2\%). Five uncertainty signals---first-token probability, margin, entropy, consistency-based sampling, and verbalized confidence---show the same failure pattern. Five post-hoc calibration correction strategies, including density-ratio reweighting and rank-preserving transformation, do not recover a useful routing signal on hard questions (best AUROC: 0.507). Cross-model comparison shows that larger parameter scale and higher base accuracy do not guarantee reliable confidence-based routing under specialist-domain difficulty shift. These findings challenge the premise of confidence-based adaptive RAG: in high-stakes biomedical settings, defaulting to always-retrieve is safer and more accurate than confidence-based routing when calibration on the target domain is unknown.

title: Is CSS-in-JS Dead? The More Interesting Question Is When CSS Gets Generated
description:
CSS Modules, Panda CSS and StyleX are changing how I think about styling architecture, component libraries and performance in production React applications.

For a long time, CSS-in-JS felt like a natural evolution of styling in React.

Styles could live alongside components. Dynamic values could be derived from props. Design tokens could be shared through JavaScript. TypeScript could help enforce consistency. And developers no longer had to worry as much about naming collisions or managing large global stylesheets.

It made styling feel like part of the component model.

But as applications grew, some of the trade-offs became harder to ignore.

I have been revisiting how I think about styling architecture, particularly in applications with large component libraries, shared design systems and increasingly complex rendering requirements.

One question keeps coming up:

Are we moving away from CSS-in-JS, or are we getting better at deciding when styling work should happen?

GitHub's migration raises a bigger architectural question

GitHub published an engineering article explaining how it migrated GitHub.com away from CSS-in-JS.

The problem was not simply that the team disliked its styling solution. The existing approach was introducing costs as the number of components on a page increased.

Style initialization affected client rendering. Server side rendering had to deal with style collection. Dynamic style updates became increasingly expensive as component counts grew.

GitHub's Primer team moved its components to CSS Modules and reported a 55% reduction in server side rendering time and a 25% reduction in component initialization time.

Those are significant improvements, especially at the scale of a product like GitHub.

What I find more interesting is the engineering decision behind the migration.

The team did not replace one styling syntax with another simply because something newer existed. It identified where styling work was happening, understood the cost, and changed the architecture to remove unnecessary work from the rendering path.

That is the part worth paying attention to.

The article also describes a gradual migration using feature flags, visual regression tests and compatibility layers. This was a substantial architectural change, not a quick dependency replacement.

Read GitHub's engineering article

The distinction that matters: authoring styles versus generating styles

I think discussions about CSS-in-JS often become unnecessarily polarised.

People compare syntax, developer experience and how convenient it is to write styles inside a component. Those things matter, but they do not tell us enough about the architecture.

Consider two separate questions:

  1. Where do developers author styles?
  2. When are those styles converted into CSS that the browser can use?

These questions are related, but they are not the same.

A developer can author styles in TypeScript while having those styles extracted during the build. Another developer can write styles in a separate CSS file and have the bundler process them into production stylesheets.

The important distinction is whether the application needs to evaluate styling logic, generate rules or inject styles while rendering components.

Traditional runtime CSS-in-JS libraries can introduce work during server rendering or browser execution, depending on the library and how it is used.

Build time approaches move much of that work earlier.

This does not mean every runtime styling solution is inherently slow, or that every build time solution is automatically faster. It means the cost model is different, and that difference becomes important as an application grows.

I think this is where CSS Modules, Panda CSS and StyleX become particularly interesting.

1. CSS Modules: native CSS with component level boundaries

CSS Modules are probably the most straightforward option in this comparison.

You write ordinary CSS in a .module.css file and import it into a component. Class names are locally scoped, so the same class name can exist in different modules without creating global collisions.

For example, imagine a component that displays the current state of an operational report.

ReportSummary.tsx

import styles from "./ReportSummary.module.css";

type ReportSummaryProps = {
  title: string;
  status: "healthy" | "warning" | "critical";
  description: string;
};

export function ReportSummary({
  title,
  status,
  description,
}: ReportSummaryProps) {
  return (
    <article className={styles.summary}>
      <div className={styles.heading}>
        <h2>{title}</h2>
        <span className={styles[status]}>{status}</span>
      </div>

      <p>{description}</p>
    </article>
  );
}

ReportSummary.module.css

.summary {
  padding: 1.25rem;
  border: 1px solid #e5e7eb;
  border-radius: 0.75rem;
  background: white;
}

.heading {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: space-between;
  gap: 1rem;
}

.healthy {
  color: #15803d;
}

.warning {
  color: #a16207;
}

.critical {
  color: #b91c1c;
}

There is nothing particularly complicated here.

The browser receives CSS through the normal stylesheet delivery process. There is no need for a component to generate and inject a new style rule during rendering.

Where CSS Modules work well

  • Applications that benefit from native CSS and straightforward component styling.
  • Teams that want minimal styling infrastructure.
  • Next.js applications using the App Router and React Server Components.
  • Codebases where component styles are relatively self contained.

Where the trade-offs appear

CSS Modules provide scoping, but they do not provide a complete design system architecture.

You still need to establish how tokens, spacing scales, typography, themes and component variants are managed.

As a component library grows, developers can end up building their own conventions for variants and shared styling patterns.

That is not necessarily a problem. It is simply additional architecture that the team needs to own.

CSS Modules give you a solid foundation, but they do not prescribe how your design system should work.

2. Panda CSS: a design system with build time CSS generation

Panda CSS approaches the problem differently.

It provides a TypeScript based styling API while generating CSS at build time. Instead of relying on runtime style injection, Panda analyses the styles in your source code and extracts the CSS it can determine ahead of time.

This makes it particularly interesting for teams building reusable component libraries.

You get an API that feels close to styling directly inside React components, but the resulting CSS is generated before the application runs.

One of Panda's most useful concepts is the recipe.

A recipe allows a component to define a controlled set of visual variants rather than repeatedly implementing conditional styling logic.

For a report summary, the styling could be expressed as:

import { cva } from "../styled-system/css";

export const reportSummary = cva({
  base: {
    padding: "5",
    borderRadius: "lg",
    borderWidth: "1px",
    background: "white",
  },

  variants: {
    status: {
      healthy: {
        borderColor: "green.300",
      },
      warning: {
        borderColor: "yellow.400",
      },
      critical: {
        borderColor: "red.400",
      },
    },

    density: {
      comfortable: {
        padding: "5",
      },
      compact: {
        padding: "3",
      },
    },
  },

  defaultVariants: {
    status: "healthy",
    density: "comfortable",
  },
});

The component can then select its appearance through named variants.

import { reportSummary } from "./reportSummary";

export function ReportSummary({
  status,
  density,
  children,
}) {
  return (
    <article className={reportSummary({ status, density })}>
      {children}
    </article>
  );
}

This becomes useful when the same component needs to support multiple visual states across different applications.

Panda also has slot recipes for components made up of multiple styled elements. Think of an analytics card with a header, title, metadata, chart area and footer. Those parts can share a variant definition without forcing every component to manage its own collection of conditional classes.

Where Panda CSS works well

  • Shared component libraries.
  • Applications with a substantial design token system.
  • Teams that want TypeScript authoring and build time CSS generation.
  • Components with multiple variants and compound states.
  • Design systems that need consistent patterns across several applications.

Where the trade-offs appear

Panda introduces a build step and a styling abstraction that the team needs to understand.

Its extraction model also has constraints. The compiler needs to be able to determine which styles should exist. If a style value is only known at runtime, the team needs to use supported techniques such as CSS variables or explicitly generated styles.

That is an important distinction when building highly dynamic interfaces.

Panda gives you more structure than CSS Modules, but that structure comes with conventions and build configuration.

For a small application, that may be unnecessary. For a shared design system, it can be a worthwhile investment.

3. StyleX: atomic CSS with compile time extraction

StyleX is particularly interesting because it takes a different route to solving the same problem.

Developed at Meta, StyleX combines JavaScript authoring with compile time style extraction and atomic CSS generation.

Instead of producing a large collection of component specific CSS declarations, it can reuse atomic declarations across components.

If several components use the same padding, font weight or colour, those declarations can share generated CSS rules.

This becomes valuable in large applications where the same styling decisions appear across many components.

A simplified example:

import * as stylex from "@stylexjs/stylex";

const styles = stylex.create({
  summary: {
    padding: "20px",
    borderRadius: "12px",
    backgroundColor: "#ffffff",
  },

  healthy: {
    borderColor: "#15803d",
  },

  warning: {
    borderColor: "#a16207",
  },

  critical: {
    borderColor: "#b91c1c",
  },
});

export function ReportSummary({ status, children }) {
  return (
    <article
      {...stylex.props(
        styles.summary,
        styles[status]
      )}
    >
      {children}
    </article>
  );
}

The example illustrates the authoring model. The actual production setup requires the StyleX compiler integration to transform style definitions and generate the corresponding CSS.

StyleX is designed to avoid runtime style injection. Its compiler generates optimised atomic CSS, while the runtime handles style composition.

Where StyleX works well

  • Large applications with many shared styling declarations.
  • Teams that value predictable style composition.
  • Design systems that need consistent styling across a large component surface.
  • Applications where reducing duplicated CSS declarations is important.

Where the trade-offs appear

StyleX is not simply a library that can be dropped into any React project without architectural consideration.

The compiler and build integration are central to how it works. Teams need to understand its supported styling model, constraints and integration requirements.

Atomic CSS also changes how developers think about generated styles. Debugging and inspecting output can feel different from working with familiar component level CSS classes.

For a large engineering organisation, those trade-offs may be justified. For a smaller team, the additional setup may not provide enough value.

Comparing the three approaches

The interesting comparison is not which syntax looks better. It is how each approach handles the needs of a growing application.

Concern CSS Modules Panda CSS StyleX
Style authoring CSS files TypeScript JavaScript
CSS generation Build pipeline Build time extraction Compile time extraction
Runtime style injection No No No
Local scoping Yes Generated classes Generated atomic classes
Design tokens Manual conventions Built in system Supported through themes and variables
Component variants Manual implementation Recipes Style composition
Multi part components Manual implementation Slot recipes Composable styles
Atomic CSS No Yes Yes
Build integration Relatively straightforward Requires Panda setup Requires compiler integration

There is no universal winner here.

CSS Modules prioritise native CSS and simplicity. Panda CSS provides a more opinionated design system toolkit. StyleX focuses on predictable composition and optimised atomic output.

The right choice depends on the constraints of the application and the team maintaining it.

What I would actually measure before choosing

This is where I think engineering teams should be more deliberate.

It is easy to compare styling libraries by writing the same component three times and deciding which API feels nicer.

That tells us something about developer experience. It tells us very little about production performance.

If I were evaluating these approaches for a production React application, I would build the same component suite with each solution.

I would include:

  • An analytics summary with multiple visual states.
  • A nested activity timeline.
  • A data table with conditional row states.
  • A filter panel with responsive layouts.
  • A notification feed with different severity levels.

The components would have the same markup, content, behaviour and visual output. The only meaningful difference would be the styling implementation.

Then I would measure several things.

Build performance

How long does a clean production build take? How much does an incremental change affect build time? Does the styling compiler introduce a noticeable cost to the development workflow?

CSS output

How much CSS is generated? What is the compressed stylesheet size? How many unique rules are emitted? Does the output grow proportionally as more components and variants are introduced?

Server rendering

How much time does server rendering take? Does the styling solution introduce additional work during rendering? Are styles available in the initial HTML and stylesheet delivery path?

Browser execution

How much JavaScript is required to initialise the styling system? Is there runtime style generation or injection? How much work happens during hydration and subsequent component updates?

User experience

I would also measure LCP, INP and CLS under realistic conditions. These metrics help reveal whether the styling architecture contributes to the experience users actually see.

I would run production builds, repeat measurements, control the environment and compare medians rather than relying on a single run.

Most importantly, I would separate the cost of generating styles from the cost of composing styles in JavaScript. They are different parts of the system and should be measured independently.

I have not run this comparison yet, so I would not attach performance numbers to it. The methodology is what I would use to make the decision rather than assuming that one library is faster because of how it describes its architecture.

What I would choose for a production application

My preference would depend on the kind of system I was building.

For a conventional application with a relatively small component library, I would be comfortable choosing CSS Modules. Native CSS is powerful, the mental model is straightforward and the amount of additional infrastructure is limited.

For a product with multiple applications sharing a design system, I would seriously consider Panda CSS. Recipes, tokens and slot recipes provide useful abstractions when consistency across a large component surface becomes important.

For a large application with substantial component reuse and a team comfortable with compiler driven tooling, I would evaluate StyleX. Its atomic output and composition model are compelling, particularly when the same styling declarations are repeated across a large codebase.

I would also consider the existing ecosystem.

How does the solution integrate with the framework? How easy is it to migrate existing components? Can the team debug generated output? What happens when a component needs a style that cannot be determined at build time? How does the system behave when multiple applications consume the same design system?

These questions matter more than whether the styling API looks elegant in a small example.

CSS-in-JS is not dead. The cost model is changing.

I do not think the industry is abandoning the idea of authoring styles alongside components.

That developer experience remains valuable.

What is changing is where the work happens.

The shift towards build time extraction, static CSS generation and atomic output reflects a broader architectural preference: move work out of the critical rendering path when it can be done ahead of time.

GitHub's migration is a useful example of what happens when the cost of a styling abstraction becomes significant at scale. It is not proof that CSS Modules are the right answer for every application, or that every CSS-in-JS approach has the same performance characteristics.

The more useful lesson is to understand the work your styling architecture asks the browser and server to perform.

When building a component library, I would evaluate the styling system as part of the architecture, alongside rendering strategy, design tokens, component composition, build tooling and long term maintainability.

Because the question is not simply how quickly we can write styles.

It is how efficiently we can generate, deliver and maintain them as the application grows.

If you were starting a large React application or a shared component library today, would you choose CSS Modules, Panda CSS or StyleX? What would influence your decision?

Further reading

  • GitHub: Improving site performance by shipping more CSS
  • CSS Modules documentation
  • Panda CSS documentation
  • Panda CSS recipes
  • Panda CSS slot recipes
  • StyleX documentation

title: Don't Waste the Population: Post-Anneal Refinement for Combinatorial Optimization
description:
arXiv:2611.33766v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Parallel annealers generate diverse candidate solutions; yet, conventional post-processing typically refines only the best, leaving much of the population's potential untapped. We introduce Iterative Path-Relinking Polish (I-PRP), a deterministic, training-free method that exploits this diversity to discover better solutions without modifying the underlying annealing process. I-PRP selects promising candidates, explores cost-guided paths between locally optimized solutions, and refines intermediate states to uncover better local minima. Newly discovered improvements are iteratively incorporated into the population, enabling further exploration. We theoretically guarantee that I-PRP never degrades solution quality relative to conventional single-candidate polishing on the same population and converges in finitely many iterations. Experiments across challenging combinatorial optimization benchmarks, including MaxCut, MaxClique, and graph coloring, demonstrate substantial improvements in several instances. Paired evaluations confirm non-degradation, while matched-runtime comparisons show that exploiting existing population diversity can outperform additional annealing. These results establish I-PRP as an effective and reliable refinement strategy for parallel annealing.

title: Web Workers and PDF Processing: Keeping the Interface Responsive
description:
The interface shouldn't freeze while a PDF is processing

One frustrating experience with browser-based file utilities is clicking a button and watching the entire interface stop responding.

The progress indicator freezes.

The page becomes unresponsive.

Sometimes the browser even displays its familiar warning about a page taking too long.

This is where Web Workers become interesting.

What is happening?

JavaScript running on the main thread shares time with important browser activities.

That includes interface updates, event handling, and rendering.

If you perform an expensive synchronous operation on the main thread, the browser cannot respond normally until that work finishes.

PDF operations can involve significant computation, depending on the library and document.

Moving work into a Web Worker

A Web Worker allows JavaScript to execute in a separate background thread.

A simplified example:

JavaScript
// main.js
const worker = new Worker("worker.js");

worker.postMessage({
task: "process",
data: fileBuffer
});

worker.onmessage = (event) => {
console.log("Processing finished:", event.data);
};

Inside the worker:

JavaScript
// worker.js
self.onmessage = async (event) => {
const { task, data } = event.data;

if (task === "process") {
// Perform the processing operation here.

self.postMessage({
status: "complete"
});
}
};

This is illustrative rather than a complete PDF implementation. The actual processing logic depends on the library being used.

A few things to consider

Workers introduce their own design decisions.

Data transfer: Large ArrayBuffers can be expensive to copy. Transferable objects can help avoid unnecessary duplication.

Communication: Workers cannot directly manipulate the DOM.

Error handling: Worker crashes and processing failures need to be communicated back to the interface.

Progress reporting: Long operations should provide meaningful updates rather than leaving users guessing.

When should you use them?

Not every PDF operation needs a worker.

For small documents and inexpensive operations, the additional complexity might not be worthwhile.

But for computationally expensive processing, workers can make the experience considerably more responsive.

A PDF utility shouldn't make the browser feel broken just because somebody selected a large document.

Have you moved any file-processing workloads into Web Workers? What complications did you run into?

title: Vercel MCP now supports Client ID Metadata Documents
description:
Any MCP client can now ask to connect to Vercel MCP. You still log in and approve each connection, but the client no longer has to be reviewed by Vercel first. Previously, Vercel reviewed and allowlisted each client and its redirect URIs by hand, and anything not on the list was rejected.

To connect, a client publishes a Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD), a JSON file on its own domain that describes it, and uses that file's HTTPS URL as its OAuth client_id. This follows the MCP authorization spec, which now recommends CIMD over Dynamic Client Registration.

Because Vercel hasn't reviewed these clients, the consent screen shows where each one comes from: its name, its logo, and the hostname that serves its metadata document, for example "Claude Code by claude.ai". CIMD clients don't get the Vercel verified badge, so the hostname is what you're trusting when you approve.

Apps already registered with Vercel are unchanged.

Read the Vercel MCP documentation to connect your client.

title: What Does RL Post-Training Teach Text-to-Image Models? A Skill-Wise Analysis of Flow-GRPO
description:
arXiv:2611.33316v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has become a standard way to improve text-to-image flow models: Flow-GRPO lifts the GenEval score of SD3.5-M from 0.63 to 0.95, a gain read as the model having learned compositional generation. We ask how much of that gain the base model's own samples already contained, by measuring pass@k over shared noise seeds, one skill at a time, before and after RL, on prompts never used in training. The answer differs by skill. On four of GenEval's six skills, where 32 base samples already solve almost every prompt, the gain is sharpening: one post-trained sample is worth 4 to 10 base samples, and pass@32 barely moves. On spatial relations it is unlocking: pass@32 rises from 0.69 to 1.00, 128 base samples do not match one post-trained sample, and prompts the base model never solved in 32 samples are solved 93% of the time, as often as those it solved. The benchmark average, 31 base samples per post-trained sample, describes no skill. Relations carry 35% of the gain; of the other 65%, selecting among 8 base samples with the judge behind the reward recovers nine tenths. We propose an account of when each occurs: within a prompt, a group-relative update re-weights only the outcomes its samples contain, and a flow policy cannot widen the noise that produces them; across prompts, shared parameters let successes on some prompts repair a deficit common to many. The same anatomy applies to a text-rendering checkpoint. The account's predictions are tested with a checkpoint trained without KL, within-prompt diversity, and controlled training that holds object classes out, where sharpening comes first and transfers, and unlocking follows, on practised objects before unseen ones.

title: Sports Agent: A Self-Evolving System for Conversational Data Analytics
description:
arXiv:2611.33700v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conversational sports analytics requires accurate, evidence-based responses with low latency. Changes in query distributions, data resources, and model behavior can degrade static agent configurations, motivating controlled evolution guided by runtime evidence.
  We present Sports Agent, a self-evolving framework integrating an Agentic SQL Model for structured-data reasoning, a harness for planning and tool orchestration, and a unified Feedback Engine connecting online execution with offline evolution. The engine assesses responses and execution trajectories, verifies factual claims, diagnoses failures, and generates evolution signals. Model evolution combines SQL-to-Question Scaling for coverage expansion with Graph-Guided Scaling for error-targeted synthesis. Generated questions undergo trajectory distillation and quality filtering for iterative supervised fine-tuning, followed by a separate Post-RL stage. Harness evolution translates recurrent failures into bounded prompt and skill updates, validated through independent audits, execution replay, and regression testing. Performance-tolerance checks guard against unacceptable degradation during simplification.
  The resulting Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-based model outperforms Qwen3.8-Max on sports question answering and analysis while achieving approximately three times the inference efficiency. Across 30 harness-evolution rounds, the aggregate performance score improves by 10.8 points. In a live sports analytics product, the evolved system improves factual correctness by 10.5 points and average response length, a proxy for answer richness, by 158.1%, while reducing average latency by 41.3% relative to the baseline.
