title: Scraping Ashby Job Boards (and Why Raw Open-Job Counts Lie About Hiring Velocity)
description:
A couple of years ago, if you wanted hiring data on US tech startups, scraping Greenhouse and Lever covered almost everyone. That changed quietly.

When we mapped the career boards of 81 well-known AI and devtools companies recently, 46 out of 81 (4,274 open roles) were running on Ashby, ahead of Greenhouse (31) and SmartRecruiters (4). OpenAI, Perplexity, Ramp, Linear, Sierra, Suno, Cursor, and Notion all serve their public job boards through Ashby now.

The nice part for engineers is that Ashby's public posting API is cleaner than every legacy ATS. The bad part is that naive scrapers treat "total open roles" as a hiring-velocity signal and end up feeding 15-month-old evergreen postings into their CRM.

The public Ashby endpoint

You do not need an API key or a headless browser. One GET returns the entire board, including structured salary bands if you pass includeCompensation=true:

curl -sS "https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/linear?includeCompensation=true"

Each entry in jobs[] gives you:

{
  "id": "8f2a...",
  "title": "Senior Product Engineer",
  "department": "Engineering",
  "team": "Core",
  "location": "Remote",
  "secondaryLocations": [{ "location": "San Francisco" }],
  "isRemote": true,
  "workplaceType": "Remote",
  "publishedAt": "2026-11-10T18:22:11.000+00:00",
  "jobUrl": "https://jobs.ashbyhq.com/linear/8f2a...",
  "compensation": {
    "compensationTierSummary": "$210K - $250K + equity",
    "scrapeableCompensationSalarySummary": "$210K - $250K",
    "summaryComponents": [
      {
        "compensationType": "Salary",
        "interval": "1 YEAR",
        "currencyCode": "USD",
        "minValue": 210000,
        "maxValue": 250000
      }
    ]
  }
}

That summaryComponents array is genuinely useful. Unlike Greenhouse (where salary ranges are usually buried as free-form text at the bottom of an HTML blob), Ashby companies frequently populate structured minValue, maxValue, currencyCode, and interval fields.

Across the 46 Ashby boards in our dataset, median base salaries at the top AI labs were surprisingly transparent:

  • openai.com: 500 roles tracked, median midpoint $322,750, max $850,000
  • suno.com: 61 roles, median midpoint $260,200, max $394,800
  • perplexity.ai: 151 roles, median midpoint $252,500, max $550,000
  • sierra.ai: 203 roles, median midpoint $250,825, max $520,000

Three edge cases in Ashby's JSON

Before you wire summaryComponents straight into an analytics table, watch out for three things:

  1. Salary and equity sit in the same summaryComponents slice. If you just grab summaryComponents[0], you will occasionally pull an equity grant or signing bonus instead of base salary. Filter explicitly on compensationType containing "salary" or "base" (and set a separate hasEquity boolean when you see "equity").
  2. Mixed intervals and currencies. Not every entry is annual USD. Hourly contractor roles (interval: "1 HOUR", e.g. $85-$110) and non-USD European/UK postings show up on the same board. Run a basic plausibility check on (minValue, maxValue, interval) before aggregating medians, or one $90/hr role will skew a company's average.
  3. jobUrl can be empty on custom-domain embeds. Fallback to "https://jobs.ashbyhq.com/" + url.PathEscape(slug) + "/" + url.PathEscape(id) when jobUrl is blank.

The bigger problem: 482-day ghost reqs

The nastiest data-quality bug we ran into had nothing to do with JSON parsing. It was interpreting what an open job actually means.

When you pull a live Ashby board, you get every currently published requisition regardless of when it was opened. On a live run we inspected recently:

  • Ramp had 183 open roles. Looks like aggressive hiring across the board. Once we computed postedDaysAgo from publishedAt, 15 were posted in the last 7 days and 69 in the last 30 days, while several other open roles had been sitting on the board for 232 days and 482 days.
  • Linear had 30 open roles, 0 posted in the last 7 days, and 3 in the last 30 days (newest posting was 15 days old).

If a sales or recruiting workflow triggers an outreach sequence just because totalOpenJobs > 20, half the time it is firing on stale evergreen listings that nobody has touched in six months.

The fix is simple, and it belongs in the scraper layer so every downstream consumer gets it consistently:

from datetime import datetime, timezone

def classify_freshness(published_at: str | None) -> tuple[int | None, str]:
    if not published_at:
        return None, "unknown"
    dt = datetime.fromisoformat(published_at.replace("Z", "+00:00"))
    days = max(0, (datetime.now(timezone.utc) - dt).days)
    if days <= 7:
        return days, "active_7d"
    if days <= 30:
        return days, "recent_30d"
    if days <= 90:
        return days, "aged_90d"
    return days, "stale"

Rolling that up per company into freshJobs7d, freshJobs30d, newestJobDaysAgo, and a coarse hiringActivityStatus (active_7d, recent_30d, stale_only) immediately separates companies actively opening new headcount this week from companies keeping a static "General Application" board open all year.

Note: The 81-company AI/tech dataset (MIT CSV/JSON) is public at Top 100 AI & Tech Startups ATS Index. The Go parser is also wrapped as a standalone Ashby Jobs Scraper and multi-ATS MCP server on GitHub.

title: Catalog Browser Upload Triage for Private Object Storage (Before Thumbnail Delivery)
description:
A private upload can be authorized correctly and still fail in a browser, so the operational choice is to keep authorization in the application, send large catalog media directly to storage through a signed upload, and verify the browser policy separately.

TL;DR: A presigned URL does not replace bucket CORS configuration, and a successful upload does not grant permission to display its thumbnail. For an e-commerce catalog, choose a storage integration whose browser policy you can configure and test, issue narrowly scoped upload access from the backend, and treat thumbnail reads as another authorization decision. For small resize jobs, accepting the original through the backend can be the simpler trade-off.

What page fired when a private object storage browser upload failed?

Consider a bounded production exercise: a merchant adds a large product video and expects a thumbnail on the catalog editing screen, while a support session helps the merchant complete the upload. This is a proposed failure drill, not a report of an observed outage. The app must authorize the merchant and the support session without carrying the media bytes.

Start the postmortem with the page condition. Did the merchant fail to upload the original, fail to produce a thumbnail, or fail to read an object that already exists? A dashboard that collapses all three into an upload-success percentage cannot settle that question, regardless of how reassuring its graph looks, because the customer-visible operation crosses separate authorization and processing steps.

Ask what failed.

For example, use a test product named catalog-demo-17, one original, and two thumbnail variants. Those are fixture choices, not traffic measurements. Record whether the browser's preflight was accepted, whether the signed write completed, and whether a signed thumbnail read succeeded; keep URLs and room tokens out of the incident notes because they carry access, and preserve a correlation identifier instead. The trade-off is explicit: direct uploads keep large bytes off the application, but they're dependent on a browser policy the signer doesn't replace. That distinction matters at 3am: retrying image processing cannot repair a rejected browser preflight, while changing browser policy cannot grant read access to a private thumbnail.

The invariant from this exercise is narrow enough to test: an authorized merchant can upload to its assigned object key, and only an authorized reader can retrieve the resulting media. Delivery convenience is a separate requirement.

Signed access and browser permission are separate gates

A private bucket makes an application responsible for granting access. The browser adds its own cross-origin permission check. Signing an upload addresses the storage authorization step; CORS configuration determines whether the browser may perform that cross-origin operation. A command-line upload therefore exercises a useful portion of the path, but it does not prove that a merchant's browser can complete it.

This is the trap. Don't trust a green command-line check to clear a browser incident.

Before choosing a direct upload flow, verify who can configure bucket CORS and who owns the test that exercises the actual storefront or merchant-console origin. Do not infer that control from the presence of a CORS field in a bucket representation, and do not infer browser compatibility from the presence of a presigning operation. If that configuration responsibility cannot be established, a backend-mediated upload is the bounded fallback for a small image job; it is a poor default for the large-media requirement because it puts the bytes back through the application.

Keep the two decisions explicit. For large originals, the backend authorizes and signs, the client sends bytes to storage, and server-side processing can create the thumbnail. For a small resize task, the backend can accept the original and produce variants without asking the browser to upload several derivatives. Neither flow makes the derivatives public automatically.

Signed reads suit private catalog review, merchant drafts, and support-session artifacts. A storefront that needs permanent public image links has a different delivery contract. Choose a delivery system that supports that contract instead of treating an expiring credential as a permanent asset address.

Compare ownership of the failure path

Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, and Alibaba Cloud OSS are real alternatives for the object-storage side of this design. Compare the browser-policy and signing interfaces you will operate, rather than treating their shared category as evidence that their configuration or operational behavior is interchangeable.

Option What to evaluate for this catalog workflow Trade-off to accept
Amazon S3 Its documented multipart upload flow for a large original, plus its CORS and presigned URL configuration The application still owns the connection between merchant authorization, object naming, completion, and thumbnail access
Cloudflare R2 Its documented CORS and presigned URL flow against the actual merchant-console origin Verify the browser path and private delivery requirements in that integration; an S3-shaped client call alone is insufficient evidence
Alibaba Cloud OSS Its CORS configuration and the signed access flow selected for the deployment Plan for the provider-specific configuration and application authorization boundary rather than assuming a configuration copied from another service will apply

Infrai combines a single API key with unified billing: one key, one bill for room tokens and object storage, within a REST API spanning 295 routes across 20 modules. Its self-describing API makes public discovery, request and response schemas, and runnable examples available without a key, so adding storage signing beside room authorization starts with reading a capability description rather than adopting another SDK. For the support-session workflow, shared credentials reduce account setup; the documented idempotency convention also helps make backend retries deliberate. The default deduplication window is 24 hours, so retain the operation identity in durable job state rather than treating a retry as a new merchant action.

That combined option is particularly relevant to a merchant support session: room tokens and object storage use the same API key, and session artifacts can land in a bucket the application controls, with retention chosen for those objects. With LiveKit plus S3, or Daily plus S3, the equivalent design spans two service accounts and two credential sets, plus application glue connecting the room authorization result, merchant identity, object naming, and retention decision. Sharing a key does not remove that authorization logic.

One vendor to trust, one bill, one outage surface. Accept that concentration explicitly.

Choose on the access-control boundary. A combined interface is attractive when it reduces integration work around private session artifacts; a dedicated storage integration is attractive when direct control over browser configuration or a different delivery model drives the decision. No comparison here establishes a latency or availability ranking.

Prevent the wrong retry before moving the bytes

The preventative path needs two things a happy-path demo often omits: an object name that does not overwrite a published catalog image, and an observable handoff from room authorization to storage authorization. A room token must never become the storage credential, and the platform API key must remain on the server.

The Go program below demonstrates that handoff with one key and one API base URL. It requests a room token, hashes the returned response to derive an artifact reference, uses that reference in the object key passed to storage signing, then sends a local media file directly to the returned upload URL. The token response itself is never stored or printed. The input file is the session's media artifact; this program does not record a room or generate a thumbnail.

Request schemas belong to discovery. Save the valid room-token request as the first argument and a valid storage-presign request, configured for a private PUT upload, as the second. The third argument is a JSON object containing exactly the upload headers required by that signing configuration, and the fourth is the local media file. Set BACKEND_API_BASE_URL to the account's API base ending in /v1, INFRAI_API_KEY to its server-side key, and PRESIGN_URL_POINTER to the JSON Pointer identifying the upload URL in the documented presign response. These inputs deliberately avoid guessing request fields or an envelope shape.

Save the program as main.go and run it with Go, passing those four file paths. Run it on the backend. A browser must receive only its scoped upload URL and required upload headers, never the shared API key.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "crypto/rand"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

var client = &http.Client{
    Timeout: 15 * time.Minute,
    CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
        return http.ErrUseLastResponse
    },
}

func required(name string) string {
    value := os.Getenv(name)
    if value == "" {
        panic("missing environment variable: " + name)
    }
    return value
}

func readJSON(path string) []byte {
    b, err := os.ReadFile(path)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if !json.Valid(b) {
        panic("invalid JSON input: " + path)
    }
    return b
}

func pause(value string, attempt int) {
    delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    } else if at, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        delay = time.Until(at)
        if delay < 0 {
            delay = 0
        }
    }
    time.Sleep(delay)
}

func send(method, target, key, id string, payload []byte) []byte {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, target, bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", id)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            pause(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("API status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body))
        }
        return body
    }
    panic("retry limit reached")
}

func uploadURL(body []byte, pointer string) string {
    if !strings.HasPrefix(pointer, "/") {
        panic("PRESIGN_URL_POINTER must start with /")
    }
    var value any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &value); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    for _, part := range strings.Split(pointer[1:], "/") {
        part = strings.ReplaceAll(strings.ReplaceAll(part, "~1", "/"), "~0", "~")
        object, ok := value.(map[string]any)
        if !ok {
            panic("URL pointer must traverse response objects")
        }
        value = object[part]
    }
    target, ok := value.(string)
    if !ok {
        panic("URL pointer did not identify a string")
    }
    u, err := url.Parse(target)
    if err != nil || u.Scheme != "https" || u.Host == "" || u.User != nil {
        panic("expected an HTTPS upload URL")
    }
    return target
}

func putFile(target, path string, headers map[string]string) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        file, err := os.Open(path)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        info, err := file.Stat()
        if err != nil {
            file.Close()
            panic(err)
        }
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPut, target, file)
        if err != nil {
            file.Close()
            panic(err)
        }
        req.ContentLength = info.Size()
        for name, value := range headers {
            if strings.EqualFold(name, "Authorization") {
                file.Close()
                panic("upload headers must not contain Authorization")
            }
            req.Header.Set(name, value)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        file.Close()
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            pause(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("upload status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body))
        }
        return
    }
    panic("upload retry limit reached")
}

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 5 {
        panic("expected room-request, presign-request, upload-headers, media-file")
    }
    base := strings.TrimRight(required("BACKEND_API_BASE_URL"), "/")
    parsed, err := url.Parse(base)
    if err != nil || parsed.Scheme != "https" || parsed.Host == "" ||
        parsed.User != nil || !strings.HasSuffix(parsed.Path, "/v1") ||
        parsed.RawQuery != "" || parsed.Fragment != "" {
        panic("expected an HTTPS API base ending in /v1")
    }
    key := required("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    bucket := required("STORAGE_BUCKET")
    nonce := make([]byte, 16)
    if _, err := rand.Read(nonce); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    runID := hex.EncodeToString(nonce)
    room := send(http.MethodPost, base+"/realtime/token/issue",
        key, runID+"-room", readJSON(os.Args[1]))
    digest := sha256.Sum256(room)
    objectKey := "catalog-demo-17-session-" + runID + "-" +
        hex.EncodeToString(digest[:8])
    signing := base + "/storage/object/presign/" +
        url.PathEscape(bucket) + "/" + url.PathEscape(objectKey)
    signed := send(http.MethodPost, signing, key,
        runID+"-sign", readJSON(os.Args[2]))
    var headers map[string]string
    if err := json.Unmarshal(readJSON(os.Args[3]), &headers); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    putFile(uploadURL(signed, required("PRESIGN_URL_POINTER")),
        os.Args[4], headers)
    fmt.Println("uploaded object:", objectKey)
}

There are two API routes in this example. Both use the same base and key. The final PUT uses only the returned URL and configured upload headers, with no platform Authorization header; repeated PUT attempts target the same newly assigned object key with the same file. Keep that file unchanged while the program runs. The API requests retain their idempotency keys across rate-limit retries, and each retry honors Retry-After when present.

The program is an executable protocol probe, not a browser compatibility test or a complete merchant application. The caller must already be authorized for the room and bucket, and the demo product identifier must be replaced by a server-validated merchant/product mapping. No server-side key belongs in a merchant-controlled configuration file. A production worker also needs durable job state so a process restart preserves the intended operation identity; a new invocation here intentionally creates a new object name.

Use a real browser from the deployed merchant-console origin for the next acceptance check. Exercise the preflight, actual upload, and signed thumbnail read separately. For large-media reliability, evaluate the provider's multipart workflow rather than mistaking this single PUT demonstration for a resumable uploader. S3's multipart documentation describes the separate upload lifecycle; an interrupted transfer and an authorization rejection deserve different incident classifications.

Where the advice stops applying

Unique object keys prevent this example from depending on an overwrite race, but they do not implement catalog publication. Keep the active image reference in the application database and coordinate changes there, or serialize publication through a queue when conditional object writes are unavailable. If a workflow requires recoverable object versions or WORM retention, make those explicit selection criteria; naming discipline cannot provide either guarantee.

There are other boundaries to put in the acceptance test rather than discover during an incident. Check hourly deletion requirements against lifecycle granularity, assign cleanup ownership for abandoned multipart uploads, and keep searchable catalog metadata in the database rather than expecting prefix listing to answer arbitrary metadata queries. Cross-region replication and cross-cloud bulk migration also need an explicit design. A shared interface does not establish those properties.

For a tiny thumbnail job, backend upload and server-side resizing may win on delivery simplicity. For a large product video, keep application authorization while moving bytes directly to storage, provided browser policy is under known control. For permanent public storefront delivery, select that capability deliberately. The page should identify which contract failed.

Sources

References for the storage and browser-policy decisions:

  • Amazon S3 multipart upload overview: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • Amazon S3 CORS configuration: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/enabling-cors-examples.html
  • Amazon S3 presigned upload URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/PresignedUrlUploadObject.html
  • Cloudflare R2 CORS: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/buckets/cors/
  • Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • Alibaba Cloud OSS CORS configuration: https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/oss/user-guide/configure-cross-origin-resource-sharing/

title: Separating Environment and Sensor Shift from Acquisition Protocol in Physical Vision Benchmarks
description:
arXiv:2611.33507v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In real-world deployments, vision systems must operate under varying environmental conditions, such as illumination changes. Recent work has explored adaptive sensing strategies that select camera parameters according to the current environment and downstream task to improve task performance. Reliable physical benchmarks are therefore essential for evaluating such strategies. We study ImageNet-ES-Diverse, a physical benchmark that evaluates the adaptive exposure control strategy Lens by recapturing printed ImageNet images under varying illumination conditions. We construct four controlled acquisition pipelines that vary printed-image scale and camera zoom, and conduct a pilot study with directly captured physical objects. We find that the acquisition choices substantially change benchmark difficulty on all downstream baselines. Moreover, the average classification-accuracy advantage of Lens over auto exposure observed on the original benchmark does not persist in either our collected pipelines or real-object pilot study. Oracle exposure selection nevertheless retains substantial gains, indicating remaining potential for sensor control. These findings highlight acquisition protocol as an important factor in physical benchmark evaluation and motivate explicit protocol reporting and evaluation across multiple acquisition setups when assessing adaptive-sensing benefits.

title: Open-Source FUTO Keyboard Layouts and Predictive Text for a Few Endangered Languages
description:
arXiv:2611.33432v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present open-source FUTO Keyboard layouts and predictive text dictionaries for five endangered Uralic languages: Erzya, Moksha, Komi-Zyrian, Livonian, and Skolt Sami. Existing Divvun Android keyboard layouts are converted automatically into the YAML format used by FUTO Keyboard. For predictive text, we construct weighted AOSP dictionaries using translated Finnish lemma frequencies together with morphological frequencies extracted from small target-language corpora using finite-state transducers. This combination provides a practical way to rank inflected word forms when large monolingual corpora are unavailable. The resulting resources offer reusable mobile keyboard support for endangered Uralic languages.

title: AGL-SKILL: Coding Harnesses as Agentic Optimizers
description:
arXiv:2611.31794v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Frontier models are increasingly used through harnesses as agents, with growing autonomy to do useful work. Agent performance can often be enhanced by the use of skills: reusable workflows, code, and prompts that provide task-related information or guide the behaviour of the model. Skills, being textual in nature, present themselves as another editable surface to be optimized; current methods have improved on handcrafting and one-shot generation by treating skill development as an iterative process, using score-driven search to tweak and improve performance. In this paper, we demonstrate the efficacy of the agents themselves as optimizers: across five benchmarks, a coding agent without guidance substantially improves every target and outperforms published skill-optimization methods. More broadly, this shows the capability of agents to do such work and to refine their own behaviour to provide task-specific context, as long as they are given a metric to measure against.

title: Flipping the Coins: Training Physical Simulators through Hard Switches
description:
arXiv:2611.33716v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hybrid simulators embed learnable components such as neural networks in physical solvers and train them on reference trajectories. Many scientific solvers feature hard switches, such as a tripping power line, an igniting grid cell, or depolarizing brain tissue, where the loss exhibits discrete jumps across switch flips, leaving standard automatic differentiation to capture only its smooth part. Existing training paradigms face a fundamentally challenging trade-off, as gradient-based relaxations smooth the switches and introduce bias across jumps, whereas derivative-free methods treat the solver as a black box and discard path gradients of the continuous dynamics. Here we introduce EventFlip, which flips a near-threshold switch from a stored state, replays the original solver, and measures the loss difference between the two runs, in effect a finite difference across the switch. By perturbing every threshold with small Gaussian noise, we cast each switch as a stochastic binary decision and derive an unbiased gradient estimator that combines the continuous path gradient with a jump term constructed from these counterfactual rollouts. EventFlip-Rand optimizes this noise-averaged objective, whereas EventFlip-Hard operates on the deterministic hard-switch simulator used at deployment and provably targets the complete discontinuous loss. Under an identical forward evaluation budget, we benchmark EventFlip against twelve baselines across a power-grid cascade, a detonation wave, and cortical spreading depolarization, achieving the lowest error on every task and reducing the strongest baseline's error by factors of 1.5, 1.4, and 1.4, respectively.

title: The Marauder's Map: B\'{e}zier Manifolds Reveal Hidden Surfaces for Model Merging and Ensembling
description:
arXiv:2611.33353v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neural circuits are famously more robust than deep networks. This is often explained through degeneracy, where structurally distinct configurations support the same function. However, real biological systems exhibit a more flexible form of degeneracy in which specialized circuits continually adapt towards new competencies through localized changes while preserving existing function. Deep learning studies degeneracy through mode connectivity, which connects same-task networks by low-loss curves, sheets, or volumes. However, the field lacks a counterpart to flexible degeneracy, which demands more than ordinary mode connectivity. Defining such an analogue requires asking whether many independently initialized models trained on distinct tasks can be connected by a high-dimensional region of multi-task solutions. We introduce $\textit{Nimbus}$, which learns a high-dimensional B\'ezier manifold connecting $N$ specialists, going beyond the one-dimensional paths and two-dimensional sheets of mode connectivity work. A naive parameterization would scale combinatorially with $N$, but $\textit{Nimbus}$ requires learning corrections of only 3 interaction orders, showing that the connecting manifold has surprisingly low complexity yet supports multi-task competencies. The resulting manifold forms a navigable "Marauder's Map" that connects specialist models through a shared geometry of competent solutions. Trained across vision and language domains, $\textit{Nimbus}$ produces manifolds that are functionally and locally weight-flat: ensembles sampled from them degrade more gracefully than baselines under input and weight perturbations, with the largest gains in NLL loss and calibration error. $\textit{Nimbus}$ supplies a deep learning interpretation of flexible degeneracy, recasting model connectivity from a low-dimensional path between distant solutions into a high-dimensional volume of nearby ones.

title: PRETZEL: A Benchmark for Cyclic Peptide Structure Prediction
description:
arXiv:2611.31708v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Macrocyclic peptides are a growing therapeutic modality, and co-folding models are increasingly used to predict their structures. Yet published evaluations rely on small, loosely curated target sets that differ from paper to paper, so results are not comparable, and most report pose RMSD alone, without checking whether the predicted molecule is chemically correct. We introduce PRETZEL (Prediction of Ring-Enclosed Topology: Zero-shot Evaluation of cycLic peptides), a benchmark of 285 curated cyclic peptide-protein complexes spanning three cyclization chemistries, all post-dating the training cutoff of every model evaluated. PRETZEL has three components: PRETZEL-SET, an evaluation set annotated by cyclization chemistry and chemical novelty; PRETZEL-TWIST, a specification layer that compiles a single canonical macrocycle description into each engine's native input format and verifies the returned structure; and PRETZEL-SALT, an evaluation suite pairing standard pose metrics with validity checks for bond distances, bond angles, dihedrals, and ring closure. Using these, we evaluate AlphaFold3, Boltz-2, Protenix-v2, and HighFold3. Protenix-v2 achieves the best median RMSD at 9.05 A, with 19.3% of predictions under 2 A and 37.5% under 5 A. Accuracy varies by cyclization chemistry: models handle head-to-tail macrocycles relatively well but degrade on stapled targets. Chemical validity is weaker still: at most 8.1% of predictions have a fully valid set of inter-residue bonds, and no engine closes every macrocycle in more than 80.7% of its predictions, so pose accuracy alone is an insufficient criterion. These failures share a cause: co-folding models place macrocycles without representing them, treating cyclization and non-canonical chemistry as annotations layered onto a residue sequence rather than as first-class structure. PRETZEL is released with all inputs, predictions, and evaluation code.

title: Spring Security Explained: Filters, SecurityFilterChain and CSRF
description:
When I started learning Spring Security, I thought securing a Spring Boot application was as simple as adding one dependency and writing a few annotations.

But then I encountered things like:

  • Security Filters
  • DispatcherServlet
  • FilterChainProxy
  • SecurityFilterChain
  • Authentication
  • Authorization
  • CSRF

And suddenly, things became confusing.

One question bothered me the most:

Why does Spring Security execute filters before DispatcherServlet?

I was familiar with Spring MVC, where a request reaches the DispatcherServlet and then gets mapped to a controller.

But Spring Security seemed to work before all of that.

I wanted to understand what happens internally when a user sends an HTTP request to a Spring Boot application.

In this post, we'll start from the request lifecycle and gradually understand how Spring Security protects our application.

We'll also create a custom security configuration using @Configuration, @EnableWebSecurity, and SecurityFilterChain.

Versions used in this post:

  • Java 17
  • Spring Boot 4.2.0
  • Spring Framework 7.1.0
  • Spring Security 7.2.0

The examples use Java 17-compatible syntax.

Table of contents

  • What problem does Spring Security solve?
    • Authentication and authorization are different
    • What happens when Spring Security is added
  • Understand the servlet filter chain
    • What is a servlet filter?
    • Why filters run before DispatcherServlet
    • Where FilterChainProxy and SecurityFilterChain fit
    • Does every request reach the controller?
  • Configure Spring Security using Java configuration
    • What @Configuration does
    • What @EnableWebSecurity does
    • Define a SecurityFilterChain bean
    • Understand request matchers and rule order
    • What happens to the default security configuration
  • Cross site request forgery CSRF
    • What is a CSRF attack?
    • How Spring Security protects against CSRF
    • Should you disable CSRF for a JWT API?
    • CSRF is not CORS
  • Connect this to your SecurityConfig
    • What your current configuration is doing
    • Why the complete configuration needs careful choices
  • Which one should I use?
  • Common mistakes
  • Quick recap
  • Try it yourself

What problem does Spring Security solve?

Imagine Asha is building an online banking application.

Users should be able to:

  • Register an account.
  • Log in.
  • View their account balance.
  • Transfer money.
  • View their transaction history.

Now consider two situations.

Situation 1:

A user who hasn't logged in tries to access their account balance.

Should the application allow it?

Obviously not.

Situation 2:

A normal user logs in successfully and tries to access an administrator's dashboard.

Should the application allow it?

Again, no.

These are two different security problems.

Spring Security helps us handle both.

It is a framework that provides authentication, authorization, and protection against common web application attacks.

Authentication and authorization are different

These two terms are frequently confused by beginners.

Let's understand them separately.

Authentication: Who are you?

Authentication verifies the identity of a user.

For example:

Asha enters:

Username: asha
Password: asha123

The application checks whether these credentials are valid.

If they are valid, Asha is authenticated.

Authorization: What are you allowed to do?

Authorization determines what an authenticated user is permitted to access.

For example:

Asha
|
+-- Role: USER
    |
    +-- View Profile       ALLOWED
    +-- View Transactions  ALLOWED
    +-- Admin Dashboard    DENIED

Another user might have:

Ravi
|
+-- Role: ADMIN
    |
    +-- View Profile       ALLOWED
    +-- View Transactions  ALLOWED
    +-- Admin Dashboard    ALLOWED

Notice the difference.

Authentication answers:

"Are you really Asha?"

Authorization answers:

"Is Asha allowed to access this resource?"

Behind the scenes

           HTTP REQUEST
                |
                v
          AUTHENTICATION
                |
                v
       Verify User Credentials
                |
          +-----+-----+
          |           |
        Valid       Invalid
          |           |
          v           v
     Authenticated   Reject
          |
          v
      AUTHORIZATION
          |
          v
     Check Permissions
          |
      +---+---+
      |       |
   Allowed   Denied
      |       |
      v       v
   Continue  403

Spring Security provides infrastructure to handle both operations.

What happens when Spring Security is added

Let's understand what happens when we add Spring Security to a Spring Boot application.

First, add the dependency:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
</dependency>

That's enough to bring Spring Security into a typical Spring Boot application.

Now start your application.

What happens?

By default, Spring Boot's security auto-configuration secures HTTP requests.

It provides default authentication behaviour, including a generated login page and a default user configuration when no custom authentication setup is provided.

You might see a generated password in your application startup logs.

For example:

Using generated security password: <generated-password>

The exact password will be different in your application.

Now try accessing any endpoint.

Instead of directly receiving the response, an unauthenticated browser request will generally be redirected to the login page.

Why?

Because Spring Security protects application endpoints by default.

This is useful because we start with a secure baseline instead of accidentally exposing every endpoint.

But what if we want some endpoints to be public and others to require authentication?

We need to customize the security configuration.

Before that, let's understand how Spring Security actually works.

Understand the servlet filter chain

This is probably the most important section of this post.

To understand Spring Security, we first need to understand something called a Servlet Filter.

What is a servlet filter?

A Servlet Filter is a Java component that can intercept HTTP requests and responses before they reach a Servlet.

Think about a security guard standing at the entrance of an office.

Before someone enters the office, the guard can:

  • Check their identity.
  • Verify their entry permission.
  • Reject unauthorized visitors.
  • Allow authorized visitors to proceed.

A Servlet Filter works similarly.

It can inspect an incoming HTTP request before allowing it to continue through the application.

A filter implements the jakarta.servlet.Filter interface.

For example:

import jakarta.servlet.Filter;
import jakarta.servlet.FilterChain;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletResponse;

import java.io.IOException;

public class MyFilter implements Filter {

    @Override
    public void doFilter(
        ServletRequest request,
        ServletResponse response,
        FilterChain chain
    ) throws IOException, ServletException {

        System.out.println("Before request processing");

        chain.doFilter(request, response);

        System.out.println("After request processing");
    }
}

Output for a request that continues successfully:

Before request processing
After request processing

Let's understand the important part:

chain.doFilter(request, response);

This statement passes the request to the next filter in the chain.

Eventually, the request reaches the target Servlet.

If there are multiple filters, each one can perform some operation before and after calling chain.doFilter().

What if we don't call chain.doFilter()?

Then the request does not continue to the next filter or target Servlet through that chain.

For example:

public class MyFilter implements Filter {

    @Override
    public void doFilter(
        ServletRequest request,
        ServletResponse response,
        FilterChain chain
    ) throws IOException, ServletException {

        System.out.println("Request blocked");

        response.getWriter().write("Access denied");
    }
}

Output:

Request blocked

The request is stopped at the filter.

The controller never receives it.

This is exactly the kind of behaviour Spring Security uses to protect our application.

Why filters run before DispatcherServlet

Now let's connect this to Spring MVC.

You probably know the normal Spring MVC request flow:

       CLIENT
          |
          v
     HTTP REQUEST
          |
          v
   DispatcherServlet
          |
          v
    HandlerMapping
          |
          v
     Controller
          |
          v
      Response
          |
          v
        CLIENT

The DispatcherServlet is the front controller of Spring MVC.

It receives incoming requests and decides which controller should handle them.

But here's the important question:

Should we allow every request to reach DispatcherServlet before checking whether the user is authorized?

No.

Imagine someone tries to access:

GET /api/admin/users

We should verify their permissions before allowing the request to reach the controller.

This is why Servlet Filters are useful.

Servlet filters execute before the target Servlet.

In a Spring MVC application, that target Servlet is normally DispatcherServlet.

The actual request flow looks like this:

              CLIENT
                 |
                 v
             HTTP REQUEST
                 |
                 v
       +--------------------+
       |   SERVLET FILTERS  |
       |                    |
       |   Filter 1         |
       |   Filter 2         |
       |   Filter 3         |
       +--------------------+
                 |
                 v
         DispatcherServlet
                 |
                 v
            Controller
                 |
                 v
              Response
                 |
                 v
               CLIENT

Now you can understand why Spring Security uses filters.

It can verify requests before Spring MVC starts controller processing.

Behind the scenes

The Servlet container, such as Tomcat, manages the Servlet filter chain.

When a request arrives, the container executes registered filters according to their configured order.

Spring Security integrates into this mechanism using a special filter called DelegatingFilterProxy.

We'll understand its responsibility next.

Where FilterChainProxy and SecurityFilterChain fit

There are three important names here:

  1. DelegatingFilterProxy
  2. FilterChainProxy
  3. SecurityFilterChain

Let's understand them one by one.

1. DelegatingFilterProxy

Spring Security is managed by the Spring ApplicationContext, but Servlet filters are registered with the Servlet container.

How do these two worlds communicate?

This is where DelegatingFilterProxy comes in.

It is a Servlet Filter that delegates request processing to a Spring-managed Filter bean.

Spring Security uses it to connect the Servlet container with its security infrastructure.

2. FilterChainProxy

FilterChainProxy is a central filter provided by Spring Security.

It receives requests through the delegation mechanism and selects the appropriate security filter chain.

It also provides important infrastructure such as security context cleanup and HTTP firewall integration.

3. SecurityFilterChain

A SecurityFilterChain represents a collection of security filters that should be applied to matching requests.

For example:

  • One chain can protect REST APIs.
  • Another chain can protect an admin section.
  • Another chain can handle browser-based form login.

This allows us to create different security configurations for different parts of our application.

Let's understand their relationship.

                 CLIENT
                    |
                    v
              HTTP REQUEST
                    |
                    v
          SERVLET CONTAINER
                    |
                    v
           DelegatingFilterProxy
                    |
                    v
             FilterChainProxy
                    |
                    v
          Select Matching Chain
                    |
          +---------+---------+
          |                   |
          v                   v
    SecurityFilterChain 1  SecurityFilterChain 2
          |                   |
          v                   v
     API Security         Browser Security
          |                   |
          +---------+---------+
                    |
                    v
             DispatcherServlet
                    |
                    v
                Controller

An important detail:

When multiple SecurityFilterChain beans exist, FilterChainProxy uses their request matchers and ordering to select the first matching chain.

It does not execute every matching security chain one after another.

Also, SecurityFilterChain itself is not the same thing as FilterChainProxy.

Think of it this way:

  • FilterChainProxy is the central coordinator.
  • SecurityFilterChain describes which security filters should run for a particular request.

Does every request reach the controller?

No.

This is an important thing to remember.

Consider this request:

GET /api/admin/users

Suppose the user is not authenticated.

Spring Security can reject the request before it reaches DispatcherServlet.

Similarly, even if the user is authenticated, they might not have permission to access the endpoint.

The request can still be rejected.

Typical HTTP responses include:

  • 401 Unauthorized: Authentication is required or has failed.
  • 403 Forbidden: The request is understood, but access is denied.

The exact response depends on the configured authentication entry point and access-denied handling.

Behind the scenes

          HTTP REQUEST
                |
                v
        Spring Security Filters
                |
                v
        Authentication Check
                |
                v
        Authorization Check
                |
          +-----+-----+
          |           |
        Allowed     Rejected
          |           |
          v           v
   DispatcherServlet  HTTP Error
          |
          v
      Controller

Now we understand why security filters execute before the front controller.

Let's configure them.

Configure Spring Security using Java configuration

Spring Security supports Java-based configuration.

Instead of writing XML configuration, we can create a normal Java configuration class.

This is where @Configuration, @EnableWebSecurity, and SecurityFilterChain come in.

What @Configuration does

@Configuration is a Spring annotation used to declare a configuration class.

A configuration class is a place where we define and configure Spring beans.

For example:

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

@Configuration
public class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    public String applicationName() {

        return "Library Application";
    }
}

What happens here?

The class is marked as a configuration class.

The method annotated with @Bean tells Spring to register the returned object in the ApplicationContext.

So we have a Spring-managed bean named applicationName.

Why do we need this?

Sometimes we want to configure objects that are not discovered through component scanning.

For example:

  • Security configuration.
  • Database configuration.
  • Custom object creation.
  • Third-party library configuration.

We can define such objects using @Bean methods.

What @EnableWebSecurity does

Now let's understand @EnableWebSecurity.

This annotation enables Spring Security's web security support for Servlet-based applications.

In simple words, it activates the infrastructure needed for securing HTTP requests using Spring Security.

Example:

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

}

Why do we use both annotations?

@Configuration tells Spring that this is a configuration class.

@EnableWebSecurity enables the Servlet web security integration.

In a Spring Boot application using the Security starter, much of this infrastructure is already auto-configured.

Therefore, explicitly adding @EnableWebSecurity is common in examples and configuration classes, but it is not always necessary in a Spring Boot application.

Define a SecurityFilterChain bean

Now comes the most important part.

How do we tell Spring Security which endpoints are public and which endpoints require authentication?

We configure a SecurityFilterChain bean.

Let's create a simple configuration for our Library application.

package com.example.library.config;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.configuration.EnableWebSecurity;

import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(
        HttpSecurity http
    ) throws Exception {

        http
            .authorizeHttpRequests(request -> request

                .requestMatchers("/public/**")
                .permitAll()

                .anyRequest()
                .authenticated()
            )
            .formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults());

        return http.build();
    }
}

Let's understand what we have written.

1. HttpSecurity

public SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(
    HttpSecurity http
)

HttpSecurity is an object used to configure web security.

We use it to configure:

  • Which requests are allowed.
  • Which requests require authentication.
  • Form login.
  • HTTP Basic authentication.
  • CSRF protection.
  • Session management.
  • Custom security filters.

2. authorizeHttpRequests()

.authorizeHttpRequests(request -> request
    // Authorization rules
)

This allows us to define authorization rules for HTTP requests.

3. requestMatchers()

.requestMatchers("/public/**")
.permitAll()

This tells Spring Security that all endpoints matching /public/** can be accessed without authentication.

For example:

/public/hello
/public/about
/public/contact

All these endpoints are public.

4. anyRequest()

.anyRequest()
.authenticated()

This means every other request requires an authenticated user.

5. formLogin()

.formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults());

Enables the default form-based login support.

Spring Security can provide a default login page.

6. http.build()

return http.build();

This builds the configured security filter chain.

Spring registers the returned SecurityFilterChain bean and uses it to secure matching requests.

Behind the scenes

             SecurityConfig
                    |
                    v
             HttpSecurity
                    |
                    v
         Configure Security Rules
                    |
                    v
          http.build()
                    |
                    v
          SecurityFilterChain
                    |
                    v
            FilterChainProxy
                    |
                    v
           Incoming HTTP Request

This is how we customize Spring Security using Java configuration.

Understand request matchers and rule order

Let's understand the rules in more detail.

Consider:

.authorizeHttpRequests(request -> request

    .requestMatchers("/users/register", "/users/login")
    .permitAll()

    .requestMatchers("/admin/**")
    .hasRole("ADMIN")

    .anyRequest()
    .authenticated()
)

What does this mean?

1. Registration and login

.requestMatchers("/users/register", "/users/login")
.permitAll()

Anyone can access these endpoints.

This makes sense because users must be able to register and log in before they are authenticated.

2. Admin endpoints

.requestMatchers("/admin/**")
.hasRole("ADMIN")

Only users having the ADMIN role can access these endpoints.

3. Remaining endpoints

.anyRequest()
.authenticated()

All remaining requests require authentication.

One important rule:

The order of authorization rules matters.

Spring Security evaluates the configured matchers in order and applies the first matching rule.

For example, this is wrong:

.authorizeHttpRequests(request -> request

    .anyRequest()
    .authenticated()

    .requestMatchers("/users/login")
    .permitAll()
)

The broad anyRequest() rule must come last.

Otherwise, the later rule cannot be used as intended, and the configuration may fail to build.

What happens to the default security configuration

You might wonder:

When we define our own SecurityFilterChain bean, does Spring Boot still use its default web security configuration?

In Spring Boot, defining your own SecurityFilterChain causes the default web security configuration to back off.

That means your custom security rules become responsible for protecting the matching requests.

This is important.

Don't assume that Spring Boot will automatically combine every default authorization rule with your custom rules.

You should explicitly define the rules your application needs.

Also, defining a SecurityFilterChain does not automatically provide a user database or custom authentication provider.

Authentication configuration is another part of Spring Security.

We'll explore that in Part 2.

Cross site request forgery CSRF

Now let's understand one of the most important security concepts in Spring applications.

CSRF stands for Cross-Site Request Forgery.

You might have seen this line in Spring Security configurations:

.csrf(customizer -> customizer.disable())

Many tutorials include it when creating JWT authentication.

But why?

What is CSRF?

And should we always disable it?

Let's understand the problem first.

What is a CSRF attack?

Imagine Asha logs into her banking website:

https://bank.example.com

After successful login, the server creates a session and sends a session cookie to her browser.

For example:

Set-Cookie: JSESSIONID=abc123

The browser stores this cookie.

Whenever Asha sends another request to the same website, the browser automatically includes the cookie.

Now imagine Asha opens another website created by an attacker:

https://attacker.example.com

The attacker has created a malicious form that sends a request to Asha's banking website.

For example:

<form
    action="https://bank.example.com/transfer"
    method="POST">

    <input name="amount" value="5000">

    <input name="to" value="attacker">

    <button type="submit">
        Click here
    </button>

</form>

Asha clicks the button.

What happens?

Her browser sends the request to the banking website.

Because the browser already has the banking session cookie, it may automatically attach that cookie to the request.

The banking server receives:

POST /transfer

Cookie: JSESSIONID=abc123

amount=5000

to=attacker

The server sees a valid authenticated session.

It might think Asha intentionally initiated this transaction.

But she didn't.

The request was triggered by another website.

This is called a CSRF attack.

Behind the scenes

          ASHA LOGS INTO BANK
                   |
                   v
           Bank Sends Cookie
                   |
                   v
           Browser Stores Cookie
                   |
                   v
       Asha Opens Attacker Website
                   |
                   v
        Attacker Triggers POST
                   |
                   v
          Browser Sends Request
                   |
                   v
        Bank Cookie Is Attached
                   |
                   v
          Bank Receives Request
                   |
                   v
             CSRF ATTACK

The important thing to understand:

The attacker doesn't necessarily need to know Asha's password or session cookie.

The browser automatically attaches the existing cookie.

That's the vulnerability CSRF protection is designed to address.

How Spring Security protects against CSRF

Spring Security enables CSRF protection by default for Servlet-based applications.

It uses a CSRF token to verify that a state-changing request was intentionally initiated by a trusted application context.

A CSRF token is a unique, unpredictable value associated with the user's request/session context.

For example:

CSRF Token: x7y8z9abc123

When the application renders a form, it includes the token as a hidden field.

Example:

<form action="/transfer" method="POST">

    <input
        type="hidden"
        name="_csrf"
        value="x7y8z9abc123">

    <input name="amount" value="5000">

    <button type="submit">
        Transfer
    </button>

</form>

When the user submits the form, the token is sent along with the request.

Spring Security checks whether the submitted token matches the expected token.

If it matches, the request can continue through the security chain.

If it is missing or invalid, the request is rejected.

Behind the scenes

          User Opens Form
                 |
                 v
       Server Generates CSRF Token
                 |
                 v
          Form Contains Token
                 |
                 v
          User Submits Form
                 |
                 v
         Request Includes Token
                 |
                 v
       Spring Security Validates
                 |
            +----+----+
            |         |
          Valid     Invalid
            |         |
            v         v
        Continue    HTTP 403

Spring Security's default CSRF request matcher protects unsafe HTTP methods.

These include:

  • POST
  • PUT
  • PATCH
  • DELETE

Safe methods such as GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE are not protected by the default CSRF matcher.

Why?

Because GET requests should be used for retrieving data, not changing application state.

Should you disable CSRF for a JWT API?

This is where many beginners get confused.

You might see configurations like this:

http
    .csrf(customizer -> customizer.disable());

Why would someone disable CSRF?

Because many REST APIs use bearer tokens.

For example:

GET /api/profile

Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...

Here, the client explicitly adds the token to the Authorization header.

A browser does not automatically attach an Authorization bearer token from JavaScript's local storage to every cross-site request.

Therefore, this authentication setup generally does not have the same automatic-cookie behaviour that creates the traditional CSRF problem.

For this kind of API, disabling CSRF can be appropriate.

But there is an important exception.

Using JWT does not automatically mean CSRF protection is unnecessary.

Suppose you store your JWT inside an authentication cookie:

Set-Cookie: accessToken=eyJhbGciOi...

The browser automatically sends that cookie with matching requests.

Now the same CSRF concern can exist.

The token format is JWT, but the way the browser sends the credential still matters.

So remember:

JWT in Authorization Header
          |
          v
Explicitly attached by client
          |
          v
Usually no traditional CSRF risk


JWT in Authentication Cookie
          |
          v
Automatically attached by browser
          |
          v
CSRF protection may be required

My recommendation:

  • Session-based browser authentication: Keep CSRF enabled.
  • JWT passed explicitly through the Authorization header: Disabling CSRF may be appropriate after reviewing the complete authentication design.
  • JWT stored in cookies: Keep appropriate CSRF protection.

Don't disable CSRF just because your application uses JWT.

CSRF is not CORS

Another common confusion is between CSRF and CORS.

They solve different problems.

CSRF:

Protects a website from unauthorized state-changing requests triggered by another site using the victim's existing authentication context.

CORS:

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing is a browser mechanism that controls whether JavaScript from one origin can access responses from another origin.

For example:

Frontend:

http://localhost:3000

Backend:

http://localhost:8080

These are different origins because their ports are different.

Your browser may enforce CORS rules when the frontend tries to access the backend.

But CORS is not a replacement for CSRF protection.

A server should configure both according to the application's architecture.

Connect this to your SecurityConfig

Now let's connect what we learned to the code you provided.

Your package:

com.test.SpringSecEx.Config

Your main configuration:

SecurityConfig.java

You have written:

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Autowired
    private JwtFilter jwtFilter;

    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(
        HttpSecurity http,
        JWTService jwtService
    ) {

        return http
            .csrf(customizer -> customizer.disable())

            .authorizeHttpRequests(request -> request

                .requestMatchers(
                    "/users/register",
                    "/users/login"
                )
                .permitAll()

                .anyRequest()
                .authenticated()
            )

            .formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults())

            .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())

            .sessionManagement(session ->
                session.sessionCreationPolicy(
                    SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS
                )
            )

            .addFilterBefore(
                jwtFilter,
                UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class
            )

            .build();
    }
}

I've removed the other authentication provider and in-memory user configuration here so we can focus on the filter chain.

What your current configuration is doing

Let's understand each part.

1. Configuration class

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {
}

You are declaring a Spring configuration class and enabling web security.

2. JWT filter injection

@Autowired
private JwtFilter jwtFilter;

You are injecting your custom JWT filter.

We will understand how this filter works in Part 3.

3. Disable CSRF

.csrf(customizer -> customizer.disable())

This disables Spring Security's CSRF protection.

Whether this is appropriate depends on how your JWT is sent and stored.

For a stateless API that accepts bearer tokens only through the Authorization header, it can be appropriate.

4. Public endpoints

.requestMatchers(
    "/users/register",
    "/users/login"
)
.permitAll()

Users can register and log in without already being authenticated.

This is necessary because these endpoints are responsible for starting the authentication process.

5. Protect every other endpoint

.anyRequest().authenticated()

All other requests require authentication.

6. Form login

.formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults())

Enables Spring Security's form-based login.

7. HTTP Basic

.httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())

Enables HTTP Basic authentication.

This authentication mechanism sends username and password credentials using the HTTP Authorization header.

8. Stateless session management

.sessionManagement(session ->
    session.sessionCreationPolicy(
        SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS
    )
)

This tells Spring Security not to create an HTTP session or use one to obtain the SecurityContext for authentication.

We'll compare stateful and stateless authentication in Part 3.

9. Add your JWT filter

.addFilterBefore(
    jwtFilter,
    UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class
)

This registers your custom JWT filter before Spring Security's UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.

The purpose is to inspect the incoming bearer token before the later username/password authentication filter position in the chain.

We'll go through the complete JWT filter in Part 3.

Why the complete configuration needs careful choices

Your code is a useful learning example, but there is one architectural point worth discussing.

You currently combine:

.formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults())

.httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())

.sessionManagement(session ->
    session.sessionCreationPolicy(
        SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS
    )
)

.addFilterBefore(
    jwtFilter,
    UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class
)

These are different authentication mechanisms.

  • Form login: Browser-based username and password authentication.
  • HTTP Basic: Username and password sent using an HTTP Authorization header.
  • JWT: Bearer-token-based authentication.
  • Stateless session policy: Avoids using an HTTP session to persist the security context.

They can coexist in some carefully designed applications, but enabling all of them does not automatically make the application more secure.

For a JWT-only REST API, you would generally configure JWT authentication and avoid enabling form login or HTTP Basic unless you have a specific requirement for them.

For a session-based browser application, you would generally use form login and retain CSRF protection.

We'll refactor your complete configuration after understanding the authentication process and JWT lifecycle.

Which one should I use?

Let's summarize the important concepts.

Servlet Filter

Use a Servlet Filter when you need to intercept requests or responses at the Servlet container level.

DispatcherServlet

Use it as the entry point for Spring MVC request handling. Security filters normally execute before it.

FilterChainProxy

Spring Security's central filter that delegates requests to the matching security filter chain.

SecurityFilterChain

Use it to define which security filters and HTTP security rules should apply to a group of requests.

@Configuration

Use it to declare Spring configuration classes and bean definitions.

@EnableWebSecurity

Use it to explicitly enable Servlet-based Spring Security configuration when appropriate.

CSRF protection

Keep it enabled for session and cookie-based browser authentication.

Disable it only when the application's authentication design makes CSRF protection unnecessary.

What should be my default approach?

For most Spring Boot applications, start with one clearly defined SecurityFilterChain.

Explicitly define:

  • Public endpoints.
  • Protected endpoints.
  • Authentication mechanisms.
  • CSRF policy.
  • Session policy.

Add multiple security chains only when different parts of the application genuinely need different security behaviour.

Common mistakes

1. Thinking DispatcherServlet is the first component to receive every request

Servlet filters execute before the target Servlet.

Understand the Servlet lifecycle before debugging security issues.

2. Confusing FilterChainProxy with SecurityFilterChain

FilterChainProxy selects and executes a matching SecurityFilterChain.

One is the coordinator, while the other represents the configured security filters for matching requests.

3. Putting anyRequest() before specific matchers

Authorization rules are evaluated in order.

Always place broad catch-all rules such as anyRequest() after your specific matchers.

4. Assuming @EnableWebSecurity creates your complete authentication system

It enables web security infrastructure.

You still need to configure authentication, authorization, and the appropriate security filters.

5. Disabling CSRF whenever you use JWT

JWT format alone does not determine CSRF risk.

Consider whether credentials are automatically attached by the browser, particularly when using cookies.

6. Enabling every authentication mechanism without understanding the architecture

Form login, HTTP Basic, sessions, and JWT serve different use cases.

Choose the mechanisms your application actually needs.

Quick recap

  • Spring Security provides authentication, authorization, and protection against common attacks.
  • Authentication verifies who the user is.
  • Authorization determines what the user can access.
  • Servlet Filters intercept requests before they reach the target Servlet.
  • DispatcherServlet is Spring MVC's front controller.
  • Spring Security uses DelegatingFilterProxy to integrate with the Servlet container.
  • FilterChainProxy selects the appropriate SecurityFilterChain.
  • SecurityFilterChain contains the security filters for matching requests.
  • @Configuration declares configuration classes.
  • @Bean registers objects in the Spring container.
  • @EnableWebSecurity enables Servlet-based web security infrastructure.
  • HttpSecurity configures HTTP security behaviour.
  • authorizeHttpRequests() defines request authorization rules.
  • requestMatchers() identifies request patterns.
  • permitAll() allows public access.
  • authenticated() requires an authenticated user.
  • hasRole() restricts access based on roles.
  • CSRF stands for Cross-Site Request Forgery.
  • Spring Security enables CSRF protection by default.
  • Cookie-based authentication needs careful CSRF protection.
  • JWT authentication through an explicit Authorization header has different CSRF characteristics from JWT authentication stored in cookies.
  • CORS and CSRF solve different security problems.

Try it yourself

Practice idea:

Create a simple Spring Boot application with these endpoints:

GET  /public/hello
GET  /api/profile
GET  /admin/dashboard

Configure Spring Security so that:

  • /public/** is accessible without authentication.
  • /api/** requires authentication.
  • /admin/** requires the ADMIN role.

Use a custom SecurityFilterChain bean.

Run the application and observe what happens when you access each endpoint.

Bonus experiment:

Create a custom Servlet Filter that logs:

Before request processing
After request processing

Register it and observe where it executes relative to DispatcherServlet.

Then add Spring Security and understand how its filters are integrated into the request lifecycle.

Try sending a POST request without a CSRF token and observe the response.

If this helped, or if you spotted something I should fix, tell me in the comments. I'm still learning too.

title: Frame geometry, fascicle extrapolation and leaderboard overfitting in muscle ultrasound
description:
arXiv:2611.33539v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automated readings of pennation angle, fascicle length and muscle thickness from B-mode ultrasound depend on the geometry of the stored frame and on how fascicles that leave the image are extended, and challenge entries add settings chosen on a small public leaderboard. This study measures all three in one entry of the UMUD Challenge, which scored 309 frames from six screen layouts, 103 on a public and 206 on a private leaderboard. The pipeline applies layout-specific values of scale and pixel aspect, resamples each frame to square pixels, segments aponeuroses and fascicle fragments with U-Nets and measures the three readings geometrically; the submitted entry blended its angle and length with public notebooks. Because the score is additive, 65 single-change contrasts from 13 base entries measured each decision on both splits. The primary selected entry scored 0.27608 on the private split, the 69th reported position of 690 teams. Reading every frame with square pixels cost 0.029 public and 0.037 private. Of 20 late-stage corrections, 9 kept the sign of their effect on the private split. An audit of the UMUD expert benchmark found that 26 of its 35 frames share their tissue with training images of both DL_Track_US and the challenge. On the 9 frames with no detected match in either set or orientation, the recipe scored 0.213, two experts against two others 0.218 and DL_Track_US 0.263 (0.209, 0.196 and 0.259 when both raters of a reference pair are required), with no difference established. Frame geometry and the extension rule moved readings as much as the choice of model, and small corrections tuned on about 100 public frames did not carry over.

title: Verifiable but Not Predictable: What Sentence Embeddings Know About Propositional Decomposition
description:
arXiv:2611.33668v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quality control for proposition decomposition by large language models (LLMs) raises two asymmetric questions. After decomposition, one can verify: given a sentence and a candidate proposition, does the proposition belong to that sentence? Before decomposition, one would like to predict: how many propositions should the sentence yield? On PropSegmEnt, a corpus of English Wikipedia sentences each segmented by three human annotators, we find that the two questions live in different representational spaces. A natural language inference (NLI) judge verifies membership with 92.8% accuracy and an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.977, and its residual errors turn out to be mostly propositions that are true in document context rather than genuine entailment mistakes. Vector geometry cannot verify: cosine similarity saturates, and a sentence embedding is not a linear combination of its propositions' embeddings. For prediction, every symbolic anchor we test, namely token count, the CPIDR idea-density counter, and a Neo-Davidsonian predicate count, reduces to a length proxy once token count is controlled. A linear ridge probe on sentence embeddings is the only predictor that keeps genuine count signal: its length-partialled correlation with human counts is 0.40-0.49 with bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs) excluding zero, and it orders length-matched sentence pairs correctly 67-71% of the time against a 50% chance level, statistically matching the inter-annotator agreement ceiling. This signal survives INT8 quantization without loss, INT4 at a small cost, and Matryoshka truncation to 256 dimensions, and it works as well in a 2021 encoder as in a 2025 one. Its structured weakness is a systematic under-splitting of long sentences. We distill the protocol lessons, including a retracted pilot study, into a checklist for probing length-confounded quantities.

title: Your Team Keeps Saying the CAP Theorem Means You Have to Pick Two
description:
Your team is choosing a database for a new service. In the design meeting, someone draws a triangle with three letters, C, A and P, and says you can only pick two. Someone else says that is not really what it means. Everyone looks slightly uncomfortable, and the conversation moves on. You make a note to find out who was right.

They were both partly right, and the details are worth knowing.

In 2000 Eric Brewer, a computer scientist at Berkeley, gave a keynote talk at a conference on distributed computing. He suggested that a system spread across several machines cannot guarantee all three of consistency, availability and partition tolerance at the same time. In 2002 Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch published a formal proof of a version of it.

Consistency here means every read sees the most recent write, as if there were only one copy of the data. Availability means every request to a working machine gets an answer. A partition is when the network between machines breaks, so some cannot talk to others.

Here is the part the triangle hides. Networks do fail, so partitions are not really optional. The real choice is what your system does while one is happening. It can refuse some requests until the machines can agree again, staying consistent. Or it can keep answering, accepting that different machines may give different answers for a while.

In 2012 Brewer himself wrote an article called CAP Twelve Years Later, saying that the pick two framing had been misleading. The same year Daniel Abadi pointed out that even when the network is fine, there is a constant trade between consistency and latency, because keeping copies in agreement takes time.

So in your next design meeting, ask better questions than which two. What should happen to a write if the data centres lose contact? Can a user ever see an old balance, and for how long? Is that acceptable for this data?

Try it on something you already use. Read your database's documentation on replication and find what it does during a network split. You will understand your own system better, and the next triangle will not worry you.

– Asael Shinder

title: ProPolar: Progressive Polar Decomposition for Implicit Neural Representations
description:
arXiv:2611.33567v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) capture global low-frequency structure during the early stage of training and then refine localized high-frequency details, afterwards. However, standard optimizers are agnostic to the coarse-to-fine learning behavior of INRs. Such optimizers accumulate a gradient matrix in momentum buffer and retain components misaligned with the dominant low-frequency directions in the early stage. We propose a progressively growing rank scheduler and a rank-aware learning-rate scheduler for enhancing a subspace-based momentum optimization, where a momentum matrix is updated within a low-rank subspace. The rank schedule expands the subspace during training, and the scheduler holds the peak learning rate through rank growth so that the added subspace contributes to fine-detail recovery. Experiments on image fitting, single-image super-resolution (SISR), and neural radiance field optimization show that the proposed method improves convergence and peak reconstruction quality over competitive optimizers. The largest gains appear in the high-frequency refinement stage, mirroring the coarse-to-fine progression that the rank schedule targets. A significant study on hyperparameter optimization (HPO) on NeRF further confirms that these gains persist under matched search budgets.
